articles.text: Measure UU would allow the City of Piedmont to issue municipal bonds to rebuild the Piedmont Pool. Measure UU is necessary if Piedmont citizens want to have a community pool, as the 56-year-old pool has outlived its viability and soon will be closed permanently. For the past decade, the City Council and staff have taken consistent steps to improve city finances. Apart from our aging infrastructure, which is increasingly expensive to maintain each year, the City stands in a very good financial position. Here are the facts: • Piedmont home sales have not plummeted. The two opponents of Measure UU claim that home sales have plummeted in Piedmont. Not true. During the first months of the pandemic, home sales did contract. However, the number of homes sold has rebounded and returned to levels consistent with prior years. • Measure UU will be paid through property taxes. The two opponents argue that Measure UU will negatively impact the City’s operating funds. Not true. Measure UU would allow the City to issue municipal bonds, which are repaid through property taxes. The bond requirements are totally unrelated to the City’s current taxes and fees. • Long-term pension planning is unrelated to Measure UU. The City has prudently provisioned and planned for the expected annual cost of pension liabilities. Long-term pension liabilities have nothing to do with rebuilding the pool. • The City has no publicly financed debt. The City is expected to receive an AA+ bond rating. Because the City has no publicly financed debt, the bond underwriters are confident the City of Piedmont will receive an AA+ bond rating. The City’s ability to borrow funds in the future will remain strong. It is important to remember that as residents, all of us have benefited from the generosity of prior Piedmont generations who built, paid for, and in many cases donated our beloved public spaces. If Piedmont is going to continue to have a pool for our community and our schools, it is our turn to step up. Instead of searching for misplaced reasons to say no, let’s say Yes to Measure UU, lock in low interest rates, and come together as a community to design, engineer, and build a safe, economical, and sustainable Community Pool for Piedmont for the next 50 years. Bob McBain is Mayor of the City of Piedmont. “We told Dude to shape up or ship out. Unfortunately, he shopped out.”
articles.title: Getting the facts straight on City finances

articles.text: The public is invited to a panel discussion organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and co-sponsored by the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee and League of Women Voters of Piedmont. The dicussion will be held tomorrow, Thursday, September 24 from 7:00-8:30 p.m. on Zoom. Registration required. As part of the ongoing struggle to achieve racial equity and justice, integrating and diversifying our neighborhoods are essential tasks. A recent UC Berkeley report on Racial Segregation in the SF Bay Area demonstrates that residential segregation is alive and well in the Bay Area. The Zoom panel will address the history of racial segregation and housing in Piedmont, and steps that the city can take to achieve a more equitable future. Panelists Gloria Bruce – Executive Director, East Bay Housing Organizations (EBHO). EBHO is the leading advocacy coalition promoting affordable housing in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Irene Cheng – Associate Professor, California College of the Arts, and co-editor, Race and Modern Architecture: A Critical History from the Enlightenment to the Present.Carol Galante – Donald Terner Distinguished Professor in Affordable Housing and Urban Policy, UC Berkeley, and Director of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation. Former Federal Housing Commissioner at the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development under President Barack Obama. The meeting will be moderated by Sarah Karlinsky, Senior Policy Advisor, SPUR (San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association). For more information: email piedmontracialequity@gmail. com. articles.text: The United States is not typically thought of as a French country; but centuries ago, when Europe began exploring America, France claimed the Great Lakes and most of the west as New France (Nouvelle-France). However, frequent skirmishes with the British, war on five continents, and draining coffers eventually discouraged France’s sweeping claims over America and Canada. France joined the competition for New World discovery in 1524, when King Francis I dispatched Giovanni da Verrazzano to explore the region between Florida and Newfoundland, map the coastline, and find a sea passage across North America to Asia. A violent storm disrupted the journey disabling three of the four-ships in the flotilla. The one surviving ship returned to port, resupplied, and with 50 men, again set sail and made land in two months at present-day Cape Fear, North Carolina. The ship then entered Pamlico Sound, a large lagoon off the coast of North Carolina near the Outer Banks; and in seeking large open water, by the notations in the Captain’s log, the crew believed they had found it and celebrated reaching the South China Sea. Exploration nearly 500 years ago was riddled with miscalculations. Thirty years earlier, Christopher Columbus calculated the size of North America at about one third its size; and never in his lifetime did he believe he had not reached India, which is why he referred to American natives as Indians. Verrazzanno sailed to New York Bay, Long Island Sound, and explored Rhode Island before sailing up the coast to Maine and Newfoundland, where the ship was resupplied before sailing home. French explorers after Verrazzano were chartered with the same mission: locate a sea passage across North America. None of them ever did. Gain and Loss of New France Explorer Jacques Cartier arrived in Newfoundland and the St. Lawrence River in 1534 to look again for a Northwest Passage. Cartier is credited with starting a few settlements, as well as originating the claims of New France and The Country of Canada. Several settlements were built at modern day Quebec City, but didn’t coalesce until a few outposts took root along the St. Lawrence River Valley. French farming was limited in scale with greater attention to establishing outposts for fur trading and attracting native Americans who were trappers. The native tribes allied readily with the French who, unlike the Brits, were not fencing off hunting grounds. At its peak in the early 1700s, New France had amassed territory from Newfoundland to the Rocky Mountains, and from Hudson Bay to the Gulf of Mexico, to include the Great Lakes. Several major French settlements are alive today, including Quebec; La Baye des Puants (Green Bay); Ville-Marie (Montreal); Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit (Detroit); La Nouvelle Orléans (New Orleans); and Baton Rouge. But France lagged far behind England’s colonization of America and was hindered by the paucity of settlements across such a large territory. The French Era in the New World from the date that Jacques Cartier declared New France to the end of the French and Indian War, 1634-1763. In the span of 230 years (1534 to 1763) on the North American continent, France did not dominate. Throughout history the French reign as a premiere European nation, or its leader. In colonizing the New World, France had largely claimed Canada and the Great Lakes, while Britain held the 13 colonies. But frontier tension over control in the Upper Ohio River Valley boiled over in the mid-1700s between Britain, France, and the native American tribes. The Battle of Fort Duquesne in 1758 ignited the French and Indian War, a seven-year conflict ending in France’s loss of its eastern American territories. Initially, the French and tribal native Americans at Fort Duquesne (near Pittsburgh) were regularly defeating the British troops. After years of skirmishes, a full-fledged war broke out and the French were eventually ousted from the eastern U.S. territories. Known also as the Seven Year War, the French were warring against England (and Spain) in the New World colonies, which coincided with warring in Europe against Prussia, while aligned with Austria, Russia, and Sweden. Britain strategically decided to aid Prussia to weaken France in the American arena. While the multiple battlefronts dragged into a long, complicated war ending in defeat for France, the French still retained New Orleans and the Mississippi River Valley. Fifty years later, France presented a purchase opportunity to the fledgling United States of America, the Louisiana Purchase, the most significant territory expansion in the nation’s history. The Northwest Passage The famed Northwest Passage is a sea route across the continent through what now is known as the Arctic Archipelago. It comprises a string of barely populated islands entirely in the Arctic circle, and from Canada’s Baffin Island to the Beaufort Sea north of Alaska, the route is 900 miles. A 15th century search for the sea passage was never realized. articles.text: On the first day of school I encouraged my students, via Zoom, to take this school year one day at a time. Even before I said it, I knew this advice would be hard to swallow. Seriously, how helpful is one day at a time in the midst of the apocalypse, especially to teenagers? But it was the only thing I could think of to say. Why? Because I think it’s true. I think taking this whole situation one day at a time is the only way through it, at least the only way through it while maintaining our sanity. There have been times when I’ve been given this advice myself and felt angry, even offended, because I understood it to mean that I should capitulate. But capitulation is not what I’m suggesting at all. Living one day at a time is not a surrender but rather an acknowledgment, a recognition that some things are out of our control, and that to fight against them heaps even more distress upon our already distressed psyches. But how are we supposed to live one day at a time, when today is so hard? We start with the breath. If you’ve never meditated or considered a mindfulness practice, now is the time to start. I begin my Psychology class each day with a minute of silence. Some students like it, others hate it, some tell me it’s useless, but I’ll keep it up. I know from years of practice that helping students create a habit of paying attention to their breathing and quieting their minds pays huge dividends. After a while, it will start to seem normal to them, even comforting, and then they are on their way to understanding what one day at a time really means. One of the best living proponents of this kind of mindfulness practice is Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen Buddhist monk. Read any of his books and they will blow you away. At the core of each he exhorts us to pay attention to our breath. That’s it, just breathe. Nhat Hanh’s authority as a teacher, for me, comes from the fact that he found peace in the midst of war. He did not retreat or capitulate or surrender. He breathed his way into the present moment, and there, here, now, he found peace. So that’s it. Just breathe, and pay attention. Nothing more, nothing less, and peace will follow. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

Guided by inspiring teachers and mentors, they create a vibrant community that is rooted in shared values of kindness, respect, and a willingness to learn from the perspectives of others. We invite you to visit us and experience College Prep first-hand. 6100 Broadway Oakland CA 94618 510.652.4364 college-prep.org By Susan Eva Porter, Ph.D. On the first day of school I encouraged my students, via Zoom, to take this school year one day at a time. Even before I said it, I knew this advice would be hard to swallow. Seriously, how helpful is one day at a time in the midst of the apocalypse, especially to teenagers? But it was the only thing I could think of to say. Why? Because I think it’s true. I think taking this whole situation one day at a time is the only way through it, at least the only way through it while maintaining our sanity. There have been times when I’ve been given this advice myself and felt angry, even offended, because I understood it to mean that I should capitulate. But capitLiving one day at a time ulation is not what I’m suggesting at all. Living one day at a time is not a surrender but rather an acknowledgment, a recognition that some things are out of our control, and that to fight against them heaps even more distress upon our already distressed psyches. But how are we supposed to live one day at a time, when today is so hard? We start with the breath. If you’ve never meditated or considered a mindfulness practice, now is the time to start. I begin my Psychology class each day with a minute of silence. Some students like it, others hate it, some tell me it’s useless, but I’ll keep it up. I know from years of practice that helping students create a habit of paying attention to their breathing and quieting their minds pays huge dividends. After a while, it will start to seem normal to them, even comforting, and then they are on their way to understanding what one day at a time really means. One of the best living proponents of this kind of mindfulness practice is Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen Buddhist monk. Read any of his books and they will blow you away. At the core of each he exhorts us to pay attention to our breath. That’s it, just breathe. Nhat Hanh’s authority as a teacher, for me, comes from the fact that he found peace in the midst of war. He did not retreat or capitulate or surrender. He breathed his way into the present moment, and there, here, now, he found peace. So that’s it. Just breathe, and pay attention. Nothing more, nothing less, and peace will follow. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. I’d love to hear from you! 2 – After my election in 2016, I saved any campaign materials I thought I could reuse if I ran for reelection. This included my kids’ “vote for my mom” t-shirts and of course my lawn signs. Well, the shirts don’t fit my kids anymore and the signs are surely showing their age as well; but they still get the message across. Reuse helps keep my campaign costs to the bare minimum. While I know many residents don’t love the aesthetic, and I agree with that sentiment, during campaign season the signs allow residents to share with undecided voters who they support. I’m not printing any new signs for this campaign so my apologies to my supporters who requested a sign but didn’t receive one since I ran out early. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – Yes. Answering our residents on any item, controversial or not, is the crux of a Councilmember’s job. My nature is to be thoughtful and thorough. I enjoy completing the necessary due diligence to understand an issue and its impact on our City. I will always present the facts as I’ve researched them and welcome discussion on any issue with any resident. What benefit do we derive from these campaign signs? None that I can see. Studies show they do not impact a voter’s decision. Meanwhile, I trust our residents to do their research and pick the candidate they feel will best serve our City. If that is me, I will be ready to work. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – I am well prepared to deal with controversy. I will also listen to experts and seek advice from people I know to have relevant insight or experience. articles.text: Witter Field reopened for the second time for public use on September 16. The Piedmont School District has announced that Witter Field has reopened for community use as of Wednesday, September 16. This is the second reopening attempt for the city’s largest sports field since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Remaining closed are the baseball and softball fields, batting cages, restrooms at the Field House, Wildwood School lower playground, and access through the Winsor Avenue gate. Access to Witter Field is available from El Cerrito Avenue, the Wildwood Ave. steps, and Piedmont Middle School’s “PE Hill.” Visitors to the field must wear face coverings, keep six-foot social distance from others who are not part of the same household, and stay home when sick with a fever, cough, or other COVID-19 symptoms. “The District previously closed Witter Field due to widespread and persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County order at the Field, and similar issues led the City of Piedmont to close the Linda Beach Playfield, as noncompliance poses a serious public health risk,” wrote the district in a press release. Staff photo Witter Field initially closed at the beginning of Alameda County’s Shelter-in-Place orders on March 17. When the county restrictions were eased on June 9, Witter Field reopened. The field was closed a second time on August 3 and remained closed until last week. The school district’s press release also states, “Witter Field is an important community resource and the decision to reopen the facility was made based on supportive public input. The Field will remain open as long as users comply with the public health orders issued by Alameda County.”
articles.title: Witter Field reopening given another chance

articles.text: Gabe Watson won league MVP, the Posts’ Athlete of the Year in 2014, and was third-team All-State. With for mer Pied mont record-nreaking running back Gabbe Watson officially transferring from Div. II Sioux Falls (South Dakota) to the University of Texas as a fifth-year senior last week, we are taking a look back at his three years as a starter: 2013 throgh 2015. Watson burst onto the scene as a sophomore under coach Scott Coats to earn a first-team AllLeague selection after rushing over 1,000 yards, it was a great preview for what was ahead. As a junior, Watson shattered school records with 1,495 total yards and 14 touchdowns. He won the Western Alameda County Conference’s MVP award and was named the Posts’ Athlete of the Year. In 2014, Piedmont High went 12-1 and won the WACC’s Shoreline championship. It was the school’s league title in 38 years. The Highlanders entered North Coast Sectionpost-season playoffs as the No. 2 seed, and Watson set a school record in the second round of the playoffs with 297 rushing yards in a 55-43 shootout against McKinleyville. It was the team’s 12th win, a school record at the time. Watosn was selected to Cal Hi Sports’ All-State third team. “Piedmont unleashed its monster running game, improving their undefeated record to 12-0 and set a school record for most wins in a single season,” wrote the Post’s Jason Eisenberg in 2014. Piedmont lost to Justin-Seina in the semifinals 14-3, and the Braves went on to win the championship. And then came 2015 with firstyear coach James Holan. The team went 9-3 and won its second consecutive Shoreline Title, but was elevated to the more competitive Foothil Division with mostly Div. schools. Watson won his second consecutive WACC Player of the Year award, and was named Athlete of the Year by the Post. But a knee injury in the quarterfinals of the NCS playoffs shelved what was set to be a historic postseason. At the time of his injury he had over 1,200 all-purpose yards and had tacked on 150 rushing yards in the first-round NCS game. He also notched a monster game with 292 rushing against San Lorenzo earlier in the season. He finished the season with 29 touchdowns. In total, Watson piled up over 4,400 rushing yards at Piedmont High and at least 6,000 all-purpose yards while scoring 78 touchdowns for Piedmont. “Watson tallied a career total of 78 touchdowns and averaged 115 yards per game. His accomplishments on the gridiron have resounded far beyond the cheering home section of Witter Field’s bleachers,” wrote the Post’s’ Kate Fratar in 2016. The Post congratulates Watson and wishes him the best of luck at Texas. As a senior in 2015, Watson won his second consecutive league MVP and our Athlete of the Year honors.

articles.text: The second week of the National Football League has come and gone with nearly everything going as expected. The Las Vegas Raiders pulled off a big 34-24 upset of the New Orleans Saints in their opening of Allegiant Stadium in Vegas, and the San Francisco 49ers posted an easy 31-13 win over the Jets, but suffered five costly injuries. The Raiders are now 2-0 and 49ers are 1-1. We wrote last week that Jon Gruden’s Raiders defense could shift its focus to running back Alvin Kamara and receiver Emmanuel Sanders in order to secure a victory with their AllPro receiver Michael Thomas out. Sanders was held to just one reception. Vegas heads to New England to play the Patriots and QB Cam Newton in Week 3. It’s harder to envision an upset this time, given that the Pats have one of the best defenses in the league. SF 49ers As the only remaining NFL team in the Bay Area, the 49ers walked out of New York with a win but with extensive injuries: defensive linemen Nick Bosa and Solomon Thomas, running backs Raheem Mostert and Tevin Coleman, and quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo. It’s a string of injuries that would leave many teams throwing in the towel on the season, especially in the ultra-competitive NFC West. But the 49ers have one of the best coaching staffs in the league with head coach Kyle Shanahan and defensive coordinator Robert Saleh. So, no time to panic. The next three weeks may determine whether the 49ers can remain in the race for the NFC West. Even without the injured players, SF is favored against the Giants in Week 3 and have meetings set with the winless Eagles and Dolphins in Weeks 4 and 5. So, the 49ers could be 4-1 with players returning by their Week 6 divisional game against the Rams. So don’t panic yet, Niners’ fans. Oakland A’s clinch AL West The compressed 60-game regular season is coming to a close. Those Swingin’ A’s have clinched first place in the American League West for the first time since 2013. It marks their third consecutive trip to the playoffs. The A’s are still in the mix for one of the top two seeds. If the season ended today Oakland would play the sixth-ranked Houston Astros. The SF Giants are a half game back of a final wildcard spot. SF has done itself no favors by losing three of their last four games. They are finishing up a series with the Colorado Rockies and have a final four games with the Padres, a must-win series. Soccer: Oakland Roots start NISA Tournament The Oakland Roots professional soccer team won the opening round group stage match 3-0 against New Amsterdam Football Club of New York on Monday, September 21. The Roots play tomorrow against Detroit City, with a final group match against Michigan Stars on Sunday, September 27. Recently promoted to the United Soccer League, the Rootes look to win Oakland’s first professional soccer championship since the Oakland Clippers won the NPSL in 1967. That’s a long time between titles. EAST BAY AGENCY FOR CHILDREN AUXILIARY PRESENTS
articles.title: A’s clinch AL West; NFL Week 2; Oakland Roots begin title run

articles.text: Staff Photos Look for this sign to start your trail at Harkins Ridge. Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve is a historic park in the MidPeninsula Open Space Preserve. Pictured here is Purisima Creek. Another view of Purisima Creek, where remnants of old logging mills from the early 1900s still exist. The Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve of San Mateo County is a part of the Mid-Peninsula Open Space Preserve. It is known for its towering redwood trees, wildflowers, ferns, and views of the rolling mountains south toward Big Basin. Purisima Creek was closed for several weeks after the nearby fire at Big Basin State Park clouded the air with smoke. It had been a few weeks since our last hike due to continued poor air quality, so the forecast on Sunday for clear skies was visibly refreshing. According to the Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve website, the coastal redwoods throughout Purisima Creek are second-growth, likely around 100 years old. Many large stumps, 10 to 20 feet in diameter, are visible in the park. The Preserve includes over 24 miles of developed trails, going down to the Purisima Creek Trail – an old logging path – up to peaks with gradients above 15 degrees. Sunday’s hike was a 6.7-mile loop along the Harkins Ridge Trail to Whitemore Gulch Trail, and then back to the parking lot. Starting at Harkins Ridge you go downhill about 230 feet for the first 3.5 miles. You pass beneath groves of redwoods and get a brief glimpse of Purisima Creek. After the creek and a right-turn through a gate, you begin to gain over 300 feet in less than a half mile, and then another 450 feet in the next mile. The final two miles of the trail back to the parking lot includes over 900 feet in elevation gain, including seven switchbacks that rise nearly 400 feet over the course of a mile. In total, this hike included over 1,600 feet in elevation gain. Although several sites list as Sometimes described as “heavily trafficked trails,” the trails on Harkins Ridge and Whittemore Gulch averaged only seven people per mile on my hike. For directions, enter Purisima Creek North Ridge Trailhead to access this loop. Nearby is the South Parking Lot, which connects you to the historic Purisima Creek Trail. The trail will take you beneath second-growth redwood trees and vast amounts of ferns native to the region. Several switchback turns provide hikers with a good workout from consistent elevation gains. Portions of the hike are in open, sunny areas. Some picturesque trees and trails of Purisima Creek’s Whittemore Gulch trail. A view of the rolling hills in San Mateo County.

pages.text: 14 Wednesday, September 23, 2020 Rev. Bill McNabb Continued from page 1 Rev. Dr. William McNabb preaching a sermon at Piedmont Community Church. he announced his retirement on May 6, 2019, more than a year in advance of leaving. He said that retiring in September 2020 was a date he and his wife, Maureen, felt good about. “We are excited about beginning this new chapter in our lives. I have hobbies I want to pursue, places we want to see, and books I want to read,” he said in his announcement. The 16 months between his announcement and retirement has given the church time to plan for an orderly transition. The church hired Dr. Steve Schibsted the week of August 24 to lead a Youth volunteers on the Mexico trip bring only the necessities, and sleep in tents for the duration of the trip. McNabb delivers a sermon during the Easter Main Service, 2017. search for McNabb’s successor. While delivering his final sermon last week, McNabb estimated that he had preached about 760 sermons in Piedmont. His legacy as Senior Minister expands well beyond Piedmont. He has maintained a lasting sister-church relationship with Imani Community Church, an African American congregation in Oakland, providing a link between the two communities. Under his tenure and with the hiring of Rev. Scott Kail as Youth Minister in 2002, Piedmont Community Church vastly expanded its commitment to build homes outside Tijuana, Mexico for impoverished families. During that time, hundreds of homes have been built by Piedmont teens and adults. McNabb’s outreach efforts have even crossed continents into Malawi, Africa, where a sister church relationship continues to blossom. Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn, the Associate Minister in Piedmont, noted that McNabb made a real difference in the world, the church and the community. He praised McNabb for opening up the Piedmont community to its neighbors near and far. “In a time when our lives are in a constant state of flux, it’s good to know we can continue to build on the solid foundation of ministry and mission he’s helped to lay. When he arrived nearly two decades ago, Piedmont Community Church — if it was known for anything at all outside of Piedmont — was seen as a close, but also somewhat closed, community. Bill did a whole lot to open us up.” “I’ll miss him as a colleague of 17 years, but I’m glad to continue calling him my friend,” Ashburn said. Building homes in Mexico a Rite of Passage The church-sponsored trip to Mexico during Spring Break each year has become a rite of passage for Piedmont’s youth. The legendary trip began in the 1970s with just a single van of teenagers bound for an orphanage across the Mexican border. Last year more than 300 people spent a week on the outskirts of Tecate. Those who volunteer to go to Mexico are equipped with the necessities only – hand tools and the basic building supplies to raise permanent homes for up to 16 families in one week. McNabb at t r ibutes the expanded interest in the program to the church’s youth minister, Rev. Scott Kail. “Shortly after I arrived here, I was asked to find the best youth minister in the country,” McNabb said with a smile. “We were told that Scott Kail was who we should pursue. It took me six months or so to talk Scott Kail into coming all the way from Long island, but we were able to move him and his family to Piedmont.” Before Kail came, the Mexico trip did not expand much from the single van of volunteers, McNabb recalled; but a year ago, 320 youth volunteers traveled across the border to help build homes. It was the largest volunteer house-building group there. It is so popular among Piedmont teens, there is a waiting list for placement. Last year, it sold out in about 14 seconds. McNabb noted that it changes people’s lives year after year. Students return home with new perspectives and a deep reflection of their own privileges. In turn, Kail recognized McNabb’s accomplishments in relation to youth ministry and charitable works. “Bill McNabb’s time as Senior Pastor of Piedmont Community Church was full of so many programs and ministries that helped the poor and those in need. In his tenure, over 300 homes were built,” Kail confirmed. A bridge to Malawi McNabb, along with members and friends of the Piedmont Community Church, established a close, permanent bond to a thriving Christian community in Malawi, Africa. Over the years, McNabb frequently visited Kafita Presbyterian Church, now Piedmont’s official sister church in Lllongwe, Malawi, fostering a bridge See Rev. Bill McNabb on page 15 Youth volunteers build houses for impoverished families in Mexico. McNabb singing with his daughter, Mackenzie, on Memorial Day weekend in 2007.

articles.text: between the two cultures. Today, a brick sanctuary stands with the words “Kafita CCAP,” a place of worship for the community. The construction of the sanctuary was made possible by the Better World Fund, and money raised from parishioners in Piedmont. McNabb said that he already had a pre-existing relationship with the Presbyterian hospitals in Malawi. “I flew over there in 1986 with Maureen to look for a mission hospital to support as part of our Capital Campaign at Miami Shores. We were going to give away 20 percent of what we were going to raise in that campaign,” he said. His church in Miami Shores donated an ambulance, but couldn’t get anyone to deliver it past Zimbabwe. Undeterred, McNabb flew to Zimbabwe with three friends and drove the ambulance about 1000 miles to Malawi. “It was one of the most incredible experiences of my life,” he said with a broad smile. McNabb’s most recent trip to Africa was in June 2019. Now inspired by the success of the outreach to Africa, the church has recently expanded its efforts to explore supporting missions in South America. Branching out to the East Bay Under McNabb’s leadership, Piedmont Community Church has formed a sister church relationships with Imani Community Church in Oakland. A chance meeting of two pastors, McNabb and Rev. Dr. George Cummings, forged a close bond between their churches. “It was after we had such positive experience with Kafita in Malawi that we tried to find a sister church closer to home,” McNabb said. McNabb started going to the Pastors of Oakland breakfast once a week to find a church that aligns with Piedmont Community Church’s mission and inclusivity. “All of a sudden, George [Cummings] got up to speak, and I knew he was different. This was an educated person who was very progressive. When he spoke, I knew that I found ‘him’,” McNabb recalled. McNabb invited Cummings to lunch, and then for dinner, finding many similarities between them – they even shared the same birthday. Through that friendship, a sister church relationship was born. Piedmont Community Church continues to raise funds for ongoing programs in Oakland and Berkeley – focusing on homelessness and food insecurity. Reflections on retirement McNabb’s beginnings in Piedmont were overshadowed by the tragic events of 9/11. His first Sunday preaching from the pulpit in Piedmont was September 9, 2001, two days before the terrorist attack on New York City and Washington, DC. And now his retirement comes upon the heels of a global pandemic, and his last sermon was delivered to an empty room. Still, McNabb reflects joyfully on the past 19 years, his beginnings, and his retirement. “It was an interesting way to start and end a ministry. We were in this together, we were going to get through it,” McNabb said. He offered similar sentiments throughout the public health crisis – in the form of short, shared video messages. P i e d m o n t C o m m u n i t y Church will celebrate Rev. Bill McNabb this Sunday, Saturday 27, with a tribute video. The video will be shown on Youtube at 9 a.m. You can view the promotional teaser on Youtube at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=9UQDrJvwFf8&feature=youtu.be. Rev. Dr. George Cummings and McNabb

And now his retirement comes upon the heels of a global pandemic, and his last sermon was delivered to an empty room. Still, McNabb reflects joyfully on the past 19 years, his beginnings, and his retirement. “It was an interesting way to start and end a ministry. We were in this together, we were going to get through it,” McNabb said. He offered similar sentiments throughout the public health crisis – in the form of short, shared video messages. articles.text: Conductor Anne Daniel works with kinder department students Part 2 in a series of the history of the youth choral organization. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir offers three departments for its 200 young singers: the Kinder Department, Training department, and Performing Department. The Kinder Department is comprised of students ages 4 through 6 in two different sets: the pre-kinder choir (ages 4-5 and in preschool), and kinder choir (ages 5 – 6 and in kindergarten). Both offer a child’s first exposure to choral music in a friendly, nurturing, and playful environment. “It’s really their first exposure to music,” said Artistic Director Eric Tuan. “We offer something that’s developmentally appropriate, like singing together, and introducing folk songs and musical games that will later be used in the training department to derive melodic patterns,” Each class in the Kinder Department meets weekly for fifty minutes. Pre-kinder choir sections are limited to 10 students, and kinder choir sections are limited to 12. Each class offers a “Family and Friends Recital” at the end of each semester. The youngest department is led by Anne Daniel, now in her fifth year, who oversees PreKinder Choir, Kinder Choir, and Girls Training 1. “She’s just terrific – with the little ones in particular,” Tuan said. Immersing students at this age in choral music has many benefits. Tuan noted the social development that comes with working in tandem. At age four and five, children begin noticing rhythmic patterns and are able to mimic them. In preschool and daycare, singing can help children improve their capacity for learning. Singing together in a choral setting is one of the first community-building exercises that a child will experience. Piedmont Children’s Choir offers teaching methods that are closely linked to the developmental stages of the growing mind, and a choir is the perfect opportunity for a young child to learn to navigate a social group in a shared activity with a common goal. “There really isn’t competition in the choir, only cooperation,” Tuan explained. “If your weakest singer does better, the whole group does better. There is a connectivity.” Most students who graduate from the kinder department continue on to the training and then performing group. The goal for many children is to be in a performing group that travels outside the state and county for summer choral competitions. Part 3 in the series will explore the training department. articles.text: Each week, Oakland Symphony is making archival footage available to patrons while its doors remain closed due to the current health crisis. This week Music Director Michael Morgan introduced Sergei Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances, Op. 45. “On this rePAST, we hear Sergei Rachmaninoff’s last major work, the Symphonic Dances. In three movements, they sum up the late compositional style of Rachmaninoff. In fact, in it he quotes several of his own earlier pieces,” Morgan explained. “The work combines the rhythmic vitality you would expect in a piece called ‘Symphonic Dances’ with the lush harmony and gift for melody one expects in RachMusic Director Michael Morgan introduces Sergei Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances maninoff. It is for large orchestra, and notable for its use of the alto saxophone as a solo wind instrument.” The piece was performed by the symphony at the Paramount Theatre on October 2, 2015. You can view the performance at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/repast/. The next concert recording will be available on Friday evening at 6 p.m.

articles.text: Musaics of the Bay’s “Stayat-home Symposium” is a virtual community collaboration and series of broadcasts featuring music premieres based on both music and art. It is a collaboration among composers, performers, artists of all types. Last week’s symposium featured violinist Maya Buchanan performing the music of composer Elise Arancio, whose work, “Wherever I Go, You Go,” was inspired by a painting entitled “Vision Unfolding” by Tim Petrin and an accompanying poem by E.E Cummings. The poem, I Carry Your Heart With Me, was a common theme throughout the broadcast. Arancio introduced the poem. “I feel like this poem is especially powerful, and this time, while so many people are separated by physical distance, it’s a great reminder that we carry the people that we love close to us no matter the circumstance,” Arancio said. Symposium composers select community-submitted pieces as the inspiration for new musical compositions to be premiered Composer Elise Arancio’s music as performed by violinist Maya Buchanan. by instrumentalists in curated weekly broadcasts. You can watch the concert at https://www.musaics.org/ symposium.

articles.text: Violinist Tessa Lark will be featured in a Cal Performances concert to be shown on October 1. Cal Performances announced a 15-episode run of full-length concerts and theater works, compiled in a series called “Cal Performances at Home.” The series will run from October to mid-January and will feature a wide variety of new and full-length videos or live events, all available to stream directly to your home screen. Main Stage performances will feature artists and programs that were set to perform for Cal Performances’ fall season, as well as a few new additions. Main Stage videos will also be accompanied by free “Beyond the Stage” talks with the artists, interviews, lectures, question and answer sessions with artists and Cal Performances staff, and with UC Berkeley faculty. Special premiere-evening “watch parties” will allow patrons to enjoy the company of other performing arts lovers from the safety of your own home. A new performance will debut each week, beginning Thursday, October 1. The first performance will feature violinist Tessa Lark, and pianist Andrew Armstrong. Throughout the fall season, the series will feature performances from New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Spain and Germany. Pricing for the “Cal Performances at Home” is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. To view suggested prices, and for more information on the series, visit https://calperformances.org/at-home/.
articles.title: “Cal Performances at Home” begins October 1

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré RBG are the initials of Ruth Bader Ginsberg, until her death on Friday this week a sitting judge on the U.S. Supreme Court. The three letters are also the title of a well-crafted documentary about a remarkable woman who, to paraphrase both Martin Luther King and Barack Obama, has time and again proven in her legal career that “The arc of a moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.” RBG in essence is a civil rights film about the pernicious effects of gender discrimination. It was Ginsberg who early in her career as an attorney decided that if it was possible to bend the arc of history toward equality for women (and men), whatever the context, then she might be able to accomplish such profound change inside of a courtroom as an advocate and later from as a judge. The arc for Ginsburg has indeed been long, beginning when she was very young. Her intellect was always present; however, her restraint, her deliberative personality, absent anger or resentment, reflects the repeated counsel of her mother, who died when Ginsburg was only 17. After law school at Harvard and Colombia, slowly and tenaciously, and despite her diminutive stature and quiet, decorous manner, she argued case after case, each buttressed by well-reasoned points of view. The film opens with a montage of anti-Ginsburg voices, each taking exception to her advocacy for equality regardless of gender. The language spoken is vitriolic and unexpected. One example is when Ginsburg stepped forward to argue that there was no legal basis for Virginia Military Institute refusing to enroll qualified women. She won, and women eagerly matriculated to VMI. It was classic RBG – not her first victory nor would it be her last. Ruth Baker Ginsberg, subject of the documentary RBG. The film seamlessly merges Ginsburg’s unparalleled work habits with her personal life, most especially her love for her husband, Martin Ginsburg, a successful New York tax attorney. Together their marriage and two children were deeply valued. While Ginsburg was reserved and focused, her husband y was easy-going and jocular. They created a charming balance, creating a much-envied harmony that lasted for decades. The film shows that while RBG had an ability to focus on the law and its historical precedents, it was when she was nominated by Bill Clinton to the Supreme Court, in 1993, that she became, ever so gradually, a judicial rock star. What caused her surprising almost pop culture fame was that the court’s pendulum was slowly swinging toward conservatism. As a result, Ginsburg found herself often penning sharp and eloquent dissents, documents that were closely read and which took an important place in the decisions of the court. Ginsburg has become an iconic symbol for feminists across the nation, her image and her initials in conjunction with the word “notorious,” referencing, tongue in cheek, rapper “Notorious B.I.G.” Hence the recent biography, titled Notorious RBG. As a film, RBG is a valentine to this remarkable woman who has, using the language of the law, spoken in courtrooms large and small and by doing so, has changed the landscape of America. Her journey has been astonishing, born of iron spine and will. And it still continues. It was suggested to her that after two bouts with cancer during Obama’s tenure she might consider retiring, allowing him to nominate a younger justice. She explained that she was committed to serving as long as she was able. And able she was until her death this week on September 18, 2020. RBG. Documentary. Directed by Betsy West and Julie Cohen. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. This review was originally printed in the Piedmont Post on May 20, 2018. articles.text: A violin made by F.O. Stanley in 1908. The piedmont Fourth of July parade is famous. There are the Oompa-Loompas and the great Piedmont Community Band. But the classic cars are viewed with excitement. I am always fascinated by the Stanley Steamers. They remain the classics of classic cars. But these classics were only a passing interest of the Stanley brothers. One of their passions will outlive the steamers by hundreds of years. If you ever need inspiration, look to the Stanley brothers. Long before cars even made an appearance on the scene, the Stanley brothers were successful. F.O. and F.E. Stanley were twins and used their initials as their names. They began their first business in an elementary school. It was some type of a maple syrup business, and it was a success. Their next success was to develop an x-ray focusing mechanism. Shortly after this, they invented a new photographic process. They sold it to George Eastman who sold it to the public as Kodak. Eastman made a fortune and so did the Stanleys. This was the seed money to start manufacturing the famous cars. Everyone knows about the Stanley Steamers. But what few may remembeer is that the best steam car ever made was made in nearby Emeryville. Moving ahead a few years, FE Stanley was killed in a traffic accident and FO Stanley came down with tuberculosis. Seeking to recover his health, he moved to Colorado. Not only did he love Colorado, but he regained his health. He invested his money wisely and went into the hotel business. The Stanley Hotel in Estes Park, Colorado remains a destination and houses the Stanley museum. But the brothers’ real interest superseded even fame and money. All those things – the cars, the x-ray machine, the photographic process, the hotel business – they all came later. The first thing the young Stanley boys learned will outlive everything else that they did. Their uncle, who had the colorful name of Liberty Stanley, was one of the first American-born violin makers. How he got his colorful name is another story. He was born in 1776, and the boys made their first violin at the age of 10. Later when they acquired a real Stradivarius violin, they took notice of the wood that Stradivarius used. They bought wood from the same forest as the great Stradivarius himself. Not only did they use it for their own violins, they used it in their Stanley Steamer cars. FE Stanley became great friends with Henry Ford. But it wasn’t their love of automobiles that cemented the friendship. No, it was their love of violins. Henry Ford bought two violins made by Stanley to accompany the two Stradivarius violins that he owned. While all those other things may be seen as passing fancies, the Stanley violins should last at least 500 years. I was said that a Stanley Steemer never needed a tuneup. But a violin? Now that’s another story. Good news It seems that good news is on the horizon. The Dallas Symphony has resumed with live concerts. They presented an all-Beethoven concert recently, and all precautions were observed. The 36 musicians on stage wore masks. The audience, which normally numbers 2000, was limited to 79. Needless to say they were very enthusiastic. The critics were happy to report that the small orchestra played with great clarity and enthusiasm. It is a start back to normalcy, and is indeed good news. F.O. Stanley
articles.title: Success is more than hot air

Not only did he love Colorado, but he regained his health. He invested his money wisely and went into the hotel business. The Stanley Hotel in Estes Park, Colorado remains a destination and houses the Stanley museum. But the brothers’ real interest superseded even fame and money. All those things – the cars, the x-ray machine, the photographic process, the hotel business – they all came later. The first thing the young Stanley boys learned will outlive everything else that they did. Their uncle, who had the colorful name of Liberty Stanley, was one of the first American-born violin makers. How he got his colorful name is another story. He was born in 1776, and the boys made their first violin at the age of 10. Later when they acquired a real Stradivarius violin, they took notice of the wood that Stradivarius used. They bought wood from the same forest as the great Stradivarius himself. Not only did they use it for their own violins, they used it in their Stanley Steamer cars. FE Stanley became great friends with Henry Ford. But it wasn’t their love of automobiles that cemented the friendship. No, it was their love of violins. Henry Ford bought two violins made by Stanley to accompany the two Stradivarius violins that he owned. While all those other things may be seen as passing fancies, the Stanley violins should last at least 500 years. I was said that a Stanley Steemer never needed a tuneup. But a violin? Now that’s another story. Good news It seems that good news is on the horizon. The Dallas Symphony has resumed with live concerts. They presented an all-Beethoven concert recently, and all precautions were observed. The 36 musicians on stage wore masks. The audience, which normally numbers 2000, was limited to 79. Needless to say they were very enthusiastic. The critics were happy to report that the small orchestra played with great clarity and enthusiasm. It is a start back to normalcy, and is indeed good news. Ruth Baker Ginsberg, subject of the documentary RBG. The film seamlessly merges Ginsburg’s unparalleled work habits with her personal life, most especially her love for her husband, Martin Ginsburg, a successful New York tax attorney. Together their marriage and two children were deeply valued. While Ginsburg was reserved and focused, her husband y was easy-going and jocular. They created a charming balance, creating a much-envied harmony that lasted for decades. The film shows that while RBG had an ability to focus on the law and its historical precedents, it was when she was nominated by Bill Clinton to the Supreme Court, in 1993, that she became, ever so gradually, a judicial rock star. What caused her surprising almost pop culture fame was that the court’s pendulum was slowly swinging toward conservatism. As a result, Ginsburg found herself often penning sharp and eloquent dissents, documents that were closely read and which took an important place in the decisions of the court. Ginsburg has become an iconic symbol for feminists across the nation, her image and her initials in conjunction with the word “notorious,” referencing, tongue in cheek, rapper “Notorious B.I.G.” Hence the recent biography, titled Notorious RBG. As a film, RBG is a valentine to this remarkable woman who has, using the language of the law, spoken in courtrooms large and small and by doing so, has changed the landscape of America. Her journey has been astonishing, born of iron spine and will. And it still continues. It was suggested to her that after two bouts with cancer during Obama’s tenure she might consider retiring, allowing him to nominate a younger justice. She explained that she was committed to serving as long as she was able. And able she was until her death this week on September 18, 2020. RBG. Documentary. Directed by Betsy West and Julie Cohen. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. This review was originally printed in the Piedmont Post on May 20, 2018. A world order, so to speak, is in transition: the balance between the forces of nature and those trying to bend the natural world to their own purpose is in conflict. articles.text: “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. This week hosts and Aurora Directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams are joined by Bay Area actors Courtney Flores, Craig and Jeanette Marker, Marissa Keltie Muterspaugh, and Jasmine Milan Williams, all graduates of the theater program at Cal State East Bay in Hayward. Along with Williams, some of them are also alumni of Impact Theatre in Berkeley’s Northside, co-founded by Costello in 1996. The episode focuses on their time at Cal State Hayward, how they’ve kept in touch since then, the history of the school’s theater department, and what makes it so strong. The guests will discuss their favorite projects they’ve done together, as well as some of their favorite Aurora shows. Flores is a Bay Area native who has worked as a freelance costume designer for 16 years Bay Area actor Marissa Muterspaugh. in the San Francisco Bay Area and outside California. Muterspaugh has worked as an actor at Aurora Theatre, Jewel Theatre, Symmetry Theatre, Magic Theatre, Marin Theatre Company, Cal Shakes, Shotgun Players, Crowded Fire, Custom Made, Central Works, California Theatre Center, San Francisco Playhouse, Berkeley Playhouse, and Impact Theatre. You can view the episode at https://www.auroratheatre.org/ auroraconnects.

articles.text: snakes. It attacks the villagers. Riding to their defense comes Ashitaka (Billy Crudup), a young prince of an isolated people. He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try and discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. It is then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a mononoke is a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. And so the story continues, a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that it is one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated films and may not be suitable for the little guys. While it is mythical history, it also engages, using action and melodrama, which for older audiences will enthrall; it never approaches anything like graphic violence. The artistry is magical and masterful, qualities that define all of the films of Hayao Miyazaki. Princess Mononoke (1999). Animé by Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Gillian Anderson and Minnie Driver. 2 hrs., 13 min. articles.text: San Francisco will get its first pop up drive-in theater at the Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture, located at 2 Marina Boulevard. Billed as Fort Mason Flix, the drive-in is located in a large parking lot at the pavilion. Flix will host a series of classic films six days a week through October 18. A 40 x 20-foot, high definition LED screen has been mounted on the festival pavilion and will be 90 times brighter than a standard movie theater projector, allowing the films to be shown in early evening light. A concession stand will be available, and all Covid-19 safety measures will be followed, including masks to be worn when leaving the vehicle. All restrooms will be deep cleaned. Contactless check-ins and tickets will be sold only online at fortmason.org/flix. Tickets are $49 per vehicle. People can bring as many people as there are seatbelts. Patrons can remain in their The Lion King will be shown at the Fort Mason Drive-in Theater on Friday, September 25. cars for the duration of the film and never have contact with anyone, according to Kinsey. Movie-goers should only come with people in their safety pod. There will be two daily screenings (see schedule below). For more information, see fortmason.org/flix.

articles.text: Walking through town, it becomes clear to me that two things stand out as chief characteristics of the architecture in Piedmont. The first is the individuality of the homes — virtually all of the homes are “one-off” designs, built before the advent of seemingly ubiquitous tract homes. Today, even in many expensive new communities, because of economy of scale, developers often build the same home in large groups, robbing the place of the rich character, individuality and texture of the streets and community that we see here. The second observation is the high quality of design and construction throughout the city. Part of the pre-tract home era in which Piedmont was started, also included noted individual architects for each house. We benefited from (and continue to benefit from) the talents and expertise of an era of excellent local architects, including Julia Morgan, Albert Farr, Miller Warneke, and W.H. Weeks. This valuable contribution continues today with top designers and architects such as Mark Becker, Glen Jarvis, and John Malick to name just a few. And with top designers seems to come a higher level of craftsmanship which results in buildings that not only look better, but last for generations. What most people immediately think of when reference is made to architecture, is the exterior appearance of a building. As we will see in this series, although the exterior shape, form or style is only part of what can be considered good architecture, it is of course very important. It is important not only for the owners, but also for the many people experiencing it: guests, neighbors and passers-by. A building and its visual relationship to adjoining buildings and landscapes (its context) necessarily is a part of and helps form the entire community. This is why building height, Well designed doors, windows, hardware and light fixtures are all among the many important details that make up the overall architectural character and quality of buildings. Building an addition onto your home is often more disruptive and expensive than renovating an existing garage. One of the best things you can do is have an experienced team behind you to make sure that your project is completed safely and efficiently. The first thing to do is understand your needs and develop a clear scope of work. Do you want extra storage space? Are you looking to add a personal workshop for hobbies and activities? A home office? Extra living space? Whatever your goals are, updating even a small garage can have a big impact. Here are some ideas from a past project (pictured) to help you make the most of your garage remodel. Aesthetics and quality craftsmanship were important to our clients for this garage remodel. Because the garage is so prominent in their backyard, a thoughtfully remodeled building that matched the style of their home and worked with the layout of their deck and yard was essential. Photography by Open Homes Photography Storage space for bike storage, a main mode of transportation for the client, was essential. Garage before remodel. Garage after remodel. Exterior style of the garage mimics the main house to make it an extension of the home. Add Storage Space Whether you’re storing tools, bikes, gear, toys, or other household items, there are endless creative options for turning your garage into a functional and accessible storage space. Take advantage of the walls and install hooks, shelves and cabinetry that can accommodate items like bikes, tools and ladders. Large floor-standing shelving units will give every item its own place. You can even add overhead racks on the ceiling to store bulky items. Create a Workshop or Home Office If you’re into gardening, carpentry, crafting, metalworking, or other DIY projects, creating a dedicated workshop is a great way to utilize extra space in your garage. Add a workbench and a place to store your tools and you’ll be all set for your home improvement projects. Alternatively, with many people now working from home these days, adding an office in your garage can provide you with a quiet space to work away from the hustle and bustle of your main house. Make it Pretty Having an aesthetically pleasing garage is just as important as having one that is functional. Choosing to match the exterior style of your main house unifies the aesthetic and makes the garage truly feel like an extension of your home and the rest of the property. It’s important to invest in quality materials to ensure an elevated look. Some upgrades you can make include adding an automatic overhead garage door to replace a sliding carriage door. articles.text: Due to the Labor Day holiday on the first Monday of September, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had their Zoom book discussion on September 14.. With the recent death of Congressman John Lewis and society’s current focus on racial and social justice, the group decided to read Lewis’ Across That Bridge. There was a solid turnout of 14 members of the group for the call. Participating were Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Jeri Lockhart, Laura Goldman, Adrienne Hamlin, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Margie Blodgett, Pat McSwain, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. John Lewis was a civil rights pioneer and icon. He was one of the leaders of the 1963 March on Washington and a speaker with Martin Luther King Jr. at the Lincoln Memorial. In 1965, Lewis led a march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, an event which became known as “Bloody Sunday.” State troopers and police attacked the marchers, leaving Lewis and others battered and bloody. Lewis later served 17 terms in the U.S. House of Representatives representing Georgia from 1987 until his death earlier this year. During this time he was a champion of civil rights and social justice. He was also the author of seven books, including Across That Bridge, drawing from his personal experiences as a civil rights leader to offer guidance on the importance of living a virtuous life and how to change the world without the use of violence. The reading group universally enjoyed Across That Bridge. Lewis followed his Christian faith and Gandhi’s principles of non-violence to accomplish change. The readers felt Lewis’ themes of love and non-violence are timeless and inspiring. The group discussed how the debate between violence and non-violence for achieving change continues. It was questioned how much the current generation knows about the power of non-violence today. The readers agreed that there has been racial progress in our country, but that we still have a long way to go, and that violence makes situations worse. It can be discouraging to see that change is not as rapid as many would like. People become impatient, but the process of change is like a relay race where the struggle is passed from one generation to the next. The group’s hope was that it will not take another hundred years to achieve true racial justice in our country. Lewis provided insights from his actions in the ‘60s which the readers felt can be used to bring change now. The group felt that this is a book for the next generation of leaders, as it reads like a guide on how to conduct themselves and accomplish change. Faith in God and Lewis’ cause kept him going on a personal level and motivated him in peaceful resistance. The group agreed Lewis was a great man, that Across That Bridge is a fine book, that it had generated a group conversation by the reading group, and that discussions are importaant even though the issues are uncomfortable. The outpouring of love for John Lewis at his death was understandable for the readers. Laura Goldman noted that actor Morgan Freeman read Lewis’s final words at his funeral. They were words that Lewis wrote at the very end of his life, Alicia Rivera had recently listened to this remarkable oratory (available at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=_i2DSkAys-8), and hoped others would listen to it as well. Alicia commented that America lost a true leader during our troubled times. In dicussing future books to read and discuss, the group selected Caste by Isabel Wilkerson for November and Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austin for December. They earlier made The Dutch House, a novel by Ann Patchett, their October selection. The group has read mostly recently written books, and thought reading a classic like Pride and Prejudice would be an interesting change. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, October 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are welcome, and there is no fee to participate. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov.

The readers felt Lewis’ themes of love and non-violence are timeless and inspiring. The group discussed how the debate between violence and non-violence for achieving change continues. It was questioned how much the current generation knows about the power of non-violence today. The readers agreed that there has been racial progress in our country, but that we still have a long way to go, and that violence makes situations worse. It can be discouraging to see that change is not as rapid as many would like. People become impatient, but the process of change is like a relay race where the struggle is passed from one generation to the next. The group’s hope was that it will not take another hundred years to achieve true racial justice in our country. Lewis provided insights from his actions in the ‘60s which the readers felt can be used to bring change now. The group felt that this is a book for the next generation of leaders, as it reads like a guide on how to conduct themselves and accomplish change. Faith in God and Lewis’ cause kept him going on a personal level and motivated him in peaceful resistance. The group agreed Lewis was a great man, that Across That Bridge is a fine book, that it had generated a group conversation by the reading group, and that discussions are importaant even though the issues are uncomfortable. The outpouring of love for John Lewis at his death was understandable for the readers. Laura Goldman noted that actor Morgan Freeman read Lewis’s final words at his funeral. They were words that Lewis wrote at the very end of his life, Alicia Rivera had recently listened to this remarkable oratory (available at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=_i2DSkAys-8), and hoped others would listen to it as well. Alicia commented that America lost a true leader during our troubled times. In dicussing future books to read and discuss, the group selected Caste by Isabel Wilkerson for November and Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austin for December. They earlier made The Dutch House, a novel by Ann Patchett, their October selection. The group has read mostly recently written books, and thought reading a classic like Pride and Prejudice would be an interesting change. The group will meet next in a Zoom call on Monday, October 5, at 1:30 p.m. New members are welcome, and there is no fee to participate. articles.text: Dryden Once again, the bicycle team Linda and Marvin will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding this Saturday, September 26, in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. You can make your donation online by simply clicking on the link at the bottom of this message. If you would prefer, you can also send your tax-deductible contribution to the address listed below. Please write the name/ Team Linda and Marvin in the memo line. Due to the Coronavirus, the ride is going virtual this year, but some of us will be riding from Oakland to the top of Mount Diablo and back, a distance of 80 miles and 7,500 feet of vertical climbing. That’s our challenge to support ALS research and care. We hope you will be compelled to support this cause in an effort to defeat this horrible disease. articles.text: Recommendations to improve the Kennelly Skate Park are still pending approval by Piedmont City Council, according to an update given to the Recreation Commission by Recreation Chair Chelle Putzer last week. A skate park subcommittee, initially comprised of Recreation Commission members Vincent Fischer, Carrie Graham Lee, and Glyn Burge, Rec. Department staff members John Wilk, surveyed the skate park last year and made recommendations on some improvements. “The subcommittee, in May 2019, came to the commission and gave their recommendations. The purpose of that committee was to review current skating and scootering options in the city, and explore ways to offer more skating opportunities,” Putzer said. Putzer also noted that the skate park is suitable only for intermediate skaters and older, information acknowledged by the subcommittee. Some recommendations pointed to a potential redesign in order to make it a better fit for the community. “[The subcommittee] wanted to make it a better fit for beginner-to-intermediate skaters, give it some space, give it shade and maybe a place to picnic,” she said. The commission approved those recommendations last year, Kennelly Skate Park is behind Coaches Field and the Piedmont Corporation Yard. but the recommendations never were formally approved by the council. “Now it’s in a bit of a holding pattern,” Putzer said. The subcommittee has since disbanded, but the recommendations still wait for council approval. Commission Chair Steve Roland noted that the subcommittee provided great insight on improvements to the park last year, but their report ultimately fell to the wayside due to COVID-19. “Eventually, the [recreation] commission passed it on to city council, and it was out of our hands. That led right up into the pandemic, and here we are,” he said. A Coaches Field master plan, currently under CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act) review, can potentially incorporate some of the intended designs for the Kennelly Skate Park. This would include a possible picnic area, as well as other design aspects that were suggested. The recommendations will probably go to council for approval at a later date, Putzer explained. The Recreation Department is currently using the skate park as a temporary preschool area, as indoor daycare services remain shuddered due to COVID-19.
articles.title: Skate park improvements waiting for council OK

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont pool has been enjoyed by generations and continuing do so is an understandable goal for Piedmont. The proposed ballot measure is not a very appropriate or responsible way for Piedmont to meet that goal. 1. The Piedmont City Council recently identified two capital improvement projects for consideration. The first project was upgrading the public facilities (police, fire and city offices) to meet “essential services” requirements to assure that they function during a natural disaster. The estimated cost was $30,000,000. The second project was a new community pool. Based on early program descriptions and no actual design documents, the estimated cost was $15,000,000. 2. Clearly the function of city services after a natural disaster would seem to be the first priority in the implementation of these projects. 3. Instead, the Piedmont City Council put a $19,000,000 bond issue on the ballot to fund a community pool, even though that same council put the estimated cost of the project at $15,000,000. 4. This project is described as a community pool. Historically, and in the promotional materials, Piedmont School District sports programs and swim classes are identified as using the facility, thus limiting community use without remuneration. Incidentally and historically, over the last 40 years at least, the School District has refused to request that Piedmont citizens fund a school pool. 5. The vaguely suggested scope of the project goes way beyond the existing facility. It seems to be tailored for water sports not community use. The specter of swim meets looms with the attendant parking nightmare. 6. A complete rehabilitation of the existing facility that would replace all piping and equipment, seal and refinish the existing pools, is certainly worth exploring, and would absolutely cost far 7. By putting the pool project ahead of public safety and putting a measure on the ballot with insufficient definition of scope of work is, to put it charitably, a mistake. Piedmont is a very small town with very limited bonding capacity and the pool is just not a first priority. We can have our pool, but not this way. Please vote no. There is time and there another way. –Alan Rudy, AIA
articles.title: A new pool? Take time and do the job right

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Measure UU, the local bond measure which will provide the funds necessary to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable new pool facility for the entire Piedmont Community. There is little dispute that the current pool has reached the end of its useful life. Despite repeated attempts by prior City Councils and community members to secure a new aquatics facility, no significant work has been undertaken to replace this critical 56-year-old community resource. I urge you to join me in supporting the decision of our bright, diligent, elected officials who have thoughtfully placed this measure on the ballot now, after significant research and consultation. Be assured, that an independent Citizen Bond Measure Oversight Committee will monitor the prudent use of all funds raised. East Bay voters had the foresight to approve the formation of the East Bay Regional Park District during the depression. Let’s emerge from this Covid cloud with the promise of a sparkling new pool facility open to all Piedmont families, students, and seniors. Please join me in voting YES on Measure UU. –Cathy Michelotti Glazier
articles.title: Building a pool open to all Piedmont families
