articles.text: Editor: In troubling times like these, it is more important than ever to elect a strong, committed, and capable leader who will work towards the common good of all, not just a few. We wholeheartedly endorse Conna McCarthy for Piedmont City Council because she has shown these qualities over her years of valuable service to the Piedmont community. We have known Conna for over 15 years and have admired her leadership on key Piedmont committees, commissions, and school boards. She tirelessly led critical initiatives on the Parent boards of both Piedmont Middle and Piedmont High School. Also, she was influential on the Parcel Tax Committees, advocating for our children and residents. In addition to championing for schools, she has worked hard as the Vice Chair of the Recreation Commission and Chair of the CIP Committee making recommendations on capital expenditures on City facilities. We have witnessed Conna being whip-smart and dedicated but also collaborative and compassionate. Conna and her thoughtful leadership will have a strong, positive impact on our town. We hope you’ll join us in voting for her on November 3 for City Council. –Debbie and Dan Lee
articles.title: McCarthy – working toward common good of all

articles.text: Editor: During this difficult time in our history, we need leadership to unite, think creatively and act for the benefit of the entire Piedmont community, especially students and teachers. As a candidate for school board, Hilary Cooper fits that bill with her vast, multi-dimensional experience as classroom teacher, volunteer and fundraiser. As president of parents’ clubs, she exhibited her ability to collaborate with different viewpoints, a much-needed skill for a school board member. With my background as a Havens teacher, parent and grandparent of Piedmont students, I see the need for an experienced individual to help the success of our schools by being able to juggle the various needs of students, teachers, administration and parents. A vote for Hilary is a vote for success for the entire community. –Elene Manolis
articles.title: Cooper able to collaborate with differing viewpoints

articles.text: Editor: I have gotten to know Cory Smegal from working together on the Wildwood Site Council and on Health & Safety preparedness, and from watching her in numerous School Board meetings. Cory is an exceptional board member. She actively listens to parents and educators, does her homework and researches best practices. Cory is a clear thinker who asks direct questions and advocates for what’s in the best interest of students. As a pediatrician, I am concerned about the health and well-being of all our students, especially now. Cory consistently ensures that the board prioritizes student mental health. She doesn’t just talk about what’s needed, she actively explores how to solve problems. Recently she’s been talking about how to find ways for students to make meaningful in-person connections while in distance learning. Cory has advocated to bring students back to the classroom as soon as it’s safely possible, starting with those who have the most difficult time with distance learning and those who pose the least risk in terms of spreading SARS-CoV-2. Cory has worked hard to secure the financial health of our District. She has led local fundraising efforts such as the Giving Campaign, actively campaigned to pass school bond measures, and advocated alongside administrators, teachers and parents for better state funding. As Board Correspondent, Cory has improved communication by making a point to respond promptly and thoughtfully to the countless emails sent to the board over the past two years. At this time of unprecedented challenges, we need experienced leaders. Cory is the current Board Vice-President and if re-elected, she is next in line to be Board President in December. Please join me in re-electing Cory to the School Board. More than ever, we need her leadership. –James E. CrawfordJakubiak, MD
articles.title: Smegal an exceptional School Board member

articles.text: Editor: I have known Conna as a parent and community volunteer and had the pleasure of partnering with her on several successful parcel tax campaigns to ensure quality public education in Piedmont. I’ve also had the opportunity to build on work she began at the Piedmont Education Foundation and the PUSD Wellness Center. Conna is the addition we need to our City Council because she is committed to public service along the entire continuum of civic engagement from volunteering to serving on commissions, and now stepping in to lead as an elected official. I have also witnessed Conna prioritize effective and inclusive community engagement as she leans in and listens to the range of voices in town. It is an exciting time to lead in Piedmont and with Conna on our City Council, our community will get an elected official it deserves. –Mahvash Hassan
articles.title: McCarthy – committed to public service

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to enthusiastically support Conna McCarthy in her candidacy for Piedmont City Council. I have had the pleasure of working with Conna over the course of many years, from serving on Parent Boards, the Booster Board, and the Piedmont Educational Foundation, to recent project collaborations in our respective roles on the City’s Recreation Commission and the City’s Park Commission. Conna comes from a background steeped in public service and civic engagement. She is caring, hardworking, and tenacious and will cut to the chase, but also maintains a healthy sense of humor. Conna doesn’t shy away from asking the tough questions and will make decisions with the best interests of all community members in mind. I know that she will govern with transparency and be accessible to the City’s residents and take heed of their concerns. Conna will continue to make Piedmont proud. Please join me in voting to elect Conna McCarthy to the Piedmont City Council. –Robin Wu
articles.title: McCarthy ­ – governing with transparency

articles.text: Editor: Piedmont is a special place to live and Conna McCarthy is the perfect person to be elected to City Council to ensure it continues to be so. Conna was raised to be politically active. As a member of City Council, she can continue to use her talents and education to improve the lives of others. Her commitment to community service is long and varied and includes the Parents Club, Boy Scouts, Booster Board, 2019 Chair of Civic Projects, serving on the Recreation Commission and many more. Conna is also a lawyer, inquisitive and a good listener. Conna and Peter have raised three wonderful children who have aspired to service in society and country, just like their mother. We highly endorse Conna McCarthy for City Council. –Daley and Mike Humphries
articles.title: McCarthy can use talents to improve lives of others

articles.text: Editor: We’re longtime friends and neighbors of Jen Cavenaugh, and we’re writing to urge Piedmonters to re-elect her to the city council. As a councilwoman, she’s been responsive to constituents, a careful steward of city resources, and an effective liaison between the council and the school board. Another term will let her continue her efforts to improve our parks and infrastructure and to promote public safety and disaster preparation. four years ago, she’d already put together an impressive volunteer resume. She served on the Piedmont Budget Advisory Committee, the Piedmont Language School, and the parent boards of Beach, PMS, and PHS. She hit the floor running at City Hall and hasn’t slowed down. Jen’s sharp, accessible, and pragmatic, and Piedmonters will benefit from another four years of her leadership. So, join us on November 3 in voting for Jen Cavenaugh for Piedmont City Council. –Matthew Goldstein and Laura Ruberto
articles.title: Making the case for re-election of Cavenaugh

In fact, I believe Hari Titan’s presence on the school board will serve the community well, ensuring the expertise so necessary in times of economic uncertainty. A vote for Hilary is a vote for success for the entire community. –Elene Manolis McCarthy can use talents to improve lives of others Editor: Piedmont is a special place to live and Conna McCarthy is the perfect person to be elected to City Council to ensure it continues to be so. Conna was raised to be politically active. As a member of City Council, she can continue to use her talents and education to improve the lives of others. Her commitment to community service is long and varied and includes the Parents Club, Boy Scouts, Booster Board, 2019 Chair of Civic Projects, serving on the Recreation Commission and many more. Conna is also a lawyer, inquisitive and a good listener. Conna and Peter have raised three wonderful children who have aspired to service in society and country, just like their mother. We highly endorse Conna McCarthy for City Council. –Daley and Mike Humphries Titan an advocate of science-based decision making Editor: I worked closely with Dr. Hari Titan on his safety summit primer. I appreciate Hari’s analytic and science-based decision making, which will be needed as we figure out how to reopen our schools safely in the future. Hari will not let closed-door politics dictate the safety of our teachers and students. –Leon Saperstein McCarthy – working toward common good of all Editor: In troubling times like these, it is more important than ever to elect a strong, committed, and capable leader who will work towards the common good of all, not just a few. We wholeheartedly endorse Conna McCarthy for Piedmont City Council because she has shown these qualities over her years of valuable service to the Piedmont community. We have known Conna for over 15 years and have admired her leadership on key Piedmont committees, commissions, and school boards. She tirelessly led critical initiatives on the Parent boards of both Piedmont Middle and Piedmont High School. Also, she was influential on the Parcel Tax Committees, advocating for our children and residents. In addition to championing for schools, she has worked hard as the Vice Chair of the Recreation Commission and Chair of the CIP Committee making recommendations on capital expenditures on City facilities. We have witnessed Conna being whip-smart and dedicated but also collaborative and compassionate. Conna and her thoughtful leadership will have a strong, positive impact on our town. We hope you’ll join us in voting for her on November 3 for City Council. –Debbie and Dan Lee Making the case for re-election of Cavenaugh Editor: We’re longtime friends and neighbors of Jen Cavenaugh, and we’re writing to urge Piedmonters to re-elect her to the city council. As a councilwoman, she’s been responsive to constituents, a careful steward of city resources, and an effective liaison between the council and the school board. Another term will let her continue her efforts to improve our parks and infrastructure and to promote public safety and disaster preparation. By the time she won her seat four years ago, she’d already put together an impressive volunteer resume. She served on the Piedmont Budget Advisory Committee, the Piedmont Language School, and the parent boards of Beach, PMS, and PHS. She hit the floor running at City Hall and hasn’t slowed down. Jen’s sharp, accessible, and pragmatic, and Piedmonters will benefit from another four years of her leadership. So, join us on November 3 in voting for Jen Cavenaugh for Piedmont City Council. –Matthew Goldstein and Laura Ruberto READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: Change could save the city $180,000 The Piedmont Recreation Department is transitioning to a new registration software, Community Pass, which could effectively save the city $180,000 in transaction fees. Maria Carson Breber, a Piedmont resident and the project manager for implementation of the new registration software, provided an update on the rollout process at the September 16 Recreation Commission meeting. “We are quickly approaching our go-live dates. We will have a phased roll-out, that will start mid-October and go through early November,” said Breber. The Recreation Department has primarily used Active Net, the current registration software, for about 14 years. Breber described it as a very expensive system. “It is about six percent per transaction that we pay to Active Net. Since Active Net was one of the first movers in the market, they were able to exploit their install base and were able to maintain high fees. In the meantime, other [companies] have rolled in are charging much less,” she explained. In 2018 and 2019 the city spent approximately $200,000 on Active Net. The new system, Community Pass, will cost around $20,000. “The industry has moved to a lower-fee model, but we will also begin to introduce a three percent convenience charge for our community members, so we can now pass through the credit card convenience fees,” Breber said. The department also took notice after Schoolmates transitioned from Active Net to a different system two years ago, which effectively saved costs in transaction rates. The Recreation Department examined other aspects beyond cost. The second priority of the transition was to improve the efficiency of user experience for both residents and staff. This means the ability to do more activities online, such as making reservations for tennis courts. “Beginning in mid-October, we are having the exact same rules and regulations. Now our users can go online 24/7, book their courts, and proceed accordingly,” Breber explained. The system will be able to integrate and extract financial data for the system in a simple fashion; previously, staff would have to manually extract this data. Online tennis reservations will “go live” with the new registration software on October 19. articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont Planning Department will soon begin updating its housing and zoning policies, known as the “Housing Element,” as part of a periodic process required by state law. Given the close connection between housing and racial segregation, this process is an opportunity to put substance behind the City Council’s recently passed Resolution Unequivocally Rejecting Racism. Piedmont’s population is 92% White and Asian, in stark contrast to the rich diversity of the surrounding region. Piedmont’s homogeneity was caused by historical practices like redlining, racial steering, deed restrictions, and explicit racial discrimination. The story of Sidney Dearing, Piedmont’s first African American homeowner, is illustrative: Dearing purchased a home in Piedmont in 1924. Bombs were found at his home on three occasions. At one point 500 neighbors gathered and protested on his lawn. Piedmont’s police chief at the time – a KKK klansman – refused to protect the family. Eventually Dearing was forced to sell his home to the City. (For more details see www.sidneydearing.com.) Such egregious practices were outlawed by the 1968 Fair Housing Act. Yet racial segregation persists. Today, one of the primary means of preserving racial homogeneity is exclusionary zoning – laws that mandate that a city’s housing consist mainly of single-family houses. Like many other predominantly white suburbs, Piedmont historically has fought to preserve its single-family zoning (which comprise 98% of the city’s housing) and to keep out dwelling types that would draw more diverse residents. In contrast, the city of Minneapolis abolished single-family zoning in 2019 and now allows up to three units on most lots. The state of Oregon recently passed a law permitting duplexes throughout the state. Piedmont should follow these examples and embrace varied and affordable forms of housing – including duplexes, triplexes, and multi-family dwellings – that will open our community to more diverse residents, while maintaining the small-town qualities that many appreciate. As a city, we have too long been governed by an ethos of preserving the status quo and allowed discussions of “neighborhood character,” “property values,” and “parking” to function as code words for upholding exclusion. As our nation grapples with the legacy of racism, we must back up our words with actions to create a more integrated and just community. We invite community members interested in the link between housing policy and racial equity to join us for a Zoom panel discussion on September 24, organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign with PADC and the League of Women Voters. To register go to padc.info. articles.text: Anne-Marie Lamarche’s homegrown edibles. This year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park this Sunday, September 27, will take place but as a virtual celebration due to restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival featured a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encouraged Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents emailed photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. The deadline for photo submissions was Friday, September 18. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest was sponsored by the Piedmont Tamisha Apodaca’s honey. Susan Hill’s biggest tomato weighs over 1 pound. Garden Club, and kids ages 14 and younger were able to download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. [This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. “We look forward to getting back to the normal harvest festival next year. It’s quite a tradition in Piedmont,” Recreation Commission Chair Steve Roland said. To view more submissions, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/cms/ one.aspx?portalId=13659823&pa geId=17046963.

articles.text: In the middle of the night on Friday morning, September 18, Piedmont police interrupted an attempted auto theft on St. James Drive. Responding to a call from a resident shortly before 4 a.m., officers quickly arrived. The suspect’s vehicle left at a high rate of speed, failed to pull over and caused a single vehicle collision near Highland Ave and Piedmont Ct. The police immediately detained Luis Villegas, 36, and Jaime Ambrez, 41, both of Oakland, who were driving a car already stolen. The Piedmont car they were attempting to steal had the door lock and ignition punched out. A third suspect fled the scene and was not located. Villegas and Ambrez were later cited and released for possession of a stolen vehicle, and burglary tools, along with several vehicle code violations. The suspects were released due to COVID-19 restrictions limiting jail capacity.

articles.text: An eerie orange haze blanketed Piedmont and the rest of the San Francisco Bay Area on Wednesday, September 9 as an unprecedented outbreak of wildfires continued to burn through California. The smoky conditions caused motorists to use their headlights as early as 8 a.m. and covered buildings, cars and yards in ash. Residents noted that the sun was essentially invisible the entire day. While the striking orange color of the sky disappeared, unhealthy air conditions continued over the next week and are projected to remain in the near term. Some 3.2 million acres have burned in the state so far over the past few weeks, according to CalFire. The orange sky in Piedmont was caused by “smoke from the various fires along the west coast” according to Fire Chief Bret Black. Experts point to the Bear and Creek fires burning to the east of the region as being some of the biggest contributors to the orange-colored sky last week. Wildfire smoke moved into the upper atmosphere and blocked out colors caused by shorter
articles.title: Bizarre orange haze disappears, but unhealthy air conditions continue

articles.text: Smoke from raging wildfires across the West Coast continues to cause unhealthy air quality in Piedmont, according to updates from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) on Monday, September 14. The Air District announced that it was again extending its “Spare the Air” alert for the entire San Francisco Bay Area until today, Wednesday, September 16. It is possible the alert could be extended again as well. The extension marks an unprecedented 30 consecutive Spare the Air days, over double the previous record of 14 days of Spare the Air alerts set in 2018. Some 3.2 million acres have burned during this devastating wildfire season so far, Cal Fire said yesterday, Tuesday, September 15. Blazes have also ravaged Oregon and Washington. Smoke from all of these fires have caused terrible air quality in the Bay Area. The severe situation was strikingly evident last Wednesday, September 9, when the skies turned a dark orange color. Although the color dissipated by the following day, the unhealthy air conditions continued. When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those who are sensitive to air conditions. articles.text: Editor: I am writing to strongly encourage the Piedmont community to vote Yes on Measure UU to provide a much-needed pool to Piedmont. The Piedmont Pool has meant so much to me during the last three years in high school and has helped shape who I am today. When I entered PHS, I was encouraged to try water polo my freshman year. I had never been on a swim team or done much swimming, but thought, why not? That decision changed the trajectory of my whole high school experience. I met the most amazing girls that first year on the water polo team, many older than me who were mentors both in and out of the water. I have cherished my years of water polo and feel the practices, games and team bonding have been some of my best high school memories by far. Being a part of the pool community through water polo opened my eyes to another great skill and opportunity – lifeguarding and teaching swim lessons. The pool provided the training and certifications for me to have a flexible work experience that was also very fulfilling. I can’t imagine a more convenient job for a PHS student. I could walk to work after school and schedule my hours around my other activities. Not only did I earn
articles.title: How the pool transformed my life

articles.text: One of the biggest understatements in the Bible might well be the statement of Jesus in the Gospel of John when He said: “In the world you will have tribulation.” It’s pretty hard to argue the truth of that statement. A quick look at local, national, and world events, not to mention taking stock of our own personal challenges, reminds us that in the world we have tribulation – and plenty of it. But Jesus put His statement about tribulation in the world into the context of the promises of His grace. He prefaced His statement by saying: “I have said these things to you, that in Me you may have peace.” Jesus was saying: “I know that tribulation is rampant. And I know it causes anxiety, discouragement, frustration, and stress of all kinds. But I am giving you My promises so that You may have My peace!” Jesus said: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart!” Literally that means to For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
articles.title: In the world you will have tribulation

articles.text: Theft, vehicle theft, auto & residential burglary significantly up Larceny (theft), vehicle theft and residential burglary incidents increased in 2020 through the second quarter of the year, as compared to the same time period, April-June, in 2019. In a report to Piedmont City Council, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said that total crimes reported jumped from 104 in 2019 to 168 in 2020, which demonstrates a 62 percent increase. Reported burglaries doubled from 17 in 2019 to 34 in 2020. Reports of vehicle thefts also doubled from 11 to 24, and larceny incidents jumped from 67 to 103. Bowers noted that vehicle theft has significantly increased in Oakland this year as well, and a spillover into Piedmont is not surprising. Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) incidents decreased this year, from 165 in 2019 to 121. Reader cameras in Piedmont resulted in the recovery of 15 stolen vehicles and nine arrests. Earlier this year, city council approved expansion of ALPR readers throughout the city; camera readers will be placed at Trestle Glen Road and Park Boulevard, Trestle Glen and Valant Place, Indian Avenue and La Salle, Harvard Avenue and Ranleigh Way, and Blair Avenue and Calvert Court. Vandalism cases were concentrated in the center of town, where most of the schools are located. “Unfortunately the school [district] has had a fair amount of folks going onto school property and damaging property. We are aware of that and are working with the schools to mitigate that the best way we can,” Bowers said. Bowers also noted that there appears to be increased vandalism in parks throughout the city. “One thing we’ve seen is that it appears someone is intentionally vandalizing our parks, by pouring a vinegar solution and killing [grass] in those areas,” he said. Mayor Bob McBain asked Bowers if he had any theories as to why crime, especially theft, has increased this year. “Short of a violent felony, criminals know they can walk away [with little punishment]. It is a factor,” Bowers said. “We need to have a long-term perspective on this, and not jump to too many conclusions [at this point] in the year.”
articles.title: City sees increase in crime in 2020

articles.text: Q: A resident just moved into a mid-20th century home. Two of the bathrooms haven’t been touched since 1953 and the estimated cost to bring them up-to-date is about $37,000. What affordable improvements could be included in a bathroom remodel to meet the proposed requirement? Since the project is more than $25,000, it will need to include at least one energy efficiency improvement. If the home is newly purchased, the home energy score, or home energy audit from the point of sale should be available. To comply with the reach code, the project can include one of the recommendations from those reports. Alternatively, the inclusion of new water efficient plumbing fixtures and the insulation of accessible hot water piping would fulfill the reach code requirements. Q: A resident has already made many low cost energy efficient improvements to their home, including attic insulation, duct sealing, LED lights, and low flow plumbing fixtures. The resident is planning a $78,000 home improvement, not related to the furnace or water heater. Would the resident be required to replace their fairly new gas-burning furnace or water heater? “No, the resident would not be required to replace the new gas-burning furnace or water heater,” stated Szasz. “In this case the resident has already completed all of the ‘low hanging fruit’ efficiency improvements, leaving just heat pumps on the improvement list. However, heat pump installation is beyond the resident’s scope of work.” So in this case, the building official would grant a modification allowing the resident not to install heat pumps. articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present a virtual screening of Suppressed 2020: The Fight to Vote, tomorrow, Thursday, September 17 at 4:30 p.m. The film will be followed by a talk with voting rights advocate Valerie Morishige. Director Robert Greenwald’s urgent and timely film focuses on the Stacy Abrams gubernatorial campaign in Georgia, revealing the rampant voter suppression that affected the outcome of that 2018 midterm election. The film exposes the threat those techniques pose to elections throughout the U.S. in November this year. The 40-minute documentary illustrates the problems of long voting lines and uncounted absentee ballots, and how Brian Kemp, who was both a candidate for governor and the Secretary of State in charge of the Georgia election, put more than 53,000 voter registrations on hold until after the election. Eighty percent of those registrations were filed by Black residents. Not surprisingly, Kemp won the election and is now Governor of Georgia. Voter suppression efforts and failures in the voting process are not limited to Georgia or other “red” states. “We might have all of the fancy policies and politicians saying all the right things about voting in California, but in practice we fail,” said Morishige. “We need to make voting accessible for all,” she said. According to a blockbuster report by the American Civil Liberties Union and just published on September 2, the state of Georgia has been quietly — and illegally — purging hundreds of thousands of valid registered voters from the state rolls for the better half of a decade. Of the more than 300,000 names that were purged from the rolls, the study discovered that “198,351 Georgia voters who supposedly moved from their registration addresses who, in fact, have not moved at all, and therefore were wrongly purged, a 63.3% error rate.” This is a conservative estimate, however, because the report “left out of this list those voters whose addresses we were unable to confirm,” the ACLU explains. Poll workers, who are overwhelmingly seniors and highly vulnerable to the coronavirus, are underpaid and undertrained on the electronic equipment used in some precincts. Director Robert Greenwald’s urgent and timely film focuses on the Stacy Abrams gubernatorial campaign in Georgia, revealing the rampant voter suppression that affected the outcome of that 2018 midterm election. The film exposes the threat those techniques pose to elections throughout the U.S. in November this year. The 40-minute documentary illustrates the problems of long voting lines and uncounted absentee ballots, and how Brian Kemp, who was both a candidate for governor and the Secretary of State in charge of the Georgia election, put more than 53,000 voter registrations on hold until after the election. Eighty percent of those registrations were filed by Black residents. Not surprisingly, Kemp won the election and is now Governor of Georgia. Voter suppression efforts and failures in the voting process are not limited to Georgia or other “red” states. “We might have all of the fancy policies and politicians saying all the right things about voting in California, but in practice we fail,” said Morishige. “We need to make voting accessible for all,” she said. According to a blockbuster report by the American Civil Liberties Union and just published on September 2, the state of Georgia has been quietly — and illegally — purging hundreds of thousands of valid registered voters from the state rolls for the better half of a decade. Of the more than 300,000 names that were purged from the rolls, the study discovered that “198,351 Georgia voters who supposedly moved from their registration addresses who, in fact, have not moved at all, and therefore were wrongly purged, a 63.3% error rate.” This is a conservative estimate, however, because the report “left out of this list those voters whose addresses we were unable to confirm,” the ACLU explains. Poll workers, who are overwhelmingly seniors and highly vulnerable to the coronavirus, are underpaid and undertrained on the electronic equipment used in some precincts. articles.text: The California State Department of Public Health announced the process for granting TK-5 grade school waivers to eventually allow some in-person learning, even while Alameda County is in the “purple” tier for COVID- 19 restrictions. Speaking at the Piedmont School Board meeting on September 9, Supt. Randy Booker stated that he had submitted an initial survey to begin the process of requesting a waiver for Piedmont’s students in grades TK to 5th for in-person learning. The Intent to Apply form, which gives basic information about the school district’s population, was submitted prior to the September 11 deadline. The actual application to Alameda County’s Public Health Department was originally due on September 17, but that date has been pushed back to October 2. The date adjustment is due in part to a delay in the distribution of the applications to school districts. At press time Piedmont still has not received its application form, and as of September 9, no school district in Alameda County had received the application. The most difficult aspect of the waiver application process Alameda County is still in the purple (most restrictive) tier for COVID- 19 restrictions. PUSD will be required to file a waiver to get elementary school students back to in-person learning. will be to prove that Piedmont School District has a contract with an outside vendor to provide testing to all elementary teachers and staff. Teachers and staff are required to receive testing prior to returning to school, then once every two months. This means a contract needs to be in place for roughly 200 tests. Booker has had a preliminary discussion with Kaiser Permanente. The application will require districts to outline plans for cleaning, disinfecting, ventilating, face coverings, health screenings and hygiene practices. Much of these plans are already outlined in Piedmont School District’s Memorandum of Understanding with staff and teachers. Even after applications are submitted, the Alameda County Public Health Department has advised that waiver requests will not be approved or denied for at least five weeks. The earliest Piedmont’s elementary schools could reopen through the waiver process would be in November. articles.text: Piedmont High School student Hamza Mahmood displays two freshly baked loaves of sourdough bread. Just a few months ago, I was in my biology class learning about fermentation and the role it plays in making sourdough. We had to turn in a loaf of bread at the end of the project. Mine was passable for the class, but as a loaf it was as hard as a rock and flat as a frisbee. Making sourdough is really a lot harder than it seems, I discovered. If someone had told me then that soon the entire world would grind to a halt, I would have called them crazy. But lo and behold, the impossible came to pass. We were all locked in our houses like pets in their kennels, only allowed to leave for necessities of life. The pandemic has been hard on everyone, but for some, it has been much worse. As businesses everywhere shut down, hardearned jobs halted. All of a sudden many people were left with no income. As a family who is more fortunate, we felt that it was our duty to help those in need. Through my grandparents’ nonprofit organization, we bought masses of food and ran several food pantries and delivered groceries to people in need. I didn’t help all that much during these food pantries; I had to stay in the car because of COVID. But I was inspired and wanted to do more. But what and how? First, I needed to pick a charity for my donations, and I wanted to pick an organization that spoke to me. I decided on the American Red Cross because I liked how it is an impartial organization providing help to people regardless of their skin color, religious beliefs, race, class or political opinions. I also like how they provide care where it’s needed most, regardless of the danger they have to face. In addition, I felt more of a connection with the Red Cross and the work that they do because it is my ambition to become a physician. But I needed to figure out how to raise money for the Red Cross. I sat and brainstormed. What was a simple way to raise money? An idea came to me. Something that we were all taught in elementary school. A bake sale. But what would I sell? My sourdough of course. If I could get good at baking sourdough and have a fundraiser for charity, I had the potential to raise a lot of money. So, the idea was set, but the bread wasn’t. I needed practice. I baked loaf after loaf, each better than the last. Slowly but surely, I was improving, and finally, I was ready to give my bread away. We started with the neighbor, and as our bread production increased, so did our demand. All sorts of people asked for loaves as we got better at baking them. As we gave bread to people, the donations started to rack up. $100, $200, $1000, all the way to $2000. We had more than doubled our goal of $1000. With all of these donations, I felt good about the community service. It was a wonderful feeling to give someone a loaf and see their eyes light up as they thank you for something you put so much time, energy and love into. Every time we gave away a loaf of bread, I felt like I was contributing to something bigger than myself. I felt like I was giving somebody a gift that they really enjoyed and were thankful for. Winston Churchill once said, “We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.” He was absolutely right. Hamza Mahmood is a sophomore at Piedmont High School.
articles.title: Hamza Mahmood – a student donating loaves to charity

articles.text: The Associated Student Body at Piedmont High extended its annual Club Day from one day to two days last week, and though everything was virtual using Google Meet, the result was a bonanza for the school. A total of 39 student organizations and clubs signed up at lunchtime on Thursday and Friday, most likely a record high. With school entrenched in distance learning, the clubs at PHS look to fill a large void in extracurricular activities and involvement between students. Connections between students outside of class have suffered, so the role of Club Day took on added meaning this year. “Club Day was more exciting this year, because it really allowed people to find something to do besides school. I have seen a lot of new clubs that people are really passionate about,” explained ASB president Grace Davies. This initial involvement with clubs is particularly impressive especially because not all existing clubs have started up, as they are not required to participate in Club Day. For example, the popular Kiva Club, which fundraises to give micro loans to people, has not begun yet. A new club, Teens4Biden, started by ASB senior class president Audrey Edel, had the highest enrollment on Club Day. At their first meeting last week, club members signed up to volunteer in various capacities. “There were more activism clubs, and some new, really creative clubs this year,” noted Edel. “There was a larger variety overall, which shows that some of our peers are dedicated and trying to uplift each other and make a difference in the school community.” Not every club had a big turnout, but of the students that did attend, there seemed to participate and engage more than in previous years. “I think it forced people to more of a commitment. You have to listen (on Zoom) to what the club presidents are saying; you can’t just put your name down and leave,” Edel said. Clubs can be created, and students can join clubs at any time throughout the year. There’s a club for everyone at PHS, including the Diversity Club, Piedmont for Consent, the Astronomy Club, the High Adventure Club and the Asian Student Union. experience College Prep first-hand.
articles.title: Though virtual, Club Day at PHS signs up a record 39 student organizations

articles.text: How does it translate online? Often, the classroom culture is what makes kids want to go to school and enjoy being there. Key words associated with a strong classroom culture include safe, pleasant, interesting, social, and community. Fostering a classroom culture that embodies these elements can be challenging in a virtual format. Humor plays a key role in creating a strong, positive learning environment. Nuanced communication skills, such as humor, are easily lost in socially distant learning spaces. One of the most common forms of humor naturally occurring in an in-person educational environment is the spontaneous, harmless violation of expectations. That is, something is funny if it contradicts one’s sense of how things are supposed to be. The shared experience of this surprising (and benign) contradiction creates community and increases morale (recall the power of “private jokes”). Shared humor increases feelings of social support, and is relationship building. Humor can also enhance the actual learning process. Shared laughter is a powerful way to reinforce learning. Humor can both capture and maintain students’ attention. For example, in an initial assessment I may include some humor with the immediate purpose of establishing rapport. More often than not, months or even years later, that child will remind me of the humor we shared in that first office visit. Lastly, and perhaps most important at this time, shared humor dampens conflict and enhances feelings of safety. Humor can be an effective coping mechanism to lessen or buffer psychological distress. Surely this is something we want to generalize to online learning. Elements that make humor effective include pacing, timing, economy of expression, vivid language, and the ability to read and respond to the energy of the group. Without the richness of verbal and non-verbal communication of in-person situations, the opportunities for shared humor decreases, and the margin for miscommunication and misunderstanding increases virtually. For example, consider the role that timing plays with humor. Digital platforms can make it difficult to know when to talk, why there may be a pause, and can be generally disruptive to the natural back and forth between students and teachers. Periods of silence create a natural conversational rhythm in real life discussions. However, when on a video call those pauses become unnatural and stressful. With regard to being able to read and respond to the energy of the group, virtual platforms make this increasingly challenging as well. It can be tricky to read key elements of discourse and humor such as body language, eye contact and facial expressions given a digital platform. By maintaining constant visual gaze at the screen, rather than shifting our gaze back and forth between people and actions as would be typical in person, we focus on too few visual cues instead of the full range of body language that we would normally be gathering. essary to demonstrate artificial eye contact on video), teachers and students both may miss other important visual cues. Since the spontaneous opportunities for humor, amusement and delight will likely be diminished with distance learning, parents and teachers can rely on more intentional and deliberate opportunities. For example, we can ask students to build humor into occasional writing assignments. We can add a humorous item to a test, or assignment. Humorous quotes or cartoons can be circulated, and maybe Fridays can be “Joke day.” Language-based humor, based more heavily on multiple meanings, allusion, puns and plays on words, can help to mitigate the loss of spontaneous, situational humor of the in-person classroom. Katie Pengilly, MA,CCC,SLP, is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.
articles.title: Humor as part of classroom culture

pages.text: Wednesday, September 16, 2020 7 S P E E C H , I N C . Humor as part of classroom culture How does it translate online? By Katie Pengilly Often, the classroom culture is what makes kids want to go to school and enjoy being there. Key words associated with a strong classroom culture include safe, pleasant, interesting, social, and community. Fostering a classroom culture that embodies these elements can be challenging in a virtual format. Humor plays a key role in creating a strong, positive learning environment. Nuanced communication skills, such as humor, are easily lost in socially distant learning spaces. One of the most common forms of humor naturally occurring in an in-person educational environment is the spontaneous, harmless violation of expectations. That is, something is funny if it contradicts one’s sense of how things are supposed to be. The shared experience of this surprising (and benign) contradiction creates community and increases morale (recall the power of “private jokes”). Shared humor increases feelings of social support, and is relationship building. Humor can also enhance the actual learning process. Shared laughter is a powerful way to reinforce learning. Humor can both capture and maintain students’ attention. For example, in an initial assessment I may include some humor with the immediate purpose of establishing rapport. More often than not, months or even years later, that child will remind me of the humor we shared in that first office visit. Lastly, and perhaps most important at this time, shared humor dampens conflict and enhances feelings of safety. Humor can be an effective coping mechanism to lessen or buffer psychological distress. Surely this is something we want to generalize to online learning. Elements that make humor effective include pacing, timing, economy of expression, vivid language, and the ability to read and respond to the energy of the group. Without the richness of verbal and non-verbal communication of in-person situations, the opportunities for shared humor decreases, and the margin for miscommunication and misunderstanding increases virtually. For example, consider the role that timing plays with humor. Digital platforms can make it difficult to know when to talk, why there may be a pause, and can be generally disruptive to the natural back and forth between students and teachers. Periods of silence create a natural conversational rhythm in real life discussions. However, when on a video call those pauses become unnatural and stressful. With regard to being able to read and respond to the energy of the group, virtual platforms make this increasingly challenging as well. It can be tricky to read key elements of discourse and humor such as body language, eye contact and facial expressions given a digital platform. By maintaining constant visual gaze at the screen, rather than shifting our gaze back and forth between people and actions as would be typical in person, we focus on too few visual cues instead of the full range of body language that we would normally be gathering. By staring at the webcam (necessary to demonstrate artificial eye contact on video), teachers and students both may miss other important visual cues. Since the spontaneous opportunities for humor, amusement and delight will likely be diminished with distance learning, parents and teachers can rely on more intentional and deliberate opportunities. For example, we can ask students to build humor into occasional writing assignments. We can add a humorous item to a test, or assignment. Humorous quotes or cartoons can be circulated, and maybe Fridays can be “Joke day.” Language-based humor, based more heavily on multiple meanings, allusion, puns and plays on words, can help to mitigate the loss of spontaneous, situational humor of the in-person classroom. Katie Pengilly, MA,CCC,SLP, is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. There’s a gravel pit, a crow’s nest, a fishing boat and a shipwreck for kids to play on. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew, a coed Venturing unit under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, holds an annual garage sale. Money raised is used to fund major projects, including building a Tiny House to provide housing for a homeless teen in Oakland, feeding the elderly, and renovating the home of an elderly low- income Oakland resident. Due to COVID-19 and the limitations imposed by Alameda County’s Shelter-in-Place order, the annual fundraiser will be ONLINE this year. To make this a success, we need the support of everyone in the community. We will be soliciting items from residents and selling the donated items online. If you have items you would like to donate, please email us at pcscgaragesale@gmail.com and include a description of the item with a photo. If you are interested in purchasing an item, please visit the “Garage Sale 2020” section https://www.pcservicecrew.org/garagesale on the crew website (pcservicecrew.org). Additional items will be added weekly so please check back with us.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: hear their perspectives and support their efforts including PUSD School Board, Piedmont Connect, League of Women Voters, Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, Parent Clubs, Piedmont Community Service Crew, Appreciating Diversity Film Series, Piedmont Parent Network, Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, and others. 2 – Measure UU is a very important ballot measure for Piedmonters. It’s about whether we want to continue to have a local pool facility for Piedmonters to learn to swim, for exercise, relaxation, injury rehabilitation, youth employment, school PE programs including adaptive PE, and HS sports teams. Or Not. It’s that simple. I’m volunteering with the campaign to reach voters so they know our 56-year-old pool is broken and is due to be permanently closed. The City has run out of cost-effective repairs, and it makes no fiscal sense to spend even more money on a failing pool that no longer meets the needs of our residents. Measure UU provides an opportunity for us to come together as a community and design a safe, affordable, and sustainable pool facility for our children and grandchildren to enjoy for the next 50 years. I am optimistic that voters understand what is at stake, and will vote Yes on Measure UU to rebuild the pool. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – I will have several ways residents can reach me: • Phone calls: I will have set office hours and be available for phone calls. Residents can also leave voicemails without requiring a call back. • Email: Residents can email me at their convenience and I will answer within 24 hours. • Zoom Chats: My website will continue to offer individual or group chat sessions with easy online scheduling. • Town Hall Forum: A Zoom event where I give my Council report and City issues can be discussed in a public forum. These events can happen as issues arise or on a scheduled basis. • Monthly Newsletter: After the Town Hall, I will post the event highlights to my website and email a newsletter to subscribers. There will be links in both to contact me. Post-Covid, I would love to meet in person with any Piedmont group or resident during my office hours. 2 – I am cautiously optimistic. The Community Pool For Piedmont group is doing a great job communicating with residents. They have a good website, informative flyer and a hard-working phone banking team. Everyone I’ve talked with is supporting the measure. Those who were undecided have changed to a “yes” vote after we talked it through. This is a difficult time to ask residents to pay more property tax. I understand and am sensitive to that. Non-users of the pool are initially reluctant to support the measure. However, after discussing, most agree the return on investing about 75 cents/day (median Piedmont home) for a new pool is a good one. We don’t want to be the only school district in Alameda County without access to a pool. Our schools are why people move here and why our property values stay high. I remain hopeful that we will vote “yes” on Measure UU. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – An upside to sheltering-in-place is that almost everyone is now expert in scheduling and participating in zoom conversations. Throughout my campaign, I have engaged residents via zoom. I became adept using Facetime and What’s App when one son was in Peace Corps in Ukraine and another son served with the US Navy in Yokosuka, Japan. I am easily contacted through my personal email and cell phone. If modern technology proves problematic, I have a home office and live near the center of town. Constituents are welcome to visit me post-pandemic. I do not foresee any barriers to making myself available to residents. I welcome and want to hear all thoughts, concerns, ideas and questions. 2 – Although passing Measure UU presents unique challenges, I remain very optimistic. While City Council candidates must achieve a plurality, passage of Measure UU requires a supermajority of almost 67%. Dozens of committed volunteers are spending their weekends walking door-to-door addressing voters’ concerns and convincing two-thirds of those voters that Piedmont’s 56 y/o pool has unfixable problems, is unsafe for public use and, most importantly, if Measure UU fails, the pool will permanently close. Piedmonters want a community pool. A survey taken months before Measure UU was placed on the ballot revealed 61% of Piedmonters consider our pool a valued community asset. As more voters understand that our pool must be replaced or permanently closed, we will reach two-thirds approval. ‘Yes on Measure UU’ signs are on display throughout Piedmont evidencing widespread community support. Review the facts at www. communitypoolforpiedmont.com We can’t let Piedmont become the only public school district in Alameda County without access to a local pool. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: original building in that it will be accessible and will include offices, expanded lobby space and classrooms for drama and set design. An initial effort to build a new theater fell through, but a subsequent measure that included building a new science and technology facility was approved. The new Alan Harvey Theater was originally scheduled to open at the start of the 2021 school year; however, pandemic related construction delays may mean a later completion date. HILARY COOPER 1 – I am deeply committed to serving our students and am happy to make myself available to Piedmont residents for questions or comments. I believe that listening is a critical component of serving on the school board. As Parent Club President at PMS & PHS, I worked with teachers, parents and administrators and made myself available to all of them. I also hosted many parent and administrator coffees, and I have always valued opportunities for our community to come together. If elected, I hope to continue to be a resource for all of our community members. I will have a designated email, and if some prefer to speak to me directly, I am happy to chat in person or over the phone. I look forward to working with our community and I will always be just a phone call or email away. 2 – Our school district is in the midst of two new building construction projects, a new STEAM building and the new Alan Harvey Theater, both at PHS. Both projects are funded by the $66M improvement bond (Measure H1). Over the past few years, I have had the opportunity to substitute teach at PHS and I have seen the need firsthand for infrastructure improvements. I was thrilled when Measure H1 passed and I am excited to see the new STEAM building, and in a year or so, the new Alan Harvey Theater. Alan Harvey Theater was one of our district’s most heavily used venues -- from speaker series to assemblies to musicals, it was packed multiple times a week. Once completed, I believe the new Alan Harvey Theater will be a source of great pride for our community. JASON KELLEY 1 – In addition to being available by email and phone, I would make a point of reaching out to school and community groups, to attend group meetings, and to solicit feedback and input from residents. As a parent who is in almost daily contact with teachers and other parents at all three school levels, I am already aware of many of the day-to-day concerns about our school district. It’s important for Piedmont residents to be able to easily communicate with their elected representatives and to know that their concerns are being heard and addressed. Being accountable to the voters is especially key in a small community such as ours. 2 – Alan Harvey was one of my teachers in high school and I performed in school musicals under his direction at the old theater, so I’m very excited about the new building. Arts education is so important to help students learn confidence and creative thinking. I’m proud that Piedmont has a strong tradition of supporting arts education and want to ensure that continues and grows. As a producer for four years of the biggest performing arts event in Piedmont, Beach Revue, I got to see first-hand how children learn from performing on stage. They become more comfortable speaking in front of groups and more confident in their own abilities. The new Alan Harvey Theater will allow more Piedmont students to gain those skills before heading to college or work, and it will be a great training facility for students who want to pursue careers in the performing arts. HARI TITAN 1 – I would make sure my email and cell number are published in the student directory and available to the local press and school district. The most convenient form of communication these days is email, however, emails sent to influence public officials are part of the public decision-making record and subject to disclosure. For confidential matters, it is better to make an appointment and discuss those matters over the phone. For school district policy matters, I would like to start moderated online wiki pages that would allow residents to quickly get up to speed on anything the board or district is working on and also make it easier to contribute to the decision-making process at a time that is convenient to each resident. This Web 2.0 facility should also reduce the volume of multiple emails to the board with the exact same advice. 2 – I have many articles on my harititan.com/search/node/aht website presenting financial arguments for a new Alan Harvey Theater. In 2014 the school board presented a plan to renovate and add classroom space to the old Alan Harvey theater. Through articles in the Piedmont Post, I discovered that our renovation cost estimate was comparable to what other school districts were paying for a brand new theater. The benefits of designing a brand new theater included 2-stories with more stadium-style seating, much better acoustics, handicap access, net-zero energy, and earthquake safety. I also analyzed our 2014 cost estimate for a brand new theater and discovered it was nearly double what other districts paid. Since labor and material costs were independent of Piedmont as a job site, I promoted getting competitive guaranteed maximum price bids for a new theater. In 2016, the district obtained much lower bids and added a new Alan Harvey Theater to Measure H1. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – Over the past four years as a School Board member, I’ve tried to make myself very accessible to all constituents. As Board correspondent for two years, I responded to all emails received on behalf of the Board. I also responded to all emails that I personally received. Pre-pandemic, I met with people in person. I’ve also reached out to people that have spoken at our Board meetings to get clarification on their views. I’ve talked to people on the phone and I’ve gone on walks with people. I am very happy when people provide input to the Board. I really try to listen to all viewpoints because I think that is the best way that decisions get made. 2 – I am very familiar with the new Alan Harvey Theater. For the last two years, I’ve served as Board liaison to the Facilities Steering Committee. This committee reviews all aspects of the current construction program and makes recommendations to the Board. Construction began in earnest on the new Performing Arts Center with the Alan Harvey Theater this spring once the schools had closed to students. It will be completed in the Fall of 2021 and includes a 487-seat auditorium, (459 fixed, 28 movable seats; the original AHT had 442 seats), a green room with dressing rooms, a separate drama classroom to minimize wear and tear on the main stage, a drama department office and a conference room. If you would like to see some renderings of the new theater, please go to: https://measureh1.org/background/updates/09-2018-update. html#new-harvey-theater-update. Once the new Performing Arts Center is completed, it will be an amazing school and community resource. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of the Argus Leader Piedmont High 2016 graduate Gabe Watson has transferred to the University of Texas after leading Division 2 football in rushing with Sioux Falls in 2018. Piedmont High has a running back on his way to pursuing a potensial career in the National Football League. Gabe Watson, Piedmont High 2016 graduated and the Piedmont Post’s two-time Athlete of the Year (2015-2016), has signed with the University of Texas as a graduate transfer student for the 2020 season. The Big-12 and the Longhorns got their season started last Saturday, September 12 with a 59-3 thrashing of University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP). Still adjusting to the offense, Watson did not appear. “I feel about as good as I can,” Watson told the Argus Leader. “I’m bigger, faster and stronger. My hamstring is fine and getting stronger. To be honest, the quarantine grind has been treating me well. I feel fantastic. articles.text: Linda Beach Playfield reopened to the public on Monday this week, September 14. Linda Beach Playfield was reopened this week on Monday, September 14, after about seven weeks of closure. The city closed the playfield on July 24 due to lack of compliance by users with the Alameda County Public Health Department’s shelter-in-place orders. Despite repeated warnings from city staff, visitors continued to play group sports, and social distancing was not observed. The field was the first public open space to be closed due to non-compliance of County Health guidelines during the coronavirus pandemic. The closure was followed one week later by the school district closing Witter Field, the largest sports field in the city. The city is asking residents and park visitors to wear a face covering, practice social distancing, and not share sports equipment with members outside of your immediate household. The use of shared sports equipment by groups outside of your household, or “social bubble”, is still not allowed by the county. Only the entrance on Linda Avenue near the Oakland Avenue Bridge will be opened for park access. During public use hours, a park ambassador will be at the entrance and will remind users of and enforce COVID-19 safety requirements. The playfield will be open Monday through Friday, 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. On Saturdays it will be open from 3 p.m. to dusk, and from 9 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Sunday mornings. Linda Beach Playfield will also be used by the Recreation Department and youth sports organizations by permit only. No public use is allowed outside of the slotted times above. For more information contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510-420-3070 (prd@ piedmont.ca.gov).
articles.title: Linda Beach Playfield reopens after nearly 2 months

articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country team in 2005. At this time last year, the cross-country teams under Jeanine Holmlund were just getting their season underway at the Lowell Invitational, where Sophia Zalewski was getting her historic senior campaign underway. The last time we looked back at the cross-country program, we mentioned the North Coast Section championship boys’ and girls’ teams of 2003. We made reference to the 2005 boys’ team as the last team to win both the NCS and State championship. Here, we take a look at the 2005 Division 4 State Champs, and the 2006 NCS runners-up. In 2005, the entire 2003 championship team returned as upperclassmen. At the State Championship at Woodward Park, Mark Ceraldi, then a junior, led the talented team with a fifth-place finish in 16:04 against 195 other runners. Senior Ricky Griffith placed seventh in 16:11. Piedmont had all five of its runners in the top-40: Jesse Baldridge, a junior, finished in 29th in 16:51, senior Dylan McCalmont placed 42nd in 17:00, and Nahoa Moya-Smith was 46th in 17:02. They defeated 2nd place Big Bear to win the State Div. 4 championship by 24 points. The previous week, Ceraldi Mark Ceraldi placed fifth out of 195 runners at State Championship meet in 2005. ran a 15:24 to win the NCS Meet of Champions in a field of 111, and Griffith was 2nd in 15:43, a remarkable 1-2 finish that put Piedmont on the map. “Piedmont’s cross-country team continued to maintain its deserved reputation for excellence,” wrote the Post’s Gray Cathrall in 2005. The squad returned in 2006 with Ceraldi and Baldridge, but marked the beginning of a drought for the boys’ program for the next decade. In 2006, Piedmont finished second at the NCS meet to St. Mary’s, 69 to 94 points. Ceraldi returned to the familiar course at Hayward High, running considerably slowed at 16:07 in 4th place. Baldridge was close behind him in 16:09 to finish 6th. New varsity member Wyatt Alt placed 18th in 16:49, Alex Hauser was 28th in 17:07 and senior Zach Sieben placed 38th in 17:34. The boys’ team qualified again for the CIF State Championship, and Ceraldi closed his PHS cross-country career with a 12th place finish in 16:15. After winning North Coast Section championships in the 2002, 2003, and 2005, Piedmont was not among the top three teams for another 11 years – until 2017. In that year, Piedmont squeaked past Miramonte by four seconds to qualify for the State meet. 2006 was a banner year for Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team, led by Mark Ceraldi (left), Jesse Baldridge, and John Weber.
articles.title: A Look Back: Piedmont 2005 & 2006 boys’ cross-country teams

articles.text: Registration for the Session 3 of Piedmont Recreation Department’s Camp Smart Start and Play Pods opened this week on Monday, September 14. Camp Smart Start provides full-day distance learning support as staff assist students log into classes on time, complete asynchronous assignments, and provide tech support as necessary. When Smart Start campers are not in class they will play games, do crafts, and socialize. Smart Start helps parents who need child care throughout the school day, and who also want to help their children stay on track in school. Department are introducing a new program called Play Pods which is focused on fun, socialization and screen-free playtime. Each afternoon trained Schoolmates and Recreation Staff lead and supervise their Play Pods while leading COVID-safe games, sports, and crafts. articles.text: Photos courtesy of CyclingNews.com Slovenian Primoz Roglic holds a 40-second lead in the Tour de France general classification through Stage 16. Primoz Roglic, a 30-year old from Slovenia, continues to lead the Tour de France general classification through Stage 16 after wearing the yellow jersey as the first=place rider since Stage 9. After the Stage 16 mountain course yesterday, September 15, Roglic holds a 40- second advantage over fellow Slovenian, Tadej Pogacar. After them are a pair of Colombians in 3rd and 4th place, Rigoberto Uran (+1:34) and Miguel Angel Lopez (+1:45). Last week’s story described Stage 15 as the start of a critical stretch of four days of mountain climbing. Cycling experts call Wednesday’s Stage 17 perhaps the most important course of this year’s Tour given its two steep ascents of 168 kilometers from Grenoble to Meribel, and the grueling climb on the 174.5 km Stage 15 and 164 km in Stage 16. Today’s Stage 17 is considered the most difficult summit finish in this year’s race It rises 2,304 meters to the peak of Col de la Loze. If Pogacar or any of the field makes a move on Roglic, Stage 17 will be the place. It’s worth noting that Pogacar and Roglic finished 1-2 in Stage 15, and then 21-22 in Stage 16 without losing any distance on the others in general classification. Stage 18’s 175 km mountain course won’t be as extreme as the previous’ two steep climbs, but will be the final alpine stage at high elevation. It includes four ascents, with the likelihood of close racing all the way to the finish line. Fellow Slovenian, Tadej Pogacar, sits close in second. Colombia’s Rigoberto Uran is in 3rd back 1 minute, 34 seconds.

articles.text: With the SCU, LNU, and CZU complex fires near full containment, the surrounding parks have begun to reopen. But keeping track of what parks are closed, or what the restrictions are, is increasingly important as air conditions change. East Bay Regional Parks has closed Del Valle, Morgan Territory, Ohlone Wilderness, Round Valley, Sunol Regional, and the ever popular Mission Peak. It is unclear when Mission Peak will re-open; it was in direct contact with the SCU blaze, so public access will not be permitted until advised by local fire officials. With smoke in the air every day, East Bay Regional announced that a health advisory warning was in place, meaning it is possible for temporary closures to occur with little advance notice. “East Bay Regional Park District advises its visitors to minimize or refrain from active outdoor recreation due to the unhealthy air quality. Should air conditions worsen, park restrictions, including temporary closures, may occur and service levels may be reduced for the safety of the public and our park staff. Any restrictions will be posted by 4pm for the following day on our website and social media,” announced park officials in a statement. able future. The Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve and Austin Creek State Recreation Area announced they are completely closed until further notice. Photo courtesy of fs.usda.gov U.S. Forest Service announced it has closed its 18 federal forests in California. U.S. Forest Service closes all 18 forests Last week, the U.S. Forest System announced its has closed all 18 of its forests in California. The list includes Angeles, Cleveland, El Dorado, Humboldt-Toiyabe, Inyo, Klamath, Lake Tahoe Basin, Lassen, Los Padres, Mendocino, Plumas, San Bernardino, Sequoia, Shasta-Trinity, Sierra, Six Rivers, Stanislaus, and Tahoe National Forests. “The number of large fires and extreme fire behavior we are seeing across the State is historic,” said Regional Forester Randy Moore. “These temporary closures are necessary to protect the public and our firefighters, and we will keep them in place until conditions improve and we are confident that National Forest visitors can recreate safely. I ask all Californians and visitors to take these closures and evacuations seriously for their own safety and to allow our firefighters to focus on the mission of safely suppressing these fires.” The news came one day after the USFS shut down eight of its parks. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Niners Nation The Arizona Cardinals upset the 49ers in Week 1, but San Francisco should be set for a Week 2 comeback against a weaker team, the Jets. Are you ready for some football? The NFL returned last week with its opening week without its regular preseason festivities. To some surprise, the 49ers lost their opener to the Cardinals 24-20 while the Las Vegas Raiders pounced on the Panthers 34-30. We wrote last week that the matchup with the Cardinals should be a perfect measuring stick, and indeed it was. Arizona quarterback Kyler Murray got it done with his feet for 91 rushing yards and a touchdown. Relinquishing some yards to a high-paced attack like the Cardinals, Murray, and HC Kliff Kingsbury shouldn’t come as a big alarm – nor should 49ers QB Jimmy Garopollo’s early season jitters. However, some of the injuries do. George Kittle’s knee sprain raises some eyebrows given that te team is already without Deebo Samuel (injured reserve) and first-round wide receive Brandon Aiyuk (hamstring injury). Kittle will be limited or left out in Week 2. Watch for newly acquired players like veteran tight end Jordan Reed to get some playing time. The 49ers will face the Jets, who are already without running back Le’Veon Bell. San Francisco is favored. That new team in Vegas, the former Oakland Raiders, were favored against Carolina, so Silver and Black fans should exeercise some caution before getting too excited. They face the high-powered New Orleans Saints this weekend, and the Saints are favored to win. AllPro receiver Michael Thomas has already been ruled out for anumber of weeks, so Vegas could pull off an upset this Sunday. Without Thomas, the Raiders can shift their focus to shutting down veteran receiver Emmanuel Sanders and running back Alvin Kamara. Naomi Osaka wins U.S. Open Naomi Osaka didn’t just win the U.S. Open, she transcended her sport and presence as a top competitor on the international sports scene. On top of defeating Victoria Azarenka in three sets – 1-6, 6-3, 6-3 – she consistently used her platform at the tournament to bring awareness to social activism, police brutality, and the Black Live Matter movement by repeatedly entering the New York tournament with apparel calling attention to fallen lives. Osaka, in the most human form of a professional athlete, said with a shaky voice rattling with nerves, that her goal is to spread awareness. “For me, I just want to spread awareness. I feel like the more people know the story, then the more interesting or interested they’ll become in it. I’m aware that tennis is watched all over the world, and maybe there is someone that doesn’t know Breonna Taylor’s story. Maybe they’ll Google it. “A lot of people ask me if I feel more stressed out ever since I started speaking out more. To be honest, not really. It’s what it is.” Photo courtesy of The Ringer Naomi Osaka won this year’s U.S. Open, and did so while calling attention to police brutality in the U.S.
articles.title: Naomi Osaka wins second U.S. Open; NFL starts regular season
