articles.text: “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the company’s YouTube channel. In season two, Aurora directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams are joined by Theatre Bay Area’s Executive Director Brad Erickson. Theatre Bay Area is one of the nation’s largest performing arts service organizations, with more than 320 theatre and dance company members and 2,200 individual members. For 13 years, Erickson has led the organization’s efforts to support, promote, and advocate for the region’s vibrant theatre and dance community. Under Erickson’s leadership, Theatre Bay Area has gained a national reputation for innovative programs and services. Its nationwide study on the intrinsic impact of the theatre experience on audiences is a leading example. For six years Erickson served as president of Californians for the Arts (CFTA) and California Arts Advocates (CAA). He currently serves as Treasurer of both CFTA Theatre Bay Area Executive Director Brad Erickson is the guest on this week’s Aurora Connects and CAA and as California State Captain for Americans for the Arts. He is the past Chair of the State Arts Action Network. Also a playwright, Erickson’s plays have won several awards and have been produced in theaters from San Francisco to Indianapolis. He is a graduate of the Goodman School of Drama (now The Theatre School) at DePaul University with a degree in acting. For more information, visit https://www.auroratheatre.org/ auroraconnects.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre features Brad Erickson in weekly series

articles.text: Even with COVID health restrictions celebrated children’s choir doesn’t miss a beat Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Artistic Director Eric Tuan –Choir Director Eric Tuan On March 16 choral programs everywhere were asked to cease operations. Six months later, the jury is still out on whether or not choir programs can begin reconvening in California. Amid the uncertainty, Chorus America and the American Choral Directors Association have advised choir groups to rehearse and perform online for the foreseeable future. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, like many other choral groups, had to change both traditional instruction and performance to comply with shelter-in-place orders brought on by the current health crisis. Under the leadership of Artistic Director Eric Tuan, the organization was quick to adapt. On June 6, rather than end its season with no final concert, the Piedmont Children’s Choir showcased one of its best events – and did it entirely online. The “Spring Sing! Virtual Concert” celebrated the musical accomplishments of the choir’s 200 singers after a full year of training and development. Since then, Tuan has gone through lengthy efforts to make the choral experience as “normal” as possible in this era of the so-called “New Normal.” A Stanford graduate, Tuan began his musical journey with Piedmont Choirs as a young chorister, and years later served on faculty as Ecco conductor and composer-in-residence before beginning his tenure as artistic director in July 2019. He is only the second artistic director in the choir’s nearly four decade-long history. As a seasoned chorister, Tuan understood the limitations of virtual instruction early on. who are beginning. In the performing arts department, the choir is offering small elective classes: songwriting, musicology, musicianship, and other ways to explore creativity through an online medium. “We’re trying to offer something like a small, music conservatory. Traditionally, in a youth choir you sing together and much of the education happens through that experience of singing together and striving as a group towards this artistic goal. Now that that process has become much more difficult, we want to offer something that’s more like a conservatory,” Tuan said. Students are now getting a more well-rounded exposure to music, he confirmed. It is not without its challenges; of course. The “new normal” requires hiring more staff, which in turn can pose some financial burden on the choir. Piedmont Choirs has hired additional vocal faculty, many who are alums or have other affiliations with the choir. Tuan said this means students can have more meaningful individual instruction over Zoom. All the instructors are essentially working double-time, too. Tuan pointed out that digital instruction can require more preparation, in addition to the other classes he has taken on to teach. Still, the choir currently has 200 students enrolled, which Tuan describes as a true testament of the community’s involvement in the program and vice versa. Part 2 in the series will explore the choral programs by age-group, starting with the kinder department. “The great limitation of [video conferencing app] Zoom, of course, is that only one person can sing at a time. So choral singing as we know it is pretty much impossible at this point. I can lead a rehearsal by singing parts and teaching different parts, but we can’t put our voice together,” he said. But there is one advantage, he noted. “It’s almost like we’re teaching every student individually at home, which has certainly made them more independent, stronger musicians,” he said. The choir is spending more time in smaller groups or cohorts, so the Choir is able to offer “pull-out lessons,” or specialized music instruction, to each student. This can prove to be an incredible advantage to singers and vocalists
articles.title: Piedmont Choirs: navigating the new normal

articles.text: It Can’t Happen Here to be shown October 13 on Youtube Photo by Kevin Berne Buzz Windrip, played by David Kelly, in Berkeley Rep’s production of It Can’t Happen Here, based on the 1935 Sinclair Lewis novel. The Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s artistic director, Tony Taccone, reimagines the Sinclair Lewis novel It Can’t Happen Here, written in 1935 during the rise of fascism in Europe. Lewis’ darkly satirical novel follows the ascent of a demagogue who becomes president of the United States by promising to return the country to greatness. The novel describes the rise of Berzelius “Buzz” Windrip, a president who foments fear and promises drastic economic and social reforms while promoting traditional values. After his election, Windrip takes complete control of the government and imposes totalitarian rule with the help of a ruthless paramilitary force in the manner of European fascists such as Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. The novel’s plot centers on journalist Doremus Jessup’s opposition to the new regime and his subsequent struggle against it as part of a liberal rebellion. In 2016, Berkeley Rep unveiled a new stage adaption of Lewis’ prescient novel. One week after that production ended, the presidential election roiled the nation. Now, the theatre company reprises that production with the same director, Lisa Peterson, but has readapted it as a radio play in four episodes. This time, the radio adaption will take place before the 2020 election. “We’re delighted to welcome back much of the original cast including David Kelly as the candidate Buzz Windrip, and to have Academy Award nominee David Strahairn join us as the liberal protagonist Doremus
articles.title: Berkeley Rep presents a Sinclair Lewis masterpiece

articles.text: Rashaad Newsome’s “Shade Compositions” at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Though temporarily closed, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is providing online content as patrons continue to shelter-in-place. Throughout September, visitors can browse a rotating selection of video and performance commissions from the past decade. Featured artwork changes every Wednesday at noon. This week’s screening is Rashaad Newsome’s Shade Compositions, in which Newsome brings together an ensemble of local performers, using live video and sound mixing to synthesize their verbal and non-verbal expressions into improvised minimalist music. With hacked video game controllers in hand, the artist acts as a conductor shaping voices and gestures in real time. “Through repetition and through technology, I’m taking the Black vernacular and turning it into contemporary music,” Newsome said. Newsome’s work blends several practices, including collage sculpture, film, photography, music, computer programming, software engineering, community organizing, and performance, to create an altogether new field. Using the diasporic traditions of improvisation, he pulls from the world of advertising, the internet, Art History, Black and Queer culture to produce his works. Born in 1979 in New Orleans, he lives and works in Brooklyn and Oakland. You can view this week’s screening as well as upcoming screenings at https:// w w w. s f m o m a . o r g / t h e m e / mfh-online-screenings/.
articles.title: Rashaad Newsome’s “Shade Compositions” September 23–30

articles.text: Cal Per for ma nces has announced a series of 15 weekly full-length concerts and theater works called “Cal Performances at Home.” The series will run from October to mid-January, and will feature a wide variety of new and full-length videos or live events, all available to stream directly to your home screen. Main Stage performances will feature artists and programs that were scheduled for the fall season this year, as well as some new additions. Main Stage videos will also be accompanied by free “Beyond the Stage” artist talks, interviews, lectures, and question and answer sessions with artists and Cal Performances staff, and UC Berkeley faculty. Special premiere-evening “watch parties” will allow patrons to enjoy the company of other performing arts lovers from the safety of your own home. A new performance will debut each week, beginning Thursday, October 1, with violinist Pianist Andrew Armstrong will be featured in Cal Performances’ online series on October 1 Tessa Lark and pianist Andrew Armstrong. Throughout the fall season, the series will feature performances from New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Spain and Germany. Pricing for the “Cal Performances at Home” is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. To view suggested prices, and for more information on the series, visit https://calperformances.org/at-home/.
articles.title: Cal Performances international online series begins October 1

articles.text: Episode 2 features Berkeley Symphony & Joseph Young The Downtown Berkeley Association (DBA), along with seven prominent arts organizations in Downtown Berkeley, presented the first ever Downtown Berkeley Summer Online Arts Festival. The performances are being delivered in one-hour episodes representing each of the seven arts organization. Every Thursday at 1 p.m. a new episode will go live with a mix of live and prerecorded musicians and performers. Episode two of the festival explores Berkeley Symphony and conductor Joseph Young. The Symphony ushered in a new era with the appointment of Young as Music Director. Young began his tenure in October 2019 with an electrifying performance of Beethoven’s 5th Symphony. The performance is featured in the second episode. The episode also explores the symphony’s youth music programs and the students it serves. The Berkeley Summer Online Arts Festival will conclude on September 24. You can view the episode at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=43v9_gICGRo&feature=youtu.be. Vardanega. sion with the artists.

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony is offering one to one concerts during shelterin-place restrictions The San Francisco Symphony is adapting to COVID-19 restrictions in a unique way by offering one-to-one concerts for patrons. The experience of seeing a concert as part of a live audience is something that has been missed dearly by musicians and music-lovers alike. In a series that San Francisco Symphony is calling “1:1,” or one-to-one, there’s only one player and one or two audience members at a safe distance. Symphony donors, subscribers, volunteers, partners and teachers have made up the majority of invitees, but there is also a lottery system available on the symphony’s website, where members of the general public can apply. One day a week, the symphony will have up to six performances. The symphony may increase the frequency and find other locations around San Francisco that are safe and conducive to the intimate solo recitals. Learn more about the program at https://www.sfsymphony.org/ OnetoOne. GET UP TO

Special premiere-evening “watch parties” will allow patrons to enjoy the company of other performing arts lovers from the safety of your own home. A new performance will debut each week, beginning Thursday, October 1, with violinist Pianist Andrew Armstrong will be featured in Cal Performances’ online series on October 1 Tessa Lark and pianist Andrew Armstrong. Throughout the fall season, the series will feature performances from New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Spain and Germany. Pricing for the “Cal Performances at Home” is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. articles.text: Clint Eastwood protrays Earl Stone in The Mule. clueless old white guy, while the trio of hard cases throw a couple of full duffel bags into the bed of his pickup, hand him a cell phone, ask him if he knows how to text (nope), and then send Earl on his way. And so begins Earl’s new journey as a drug mule. The story is based on a news report about a Leo Sharp, 87, who was arrested with 87 kilos of cocaine and in the employ of the Mexican Sinaloa Cartel. After each run, the load gets larger and the cash waiting in a manila envelope in Earl’s glove compartment thicker. Suddenly, he is flush with cash, gets his farm back, and his generosity regarding his family and VFW buddies allows him to get his life back on track. He is now driving a new pickup. He also becomes more relaxed about the drive, stopping to help a black family change a tire, taking a break for fast food with his minders and refers to them as “beaners” sitting with a white guy. He also enjoys a layover at a motel where he hires two curvy escorts for a sleepover. The problem is that while he is being carefully monitored by the follow-from-behind Cartel, the drug runs have also come to the attention of the DEA, two agents in particular, Bradley Cooper as agent Bates and Michael Pena as agent Trevino. If there is an obvious theme to the film it has to do with Earl’s growing realization that he has missed countless opportunities to be with his family because he put his flower business first. He’s made countless choices, all of which, in the aggregate, have brought him to these last years of his life; regret tenaciously stalks him. In a reflective moment he tells his daughter that he thought it was “more important to be somebody out there” than be at home with his family. The Mule is a spare elegy, having to do with drug-running only incidentally. Eastwood, with a sense of delight and sadness, embraces the role of an old man looking in the rearview mirror and discovering that what he sees is increasingly wanting. There is a scene in the film that proves to be one of the most heartfelt, a long moment between Earl and Mary that shakes Earl to his core. The Mule is a nicely told story and hopefully not the last one in which Eastwood will appear. But I’m reminded, if memory serves, that he said something about Gran Torino being his final on screen performance. But Redford also said that his role in Old Man and the Gun would close out his acting career. I hope that neither actor stops working in front of the camera. There are plenty of stories yet to be told featuring old guys who are still very able to stand stage center. The Mule. Directed by Clint Eastwood. Starring Clint Eastwood, Diane Wiest and Bradley Cooper. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on December 17, 2018.

articles.text: In viewing Clint Eastwood’s recent film, The Mule, one might characterize it as a quiet meditation on regret. All we ultimately have in life is time and there are no do-overs. Things change. The film, Eastwood’s 38th behind the camera, also stars Eastwood portraying Earl Stone, a celebrated horticulturist. He is the owner of a small farm where he raises prize-winning Daylight Lilies, a fragile flower that blooms in spring and summer; each stalk lasts only 24 hours. The year: 2005. The place: Peoria, Illinois. The film opens with a long scene in which Earl, dressed to the nines with a rakish straw hat and seersucker suit with bow tie, attends an award ceremony for the Lily. Later, savoring the moment, seated at the bar and ordering drinks all around, he is reminded that at that very moment his daughter is getting married and he had promised to walk her down the aisle. He chooses, instead, to stay on his bar stool. His estranged wife, Mary (Diane Wiest), tells his fraught daughter, Iris (played by Eastwood’s daughter, Alison), “Your father always chose work over family.” Thus is the thread that stitches this narrative together. Cut to 2017: Earl, now on the cusp of turning 90, visibly aged, bent slightly forward, is an old coot facing decidedly different circumstances. His farm is in foreclosure and with his hardused pickup filled with a few sticks of furniture and incidentals. Earl is on his way to his granddaughter’s pre-wedding bash. Arriving unannounced, he is loudly asked to leave by Mary and Iris, both decidedly estranged and not happy to see him. While walking back to his pickup and muttering, a member of the wedding party hears him and offers Earl a job driving from El Paso to Chicago. That’s it. Strapped for cash, Earl is next seen driving into a tire shop to meet his new bosses. This is a nifty scene in so many ways. The guys waiting in the garage are Chicanos with buzzed hair, one holding an AR-15 rifle. Clearly, Earl understands that he will not be delivering bags of pecans. But he keeps a cool grip, adopts the mien of a doddering, Julia Roberts and James Franco star in Eat Pray Love. Movie review by Christ Honoré Elizabeth Gilbert’s best-selling memoir, Eat Pray Love, clearly resonated with some 8 million readers, mostly women. And it is women who are turning out to see the screen adaptation. In the film’s opening scenes, Elizabeth (Julia Roberts), married for more than five years to Stephen (Billy Crudup), is suffering from a pervasive sense of ennui. She feels something is missing in her life. All seems so mundane, lacking purpose, no matter that her husband seems a nice guy and she has found success as a writer. She’s certain that there’s fulfillment to be found, she simply has yet to find it. A hint is in the book’s subtitle: “One woman’s search for everything across Italy, India and Indonesia.” It’s assumed that the meaning of “everything” will be revealed. Elizabeth divorces Stephen, falls into the arms of David (James Franco), winds up sleeping on the floor and not in his bed, explaining that her dissatisfaction with life, briefly held in abeyance, has returned. What to do? Answer: travel. What now is lost may be found. Out there. And so she packs, leaving friends and New York behind, and sets out on a quest: Italy to eat, India to pray, and Bali to find enlightenment or love. Because the film is a travelogue, with no backstory regarding the characters, the audience is treated to a ravishing view of Italy and sumptuous food consumed with friends around countless tables. After several months she travels to India and a Hindu ashram, there to chant and pray and find what is defined as “balance.” The final chapter of her quest takes place in gentle, lovely Bali where she does find love with a Brazilian businessman (Javier Bardem). As for as the quest for ultimate answers, the embedded message seems to be that to find “balance,” you have to leave home and, in effect, be off balance. There is something about being away, in a different culture, that can aid in acquiring renewed perspective and insight. Perhaps a more applicable message for the book and the film might be: No matter where you go, there you are. You take all your personal baggage with you; it never has to go in the overhead bin. And you don’t need a National Geographic journey to discover certain truths. Elizabeth’s journey seems a bit shallow, tedious, even self-indulgent. The best moments in the movie involve Richard (Richard Jenkins), an ex-pat from Texas who has led a life consumed by alcohol and has been staying at the same ashram as Elizabeth. One afternoon, he takes Elizabeth to the roof of the meditation center and shares a vignette from his life that is harrowing and disturbing. Jenkins is a superb character actor and is the best part of this movie. What Eat Pray Love amounts to is an opportunity to watch Julia Roberts – a lot. She is lovely and emotive and appears in every scene. The problem is that even she can’t lift what is essentially insubstantial material to an engaging level. Eat Pray Love. Starring Julia Roberts, James Franco, Javier Bardem, Richard Jenkins, Viola Davis and Billy Crudup. Directed by Ryan Murphy. Rated PG-13. A scene from Eat Pray Love.

articles.text: A scene from Miyazaki’s The Wind Rises. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Wind Rises was intended to be Hayao Miyazaki’s final film. It would also serve as this intensely creative animator and storyteller’s tribute to Jiro Horikoshi, known in Japan as a master aeronautical engineer and a pioneer in aircraft design during the first half of the 20th century. Through Miyazaki’s prism, Jiro (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is portrayed as a bookish, bespectacled boy and young man (not dissimilar from Harry Potter) who possessed a dreamy, distracted manner, often lost in his imagination, his visions of airplanes filling his thoughts. Early on, Jiro so loved the idea of flight that he imagines meeting the Italian aeronautical engineer Giovanni Battista Caproni, who encourages him to pursue his love of airplanes and design. As it turns out Jiro cannot be a pilot himself because of his poor eyesight. And yet fly he does. As part of the story, Miyazaki includes a sad and tender romance between Jiro and a young woman, Naoko Satomi (Emily Blunt). They meet in Tokyo during Japan’s most devastating Great Kanto Earthquake, in 1923, a natural disaster that all but leveled Tokyo. It is grippingly captured in the film’s intense images. And it is Naoko who quotes to Jiro the words of the poet Paul Valéry. “As the wind rises, we must try to live,” the source of the film’s title. In Jiro, Miyazaki creates a A scene from Miyazaki’s The Wind Rises. character of inherent idealism and innocence, qualities that thread their way through the wide spectrum of his own work. With insight and a languid beauty, using the resilient metaphor of wind, he mesmerizes those who gaze upon his wondrous animation, which never fails to transcend. Tweens and young teens will be enamored of Jiro and his personal quest to follow his dream. The will undoubtedly see the story as a place apart, a young man’s search for benevolent possibilities. For others, those jaded by life and reality, they will recall that it was also Jiro Horikoshi who would one day design the Japanese Zero fighter aircraft used to deadly effect during WWII (Kamikaze meant “Divine Wind”). As a resut, The Wind Rises opened worldwide to controversy. It soon became Japan’s highest grossing film in 2013, was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, received a Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and won the Japan Academy Prize for Animation of the Year. The Wind Rises (2013). Animated from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Emily Blunt and Martin Short. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS The Wind Rises – Miyazaki’s story of a boy whose dream was fulfilled

articles.text: Kathryn Prescott and Henry Lau star in A Dog’s Journey. Movie review by Chris Honoré A Dog’s Journey follows the 2017 release of A Dog’s Purpose, a film I did not see but understand was about a very sizable dog named Bailey (part St. Bernard and Australian shepherd). Journey carries on with Bailey, still living on a bucolic Michigan farm with his warm-hearted owners, Ethan (Dennis Quaid) and Hannah (Marg Helgenberger). Apparently, their son was killed in an accident and his widow, Gloria (Betty Gilpin), and small granddaughter CJ, are staying with them. Bailey, we’re told in voiceover (Josh Gad as Bailey), has made it his mission to keep a watchful eye on CJ as she wanders from house to field and corral, essentially ignored by her mother who is frustrated and angry and not taking well to motherhood. Soon Gloria, defensive, self-destructive, takes CJ and leaves for Chicago and Bailey is heartbroken. CJ is his best bud. Gloria, not so much. So far so good. Until it isn’t. At the end of act one the first of what will be a series of dogs dying occurs. Bailey, it turns out has cancer, and passes away in Ethan’s arms, and thus begins a Buddhist script involving reincarnation. In the last moments of Bailey’s life, Ethan has asked his big wonderful dog to somehow return in the body of another dog and find CJ and, well, keep an eye on her – fulfill the mission. And so it happens. Bailey soon returns as a Beagle named Molly, and when Molly is killed in a car accident, Bailey returns as an African Boerboel, called by his owner Big Dog. When BD grows old and dies, Bailey returns as a snippy and intuitive Yorkshire terrier, Max. Meanwhile, CJ has grown up, moved to New York to pursue a singing career, leaving behind he mom, Gloria. Plus there’s an old boyfriend, of sorts, Trent (Henry Lau) who has been her friend since elementary school. Serendipitously, Max, on the verge of being put down at a shelter, finds CJ. Since Max is really Bailey, well, all is again well. Sort of. The journey continues. I was surprised by the amount of death, however gently handled (there is an Elysian field where each dog ends up, running along a golden path into a mist of eternity). There is also illness. Ethan and Hannah grow old. CJ’s Trent, also found by Max, grows ill. And all I can conclude is that the writers missed the Disney formula that avoids dark narratives and thrives on happily-ever-after plots. None of the above qualifies as a spoiler-alert; if it’s not one dog, well, it’s the next with Bailey holding down the spiritual voiceover fort. It does beg the question: who did the moviemakers have in mind as the target audience? Perhaps tween/teen girls; however, definitely not the little guys. There were moments when all I could say to myself was “good grief, what next?” A Dog’s Journey. Directed by Gail Mancuso. Starring Josh Gad, Dennis Quaid, Marg Helgenberger, Betty Gilpin, Kathryn Prescott, and Henry Lau. 1 hr. 48 min. Rated PG. Dennis Quaid and Marg Helgenberger star in A Dog’s Journey.
articles.title: A Dog’s Journey – with 4 dogs in one lifetime

They meet in Tokyo during Japan’s most devastating Great Kanto Earthquake, in 1923, a natural disaster that all but leveled Tokyo. It is grippingly captured in the film’s intense images. And it is Naoko who quotes to Jiro the words of the poet Paul Valéry. “As the wind rises, we must try to live,” the source of the film’s title. In Jiro, Miyazaki creates a A scene from Miyazaki’s The Wind Rises. character of inherent idealism and innocence, qualities that thread their way through the wide spectrum of his own work. With insight and a languid beauty, using the resilient metaphor of wind, he mesmerizes those who gaze upon his wondrous animation, which never fails to transcend. Tweens and young teens will be enamored of Jiro and his personal quest to follow his dream. The will undoubtedly see the story as a place apart, a young man’s search for benevolent possibilities. For others, those jaded by life and reality, they will recall that it was also Jiro Horikoshi who would one day design the Japanese Zero fighter aircraft used to deadly effect during WWII (Kamikaze meant “Divine Wind”). As a resut, The Wind Rises opened worldwide to controversy. It soon became Japan’s highest grossing film in 2013, was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, received a Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film, and won the Japan Academy Prize for Animation of the Year. The Wind Rises (2013). Animated from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Emily Blunt and Martin Short. 2 hrs., 6 min. Rated PG-13. Kathryn Prescott and Henry Lau star in A Dog’s Journey. Movie review by Chris Honoré A Dog’s Journey follows the 2017 release of A Dog’s Purpose, a film I did not see but understand was about a very sizable dog named Bailey (part St. Bernard and Australian shepherd). Journey carries on with Bailey, still living on a bucolic Michigan farm with his warm-hearted owners, Ethan (Dennis Quaid) and Hannah (Marg Helgenberger). Apparently, their son was killed in an accident and his widow, Gloria (Betty Gilpin), and small granddaughter CJ, are staying with them. Bailey, we’re told in voiceover (Josh Gad as Bailey), has made it his mission to keep a watchful eye on CJ as she wanders from house to field and corral, essentially ignored by her mother who is frustrated and angry and not taking well to motherhood. Soon Gloria, defensive, self-destructive, takes CJ and leaves for Chicago and Bailey is heartbroken. CJ is his best bud. Gloria, not so much. So far so good. Until it isn’t. At the end of act one the first of what will be a series of dogs dying occurs. Bailey, it turns out has cancer, and passes away in Ethan’s arms, and thus begins a Buddhist script involving reincarnation. In the last moments of Bailey’s life, Ethan has asked his big wonderful dog to somehow return in the body of another dog and find CJ and, well, keep an eye on her – fulfill the mission. And so it happens. Bailey soon returns as a Beagle named Molly, and when Molly is killed in a car accident, Bailey returns as an African Boerboel, called by his owner Big Dog. When BD grows old and dies, Bailey returns as a snippy and intuitive Yorkshire terrier, Max. Meanwhile, CJ has grown up, moved to New York to pursue a singing career, leaving behind he mom, Gloria. Plus there’s an old boyfriend, of sorts, Trent (Henry Lau) who has been her friend since elementary school. Serendipitously, Max, on the verge of being put down at a shelter, finds CJ. Since Max is really Bailey, well, all is again well. Sort of. The journey continues. I was surprised by the amount of death, however gently handled (there is an Elysian field where each dog ends up, running along a golden path into a mist of eternity). There is also illness. Ethan and Hannah grow old. CJ’s Trent, also found by Max, grows ill. And all I can conclude is that the writers missed the Disney formula that avoids dark narratives and thrives on happily-ever-after plots. None of the above qualifies as a spoiler-alert; if it’s not one dog, well, it’s the next with Bailey holding down the spiritual voiceover fort. It does beg the question: who did the moviemakers have in mind as the target audience? Perhaps tween/teen girls; however, definitely not the little guys. There were moments when all I could say to myself was “good grief, what next?” A Dog’s Journey. Directed by Gail Mancuso. Starring Josh Gad, Dennis Quaid, Marg Helgenberger, Betty Gilpin, Kathryn Prescott, and Henry Lau. 1 hr. 48 min. Rated PG. Dennis Quaid and Marg Helgenberger star in A Dog’s Journey.

articles.text: Think of it as one more coronavirus pandemic work-around, or call it an adaptation whose time has come (again). And now, here it is. San Francisco will get its first pop up drive-in theater at the Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture, 2 Marina Boulevard, with the first movie to be shown this Friday night, September 18. Billed as Fort Mason Flix, the drive-in will be located in a large parking lot where Flix will host a series of classic films six days a week through October 18. The first offerings will include Matrix, Xanadu, Frozen, Purple Rain and The Big Lebowski. “It’s been a hard six months for everybody,” said organizer Nick Kinsey, Director of External Affairs at Fort Mason. “We’re excited to invite people back to our campus and have the opportunity to do something that provides them with a little bit of fun and excitement.” A 40 x 20-foot, high definition LED screen will be mounted on the festival pavilion and will be 90 times brighter than a standard movie theater projector, allowing the first films to be shown in early evening light. A concession stand will be available, and all Covid-19 safety measures will be followed, including masks to be worn when leaving the vehicle. All restrooms will be deep cleaned. Contactless check-ins and tickets will be sold only online at fortmason.org/flix. Tickets are $49 per vehicle. People can bring as many people as there are seatbelts. There will be two daily screenings (see sidebar for schedule). Patrons can remain in their cars for the duration of the film and never have contact with anyone, according to Kinsey. Movie-goers should only come with people in their safety pod. The new drive-in theater site will also be available for fund raising, and depending on response, may usher in live events such as stand-up comedy and concerts. For more information, see fortmason.org/flix.

articles.text: The coronavirus has had a strange effect on the arts. To some it is a forced hibernation. To others it is suspended animation. Artistically speaking, there is a huge difference to both the performers and the audience. In pre-pandemic days the concert season began in the Fall and ended before Summer. Concert artists went to the resorts for a vacation. Perhaps there were a few concerts at the spas, but it was a time for relaxation and reflection. Composers composed. But also took time to relax. Then, preparation for the new concert season began. The concert artists began by playing far from the main concept centers. These were “tune -up concerts”, so to speak. It was like sports, when the season always begins with practice games. Once they were in shape, the real season began. Yes, those were the good old days. Sometime later the concert season was extended until it lasted all year. Musicians had no time to grow artistically. Jascha Heifetz urged a return to the more relaxed schedule, past to no avail. It remained for the coronavirus pandemic to throw the musical world back about 100 years. Can today’s artists use this hibernation or suspended–animation time to artistic advantage? Will the perfection-seeking automatons discover their souls? That is a very important question. Stay tuned. For violinist Fritz Kreisler, there was no question. Kreisler was so popular people said he would sound marvelous playing on a cigar box. He sounded even better when he played on a Stradivarius. No musician anywhere was as loved as Kreisler. Americans even loved him when he was an enemy alien during the First World War. Kreisler was the very personification of the violin. No less was said of him by famed conductor Bruno Walter. “When Kreisler played the violin, he became the violin.” His fame enabled him to play a Stradivarius. But he actually did play a cigar box. It was his first musical instrument… and he made it with shoelaces. A caricature of Fritz Kreisler, the most popular violinist of all time. Perhaps he was the most liked musician of all time. It’s hard to tell what kind of a violin he is using in this picture. It doesn’t look like a Stradivarius – in fact it doesn’t even look like a violin.

articles.text: Staff photo Residents and visitors came to Piedmont Park in 2018 to enjoy the many activities at the annual Harvest Festival. This year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 27, will be a virtual celebration due to gathering restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival will feature a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encourages Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents and school district employees can email photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. Photos may be sent directly to Putzer at cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Submissions must include your name, category entered, email and home address. The deadline for photo submissions is Friday, September 18. Everyone who enters will get a participation ribbon and will be entered into a random drawing for a $60 gift certificate from Ace Grand Lake Nursery on October 5. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest is sponsored by the Piedmont Garden Club. Kids ages 14 and younger can download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. E-mail a copy of the project to cputzer@piedmont.ca.gov. “[This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. For more infor mation, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/ harvestfestival.
articles.title: Harvest Festival will be virtual on Sept. 27

The younger students attended classes from 8:30 to 12:45; the older students were in class until 1:15. The school served bouillon or hot chocolate and crackers at morning recess and lunch at 1:15. The afternoons were for study, music, drawing and outdoor activities. For the boarding students, dinner was served at 6:30, and lights out were at 8:30, 9:30 for the older girls. Ransom-Bridges School flourished into the prosperous 1920s. In 1924 there were 186 students; 123 in high school and 63 in the lower school (grades 1-8). In 1928, there were 21 instructors and 42 graduating seniors. The school struggled financially after the Stock Market Crash of 1929 and the Depression that followed. Many families could no longer afford to send their daughters to private school. Piedmont High School was built in 1921 and offered a less expensive opportunity for education. Ransom-Bridges enrollment declined, and by 1932, there were only 12 graduating seniors. Shortly after graduation in June that year, the school closed. In 1936, the school was demolished, and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The first house was built at 152 Hazel Lane. Today, the redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane marks the entrance to the former Ransom-Bridges School. Redwood trees between 100 and 114 Hazel Lane lined the entrance to the school and mark the eastern edge of the school property. The main school building was built where 141 Hazel Lane stands. The path from Hazel Lane into Piedmont Park was called Ransom Way, named for the school. For more information on Piedmont’s history, please visit our website: Piedmonthistorical. org. articles.title: History of Piedmont

articles.text: Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls was a small but important part of Piedmont’s history. It was the first school to offer a college preparatory high school education in Piedmont. Somewhat isolated in Hazel Lane, yet accessible by streetcar, the school enjoyed a reputation as one of the prestigious private schools in the Bay Area. It all started with Amy Requa Long, who wanted her daughters to have a good education. When the girls were old enough for school, Isaac Requa built a oneroom schoolhouse on his property, and Amy hired a school teacher for her daughters and a few children from the neighborhood. It was the first school in Piedmont. Interest in a private school in Piedmont grew, and in 1905 Amy leased the rambling Fridheim house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges, both teachers from Anna Head School in Berkeley. The school accepted day and boarding students and attracted the daughters of many of Piedmont’s and California’s prominent families. It quickly outgrew the Fridheim site, and in 1908, Amy Requa Long hired Julia Morgan to design a modern school with classrooms and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that today is Hazel Lane. The new school opened in 1913 as the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls. It was strictly a college preparatory school, not a finishing school. Morgan returned in 1913 to build additional classrooms, and in 1916 added a gymnasium for the growing school. The curriculum included History, Math, English and foreign language classes in French, Latin and German. The school also offered special courses in Music, Drawing and Oral Expression. The Music class included piano, singing, harmony and Glee Club. The Drawing class taught painting, costume design, architecture and sculpture. The Oral Expression class ended with a full-dress presentation of a Shakespeare play in the school’s courtyard. Athletics were also important, and the school had basketball, field hockey, tennis and baseball teams, and even hiking and riding clubs. It also sponsored outings to plays and concerts, hiking and riding on trails in the East Bay hills, and picnics at local beaches. Ransom-Bridges offered classes from first grade through high school. The younger girls lived in Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and attended as day students. The school had dormitory rooms for up to 70 students. Some of the high school girls who boarded came from as far away as Washington, Oregon, Washington, D.C. and Maine. Almost all the graduates went on to the University of California in Berkeley, Stanford and other comparable colleges. Uniforms were required for the older girls – white middy blouses, dark ties and dark or white pleated skirts. articles.text: Right now, the pandemic is causing chaos and uncertainty for colleges and students. But it won’t always be that way. If you have children who will be heading off to school in the next few years, you’re probably thinking about more typical concerns – such as expenses. How will you pay for the high costs of higher education? Most colleges do offer financial aid packages that can greatly help with these expenses. But it pays to know well in advance how financial aid works. The key platform for determining much of your child’s financial aid is the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). In fact, if you have children starting college next year, now is the time to get going on the FAFSA, which becomes available on October 1 for the 2021-22 award year. Filling out your FAFSA will provide you with what’s known as your Expected Family Contribution (EFC). The EFC calculation takes into account four separate areas: parent income, parent assets (excluding retirement funds, such as 401(k) plans and IRAs, home equity and small family businesses), student income and student assets. The EFC does not calculate the exact amount you must pay for college, rather it’s an estimate. The amount you pay may be below or above this number. Nonetheless, the EFC is important in determining your financial aid package, and your actions can influence the results. Here are a few suggestions for future years: • Save money in your name – not your child’s. FAFSA will just consider up to 5.64 percent of a parent’s assets, compared to 20 percent of a student’s assets. • Be aware of how retirement plan contributions can affect aid. Many of your current assets, such as your retirement accounts, may be excluded from the EFC calculation. However, any voluntary contributions you make to your 401(k) or traditional IRA during the “base” year (the prior tax year) generally must be reported on the FAFSA and are counted as untaxed income; consequently, these contributions may have a similar effect on aid eligibility as taxable income. Mandatory contributions, such as those made by teachers to a state retirement system, are generally not reported on the FAFSA. • Avoid withdrawals from your 401(k) or traditional IRA. The money you take out from these accounts in the years you fill out the FAFSA, and the prior tax year, may count as taxable income in the financial aid calculations. If you really need the money, you may want to consult with your financial professional for alternatives. • Consider having children put earnings into a Roth IRA. Money from after-school or summer jobs your children put in a Roth IRA may not be included in EFC – plus, your kids will get a head start on a tax-advantaged retirement account. Keep in mind, though, that Roth IRA withdrawals could be considered as taxable income on the FAFSA if the account owner is younger than 59 ½, which will be the case for your children, or the account is less than five years old. Not all these suggestions will be appropriate for everyone, but they’re worth thinking about. You might also want to consult with a college’s financial aid officer before you complete the FAFSA, as aid calculations can be complex. An investment of your time and effort early in the process may pay off when the aid packages are finally delivered. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 16, 2020 Features BUSINESSES ADAPTING Can you influence your Financial Aid award? By TJ Stevko Right now, the pandemic is causing chaos and uncertainty for colleges and students. But it won’t always be that way. If you have children who will be heading off to school in the next few years, you’re probably thinking about more typical concerns – such as expenses. How will you pay for the high costs of higher education? Most colleges do offer financial aid packages that can greatly help with these expenses. But it pays to know well in advance how financial aid works. The key platform for determining much of your child’s financial aid is the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). In fact, if you have children starting college next year, now is the time to get going on the FAFSA, which becomes available on October 1 for the 2021-22 award year. Filling out your FAFSA will provide you with what’s known as your Expected Family Contribution (EFC). The EFC calculation takes into account four separate areas: parent income, parent assets (excluding retirement funds, such as 401(k) plans and IRAs, home equity and small family businesses), student income and student assets. The EFC does not calculate the exact amount you must pay for college, rather it’s an estimate. The amount you pay may be below or above this number. Nonetheless, the EFC is important in determining your financial aid package, and your actions can influence the results. Here are a few suggestions for future years: • Save money in your name – not your child’s. FAFSA will just consider up to 5.64 percent of a parent’s assets, compared to 20 percent of a student’s assets. • Be aware of how retirement plan contributions can affect aid. Many of your current assets, such as your retirement accounts, may be excluded from the EFC calculation. However, any voluntary contributions you make to your 401(k) or traditional IRA during the “base” year (the prior tax year) generally must be reported on the FAFSA and are counted as untaxed income; consequently, these contributions may have a similar effect on aid eligibility as taxable income. Mandatory contributions, such as those made by teachers to a state retirement system, are generally not reported on the FAFSA. • Avoid withdrawals from your 401(k) or traditional IRA. The money you take out from these accounts in the years you fill out the FAFSA, and the prior tax year, may count as taxable income in the financial aid calculations. If you really need the money, you may want to consult with your financial professional for alternatives. • Consider having children put earnings into a Roth IRA. Money from after-school or summer jobs your children put in a Roth IRA may not be included in EFC – plus, your kids will get a head start on a tax-advantaged retirement account. Keep in mind, though, that Roth IRA withdrawals could be considered as taxable income on the FAFSA if the account owner is younger than 59 ½, which will be the case for your children, or the account is less than five years old. Not all these suggestions will be appropriate for everyone, but they’re worth thinking about. You might also want to consult with a college’s financial aid officer before you complete the FAFSA, as aid calculations can be complex. An investment of your time and effort early in the process may pay off when the aid packages are finally delivered. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery, located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek, is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. Bancroft created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. articles.text: Piedmont native Ben Gandesbery married Julie Ivy of Guildford, Connecticut on September 9. Ben Gandesbery, a 2011 Piedmont High graduate, and Julie Ivy of Guilford, Connecticut, had been planning their wedding for over a year and did not let the coronavirus cancel their plans. The couple scaled back the invite list from over 100 to closer to 20 with just immediate family and a few friends in physical attendance. The wedding ceremony on September 9 was livestreamed over the internet with more than 60 friends and family members attending from across the country. The wedding was held at the beautiful and bucolic Sunflower Hill Farm, in the rolling hills of rural Missouri, about 20 miles outside of Saint Louis, where both of them are doctors at Washington University. The venue featured lush gardens and a barnlike hall that is open on all sides, something that helped ensure social distancing. The midwestern weather was in full cooperation with balmy temperatures and clear blue skies. Californians in attendance were envious of the Missouri weather. The son of Tom and Mary Gandesbery of Piedmont, the groom attended Cornell University and graduate from Case Western Reserve University Medical School in 2019. He is currently a resident in Internal Medicine at Barnes-Jewish Hospital at Washington University in St. Louis. The bride is the daughter of Mike and Alice Ivy of Guilford Connecticut. She graduated from Guildford High School in 2011, earned her undergraduate degree at Dartmouth in 2015 and was a classmate of her husband at Case Western Reserve University Medical School in 2019. She is a pediatric physician at Children’s Hospital at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri Laura Ivy, the bride’s sister, was Maid of Honor. Following the wedding they planned a honeymoon to the Southwest, to include Zion National Park, Grand Canyon, and Sedona, Arizona.
articles.title: Ben Gandesbery weds Julie Ivy

articles.text: The Wellness Center has announced a Walk for Wellness as its annual fundraiser this year. It will take place from September 21-27, and is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Event co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener and Nicki Gilbert said that in future years Walk for Wellness will be a fundraiser that will bring the community together in person to celebrate the Wellness Center and advocate for student mental health. This year, participants will receive a Walk for Wellness visor and access to eight maps detailing various walks around town. “Families and small groups of friends should complete as many of the suggested walks as possible during the week of September 21 Everyone should post photos from their walks to @piedmontwellness on Instagram!” said Gilbert. “We hope to raise muchneeded funding for the Wellness Center while increasing awareness of the need for mental health services for our students,” Hohener added. Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. For registration and donation information, visit www. piedmontwalkforwellness.org or email piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com. Photo by Zak Gilbert Walk for Wellness co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener (left) and Nicki Gilbert display the banner for this year’s event.
articles.title: Wellness Center annual fundraiser starts September 21

articles.text: Once again, the bicycle team Linda and Marvin will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding Saturday, September 26 in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. You can make your donation online by simply clicking on the link at the bottom of this message. If you would prefer, you can also send your tax-deductible contribution to the address listed below. Please write the name/ Team Linda and Marvin in the memo line. Due to the Coronavirus, the ride is going virtual this year, but some of us will be riding from Oakland to the top of Mount Diablo and back, a distance of 80 miles and 7,500 feet of vertical climbing. That’s our challenge to support ALS research and care. We hope you will be compelled to support this cause in an effort to defeat this horrible disease. Thank you for your support. A link to Linda Lettieri Memorial Website, which has been updated this year with more compelling photographs, is at: http://www.olivemurphy.com. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding Saturday, September 26 in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. You can make your donation online by simply clicking on the link at the bottom of this message. If you would prefer, you can also send your tax-deductible contribution to the address listed below. Please write the name/ Team Linda and Marvin in the memo line. Due to the Coronavirus, the ride is going virtual this year, but some of us will be riding from Oakland to the top of Mount Diablo and back, a distance of 80 miles and 7,500 feet of vertical climbing. That’s our challenge to support ALS research and care. We hope you will be compelled to support this cause in an effort to defeat this horrible disease. Thank you for your support. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Linda Trowbridge died on August 28 Linda Patrice Trowbridge, a Piedmont resident for 37 years, passed away on August 28, 2020 after battling cancer for six years. She was 65. First and foremost, Linda was a wonderful partner and spouse, a loving mother and an elated and doting grandmother. She raised three wonderful children, all left mourning her with their spouses, Brian (Diana), Daniel (Kaitlin) and Patrice (Matt). Linda was overjoyed by the arrival of her now 2 year old granddaughter, Cecilia (Ceci), who “misses grandma already.” In addition to her children and grandchild, Linda is survived by Jeff. her husband of 42 years, and her beloved Cocker Spaniel, Emerson. You would think a stage 4 ovarian cancer diagnosis in 2014 might slow down and define a person. But not Linda, who kicked its butt for almost six years, resolving work issues and planning family engagements up to her next to last day. Born in Casper, Wyoming on September 27, 1955, she met Jeff, her husband to be, at Golden High School in Colorado at age 15. Marrying after obtaining BA degrees at the University of Colorado, Linda and Jeff headed to the Bay Area, where she obtained her MBA at San Francisco State well as being a board member of Hospice East Bay. Linda loved working with youth, and served in various positions with her sons’ Boy Scout troop in Piedmont. She was Troop Committee Chair, sending Troop 15 Piedmont Scouts off to many amazing High Sierra backpacking trips and community service activities. After her sons obtained their Eagle Scout awards, Linda offered her executive talents, skills and empathy to approximately 70 young men in Piedmont to shepherd them through the process of obtaining their Eagle Scout awards. Linda was recognized by the Piedmont Council for such service in 2018 with the Sidney C. Singer Service to Youth Award. Linda met with and counseled many of such young men while actively undergoing cancer treatments. Linda co-led a Girl Scout troop in Piedmont, with members of such troop, including her daughter, obtaining the Gold Award. Linda insisted that the Girl Scouts have all of the advantages and challenges of the Boy Scouts, including working on and satisfying Boy Scout merit badge requirements and camping. Linda loved her church, College Avenue Presbyterian Church, serving on its Board of Elders. Linda and Jeff enjoyed cheering on the Oakland A’s baseball team. Linda helped pave the way for future ovarian cancer patients, participating in aggressive studies and treatments and entering into a clinical trial at Mayo Clinic requiring significant travel to Rochester, Minnesota, during the last several months of her life. Linda was a tireless, loving, loyal, champion of her family, friends, co-workers and those in need. Linda was an amazing listener, always genuinely interested in learning more about her family, friends, and colleagues. She loved traditions, family gatherings, and events, and had the ability to make a celebration out of any activity or gathering. The family thanks Linda’s long-time caring providers, Gary Cecchi, MD, and Robin Fernandez, NP. Linda’s beloved charities include: CEI (cei.elders.org), Hospice East Bay (hospiceeastbay.org), Piedmont Boy Scouts (piedmontbsa. org) and College Avenue Presbyterian Church (capcoakland.org). Donations in Linda’s name to any of these organizations would go to amazing good works. A celebration of life for Linda will be scheduled in the future as COVID-19 permits. and began a 35-year career as a healthcare executive. She worked for the Sisters of Providence Health System, Catholic Healthcare West (now Dignity Health), St. Joseph Health System and Kaiser Permanente. where she was the Executive Director for the Continuum for Northern California. While serving on the Board of Directors of On Lok Lifeways in San Francisco, Linda became a great advocate of PACE programs (Program of All-inclusive Care for the Elderly). PACE programs are dedicated to providing frail, mostly low income elders with an alternative to nursing home care. When an opportunity opened up to lead such an organization, Linda jumped at the chance. During the last seven years of her life, including six years while managing her own cancer, Linda served as the CEO of the Center for Elders Independence in Oakland. In that role she greatly increased the number of elders served, opened up and staffed new beautiful day centers, and advocated strongly with state and federal regulators for the program she loved. Under Linda’s leadership, the organization’s motto was, “Your life just got better.” She chaired the California state CalPACE organization and was given the 2020 PACE Champion Award, as WE PROVIDE: • Excellent in-home care • Quality caregiver training • Errands and transportation Start home care today. articles.text: Editor: Piedmont needs Jen Cavenaugh’s re-election to the City Council. Jen brings her energy, enthusiasm and business acumen to keeping Piedmont a wonderful place to live. She provides thoughtful analysis, based on careful inquiry into underlying facts and options, to the Council’s decision-making. Having known Jen for years, she is focused relentlessly on the need to improve the City’s deteriorating infrastructure, an issue long ignored, while remaining fiscally prudent. She also has emphasized the City’s need for strategic planning across its operations, and participation in the effort to respond to climate change. We need motivated and talented people who are willing to serve their community. Please join me in voting to re-elect Jen. –Richard Raushenbush
articles.title: Cavenaugh brings energy, knowledge to the job

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to encourage Piedmonters to re-elect City Council member Jen Cavenaugh. Jen is a Whirling Dervish of energy and dedication to Piedmont. She always does her homework and is very aware of the fiscal issues facing our wonderful City. Jen will continue to work hard to find the best solutions. As an incumbent, she has the experience, common sense and knowledge to “hit the ground running” when the new Council is sworn in. A busy mom of three teenagers, Jen still manages to fit in occasional trips down the coast to surf with her kids. Please vote to re-elect Jen Cavenaugh. Piedmont needs her energy and continued commitment to making Piedmont the best it can be. –Patty White Former Mayor
articles.title: Jen Cavenaugh – helping Piedmont be the best it can

Her endorsements reflect the broad range of her support among Piedmonters as well as leaders in Alameda County and the State of California. We’ll be voting for Conna McCarthy and hope you will, too. –Jane Cullinan & Cal James
articles.title: Why we’re voting for McCarthy

articles.text: Regarding Measure UU, I would like to address the sports of swimming and water polo and the City’s need for a local, viable, competition pool. When living in Oakland, my husband and I joined Orinda Park Pool; we wanted our three daughters to learn how to swim. What was then an innocent priority became the tail that wagged the dog. All three loved swimming for Park Pool Swim Team and every summer was spent transporting them through the tunnel to swim practice and meets. We moved to Piedmont and the girls looked forward to participating on the high school swim and water polo teams. We were surprised by what we found. The situation at the community pool was untenable. The school was at odds with the pool membership. Lane space was at a premium. The swim team was driving to other cities to practice. Water polo team was trying to practice while community pool members tried to swim laps. The pool wasn’t even deep enough for regulation play. The parents met to discuss how difficult it was for the school to reserve swim and water polo times. Talk circulated. How could the pool be redesigned to accommodate necessary changes? . .This was in the 1990s! It is time for the Piedmont community to support the building of a community pool complex. The reasons are irrefutable. Swimming is an essential life skill. Everyone must learn to swim. Safety demands it. Swimming supports all levels of ability and ages. It’s an inexpensive, lifetime, low impact sport. Children improve and gain confidence as they learn different strokes. Seniors improve endurance, muscle strength and cardiovascular fitness. With a proper pool, Piedmont could support a community swim team and a masters swim program. Piedmont High School needs a serviceable, city pool, both for swimming and water polo. Let’s support a swim tradition in Piedmont by voting YES on Measure UU. Everyone benefits.
articles.title: Everyone will benefit with a new pool

articles.text: Editor: I am honored to enthusiastically support Cory Smegal for a second term on the Piedmont School Board. I am grateful for Cory’s unending dedication to our schools over the past 16 years, and especially over the past four years on the School Board. I am continually impressed with her thoughtful feedback during School Board meetings and her ability to work collaboratively with parents, teachers, students, District staff, other School Board members as well as with other districts. Cory’s clear communication and willingness to stand up for what she believes is best for our children and teachers is exactly what we need – especially during these uncertain times. Cory has her MBA from the Haas School of Business at UC Berkeley and has over 15 years of experience as a business consultant and marketing executive. This business expertise, as well as her keen understanding of the school budget, will be invaluable over the next four years as our district faces so many fiscal challenges. Both of Cory’s children, Anna and Tommy, have attended Piedmont schools since kindergarten. Anna graduated from Piedmont High in 2019 and Tommy is in his senior year of high school. In my opinion, this first-hand experience as a parent at all three levels of the Piedmont school system has been essential in her understanding of the issues facing our school district. Cory has clear priorities for our District:

articles.text: We have known Cory Smegal since our kids began kindergarten at Wildwood over a dozen years ago. articles.text: Editor: I believe that, for a variety of reasons, many Black, Latino, Asian and other minorities have faced financial roadblocks in finding economic success. It is indisputable that pre-Pandemic, President Trump’s policies ushered in the best economy our country has seen in decades. This resulted in enhanced minority opportunities judged by the following: 1) Lowest minority unemployment rates, including minority youth, seen in decades; 2) Highest minority home ownership, 3) Opportunity Zones, enabling minority entrepreneurs: 4) Funding Black Colleges; 5) Stock Market Highs, helping increase 401 Ks; 6) Signed historic criminal justice reform; 7) Lifted 2.4 million out of poverty; among other policies such as lowering taxes, and bringing back jobs from overseas. President Trump did this with the most vitriolic hatred aimed at anyone I’ve ever seen. In spite of this, he is on his way to rebuilding the economy to its former heights. This coming election is a choice between socialism and free enterprise. Socialism never worked anywhere. If you want to help minorities, vote for President Trump. It certainly worked before and will again. –Mary Lou Weggenmann
articles.title: A vote for Trump

articles.text: I am writing to share my strong support for Measure UU. Let me preface this by saying that I don’t like getting wet. I hate being cold. And, to this day I believe there is a great white shark waiting for me at the bottom of every body of water. The reason I support a new and improved community pool is because swimming saved my life. Five years ago at the age of 47, I injured my lower back (bulging discs L4 and L5). I was in crippling pain. The doctors prescribed drugs, rest, and ice. Months passed and my situation did not improve. MRIs, steroids and cortisone shots did nothing for the pain. I was getting depressed. After months of agony, a good friend begged me to try swimming. Keep in mind at this point I was not a swimmer, but I was desperate for exercise and was willing to try anything to get my life back. My first swim lesson did not go well. I spent the hour holding on to the side of the pool learning how to blow bubbles. In a few weeks of swimming, my back was significantly better.

I hate being cold. And, to this day I believe there is a great white shark waiting for me at the bottom of every body of water. The reason I support a new and improved community pool is because swimming saved my life. Five years ago at the age of 47, I injured my lower back (bulging discs L4 and L5). I was in crippling pain. The doctors prescribed drugs, rest, and ice. Months passed and my situation did not improve. MRIs, steroids and cortisone shots did nothing for the pain. I was getting depressed. After months of agony, a good friend begged me to try swimming. Keep in mind at this point I was not a swimmer, but I was desperate for exercise and was willing to try anything to get my life back. My first swim lesson did not go well. I spent the hour holding on to the side of the pool learning how to blow bubbles. In a few weeks of swimming, my back was significantly better. Now I swim 5 days a week. My back, though not perfect, needs the low impact movement that only water can provide. The Piedmont pool is not just a place where children learn to swim and have birthday parties or a venue for swim meets and water polo. It’s a place where middle aged people like myself can find rehabilitation and an incredible source of exercise that we can benefit from well into our golden years. I believe there are many more ‘older’ Piedmonters like myself who will benefit tremendously from a rebuilt community pool. Without a pool, Piedmont will literally have a gigantic, empty hole in the ground, and we will have lost more than a place for recreation and rehabilitation. We will have lost a part of our community. I urge everyone to vote yes on Measure UU. Everyone will benefit with a new pool By Barbara Reding Regarding Measure UU, I would like to address the sports of swimming and water polo and the City’s need for a local, viable, competition pool. When living in Oakland, my husband and I joined Orinda Park Pool; we wanted our three daughters to learn how to swim. What was then an innocent priority became the tail that wagged the dog. All three loved swimming for Park Pool Swim Team and every summer was spent transporting them through the tunnel to swim practice and meets. We moved to Piedmont and the girls looked forward to participating on the high school swim and water polo teams. We were surprised by what we found. The situation at the community pool was untenable. The school was at odds with the pool membership. Lane space was at a premium. The swim team was driving to other cities to practice. Water polo team was trying to practice while community pool members tried to swim laps. The pool wasn’t even deep enough for regulation play. The parents met to discuss how difficult it was for the school to reserve swim and water polo times. Talk circulated. How could the pool be redesigned to accommodate necessary changes? . .This was in the 1990s! It is time for the Piedmont community to support the building of a community pool complex. The reasons are irrefutable. Swimming is an essential life skill. Everyone must learn to swim. Safety demands it. Swimming supports all levels of ability and ages. It’s an inexpensive, lifetime, low impact sport. Children improve and gain confidence as they learn different strokes. Seniors improve endurance, muscle strength and cardiovascular fitness. With a proper pool, Piedmont could support a community swim team and a masters swim program. Piedmont High School needs a serviceable, city pool, both for swimming and water polo. Let’s support a swim tradition in Piedmont by voting YES on Measure UU. Everyone benefits. Continued from page 3 best they can be. articles.text: ovation The resident’s old gas furnace stopped working last night and a contractor is coming next week to install a new one. Do they have to install an electric heat pump furnace? “No, not at all,” Jackson said. “Most furnace replacements are less than $10,000. If renovations amount to less than $25,000, it would be exempt from the reach code requirements.” Q: A resident is developing the basement and crawlspace area into a family room with a half bath. The total project cost will be greater than $100,000, and the resident will be relocating the furnace and water heater as part of the project. Does the resident have to replace their gas furnace and water heater with electric heat pumps? No, according to Jackson. The ordinance does not require anyone to replace their gas furnace with a heat pump, or a gas water heater with a heat pump. However, projects that total more than $100,000 must include two energy-efficient improvements. Q: Are there any rebates available to Piedmonters to help pay for a heat pump? Including all available rebates, about how much would it cost a resident to install a heat pump compared with a new gas furnace and water heater? Rebates available to Piedmont residents currently are through Bay Area Regional Energy Network; they offer a $1000 rebate to replace a gas heating system with a heat pump, explained Muthig. PG&E is only offering rebates for ‘smart thermostats.’ “Due to the wide range of homes in Piedmont, it is difficult to give an exact cost, but it generally is in the $15,000-$20,000 range.”
