articles.text: The number of total COVID- 19 cases in Alameda County is now 20,022 as of Monday, September 14, making it the first and only county in the San Francisco Bay Area to surpass the threshold of 20,000 cases. The number of new cases added per day has been relatively low in the county over the past seven days, with 31 cases added as of Sunday, September 13. This is a marked decrease since the peak of 425 daily new cases recorded on August 13, a record high according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. Tragically, 32 more deaths have been recorded over the past seven days in Alameda County, increasing the total number of fatalities to 332. Last Friday, September 11 was the deadliest day yet of the coronavirus pandemic in the Bay Area, with 34 deaths recorded across the region. The majority occurred in Alameda and Santa Clara counties. No new cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, were recorded amongst Piedmont residents. The total number of cases for the City stands at 33, with only one new case reported so far in September. In Oakland, the most populous city in the county, the number of cases since the pandemic was declared in March is now 7,959. In Hayward, 2,857 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,354 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,091. The rolling seven-day percentage of positive tests has trended slightly downward through September, with 5 percent of COVID-19 tests now coming back positive in Alameda County. Santa Clara County, the initial epicenter of the pandemic until cases shot up in Alameda County in June, has recorded a total of 19,613. Contra Costa County has a caseload of 15,489. San Francisco has recorded a total of 10,430 and San Mateo County has recorded 9,242. Along with 29 other counties in California, Alameda County remains in the state’s Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier for reopening businesses and other activities as per a new system put in place by the state government on August 31. Alameda County started the new system in this most restrictive tier after being put on a state “watchlist” back on July 12. There are four color-coded tiers in the new system that have different rules for how the economy can be reopened. San Francisco, Santa Cruz, Santa Clara and Marin counties are all currently in the slightly less restrictive red tier. On Friday, September 11, the Alameda County Public Health Department updated its health orders to allow for vehicle-based gatherings for live music, religious services and other events. Officials also worried about a possible spike from the Labor Day holiday. Because symptoms of the virus can take some time to develop and so many carriers can be asymptomatic, it will likely be several days before officials will know whether the holiday weekend resulted in an increase in cases. Statewide, the total number of COVID-19 cases recorded so far is now 760,013 and there have been 14,451 deaths. California has by far the most cases of COVID-19 in the United States and is the only state with over 700,000 cases. The City of Piedmont keeps its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ covid-19
articles.title: Alameda County is first in region with over 20,000 COVID-19 cases

pages.text: Wednesday, September 16, 2020 29 Reach Codes Continued from page 5 ovation The resident’s old gas furnace stopped working last night and a contractor is coming next week to install a new one. Do they have to install an electric heat pump furnace? “No, not at all,” Jackson said. “Most furnace replacements are less than $10,000. If renovations amount to less than $25,000, it would be exempt from the reach code requirements.” Q: A resident is developing the basement and crawlspace area into a family room with a half bath. The total project cost will be greater than $100,000, and the resident will be relocating the furnace and water heater as part of the project. Does the resident have to replace their gas furnace and water heater with electric heat pumps? No, according to Jackson. The ordinance does not require anyone to replace their gas furnace with a heat pump, or a gas water heater with a heat pump. However, projects that total more than $100,000 must include two energy-efficient improvements. Q: Are there any rebates available to Piedmonters to help pay for a heat pump? Including all available rebates, about how much would it cost a resident to install a heat pump compared with a new gas furnace and water heater? Rebates available to Piedmont residents currently are through Bay Area Regional Energy Network; they offer a $1000 rebate to replace a gas heating system with a heat pump, explained Muthig. PG&E is only offering rebates for ‘smart thermostats.’ “Due to the wide range of homes in Piedmont, it is difficult to give an exact cost, but it generally is in the $15,000-$20,000 range.” Q: The federal government has minimum efficiency standards for gas furnaces. Can the ordinance set more stringent efficiency standards for new gas furnaces installed in Piedmont? No, it cannot. State and local governments are prohibited from adopting higher minimum efficiencies than the federal standards, confirmed Jackson. Q: Will a resident need to install solar panels when they: get a $25,000 renovation, replace the roof material of their home, or install a new underlayment under roof tiles? No, a resident will not need to install solar panels in any of these cases, according to Muthig. Residents will only need to install solar panels if they are adding an entire new upper level to their house, or increasing their total roof area by 30 percent or more. Q: A resident is planning to increase their home’s floor and roof area by 50 percent. Will they need to install solar panels? Yes, if a resident is increasing their total roof area by 30 percent or more, they need to install solar panels. Q: If a house is undergoing a significant expansion and is required to install solar panels, how will the city determine the number or solar panels that must be installed? The California Energy Code already requires that newly constructed homes have rooftop solar panels, and the energy code has a formula for determining the number of solar panels that must be installed based on the floor area, Szasz said. Piedmont’s Reach Code uses the same formula, making it consistent with the California energy code formula. Q: What if a house is increasing roof area by 40 percent, but the roof is shaded so solar panels are impractical, would the house still be required to install solar panels? In this case, it would not. “The California Energy Code also has a list of exceptional cases in which a new home would not need to install solar panels,” Szasz said. The list of exceptions form the California Energy Code would also be applied. Q: Why does the ordinance require the installation of solar panels on existing houses getting a new upper level, or increasing roof area by 30 percent or more? “The goal is to move Piedmont and the electrical grid to local renewable sources of energy. The state of California is requiring that by the year 2045, all electricity in use in California be generated by renewable sources,” Jackson said. To meet this goal, and Piedmont’s climate action goals, the plan includes requiring the installation of solar panels. Q: A resident is renovating the landscaping of their backyard, installing an outdoor kitchen and reconfiguring the swimming pool to add a spa. The project is expected to cost $175,000. Would the proposed Ordinance affect this project in any way? No. Projects that do not alter the buildings structure are not subject to the ordinance. The resident might explore options to include electric appliances in an outdoor kitchen to reduce their carbon footprint, but it is not required, according to Jackson. The City Council has not yet set a date for the second reading of Reach Codes. articles.text: It has been 19 years and one week since the Twin Towers fell in a terrorist attack in New York City and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001. Ripples of the attacks were felt coast to coast, and no one was spared from the destruction that day. In Piedmont, a giant American flag was raised in solidarity and residents held an impromptu candlelight vigil at the Exedra in the middle of town. Nineteen years ago, a nation came together, united by tragedy.

An essential term to Racial Equity policy (BP 0415.1) is BIPOC which refers to Black, Indigenous, and People of Color. articles.text: When the Coronavirus pandemic caused everythng to close earlier this year, it interrupted the Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner scheduled for March 26. That forum annually is when the Council is able to publicly thank the almost 200 volunteers that serve some 1000 of our community’s youth. What the Council had hoped would be merely a postponement of the event turned into a cancellation. In lieu of the Recognition Dinner, the Council will celebrate John Stewart’s lifelong contributions to Scouting and present him with the Silver Beaver Award at a virtual ceremony on Wednesday, September 16 from 6:30-7:00 p.m. via Zoom. Everyone is invited to attend, but must register at https:// tinyurl.com/pbsa-JohnStewart. Attendees will receive a link by e-mail. For details, contact the Scout office at 547-4493, or Jo Hazelett at Jo.Hazelett@scouting.org. The John Stewart story A Berkeley native and son of an Eagle Scout, Stewart began his Scouting career at Crocker Highlands Elementary with Troop 295. Highlights included passing his 1st Class Morse Code and being the only Scout to slip off a pontoon raft and into the turbulent waters of the Snake River in Idaho. Rumors persist that he struck his head. He moved to Piedmont in the 8th grade and joined Troop 11. He enjoyed a year of Camp Wallace Alexander, Piedmont’s early Scout camp, where he earned his 50-Mile Patch. In ninth Grade he earned his God and Country Award at Piedmont Community Church. He served his Troop and Scoutmaster John Sullivan, The venerable John Stewart, a longtime former Scoutmaster of Troop One and recently Vice President of Scouting for the Piedmont Council, will be celebrated on September 16 with a presentation of the Silver Beaver, the highest honor given by local Scout Councils
articles.title: Lifetime Scouter to be awarded Silver Beaver on Sept. 16

articles.text: Red Flag Warning for East Bay Hills, Piedmont until Wednesday morning The Bay Area Air Qualit y Management Dist r ict (BAAQMD) announced Monday, September 7 that it was extending a “Spare the Air” alert for the Bay Area, including Piedmont, until today, Wednesday, September 9. It marks 23 consecutive days of Spare the Air alerts, a bleak record for the agency. When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those with who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. BAAQMD said that very hot temperatures inland mixed with vehicle emissions caused smog to accumulate in the beginning of the week. Additionally, several wildfires burning nearby added to unhealthy air conditions in the Bay Area. “The Labor Day weekend heat wave, combined with tailpipe exhaust and lingering wildfire smoke, is expected to cause unhealthy air quality in the region,” Jack Broadbent, the executive officer of the Air District, said in a statement. “Driving less can help reduce smog and heading indoors when smoke is present can help protect our health.” Three massive fires caused by lightning strikes in mid-August are nearing containment but continue to burn around the Bay Area. (See details on page 14.) The Air District pointed to some other fires in Northern California that might impact air quality in Piedmont as well. Most fires were caused by lightning last month. The Woodward Fire has burned over 4,800 acres in Point Reyes National Seashore in Marin County and was 95 percent contained as of press time. The August Complex fire in Mendocino National Forest in Mendocino County has burned over 356,000 acres and is only 24 percent contained. This week, the National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning for parts of the Oakland Hills, including some portions within Piedmont. The Red Flag Warning, which indicates a high fire risk, was issued from Monday, September 7 at 10 p.m. to 8 a.m. today, Wednesday, September 9. Fire Chief Bret Black urges residents to create two emergency preparedness kits – a Go Bag and an Emergency Stay Kit. A Go Bag is a portable bag of items that should be prepared ahead of time in case an immediate evacuation is ordered. Information on creating a Go Bag can be found at ready.gov/kit An Emergency Stay Kit is a collection of gear in case a natural disaster, like an earthquake, limits mobility and requires residents to survive on what is at hand. More information can be found at resilience.abag.ca.gov/ preparedness/kit/ For more information, contact the Fire Department at 420-3030.
articles.title: Air District declares record 23-day Spare the Air alert in Piedmont

articles.text: Editor: Running for City Council in Piedmont is no small undertaking. It requires dedication, responsibility, and most of all commitment: • A commitment to community service. • A commitment to listen to Piedmonters’ input on the issues that are the most important to them. • A commitment to transparency and accountability for the decisions made by the City Council that greatly impact the quality of life and safety of the town we all love. • A commitment to be polite and courteous, even to those constituents with whom you might disagree. We have known Conna McCarthy for about 15 years and have been consistently impressed with her deep commitment to community service and her willingness to work hard on behalf of everyone in Piedmont. articles.text: Editor Now is the time for the City of Piedmont to build a new swimming pool complex. That the existing pool is beyond repair is indisputable. It has given us many years of service, fully justifying the expense incurred from the time of construction to the last dollar spent on maintenance and repair. The need for Piedmont to have a swimming pool was clear 50 years ago. That is true even more now. Recreational swimming is one of the few forms of exercise that can be done throughout life. Competitive swimming is more popular than ever. Both are in jeopardy in Piedmont. Economics favor doing the pool now. Piedmont’s bonding capacity could not be stronger. Interest rates are at historic lows. Piedmont’s leaders are unanimous in wanting to go forward now. The stars may not soon again line up so clearly. Piedmont’s realtors are telling us the availability of recreational and competitive swimming is important for our property values. I can personally attest to that fact. My mother Jean Brown Wolfe’s parents built a home in Piedmont in 1921, and she attended Piedmont schools from 2nd grade through graduation from Piedmont High. She and my dad would have loved to raise their children in Piedmont but for one major problem: Both my middle brother and I were competitive swimmers, and there was no community or high school pool in Piedmont during the 50’s. Oakland High did have such a pool. That was one of the major reasons they bought a home in the Crocker Highlands area of Oakland and did not move back to Piedmont until we graduated. Piedmont should never again be without a pool. It is fortuitous that the bond measure to authorize construction of a pool is labeled Measure UU. Our leaders have done their part in putting Measure UU on the ballot. It is now time for YOU to do your part and vote YES on Measure UU. –Cameron Wolfe, Jr. For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. Born in 1836 in Nantes, a port city of Atlantique-Loire, his father was a prosperous textile merchant in the drapery business, and his mother created millinery fashions. From childhood he retained a fascination with fashion and boats, and elements of ships and fashion would show frequently in his mature work. His parents sent him for schooling at the Jesuit Brugelette in Flanders, which borders northeast France; and he grew in admiration for the Belgian painter Henri Leys and Dutch masters of the past century painting captivating scenes of village life. When he showed a talent for sketching, his father tried to steer him to architecture; but determinedly, he moved to Paris at age twenty to become an artist and attend Ecole des Beaux-Arts. As artists commonly practice, he honed his copying skills at the Louvre. In Paris, he called himself James, a first name he had used since his youth, dropping his birth-name of Jacques Joseph. He’d always tilted toward anything Anglicized which was all the rage in France at the time; and his upbringing close to the Atlantic channel spanned England and France by commercial trade. Some of his early paintings were earnest efforts but were panned as pastiche, showing village scenes and people with enigmatic interactions, arranged at a dockside crowded with large boats (reminiscent of his youth); but criticized for lacking a central story or theme. His drawing technique showed promise, but the background and settings were too bland and flat, unaided by any social context. He painted several classical scenes in church interiors, one of which was purchased at his first public showing. By the next year and through the 1860s, Tissot proved very entrepreneurial in Paris. Tissot was an early enthusiast of Japanese arts, integrating Asian cultural elements into his paintings and collecting artifacts. His interest was piqued by the Japanese Pavilion at the Paris International Exposition in 1867, following Japan’s formal opening of their borders to foreigners in 1854. He entered his works into the Paris Salon, known as Salon, the most famous French venue in the world. The Salon was trumpeted as the finest exhibitor of painters, sculptors, and engravers trained at the Paris L’Académie des Beaux-Arts. Annual and bi-annual exhibitions at Salon were judged art shows where critical acclaim lifted the artist’s career, and rejection shattered reputations. Tissot made haste in building a following and getting famous; dealers displayed his work; and his friends were Edgar Dégas, Edouard Manet, and (ex-pat American) James Whistler. Before the Late Renaissance, portrait painting was the covenant of European royalty and the Catholic church for many centuries. The 17th century master painters, such as Rembrandt and Johannes Vermeer, are credited with creating genre art, that is, scenes of ordinary people doing everyday activities. Portrait painters such as Tissot excelling in genre style were in high demand as society mavens and critics were exhilarated by their realism. But the Franco-Prussian war of 1870 changed the Paris landscape into a disaster. The cost of foreign aggression under Napoleon III’s Second French Republic bankrupted the nation, and the Republic collapsed when the (Prussian) Germans invaded Paris. Emperor Napoleon was captured, deposed and jettisoned to England. Tissot who had joined the National Guard volunteering to protect Paris fell in with the anarchist Paris Commune during the chaotic German occupation. The Commune was a radical socialist, anti-religious, unruly group that was mostly out of control during the lawless months the Third French Republic was struggling. Tissot, realizing the risk for associating with radical forces, or to better his situation, fled Paris for London. He was advantaged in that he already had a London art dealer and figured his prospects to burnish his reputation would land him commissions as a fine art painter to a high society clientele. In 1876, at the age of forty, Tissot met a young Irish divorcée, Kathleen Newton, who became his model, muse, and mistress. With her young daughter, and later a son, she moved into Tissot’s house. Although they never married, the family grew happy and content living in their private world during an era when misEn Plein Soleil, Open Air, 1881. Kate and children, along with her sister Mary Hervey. Kathleen “Kate” Newton, 1876 tresses were commonplace, and artists lived in open and unmarried relationships. Their friends were artists, and the family socialized openly; but unfortunately, it was the Victorian Age in England, and Tissot felt the sting barring him from society gatherings and getting dropped by clientele who previously respected his work. In short, commissions dried up. Tissot refused to disguise his relationship with Kate, who became the love of his life. He was inspired to paint her loveliness onto every canvas, creating some of his most beautiful and emotional works. Sadly, Kate became ill with tuberculosis and suffered for two years before overdosing and taking her own life in 1882, at just age 28. His grief was enormous, and within a week of her death, Tissot abandoned his home, paints, brushes, and unfinished canvases, and left London to return to Paris. A retrospective of Tissot’s work was first exhibited recently at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, and then to Paris’s D’Orsay Musée. The San Francisco retrospective was titled “Fashion and Faith.” The Fashion is evident by the telling of his youth and how Tissot elegantly clothes his subjects. Faith is another matter. Significantly, he was raised by his mother to be a pious Catholic and regained his faith late in life when he suffered a tragedy that dramatically shifted his work. At the D’Orsay, the same 60-works exhibition is themed “L’Ambigu Moderne” meaning “An Ambiguous Figure of Modernity” or possibly “Ambiguously Modern.” The French acknowledge the artist’s shift from temporal subjects to ecclesiastic. articles.text: Does your teenager want to explore his or her creative voice? Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is offering a new online vocal music course for high school students. Called Future Voices: Foundations of Vocal Music, it will guide young people through a semester of training in vocal technique, rhythm and harmony, music literacy, and a special virtual choir project. The skills learned will support them in choir, musical theater, solo vocal lessons, and songwriting. No prior musical experience is required. The course will meet weekly on Tuesdays from 6:30-8:00 pm on Zoom, beginning September 8. The semester runs from September 8 through January 9, 2021. PEBCC instructor Tim Silva is a skilled vocalist, singer-songwriter, and musicianship coach with a special gift for sparking creativity in young people. For details contact Silva at tsilva@piedmontchoirs.org. To sign up, contact registrar Anastasia Fegbeitel-Finn (afegbeitel-finn@piedmontchoirs.org). If there is sufficient interest, an AP Music Theory may be available. If interested, contact Artistic Director Eric Tuan at etuan@piedmontchoirs.org.

articles.text: Simplified Mandarin will be taught online through Zoom technology in small classes this fall through Piedmont Language School. It is a non-profit designed to help students ages 5-12 enjoy learning Mandarin and develop a strong foundation in learning Chinese language and culture. • Early Mandarin Early Mandarin is for the youngest students (TK to 1st grade) and provides a foundation for learning at the higher levels. articles.text: On August 2nd, American astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley returned from the International Space Station with a splashdown. Splashdown is a water-based landing in which a reentry capsule lands in a large body of water, often the ocean. The astronauts inside are brought to shore and safely returned home. Splashdown landings were used in the return of the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo capsules. More recently, the SpaceX capsule, Crew Dragon, was added to the list as it successfully completed its first crewed landing in the Gulf of Mexico in early August, 2020. This marked history as astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley became the first astronauts to launch and land on American soil in over nine years due to the retirement of the Space Shuttle program. This mission’s purpose was to serve as a test-run and has already revealed ways to improve the design for the next launch. Now, we’re challenging you at home to design your own model capsule to survive the challenges of splashdown and protect the astronauts inside. CRITERIA • The capsule must stay together during landing. • The capsule must be able to float on the water’s surface for one full minute after landing. • Two astronauts must be secured inside of the capsule at all times. • The astronauts must be kept dry throughout the landing and floating period. MATERIALS Bucket, bin, sink, or tub Two objects to represent astronauts Containers or cups Coffee filters Pipe cleaners Popsicle sticks Glue or tape Markers Balloons Rubber bands Bubble wrap Foil Foam Cardboard Scissors Water ACTIVITY 1. Gather your materials. 2. Get thinking with some questions: a. How do you think astronauts return to Earth from space? b. How do you think astronauts are kept safe during return? c. What do you think are some of the challenges (or benefits) of landing astronauts in the ocean on their return? 3. Set up your “splashdown” site. a. This can be a bowl, bucket, sink, or tub filled with water. This represents the Photo courtesy of NASA/Bill Ingalls Crew Dragon capsule splashdown on August 2nd. Photo courtesy of NASA/Bill Ingalls Support teams arrive at the SpaceX Crew Dragon shortly after it landed. ocean that the astronauts will be landing in during their return to earth. 4. Select two objects to represent astronauts. a. Anything with a little weight – washers, figurines, toys, coins, etc. 5. Explain the design challenge and review the criteria (above). 6. 7. Design and build the capsule. Once it’s ready, test the capsule in splashdown! a. Hold your capsule high above the splashdown site. b. Give a countdown and drop it into the water! c. Determine whether the capsule survived impact by staying intact. d. If so, wait 60 seconds to determine whether your capsule can float. e. After, remove it from the water and check if the astronauts stayed dry. 8. Discuss the results of your first round of capsule testing: a. What did you try in your design? b. What did you notice happen during landing? c. What worked well and what could be improved? d. What else would you like to try in the next round? 9. Re-design and re-build the capsule with improvements. a. If the capsule did not survive, start over, using what you can. b. If it did survive, how can you improve the current design? 10. Once it’s ready, test the capsule again using steps 7a-7e. 11. Discuss the results of your second round of capsule testing using questions 8a-8d. 12. Repeat this process as many times as desired or until you’ve met all criteria. Haley Thiltgen is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd., Oakland. It is a center for science learning featuring interactive exhibits, planetariums, a large screen theater, hands-on activities and three powerful telescopes. For more information see: chabotspace.org.

articles.text: School started three weeks ago, and it has been quite intriguing. Online classes are working much better than I thought possible. I think one reason is because teachers had more time to prepare over the summer. I know that my friends are enjoying the distance learning now in place. We’re even able to do group projects, thanks to breakout groups. Seeing what the assignments are on Google Meets works so much better than Schoology conferences. I thought I would hate distance learning this fall, but I don’t – even though I’d rather be in school. There are some pros to distance learning. For instance, you don’t have to get out of bed at 7 in the morning (unless you wake up that early anyway). School starts at 8:50 or 10:15 a.m., so I could not be happier. Homework is now being given with more explanation, not just “go write an essay in two weeks.’’ The teachers try to engage us and ensure that we partake in the activities. Also, the schedule isn’t as complicated as last spring. We are advised where to go and what links to click to get to various places. But there are some flaws in the plan. As example, people with poor wi-fi reception can’t really pay attention to the class because they are too busy trying to hold the wi-fi router in place to get into class. Once there, they can’t move for the fear of losing the wi-fi connection. Another issue is that it’s only a matter of time before Schoology, the online learning system, overloads and shuts down. it’s already happened once and was a problem across the U.S. There must be a better way for students and teachers to get into the classroom without accessing Schoology. Maybe teachers could send out an email that contains the link to the classroom as backup for when Schoology fails. For the kids with bad wi-fi, either get a new router or happy trails – because it’s going to be a tough ride. Let’s talk about distractions Then there are all these home distractions the teachers can’t do much about (nor can the kids). Last Wednesday when the heat was pretty unbearable, I was on the computer taking my history class, the final class of the day. I noticed that the faucet in the bathroom had been going for about 20 minutes, so I thought that someone was taking a bath. But when I turned my chair around, I saw water coming through the doorway. Hmmm. It seems that my mother had decided to cool the house down by filling a bathtub with cold water, but completely forgot about it. My sister, mom and I got down on our hands and knees to scoop water off the bathroom floor with a bucket and a dustpan. The whole time my camera was off, so my classmates had no idea I was running around trying to stop my house from flooding. Now that everyone is home and usually on a call, the wi-fi can get bad and people can get on your nerves. The whole thing seems like a mess. My sister is in the room next to mine doing her classes. and it gets annoying every day. At some point you just feel like walking into a wall and forgetting everything. But then you remember that everyone is trying to do their best while stuck in a house. So we keep our game face on, thank the teachers for their hard work, thank our classmates, and keep pushing through. We have four months left of 2020, and only God knows what will happen. Maybe we will have a zombie apocalypse – maybe we will find out that unicorns exist. But for now, congrats on getting through the first three weeks of school. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.
articles.title: Virtual School: Oh boy, here we go

pages.text: Wednesday, September 9, 2020 9 Virtual School: Oh boy, here we go By Crystal Vacker School started three weeks ago, and it has been quite intriguing. Online classes are working much better than I thought possible. I think one reason is because teachers had more time to prepare over the summer. I know that my friends are enjoying the distance learning now in place. We’re even able to do group projects, thanks to breakout groups. Seeing what the assignments are on Google Meets works so much better than Schoology conferences. I thought I would hate distance learning this fall, but I don’t – even though I’d rather be in school. There are some pros to distance learning. For instance, you don’t have to get out of bed at 7 in the morning (unless you wake up that early anyway). School starts at 8:50 or 10:15 a.m., so I could not be happier. Homework is now being given with more explanation, not just “go write an essay in two weeks.’’ The teachers try to engage us and ensure that we partake in the activities. Also, the schedule isn’t as complicated as last spring. We are advised where to go and what links to click to get to various places. But there are some flaws in the plan. As example, people with poor wi-fi reception can’t really pay attention to the class because they are too busy trying to hold the wi-fi router in place to get into class. Once there, they can’t move for the fear of losing the wi-fi connection. Another issue is that it’s only a matter of time before Schoology, the online learning system, overloads and shuts down. it’s already happened once and was a problem across the U.S. There must be a better way for students and teachers to get into the classroom without accessing Schoology. Maybe teachers could send out an email that contains the link to the classroom as backup for when Schoology fails. For the kids with bad wi-fi, either get a new router or happy trails – because it’s going to be a tough ride. Let’s talk about distractions Then there are all these home distractions the teachers can’t do much about (nor can the kids). Last Wednesday when the heat was pretty unbearable, I was on the computer taking my history class, the final class of the day. I noticed that the faucet in the bathroom had been going for about 20 minutes, so I thought that someone was taking a bath. But when I turned my chair around, I saw water coming through the doorway. Hmmm. It seems that my mother had decided to cool the house down by filling a bathtub with cold water, but completely forgot about it. My sister, mom and I got down on our hands and knees to scoop water off the bathroom floor with a bucket and a dustpan. The whole time my camera was off, so my classmates had no idea I was running around trying to stop my house from flooding. Now that everyone is home and usually on a call, the wi-fi can get bad and people can get on your nerves. The whole thing seems like a mess. My sister is in the room next to mine doing her classes. and it gets annoying every day. At some point you just feel like walking into a wall and forgetting everything. But then you remember that everyone is trying to do their best while stuck in a house. So we keep our game face on, thank the teachers for their hard work, thank our classmates, and keep pushing through. We have four months left of 2020, and only God knows what will happen. Maybe we will have a zombie apocalypse – maybe we will find out that unicorns exist. But for now, congrats on getting through the first three weeks of school. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time. In working for solutions for Piedmont, I will leverage my deep community connections, including with school district partners, to engage and promote diverse perspectives, develop mutually beneficial solutions, and increase equity and inclusiveness. 2 – As a member of Piedmont’s Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee before joining the City Council in 2016, I worked with my colleagues to develop a comprehensive Facilities Maintenance Plan, which identified millions in deferred maintenance and unfunded liabilities. The work of this committee has provided independent budget oversight, transparency and in-depth understanding of city finances, By implementing recommendations of this committee, the city has strengthened its financial position. Measure TT generates much-needed resources to take care of the city’s old and ailing infrastructure and facilities. The proposed transfer tax increase brings Piedmont’s rate in line with neighboring Berkeley and Oakland rates. The is a one-time tax which occurs at the point of sale of a home and is generally shared by buyers and sellers alike; few homeowners will pay this tax. The proposed increase will provide necessary funds for maintaining and improving city facilities, streets, sidewalks, and parks. I strongly support it as do all of my colleagues on the City Council and the members of the BAFPC. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – My top priority will always be to listen to the citizens of Piedmont and bring their input to the Council. That includes transparency in communication. Gathering and reporting diversity of opinion is critical to widespread representation and also to the making of good, solid decisions. From an issue standpoint, I believe I will not have the luxury of picking one top priority. An excellent decision-maker must be able to assimilate large quantities of quickly changing data, work with a constantly shifting landscape and all the while staying focused on the most optimal end result. So I expect there to be many top priorities. From attending City Council meetings and reading staff reports, I see the following areas currently floating to the top: new community pool, Reach Codes, essential building upgrades for police and fire, City budget requirements (transfer tax increase,) diversity and BLM, increased crime and emergency readiness. 2 – Yes, I support Measure TT. Property related taxes (comprised of property, parcel and transfer taxes) account for 72% of our City’s revenues. In the 2020-21 City budget, we are anticipating a decrease of $414,000 over the 2019-20 projected actual. The decrease is mainly in transfer tax revenue due to slowing home sales in a COVID-affected market. Since 1968, the transfer tax rate has been set at $13.00 per one thousand dollar of the sale. Every year we budget to receive $2.8M in transfer taxes. The amount we receive fluctuates based on number of home sales and sales prices. The surplus, designated for general use, can be used to fund facilities maintenance. We have $38M in needed major capital improvements – fire/police/veterans/ recreation buildings, Coaches/Linda fields and the pool. Raising the transfer tax from $13.00 to $17.50 will create much needed additional revenue with minimal impact to our residents. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – My priorities are determined by the needs and interests of our residents:1.) Public Safety is consistently identified as a primary concern. We must continue to maintain high level police and fire services and, during the current pandemic, we must be vigilant to protect our vulnerable residents; 2.) We must continue to exercise fiscal responsibility to maintain high quality services including well-tended parks and good recreation programs; 3.) We must address aging infrastructure. Years of deferred maintenance and coping with outdated facilities is untenable in light of the changing needs of our residents. It is time for important community conversations challenging us to define our vision of Piedmont for present and future generations, and to determine how we will act upon that shared vision; 4.) Enact consensus driven policies for sustainability and energy conservation, and; 5.) Actively work for inclusiveness and equity in accordance with the August 3, 2020 Anti-racism Resolution. 2 – I favor Measure TT which allows for an increase in the Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT). Piedmont has not increased the RPTT in 27 years. If approved, Measure TT will provide additional needed funding for ordinary current expenses of our City including, but not limited to, maintenance of city facilities, streets, sidewalks, and parks. And, the RPTT is one of the few ways Piedmont is able to generate income for essential services like police and fire. Estimated revenues will generate approximately $948,462 annually. Piedmont‘s current RPTT rate is lower than neighboring Berkeley or Oakland. Moreover, the proposed increase in the RPTT impacts a minimal number of residents on a one-time basis. Local Real Estate agents advise that an increase in our RPTT will not have an adverse effect on real estate values or demand. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: Friday is the deadline for districts to submit an in-person learning readiness survey. (PUSD has already submitted its response.) Districts that the county deems eligible to reopen will then receive a formal application to apply for a waiver. Those will be due September 17. Meanwhile, a much-anticipated fast track to get students with special needs back to school may be discussed at this week’s School Board meeting. HILARY COOPER 1 – My priority will always be the students. Re-opening our schools safely and effectively is going to be the most significant challenge our district has ever faced. It is incumbent on all stakeholders to come together at this moment to find a solution. I am very aware of the anxiety and fear that constrain our decisions, but we must continue to move forward with action. If we can acknowledge that there may not be a perfect solution for quite some time, then we can work on finding a solution. Beyond that, I think that our children’s social and emotional well-being must be addressed because no child can learn when they are struggling with motivation or self-esteem. Our students are missing the personal interaction of being in the classroom with their peers and teachers -- most especially our young learners. It is imperative that we find a way back into the classroom. 2 – Returning to in-person learning is a priority of my campaign. Many schools in the state have already applied for a K-6 waiver and that could afford us the opportunity to learn from each other and implement best practices. It’s important to let science drive our decisions, and studies have suggested that children under the age of 16 are far less likely to spread COVID than adults, and that it is unlikely for someone to contract COVID from surfaces. As we learn more and develop guidelines to ensure the safe return of our students to the classroom, I support applying for a special waiver for our youngest students. I am also interested in exploring how we can provide COVID testing for our students and teachers. We should strive to secure funding for such a program. We need to create a safe environment and get our kids back in the classroom. JASON KELLEY 1 – I’m running to: • Protect the whole community – students, teachers, families, and all Piedmont residents – by opening schools safely when the time is right. Families need as much stability as possible to plan for work and child care. • Make sure there’s a welcoming place for every learner in Piedmont schools. I want to see every student nurtured and challenged, whatever their ability, background or trajectory after graduation. • Plan carefully for what education will look like in the years to come. Students learn best in the classroom and need to be with peers to thrive, but lessons we’ve learned this year – and continue to learn – should help us prepare students for colleges and careers that may increasingly rely on remote learning and working. 2 – To apply for waivers to open in-person learning for elementary grades, schools must demonstrate compliance with a broad set of criteria designed to maximize safety. Applications must also show administrations have consulted with all parent and labor groups at each school site for which an application is being submitted. I think that consultation should be underway and ongoing. The principles that would guide me in making decisions about return to in-person learning if I were elected to the school board are: 1. Safety – ensuring schools have the resources to comply with health regulations to protect students, families, educators and the whole Piedmont community, 2. Stability – finding ways to make transitions stable and lasting so families can plan for work and childcare, and 3. Consensus – engaging in ongoing consultations to ensure all parties are heard so that any waiver application can be supported by the broadest range of stakeholders possible. HARI TITAN 1 – My focus would be a safe return to educational excellence. The spring 2020 incarnation of distance learning was more “crisis learning”. The new distance learning is working much better, however I see many issues needing a follow-up. I would focus on the correct scientific evaluation of the new distance learning model and would fight against positive spin. My focus would be on measuring learning loss of distance learning compared to classroom instruction as well as the social and emotional impact on students. After we got placed on the Governor’s watchlist, I began focusing on alternatives, like outdoor spaces and using larger rooms to teach subjects that need it most. Piedmont epidemiologist, Dr. Steve Sydney proposed that we do a small pilot study so we can figure out if students will actually comply with social distancing and masking rules in the classroom. I would work towards these goals while maintaining parent choice between hybrid and distance learning models based on what works best for each household. 2 – The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) announced Wednesday, September 2nd that it will begin the process of accepting waivers for classroom instruction. Alameda County waiver applications will have to pass through the county education office, the county health department, and then the state health department. The waiver process is rigorous (see: covid-19.acgov.org/schools. page. Applicants must involve labor, parent, and community groups in the reopening process. The entire process is expected to take weeks. In contrast, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) reports many applications processed, mostly from independent schools. As of September 4, a total of 332 elementary schools applied for waivers and all but 9 were approved. The CDPH approved 16 schools in Marin, 15 schools in Santa Clara, 10 schools in Contra Costa, and 5 schools in San Mateo. No school district in Alameda County has applied for CDPH approval. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent My priorities are: 1) Maximizing safe learning environments, 2) Creating opportunities to improve mental health, and 3) Maintaining fiscal responsibility. I believe it is critical during this crisis to focus on both student learning and mental health. From an educational perspective, many changes have been made to our distance learning process this fall that have improved the experience for our students. There is a consistent schedule, clear assessments, and accountability. While all would agree that in-person learning is preferred, teachers and administrators are working extremely hard to maximize student learning during this time of physical distance. We must not lose sight of the fact that distance learning is very hard on students and teachers from a mental health perspective. We need to create opportunities for all members of our community to make safe in person connections. I’ve suggested opening Witter Field for controlled student activities, such as small club meetings and more. My final priority is to maintain fiscal responsibility during and after the pandemic. 2 – I have been consistent and public in my views that we must prioritize bringing our youngest learners back for some in-person instruction. To apply for a waiver for elementary schools, districts must provide information that will show the ability to open sites safely. PUSD will detail the many precautions it plans to have in place that will protect both students and staff. For example, all students, even our youngest ones, plus teachers and staff, will be required to wear masks at all times. Students will be split into two cohorts to facilitate social distancing in classrooms. Extra cleaning protocols and proactive symptom screening will be diligently enforced. These precautions and others will help PUSD open our tri-schools safely so that our youngest learners, who may have the most challenges with distance learning, can safely receive some in person instruction. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

This School Board Election – Candidates Q&A Friday is the deadline for districts to submit an in-person learning readiness survey. (PUSD has already submitted its response.) Districts that the county deems eligible to reopen will then receive a formal application to apply for a waiver. Those will be due September 17. Meanwhile, a much-anticipated fast track to get students with special needs back to school may be discussed at this week’s School Board meeting. HILARY COOPER 1 – My priority will always be the students. Re-opening our schools safely and effectively is going to be the most significant challenge our district has ever faced. It is incumbent on all stakeholders to come together at this moment to find a solution. I am very aware of the anxiety and fear that constrain our decisions, but we must continue to move forward with action. If we can acknowledge that there may not be a perfect solution for quite some time, then we can work on finding a solution. Beyond that, I think that our children’s social and emotional well-being must be addressed because no child can learn when they are struggling with motivation or self-esteem. Our students are missing the personal interaction of being in the classroom with their peers and teachers -- most especially our young learners. It is imperative that we find a way back into the classroom. 2 – Returning to in-person learning is a priority of my campaign. Many schools in the state have already applied for a K-6 waiver and that could afford us the opportunity to learn from each other and implement best practices. It’s important to let science drive our decisions, and studies have suggested that children under the age of 16 are far less likely to spread COVID than adults, and that it is unlikely for someone to contract COVID from surfaces. As we learn more and develop guidelines to ensure the safe return of our students to the classroom, I support applying for a special waiver for our youngest students. I am also interested in exploring how we can provide COVID testing for our students and teachers. We should strive to secure funding for such a program. We need to create a safe environment and get our kids back in the classroom. JASON KELLEY 1 – I’m running to: • Protect the whole community – students, teachers, families, and all Piedmont residents – by opening schools safely when the time is right. Families need as much stability as possible to plan for work and child care. • Make sure there’s a welcoming place for every learner in Piedmont schools. I want to see every student nurtured and challenged, whatever their ability, background or trajectory after graduation. • Plan carefully for what education will look like in the years to come. Students learn best in the classroom and need to be with peers to thrive, but lessons we’ve learned this year – and continue to learn – should help us prepare students for colleges and careers that may increasingly rely on remote learning and working. 2 – To apply for waivers to open in-person learning for elementary grades, schools must demonstrate compliance with a broad set of criteria designed to maximize safety. Applications must also show administrations have consulted with all parent and labor groups at each school site for which an application is being submitted. I think that consultation should be underway and ongoing. The principles that would guide me in making decisions about return to in-person learning if I were elected to the school board are: 1. Safety – ensuring schools have the resources to comply with health regulations to protect students, families, educators and the whole Piedmont community, 2. Stability – finding ways to make transitions stable and lasting so families can plan for work and childcare, and 3. Consensus – engaging in ongoing consultations to ensure all parties are heard so that any waiver application can be supported by the broadest range of stakeholders possible. HARI TITAN 1 – My focus would be a safe return to educational excellence. The spring 2020 incarnation of distance learning was more “crisis learning”. The new distance learning is working much better, however I see many issues needing a follow-up. I would focus on the correct scientific evaluation of the new distance learning model and would fight against positive spin. My focus would be on measuring learning loss of distance learning compared to classroom instruction as well as the social and emotional impact on students. After we got placed on the Governor’s watchlist, I began focusing on alternatives, like outdoor spaces and using larger rooms to teach subjects that need it most. Piedmont epidemiologist, Dr. Steve Sydney proposed that we do a small pilot study so we can figure out if students will actually comply with social distancing and masking rules in the classroom. I would work towards these goals while maintaining parent choice between hybrid and distance learning models based on what works best for each household. 2 – The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) announced Wednesday, September 2nd that it will begin the process of accepting waivers for classroom instruction. Alameda County waiver applications will have to pass through the county education office, the county health department, and then the state health department. The waiver process is rigorous (see: covid-19.acgov.org/schools. page. Applicants must involve labor, parent, and community groups in the reopening process. The entire process is expected to take weeks. In contrast, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) reports many applications processed, mostly from independent schools. As of September 4, a total of 332 elementary schools applied for waivers and all but 9 were approved. The CDPH approved 16 schools in Marin, 15 schools in Santa Clara, 10 schools in Contra Costa, and 5 schools in San Mateo. No school district in Alameda County has applied for CDPH approval. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent My priorities are: 1) Maximizing safe learning environments, 2) Creating opportunities to improve mental health, and 3) Maintaining fiscal responsibility. I believe it is critical during this crisis to focus on both student learning and mental health. From an educational perspective, many changes have been made to our distance learning process this fall that have improved the experience for our students. There is a consistent schedule, clear assessments, and accountability. While all would agree that in-person learning is preferred, teachers and administrators are working extremely hard to maximize student learning during this time of physical distance. We must not lose sight of the fact that distance learning is very hard on students and teachers from a mental health perspective. We need to create opportunities for all members of our community to make safe in person connections. I’ve suggested opening Witter Field for controlled student activities, such as small club meetings and more. My final priority is to maintain fiscal responsibility during and after the pandemic. 2 – I have been consistent and public in my views that we must prioritize bringing our youngest learners back for some in-person instruction. To apply for a waiver for elementary schools, districts must provide information that will show the ability to open sites safely. PUSD will detail the many precautions it plans to have in place that will protect both students and staff. For example, all students, even our youngest ones, plus teachers and staff, will be required to wear masks at all times. Students will be split into two cohorts to facilitate social distancing in classrooms. Extra cleaning protocols and proactive symptom screening will be diligently enforced. These precautions and others will help PUSD open our tri-schools safely so that our youngest learners, who may have the most challenges with distance learning, can safely receive some in person instruction. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received. READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present a virtual screening of Suppressed 2020: The Fight to Vote, on Thursday, September 17 at 4:30 p.m. The film will be followed by a talk with voting rights advocate Valerie Morishige. Director Robert Greenwald’s urgent and timely film focuses on the Stacy Abrams gubernatorial campaign in Georgia, revealing the rampant voter suppression that affected the outcome of that 2018 midterm election. The film exposes the threat those techniques pose to elections throughout the U.S. in November this year. The 40-minute documentary illustrates the problems of long voting lines and uncounted absentee ballots, and how Brian Kemp, who was both a candidate for governor and the Secretary of State in charge of the Georgia election, put more than 53,000 voter registrations on hold until after the election. Eighty percent of those registrations were filed by Black residents. Not surprisingly, Kemp won the election and is now Governor of Georgia. Voter suppression efforts and failures in the voting process are not limited to Georgia or other “red” states. “We might have all of the fancy policies and politicians saying all the right things about voting in California, but in practice we fail,” said Morishige. “We need to make voting accessible for all,” she said. According to a blockbuster report by the American Civil Liberties Union and just published on September 2, the state of Georgia has been quietly — and illegally — purging hundreds of thousands of valid registered voters from the state rolls for the better half of a decade. Of the more than 300,000 names that were purged from the rolls, the study discovered that “198,351 Georgia voters who supposedly moved from their registration addresses who, in fact, have not moved at all, and therefore were wrongly purged, a 63.3% error rate.” This is a conservative estimate, however, because the report “left out of this list those voters whose addresses we were unable to confirm,” the ACLU explains. Poll workers, who are overwhelmingly seniors and highly vulnerable to the coronavirus, are underpaid and undertrained on the electronic equipment used in some precincts. Many businesses and public facilities can’t or won’t provide space for polling places because of stringent regulations and the added burden of the patchwork of local public health guidelines for COVID-19. These conditions have led to a scarcity in in-person voting locations, resulting in long lines and missed opportunities to vote. Voting rights advocate Valerie Morishige will be available for questions following a screening of the film, Suppressed 2020: The Fight to Vote, on Thursday, September 17. “Pull back that veneer and you see something really rotten happening. It’s almost like termites,” commented Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University, in the film. “We’ve got to understand: this stuff is bureaucratic. It’s mundane. It’s routine. But it is lethal.” Please join the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee for this fascinating, infuriating film and learn how to recognize and prevent voter suppression here in California. For details on how to watch the film and attend the post-film discussion on Zoom, go to the ADFS website at diversityfilmseries.
articles.title: Diversity Film Series opens fall with Sept. 17 film on voting ills

articles.text: Back in 1776, only select people had the right to vote: white men age 21 and older who owned land. Today all U.S. citizens age 18 and older can vote. So many more people have the opportunity to vote now, compared to 1776. Casting a ballot should be encouraged because it is not only a legal right, but also a privilege that many people do not have worldwide. When people have the chance to be heard, they should take the opportunity and an active role in our nation’s democracy by voting. For many years women, people of color, those who lived in poverty, or those who were uneducated were forbidden to vote. People in our nation’s history devoted considerable time and effort to fight for the right to vote. In the mid-19th century, many courageous women fought for suffrage, often sacrificing their safety and freedom as they were threatened, beaten, or arrested. It was not until 1920 that women were finally allowed to vote, a right that was legally recognized and added as the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Yet, according to The Washington Post, about 100 million people who were eligible to vote in 2016 did not vote and “[r] oughly 43 percent of eligible voters didn’t bother filling out a ballot”. That is a lot of people who gave up their vote. Americans only get to vote every four years for President, a person who has enormous influence and power over the well-being of our nation. Since the President can impact a person’s everyday life, voting can help choose someone best fit for the country. If people who did not vote are dissatisfied with certain policies or political leaders, they should take an active role so that their vote could work toward securing positive changes. In the end, voting should be highly encouraged because our ancestors had to fight for the right for all Americans to cast their ballots on election days. We are very privileged to be able to vote. Adding our voices to our nation’s decisions is a privilege and duty, and all American citizens should be encouraged to vote. Eileen Liu is an eighth grade student at Piedmont Middle School.
articles.title: ESSAY Americans need to take part in decisions that govern our land by voting

articles.text: LWV to host Sept. 20 discussion with polling expert Amy Simon The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host an event on the credibility and mechanics of election polling with Amy Simon, a founding partner of Goodwin Simon Strategic Research. This free event will be live-streamed on the League’s YouTube channel from 4:00-5:00 p.m. on Sunday, September 20. With the November election close at hand, viewers will learn how polls are constructed, fielded, and analyzed, and will have a better understanding of how to interpret them. A founding partner at Goodwin Simon Strategic Research, a national public opinion research firm, Amy Simon brings more than three decades of political experience to her work as a pollster and communications strategist. She conducts public opinion research on a variety of public policy issues domestically and globally. She has special expertise in conducting innovative qualitative and quantitative research on socially controversial and emotionally complex issues, with particular attention to developing effective messaging that has yielded a winning record on ballot measure campaigns. Simon is one of the leading architects of the freedom-tomarry messaging that helped propel voters in Maine and Washington state to support allowing marriage for same-sex couples in the 2012 elections. She has also Polling expert Amy Simon helped craft winning strategies on abortion, marijuana, medical aid-in-dying, climate change, insurance reform, and medical malpractice. With support from the David and Lucile Packard Foundation, Amy and her frequent collaborator, Robert Perez of Wonder: Strategies for Good, co-wrote Heartwired: Human Behavior, Strategic Opinion Research and the Audacious Pursuit of Social Change, a strategy guide to share lessons learned from their decades of experience on the front lines of social change. Their new, integrated approaches to audience research, storytelling, and persuasive communication have supported historic wins. In the guide, they share stories, tools, and some secrets of success
articles.title: Can you trust the polls?

articles.text: Mackie McDonald, Tennis; A’s playoff run ahead; Oakland Roots returns Photo courtesy of USOpen.com Mackenzie McDonald (left) made it to the quarterfinals of the U.S. Open with Christopher Eubanks as his doubles teammate. Piedmont’s Mackie McDonald stayed alive at the U.S. Open in New York after getting eliminated from the tennis singles’ bracket in the opening round last week. Playing with doubles partner 24-year old Christopher Eubanks, they won their second-round match, 6-3, 6-2, against Ben McLachlan and Luke Bambridge on Wednesday, September 2. The following day they beat Marcus Daniell and Philipp Oswald in the Round of 16, 7-6 (5), 6-3. In the Quarterfinals on September 5, McDonald and Eubanks lost to the No. 3 ranked team of American Rajeev Ram and England’s Joe Salosbury, 6-2, 7-6 (5). The next Grand Slam tournament is the French Open, which will begin September 27. McDonald could also appear in the Internazionali BNL of Italy, an ATP tournament that runs from September 14-21. A’s No. 3 in American League The Oakland A’s are distancing themselves from the Houston Astros and are No. 1 in the American League West division. They hold a 5-1/2 game lead as of September 8 and are the No. 3 seed heading into the 2020 Major League Baseball playoffs with a 24-14 record. The MLB’s 2020 seeding system qualifies the top top-eight teams to playoffs, similar to the National Basketball Assn. They currently are in the midst of a 5-game series with the Astros. The regular season concludes on September 27. The Giants are still in the hunt for a wild card berth as the No. 7 seed with a 21-21 overall record. They have a half-game lead over the No. 9 seeded Colorado Rockies. Oakland Roots soccer is back Professional soccer is back in Oakland… Well, sort of. The brief two-game fall schedule is already halfway done, after the Oakland Roots beat the Los Angeles Force 2-0 on the road last Sunday, September 6. Their next game will be played in Southern California on September 13 against the California United Strikers. A win would solidify the top spot in NISA’s postseason tournament, starting September 21. Some bigger news for Roots fans is on the way this week. Multiple news agencies have confirmed that Oakland is leaving NISA, a Division 3 league, and moving up to Division 2 in the USL Championship. Those game are telecast on ESPN’s streaming service and considered a pipeline toward Major League Soccer expansion. The deal to join USL is monumental toward building a stadium in Oakland now that a planned USL organization for Concord fell through. Residents there voted against a 15,000-seat stadium in favor of a 5,000 capacity. The Roots are expected to make their formal announcement later this week. Photos courtesy of Oakland Roots The Oakland Roots soccer team won its fall opener 2-0 over the LA Force. The bigger news is they are joining a larger and better league in the USL Championship.

articles.text: Primoz Roglic jumps to the top of classification Don’t look now; the favorite has made his way to the front. 30-year old Primoz Roglic of Slovenia was mentioned as the Vegas favorite in our Tour de France preview a couple of weeks ago. The Slovenian won Stage 4 to put himself in second place overall. Several days later, he was 2nd in the Stage 9 mountain course on September 6 to become the overall leader, proudly wearing the yellow jersey to the delight of his countrymen. After Stage 10 on September 8, Roglic holds a 21-second lead over 2019 champion Egan Bernal. In last week’s story, Frenchman Julian Alaphilippe held the yellow jersey after Stage 4. He since has fallen far behind to 41st with a 52-minute, 9-second deficit due to a time penalty he received for an illegal feed during Stage 5. Virtually out of it, he says that he did not expect to compete for the jersey this year. “I never expected to repeat what I did last year. Last year was an exceptional season and an exceptional Tour de France,” said Alaphilippe in a story with Cycling News. After Alaphilippe, England’s Adam Yates held the top spot over Roglic until Stage 9, when he relinquished 54 seconds and subsequently fell to No. 8 in classification. As mentioned last week, the mountains are proving to be the changing ground when it comes to advancing or falling behind in the General Classification (overall standings). On Stage 9, Roglic and stage winner Tadej Pogacar distanced themselves from Yates up the double-digit gradient ascent of the Col de Marie Blanque. Looking ahead, four succesPhotos courtesy of CyclingNews.com Slovenia’s Primoz Roglic gained the yellow jersey after a mountain course on Stage 9. 2019 champion Egan Bernal is in 2nd place 21 seconds back. sive mountain courses come on Stage 15 (174.5 km) on Sunday, September 13, followed by rest day on Monday, then Stage 16 (164 km), Stage 17 (170 km), and Stage 18 (175 km). If Colombia’s Bernal or Pogacar, a fellow Slovenian, make a push for the yellow jersey, it’ll likely will take place during the mountain runs. CURRENT STANDINGS 1. Primoz Roglic (Jumbo-Visma) - 42:15:23 2. Egan Bernal (INEOS) - +:21 3. Guillaume Martin (Cofidis)- +:28 4. Romain Bardet (AG2R) - +:30 5. Nairo Quintana (Arkea-Samsic) - +:32 6. Rigoberto Uran (EF Pro Cycling) - +:32 7. Tadej Pogacar (Team Emirates) - +:44 8. Adam Yates (Mitchelton-Scott) - +1:02 9. Miguel Angel Lopez (Astana) - +1:15 10. Mikel Landa (Bahrain - McLaren) - +1:47 Julian Alaphilippe held the top spot until receiving a time penalty in Stage 5. adej Pogacar won the Stage 9 mountain course. He is a rider to watch in Stages 15-19, all mountain tracks.

articles.text: Staff Photos The Five Lakes Trail of Alpine Meadows in north Lake Tahoe provides a 1,100-foot climb to a group of alpine lakes. Figuring out how to hike recently is an ongoing battle with smoke still settling around California. Even when traveling outside of the Bay Area, frequently tracking the changes to air quality is important. Temperatures began to scorch the East Bay last weekend, but Lake Tahoe and the surrounding Tahoe National Forest provided a brief escape from triple-digit heat and poor air quality. Which ranged all the way to nearly 200 on the Air Quality Index. But at North Lake Tahoe the air was consistently clear – and clean. Our Sunday morning the AQI was 57, though this writer did not experience affects from the smoke. Here are some guidelines to hiking during fire season and COVID-19: • Track air quality the day prior and morning of your hike. • Consider multiple locations given that smoke travels. • Always bring a mask, COVID is ongoing. • Check specific park websites for limitations, restrictions, or closures. • No large groups. Park officials request no groups over four. Some back-country hikers will search hours to find a location like Five Lakes, but with an hour’s worth of walking, the trail brings you to one of the most picturesque day hikes in California. Alpine Meadows is principally a ski resort community just south of Squaw Valley along Bear Creek on Alpine Meadows Road. The Five Lakes Trail is a 4.95- mile hike in total but provides around 1,100 feet of elevation gain in Tahoe National Forest’s Granite Chief Wilderness. Although a brief trail, it’s a good location for acclimating at altitude. The hike started at an elevation of 6,450 feet and topped out at near 7,600 feet. The trail connects with the historic Pacific Crest Trail. The trail goes on the southern ends of the KT-22 and Squaw One of the five accessible lakes, this is among the three in which you can swim. In the back is Squaw Peak. mountain peaks. To your left will be views of the pine tree-covered mountains of Scott Peak and the mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak. But given its location – surrounded by resorts and tourist destinations of Truckee, Tahoe City, Kings Beach and other North Lake Tahoe destinations – this hike can be a traffic jam. We passed 105 other hikers on the way to the summit and another 51 on the way back down, an average of 32 people per mile. This means your mask, along with some patience, is of utmost importance. Long portions of the hike are less than six-feet wide, making you stepping aside for groups a certainty. I passed at least three groups with more than 10 people, and many families with children miserably making their way up the mountainside. Faster hikers may find themselves behind slower traffic without a clear pathway around. But at the summit, a group of five alpine lakes are waiting for you. Despite the foot traffic and patience required to reach them, you can easily find your own area on one of the three swimmable lakes. Three of them had people cooling off in the water. Finding all three lakes could be tricky for some. The largest lake is near the main trail. Hugging its eastern shore brings you to another interconnecting lake, This lake is more marshy and un-swimmable, but equally as picturesque. Pictured is the first lake upon your arrival to the summit. The hike takes you under a tramway toward the summit of KT-22 above Alpine Meadows. A view of Ward Peak on the right.

articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department’s registration for the next session of fall programs opened up today, Wednesday, September 9 at 8:00 a.m. for residents. The classes begin on September 21 and will include some safe and fun in-person classes and sports. Most programs will be in three-week long camps in stable pods of 12 campers each, with social distancing and shared equipment only among pod members of each pod. Class registration is on an individual day-to-day enrollment, without participants being put into pods. Pick and play classes operate with strict social distancing under the county restrictions for “Outdoor Non-Contact Fitness” classes. Another option is to bring your own pod for Camp Games with Michael Murphy. All programs require mask wearing and temperature screenings. For more information call 420-3070, or see: www.apm.activecommunities.com/piedmontrecreation/Activity_Search. Current programs offered are: 3-Week Camps Soccer Camp Baseball Camp Art and Action Triple Threat Basketball Flag Football Multi-Sport Camp for Middle Schoolers Jr. Fencing Team Breakdancing and Grooves Dance Camp Camp Smart Start Plug and Play 1-Day Classes Move & Groove Yoga Teen Yoga Camp Games with Michael Murphy Qi Stretches (adults) Agility, Coordination & Fun Bike Fun Hip Hop Dance Another of the three alpine lakes. where you also can swim. Perhaps the most hidden lake is just east. Staying on its eastern shore takes you to an open ridgeline where you’ll find the green valley of Alpine Meadows below you. The first mile of the trek has ab elevation gain of 660 feet, 430 of which is in the initial half mile, followed by a quick gain of 200 feet up two switchbacks. The next mile mostly levels out, gaining another 370 feet to the group of lakes. Most of your journey is in open space, so prepare with sunscreen and proper hydration. According to Granite Chief Wilderness officials, camping at the Five Lakes Basin – 600 feet away from the lakes’ shorelines – is allowed without the need of acquiring wilderness permits. Proper food storage and gas-powered stoves are required. San Francisco Chronicle outdoor writer Tom Stienstra ranked Five Lakes in 2012 as No. 10 on a list of the best hikes at Tahoe. Trailhead: Look for this sign off of Alpine Meadows Road to start your hike.

articles.text: Big Basin Redwoods State Park in San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties confirmed on Friday, August 28 that many of the famous old-growth redwood trees throughout the park remain healthy. Further assessment must be done to determine the extent of damage to trees from the CZU Complex Fire. Park officials state that their most famous grove, the “Mother of the Forest” and “Father of the Forest” were impacted but “generally healthy.” “Based on its initial appearance, the Mother of the Forest and the Father of the Forest trees were both affected by the wildfires but remain generally healthy. The Auto Tree sustained moderate to extensive fire damage but remains standing. Old growth stands in the vicinity of the entrance road and lower campgrounds appear to have experienced a range of fire intensities, with the upper crowns of some trees burned while other trees remained unburned. Additional assessments still need to be done to understand the health of these trees,” according to the park’s press release. The Mother tree has a 70-foot circumference and height of 329 feet make it a frequent visit for tourists. Another tree of mention, the Auto Tree, stands with a hollowed out interior and is a famous photo op in the park. Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating back to 1902 and preserves some Redwood Trees that are more than 2,000 years old. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 of old-growth Redwood Trees. The old growth trees itself are known to be resilient. The trees within Big Basin, in particular, have experienced burns before. Despite some trees losing its canopies, they will make a return in time. That’s what makes the trees in Big Basin vastly different than the third- and fourth-generation redwoods at Joaquin Miller and Redwood Regional here in the Oakland Hills. “Old-growth redwoods have Photo courtesy of San Mateo County Parks Twitter Big Basin Redwoods State Park officials wrote in an official statement that many of its old growth redwood trees are “generally healthy” in spite of the CZU Complex Fire. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. The Mother of the Forest, the park’s oldest tree, is still standing. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. Another of the older trees in the park, the Father of the Forest, is also confirmed to be intact. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. Gov. Newsom stands within the “Auto Tree”, visibly burned, but still upright. experienced fire many times over the centuries, as evidenced by fire scars and dendrochronology. Mature coast redwoods’ thick bark and unique chemical composition make them highly resistant to fires,” according to a Big Basin statement. The CZU Complex Fire remains at 43 percent containment with 85,218 acres burned. Due to the fires in San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties the following parks and campgrounds remain closed: Año Nuevo State Park, Bean Hollow State Beach, Butano, Pescadero, Pigeon Point Light Station State Historic Park, Pomponio, Portola Redwoods, San Gregorio, Big Basin Redwoods, Castle Rock, Henry Cowell Redwoods, Wilder Ranch. Other fires Although the CZU sizably less acreage than the LNU and SCU complexes, it has the least containment of the three with the LNU at 69 and SCU at 70 percent containment as of Tuesday afternoon. The LNU has 375,298 acres burned and ranks third largest wildfire in California history; the SCU containment has ravaged 390,157 acres, ranking second in state history. The LNU has destroyed 1,288 buildings. Cal Fire officials announced that at least 274 homes were razed in Napa County, 268 in Solano County, and 118 in Sonoma County. Photo courtesy of Associated Press. Governor Gavin Newsom visits Big Basin Redwoods Park to see the fire damage. The SCU has burned down 120 structures through five different counties: Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Joaquin, Merced, and Stanislaus. Although no historic structures were burned, fires reached the Lick Observatory on August 20—but have since been contained without damage to the observatory.
articles.title: Big Basin park officials address old-growth tree concerns
