articles.text: Each week, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English invites playwrights to join him for a half-hour conversation about their craft, the sources of their inspiration, and the future of theatre. On August 28, English invited playwright Betty Shamieh to discuss her work, what it takes to get a play produced, and how the world of theatre will change in the post-pandemic world. Shamieh is also an author, screenwriter, and actor, and has written 15 plays. Born in San Francisco, she holds degrees from Harvard University and the Yale School of Drama. In 2004, she was a Clifton Visiting Artist at Harvard University and the following year was selected as a Playwriting Fellow at Harvard University’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Studies in 2005. She currently is a professor at Marymount Manhattan College Playwright Betty Shamieh in New York City. She also serves on the Screenwriting/Playwriting Advisory Board for the New York Foundation for the Arts and is working on a commission from Time Warner Second Stage Theatre. SF Playhouse’s Fireside Chat conversations are available on Youtube and have a runtime of approximately 50 minutes. You can view the chat at https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=uxFpxLyoqiU&feature=youtu.be.
articles.title: SF Playhouse fireside chat with Betty Shamieh

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre is presenting Romantics Anonymous online on Saturday, September 26 at 1 p.m. Directed by Emma Rice, the play is based on the film Les Emotifs Anonymes, written by Jean-Pierre Ameris and Philippe Blasband. Wise Children, Bristol Old Vic, and Plush Theatricals will produce Rice’s critically acclaimed musical adaption of Romantics Anonymous, performed at Bristol Old Vic and broadcast live, direct to homes. The play’s protagonist, Angélique, is a gifted chocolate maker crippled by social anxiety. Jean-René is the boss of a failing chocolate factory. Angélique is so timid, she faints when people look at her; Jean-René so awkward he relies on self-help tapes and is prone to embarrassing sweating. When Angélique takes a job in Jean-René’s struggling factory, a fragile love affair unfolds. Factory owner Jean-Rene is played by Dominic Marsh, and Angelique is played by Carly Bawden. The cast also includes Marc Antolin, Philip Cox, Joe Evans, Natasha Jayetileke, Joanna Riding, Lauren Samuels, and Gareth Snook. Lyrics are by Christopher Dimond, and music by Michael Kooman. Rep 7-Play season subscribers will get free access to Romantics Anonymous. Log in to your account to renew online or select the Rep 7-Play subscription package of your choice. You must subscribe to the Rep 7-Play package by 5 p.m. on September 23 to get free access to Romantics Anonymous. On September 25, you’ll receive an email from Ticket Co with your unique reference code for the live broadcast. If you subscribed to a 2021 Rep 7-Play package before September 2, you’ll receive an email from Berkeley Repertory Theatre asking if you’d like to see Romantics Anonymous.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep presents Romantics Anonymous on Sept. 26

articles.text: Antioch Dunes Evening Primrose, on the federal endangered species list, can be seen at the Botanic Garden in Tilden Park. The East Bay Regional Parks Botanic Garden in Berkeley’s Tilden Park is open by reservation to individuals and households for up to five individuals per reservation. The Botanic Garden is a living museum of California native plants. The sizeable 10-acre garden is a sanctuary for many of the state’s rare and endangered plants and a place for visitors to wander among trees, shrubs, flowers, and grasses from plant communities throughout California. The garden is now open on Saturdays, Sundays, Tuesdays, and Thursdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Same-day reservations are not available. The maximum number of visitors per open day is 120 visitors. When making a reservation: please provide your name, phone number, email address, home address, and the number of individuals in your reservation. Social distancing requirements are in full effect at the garden, and visitors must wear a mask at all times. articles.text: From a Yuja Wang-inspired “fashion show” to performances by Kay Stern and other top Bay Area musicians, the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will host a virtual Telethon this Sunday, September 13 from 12-8 pm. The event will launch their 2020-21 season of concerts. Admission to the Virtual Telethon is free, with performers and presenters encouraging viewers to make donations throughout the day. The CMS of SF Virtual Telethon will be a day of entertainment and fun, featuring performances and presentations - all with a musical twist. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, September 9, 2020 Arts & Entertainment SF Playhouse fireside chat with Betty Shamieh By Allyson Aleksey Each week, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English invites playwrights to join him for a half-hour conversation about their craft, the sources of their inspiration, and the future of theatre. On August 28, English invited playwright Betty Shamieh to discuss her work, what it takes to get a play produced, and how the world of theatre will change in the post-pandemic world. Shamieh is also an author, screenwriter, and actor, and has written 15 plays. Born in San Francisco, she holds degrees from Harvard University and the Yale School of Drama. In 2004, she was a Clifton Visiting Artist at Harvard University and the following year was selected as a Playwriting Fellow at Harvard University’s Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Studies in 2005. articles.text: Opera San Jose is presenting its resident artists in a showcase, allowing audiences to get to know them better while enjoying their talents. The showcase is a popular annual event that features music, song, and celebration while welcoming the opera’s newest company of resident artists. Opera San Jose recently created a video recording studio that can double as rehearsal and performance space and is used for live-stream. Singers will be tighter-knit than usual, living and rehearsing as a pod, in order to do so safely. articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players has announced plans for two new series of virtual concerts: Bach Shorts and Main Stage Concerts. The first series, Bach Shorts, consists of three one-hour, livestreamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of Bach’s Cello Suites. Three leading Bay Area cellists partner with professors, composers, and musicians from around the globe for uniquely personal performances and collaborations. The series begins this Sunday, September 13 at 4 p.m. with cellist Christopher Costanza, from the St. Lawrence String Quartet. He will perform Bach’s Second and Sixth Cello Suites and will partner with Stanford Professor Jonathan Berger, who will discuss the effect music has on the brain, hence the concert title, Bach and the Dancing Brain. On October 11, GCCP presents Bach Inspired, a concert featuring Jennifer Kloetzel, former cellist with the Cypress Quartet. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler. Elena will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. The Bach Shorts series concludes on Sunday, November 8 with Bach Connections, with cellist Robert Howard from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra. He will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. More Music Next Year After the New Year, Gold Coast Chamber Players plan to offer four live-streamed Main Stage performances with a feeling similar to what Gold Coast audiences have come to enjoy. Tickets for the Main Stage concert series will go on sale later this year. Bach Shorts tickets are $20 per concert, or $50 for all three performances in the series. Concerts are live-streamed via YouTube LIVE. Purchase online at www.GCCPmusic.com or by calling (925) 283-3728. See the website, gccpmusic.com, for regular updates about concert offerings, to purchase tickets and to make donations. Elena Ruehr, composer

articles.text: Composer Kev Choice The San Francisco Symphony has launched its summer 2020 digital programming, to include “Currents”, a four-part series. The performances are curated and hosted by Oakland Symphony conductor Michael Morgan in collaboration with San Francisco Symphony musicians and guest artists from the Bay Area. The Currents video series and companion podcast series explores the intersections between classical music and Chinese, Jazz, Mexican, and Hip Hop musical cultures. A concert will be performed every two weeks, and will illuminate the connections and ways that cultures influence each other and evolve together. The third episode, “From Scratch,” will explore the threads of Oakland’s dynamic Hip Hop culture. “Oakland is a city unafraid to speak up and speak out, with residents who loudly and proudly claim it as their own. I’m one of them. Art and activism go hand in hand here, and drive this city’s culture,” Morgan said. Emcee and lyricist Aima The Dreamer and pianist and composter Kev Choice describe how the culture of Oakland has shaped the genre of Hip Hop, The episode also features a new song by both musicians. Choice also discusses how he has been influenced by Bach, Stevie Wonder, Rakim, and A Tribe Called Quest. You can watch the episode at https://www.sfsymphony.org/. articles.title: SF Symphony explores Oakland’s Hip-Hop culture

articles.text: Each week, Oakland Symphony is making archival footage available to patrons while its doors remain closed due to the current health crisis. This week, Music Director Michael Morgan introduces Martin Rokeach’s Concerto for Piccolo and Orchestra and George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. Morgan describes Rokeach’s Concerto as a new and unusual work for a soloist and orchestra. “When Oakland Symphony flute player Amy Likar approached me about a Piccolo concerto, she wanted to commission from composer Martin Rokeach, I thought Jazz pianist Taylor Eigsti performs Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. Oakland Symphony flautist Amy Likar performs Martin Rokeach’s Concerto for Piccolo and Orchestra with the Symphony. the least we could do to encourage such enterprise was to play the resulting piece. It was so successful that we have another project with him in the works,” Morgan said. The newly commissioned piece will be an oratorio based on the Flint, Michigan “sit down” strike of 1936. The piece, titled Bodies on the Line, honors America’s labor movement and will debut in 2022. Rhapsody in Blue featured Jazz pianist Taylor Eigsti. “This is one of my favorite performances of this piece because of the way Taylor uses the various solos as points of departure and improvises on them. I have no doubt Gershwin would completely approve,” Morgan said. You can view the performances by visiting https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/repast/.

articles.text: A scene from Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma. Movie review by Chris Honoré Roma – the title is taken from the name of the middle-class barrio in Mexico City where director-writer Alfonso Cuaron grew up. It is, in the most wonderful, understated way. a poetic tribute to the women who raised him. Of all his films – Y Tu Mama Tambien, Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, Children of Men and Gravity – this is his most personal. It is also shot in 65mm black and white. The time is the early 1970s. The film opens with sudsy water thrown across a kaleidoscope of tiles. As the camera pulls back we see the maid/nanny, Cleo (Yoritza Aparicio), walking away, down a corridor, carrying a bucket and broom. She cleans the house, washes the clothes, nurtures the children, and brings them their meals, The family she cares for is composed of a mother, Sofia (Marina de Tavira), a father, Antonio (Fernando Grediaga), a grandmother (Veronica Garcia) and four young children. For the first hour of the film Cuaron allows us to dwell on the minutiae of their daily lives, all told from the point of view of Cleo. It’s obvious that she is indigenous, her skin a deep latté brown, her hair deeply black, while the family is as white as Nordic Europeans. Her wide face and deeply black hair say that while she is a member of the family, she also resides on its periphery. She soothes the children at bedtime, wakes them in the morning, and as the children cling to her it is obvious their bond is profound. Even when Cleo discovers she is pregnant, her place in the family is unaffected. What is significant is that the father of the child, Fermin (Jorge Antonio Guerrero), an obsessed kung fu neophyte and a coward, upon learning that Cleo is pregnant, immediately abandons her. In a movie theater, she sits and waits for him to return with ice cream. The second male to leave her is Antonio, a hospital doctor, who says he is going on a business trip to Quebec. In reality, he takes his mistress to a resort on the coast. Sofia, growing ever distraught, maintains a lie to protect her own children who begin to sense their father’s prolonged absence means more than they’re being told. And so we, the audience, are drawn into the very ordinary experiences of this family. Days pass. Months pass. Cleo grows larger. Still Antonio does not return. Life goes on. Patience required to know this family proves worthwhile. At first I was a bit distracted by the repeated wide screen shots. I wanted to move closer to Cleo. Observe the look in her eyes, the set of her mouth, see her protective hand placed on her expanding stomach. Gradually the camera does move closer. The pace begins to accelerate and Cuaron engages us, culminating in several scenes that are heartbreaking and breathtaking in their stark loveliness. Later, there is a long wide angle shot of two of the children wading out in the ocean, going too far, suddenly in trouble, and Cleo, who cannot swim, walking deliberately through the waves, on the precipice of being overcome, unwavering in her attempt to rescue them. It’s a wrenchingly beautiful moment, the connection between her and the children touchingly inviolable. Roma repeatedly asks the question: what is the relationship between the moviegoer and the story? What are our expectations? To select a film, sit in a theater, which is where Roma should be seen (not on a small screen of any kind), is aspirational. We want to be pulled into a narrative that in some way touches us, that exists somewhere on the spectrum of emotions. Cuaron’s movie asks a great deal of us. Wait. Watch. Allow the vignettes – and Roma is constructed of a series of tightly crafted moments – to build, allow them to be slowly fitted together. And then relish the final scenes that are so wonderfully human, each a revelation. Nominated for seven Academy Awards, Roma and Cuaron walked away with an Oscar for Best International Feaature Film. Clearly it was embraced by the Academy of Motion Pictures in acknowledging the fine work of its director, Alfonso Cuaron Roma (2018). In Spanish with subtitles Written and directed by Alfonso Cuaron. 2 hrs., 15 min.
articles.title: Roma a deeply personal story

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré It’s supremely difficult to make a good movie about adolescents. It’s the equivalent of trying to capture lightning in a bottle: years of emotional riptides, dramatic changes, layered with confusion and clarity and idealism. Which is why so many Hollywood teen movies seem shallow, trivial, and too often buried beneath an avalanche of stereotypes and clichés. Unexpectedly, It’s Kind of a Funny Story gets it just about right. It’s sweet and poignant, certainly relevant, and it’s aimed directly at young people who should instantly recognize the existential crisis of 16-year-old Craig (Keir Gilchrist) who is definitely one of their own. Craig, nudged by depression (he’s seeing a therapist, taking some Zoloft), feeling overwhelmed by the pressures of high school and the expectations of his parents, is stalked by thoughts of suicide. He heads toward the George Washington bridge in New York one morning, contemplating jumping. Instead he detours to Argeron Hospital, in Brooklyn, and, after a cryptic conversation with one of the Docs, unwittingly checks himself into the psych ward. Because the children’s ward is closed for renovations, he finds himself among the general population and quickly realizes – whoops! — perhaps it would be better if he just, like, went home. No harm, no foul. Plus, well, he’s got school the next day and a paper is due. He soon learns that he is there for a five-day evaluation. His parents, as it turns out, agree, and thus begins Craig’s very strange and enlightening odyssey. Writers and directors Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden walk a precarious line between the dark tragedies that define severe mental illness and the comedic and the light-hearted moments encountered by Craig as he navigates the ward. He is mentored, in a touching and heartfelt way, by Bobby (Zach Galifianakis), who has a wife and young daughter, and who not only has suicide ideation, but has tried to kill himself several times. And there’s Noelle (Emma Roberts), a love interest, who is hospitalized because she is a cutter. Craig is also gently guided and helped by the resident psychiatrist, Dr. Minerva (Viola Davis), who gives him increasing support and insight as he sorts out his feelings. While watching the relationship between Craig and Noelle grow, as they reach out to one another for understanding and tentative love, it begs an interesting question: can adolescents truly help one another through their long and often painful rite of passage? The answer is probably yes – and no. The fact is that turning to one another is the default response of most teenagers to the exigencies of growing up. Friends have an exalted status. Their counsel is weighted heavily. Adults, in contrast, have to tenaciously insert themselves into the lives of adolescents, no matter the reflexive resistance – which is what happens to Craig in a kind of wonderful way during his remarkable five days on the ward. It’s Kind of a Funny Story would be a great movie to see with a teenager, a son or daughter, hopefully resulting in a conversation post-screening. Know that the film strikes just the right note between the realities of teen suicide, and the ability of a young, intelligent kid to realize that the gestalt of emotions that seem so perplexing and contradictory can ultimately be understood and dealt with. It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Starring Keir Gilchrist, Emma Roberts, Zoe Kravitz, Zach Galifianakis and Viola Davis. Written and directed by Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: It’s Kind of a Funny Story a charming tale for parents and teens

He is mentored, in a touching and heartfelt way, by Bobby (Zach Galifianakis), who has a wife and young daughter, and who not only has suicide ideation, but has tried to kill himself several times. And there’s Noelle (Emma Roberts), a love interest, who is hospitalized because she is a cutter. Craig is also gently guided and helped by the resident psychiatrist, Dr. Minerva (Viola Davis), who gives him increasing support and insight as he sorts out his feelings. While watching the relationship between Craig and Noelle grow, as they reach out to one another for understanding and tentative love, it begs an interesting question: can adolescents truly help one another through their long and often painful rite of passage? The answer is probably yes – and no. The fact is that turning to one another is the default response of most teenagers to the exigencies of growing up. Friends have an exalted status. Their counsel is weighted heavily. Adults, in contrast, have to tenaciously insert themselves into the lives of adolescents, no matter the reflexive resistance – which is what happens to Craig in a kind of wonderful way during his remarkable five days on the ward. It’s Kind of a Funny Story would be a great movie to see with a teenager, a son or daughter, hopefully resulting in a conversation post-screening. Know that the film strikes just the right note between the realities of teen suicide, and the ability of a young, intelligent kid to realize that the gestalt of emotions that seem so perplexing and contradictory can ultimately be understood and dealt with. It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Starring Keir Gilchrist, Emma Roberts, Zoe Kravitz, Zach Galifianakis and Viola Davis. Written and directed by Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma. Movie review by Chris Honoré Roma – the title is taken from the name of the middle-class barrio in Mexico City where director-writer Alfonso Cuaron grew up. It is, in the most wonderful, understated way. a poetic tribute to the women who raised him. Of all his films – Y Tu Mama Tambien, Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, Children of Men and Gravity – this is his most personal. It is also shot in 65mm black and white. The time is the early 1970s. The film opens with sudsy water thrown across a kaleidoscope of tiles. As the camera pulls back we see the maid/nanny, Cleo (Yoritza Aparicio), walking away, down a corridor, carrying a bucket and broom. She cleans the house, washes the clothes, nurtures the children, and brings them their meals, The family she cares for is composed of a mother, Sofia (Marina de Tavira), a father, Antonio (Fernando Grediaga), a grandmother (Veronica Garcia) and four young children. For the first hour of the film Cuaron allows us to dwell on the minutiae of their daily lives, all told from the point of view of Cleo. It’s obvious that she is indigenous, her skin a deep latté brown, her hair deeply black, while the family is as white as Nordic Europeans. Her wide face and deeply black hair say that while she is a member of the family, she also resides on its periphery. She soothes the children at bedtime, wakes them in the morning, and as the children cling to her it is obvious their bond is profound. Even when Cleo discovers she is pregnant, her place in the family is unaffected. What is significant is that the father of the child, Fermin (Jorge Antonio Guerrero), an obsessed kung fu neophyte and a coward, upon learning that Cleo is pregnant, immediately abandons her. In a movie theater, she sits and waits for him to return with ice cream. The second male to leave her is Antonio, a hospital doctor, who says he is going on a business trip to Quebec. In reality, he takes his mistress to a resort on the coast. Sofia, growing ever distraught, maintains a lie to protect her own children who begin to sense their father’s prolonged absence means more than they’re being told. And so we, the audience, are drawn into the very ordinary experiences of this family. Days pass. Months pass. Cleo grows larger. Still Antonio does not return. Life goes on. Patience required to know this family proves worthwhile. At first I was a bit distracted by the repeated wide screen shots. I wanted to move closer to Cleo. Observe the look in her eyes, the set of her mouth, see her protective hand placed on her expanding stomach. Gradually the camera does move closer. The pace begins to accelerate and Cuaron engages us, culminating in several scenes that are heartbreaking and breathtaking in their stark loveliness. Later, there is a long wide angle shot of two of the children wading out in the ocean, going too far, suddenly in trouble, and Cleo, who cannot swim, walking deliberately through the waves, on the precipice of being overcome, unwavering in her attempt to rescue them. It’s a wrenchingly beautiful moment, the connection between her and the children touchingly inviolable. Roma repeatedly asks the question: what is the relationship between the moviegoer and the story? What are our expectations? To select a film, sit in a theater, which is where Roma should be seen (not on a small screen of any kind), is aspirational. We want to be pulled into a narrative that in some way touches us, that exists somewhere on the spectrum of emotions. Cuaron’s movie asks a great deal of us. Wait. Watch. Allow the vignettes – and Roma is constructed of a series of tightly crafted moments – to build, allow them to be slowly fitted together. And then relish the final scenes that are so wonderfully human, each a revelation. Nominated for seven Academy Awards, Roma and Cuaron walked away with an Oscar for Best International Feaature Film. Clearly it was embraced by the Academy of Motion Pictures in acknowledging the fine work of its director, Alfonso Cuaron Roma (2018). In Spanish with subtitles Written and directed by Alfonso Cuaron. 2 hrs., 15 min.

articles.text: Jennifer Aniston and Owen Wilson in Marley and Me. Movie review by Chris Honoré Marley and Me initially has all the signs of a filler film. You know, one of those saccharine movies that’s far from any reality being experienced by families today. When it comes to depicting suburban life in America, surreal is often the screenwriter’s default position. Consistently, there is a glow about these films, and often they leave the audience feeling a bit empty. But Marley and Me tries for more and surprises. Though it’s billed as a film about a sweet, ever disobedient Golden Lab, it proves instead to be about a couple, Jenny (Jennifer Aniston) and John (Owen Wilson), who adopt an irresistible pup, Marley, and then, over the next 12 years, go on to have three children, transforming their lives. Marley is the sixth member of a family and though his antics often dominate, making for some comedic moments, he never overwhelms what turns out to be a nicely told movie about the messiness and compromises involved in having children and keeping everything and everyone afloat. Marley, as it turns out, represents nicely all those aspects of life that seem impossible to contain. Shirttails are always slightly un-tucked. Nothing is ever symmetrical. The surprises, the unexpected, the maddening feel of things being slightly out of control, the arguments and moments of sadness and disappointment are all wrapped up with Marley. Kids will enjoy Marley and Me if they’re middle schoolers or older. The film does grow sad as time passes and Marley begins to age. But there is much to be said for this lighthearted film. For anyone who has let a dog into his or her life and has experienced the unconditional love offered each day by such a pet, well, Marley and Me is a must see. Marley and Me. Starring Jennifer Aniston, Owen Wilson and Eric Dane. Directed by David Frankel. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Marley and Me a sweet story of a Golden Lab

articles.text: During the dark days of life in a time of a worldwide pandemic due to coronavirus, some levity distinctly is in order. For fans of the English language, and those who can remember being taught the many parts of the language, here’s a little refresher, all based upon the well-worn joke, “A man walks into a bar….” • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • The past, present, and future walked into a bar. It was tense. An Oxford comma walks into a bar where it spends the evening watching the television getting drunk and smoking cigars. A dangling participle walks into a bar. Enjoying a cocktail and chatting with the bartender, the evening passes pleasantly. A bar was walked into by the passive voice. An oxymoron walked into a bar, and the silence was deafening. Two quotation marks walk into a “bar.” A malapropism walks into a bar, looking for all intensive purposes like a wolf in cheap clothing, muttering epitaphs and casting dispersions on his magnificent other, who takes him for granite. Hyperbole totally rips into this insane bar and absolutely destroys everything. A question mark walks into a bar? A non sequitur walks into a bar. In a strong wind, even turkeys can fly. Papyrus and Comic Sans walk into a bar. The bartender says, “Get out -- we don’t serve your type.” A mixed metaphor walks into a bar, seeing the handwriting on the wall but hoping to nip it in the bud. A comma splice walks into a bar, it has a drink and then leaves. Three intransitive verbs walk into a bar. They sit. They converse. They depart. A synonym strolls into a tavern. At the end of the day, a cliché walks into a bar -- fresh as a daisy, cute as a button, and sharp as a tack. A run-on sentence walks into a bar it starts flirting. With a cute little sentence fragment. Falling slowly, softly falling, the chiasmus collapses to the bar floor. A figure of speech literally walks into a bar and ends up getting figuratively hammered. An allusion walks into a bar, despite the fact that alcohol is its Achilles heel. The subjunctive would have walked into a bar, had it only known. A misplaced modifier walks into a bar owned by a man with a glass eye named Ralph. A dyslexic walks into a bra. A verb walks into a bar, sees a beautiful noun, and suggests they conjugate. The noun declines. A simile walks into a bar, as parched as a desert. A gerund and an infinitive walk into a bar, drinking to forget. A hyphenated word and a non-hyphenated word walk into a bar and the bartender nearly chokes on the irony.
articles.title: ENGLISH, ANYONE?

The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet My list of all the all-time greats begins with Johan Sebastian Bach. He wasn’t even on the YouTube list. How is this possible? My rationale is that the entire history of music would Stream of consciousness on substance vs. glitz be poorer if Bach had not written his six solo sonatas for violin. That alone should put Bach on the list. How could any listmaker overlook this stupendous musical monument and Bach’s legacy? Well, as I said, rationale does not exist. But media manipulation – that’s real big these days. The next monument to musical history was the Italian violinist Viotti. His contributions consisted of 29 violin concertos. These works changed the course of music history when Viotti introduced a completely new way of composing concertos. The second thing that he did was to establish the French school of violin playing which influenced music for more than 200 years. His pupils are in all of the history books. And as if these accomplishments were not enough, it was Viotti whose experiments resulted in the invention of the modern violin bow. He’s not on the list either. Fortunately the list does include the important names of Nicolo Paganini, Joseph Joachim, Pablo de Sarasate, Fritz Kreisler Jascha Heifetz and David Oistrakh. Every one of these players changed the course of music. In addition to what they did as players, they inspired countless composers to write music for them. The same cannot be said for the players of today. Of course, the players of today are obsessed with social media. And the gullible public is...well they are the gullible public. My avid readers must surely be interested to know the players who are still before the public and are on the list. Two of these are English violinists. The first one is notable for his public vulgarity, his galumphing around the stage wearing army boots, and decorating a black shirt prominently with safety pins. These antics have drawn praise in many quarters. The other English violinist who is making the rounds is also noted as a prominent teacher. When she was presented by a local university, I went to see what she had to offer. What a disappointment! I asked her what her philosophy of the violin is. She stared at me blankly. I also asked her if she had any “golden rules” to share with her audience. The answer was utter silence. How impressive is this? And the list goes on. Almost all of today’s prominent violinists are into social media. It is their image that is all-important. The women, usually very attractive, strut their stuff. The guys are also interested in their image; and they capitalize on it in any way they can. Don’t misunderstand me. Almost all of these players approach a perfection unknown in the past – but let’s be realistic. Try to put aside the social media glitz. Planting, the most obvious of the landscape elements, creates a wonderful soft, organic visual counterpoint to the necessarily hard straight lines of the surrounding building(s). pages.text: Wednesday, September 9, 2020 21 Features Landscape Architecture - Overview Trellises & Gazebos are part of the landscape concept. By Will Adams Part two in a series No matter how dense or “urban” a place is, it can be unified, softened, and made more inviting by thoughtful landscape treatment as an integral part of the design, coordinated with the architecture. With this in mind, walking through the city, it is clear that one of the key components that makes Piedmont such a beautiful place, is the successful landscaping. Many people think of landscape architecture as limited to planting. But it also of course includes everything outside of buildings: roads, parks, pools, fountains, plazas, walkways, benches, fences, retaining walls, play fields, tennis courts, monuments, and even lighting and signage. From manicured and formal to natural and informal— there are many “right” ways to select or design these various landscape components, but they really must be considered all together along with the architecture to form a clear design concept. Planting, the most obvious of the landscape elements, creates a wonderful soft, organic visual counterpoint to the necessarily hard straight lines of the surrounding building(s). It is often successful if there are complementary different scales or sizes of planting involved. This starts with large trees. In addition to providing shade, thoughtfully placed trees can visually frame and anchor the adjacent buildings. And street trees also have the wonderful effect of visually unifying the sometimes very different architectural building styles seen on a single street in a city like Piedmont. Smaller shrubbery can provide screening between uses, a soft background to open space, or a foreground and transition to yet smaller plantings. The small scale of potted plants, window boxes or hanging planters is also a way to introduce flowers and color to the garden or street scene. This kind of detail is also valuable to the community because it exhibits care and ownership Different scales of planting. — clearly it takes someone to plan and continually maintain beautiful landscaping. There are many kinds of fences and gates possible: stone, masonry, iron, stucco, and wood of different designs and finishes. The most successful of all these elements are clearly those that complement the materials and architectural style of the home to which they are a part. When neglected or treated as an afterthought, often the whole aesthetic of the property is compromised. This is also true of paving. There is nothing nicer than a front entry or private patio that has a paving material and pattern that complements and enhances both the adjacent building and its outdoor space. Fountains, sport courts, patios, and sculptures, must first be located in the right spot relative to a host of considerations, such as views, privacy, and connection to the building, before their detail design can be considered. Each one of these landscape elements is a topic in itself on which we will expand in future columns. articles.text: Whatever I have to say on any topic, there will be parallels. I will take one idea and cross-pollinate it over multiple perspectives. Right now, that idea is slow. If nothing, the current times have forced us to slow down. Roughly 30 years ago, the idea of Slow Food first gained a foothold in popular consciousness. Food grown and procured consciously and consumed with attention and awareness results in a healthy, satisfied, and whole mind, body, and spirit. These days, I am looking at design through the Slow lens. Not that I want all of my clients to have to wait a long time for their furnishings to arrive, or other design elements to be implemented and installed. But actually, sometimes I do. As I often remind clients and friends, it’s the rule of the Iron Triangle: Fast, Cheap, or Good. You cannot have all three. And frankly, if your emphasis is quality, you might as well let go of any attachments to cheap or fast. Similar to the Slow Food movement, a choice to emphasize quality, which often takes time and a bigger financial investment, will lead to you feeling more nourished. Your design, your home – everything will taste better. The photos accompanying this month’s column are from a designers’ tour at Studio Bel Vetro and an accompanying lunch at Reeve Winery in Healdsburg in 2019. The chandeliers perfectly demonstrate the values of Slow Design I am describing here. An artist at work at Studio Bel Vetro in Healdsburg. Studio Bel Vetro owners, the husband-wife team of Paulo DiLima (chief glassblower) and Lisa Spinella (artist).
articles.title: Focusing on Slow design

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, September 9, 2020 Focusing on Slow design By Laura Martin Bovard Whatever I have to say on any topic, there will be parallels. I will take one idea and cross-pollinate it over multiple perspectives. Right now, that idea is slow. If nothing, the current times have forced us to slow down. Roughly 30 years ago, the idea of Slow Food first gained a foothold in popular consciousness. Food grown and procured consciously and consumed with attention and awareness results in a healthy, satisfied, and whole mind, body, and spirit. These days, I am looking at design through the Slow lens. Not that I want all of my clients to have to wait a long time for their furnishings to arrive, or other design elements to be implemented and installed. But actually, sometimes I do. As I often remind clients and friends, it’s the rule of the Iron Triangle: Fast, Cheap, or Good. You cannot have all three. And frankly, if your emphasis is quality, you might as well let go of any attachments to cheap or fast. Similar to the Slow Food movement, a choice to emphasize quality, which often takes time and a bigger financial investment, will lead to you feeling more nourished. Your design, your home – everything will taste better. The photos accompanying this month’s column are from a designers’ tour at Studio Bel Vetro and an accompanying lunch at Reeve Winery in Healdsburg in 2019. The chandeliers perfectly demonstrate the values of Slow Design I am describing here. An artist at work at Studio Bel Vetro in Healdsburg. Studio Bel Vetro owners, the husband-wife team of Paulo DiLima (chief glassblower) and Lisa Spinella (artist). Chandelier crystals made of handblown glass, by Studio Bel Vetro. They are handmade and incorporate classical Murano-glass-blowing techniques. The lunch was a lovely and delicious Slow Food farm-to-table meal. Slow design is better for you, better for the local economy, and better for the planet. Emphasizing eco-conscious and local production, human-scale handmade techniques, and minimizing the carbon footprint, Slow design can be a socially conscious act. If you know me, you know that in addition to design, my passion is personal growth. Thus, I am also seeing the choice of fast design and fast food as equivalent to a spiritual bypass. When someone uses a spiritual bypass to get through a difficult time in their lives or to deal with confrontation, they are looking for a quick fix. Spiritual bypass is about doing things that may feel good or make you happy in the short term, They include glossing over difficulties with affirmations or going on spiritual retreats, while skipping the hard work of looking at underlying systems of feeling the grief or pain that might be underneath the issues one is facing, all of which mean slowing down. Spiritual seekers and homeowners both can benefit from slowing down. I am a person who has high reverence and regard for connection — to people, to process, and to quality of results, which is what we receive when we slow down and plug into what is true and real. It may be easier to order food delivered or order an entire room design from an online retailer, or to pull together with a quick meditation or prayer and avoid the deeper issues. But in the end, we will have to face the impact of our choices and be with ourselves. Which is why I am so emphatic about the importance of good, healthy food; spiritual practices that invite us to look deeply, connect, feel, grieve, and be reborn; and design that takes the values of quality and health into account to create spaces that support humanity and community, and that are as harmonious as possible with caring for our earth. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. Her approach to work and life has earned her firm numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s best and most sought after interior design agencies. For information see laura@lmbinteriors.com. Photos by Laura Martin Bovard A chef plates a Slow Food lunch at Reeve Winery in Healdsburg. Farm-to-table deliciousness is offered at Reeve Winery. pages.text: Wednesday, September 9, 2020 23 INSTRUCTIONS Chocolate Coconut Tart – delivering taste, texture… and looks Photo by Deborah Quok Chocolate Coconut Tart, a dessert that’s easy to make and delicious to eat. By Deborah Quok you like the chocolate. It’s early September in Piedmont and it is rough going outside for myriad reasons. There’s the pandemic, unhealthy air quality from wildfires, and an excessive heat wave happening as I type. If there was ever a time to rely upon preparing food with what is at hand, this is it. Using a dozen ingredients, this chocolate tart delivers on taste, texture, and is a looker. The crust is press-in and needs minimal use of the oven. I made it in a toaster oven, which avoids heating up the entire kitchen for a few short baking periods. The ganache is as easy as boiling water, well, heavy cream. Stir. Fill. Chill. Serve. Note: Do not use chocolate chips for the ganache. Chocolate chips are designed to not melt. Choose a chocolate you enjoy eating on its own. It is the primary flavor of the tart and important Easy Chocolate Coconut Tart Adapted from Bake or Break (crust) and Delish (filling) INGREDIENTS Coconut crust: • 1/2 cup unsalted butter, very cold and cut into 1/2” pieces • 3/4 cup unsweetened finely shredded coconut • 1-1/4 cups all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt • 2 tablespoons heavy cream, very cold • 1/2 teaspoon coconut extract Chocolate ganache filling: • 9 ounces semi-sweet chocolate, roughly chopped • 1/3 cup heavy cream • 1/4 cup sour cream • 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • Additional toasted coconut flakes for garnish, optional Prepare the crust: 1. Preheat oven to 350°F. Place the coconut in a single layer on a flat pan or dish. Bake until just golden, about 5 minutes in a toaster oven. Check frequently and stir as needed for even toasting. Set aside to cool completely. 2. Place the cooled coconut, flour, sugar and salt in the bowl of a food processer. Pulse a few times to mix. Add the chilled butter and pulse 8 – 10 times until the butter is the size of small peas. Add the chilled heavy cream and coconut extract and pulse another 4 – 5 times to fully incorporate. (This can also be done using a pastry blender, the 2-knives cutting method, or with your fingers.) 3. Transfer the mixture into a 9-inch round pie plate or tart pan with removable bottom. Spread it evenly, but with more around the edges. First press the crust up the sides of the pan, using your fingers, to firmly affix about a 1/ 4-inch edging. Press the remainder of the mixture evenly across the bottom. Using a flat-bottomed measuring cup or wide spoon will help with evenness and minimize melting the butter. 4. Bake in a 350° F oven for 15–18 minutes, until golden brown. Set aside, cool completely. Prepare the chocolate ganache filling: 1. Place chopped chocolate in a heat proof bowl. In a small pot over low heat, bring the heavy cream to a simmer. Pour hot cream over the chocolate and let stand 1 – 2 minutes, then stir to ensure the chocolate has melted. Add sour cream and salt, then whisk until completely smooth. 2. Pour ganache over the cooled crust and smooth the top with an offset spatula. Refrigerate at least 1 hour, until the filling is set. Add toasted coconut flakes as a garnish before serving. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. articles.text: Alyssa Maldonado, Veterinarian Technician, performs an initial examination on one of the 20 Riparian Brush rabbits temporarily housed at Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital while undergoing vaccinations against the Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV2). Oakland Zoo’s focus on species conservation now includes an effort to help prevent the possible extinction of the Riparian Brush rabbit. The sub-species is threatened by Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV2); a European-borne virus that has spread to many species of wild rabbit populations across the United States. The Oakland Zoo has partnered with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, California Department of Fish and Wildlife, U.S. Geological Survey, and River Partners, to conduct ‘rabbit captures’ in the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge in Modesto since August. Over the past three weeks, 20 captured rabbits were brought to Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital, where they received thorough physical exams and the RHDV2 vaccination. The rabbits are being closely monitored by Zoo veterinarians and staff to ensure that the vaccination has no adverse effects. Prior to this conservation effort, the RHDV2 vaccine has only been used on domestic rabbits, The current 20 rabbits serve as a safety trial for the use of the RHDV2 vaccine on wild populations. Monitoring of the rabbits at Oakland Zoo in the coming weeks will be key to predicting the success of more widespread vaccinations of this sub-species. “Conservation of species is very important to Oakland Zoo, both in captivity and in the wild. We, and all AZA-accredited zoos, play a unique role in conservation, in that we are able to use our extensive knowledge of animals and the care to also aid in saving those in the wild,” says Darren Minier, Assistant Director of Animal Care, Conservation & Research at Oakland Zoo. Following the monitoring period, if successful, the Riparian Brush rabbits will be returned to the wild at the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge. Oakland Zoo will then help administer vaccinations to an additional 200 rabbits in the wild to protect them from the Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease Virus. Rabbits are an essential part of ecosystems as herbivores and as a primary food source to other animals. This program will help maintain their place in the ecosystem. Oakland Zoo continues in the practice of rescuing and rehabilitating animals for release back into the wild. For more information visit www.oaklandzoo.org/conservation-society-of-california.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo fighting a different virus

articles.text: Like many other seasonal events across the Bay Area, this year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 27, will be a virtual celebration due to gathering restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival will feature a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encourages Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents and school district employees can email photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. Photos may be sent directly to Putzer at cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Submissions must include your name, category entered, email and home address. The deadline for photo submissions is Friday, September 18. Everyone who enters will get a participation ribbon and will be entered into a random drawing for a $60 gift certificate from Ace Grand Lake Nursery on October 5. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest is sponsored by the Piedmont Garden Club. Kids ages 14 and younger can download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. E-mail a copy of the project to cputzer@piedmont.ca.gov. [This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. For more infor mation, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/ harvestfestival.
articles.title: Harvest Festival goes virtual on Sept. 27

articles.text: A panel discusssion organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign and cosponsored by Piedmont Advocating Diversity Committee and League of Women Voters of Piedmont will take place on Thursday, September 24, 2020, 7-8:30 pm on Zoom. Register here: https://forms. gle/FQB4BG5mqU6YJqiA9 As part of the ongoing struggle to achieve racial equity and justice, integrating and diversifying our neighborhoods are essential tasks. A recent UC Berkeley report on Racial Segregation in the SF Bay Area (https://belonging.berkeley.edu/ racial-segregation-san-francisco-bay-area-part-5) demonstrates that residential segregation is alive and well in the Bay Area. How did we get here? What can we do about it? Join us for a Zoom panel addressing the history of racial segregation and housing in Piedmont, and steps that our city can take to achieve a more equitable future. FEATURING: Gloria Bruce Executive Director, East Bay Housing Organizations (EBHO). EBHO is the leading advocacy coalition promoting affordable housing in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. Irene Cheng Associate Professor, California College of the Arts, and co-editor, Race and Modern Architecture: A Critical History from the Enlightenment to the Present Carol Galante, Piedmont resident Donald Terner Distinguished Professor in Affordable Housing and Urban Policy, UC Berkeley, and Director of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation. Former Federal Housing Commissioner at the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development under President Barack Obama Moderated by Sarah Karlinsky, Senior Policy Advisor, SPUR (the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association)
articles.title: Racial Segregation and Housing in Piedmont: How Did We Get Here? What Can We Do About It?

articles.text: The city is looking for volunteers to serve on a Pedestrian-Bicycle Advisory Committee, which will assist in updating the current Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan (PBMP). The process is expected to begin in October and go through May 2021. The efforts of the committee will focus on assisting staff and city consultants with the development of the PBMP update, specifically in reviewing and providing feedback on the following materials: a community needs assessment, a draft action plan of recommendations, opportunities for public participation and input regarding the draft action plan of recommendations, a public draft of the PBMP update, and opportunities for public participation and input regarding the draft. City Council called out two specific groups it would like to be represented: Piedmont and Millennium High School students who reside in Piedmont, and former members of the Planning Commission, Public Safety Committee and CIP Review Committee. Interested residents may view the City Council resolution establishing the Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee, download the Application for Appointive Vacancy, and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall on or before 5 p.m. on Friday, September 25. Interviews with the City Council for the volunteer positions will be scheduled for Wednesday evening, September 30. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. For more information, contact the City Clerk’s office at 420-3040.
articles.title: High school students eligible to apply

articles.text: The Wellness Center has announced a Walk for Wellness as its annual fundraiser this year. It will take place from September 21-27, and is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Event co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener and Nicki Gilbert said that in future years Walk for Wellness will be a fundraiser that will bring the community together in person to celebrate the Wellness Center and advocate for student mental health. This year, participants will receive a Walk for Wellness visor and access to eight maps detailing various walks around town. “Families and small groups of friends should complete as many of the suggested walks as possible during the week of September 21 Everyone should post photos from their walks to @piedmontwellness on Instagram!” said Gilbert. “We hope to raise muchneeded funding for the Wellness Center while increasing awareness of the need for mental health services for our students,” Hohener added. Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one third of high school and one quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. For registration and donation information, visit www. piedmontwalkforwellness.org or email piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com. Photo by Zak Gilbert Walk for Wellness co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener (left) and Nicki Gilbert display the banner for this year’s event.
articles.title: Wellness Center annual fundraiser starts Sept. 21

articles.text: Once again, the bicycle team Linda and Marvin will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. By leading the way in global research, providing assistance for people with ALS through a nationwide network of chapters, coordinating multidisciplinary care through certified clinical care centers, and fostering government partnerships, The Association builds hope and enhances quality of life while aggressively searching for new treatments and a cure. Team Linda and Marvin will be riding Saturday, September 26 in their memory and we are soliciting your support to help our team exceed our fundraising goal for ALS research. Last year, through the amazingly generous donations of friends, family, and clients, we raised over $70,000 for ALS Research. The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. pages.text: Wednesday, September 9, 2020 25 City seeks volunteers for pedestrian-bicycle committee High school students eligible to apply By Allyson Aleksey The city is looking for volunteers to serve on a Pedestrian-Bicycle Advisory Committee, which will assist in updating the current Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan (PBMP). The process is expected to begin in October and go through May 2021. The efforts of the committee will focus on assisting staff and city consultants with the development of the PBMP update, specifically in reviewing and providing feedback on the following materials: a community needs assessment, a draft action plan of recommendations, opportunities for public participation and input regarding the draft action plan of recommendations, a public draft of the PBMP update, and opportunities for public participation and input regarding the draft. City Council called out two specific groups it would like to be represented: Piedmont and Millennium High School students who reside in Piedmont, and former members of the Planning Commission, Public Safety Committee and CIP Review Committee. Interested residents may view the City Council resolution establishing the Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee, download the Application for Appointive Vacancy, and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall on or before 5 p.m. on Friday, September 25. Interviews with the City Council for the volunteer positions will be scheduled for Wednesday evening, September 30. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. For more information, contact the City Clerk’s office at 420-3040. Wellness Center annual fundraiser starts Sept. 21 The Wellness Center has announced a Walk for Wellness as its annual fundraiser this year. It will take place from September 21-27, and is an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Event co-chairs KeriAnne Hohener and Nicki Gilbert said that in future years Walk for Wellness will be a fundraiser that will bring the community together in person to celebrate the Wellness Center and advocate for student mental health. This year, participants will receive a Walk for Wellness visor and access to eight maps detailing various walks around town. “Families and small groups of friends should complete as many of the suggested walks as possible during the week of September 21 Everyone should post photos from their walks to @piedmontwellness on Instagram!” said Gilbert. “We hope to raise muchneeded funding for the Wellness Center while increasing awareness of the need for mental health services for our students,” Hohener added. Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center provides confidential, free on-campus and online counseling to all Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Piedmont Middle School students. The Wellness Center helps students manage common emotional and social challenges of middle and high school including stress, depression, grief, family or friendship conflicts, and substance use concerns. The Garden Bench, 1882 Continued from page 2 recording and materials make it clear that the City’s Reach Code effort has been very careful and balanced and does not impose an undue burden on homeowners. Energy efficiency and electrification options, only required for certain renovations over $25,000 under the proposed Reach Codes, start at a few hundreds of dollars for the least expensive options, with financial payback within just a few years. State and City Code allow for substantial exemptions to the proposed Code provisions to ensure no unwarranted requirements. There is no Reach Code requiring replacement of your gas cooktop with an electric model. As an aside, many homeowners and top chefs prefer induction cooktops to gas. An electric induction cooktop heats faster and hotter, can sear, and adjusts as instantaneously as gas. I know, because we have had both in our home. We have induction now, and we will never go back. The electrification encouraged by the proposed Piedmont Reach Codes moves us towards a more resilient electrical grid. Rooftop solar reduces grid load as use and production are at the same location. The addition of home battery storage extends this local electricity production benefit to nighttime and cloudy days. The pairing of sufficient rooftop solar panels and home batteries also allows you to be immune to PG&E blackouts as well. Some fact-checking on natural gas vs. electric posted on FaceBook. 1. Most electricity we consume in Piedmont does not come from burning carbon. In Piedmont we have by default 100% renewable electricity. Even if one purchases from PG&E, the percent from fossil fuels is about 15%. The transmission (and distribution) losses are about 5%, not 35%, and gas system drilling, transmission and distribution losses are significant source of high global warming methane. 2. Cooking with electricity does not take more energy than cooking with gas. There appears to be some confusion concerning the laws of thermodynamics in the letter writer’s comment. “Warming up energy” is not wasted if you put your pot or pan on the burner, just as the heat from a gas burner is not wasted. Although conventional electric burner will take longer to warm up, the energy is not wasted. 3. Electric stovetops can provide all the cooking quality and flexibility of gas cooktops - without having an indoor source of combustion pollution. The author seems to not be aware of current technology (actually a 50-year old technology) called induction stoves. Induction cooktops heat 25-50 percent faster and distribute heat more evenly than radiant stovetops, and they offer quick, fine temperature adjustment. Induction cooktops are among the safest technologies for your kitchen, boasting high-end luxury appeal and unmatched energy efficiency. The appliance science used in these products has been perfected and fine-tuned for over 50 years. Natural gas cooking appliances can contribute to poor indoor air quality, especially when used without an exhaust hood. Gas stoves emit nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), and formaldehyde (HCHO), each of which can exacerbate various respiratory and other health ailments. –Steve Schiller Jesus at Bethany, watercolor, series 1886-1894 Editor: Really….a little fact checking would’ve shown that Mr. Joffe had all his facts wrong in last week’s Post. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Editor: We have been so fortunate to have Cory Smegal on the Piedmont School board that it would seem a foregone conclusion we need to elect her for a second term. I have listened to Cory at Parent Club meetings where she is able to articulate clearly and extensively on a myriad of issues facing the district. I have sat in Budget Advisory Committee meetings with Cory where her facility with numbers and deep understanding of district financials have proven invaluable when budgets were constrained. As we face new COVID-related budget challenges, her financial background will be even more critical in ensuring fiscally prudent decisions. She has a demonstrated record of working collaboratively with teachers, administrators and parents with a straight-forward style that is widely appreciated. articles.text: On Friday, August 28, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a shift from its statewide monitoring list to a color-coded four-tier blueprint for “Safe Reopening.” While the governor has set guidelines and restrictions, it is ultimately up to the Alameda County Public Health Office (ACPHD) on whether or not salons and barbershops can reopen indoors. On August 31, when asked if salons were permitted to reopen in the county, ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram did not specifically answer the question, but instead pointed to the office’s process in determining the safety of reopening. “We are evaluating next steps and options for alignment with the State, while ensuring a reopening plan that reflects the specific disease conditions and needs in Alameda County. In doing so, we are considering the risk, timing and cadence of reopening activities, as well as their downstream impact on local disease conditions that could limit future activities. We will issue another update this week on how we plan to proceed as we work through our options and concerns,” Balram said. In a revised list provided by Balram, hair salons and barbershops are listed as “permitted to open outdoors only, as of August 28.” But the most recent change came last Friday, September 4. Salons are now permitted to open indoors, at limited capacity, if they meet certain guidelines imposed by the ACPHD. The county public health department issued an eight-page reopening guidance update for businesses, including hair and barber services, on September 1, with a strict list of requirements for these personal services businesses to reopen. The requirements maintain that each business must: prepare and implement a COVD-19 site specific protection plan based on local and state industry guidance, train employees on COVID-19 prevention including symptom screening, face coverings and hygiene, implement symptom screening for all employees, develop and implement cleaning and disinfecting protocols, establish physical distancing guidelines, ensure compliance with face covering orders which require both stylists and clients to wear a mask at all times, including during washing. Services that would require a client to remove their face covering are prohibited. This includes eyebrow waxing, eyelash treatments, and removal of facial hair. Alameda County, as of Tuesday afternoon, is still in the purple tier, the most restrictive. In the greater Bay Area, only four counties are in the lesser “red” tier: San Francisco, Santa Clara, Santa Cruz, and Napa counties. Marin County was expected to be moved from “purple” to “red,” but the state opted to hold off on moving the county into a new category so that its coronavirus trends can be monitored for another week. articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission approved Autumn Blaze Maple trees as replacement of liquidambars on Bellevue Avenue. At the request of the residents at 60 Bellevue Avenue, the city’s Public Works staff met in December 2019 to review the street trees in front of their property. An outside arborist was called in to assess the condition of seven trees, three Liquidambar (Sweetgum) trees at 60 Bellevue, two Liquidambars at 64 Bellevue, and two Liquidambars and a Birch tree at 57 Bellevue. Kent recommended that city inspect adjacent trees if the streets, roadway, curb or gutter were to be repaired. If the roots can be pruned, then the trees could be saved. Across the street, at 47 Bellevue, a lone Liquidambar tree was approved for removal. The trees at 57 Bellevue are located “under high voltage lines,” Kent explained, which means they get severely pruned by PG&E. Because of that pruning, those trees have been recommended for removal. Residents at 60 Bellevue are currently planning a landscaping project, which is under review by the city Planning Commission. While all seven trees were assessed, Park Commissioners considered removing only three trees located at 60 Bellevue at the most recent Park Commission meeting, on September 2. “The applicant is requesting removal of these trees to accommodate the proposed construction, and proper replacement of the sidewalk, curb and gutter,” Kent said. One Liquidambar is causing substantial damage to the curb and roadbed, causing a depression, which is interrupting the drainage along Bellevue Avenue. It is expected that during the repair of the curb, substantial tree roots will be encountered from the mature Liquidambar. Following arborist recommendations, the root system needs to be exposed during demolition, and evaluation will be determined then if the tree can be preserved. Two species of trees were considered for the Bellevue block: Chinese Pistache and Autumn Blaze Maple. Both species are known to provide substantial shade and canopy, with impressive autumn colors. Chinese Pistache is a small to medium-sized tree, native to central and western China. The species is planted as a street tree in temperate areas worldwide due to its attractive fruit and autumn foliage. Autumn Blaze Maple, or Freeman maple, is a naturally occurring hybrid maple that is the result of a cross between Acer rubrum and Acer saccharinum. Wild specimens are found in eastern North America. Commissioner Jim Horner recommended the tree species Autumn Blaze Maple in place of Liquidambar, if the existing trees are to be removed. “The Liquidambar trees [on Bellevue] seem to have been doing well for a really long time. If the city is [trying] to gradually rotate out of Liquidambar to other species, the Autumn Blaze Maple is more consistent and would be a less dramatic change,” Horner said. Liquidambar tree branches can grow horizontal and vertical directions, which require considerable pruning. The recommendation to replace Liquidambar trees with Autumn Blaze Maple was also supported by Dave Frankel, former Public Works Supervisor. Commissioner Amber Brumfiel questioned whether residents were notified in a timely manner when asked to weigh in on which species tree they would like to see replace the Liquidambars. Commission Chair Patty Dunlap pointed out that the process will be gradual, and that the tree replacement at 60 Bellevue will take some time. “The street trees will take a long time to replace; it’s not going to happen overnight,” Dunlap explained. A motion was made to designate the Autumn Blaze Maple for Bellevue Avenue. Six commissioners were in favor of the motion, with Amber Brumfiel abstaining.
articles.title: Liquidambar trees on Bellevue may be removed

articles.text: Alameda County allows public pools to open After five months of closure, Alameda County swimming pools are now allowed to re-open under loosened shelter-in-place guidelines. The guidance came in a statement from Alameda County Public Health Department more than a week ago, on August 21. “[This] outdoor activity we are allowing to reopen is relatively low-risk,” Interim Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss said. This is the first guidance issued by Alameda County for the reopening of pools. The Piedmont Community Pool has remained closed due to COVID- 19, but has now been given the green-light to reopen. City staff is determining whether the conditions imposed by the order can be applied in a way that makes sense to reopen the pool. Recreation Department staff members had previously developed reopening frameworks based upon guidance from other health jurisdictions. The 56-year-old pool is showing its age and is leaking approximately 3,000 gallons of water each day. City Council has decided to place a measure on the November 3 ballot that aims to address these problems. Measure UU, a $19.5 million bond, would replace the three existing pools with two pools. The measure is supported by Mayor Bob McBain, councilmember Betsy Andersen, Recreation Chair Steven Roland, Board of Education member Sarah Pearson, and retired Beach School Principal Nancy McHugh. The September 8 City Council agenda will include an update from city staff on the feasibility of reopening the pool in its current condition. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer, Finance Director Michael Szczech, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand are currently working on a report that will be presented publicly at the meeting.
articles.title: City Council to consider reopening pool

articles.text: Unhealthy air quality conditions shrouded Piedmont this week as a trio of wildfires continued to blaze around the Bay Area. The Bay Area Air Qualit y Management Dist r ict (BAAQMD) extended a “Spare the Air” alert for the Bay Area, including Piedmont, through Tuesday, September 1. This marked 15 consecutive days of Spare the Air alerts, a bleak record for the agency. When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. Three fires caused by lightning strikes in mid-August are the cause of the unhealthy air quality. The SCU Lightning Complex, which has burned over 390,000 acres and has the largest footprint of the three blazes, is burning in rural Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. It was 70 percent contained as of press time. Fires in Napa and Sonoma counties, the LNU Lightning Complex, have proven to be the deadliest and most destructive. Five people have died, and 1,288 structures have been destroyed. CalFire reports that over 3,300 structures are still threatened, even as the fire is now 69 percent contained. With a size of 85,218 acres, the CZU Lightning Complex, between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, is the smallest of the three fires is the least contained. Cal Fire said that it was only 43 percent contained as of yesterday. One person has died in this wildfire. articles.text: Alameda County falls under most restrictive “purple” tier During a press briefing on August 28, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced new guidelines for reopening the counties that have previously been on the state watch list. The watch list has been replaced with a new, four-tiered color-coded reopening system based on coronavirus prevalence and testing rates. The new model is officially named “The Blueprint for a Safer Economy,” and its primary focus is to determine what businesses can and cannot open. “COVID-19 will be with us for a long time and we need to adapt,” Newsom said. The new model went into effect this week on Monday, August 31. “Counties fall into one of four color-coded categories depending on the number of positive COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents, and the percentage of tests that come back positive,” Newsom said. The four tiers, based on virus spread, range from widespread (purple), substantial (red), moderate (orange), and minimal (yellow). Alameda County is in the most restrictive, widespread “purple” tier. The county has 10.6 new COVID-19 positive cases per 100,000 residents, and a 5.6 percent positivity rate. Schools in the widespread tier aren’t permitted to reopen for in-person instruction, unless they receive a waiver from their local health department. As of August 31, counties in the widespread tier have been given clearance to open some businesses and activities with modifications. This includes all retail business, shopping centers, indoor hair salons and indoor barbershops subject to maximum capacity of 25 percent capacity. Alameda County Public Health Department however released a revised health order that limits hair salons and barber shops to open outdoor only. Gov. Newsom said that despite the roll out of this new model, individual counties can move slower than state guidelines allow. For example, both San Francisco California Governor Gavin Newsom and Napa counties were given the green light to reopen businesses indoors at 25 percent capacity. Napa County will move forward with the allowance, but San Francisco County has made no plans to loosen restrictions. They are the only two counties in the Bay Area with a less restrictive classification under the new reopening plan. The model also sets in place plans to reopen the majority of non-essential businesses. To move forward in the reopening

Gavin Newsom announced new guidelines for reopening the counties that have previously been on the state watch list. The watch list has been replaced with a new, four-tiered color-coded reopening system based on coronavirus prevalence and testing rates. The new model is officially named “The Blueprint for a Safer Economy,” and its primary focus is to determine what businesses can and cannot open. “COVID-19 will be with us for a long time and we need to adapt,” Newsom said. The new model went into effect this week on Monday, August 31. “Counties fall into one of four color-coded categories depending on the number of positive COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents, and the percentage of tests that come back positive,” Newsom said. The four tiers, based on virus spread, range from widespread (purple), substantial (red), moderate (orange), and minimal (yellow). Alameda County is in the most restrictive, widespread “purple” tier. The county has 10.6 new COVID-19 positive cases per 100,000 residents, and a 5.6 percent positivity rate. Schools in the widespread tier aren’t permitted to reopen for in-person instruction, unless they receive a waiver from their local health department. As of August 31, counties in the widespread tier have been given clearance to open some businesses and activities with modifications. This includes all retail business, shopping centers, indoor hair salons and indoor barbershops subject to maximum capacity of 25 percent capacity. Alameda County Public Health Department however released a revised health order that limits hair salons and barber shops to open outdoor only. Gov. Newsom said that despite the roll out of this new model, individual counties can move slower than state guidelines allow. For example, both San Francisco California Governor Gavin Newsom and Napa counties were given the green light to reopen businesses indoors at 25 percent capacity. Napa County will move forward with the allowance, but San Francisco County has made no plans to loosen restrictions. They are the only two counties in the Bay Area with a less restrictive classification under the new reopening plan.
