Tour de France: Julian Alaphilippe in yellow jersey through Stage 4 Photos courtesy of LeTour.FR Julian Alaphilippe holds the yellow jersey through Stage 4 after gaining the top spot in general classification in Stage 2. By Jonathan Comeaux The 107th edition of the Tour de France is underway, the latest start ever due to COVID-19’s world impact. Through Stage 4, Frenchman Julian Alaphilippe leads, wearing the yellow jersey in general classification. For Alaphilippe, his ascent to the top spot is a bit of a triumph after leading last year’s tour at Stage 19. A landslide across the roadway and allowed Egan Bernal to eventually take over the top spot. Alaphilippe made his way to the front by winning Stage 2’s 186-kilometer mountain course, placing 58th in Stage 3’s 198-km flat course, then finished No. 5 on Stage 4’s hilly course, a length of 161 km from Sisteron to Orcrerer-Merlette. Alaphillippe said he was hoping to win Stage 4, but he relinquished six seconds to No. 4 Tadej Pogacar, who many marked as a favorite this year. “I had the double goal to retain the yellow jersey and to win the stage. It would have been special to win a second stage. I have no regret because the team perfectly executed the plan. I gave it all and I’ve been beaten by someone stronger than me. Moreover, I’m happy with my shape even though it’s hard to compare with last year. We won’t be able to keep that rhythm for three weeks. Soon it won’t be up to us to control the race,” said Alaphilippe. Bernal, last year’s champion, was able to hang around the top-five in 2019 before his fortunate turn in Stage 19.Traiing by 17 seconds, he faces a trio of mountain courses from Stages 16-18. Looking ahead this week, Stage 5’s flat course likely won’t provide any headway for the top riders, unless something catastrophic happens – like a crash. Even then, the mostly downslope course will provide relatively even times. Stage 6 is classified as a hilly course from Le Teil to Mont Aigoual, but it is mostly flat until the final 17 km ascent. After a flat Stage 7, the mountain courses of Stages 8 and 9 could be where the climbers like Bernal or Pogacar make their move. Here is the current top 10: 1. articles.text: When Piedmont had fire alarm boxes Today, we’ll turn our attention to some of Piedmont’s more recent history. Readers of a certain age may remember fire alarm boxes. Before telephones were considered reliable, and before every house had a telephone, the fire alarm box was the main way to summon the fire department. Piedmont maintained more than 50 fire alarm boxes on street corners. To report a fire, you ran to the nearest fire alarm box, lifted the cover and pulled the handle. A blue light on top of the alarm box lit up when the alarm was activated. You were to stay at the alarm box to direct the firefighters to the fire. The boxes were connected directly to the Piedmont Fire Department through a low voltage wire which allowed them to work even in a power failure. The alarm box sent out a coded signal to a ticker tape machine in the fire station and to a large panel (see photo). The location of the alarm box would quickly be identified, and the fire engines were off. In the Fall of 1955, there was a telephone strike, and phone service was undependable. On October 14, 1955, The Piedmonter published a list of fire alarm boxes and encouraged residents to use them in case of fire. The list shows 51 fire alarm boxes installed at street corners throughout Piedmont. Where was the fire alarm box in your neighborhood? The first call boxes were developed in Boston in 1852. San Francisco still maintains active fire alarm boxes within two blocks of any part of the city and considers the alarm boxes faster than calling 911 by phone to report a fire. These fire alarm boxes send a signal directly to the nearest fire station and are still considered crucial in the event of a power failure. The alarm boxes in San Francisco worked during the Loma Pieta earthquake in 1989 when electricity failed. In most parts of the state alarm boxes have been replaced by the calling 911 as an emergency phone number. In addition to San Francisco, Nevada City, Sacramento and Ventura continue to use fire alarm boxes in California. Fire alarm boxes were removed in Piedmont in 1978, and were offered for sale for $50 each. At that time the Fire Department said they were 50 years old. For a detailed hstory of Piedmont and more informaation, visit the website: Piedmonthistorical.org. If you are enjoying reading the biweekly columns on the history of Piedmont, consider becoming a m,member of the Peidmont historical Society by e-mail with your name, address, phone number and e-mail address, or contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@pacbell.net. Previously published in the Post on May 23, 2018. In a photo from the 1960s, Piedmont’s Fire Chief is shown with the fire alarm box equipment. Ticker tape machines are shown in the background. A list of fire alarm boxes was printed in The Piedmonter in 1955. Where was the fire alarm box in your neighborhood? A photo of an early fire alarm box in Piedmont is in the Piedmont Historical Society collection. It originally had a blue light bulb on top that lit up when the alarm was activated. A ticker tape machine in the Piedmont Fire Station would receive the coded location of an activated fire alarm box. The ticker tape machine now is part of the collection of the Piedmont Historical Society – and still has ticker tape.

The series offers a look inside the process of how a director and actors work together. You will see directors share their vision for the play and give actors a few words of inspiration. articles.text: From a Yuja Wang-inspired “fashion show” to performances by Kay Stern and other top Bay Area musicians, the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will host a virtual Telethon on Sunday, September 13 from 12-8 pm. The event will launch their 2020-21 season of concerts. Admission to the Virtual Telethon is free, with performers and presenters encouraging viewers to make donations throughout the day. The CMS of SF Virtual Telethon will be a day of entertainment and fun, featuring performances and presentations - all with a musical twist. A m o n g t h e p e r fo r m - ers are Queen Elizabeth and Tchaikovsky Competition laureate pianist Stephen Prutsman, actor and comedian Tom Lenk, SFCM cello professor Jean-Michel Fonteneau, San Francisco Opera concertmaster Kay Stern, as well as demonstrations in french cooking, high-end coffee making and much more. The day will be capped with a grand finale concert at 6 pm featuring the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco performing music of Mendelssohn, Bach, and Haydn, as well as a preview of its 2020-21 season. “People have been doing telethons to fundraise forever and we thought it would be a fun way to bring fundraising online, with a The Chamber Music Society of SF prepares for its first virtual telethon, scheduled for Sunday, September 13. huge diversity of kinds of entertainment for people to tune in to,” said Telethon Chair Mariana Roytman Schiffner. “We are thrilled to bring so many different voices to the conversation of why music, and chamber music matter so much, and how we can all support to ensure that CMS of SF comes out of this challenging period even stronger.” HOW TO REGISTER Telethon: Sunday, September 13th from 12 - 8 pm. Register at: https://chambermusicsocietysf. org/events About CMSSF Founded in the spring of 2013, the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco was born out of a collective desire to perform the great chamber music repertoire. Dedicated to bringing these masterworks to diverse audiences, CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners, and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Clio Tilton and Samsun van Loon came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets, forming a core to collaborate with beloved Bay Area musicians as guest artists. CMS of SF brings together Bay Area musicians of diverse musical experience. They can be heard performing with the San Francisco Symphony, San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, Oakland Symphony, Magik Orchestra, as well as many other chamber ensembles, including early music, jazz, tango, and pop.
articles.title: Chamber Music Society of SF in telethon concert Sept. 13

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony and the San Francisco Conservatory of Music have collaborated to create the Emerging Black Composers Project, which will commission works from ten early-career Black American composers. Each composer selected will receive $15,000, as well as workshops and performances by either the symphony or conservatory orchestras. They will also have the opportunity to be mentored by conductors Michael Morgan, Edwin Outwater, and conductor-composer Esa-Pekka Salonen. The call for applications is open through the end of the year, and the first commissioned piece will have its world premiere during the 2021-2022 season. David Stall, President of the SF Conservatory, said the goal is to elevate Black voices and expand the American canon. “When Black talent is nurtured, we strengthen our culture of excellence. We look forward to deepening the impact of the Emerging Black Composers Project through this partnership with San Francisco Symphony,” Stall said. San Francisco Symphony CEO Mark Hanson said that the classical music industry has a long history of excluding Black artists due to systemic racism. “We believe that the work of Black composers often does not receive the exposure or prominence it deserves. We believe that [the project] is a small step towards reducing some of the barriers these talented artists unjustly face in our field, and we look forward to performing and promoting these new works in future symphony seasons,” Hanson said. This initiative is part of a larger action plan at the SF Conservatory, which includes specific and funded commitments to create a truly equitable space for Black talent and leadership. Beginning this fall, the conservatory will program works by Black composers in all ensemble programs and host Black artists-in-residence for master classes and lessons each year. For more information on the project, visit https://sfcm.edu/ newsroom/san-francisco-conservatory-music-and-san-francisco-symphony-announce-emerging-black.
articles.title: SF Symphony, Conservatory of Music create Emerging Black Composers Project

articles.text: “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A live broadcast is scheduled for every Friday at 4 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. In season two, Aurora directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams are joined by Fusion Theatre Project at Laney College. The broadcast will feature Michael Torres, Alejandro Navarro, and Storm White. Torres was last seen at Aurora in 2019’s The Importance of Being Earnest. He co-founded Campo Santo in 1996, where he originated roles for Dave Eggers, Denis Johnson, Jose Rivera, Jessica Hagedorn, Octavio Solis and more. An award-winning actor, Torres has played at Shotgun Players, Crowded Fire, Word for Word, Berkeley Repertory, Teatro Campesino, California Shakespeare Theatre, Magic Theater, and TheatreFirst, He has also toured the U.S. and Europe in shows. Recently, he co-directed The Michael Torres Farm with Elena Wright, a show by Jon Tracy for TheatreFirst. He appeared in films in About Cherry and The Other Barrio. Torres is Chair of the Laney College Theatre Arts Department where he founded The Fusion Theatre Project. He holds a BA from San Francisco State and an MFA from the University of California at San Diego. You can watch the episode at https://youtu.be/bGt-zKyROTE.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre hosts Laney’s Fusion Project founder

articles.text: Join Berkeley Symphony this fall for “Joseph Young and Friends”, a series of online musical gatherings hosted by the symphony’s Music Director, Joseph Young. He is inviting viewers to share intimate musical experiences offered by symphony musicians and their colleagues. From Symphony musicians, to local composers, to special guest artists, patrons will be able to interact with familiar faces and make new friends in an engaging musical journey. The first episode will air on Thursday, September 10 at 5 p.m. Young will share his life story and career path, including vintage performance highlights captured in concert halls from around the world. For more information, visit https://www.berkeleysymphony. org. Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young.
articles.title: “Joseph Young and Friends” concert to air September 10

In season two, Aurora directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams are joined by Fusion Theatre Project at Laney College. The broadcast will feature Michael Torres, Alejandro Navarro, and Storm White. Torres was last seen at Aurora in 2019’s The Importance of Being Earnest. He co-founded Campo Santo in 1996, where he originated roles for Dave Eggers, Denis Johnson, Jose Rivera, Jessica Hagedorn, Octavio Solis and more. An award-winning actor, Torres has played at Shotgun Players, Crowded Fire, Word for Word, Berkeley Repertory, Teatro Campesino, California Shakespeare Theatre, Magic Theater, and TheatreFirst, He has also toured the U.S. and Europe in shows. Recently, he co-directed The SF Symphony, Conservatory of Music create Emerging Black Composers Project By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Symphony and the San Francisco Conservatory of Music have collaborated to create the Emerging Black Composers Project, which will commission works from ten early-career Black American composers. Each composer selected will receive $15,000, as well as workshops and performances by either the symphony or conservatory orchestras. They will also have the opportunity to be mentored by conductors Michael Morgan, Edwin Outwater, and conductor-composer Esa-Pekka Salonen. The call for applications is open through the end of the year, and the first commissioned piece will have its world premiere during the 2021-2022 season. David Stall, President of the SF Conservatory, said the goal is to elevate Black voices and expand the American canon. “When Black talent is nurtured, we strengthen our culture of excellence. We look forward to deepening the impact of the Emerging Black Composers Project through this partnership with San Francisco Symphony,” Stall said. San Francisco Symphony CEO Mark Hanson said that the classical music industry has a long history of excluding Black artists due to systemic racism. “We believe that the work of Black composers often does not receive the exposure or prominence it deserves. We believe that [the project] is a small step towards reducing some of the barriers these talented artists unjustly face in our field, and we look forward to performing and promoting these new works in future symphony seasons,” Hanson said. This initiative is part of a larger action plan at the SF Conservatory, which includes specific and funded commitments to create a truly equitable space for Black talent and leadership. Beginning this fall, the conservatory will program works by Black composers in all ensemble programs and host Black artists-in-residence for master classes and lessons each year. He holds a BA from San Francisco State and an MFA from the University of California at San Diego. articles.text: Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan introduces Britten’s Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings and Elgar’s In the South. Each week, Oakland Symphony is making archival footage available to patrons while its doors remain closed due to the current health crisis. This week, Music Director Michael Morgan introduced Edward Elgar’s In the South Overture, Op. 50, originally performed by the symphony at the Paramount Theatre on October 14, 2016. In the South was written as an overture, or tone poem, in 1903. meant southern Europe and more specifically, the town of Alassio on the Italian Riviera. “Elgar had vacationed there and was inspired by the scenery to remember the great battles that had been fought there in centuries past. It is a thrilling depiction of sun, sea, and land. Notable for its energy, and the viola solo in the middle section,” Morgan explained. An additional recording of the symphony’s performance of Benjamin Britten’s Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings, Op. 31, is also available. The symphony originally performed Serenade at the Paramount Theatre on February 9, 2018. Morgan said that Britten wrote Serenade for his partner, tenor Peter Pears, at the request of hornist Dennis Brain. “It sets six poems by various poets, each a mediation on aspects of the night plus a prologue and an epilogue played on the natural horn, that is playing the horn without using the valves. You could call it a series of nocturnes. In this performance, from our ‘Notes from LGBTQ America” concert, the famously difficult horn part is taken by our Principal Horn Meredith Brown, and the tenor – with the perfect voice for Britten – is Jonathan Blalock,” Morgan said. To listen to these archived performances, visit https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/repast/.

articles.text: Musaics of the Bay founder and artistic director Audrey Vardanega. Starting on September 27, Musaics of the Bay will present virtual chamber music concerts featuring Bay Area musicians while closely respecting California’s health guidelines. The first series of live-stream chamber performances, produced by Grittani Creative, will feature works by Dvorak and Schubert. The virtual season begins with Dvorak’s Piano Trio No.3 in F Minor, Op. 65 on Sunday, September 27 at 4 p.m. The concert will feature violinist Alexi Kenney, cellist Peter Myers, and pianist Audrey Vardanega, founder of Musaics of the Bay. Kenney is the recipient of a 2020 Borletti Buitoni Trust Award, and a 2016 Avery Fisher Career Grant. He has been named a “talent to watch” by the New York Times, which also noted his “architect’s eye for structure and space and a tone that ranges from fragile to full-bodied robustness.” Kenney has performed at a range of festivals, including Marlboro, Bridgehampton, Festival Napa Valley, Prussia Cove, Ravinia, and Yellow Barn. He is a member of the Bowers Program at the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, and has performed as guest concertmaster of both the Pittsburgh Symphony and the Mahler Chamber Orchestra. Myers has served as Assistant Principal Cellist of the San Francisco Opera Orchestra since 2017 and is internationally known as a chamber musician. For several years, he served as Co-director of Music for the American Contemporary Ballet in Los Angeles. Vardanega has performed as a solo and collaborative pianist across Europe, China, and the United States. She is the Founder and Artistic Director of Musaics of the Bay, a nonprofit chamber music series dedicated to music mentorship in the Bay Area. For more information and access to the concert on Sunday, September 27, see https://www. musaics.org/virtualconcerts.
articles.title: Musaics of the Bay season to begin September 27

articles.text: Bach’s cello suites featured in Bach Shorts on Septmeber 13 Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players has embarked on two new series of virtual concerts: Bach Shorts and Main Stage Concerts. The first series, Bach Shorts, consists of three one-hour, livestreamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of Bach’s Cello Suites. Three leading Bay Area cellists partner with professors, composers, and musicians from around the globe for uniquely personal performances and collaborations. The series begins on Sunday, September 13 at 4 p.m. with cellist Christopher Costanza, from the St. Lawrence String Quartet. He will perform Bach’s Second and Sixth Cello Suites and will partner with Stanford Professor Jonathan Berger, who will discuss the effect music has on the brain, hence the concert title, Bach and the Dancing Brain. On October 11, GCCP presents Bach Inspired, a concert featuring Jennifer Kloetzel, former cellist with the Cypress Quartet. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler. Elena will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. The Bach Shorts series concludes on Sunday, November 8 with Bach Connections, with cellist Robert Howard from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra. He will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. More Music Next Year After the New Year, Gold Coast Chamber Players plan to offer four live-streamed Main Stage performances with a feeling similar to what Gold Coast audiences have come to enjoy. Tickets for the Main Stage concert series will go on sale later this year. Bach Shorts tickets are $20 per concert, or $50 for all three performances in the series. Concerts are live-streamed via YouTube LIVE. Purchase online at www.GCCPmusic.com or by calling (925) 283-3728. See the website, gccpmusic.com, for regular updates about concert offerings, to purchase tickets and to make donations. Robert Howard, cello

articles.text: The first performance on October 1 will feature violinist Tessa Lark. Cal Per for ma nces has announced its plans for a 15-episode run of full-length concerts and theater works, compiled in a series called “Cal Performances at Home.” The series will run from October to mid-January and will feature a wide variety of new and full-length videos or live events, all available to stream directly to your home screen. Main Stage performances will feature artists and programs that were set to perform for Cal Performances’ fall season, as well as a few new additions. Main Stage videos will also be accompanied by free “Beyond the Stage” artist talks, interviews, lectures, and question and answer sessions with artists and Cal Performances staff, and UC Berkeley faculty. Special premiere-evening “watch parties” will allow patrons to enjoy the company of other performing arts lovers from the safety of your own home. The series will begin on Thursday, October 1 with a concert by violinist Tessa Lark, and pianist Andrew Armstrong. Throughout the fall season, the series will feature performances from New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Spain and Germany. Pricing for the “Cal Performances at Home” is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. To view suggested prices, and for more information on the series, visit https://calperformances.org/at-home/.

articles.text: While Dragon Tattoo is a whodunit procedural, the recently released film, The Girl Who Played With Fire, though it involves the same central characters – Salander and Blomkvist – is really the beginning of a two book and two film series, ending with The Girl Who Kicked the Hornets’ Nest. The stories merge, hence Played With Fire is prologue to what will be the climactic and perhaps best film in the trilogy and should be judged accordingly. Of course, for fans of the Millennium Trilogy, which has proven to be a cultural phenom, this second film is a must see. It possesses a building intensity, taut and violent while Noomi Rapace continues to create an unforgettable character. One final comment about these books being adapted to the screen: for those who have read the trilogy, it becomes quickly evident that narratives as complex and multi-layered as Larsson’s pose a challenge. Movies are only two hours. It is impossible to explore the countless cul-de-sacs, the many characters, their backstories, and all of the elements that make the books so satisfying telescoped into a screen adaptation. Hence the films may feel spare and a bit truncated. That’s not to say that they’re not compelling. They’re a wonderful adjunct to the books. Rapace as Salander and Michael Nyqvist as Blomkvist are perfect. Of course, Hollywood will also adapt the trilogy, so hold your breath. Daniel Craig, of James Bond fame reportedly has been cast as Blomkvist. The role of Salander is still open. The Girl Who Played With Fire. Starring Noomi Rapace, Michael Nyqvist, Annika Giannin, and Yasmine Garbi. Directed by Daniel Alffredson. Rated R. A scene from They Shall Not Grow Old. Movie review by Chris Honoré What Peter Jackson has accomplished in They Shall Not Grow Old is extraordinary, bordering on the magical. Given access to hundreds of hours of World War I archival news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum, he began what was to be a 30-minute short. Soon it grew into an astonishing, yearslong restorative achievement. Using computer-generated, state-of-the-art technology Jackson undertook what was a meticulous cleaning of the dusty, scratched, grainy film. Realizing that the footage was hand cranked, shot at various speeds, he synched it to a standard 24-frames-per-second. Then he and his talented group began the painstaking process of adding color, going to astonishing lengths to achieve accuracy. The filming crew traveled to actual locations where they shot countless reference photos. Additionally, they took pains to get the soundtrack spot-on. Where soldiers were shown speaking in the archival films, they hired lip readers to determine what was said, then hired local actors to get the accents just right. No narration was used; rather they listened to some 600 hours of BBC recordings of veterans of the war and used 100 voices. We hear them reflecting on their experiences, offering their memories without a hint of cynicism. The result is almost surreal. It’s as if we are literally stepping back in time and observing from the camera’s point of view what is taking place. The story is told chronologically, beginning with contextual images shot in black and white of enlistees (some as young as 14 and 15) arriving at boot camp as civilians and then gradually turned into disciplined soldiers. We learn from the voice overs that to a man they believed they were embarking on an unrivaled adventure, one not to be missed, wrapped in patriotism and heroism and a promise that the war would end within months. England vibrated with war fever. Train stations were filled with cheering, flag waving crowds saying goodbye. Men on the streets of London and other towns were often approached by young women who handed them white feathers, symbols of cowardice, urging them to join their comrades. On walls and buildings were posters, appealing to men (and boys) to enlist and do their part. It’s at this point in the narrative that the screen fills with color and we, the audience, begin in earnest to comprehend that what Jackson has done is create a work of art. We are there. All but shoulder to shoulder with these young men who soon came to realize that the much anticipated adventure proved to be an unimaginable ordeal, harsh, stark, life maiming and life ending. What the young Brits found out was that this was a war fought from the warrens of crooked trenches, often filled with the stench of death, filled with water and partially buried bodies, blackened hands and arms sticking out of layers of mud. To confront the enemy was to climb up and over the top, onto the field of battle, often into withering machine gun fire and exploding shells, later spending nights trying to sleep in shallow hollowed out caves while an unrelenting bombardment shook the ground. Those who stopped and looked into the box-like cameras, gave stoic smiles or long gazes of brittle confidence; in truth they now knew what was ahead. World War I (1914-1918) was referred to as The War to End All Wars. And most especially, after watching They Shall Not Grow Old, it is clear why it was unimaginable that such carnage and awfulness would ever be repeated. The toll was staggering: there were 5.5 million military deaths; 12 million were wounded. Poison gas was used, inflicting 1.3 million casualties. Civilian deaths totaled over 4 million. And 1 million British boys were killed, an unimaginable loss for a small island nation. At no time during the film is there any commentary by Jackson or others about the nature of war. And yet, after the last frame fades from the screen, it is all but impossible not to conclude that what was created is an anti-war film. To see WWI as it was, while knowing that the horror was far worse (the archival footage was meant for audiences back in England), is revelatory. And, of course, embedded in those 99 minutes is the haunting question: why does war seem to be ever with us? They Shall Not Grow Old. World War I Documentary. A Centenary Restoration by Peter Jackson. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated R. Originally printed in the Post on February 6, 2019. An example of how original World War I footage was restored and colorized for Peter Jackson’s documentary, They Shall Not Grow Old.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS They Shall Not Grow Old – Peter Jackson’s extraordinary film on World War I

articles.text: Noomi Rapace as Lisabeth Salander in The Girl Who Played With Fire Movie review by Chris Honoré The summer of 2010 will always be, in part, defined by the arrival of what is known as the Millennium Trilogy – The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo, The Girl Who Played With Fire, and The Girl Who Kicked the Hornets’ Nest – three novels, written by Stieg Larsson, that have caused a small tsunami in the publishing world. The first book (and film) is a stand-alone murder mystery that initially focuses on Mikael Blomkvist, a muckraking journalist living in Stockholm, who is hired by a patrician industrialist in northern Sweden to investigate the disappearance of his young niece more than 20 years ago. Though her body was never found, it’s believed she was murdered. It’s in book one that Lisabeth Salander appears, initially as a secondary character. She’s a superb researcher and investigator, a computer hacker, possessing a photographic memory, and is hired by Blomkvist as an assistant. Salander seems, at first blush, an unlikely choice: she’s skinny – five feet zip, 90 pounds – New Age gothic, seemingly feral, her back covered with a dragon tattoo, nose pierced, and fearless. Salander’s childhood was a nightmare. Committed to a psychiatric hospital at the age of 12 for trying to kill her pathologically abusive father – she throws gasoline on him, followed by a lighted match – where she was raped and tormented by the very people who were charged with her care. She is instantly enigmatic and hugely appealing and gradually, as the book evolves, emerges as the central character, proving to be one of the strongest female characters to emerge in literature in a decade or more. A scene from The Girl Who Played With Fire.
articles.title: Girl Who Played With Fire a gem from Sweden

All but shoulder to shoulder with these young men who soon came to realize that the much anticipated adventure proved to be an unimaginable ordeal, harsh, stark, life maiming and life ending. What the young Brits found out was that this was a war fought from the warrens of crooked trenches, often filled with the stench of death, filled with water and partially buried bodies, blackened hands and arms sticking out of layers of mud. To confront the enemy was to climb up and over the top, onto the field of battle, often into withering machine gun fire and exploding shells, later spending nights trying to sleep in shallow hollowed out caves while an unrelenting bombardment shook the ground. Those who stopped and looked into the box-like cameras, gave stoic smiles or long gazes of brittle confidence; in truth they now knew what was ahead. World War I (1914-1918) was referred to as The War to End All Wars. And most especially, after watching They Shall Not Grow Old, it is clear why it was unimaginable that such carnage and awfulness would ever be repeated. The toll was staggering: there were 5.5 million military deaths; 12 million were wounded. Poison gas was used, inflicting 1.3 million casualties. Civilian deaths totaled over 4 million. And 1 million British boys were killed, an unimaginable loss for a small island nation. At no time during the film is there any commentary by Jackson or others about the nature of war. And yet, after the last frame fades from the screen, it is all but impossible not to conclude that what was created is an anti-war film. To see WWI as it was, while knowing that the horror was far worse (the archival footage was meant for audiences back in England), is revelatory. And, of course, embedded in those 99 minutes is the haunting question: why does war seem to be ever with us? They Shall Not Grow Old. World War I Documentary. A Centenary Restoration by Peter Jackson. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated R. Originally printed in the Post on February 6, 2019. An example of how original World War I footage was restored and colorized for Peter Jackson’s documentary, They Shall Not Grow Old.

articles.text: Will Smith and Matt Damon star in The Legend of Bagger Vance. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Legend of Bagger Vance is based on the novel by Steve Plessfield who extended the title, reassuring the reader that his book was also A Novel of Golf and the Game of Life. The film keeps that promise, beginning with a brief montage of the romance of two young people, Rannulph Junuh (Matt Damon) and a wealthy southern belle, Adele (Charlize Theron). Both are residents of Savannah, Georgia. It is just prior to World War I, and Junuh, known as one of the state’s premier golfers, enlists to fight on the war like so many of his contemporaries. Many did not return from what was initially called “The war to end all wars.” , Junuh survived, though deeply damaged by what he experienced. Upon returning vanished into the remote fringes of Savannah, refusing to see even Adele. And then it was 1931, and the Great Depression was underway. Adele’s father committed suicide and his legacy, to include a startling beautiful golf course, is threatened. She is determined to hang on to the property, despite the bank’s insistence that she should sell it for pennies on the dollar and avoid foreclosure. She informs the bank and the town council that she will sponsor a spectacular golf tournament that will feature two nationally known golfers, Bobby Jones (Joel Gretsch) and Walter Hagen (Bruce McGill). The exhibition match will have at stake a purse of $10,000. But the town fathers insist that a local Savannah boy is needed as a draw. At this point Junuh’s name is mentioned. He’s well known locally, and was once a gifted golfer. He first says no, he won’t play, and explains to Adele that he has “lost his swing” and without it he has no business stepping up to any golf tee. But mysteriously, out of the night, a man appears. His name is Bagger Vance, and he explains that if Junuh has lost his swing, well, let’s set out to find it, along with some confidence. Both essential if Junuh is to have any chance to hold his own on the links with Jones and Hagen. And so the three-day match begins. Bagger’s light touch and deep Zen-like instruction slowly begins to transform Junuh’s game and his life. This film has a deep bench of fine actors and the 18th hole on the third day of the tournament is hardly in doubt. But it’s not the end that so much matters – balls hit, putts made, sand traps waiting – but the laconic, spare support and advice supplied by Bagger. And then there is a 12-year-old boy, Hardy (J. Michael Moncrief), who signs on as the assistant caddy, and loves the game while basking in the magical glow that defines the game and surrounds Bagger. The film has a silky look with soft golden tones, the story told beautifully by Robert Redford. It never feels burdened by cliché’ or shallow resolution. Golf and life co-mingle and the lessons are made manifest on the field of play. Bagger counsels Junuh to peer down the fairway, choose his clubs wisely, and visualize the life that awaits him. Redford conveys all of this with restraint and respect for what is a wonderful American tale. The Legend of Bagger Vance. Directed by Robert Redford. Starring Will Smith, Matt Damon and Charlize Theron. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG-13. Charlize Theron and Matt Damon in The Legend of Bagger Vance.
articles.title: Redford’s deft directorial touch shown in The Legend of Bagger Vance

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré From the world-renowned Japanese Studio Ghibli, The Secret World of Arrietty, made in 2010, was co-written by two of its principal storytellers, Hiromasa Yonebayashi and Hayao Miyazaki. It is based on the famed children’s fantasy novels titled The Borrowers, by British writer Mary Norton. Set in 1950s England, the borrowers are a race of teacup size people who make their confortable if diminutive home under the floorboards of an old-fashioned English cottage. At the center of this delightful narrative is Arrietty, an adventurous 14-year-old girl (Bridget Mendler) who lives with her mother, Homily (Amy Poehler), and father, Pod (Will Arnett). They survive day to day by “borrowing” bits of food and objects from the “human beans” who live above the floorboards. It is important to know that a sacrosanct rule, even law, is that a Borrower must, at all cost, never reveal him or herself to a “bean.” Should that happen, alas, the Borrowers, they believe, are put in real danger and must find a new residence. But then a sickly 12-yearold boy, Shawn (David Henrie), comes to stay at his aunt’s home to convalesce. He is keen-eyed and curious. Meanwhile, Arrietty and her father go on a mission above the floorboards to borrow a cube of sugar, an adventure to be sure for she is fascinated by the sheer size of the bean world, something she views in all its gigantic splendor and potential danger. But, as it turns out, she is also drawn into Shawn’s personal world and is soon discovered by the bean boy. Surprisingly these two most disparate characters fashion a friendship and a bond of trust. Of course, one of the beans, an elderly housekeeper, Hara (Carol Burnett), is ever on guard, intent on ridding the bean’s home of any “pests.” The danger to Arrietty and family is palpable. The Secret is a wonderful tale, lush and beautiful, hand drawn animé that brings to life this contrasting world of Borrowers and beans. It is also a coming-ofage story featuring a strong and courageous early teenage girl who yearns to expand her horizons above the floorboards. She exhibits a focused fearlessness and kindness, qualities that are endearing. This film tells a tender story and is a visual stunner while avoiding the fantastical, extraordinary, shape-shifting characters that are often part of the Ghibli world. The Secret World of Arrietty (2010). Animaé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hiromasa Yonebayashi. With the voices of David Henrie, Bridget Mendler, Amy Poehler and Carol Burnett. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated G. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty.
articles.title: The Secret World of Arrietty another gem from Studio Ghibli

articles.text: In this world, there are a lot of complainers. The news media seems to enjoy these folks. Fortunately, there are a few doers. The conflagration in the Santa Cruz mountains featured a few of these doers on the front page. Did you see the name John Lingemann? I hope you took note of what he did. I know John. He married a girl who was a classmate of mine since nursery school. John is one of those builders of society. He is also a savior of society. That’s just how he is... all the more amazing since he is 77 years old. John studied architecture, but he is a mountain man at heart. He designed his own house in Bonny Dune and built it around some pretty big trees – trees that are inside the house. After designing the house by sketching it in the dirt, he made his own lumber from the trees on his property and drilled his own water well. Nothing was wasted. When the inspector saw John’s house his jaw dropped in amazement. “How did you do it?“ he asked. John answered in his modest manner. Last week John saved his house from the fire and the houses of others in his zone. John and wife Nancy are the doers of society. Who would you rather have in an emergency, a whining complainer or John Lingemann? Toasting success Focaccia is an Italian classic. But you can’t go to Italy now. My daughter-in-law introduced me John Lingemann, 77, fighting fires in Bonny Dune during the recent fires above Santa Cruz. to some locally made focaccia. Lisa Chan has opened her shop, Sweet-Wheezy-Treats.myshopify. com, and bakes a California-inspired version of focaccia which is every bit as good as focaccia in Italy. Hers is a success story at every turn. She came from a career in the fashion industry to bexomw Pastry Sous Chef for Michelin-starred State Bird Provision and The Progress in San Francisco. When she was laid off because of the pandemic, she decided to open her own business making focaccia. I never had any that was better. Leaving you with laughter Seeking humor can be difficult these days. Perhaps this will bring a smile: What wears a mask all the time, is obsessed with handwashing, and its name can be re-arranged to spell corona? Answer: racoon

articles.text: The San Francisco Botanical Garden reopened to the public on June 1, with regular operating hours of 7:30 a.m. to 7 p.m. On Tuesday, September 8, it is offering a “garden free day.” From 7:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., the garden will be free to everyone. The garden closed in midMarch to comply with shelter-inplace orders. “The garden is essential, now more than ever, as a place of peace, calm, and reflection. Research shows that outdoor places like the garden promote well-being, good health, and empathy,” said Executive Director Stephanie Linder. Upon reopening, the garden has implemented all necessary measures to ensure visitor, staff, and volunteer health, manage social distancing, and other operational guidelines. The Plant Arbor is now open on weekends, from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. The Children’s Garden is open daily with the same hours as the rest of the garden. The Helen Crocker Russel Library of Horticulture and Garden Bookstore remain closed. Buying advanced tickets is recommended for all garden visitors, including members as well as residents. Face coverings must be worn by all staff and visitors. Restrooms, drinking fountains, and waste receptacles are all open and available for visitors. However, advance tickets are not needed for the garden free day on September 8. This is a continuing event every second Tuesday of every month. For more information, visit https://www.sfbg.org/events.
articles.title: SF Botanical Garden offers free day on September 8

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California The Oakland Museum of California is offering many of its collections online to view while its doors remain closed due to shelter-in-place restrictions. The museum’s extensive collection of California’s historical artifacts, works of art, ethnographic materials, and natural specimens represents the material legacy of California and its people. You can view the collection homepage from any location. Throughout the site, you will find numerous links to related topics or expanded information. The project is supported by a 2010 federal grant award to the Oakland Museum of California, secured through the assistance of Rep. Barbara Lee. Featured collections include work from environmental activist and photographer Bob Walker, political posters, Chinese “snuff bottles,” arts and crafts followers Arthur and Lucia Mathews, iconic photographer Dorothea Lange, archived photographs from the Oakland Tribune, and jewelry pioneer Margaret De Patta. You can tour the featured collections of art, grouped by specific topics, or you can search the collection to access information on all of the more than 27,000 objects on the museum’s online collection. To view what the Oakland Museum of California has to offer, visit http://collections. museumca.org/.
articles.title: Featured collections include work by Dorothea Lange and Margaret De Patta

articles.text: The overwhelming majority of Piedmoners – 94% – grasp the reality of climate change, and most of those understand that climate change is caused primarily by human activities, according to a representative survey of residents commissioned by the City and conducted in June 2020 by FM3 Research. In our community’s spirit of stewardship for future generations, 90% of the survey respondents are concerned that future generations will be significantly impacted by climate change and believe that taking action is important. “It’s clear from the results of this survey that Piedmonters support efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions,” said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “That support will be critical to the heavy lifting that needs to occur if we are going to meet the community’s emissions reduction targets for 2030 and 2050. All the ‘low hanging fruit’ has already been accomplished, including Piedmonters’ switch to purchasing electricity from East Bay Community Energy that is generated by 100% renewable sources.” Describing the “heavy lifting, Jackson said, “About 90% of Piedmont’s in-boundary emissions come from vehicles and the burning of natural gas appliances. To meet the 2050 target of reducing emissions to less than 20% of current emissions, we will all need to start driving electric vehicles and greatly reduce or eliminate the use of natural gas in our homes. “This won’t be easy or convenient, but given the results of this survey I believe Piedmonters are up to the task,” he stated. The survey showed strong support for Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, adopted in 2018, which commits our community to reduce greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 40% by 2030 (just a decade out) and 80% by 2050, from our 2005 baseline emissions. Despite some gaps in familiarity with the particulars of the plan, 75% of residents agreed these goals are “extremely” or “very important” to meet. In a sign of Piedmonters” commitment to reducing emissions, one-quarter of us already own electric vehicles (EVs). Nearly 79% of the respondents support the expansion of publicly available EV charging stations in Piedmont, which half of non-EV owners report might help them to make the switch away from gas vehicles, depending on the location of the chargers and how the parking spaces are managed. Two-thirds of residents supported a proposal to revise building codes – called “Reach Codes” – to encourage less natural gas use when homes are remodeled and reduce emissions from natural gas. The City Council supported Reach codes in a preliminary vote last month, and the city will hold a town hall meeting Sept. 3 to educate residents about them and answer questions. Over half of residents expressed support for the variety of different reach code options under consideration, such as improving home insulation, adding solar panels, and increasing capacity for future home electrification. Over half of respondents said they would consider upgrading their home to all-electric if incentives were provided. Residents were mixed on their support for increasing Piedmont’s gas tax to discourage natural gas use and provide incentives and funds to help homeowners electrify. It’s heartening to know that a community as resourceful and capable as Piedmont can set its sights on tackling climate change as aggressively as possible at the local level, resting assured that we are collectively up for this critical and urgent challenge. mont Climate Survey at https:// bit.ly/2GggoeE. Learn more about Reach Codes on the city website at https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_news___notifications/ reach_codes. GET UP TO
articles.title: Piedmonters taking on climate change

articles.text: Hanno has handed over the winemaking duties to his daughter, Dorothee, who carries the tradition forward with the help of Hanno and Ruth and Dorothee’s husband Philipp. A few months ago I was elated to receive a press release from Loosen Bros. a U.S. Importer of German wines, announcing the addition of Zilliken to their portfolio. It had been many years since I had tasted their wines and I was interested to see if the magic was still there. I am pleased to report in my tasting notes below that the answer is…….YES! I was so lucky 35 years ago to be traveling in Germany and happened to find the Zilliken estate in the little town of Saarburg on the tiny Saar River. Hanno Zilliken and his wife Ruth invited me into the living room of their house perched above the winery and opened an antique cabinet, retrieved some exquisite green stemmed wine glasses and proceeded to pour me samples of their wines. I will never forget the pristine, delicate loveliness of their Rieslings. How lean and racy they were, yet fruity enough to mask the high acidity. These were handcrafted wines made with obvious love and care that Hanno and Ruth presented with pride, but with great humility. The origin of the winery dates to 1742. Since then it has been passed on from generation to generation. In 1944 it was destroyed by Allied forces bombing during World War II. The Zillikens rebuilt the home over a deep wine cellar cave with natural conditions of 100% humidity and constant cool temperatures. All the wines are made and aged in 1,000-liter, neutral oak Fuder casks, with an annual production of about 6,000 cases a year. Zilliken Winery’s 2019 Butterfly Riesling is a great value. 2019 Zilliken Butterfly Riesling (Great Value) (see photo) This is Zilliken’s entry-level wine. The label declares it as Piedmonters taking on climate change By Ronna Abramson The overwhelming majority of Piedmoners – 94% – grasp the reality of climate change, and most of those understand that climate change is caused primarily by human activities, according to a representative survey of residents commissioned by the City and conducted in June 2020 by FM3 Research. In our community’s spirit of stewardship for future generations, 90% of the survey respondents are concerned that future generations will be significantly impacted by climate change and believe that taking action is important. “It’s clear from the results of this survey that Piedmonters support efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions,” said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “That support will be critical to the heavy lifting that needs to occur if we are going to meet the community’s emissions reduction targets for 2030 and 2050. All the ‘low hanging fruit’ has already been accomplished, including Piedmonters’ switch to purchasing electricity from East Bay Community Energy that is generated by 100% renewable sources.” Describing the “heavy lifting, Jackson said, “About 90% of Piedmont’s in-boundary emissions come from vehicles and the burning of natural gas appliances. To meet the 2050 target of reducing emissions to less than 20% of current emissions, we will all need to start driving electric vehicles and greatly reduce or eliminate the use of natural gas in our homes. “This won’t be easy or convenient, but given the results of this survey I believe Piedmonters are up to the task,” he stated. The survey showed strong support for Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, adopted in 2018, which commits our community to reduce greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 40% by 2030 (just a decade out) and 80% by 2050, from our 2005 baseline emissions. Despite some gaps in familiarity with the particulars of the plan, 75% of residents agreed these goals are “extremely” or “very important” to meet. In a sign of Piedmonters” commitment to reducing emissions, one-quarter of us already own electric vehicles (EVs). Nearly 79% of the respondents support the expansion of publicly available EV charging stations in Piedmont, which half of non-EV owners report might help them to make the switch away from gas vehicles, depending on the location of the chargers and how the parking spaces are managed. Two-thirds of residents supported a proposal to revise building codes – called “Reach Codes” – to encourage less natural gas use when homes are remodeled and reduce emissions from natural gas. The City Council supported Reach codes in a preliminary vote last month, and the city will hold a town hall meeting Sept. 3 to educate residents about them and answer questions. Over half of residents expressed support for the variety of different reach code options under consideration, such as improving home insulation, adding solar panels, and increasing capacity for future home electrification. Over half of respondents said they would consider upgrading their home to all-electric if incentives were provided. Residents were mixed on their support for increasing Piedmont’s gas tax to discourage natural gas use and provide incentives and funds to help homeowners electrify. It’s heartening to know that a community as resourceful and capable as Piedmont can set its sights on tackling climate change as aggressively as possible at the local level, resting assured that we are collectively up for this critical and urgent challenge. See the full results of the Piedmont Climate Survey at https:// bit.ly/2GggoeE. Learn more about Reach Codes on the city website at https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_news___notifications/ reach_codes. articles.text: Construction on the STEAM building has moved to exterior ground floor items like retaining walls, and the curb, gutters, and sidewalks on Magnolia. Construction on Piedmont High’s new three-story classroom building, which was to have opened on the first day of school, has been delayed. Teachers and staff may be able to use the completed building by October 26. In an update by Facilities Director Pete Palmer to the school board on August 26, he explained the reason for the delay in the building’s completion. PG&E was four weeks late in installing full power to the building. The initial plan aimed for completion by August 17, which was to have been the first day of classes. “PG&E’s delay affected phone-fiber-internet connections between the STEAM and 40s building which, in turn, delayed state-required fire/life/safety inspections, elevator inspections, and accessibility inspections,” explained Supt. Randy Booker in a memo to the School Board. All classes were moved to online instruction, making the issue of an empty classroom building somewhat moot. COVID-related delays also slowed the project’s access to materials, including “epoxy tabletops and sinks for all science and prep rooms, operable windows and actuators, certain doors and electronic hardware. In some cases, the general contractor has had to find entirely new vendors and subcontractors due to Covid- 19.” Booker noted. “It has been very frustrating and challenging and I really wanted to come through for the community and the district to say we are finishing on time and are moving onto the theater. But we just couldn’t pull it off,’ said Palmer. He noted that a lot of the cabinets are in, and the floors are polished. Internet installation occurred August 26 and the building now has permanent power. The July 14 decision to begin the year with distance learning gave the contractor some latitude on the actual date of completion. In turn, the School Board stopped paying overtime to workers and work stopped on weekends. The district expects teachers to start moving their belongings into the STEAM building on October 19 when a Certificate of Occupancy is obtained from the state. One week later teachers should be able to use their classrooms to conduct their distance learning classes. A few yards away, construction on the new theater building has begun with the foundation, including 30-foot support beams dug into bedrock. The new theater building will be closer to Magnolia Avenue, resulting in the sidewalk being shored up.
articles.title: STEAM building opening delayed to Oct. 26

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has announced that it will begin accepting “text-to-911” calls throughout the city, beginning on August 31. Wireless customers can now send messages to 911 in an emergency. The text-to-911 feature should only be used in an emergency when placing a call is not possible. The department is asking residents to “call if you can, text if you can’t.” Location accuracy varies depending on your wireless carrier and should not be relied upon. If you do send a text, be sure to include your location and street address, including city, in your text. Text-to-911 will not be available if the wireless carrier cannon ascertain a location of the device sending the message. Do not send acronyms, short code messages, or animations. This new feature is intended primarily for use in three emergency scenarios: for an individual who is deaf, hard of hearing, or has a speech disability, for someone who is in a situation where it is not safe to place a voice call to 911, or in a medical emergency that renders a person incapable of speech. Call 510-420-3000 to reach Piedmont Police Department for any non-emergencies.
articles.title: Police Dept. rolls out “text-to-911” option

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department firefighters returned yesterday from assisting in the SCU lightning complex. Piedmont Fire Engine 2880 was deployed on the evening of August 21 for an “immediate need” assignment as part of a local task force assigned to the SCU lightening complex. The engine was staffed with three firefighters. The threeman crew was led by Lt. Justin McNulty, with engineers Russ San Fillippo and Justin Morris. At the time of their deployment, the SCU lightning complex fire was the 7th largest wildfire in California’s history. The fires continue to burn in Santa Clara, Alameda, and San Joaquin counties, but are 60 percent contained as of August 31. Cal Fire says that this largest of the August lightning fires will reach 100 percent containment later this week, possibly by Thursday, September 3. Cal Fire explained that the continued firefight is a combination of controlling the burning that is ongoing as it consumes “heavy dead and down fuels,” and “scouting for safe access points in order to construct direct and indirect fire line. All evacuation orders in Alameda, Santa Clara, and San Joaquin counties were lifted on Monday. The fire has burned over 380,000 acres in 12 days, making it the second-largest wildfire in California history.
articles.title: Piedmont firefighters return from SCU wildfire

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department hosted a screening of the award-winning documentary Wilder than Wild: Fire, Forests and the Future on Monday, August 31. The film will be shown daily on KCOM, Channel 27, from Friday through Monday, September 4-7 at 4:30 p.m. Wilder than Wild is a one-hour documentary that reveals how fuel build-up and climate change have exposed Western wild lands to large, high intensity wildfires, while greenhouse gases released from these fires contribute to global warming. The film explores strategies that are being developed to help mitigate the impact of these fires. Cal Fire Director Ken Pimlott described the documentary as “an absolutely wonderful production. The messages in this film are spot on.” A panel featuring the film’s director and producer, Kevin White, and Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black, followed the screening held on August 31. “The city of Piedmont wants to build community awareness about mitigation strategies in this new age of wildfire,” Black said. “The screening is part of a larger effort by the city to engage the community in conversations about the future of wildfire, specifically in an urban setting.” You can view the August 31 screening and panel discussion at http://piedmont.granicus.com/MediaPlayer.php?view_id=3&clip_id=2215.
articles.title: Wilder than Wild documentary on KCOM September 4 - 7

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Rob Bond, a resident of Piedmont from 1971 to 2014, died on August 5 in Orinda, where he and his wife Leslie resided for the past six years. Born Robert Elder Bond on February 15, 1941 in Louisville, Kentucky, he was the son of Roberta Elder and Allen McKee Bond. He spent most of his childhood in Louisville, and after graduating from Louisville Country Day, he attended Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut. At Trinity, he was an active member of St. Anthony Hall fraternity and rowed crew. Upon graduation in 1963, he joined the Navy and attended Officer Candidate School in Newport, Rhode Island. He became an Explosive Ordnance Disposal Officer, a job that involved diving and bomb disposal operations. He finished his time in the Military with a tour in VietNam. He relished his military service and had a strong sense of patriotism. Following graduation from Stanford Business School, he married Leslie Antonius of Madison, Wisconsin. After a threemonth honeymoon in Europe, his first job was with Monsanto. Two years later, he took a job with Kaiser (and subsequent subsidiaries). In 1987, Rob founded the World Franchising Network. The Network involved annual directories, websites, databases and, more recently, franchise analytical services. He also published numerous art books under the brand name Half Full Press. He and Leslie lived in Palo Alto, St. Louis, and Piedmont, where they raised their two sons and where he coached youth sports for many years. In 2014 they moved to Orinda. His love of travel and adventure took him to 94 countries and 49 states. Innumerable trips involved hiking, climbing, motorcycling and diving. Many were with his sons and/or Navy buddies. He was never shy about traveling solo with a backpack to out-of-the-way places he wanted to explore. An important part of his love for this kind of travel was meeting and learning from strangers he met along his route. Rob Bond, a resident of Piedmont for 43 years, died on August 5. He was 79. He lived a rewarding and full life, and one that was lovingly centered around Leslie and their two sons, Chris and Jeff. At 79, he lived a life filled with adventure, humor, curiosity, entrepreneurialism and sacrifice to his country. He raised his boys with a strong sense of integrity, passion for adventure travel, and, above all, respect for others. He prided himself on his daily commitment to fitness - walking, working out and swimming. He was often seen walking to and from work (six miles round trip) with his trusty weighted backpack. Rob was also known as the ultimate prankster, who loved tricking his friends and family – and was often his own best audience. The Bond family has a wide circle of longtime friends who Rob truly cherished, as they cherished him. Rob will be sorely missed, and so fondly remembered by his family. He is survived by Leslie, his wonderful wife of 51 years, son Chris and wife Gretchen of Wayne, Pennsylvania, and son Jeff and wife Jenny of Orinda. He is also survived by seven independent, spirited and fun-loving grandchildren, (McKee, Peyton, Fisher, Kennedy, Derek, Sadie and Sawyer). Affectionately known as “Poppy” to his family, his greatest joys were watching his grandchildren grow, prosper and become solid citizens. He is also survived by his two brothers, Allen McKee Bond, III and Charles Willis Bond, both of Louisville, KY. He is pre-deceased by his sister, Tacie Jarrett Bond. A Celebration of Life will be held at a future date. In his memory, contributions may be sent to: George Mark Children’s House, 2121 George Mark Lane, San Leandro, CA 94578 or http://www.georgemark.org. “He lived, and laughed, and loved, and left…and the world will never be the same.”
articles.title: Longtime Piedmont resident Rob Bond dies on August 5

articles.text: Editor: Hari Titan is a parent, a data scientist, and a former college professor running for School Board. We’ve worked together on a wide variety of school board matters since 2014. Hari is uniquely adept at using aggregated student, teacher and taxpayer data before formulating his judgment. He seeks out the most applicable expertise for each matter. I also like Hari’s idea to allow busy working people to participate in decision making via moderated online forums, open 24/7 and surveying parents and teachers. We need board members with a track record of explaining controversial decisions made by the board, and thoroughly answering questions from the public. Hari is the only candidate committed to full-disclosure transparency, which is especially important for decisions being made regarding distance learning and the future option of classroom instruction. For me, Hari represents a refreshing change to how business is conducted, and provides hope that even as busy parents, we too can have a voice. –Alicia Gruber Kalamas, M.D.
articles.title: Hari Titan committed to full disclosure by school board

articles.text: Editor: I have known Connie Herrick for many years. She is a wonderful combination of kindness, compassion, approachability and truly caring with a highly analytical, problem- solving kind of brain. She will listen and truly care about the concerns of others. We need people like that on our City Council. She is passionate about including all Piedmonters in making decisions that impact all of us. Connie grew up in Piedmont. Her son graduated from PHS. She loves our City and will work hard for us. She is running a different kind of campaign. She’s not taking donations, doing lawn signs or bothering us with phone calls asking for our endorsements. She is spending her time reading through staff reports, attending City Council and Committee meetings and talking with as many of us as she can. This is Connie’s first time running for office, so you likely have not seen her name before. Please go to her website (VoteHerrick.com) and learn about her. You can book an online chat and meet her. And If you decide to support her, you can download window posters. I already have one on display. Please join me and vote for Connie Herrick for City Council. We need people like her on the Council. –Patty White Former Piedmont Mayor
articles.title: Ex-Mayor voting for Connie Herrick

articles.text: Editor: As a long time resident of Piedmont, I have read the Measure UU document and arguments both pro and con. I have also read Andy Wasserman’s articulate article of the specific financial reasons stating that this would be a foolish spend of $19 million of public funds. All this for a swim club that has a small membership and usage. I can hardly fathom what grandiose plans they have for this property. This pool measure is approximately 1/3 of the $66 million cost of current high school bond measure. They receive a new campus and this would provide two new pools. The argument in favor of this measure, signed by our mayor and four Piedmonters, makes the greatest reasons not to vote on this measure. Which Piedmonters would be picked for a Citizens Bond Oversight Committee and how are they to be vetted? No information was given on this topic. Review the current $66 million school bond oversight committee’s use of funds. That bond issue was rammed through the voter process with a “special” and costly election so the Piedmont government could reach the required threshold to pass a bond measure mandated by California. Here we go again! “It will only cost 75 cents a day for the median-price home” states the proposal. I calculate a much higher figure. Our local government must think that loading our tax bills with luxury projects is appropriate. –Bob Morrison
articles.title: Voting No on pool bond measure on Nov. 3

articles.text: Last weekend Piedmonters of all ages from all corners of the city kicked off the Community Pool for Piedmont campaign to pass Measure UU. For more than 50 years, the Piedmont Pool has been at the literal and figurative heart of the community. Generations of children have learned to swim in the city’s only public pool. Since its closure in March due to the Coronavirus, it has become even more evident how much Piedmont needs this pool. “After serving families and high school athletes well beyond its useful life, our pool no longer functions reliably or cost-effectively,” said Piedmont native Anne Callahan, one of three Co-Chairs of the Community Pool for Piedmont campaign. “The time has come to replace this indispensable civic asset with an affordable new facility to provide Piedmont citizens with a safe and sustainable community pool for the next 50 years.” “Measure UU will pay for the rebuilding of the Piedmont Pool. With historically low interest rates, the cost to median homeowners will be less than 75 cents a day. If Piedmont does not replace this facility, we will become the only school district in Alameda County that doesn’t have a local pool
articles.title: Campaign begins for Community Pool bond

articles.text: Editor: I am pleased and honored to endorse Hilary Cooper’s candidacy for Piedmont School Board. I am a grateful and proud alumna of Piedmont public schools so, when my husband and I returned to the Bay Area in 2012 as our youngest child was entering 9th grade, we chose Piedmont. Like so many of our neighbors, we moved to Piedmont for the quality of public education and the strength of community. I became involved as a high school Parent Club Board member and later was a member of the board of the Piedmont Education Foundation Through these, I was fortunate to work with Hilary at PHS on the Giving Campaign and Measures H & G. Hilary exemplifies the reason we made the decision to live in Piedmont. She is a creative and resourceful volunteer and has earned this community’s highest volunteer recognition with the Art Hecht Award. For our schools, she has been a committed volunteer who has given an enormous amount of time and energy. Now, at a time when she could be resting on her laurels as a new empty-nester, she has made the admirable choice to deepen her commitment to our schools and run for a place on our School Board. articles.title: Piedmont alum voices support for Hilary Cooper

articles.text: Editor: My name is Jace Porter and I served on the Piedmont School Board as the PHS Representative and was the 2019-2020 PHS Associated Student Body President. I had many opportunities to work closely with Cory Smegal and I am thrilled to be voting for her in my first election. The first quality I noticed about Cory was her strong communication skills. She was the first to reach out to me and help guide me to what my responsibilities would entail. She never lost touch, even after the closing of in-person school and board meetings. During School Board meetings Cory was the first to ask presenters a question and reevaluate the information being shared, proving her thoroughness in her work. Cory always worked to acknowledge each accomplishment of our community. From school performances, to the extraordinary Giving Campaign, Cory made each member of our school district feel valued. During these uncharted times it is important to think outside the box and Cory does just that. From working with her on the Red for Ed campaign and joining her in meetings with Buffy Wicks, I know that Cory will do whatever she can for Piedmont Schools while supporting the broader community. Cory also utilizes these experiences outside of Piedmont to discover new, successful solutions that inform her view on impactful issues for Pied-
articles.title: Student leader in support of Cory Smegal

articles.text: Editor: I understand the City needs money which is why the City Council voted to increase taxes (transfer, etc.). The City always needs money. So why do they want to increase debt at the same time? Putting the new pool bond on the ballot just doesn’t make sense. At a big expense, I had my pool removed, filled with dirt and landscaped with 14 trees, dozens of plants and open space. This helps the Reach Code goals. No more gas pool heater (the expense of an electric heater is prohibitive), and now with trees and plants to improve climate change. I wish all members of this Council were on the ballot. I would vote all of them out. –Patricia Markovich
articles.title: Why I’m voting for Pool bond doesn’t make sense

articles.text: 35% increase sparks discussion both for and against On August 3, Piedmont’s City Council quietly but unanimously passed and adopted resolution 59-2020, placing a real estate transfer tax measure on the November 3 ballot. The Alameda County Registrar of Voters officially assigned a letter to the measure on August 10, now formally referred to as Measure TT. If adopted by voters, Measure TT would increase the existing real property conveyance tax (otherwise known as real estate transfer tax) from the existing rate of $13 per $1,000 of transfer price, to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price. If passed, the 35 percent increase would make Piedmont’s real estate transfer tax the highest in the state. DJ Grubb, President of The Grubb Company, noted that the real estate community understands that these generated dollars are earmarked for infrastructure maintenance. “The 35 percent seems to be a little overreaching in this very tight marketplace. The city needs to promote mobility (affordability), not over-tax the process,” Grubb said. Grubb added that many people are held hostage in their homes due to over-taxation on capital gains, and that this additional taxation does not help that perception. “Mobility would create more transactions which would obviously increase the City’s revenue,” he said. It is estimated that revenues from this tax will generate approximately $948,462 of additional revenue annually, according to City Attorney Michelle Kenyon’s analysis of Measure TT. Funds generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used for any city general revenue purpose. The city intends to use the funds to repair and maintain existing facilities, to include city hall, the fire department and police department The ballot measure reads: “Shall the City of Piedmont, to be in alignment with neighboring East Bay Cities, increase the real estate transfer tax from $13 to $17.50 per $1000 of transfer price, generating $948,462 annually until ended by voters, to provide general tax revenue for city services and to repair and maintain city facilities including police and fire stations, parks, recreation facilities, and other city infrastructure, be adopted?” A “Yes” vote would be in favor of increasing the real estate transfer tax to the new rate of $17.50 per $1,000. A “No” vote would be against the increase in the real estate transfer tax. Unlike the pool bond, which requires a 2/3 majority of votes, the Measure TT requires only a simple majority (50.1%) for passage. The new rate would go into effect on July 1, 2021. The last day for filing direct arguments for or against the measure was August 14 and the last day for filing rebuttal arguments was August 21. Argument in favor Mayor Bob McBain, Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King, Budget Advisory Chair Bill Hosler, former mayor John Chiang, and Budget Advisory member Chris Kwei submitted an argument in favor of Measure TT. The argument in favor states, “Measure TT is assessed only on property when it is sold. The average number of home sales in Piedmont is 138 annually, so relatively few residents will be affected. Measure TT is paid at close and negotiated between the buyer and seller. Revenue from the Transfer Tax depends on the number and prices of homes sold each year. The city must forecast conservatively for this variable tax revenue to ensure budgeted expenses do not exceed expected proceeds from home sales. When tax revenue exceeds the forecast, Council allocates the excess for equipment replacement, facilities maintenance, and to address long-term liabilities. This approach has significantly strengthened the City’s financial condition. However, the age and condition of Piedmont’s streets, sidewalks and pathways, not to mention aging buildings demands attention.” The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee strongly recommends that the City raise additional funds to deal with critical infrastructure needs. Argument in opposition The argument in opposition is authored by Eric Wong, President of Berkeley-based Bridge Association of Realtors, a trade association representing 1800 realtors in the Oakland-Berkeley area. Wong argued that the proposed increase of the city’s transfer tax would make it the highest flat rate in the entire state, and could cost homeowners tens of thousands of dollars when buying or selling their home. “Unfortunately, Measure TT has no sunset date. The authors have simply crossed out the old tax rate and inserted a much higher rate without any safeguards that the money will be used as voters intend. In fact, there is no guarantee that the money from this tax will be directed to repair and maintain city facilities including police and fire stations, parks and recreation facilities, and other city infrastructure like the ballot language suggests,” the argument stated. Wong said that this means the tax can be used for anything, including salaries, pensions, or project overruns. “Piedmont already has an extremely high transfer tax rate. Increasing it will set a bad precedent in the region and could adversely affect homeowners that wish to sell their home in order to move into a retirement community,” the argument stated. Rebuttals In a rebuttal to argument in favor of Measure TT, Wong argued that “The City’s polling results indicate that well over 60 percent of Piedmonters are satisfied with city facilities as they are. Why then is the City insisting on making housing costs even more expensive for residents? It is probably the same reason a loophole was written into the measure allowing money from TT to be spent on anything. Cities, like Berkeley, include something called a “sunset clause” to their transfer taxes so they end when the money is no longer needed. Supporters claim that they want to increase taxes to fix facilities and infrastructure. If that’s the case, shouldn’t the tax end after the fixes are made? There is no sunset clause in Measure TT.” Wong added that now is not the time to make housing costs even higher for new homeowners and retirees. In a rebuttal to Wong’s argument in opposition to Measure TT, the authors stated that “Berkeley and Oakland have higher real estate transfer taxes than Piedmont. Piedmont’s transfer tax has not been increased in 27 years. All the money from Measure TT stays in our community. Revenue from transfer taxes is one of the few ways Piedmont is able to generate income for essential services like police and fire.” The authors added that, unlike annual taxes, transfer taxes are applied only when a property is sold, so Measure TT is a tax many never pay. SUDOKU SOLUTION CROSSWORD SOLUTION
