articles.text: I correspond by with a close friend who lives in Tucson, Arizona. We have shared our experiences coping with the pandemic and how it has redefined our lives. We agree that its tenacious presence continues to be unsettling at best and deeply disturbing at worst. Ongoing is the seemingly intractable issue of systemic racism in America, with a renewed focus brought about by the anguish-filled death of George Floyd. How do we fully grasp the presence of evil and injustice in a moral universe – mysterium iniquitatis? Charles Blow, an op ed columnist for the New York Times, recently shared his painful attempt to understand that which is beyond understanding. How is it possible that slavers and owners could justify to themselves that they had the right to own another human being? He puzzles and then comments that slavery, however framed, is profoundly abhorrent and depraved and was enforced by a violence both barbaric and unimaginable. What those Africans endured, kidnapped and shipped to America, was a cruel and willful horror that escapes language. Relying on the rare 1829 written record of Rev. Robert Walsh, an Englishman, Blow describes what Walsh encountered when he boarded an intercepted slave ship. “The ship had been at sea for 17 days. There were over 500 kidnapped Africans onboard. Fifty-five had already been thrown overboard. The Africans were crowded below the main deck. Each deck was only 3 feet 3 inches high. They were packed together so tight that they were sitting between one another’s legs, everyone completely nude,” the choking air so foul and fetid it repelled. “Each had been branded on their breast or arm. Many were children, little girls and little boys.” Mysterium iniquitatis in a moral universe. “Let us realize the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.” -Rev. Jen is a valued member of our City Council who is also deeply invested in our community. Because her three children attend(ed) schools at every grade in Piedmont, she brings relevant knowledge to the collaboration required with our school district -- the very heart of our city. She has a genuine warmth and enjoys engaging directly with people in our community. Jen loves attending Piedmont events and is passionate about hearing from a diverse set of citizens. I have seen first hand during the most recent discussion of city infrastructure needs in June and July how Jen is detail-oriented, strategic, and biased towards action. She displayed a very detailed understanding of the history and issues for both essential services as well as our pool facilities. Jen was also able to deftly place the plan for addressing these needs within the context of our political and budgeting processes. Further, as a citizen herself she has educated and mobilized other prominent Piedmonters to take up the leadership mantle of helping pass Measure UU. City Council representation requires a heavy investment from both the candidate and the community. Let’s take advantage of the four years Jen and Piedmont have invested and reap more fruitful work from a capable professional who is already up to speed on our city’s issues and dynamics. We supported Jen during her original campaign and are even more enthusiastic in our endorsement of her candidacy four years later. –Dion and Amy Lim

articles.text: The decision to place a $19 million bond on the November 3 ballot to build a new community pool was approved by the Piedmont City Council on August 3. Now known as Measure UU, the money would be used to finance the cost of replacement and enhancement of the current pool, located next to the Recreation Department on Hillside Avenue. Language from the ballot includes the following: The amount of the principal of the bonds shall not exceed $19,500,000. The final costs, locations, designs, layouts, and other details of the improvements will be determined as plans are finalized, construction bids are awarded, and projects are completed. Therefore, the city council cannot guarantee that the bonds will provide sufficient funds to allow completion of all needed improvements. No current renderings have yet been released. Amy Aubrecht, Anne Callahan, and Vince Saunders are co-chairing the campaign for YES on Measure UU. Cathie Geddeis is treasurer and Margaret Hiller is assistant treasurer on the campaign. An opportunity for rebuttal arguments ends on Monday, August 31. Arguments for and against are shown below. Argument in favor The argument in favor of Measure UU is authored by Mayor Bob McBain, councilmember Betsy Andersen, Piedmont Recreation Chair Steven Roland, Piedmont Board of Education member Sarah Pearson, and retired Beach Elementary Principal Nancy McHugh. The argument in favor states that “Measure UU will provide the funds necessary to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility to serve Piedmont families, students and seniors for the next 50 years. Measure UU will allow the city to take advantage of historically low interest rates, currently less than 3 percent, and will cost the median homeowner less than 75 cents a day.” A vote YES on the measure will ensure that Piedmont has a pool for lessons, recreation, exercise, and school sports. articles.text: LNU, SCU, CZU Lightning Complex fires have burned over 800,000 acres On August 17, lightning strikes started hundreds of fires across Northern California. In the days since, over one million acres have burned. California is currently under a state of emergency, and all Cal Fire resources are overextended in battling these fires. Since they broke out a week ago, three of the largest wildfire complexes (LNU, SCU, and CZU) have burned over 800,000 acres combined, and have destroyed 1,000 structures as of press time. Two of the complexes have already ranked as the second and third largest in California history. The complexes encircle the San Francisco Bay Area in Napa and Sonoma counties (LNU complex), Santa Cruz county (CZU complex), and Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties (SCU complex). The complexes are named with acronyms to indicate geographical locators based on Cal Fire administrative unit codes. LNU, for example, designates the areas that are part of the Sonoma-Lake-Napa unit, comprising Sonoma, Lake, Napa, Colusa, Solano, and Yolo counties. Fires managed by that unit are grouped under that prefix. SCU refers to the areas that are administratively under the Cal Fire SCU unit – Santa Clara, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties. CZU refers to the San Mateo-Santa Cruz unit. Piedmont Fire Engine 2880 was deployed after 9 p.m. on Friday night, August 21, for an “immediate need” assignment as part of a local Task Force assigned to the SCU Lightning Complex. The three-man crew is led by Lt. Justin McNulty, with engineers Russ San Fillippo and Justin Morris. “Piedmont Fire Department immediately accepted the call for assistance,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. The SCU Lightning Complex has burned the most acres of the three, making it the second largest wildfire in state history. The majority of the destruction has been limited to Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. As of press time, it had burned 360,055 acres, with 15 percent containment as of Tuesday morning, August 25. Joining the Piedmont firefighters on the task force are firefighters from Hayward, Alameda, East Bay Regional Parks and San Mateo departments. Black added that the fire is not a threat to Piedmont. The CZU Lightning Complex, the smallest of the three fires, is also the least contained. It had burned 78,869 acres and was 17 percent contained on Wednesday morning. One Santa Cruz county man died and seven others have been reported missing, and 330 structures have been destroyed. The LNU Lightning Complex is, thus far, the deadliest and most destructive of the three fires in terms of structure damage. It has burned 352,913 acres and was 27 percent contained as of Tuesday morning. Five people died in Napa and Sonoma counties, and 1,188 total structures have been damaged or destroyed.

articles.text: No new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters over the past seven days, but the number of positive cases in Alameda County continued to grow. As of yesterday, August 25, the number is 16,738 according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. This represents a 12 percent increase. Health officials reported 10 more deaths since last Tuesday, August 18, bringing the total number of fatalities due to COVID-19 to 234 in Alameda County. Six cases were reported in Piedmont earlier in August and the total number of cases for the City stands at 29. Earlier in the month, officials said that an electronic reporting issue was resolved and this resulted in a sudden uptick in cases. However, some of the newly reported cases due to the repaired process come from early in the year, and it is not clear if the new Piedmont cases are all from August or were from prior months. Oakland, the most populous city in the county, now has 6,866 cases. Hayward counted 2,357 cases and Fremont has 1,120. The state still has Alameda County on a COVID-19 “watchlist” along with most other counties in California. Alameda County has been on the list since July 12, meaning many indoor businesses and activities are prohibited by state regulations. On Friday, August 21, county officials allowed some new sectors of the economy to reopen for the first time in weeks. Outdoor public pools are now allowed to open as long as they follow protocols, as well as some personal services, like barbers, nail salons and non-medical massages, but the business has to be conducted completely outdoors.

Alameda County COVID-19 cases soar to nearly 17,000 By Barry Eitel No new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters over the past seven days, but the number of positive cases in Alameda County continued to grow. As of yesterday, August 25, the number is 16,738 according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. This represents a 12 percent increase. Health officials reported 10 more deaths since last Tuesday, August 18, bringing the total number of fatalities due to COVID-19 to 234 in Alameda County. Six cases were reported in Piedmont earlier in August and the total number of cases for the City stands at 29. Earlier in the month, officials said that an electronic reporting issue was resolved and this resulted in a sudden uptick in cases. However, some of the newly reported cases due to the repaired process come from early in the year, and it is not clear if the new Piedmont cases are all from August or were from prior months. Oakland, the most populous city in the county, now has 6,866 cases. Hayward counted 2,357 cases and Fremont has 1,120. The state still has Alameda County on a COVID-19 “watchlist” along with most other counties in California. Alameda County has been on the list since July 12, meaning many indoor businesses and activities are prohibited by state regulations. On Friday, August 21, county officials allowed some new sectors of the economy to reopen for the first time in weeks. Outdoor public pools are now allowed to open as long as they follow protocols, as well as some personal services, like barbers, nail salons and non-medical massages, but the business has to be conducted completely outdoors. articles.text: Editor: Jen Cavenaugh is a true gift to the Piedmont community and has been an outstanding member of our city council. Her contributions to the council and our city have been numerous and exemplary. There is no question in my mind that Jen should be reelected to our city council. Jen approaches opportunities in the way that you would expect of a University of Chicago MBA, Accenture (Andersen Consulting) executive, and Clorox manager. She identifies opportunities, analyzes them, develops solutions, connects with people, enlists them in the efforts, manages the processes, and gets results. My first exposure to Jen and her work was a community research plan she did in 2014 for the Recreation Commission as a volunteer consultant. It defined Piedmont community recreational interests, priorities, and unmet needs. It was an outstanding, highly professional report that inspired me. Since that first exposure to Jen, I have been constantly amazed by the breath of her interests, her energy, her desire to take on new challenges, and make Piedmont better. But this is what she just naturally does. Jen Cavenaugh is a force that Piedmont needs, and I am thankful we have her. I strongly support and recommend Jen’s reelection to the Piedmont City Council. –Dick Carter of the city council. She is honest, direct, compassionate, and a good listener. One aspect of Jen that I find particularly engaging--and is such a gift for our city--is that she is always pressing forward. She doesn’t dwell on past decisions or judge others; she continually works to identify needs and consider solutions, to reach out to others to gain information or spread the word. Whether there is a community need or celebration, she shows up. She doesn’t hesitate to do the hard work or cast an unpopular vote to support what she believes is best for Piedmont. Jen has a quick mind, strong business acumen, and a deep knowledge of Piedmont. She respects our history while recognizing areas of needed improvement, and understands how to use our limited resources and prioritize our most critical issues. Please join me in voting to reelect Jen Cavenaugh for Piedmont City Council in November. Sincerely, –Megan Pillsbury Piedmont Board of Education
articles.title: Jen Cavenaugh – working to make Piedmont better

City ordinance 517 N.S. banned gas powered leaf blowers in 1990 because of their noise pollution. Many proponents of the REACH codes insist that stopping climate change necessitates elimination of natural gas appliances. How about enforcing the leaf-blower ban first? That’s a GHG-reducing measure that would be music to our ears. –Dai Meagher For sake of climate, residents urged to support Reach Codes Editor: Along with 90% of our fellow Piedmonters (according to recent survey results), we worry about the world we will leave behind if we don’t take serious action to prevent the worst-case scenarios for climate change. Case in point: this week’s smoke-filled air becoming the new normal with more frequent and intense wildfires. The Reach Codes now before City Council offer a reasonable and concrete step in the right direction, by assisting our transition away from natural gas, a greenhouse gas-emitting fossil fuel that contributes to climate change. Heating our homes and water with natural gas accounts for almost half of the emissions created within Piedmont’s boundaries. We can’t move the needle on our climate goals without using less natural gas, whether through better insulating our homes and pipes, adding rooftop solar, or replacing natural gas appliances over time with new, efficient electric appliances. As many as 30 other leading California cities are adopting Reach Codes, and even PG&E supports this long-term shift away from natural gas. City staff led a thorough, year-long process to develop the Codes, incorporating a great deal of public input. In particular, staff responded to concerns about one-size-fits-all requirements by developing a menu of options for energy upgrades, based on the preferences, budget, and individual circumstances of each homeowner, including many low-cost options. The upgrades will be triggered by sizable renovations or expansions to Piedmont’s aging housing infrastructure, when it is most pragmatic and cost-effective to do so. For more details, visit https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/city_news___notifications/council_consideration_ of_reach_codes_deferred. Reach Code requirements are relatively minor in the scheme of home renovations, but are important steps in tackling climate change. It would be a real shame if we shirk our collective responsibility by passing up on this opportunity. We urge our fellow residents to show that this community cares about climate action by writing to Council today (citycouncil@ piedmont.ca.gov) to support the adoption of Reach Codes. –Signed Katie Aubrecht, Indira Balkisoon, Elizabeth Behrens, Marj Blackwell, realtor Moira Chapman, Irene Cheng, Ellington Davis (PUSD alum), Jonathan Davis, Jezabel Droga (PHS student), Glenn Friedman, Amy Griffith (PUSD parent), Claudia Harrison, Toby Jacob (PHS student), Garrett Keating, Judy Kelly, Ronna Kelly, Russell Griffith (PUSD parent), Zenobia Lloyd (PHS student), Mara Lovric (PHS student), Marianne Mitosinka, George Wick, Samantha Miller, Susan Miller-Davis, Margaret Ovenden, Henri F. articles.text: Yes, there are hundreds of wildfires all over our state right now, most out of control. The biggest negative for most, surprisingly, will be mental health, I’m convinced. Apart from Santa Cruz, Vacaville and Healdsburg, these fires are mostly in remote parts with few inhabitants, few homes. But the situation is unexpectedly depressing, piled on top of other existing news: The killer Coronavirus that just won’t go away, and the related health and expense for both teachers and schools, plus the isolation it causes from friends and most relatives. And then we have a depressed economy and unemployment both real and anticipated, the instability and deadlocks in our national government, virtual schooling that forces parents to stay home and not work, the drought, our troubled foreign policy, foreign governments known to meddle in our upcoming election, and the uncertainty about the future resultant from the multiple distresses. Then too the officially “unhealthy” smoky air over so many of our cities day after day. All these negatives will be weighing on the citizenry even after long-overdue November rains wipe out the fires. Just consider the kids locked out of classrooms now for six-plus months, with brains ill-equipped to catch up. Nonetheless, my conviction is that after all these trials pass, we will all emerge stronger and more resilient than ever. Only we’re not in Nirvana any more. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, August 26, 2020 Local Items Reflections on our current state (of mind) By Paul Hertelendy Yes, there are hundreds of wildfires all over our state right now, most out of control. The biggest negative for most, surprisingly, will be mental health, I’m convinced. Apart from Santa Cruz, Vacaville and Healdsburg, these fires are mostly in remote parts with few inhabitants, few homes. But the situation is unexpectedly depressing, piled on top of other existing news: The killer Coronavirus that just won’t go away, and the related health and expense for both teachers and schools, plus the isolation it causes from friends and most relatives. And then we have a depressed economy and unemployment both real and anticipated, the instability and deadlocks in our national government, virtual schooling that forces parents to stay home and not work, the drought, our troubled foreign policy, foreign governments known to meddle in our upcoming election, and the uncertainty about the future resultant from the multiple distresses. Then too the officially “unhealthy” smoky air over so many of our cities day after day. All these negatives will be weighing on the citizenry even after long-overdue November rains wipe out the fires. Just consider the kids locked out of classrooms now for six-plus months, with brains ill-equipped to catch up. Nonetheless, my conviction is that after all these trials pass, we will all emerge stronger and more resilient than ever. Only we’re not in Nirvana any more. articles.text: Camp Smart Start is the Piedmont Recreation Department’s (PRD) response to in-person childcare during this unusual academic school year. “We’re trying to support working families and working parents by providing childcare and support for elementary school students during their distance learning,” Recreation Supervisor Jackson Stearns said. The camp is following the same model as Camp Almost Everything, that was rolled out by the recreation department this summer. Camp Smart Start consists of small cohorts of students, and “pods” are no greater than 12 children. Students are required to wear masks and socially distance themselves from one another. Daily health screenings are provided. As a three-week session, it is similar in length to Camp Almost Everything. Stearns said the biggest difference is the support given to Piedmont students in distance learning. “School staff and Recreation Department staff are working with students during the school day, making sure they log in [to class] on time to their synchronous learning classes, as well as complete their asynchronous assignments and submit those in a timely manner,” Stearns said. Currently, 57 students are enrolled, divided into six groups operating at all campsites. One group is at Wildwood Elementary, two groups are at Beach, and three groups are at Havens. There is currently a waiting list for a 2nd session. Stearns admits that the first day provided a learning curve for staff, as both students and staff became acclimated to distance learning programs. “Because this is brand new both for the district and the staff, we knew there would be some challenges just learning the computer systems. I’m happy to say that the majority of the students were able to log in successfully, complete their assignments and do the work,” Stearns said. He confirmed that he plans to work closely with the principals of the three schools. Smoke in the air from surrounding wildfires presented the camp’s “first big curveball” on Monday, Stearns acknowledged. “We did shut down the program around lunchtime, and will be closed for the foreseeable future until air conditions improve,” he said. Camp Smart Start is for students from transitional Kindergarten through grade five, and is entirely outdoors. Residents can register for the lottery based upon their child’s school assignment. All “pods” will match school district cohorts to the best of the department’s capability. The school district provides students with Chromebook laptops, and students are asked to come to camp with their laptop, charger, headphones, and stationary. “We are asking the parents to treat [this camp] as school,” Stearns said. While the camp is not to be treated as a replacement for school, staff will support both teachers and students in distance learning. Camp Smart Start staff are not teachers or tutors, but they communicate and work closely with parents to support students in their distance learning classes and assignments. For more information on the camp, visit https://piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ recreation/camp_smart_start.

articles.text: Abby Bleich of Piedmont was named to the Dean’s List at Bates College for the winter semester. A 2017 graduate of Athenian School, she will be entering her senior year at Bates. To achieve the Dean’s List recognition, students must have a cumulative grade point average of 3.8 or higher. Located in Lewiston, Maine, Bates is internationally recognized as a leading liberal arts college, attracting 2,000 students from across the U.S. and around the world. Since 1855, Bates has been dedicated to educating the whole person through creative and rigorous scholarship in a collaborative residential community. Cultivating intellectual discovery and informed civic action, Bates prepares leaders sustained by a love of learning and zeal for responsible stewardship of the wider world.

articles.text: Like many other seasonal events across the Bay Area, this year’s Harvest Festival, originally scheduled for Piedmont Park on Sunday, September 27, will be a virtual celebration due to gathering restrictions brought on by the pandemic. “As disappointing as not having an in-person event is, the city recognizes that the most important thing right now is to keep the community safe and healthy,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “Because of the nature of the Harvest Festival, social distancing measures would not be possible to achieve, let alone enforce, during this event,” This year’s Festival will feature a photo contest and a youth coloring, drawing, and collage contest. The Recreation Department encourages Piedmont residents to share harvest gardening successes with the virtual festival. Residents and school district employees can email photos of their home-grown edibles, preserves and cooking at one photo per category. Photos may be sent directly to Putzer at cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Submissions must include your name, category entered, email and home address. The deadline for photo submissions is Friday, September 18. Everyone who enters will get a participation ribbon and will be entered into a random drawing for a $60 gift certificate from Ace Grand Lake Nursery on October 5. Categories for submissions include: tomato, pumpkin, squash, jam, bread, mustard, best cookie, dried fruit and veggie, salsa, unusual fruit, curds and butters, jam, apple pie, cake, cucumber pickles, ugly edible, honey, preserved edible, “other” pie, pesto and sauce, preserved veggie, and compost pile. The youth coloring contest is sponsored by the Piedmont Garden Club. Kids ages 14 and younger can download a poster, create their own vegetable drawing or make a collage from the nature scavenger hunt page found on the recreation department’s website. E-mail a copy of the project to cputzer@piedmont. ca.gov. “[This] is essentially a way to engage all the ages as we’re all sheltering in place,” said Susan Hill, founder of the Harvest Festival. She added that designing the festival virtually allows for a wider breadth of possibilities. For more infor mation, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/ harvestfestival. articles.text: Outreach Project Leader. I have been volunteering in our schools since 2005, including on every Parent Club Board and as President of Piedmont Language School. I am an active member of the League of Women Voters and Piedmont Connect. In Oakland, I taught strategic and financial decision-making skills to underserved youth through Game Theory Academy, developed a professional mentoring program, and was Co-Founder and Director of the Oakland Treasure Hunt. I have a deep commitment to the social/emotional development of our youth: I developed Healthy Relationships programs for the Recreation Dept, lead the high school Coaching Boys into Men and Athletes as Leaders program rollout, and serve with Change a Path Foundation, a donor circle to fund anti-sex trafificking initiatives. For over a decade I was the General Manager (and below average player) for the Baja Bombers adult softball team. 2 – I am intimately familiar with Yes on Measure UU to rebuild Piedmont’s Community Pool. The campaign has great campaign chairs leading the grassroots effort. I am using my experience with countless City Council, School Board, and financing measure campaigns to help with strategy, volunteer recruitment, and voter outreach. The goal is to personally reach every voter to educate them about the current state of the pool, which has been the literal and figurative heart of our community for over 50 years. Unfortunately, our current pool has surpassed its useful life and can no longer serve children, adults of all ages, and our public schools and athletic teams. Measure UU will provide the funds necessary to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable pool facility for our community for the next 50 years. These are challenging times to be working on a campaign, but now is the time to support an investment in our future. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – For 25 years, I have been part of the Charlotte Maxwell Clinic (CMC). We provide integrative cancer care for low-income, underserved Bay Area women with cancer. Our clients are mainly Latina, African-American and Asian, many are monolingual and 70% live below the federal poverty level. I have faced breast cancer twice. Even with incredible support, the experience was grueling and my life was never the same. CMC clients get chemotherapy and go back to work the same day. Many work two jobs. There is no respite for these women. Our clinic is their community, their place to receive care and support. I’ve been honored to volunteer at CMC in many capacities: acupuncturist, board vice president, medical advisor and executive director. 2 – In 2002, Josh Bernstein asked my support for a new pool and I gladly gave it. Our pool was already old and worn then, two decades ago. I hear the concerns about incurring $19.5M in debt. However, now is a good time to take advantage of low interest rates. If we continue to delay, replacement costs keep skyrocketing, the pool keeps leaking, and we keep spending more and more to maintain its degrading infrastructure. Our pool is a midtown jewel that strengthens our property values. Potential home buyers find our community amenity extremely attractive. I hope for a modern, green facility that can easily accommodate all our swim, health, recreation and community gathering needs. As a swimmer and enthusiastic advocate for aqua circuit training, I will vote Yes on Measure UU. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – For 25 years my volunteer efforts focused on our City and PUSD. I chaired the 2019 CIP and continued in 2020 reviewing resident proposals and ongoing long-term projects. City Council appointed me to Recreation Commission in 2017; I now serve as Vice Chair. Since 2015, I’ve served on Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame Board. In 2012, I joined Mayor Chiang leading Measure Y to victory. I’ve served on the Budget Advisory Committee reviewing 5-year financial projections, funding and expenditures. I volunteered during a series of PUSD Parcel Tax campaigns. I co-chaired the 2006 Seismic Safety Bond Program. I served with Piedmont Educational Foundation 2007-11. I served as PMS Parent Club President, with Beach Parents Organization, PHS Parent Club and on the Support Committee for PHS Wellness Center. I served PHS Boosters 2008- 14 and PHS/PMS “Every 15 Minutes” 2011. I chaired the Tri-school fundraiser, started Meet the Masters, and led PEP. 2 – Five studies, (2002-2016) each concluded the same sad fact: The Piedmont Pool, as it currently exists, does not meet the needs of our community. Staff reporting to City Council confirms: pool expenses remain stable but operating costs continue to accelerate due to irreparable wear and tear. While Alameda County is now re-opening community pools, our Piedmont pool will remain closed. Public testimony and resident surveys reveal a groundswell of deep attachment to our pool. As a resource for lap swim, recreation swim, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, competitive swim and water polo, there is no dispute that our pool is a valued community asset. Taking advantage of historically low interest rates, Measure UU funds construction of a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility. The June BAFPC analysis indicates a favorable operational recapture rate depending on fee structure. I endorse Measure UU and campaign for its passage. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: distance learning, everyone is feeling the pressure. Students are transitioning from unstructured summer months at home to five days of classes sitting at a computer screen – still at home. Working parents struggle to balance office responsibilities with parenting, a particularly challenging dance for parents of young children. And teachers are working mightily to adjust to new technologies in remote environments. COVID has presented us with the challenge of how we educate our children in a different way that is effective and fulfilling. With great challenge comes great opportunity. I am looking forward to working with Piedmont families to find solutions that meet the needs of our children. HILARY COOPER 1 – Since moving to town, I have been involved with the Havens Parent Club, PMS Parent Club and PHS Parent Club. At Havens, I co-chaired the tri-school’s Spring Fling fundraiser. And at both PMS and PHS, I served as Vice President and President. I have co-chaired the Giving Campaign twice, which is the largest fundraiser for the Piedmont Education Foundation. I volunteered during the Measure A Parcel Tax Campaign and I co-chaired the Measures G&H Parcel Tax Campaign. I am a board member of The Cancer League and I just became a provisional member of the Piedmont Garden Club. My daughter and I were also involved with the National Charity League for seven years where we focused most of our time at Piedmont Gardens, a local senior living community. 2 – I believe the biggest loss our students are experiencing is the lack of social interaction with their peers, teammates, teachers and coaches. Humans are social beings and distance learning is not an ideal substitute for in-person teaching and learning. However, since the state mandated that all schools begin with distance learning, we must look for creative ways to find alternatives to get our students together (while minding the guidelines). We should look to partner with some of our excellent resources, like the Wellness Center or the Piedmont Makers, to collaborate on gatherings of smaller groups of students. Once we are able to re-open, we should look into sending the students whose need for in-person instruction is greatest, like our elementary students. I am hopeful that we could have a successful rollout by grade that would ensure we remain open safely. JASON KELLEY 1 – My main volunteer commitment for the past four years has been producing the Beach Revue at Beach School, heading up 50 parent volunteers to put on the annual live musical that sees 200-plus students and a live band perform in four shows – and earning Piedmont schools about $20,000 each year. I’ve also been on the boards of the Piedmont Middle School and Beach Elementary. I’ve been a board member of PRAISE, the special education parents’ organization, and I was a member of the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee. Outside of Piedmont, I’ve volunteered for charities focused on helping LGBTQ youth by raising money and awarding scholarships, as well as finding services and shelter for young people who have been thrown out of their homes because of their sexual orientation. 2 – Students, parents, and teachers are adapting to online learning, but students are really missing direct teacher contact and the classroom setting. Although online learning is much more organized and thought out this fall as compared to the emergency situation in the spring, younger students especially are having a hard time learning remotely. Students are also missing their friends and the growth that comes from interacting with their peers academically, athletically, and socially. An additional loss is the delay in the natural childhood progression of ever-increasing independence. Normally, every year brings new milestones of independence. Children go out into the world on their own farther and for longer times as each year passes. That forward momentum has been interrupted, and I think it’s important to find ways to help our kids continue to become more independent even though they’re spending almost all of their time home with us these days. HARI TITAN 1 – My volunteer experience includes active participation with Piedmont Neighbors’ and Newcomers’ Club, Havens Parents Club, Havens Dads Club, Piedmont Asian American Club, Piedmont Makers, PMS Parents’ Club, Yes on Measure H1, Yes on Measures G & H, Piedmont Parents Network, PREC Education Subcommittee, PHS Parents Club, Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, STEAM Funding and Marketing Committee. 2 – I think the biggest loss is the loss of social and emotional connection of seeing friends every school day and having a shared experience at school. Working alone at home is not a substitute. Some students with advanced executive functions may be able to use the lack of distraction at home to their advantage to get their work done more quickly. It is going to be hard to measure this impact. Another impact is the loss of freedom from the tyranny of staring at a computer screen. Most of the Chromebooks were chosen and purchased before the pandemic and we didn’t anticipate online instruction for anywhere from 2 to 5 hours per day. Learning loss is the result of a less than robust educational model being implemented to cover the same amount of subject matter. We won’t know what this learning loss will be until after grading at year-end. At that point we can compare the average standardized test scores with years prior to measure the actual learning loss. McKinsey & Company did a meta-study that estimated learning loss ranging from no impact to months of learning loss per year depending upon the financial resources of the parents among other factors. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – My volunteer experience includes the following: Current School Board member, 4 years ; Vice President and Correspondent, 2 years; Facilities Steering Committee, Board Liaison; Measures G&H Parcel Tax Campaign, Board Liaison; Giving Campaign, Committee, 6 years, co-chair 2 years, raised more than $3.4 million over two campaigns; Wildwood Parent Club, 7 years, including Club President; Piedmont Education Foundation Co-Treasurer; APCP Treasurer and Tri-School Treasurer; Piedmont Education Foundation Grants Committee Co-Chair; Piedmont Middle School Site Council, 2 years; Appointed to Math Task Force that relaunched District curriculum; Piedmont Middle School March Mingle Founder; Piedmont Middle School Learnscape Legacy Wall Creator; Piedmont Community Church Mexico Trip Team Leader ; Piedmont Scouts BSA Merit Badge Counselor; Piedmont Baseball/Softball Board Member, 9 years; Piedmont High School Booster Board – chaired Highlander Classic; Youth sports coach – soccer and softball 2 – Our students and teachers are missing the daily in-person connections with one another, from kindergarteners who couldn’t get a hug from their teacher on the first day of school to the middle and high schoolers who just want to walk through the halls and see the casual smiles of their classmates. No student should be at home in front of a screen all day. The pandemic is clearly taking a toll on our students’ emotional health. At our School Board meetings this summer, I advocated strongly for as much in-person learning as possible. If re-elected, I will continue to encourage the District to make decisions that address student mental health and, as public health recommendations allow, to creatively develop ways of supporting vital in-person connections. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: In advance of the November 3 municipal election in Piedmont, School Board candidates were asked two questions: 1) What volunteer organizations are you or have you been a member of? 2) What do you believe is the biggest loss students are experiencing during distance learning? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. VERONICA ANDERSON THIGPEN 1 – I am always actively engaged in civic life and community service. As a young adult in Chicago, I was a volunteer math teacher for a community GED program. I have served on several nonprofit boards, including Congo Square Theatre Company; Healthy Schools Campaign; Genesys Works Chicago; and Community Organizing and Family Issues, where I was board president. When I moved to Piedmont, I immediately joined the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, August 26, 2020 By Allyson Aleksey Part 2 in a series In advance of the November 3 municipal election in Piedmont, City Council candidates were asked two questions: 1) What volunteer organizations are you or have you been a member of? 2) How familiar are you with the council’s decision to place a $19 million bond on the Nov. 3 ballot for a new community pool? Will you be involved with the campaign? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. JEN CAVENAUGH, Incumbent 1 – I have a long history of and passion for community service. During this current crisis, I have been a weekly volunteer with the Alameda County Community Food Bank and have supported AC Census 2020 outreach. Equity and inclusion are priorities for me: I am an active member of Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee and the newly-formed Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign, Let’s Talk Co-program Organizer, and Different Together Program Advisor through Glide Memorial Church. In Piedmont, I served on the city’s Budget Advisory Committee and was the Recreation Department Community Election Preview – City Council candidates Q&A Outreach Project Leader. I have been volunteering in our schools since 2005, including on every Parent Club Board and as President of Piedmont Language School. I am an active member of the League of Women Voters and Piedmont Connect. In Oakland, I taught strategic and financial decision-making skills to underserved youth through Game Theory Academy, developed a professional mentoring program, and was Co-Founder and Director of the Oakland Treasure Hunt. I have a deep commitment to the social/emotional development of our youth: I developed Healthy Relationships programs for the Recreation Dept, lead the high school Coaching Boys into Men and Athletes as Leaders program rollout, and serve with Change a Path Foundation, a donor circle to fund anti-sex trafificking initiatives. For over a decade I was the General Manager (and below average player) for the Baja Bombers adult softball team. 2 – I am intimately familiar with Yes on Measure UU to rebuild Piedmont’s Community Pool. The campaign has great campaign chairs leading the grassroots effort. I am using my experience with countless City Council, School Board, and financing measure campaigns to help with strategy, volunteer recruitment, and voter outreach. The goal is to personally reach every voter to educate them about the current state of the pool, which has been the literal and figurative heart of our community for over 50 years. Unfortunately, our current pool has surpassed its useful life and can no longer serve children, adults of all ages, and our public schools and athletic teams. Measure UU will provide the funds necessary to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable pool facility for our community for the next 50 years. These are challenging times to be working on a campaign, but now is the time to support an investment in our future. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – For 25 years, I have been part of the Charlotte Maxwell Clinic (CMC). We provide integrative cancer care for low-income, underserved Bay Area women with cancer. Our clients are mainly Latina, African-American and Asian, many are monolingual and 70% live below the federal poverty level. I have faced breast cancer twice. Even with incredible support, the experience was grueling and my life was never the same. CMC clients get chemotherapy and go back to work the same day. Many work two jobs. There is no respite for these women. Our clinic is their community, their place to receive care and support. I’ve been honored to volunteer at CMC in many capacities: acupuncturist, board vice president, medical advisor and executive director. 2 – In 2002, Josh Bernstein asked my support for a new pool and I gladly gave it. Our pool was already old and worn then, two decades ago. I hear the concerns about incurring $19.5M in debt. However, now is a good time to take advantage of low interest rates. If we continue to delay, replacement costs keep skyrocketing, the pool keeps leaking, and we keep spending more and more to maintain its degrading infrastructure. Our pool is a midtown jewel that strengthens our property values. Potential home buyers find our community amenity extremely attractive. I hope for a modern, green facility that can easily accommodate all our swim, health, recreation and community gathering needs. As a swimmer and enthusiastic advocate for aqua circuit training, I will vote Yes on Measure UU. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – For 25 years my volunteer efforts focused on our City and PUSD. I chaired the 2019 CIP and continued in 2020 reviewing resident proposals and ongoing long-term projects. City Council appointed me to Recreation Commission in 2017; I now serve as Vice Chair. Since 2015, I’ve served on Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame Board. In 2012, I joined Mayor Chiang leading Measure Y to victory. I’ve served on the Budget Advisory Committee reviewing 5-year financial projections, funding and expenditures. I volunteered during a series of PUSD Parcel Tax campaigns. I co-chaired the 2006 Seismic Safety Bond Program. I served with Piedmont Educational Foundation 2007-11. I served as PMS Parent Club President, with Beach Parents Organization, PHS Parent Club and on the Support Committee for PHS Wellness Center. I served PHS Boosters 2008- 14 and PHS/PMS “Every 15 Minutes” 2011. I chaired the Tri-school fundraiser, started Meet the Masters, and led PEP. 2 – Five studies, (2002-2016) each concluded the same sad fact: The Piedmont Pool, as it currently exists, does not meet the needs of our community. Staff reporting to City Council confirms: pool expenses remain stable but operating costs continue to accelerate due to irreparable wear and tear. While Alameda County is now re-opening community pools, our Piedmont pool will remain closed. Public testimony and resident surveys reveal a groundswell of deep attachment to our pool. As a resource for lap swim, recreation swim, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, competitive swim and water polo, there is no dispute that our pool is a valued community asset. Taking advantage of historically low interest rates, Measure UU funds construction of a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility. The June BAFPC analysis indicates a favorable operational recapture rate depending on fee structure. I endorse Measure UU and campaign for its passage. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received. By Allyson Aleksey Part 2 in a series In advance of the November 3 municipal election in Piedmont, School Board candidates were asked two questions: 1) What volunteer organizations are you or have you been a member of? 2) What do you believe is the biggest loss students are experiencing during distance learning? The Post will ask each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. VERONICA ANDERSON THIGPEN 1 – I am always actively engaged in civic life and community service. As a young adult in Chicago, I was a volunteer math teacher for a community GED program. I have served on several nonprofit boards, including Congo Square Theatre Company; Healthy Schools Campaign; Genesys Works Chicago; and Community Organizing and Family Issues, where I was board president. When I moved to Piedmont, I immediately joined the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee. At the first meeting I attended, I volunteered to co-chair the MLK Day Celebration, a longstanding Piedmont tradition and PADC’s signature event. When I became co-president of PADC, I worked with students and educators to launch a Black student affinity group and partnered with community advocates and district administrators to submit a racial equity policy. At PHS, I carpooled for my daughter’s badminton team and I was a parent volunteer for this year’s Musical. 2 – During this time of physical distancing, masks and social bubbles, we all miss the way we walked through the world six months ago. Obviously, the absence of personal contact with teachers and classmates is the biggest loss. In our current state of School Board Election – Candidates Q&A distance learning, everyone is feeling the pressure. Students are transitioning from unstructured summer months at home to five days of classes sitting at a computer screen – still at home. Working parents struggle to balance office responsibilities with parenting, a particularly challenging dance for parents of young children. And teachers are working mightily to adjust to new technologies in remote environments. COVID has presented us with the challenge of how we educate our children in a different way that is effective and fulfilling. With great challenge comes great opportunity. I am looking forward to working with Piedmont families to find solutions that meet the needs of our children. HILARY COOPER 1 – Since moving to town, I have been involved with the Havens Parent Club, PMS Parent Club and PHS Parent Club. At Havens, I co-chaired the tri-school’s Spring Fling fundraiser. And at both PMS and PHS, I served as Vice President and President. I have co-chaired the Giving Campaign twice, which is the largest fundraiser for the Piedmont Education Foundation. I volunteered during the Measure A Parcel Tax Campaign and I co-chaired the Measures G&H Parcel Tax Campaign. I am a board member of The Cancer League and I just became a provisional member of the Piedmont Garden Club. My daughter and I were also involved with the National Charity League for seven years where we focused most of our time at Piedmont Gardens, a local senior living community. 2 – I believe the biggest loss our students are experiencing is the lack of social interaction with their peers, teammates, teachers and coaches. Humans are social beings and distance learning is not an ideal substitute for in-person teaching and learning. However, since the state mandated that all schools begin with distance learning, we must look for creative ways to find alternatives to get our students together (while minding the guidelines). We should look to partner with some of our excellent resources, like the Wellness Center or the Piedmont Makers, to collaborate on gatherings of smaller groups of students. Once we are able to re-open, we should look into sending the students whose need for in-person instruction is greatest, like our elementary students. I am hopeful that we could have a successful rollout by grade that would ensure we remain open safely. JASON KELLEY 1 – My main volunteer commitment for the past four years has been producing the Beach Revue at Beach School, heading up 50 parent volunteers to put on the annual live musical that sees 200-plus students and a live band perform in four shows – and earning Piedmont schools about $20,000 each year. I’ve also been on the boards of the Piedmont Middle School and Beach Elementary. I’ve been a board member of PRAISE, the special education parents’ organization, and I was a member of the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee. Outside of Piedmont, I’ve volunteered for charities focused on helping LGBTQ youth by raising money and awarding scholarships, as well as finding services and shelter for young people who have been thrown out of their homes because of their sexual orientation. 2 – Students, parents, and teachers are adapting to online learning, but students are really missing direct teacher contact and the classroom setting. Although online learning is much more organized and thought out this fall as compared to the emergency situation in the spring, younger students especially are having a hard time learning remotely. Students are also missing their friends and the growth that comes from interacting with their peers academically, athletically, and socially. An additional loss is the delay in the natural childhood progression of ever-increasing independence. Normally, every year brings new milestones of independence. Children go out into the world on their own farther and for longer times as each year passes. That forward momentum has been interrupted, and I think it’s important to find ways to help our kids continue to become more independent even though they’re spending almost all of their time home with us these days. HARI TITAN 1 – My volunteer experience includes active participation with Piedmont Neighbors’ and Newcomers’ Club, Havens Parents Club, Havens Dads Club, Piedmont Asian American Club, Piedmont Makers, PMS Parents’ Club, Yes on Measure H1, Yes on Measures G & H, Piedmont Parents Network, PREC Education Subcommittee, PHS Parents Club, Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, STEAM Funding and Marketing Committee. 2 – I think the biggest loss is the loss of social and emotional connection of seeing friends every school day and having a shared experience at school. Working alone at home is not a substitute. Some students with advanced executive functions may be able to use the lack of distraction at home to their advantage to get their work done more quickly. It is going to be hard to measure this impact. Another impact is the loss of freedom from the tyranny of staring at a computer screen. Most of the Chromebooks were chosen and purchased before the pandemic and we didn’t anticipate online instruction for anywhere from 2 to 5 hours per day. Learning loss is the result of a less than robust educational model being implemented to cover the same amount of subject matter. We won’t know what this learning loss will be until after grading at year-end. At that point we can compare the average standardized test scores with years prior to measure the actual learning loss. McKinsey & Company did a meta-study that estimated learning loss ranging from no impact to months of learning loss per year depending upon the financial resources of the parents among other factors. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – My volunteer experience includes the following: Current School Board member, 4 years ; Vice President and Correspondent, 2 years; Facilities Steering Committee, Board Liaison; Measures G&H Parcel Tax Campaign, Board Liaison; Giving Campaign, Committee, 6 years, co-chair 2 years, raised more than $3.4 million over two campaigns; Wildwood Parent Club, 7 years, including Club President; Piedmont Education Foundation Co-Treasurer; APCP Treasurer and Tri-School Treasurer; Piedmont Education Foundation Grants Committee Co-Chair; Piedmont Middle School Site Council, 2 years; Appointed to Math Task Force that relaunched District curriculum; Piedmont Middle School March Mingle Founder; Piedmont Middle School Learnscape Legacy Wall Creator; Piedmont Community Church Mexico Trip Team Leader ; Piedmont Scouts BSA Merit Badge Counselor; Piedmont Baseball/Softball Board Member, 9 years; Piedmont High School Booster Board – chaired Highlander Classic; Youth sports coach – soccer and softball 2 – Our students and teachers are missing the daily in-person connections with one another, from kindergarteners who couldn’t get a hug from their teacher on the first day of school to the middle and high schoolers who just want to walk through the halls and see the casual smiles of their classmates. No student should be at home in front of a screen all day. The pandemic is clearly taking a toll on our students’ emotional health. At our School Board meetings this summer, I advocated strongly for as much in-person learning as possible. If re-elected, I will continue to encourage the District to make decisions that address student mental health and, as public health recommendations allow, to creatively develop ways of supporting vital in-person connections. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received.

articles.text: The show must go on! And so, the 107th edition of the world’s most famous cycling race, the Tour de France, is set to begin in real time on August 29 in Nice. The storied race will end on September 20 in Paris. The coronavirus pandemic forced race officials to delay the start of the race from June 27 to the end of this month. The race will continue on its normal 3,470-kilometre course starting with the 2020 Grand Départ from Nice; a 170 km ride into France’s Var Valley to Sisteron. Stage 2 climbs 187 km to the Nice Haut Pays with nearly 4,000 meters of ascent. Stage 8 and 9 provide back-toback mountain courses, respective 140 km and 154 km courses. Like the first mountain stage, Stage 8 will include three cols (mountain passes) and require more than 4,000 meters of rising for cyclists. Stage 9 has one steep ascent up Cole de la Hourcere at 1,440 meters. From there, Stages 16, 17, and 18 are three consecutive mountain stages. Stage 16 goes 164 km from La Tour de Pin to Villard de Lans; Stage 17 travels 168 km from Grenoble to Col de la Loze; and 18 goes another 168 km from Méribel to La Roche-sur-Foro. But for cycling fans, a shocking move was Team INEOS electing to keep 2017 champion Christopher Froome and 2018 champion Geraint Thomas at home despite both reportedly being healthy after recovering from injuries. articles.text: East Bay Regional closes all of its inland parks With extreme fire activity returning to Northern California and the Bay Area, parks and other outdoor activities have been closed. East Bay Regional Parks announced this week on Monday, August 24, that all of its inland parks are officially closed. The East Bay Parks that remain open are Crown Beach in Alameda, Hayward Shoreline, MLK Shoreline I Oakland, Berkeley Marina’s McLaughlin Eastshore, San Leandro’s Oyster Bay, Point Isabel in Richmond, and Quarry Lakes in Fremont. Six East Bay Regional Parks are currently within the SCU complex; Del Valle, Mission Peak, Morgan Territory, Pleasanton Ridge, Round Valley, and Sunol. The total number of park closures is estimated at 200, the highest in history. As of Tuesday morning, 795,554 total acres surrounding the Bay Area have burned due to LNU, SCU, and CZU lightning complex fires. Three more fires have burned another 125,473 acres thus far: Tehama/Glenn Zone, River Fire, and Sheep Fire. The SCU Complex Fire hits closest to home for residents of the East Bay with the fire raging through five counties: Alameda (southern end), Contra Costa, Santa Clara, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus. Its 363,772 acres already make it the second-largest fire in state history with just 15 percent containment as of Tuesday, overtaking LNU’s 352,913 acres, the third largest, with 27 percent containment yesterday. The SCU encompasses three zones: Calaveras (Alameda, Santa Clara, Stanislaus counties), Canyon (Stanislaus, San Joaquin, Merced counties), and Deer— which has been fully contained as of Tuesday in the Morgan Territory. Nearest to Piedmont, the SCU’s northernmost burn area of the Morgan Territory Regional Preserve and Los Vaqueros Reservoir shutdown Mt. Diablo. SCU has engulfed Henry W. Coe State Park near Morgan Hill, Joseph D. Grant County Park and Blue Oak Ranch Reserve approaching San Jose, while Mission Peak, the Sunol Regional Wilderness, Ohlone Wilderness, and Calaveras Reservoir have been impacted by flames. Although most of the SCU Photo courtesy of California State Parks California State Parks have announced several closures. area has been open space, the fire is rapidly approaching Patterson in Stanislaus County, with an estimated population of 22,524 and has caused destruction in the nearby Diablo Grande community. In Fremont near Mission Peak, residents along Mission Boulevard have received evacuation warnings. Residents south of Livermore and Pleasanton have also been warned. The SCU fire, only 15 percent contained, has destroyed 18 structures and damaged another six, while injuring five individuals. In the CZU zones, fires in Santa Cruz and San Mateo counties have resulted in approximately 77,000 evacuations as of Tuesday. The CZU has closed all San Mateo County parks and State Beaches. It’s destroyed 330 structures and damaged 32 with just 17 percent containment, notably overtaking the historic Big Basin Headquarters and nature center. The State Park is the oldest in California, established in 1902 to preserve some of the state’s oldest stand of old-growth redwoods. The park’s headquarters’ walls were erected in 1932. (See story on page 15 for more information) In Pescadero, the historic Pie Ranch farmhouse – built in 1863 – was destroyed after an ember fell onto their grounds. The mountain town of Boulder Creek is in the midst of a firefight, causing the destruction of 100 homes. A death was recorded in Davenport. Although the SCU and CZU fires are nearest to the Bay, the LNU has been the most destructive with nearly 1,000 structures destroyed along with four injuries and five deaths. articles.text: The JV football team has room for more players. Staff Photo Varsity football coach Jerome Johnson (right) plans a virtual program via Zoom for the JV team, similar to what they used during the summer. JV head coach Daniel King, and assistant Scott Kail are eager to implement a virtual program similar to college and the pros. “Daniel, Scott, and I would like to put kids in our virtual program and show them that football is not all physical – show them the nuances of the game,” said Johnson. “High football IQ goes such a long way. You may not be the fastest, strongest, or biggest, but if you know how to plan for an opponent, study concepts, take angles correctly, it pays such larger dividends,” he said. Through Zoom technology, student athletes are getting acclimated to football in the classroom setting, building their IQ of the game. The goal: put the brains to brawn and see what translates onto the field. “We can really go step-bystep. Kids are engaged, ask a lot of questions and we can go over teaching the game of football. Now the teachable moments are unique since we’re in a classroom setting. Usually when we have a lot of open space, kids are more engaged with each other as compared to with the coaches in this virtual setting,” said Johnson. The JV program currently has around 20 players, and it is eager to find more young talent. Although there will be some expected holdovers from the previous team, the Scots have perpetually been the pipeline for many instant starters. “We would like to add 10-15 more players. We’re going to keep kids engaged and make sure we’re having our program improve while doing it safely,” said Johnson. Despite last year’s Scots winning just one game last fall, the 2018 team was undefeated in its 10-game schedule. It included RB Brian Cain, DB/WR Ben Marshburn, CB/WR Alex Hilton, QB/ WR Tommy McNeal, and QB Cal Barna. Former JV players from 2019, such as running back Nico Defazio were praised by OL coach Dick Carte, who mentioned that Evan McConathy and Lucas Bernales will likely have larger roles on the varsity this coming season. Staff Photo In today’s age of COVID-19, uncertainty has been the middle name for each of the sports at Piedmont High. For the football team, it’s a matter of filling a full roster for the Junior Varsity team. “We want to get more kids. Right now, we’d be in the middle of our offseason and we haven’t had the opportunity to look at our JV roster and work with them at the virtual level. We’re looking to start our program mid-September,” said varsity coach Jerome Johnson. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Time Magazine The charred remains of the Big Basin Redwoods State Park headquarters. Last week on Thursday, August 20, park officials announced that the CZU Fire waging in San Mateo County and the Santa Cruz Mountains have destroyed Big Basin Redwood State Park’s historic headquarters, visitor’s center, and campgrounds. The headquarters building was created as a WPA project and is made of stone and redwood logs. It served as park headquarters until its destruction by fire this week. “The historic structures in California’s first state park are almost completely destroyed. It’s awful,” said Save the Redwoods League President Sam Hodder. “We are grateful that everybody got out and everybody is safe. “To have lost something that has been transforming people’s lives for years, such an iconic place, such a terrific example of what parks mean to communities, it’s heartbreaking.” Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating back to 1902, and contains some redwood tees believed to be 2,000 years old. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 acres of oldgrowth Redwoods. As of Tuesday, the Associated Press confirmed that “most” of the park’s old-growth redwoods had survived the burn. Among them, the “Mother of the Forest,” a tree with a 70-foot circumference and height of 329 feet – the equivalent of a 33-story building. Santa Cruz park superintendent Chris Spohrer indicated that damage to trees was widespread and that much of the canopy had been scorched. “From what they described, it was a high-heat, high-intensity fire,” Spohrer said. “A lot of the canopy burned. It is too early to tell what the long-term damage is Photo courtesy of Time Magazine The original Big Basin headquarters building. Photo courtesy of Time Magazine Photo courtesy of the Santa Cruz Sentinel A down redwood tree in Big Basin. Another angle of the Big Basin Headquarters. going to be to those trees.” Although stretches of redwoods will lose their canopies, Save the Redwoods’ scientist and ecologist Kristen Shive mentioned that burn marks will be visible for a while, but the resilience of Redwood trees will help “eventually recover.” “An active crown fire could kill trees,” said Shive. “In many cases, they will look sickly and sad for a while, but they can eventually recover.” Regarding misleading reports of the State Park being totally destroyed, Sempervirens Fund conservationist Laura McLendon agreed that redwoods will recover from the fire and make them stronger. “The forest is not gone,” McLendon said. “It will regrow. Every old growth redwood I’ve ever seen, in Big Basin and other parks, has fire scars on them. They’ve been through multiple fires, possibly worse than this.” As of Tuesday morning, the CZU Lightning Complex fire had burned 78,869-acres and was 17 percent contained. It is connected to six other parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Photo courtesy of the Santa Cruz Sentinel The “Mother of the Forest” still stands at Big Basin State Park. Photo courtesy of Cal Fire. A map of the CZU fire burning the Santa Cruz mountains.

Big Basin State Park Headquarters destroyed Old Growth 300-foot “Mother of the Forest” Redwood still standing By Jonathan Comeaux Last week on Thursday, August 20, park officials announced that the CZU Fire waging in San Mateo County and the Santa Cruz Mountains have destroyed Big Basin Redwood State Park’s historic headquarters, visitor’s center, and campgrounds. The headquarters building was created as a WPA project and is made of stone and redwood logs. It served as park headquarters until its destruction by fire this week. “The historic structures in California’s first state park are almost completely destroyed. It’s awful,” said Save the Redwoods League President Sam Hodder. “We are grateful that everybody got out and everybody is safe. “To have lost something that has been transforming people’s lives for years, such an iconic place, such a terrific example of what parks mean to communities, it’s heartbreaking.” Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating back to 1902, and contains some redwood tees believed to be 2,000 years old. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 acres of oldgrowth Redwoods. As of Tuesday, the Associated Press confirmed that “most” of the park’s old-growth redwoods had survived the burn. Among them, the “Mother of the Forest,” a tree with a 70-foot circumference and height of 329 feet – the equivalent of a 33-story building. Santa Cruz park superintendent Chris Spohrer indicated that damage to trees was widespread and that much of the canopy had been scorched. “From what they described, it was a high-heat, high-intensity fire,” Spohrer said. “A lot of the canopy burned. It is too early to tell what the long-term damage is Photo courtesy of Time Magazine The original Big Basin headquarters building. Photo courtesy of Time Magazine Photo courtesy of the Santa Cruz Sentinel A down redwood tree in Big Basin. Another angle of the Big Basin Headquarters. going to be to those trees.” Although stretches of redwoods will lose their canopies, Save the Redwoods’ scientist and ecologist Kristen Shive mentioned that burn marks will be visible for a while, but the resilience of Redwood trees will help “eventually recover.” “An active crown fire could kill trees,” said Shive. “In many cases, they will look sickly and sad for a while, but they can eventually recover.” Regarding misleading reports of the State Park being totally destroyed, Sempervirens Fund conservationist Laura McLendon agreed that redwoods will recover from the fire and make them stronger. “The forest is not gone,” McLendon said. “It will regrow. Every old growth redwood I’ve ever seen, in Big Basin and other parks, has fire scars on them. They’ve been through multiple fires, possibly worse than this.” As of Tuesday morning, the CZU Lightning Complex fire had burned 78,869-acres and was 17 percent contained. It is connected to six other parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Photo courtesy of the Santa Cruz Sentinel The “Mother of the Forest” still stands at Big Basin State Park. Photo courtesy of Cal Fire. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, August 26, 2020 Back to School By Beatriz Martinez When shelter in place began, a lot of us in Piedmont had to quickly adapt study and work areas in our home. It was then that I realized that no-one in our home had the right set up to be eight hours sitting in front of a computer. My daughter did her homework on the floor or on her bed, my home office wasn’t ready for daily zoom calls or privacy, my living room became my zoom meditation studio, and my son converted our garage into a teen lounge room. Once it was clear that we had entered a new way of home living, it made me rethink my entire home-live-work flow. I had to quickly find effective solutions in creating homeschool spaces for my kids. As a designer I love learning about a problem and finding functional solutions while creating a beautiful environment. So, my business partner and I got on the task and created a list of design components that will help parents the way it helps us when we are designing. 1. LIGHTING – Natural & Artificial Natural lighting is proven to help improve focus, alertness, productivity, and happiness. Adequate artificial lighting helps improve mood and energy, while poor lighting contributes to depression and deficiencies in the body. Additionally, a lack of lighting can result in eye fatigue and headaches. While overhead lighting allows for general room illumination, a desk lamp provides focused light on the desk surface. articles.text: As the Head of a school, I deliver a pretty standard Backto-School message under normal circumstances. You all know the drill: a fresh start, the smell of new pencils, setting goals. Blah, blah, blah. In fact, if you’re like most parents, you probably don’t really listen to these messages because they’re often predictable and dull. I don’t blame you. But these are not normal circumstances. This year, as the school year begins, I am called to address a situation so alarming and unprecedented that I am truly at a loss for words. There’s literally nothing I can say that can put this crisis into perspective, given that perspective is the exact thing you don’t have in the middle of a crisis. I also can’t offer much hope by, say, predicting when we’re going to get a vaccine and return to school full time. I can’t even say for sure which risks are worth taking and which ones aren’t Education is important Commit to supporting each other through the pandemic. because every family is different. So, as the school year begins, I am speechless, or more accurately, I have nothing of consequence to say. Except, maybe, for this. What has buoyed me these past few months, as I plan for the opening of school, are the strikingly honest conversations I’ve had with parents who have contacted me to share their concerns. What Covid has done is stripped away the need for the social niceties that often get in the way of the truth. As a result, every conversation I’ve had has been meaningful, sometimes poignant, and often soulful. People are speaking from the heart, and sometimes their hearts are breaking, and this is sacred ground. The war against this virus, and all of its attendant complications, has many fronts, and it doesn’t need one more. Let’s make it our goal not to wage a battle against each other as school begins. No one has a clear answer about how to navigate this uncharted territory, therefore we can all learn something from each other. And more than that. We can support each other on this journey because, the truth is, all of our hearts are breaking. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast is live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the company’s YouTube channel (see link below). The broadcast’s first season invited leading industry professionals to discuss Aurora’s upcoming shows and season, and hold interviews with question and answer segments and roundtable discussions. This week on Aurora Connects, theater directors Josh Costello and Dawn Monique Williams welcome famed Bay Area actor James Carpenter and his wife, costume designer Cassandra Carpenter. Audiences will get to know the Carpenters professionally: they will discuss how each started working in theatre, what they enjoy most about working in theatre, and some of their favorite shows. Costello and Williams will ask how they met, learn more about their family, and reminisce about their favorite Aurora memories. James Carpenter is an Associate Artist with California Shakespeare Theater and a former Associate Artist with Berkeley Repertory Theatre. Former shows at Aurora include American Buffalo, John Gabriel Borkman, The Birthday Party. Other credits include: Magic Theatre, Marin Theatre Company, Mark Taper Forum, The Old Globe, the Oregon Shakespeare Festival, Yale Repertory Theatre, Santa Cruz Shakespeare, the Huntington Theatre Company, and Intiman Theatre. Screen credits include feature films The Rainmaker and Metro, the independent films Bay Area actor James Carpenter. Singing and For the Coyotes, and the series Nash Bridges. Cassandra Carpenter has been a professional costume designer in the Bay Area for over 25 years. Theatre credits include: American Conservatory Theatre School of Theatre productions, Berkeley Repertory Theatre, Marin Theatre Company, San Jose Repertory Company, San Jose Stage Company, The Magic Theatre, Word for Word, Aurora Theatre Company, San Francisco Shakespeare Festival, Center Repertory Company, and Chanticleer. She has provided dance design for Smuin Ballet, Oberlin Dance Collective, Anne Bluthenthal Dancers. She operated her own costume studio, CMC & Design, in downtown San Francisco for nearly 20 years, from 1997 to 2016. Clients included Smuin Ballet, San Francisco Ballet, San Francisco Opera, Macy’s Passport, Baz Luhrman’s La Boheme, and many more. articles.text: West Edge Opera has announced the launch of “Aperture,” an online platform to create a new opera and music theater in a world where artists are separated from their audiences. The announcement follows the postponement of the Opera’s 2020 season. West Edge Opera is taking the time to invent a program that brings the creative process of new opera directly to the people who are most invested in the art form. “Aperture” seeks to redefine the way operas are chosen for commission and will provide opportunities for both experienced composers and librettist teams, as well as new talent from diverse backgrounds. Select teams will receive commissions of $60,000 and a live performance of the work when it is safe to gather again. Subscribing members of the new program will receive twiceweekly emails filled with video progress reports, analysis, and mini documentaries that discuss the work being made, as well as candid glimpses into the featured artists’ lives. West Edge Opera General Director Mark Streshinksy says he found inspiration for the program in his daily rituals. “The pandemic has been really hard for everyone in the performing arts,” he said. “For me, some days it felt like [actor] Leslie Jordan’s little 90-second updates on Instgram were the highlights of my day. I thought, what if we could do that for new opera? West Edge has found such success with Snapshot [a new work series]. I thought maybe an online version could keep people connected and creating,” he said. “As a composer without much hope of in-person performance any time soon, I found myself without much incentive to write,” said Snapshot co-creator Brian Rosen. “A program like this could bring creators closer to the people who care that these works are still being made. That sort of interaction could keep creativity going Photo by Mark Mayfield West Edge Opera General Director Mark Streshinksy. while we’re trapped in our home.” Aperture will be open for submissions in late August and selected artistic teams will start to be notified in late September. General Membership will be open to the public in late October and will range from $15 to $90 per month, with more access and interactivity offered at higher levels of membership. For more information, visit http://westedgeopera.org/aperture.
articles.title: West Edge Opera announces “Aperture,” a new online commissioning residency

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department will host a screening of the award-winning documentary Wilder than Wild: Fire, Forests and the Future on Monday, August 31, at 6 p.m. It will be shown on the city’s television station, KCOM, Channel 27, to be followed by a panel discussion on wildfire preparation and disaster preparedness. Wilder than Wild, the 2018 documentary written, directed a produced by Emmy Award winners Kevin White and Stephen Most, is a one-hour documentary that reveals how fuel build-up and climate change have exposed Western wild lands to large, high intensity wildfires, while greenhouse gases released from these fires contribute to global warming. The film explores strategies that are being developed to help mitigate the impact of these fires. Ken Pimlott, Director of California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire), described the documentary as “an absolutely wonderful production. The messages in this film are spot on.” A panel featuring the director and producer Kevin White, and Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black will follow the screening. “The city of Piedmont wants to build community awareness about mitigation strategies in this new age of wildfire,” Black said. “The screening is part of a larger effort by the city to engage the community in conversations about the future of wildfire, specifically in an urban setting.” Residents can view the screening by tuning in to KCOM or AT&T channel 99. Residents can also watch Wilder than Wild on the Zoom platform by clicking the following link: https://us02web. zoom.us/j/84429317342. For additional information, contact Bret Black at bblack@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City to show Wilder than Wild film on Aug. 31
