articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players has announced plans for two new series of virtual concerts: Bach Shorts and Main Stage Concerts. The first series, Bach Shorts, consists of three one-hour, livestreamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of Bach’s Cello Suites. Three leading Bay Area cellists partner with professors, composers, and musicians from around the globe for uniquely personal performances and collaborations. The series begins on Sunday, September 13 at 4 p.m. with cellist Christopher Costanza, from the St. Lawrence String Quartet. He will perform Bach’s Second and Sixth Cello Suites and will partner with Stanford Professor Jonathan Berger, who will discuss the effect music has on the brain, hence the concert title, Bach and the Dancing Brain. On October 11, GCCP presents Bach Inspired, a concert featuring Jennifer Kloetzel, former cellist with the Cypress Quartet. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler. Elena will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. The Bach Shorts series concludes on Sunday, November 8 with Bach Connections, with cellist Robert Howard from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra. He will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. More Music Next Year After the New Year, Gold Coast Chamber Players plan to offer four live-streamed Main Stage performances with a feeling similar to what Gold Coast audiences have come to enjoy. Tickets for the Main Stage concert series will go on sale later this year. Bach Shorts tickets are $20 Jennifer Kloetzel, cello per concert, or $50 for all three performances in the series. articles.text: Jude Law as conspiracy theorist Alan Krumwiede in Contagion. Movie review by Chris Honoré Consider the still memorable template: The year is 1918, World War I is underway, and for almost two years a pandemic, also known as the Spanish Flu, grips the world. It’s origin is still unknown, its impact staggering. Some 500 million people were infected and an estimated 50,000,000 to 100,000,000 people died. Panic swept the globe, white masks were ubiquitous, required in all public places, the signature image of a virus that no one was equipped to deal with. But that was then and this is now. Or, more accurately, this is Hollywood where all of life’s events and vagaries offer material for screenwriters, especially a harrowing epidemic and all its contemporary possibilities. Recall Outbreak, released some years back. In the film’s setup we see an infected person sneezing in a movie theater. It was a hold-your-breath moment as the small particles went aerosol. Contagion has countless such moments, small and large. The film opens with a dark screen and the sound of a dry, hacking cough. Then the image of Beth Emhoff (Gwyneth Paltrow) comes into focus, her face a sheen of sweat. She’s in a nightclub in Macao, gambling, having drinks with business associates, and talking intimately with someone not her husband on a cell phone. She coughs again and is asked if she feels all right. She insists that it’s just jet lag. At that moment, the audience knows more than she does; this will not end well. Everything she touches, every person she comes into contact with, warrants a tight shot and each image is chilling. And so this well-crafted thriller begins with a virus (ME- 1) that quickly manifests in ways indicating it is terminal and not amenable to any known medical protocols; a serial killer out of control. Soon the Center for Disease Control and the World Health Organization, and its SWAT teams of doctors, are in a desperate hunt to find its source as well as a vaccine that can be given worldwide. Contagion has a deep bench of solid actors, all focused on an analysis of what it is and how to respond quickly. They know that millions are dying. The urgency is palpable. On the front line is Dr. Ellis Cheever (Laurence Fishburn), of the CDC, who heads up the investigation. His chief field investigator is Dr. Erin Mears (Kate Winslet). Working for WHO is Dr. Leonora Orantes (Marion Cotillard). And there’s everyman Mitch Emhoff (Matt Damon), husband of Beth, and his daughter, Jory (Ana Jacoby-Heron). What is also interesting about a film that flirts with apocalypse is the its examination of the fragility of society’s rule of law and decorum. It soon becomes evident in Contagion that just beneath the patina of civilization resides the instinct for survival at any cost, a Darwinian response that can, like the virus, be just as lethal. The thread of civility is slender, and one event can change everything. Contagion is about such an event. Contagion. Starring Matt Damon, Kate Winslet, Gwyneth Paltrow, Laurence Fishburn, Jude Law, Marion Cottillard, Jennifer Ehle and Ana Jacoby-Heron. Directed by Steven Soderbergh. Rated PG-13. Beethoven’s persona was that of an absent minded and disheveled street person. Jascha Heifetz attempted to look inconspicuous, and in doing so attracted even more attention. One of these The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet delights was Babes in Toyland which featured comedians Laurel and Hardy to best advantage. But that is not what made Victor Herbert great. As a bon vivant, he was the talk of the entire nation. People talked about him wherever he went. He delighted in the attention. As a great conversationalist, he also delighted his audience. When aroused, he was a virtuoso of the most “colorful” vocabulary. But he could calm down just as quickly. This delighted those who were around him. One of my old friends knew Victor Herbert very well. My friend told me of these incidents in great detail. Another thing that endeared Victor Herbert to his public was his immense generosity. He made lots of money and he gave it away with equal enthusiasm. But that is not what made Victor Herbert great. In him, America saw what they wanted to be - the consummate genius who knew success worn with grace and generosity. Americans said about him “what a guy!” But there is much more. Victor Herbert was also the greatest cellist. And herein lies the rest of the story (as radio announcer Paul Harvey famously said). There are two things which remain to be mentioned. It was Victor Herbert who inspired Dvorak to write the greatest cello Concerto of all time. And we must remember that it was Victor Herbert who established that most important organization ASCAP – the first professional organization for composers, authors and publishers. articles.text: A scene from Howl’s Moving Castle. Review by Chris Honoré Howl’s Moving Castle represents another tour de force from the extraordinary imagination of writer-director Hayao Miyazaki and his world-renowned Studio Ghibli. Adapted from the novel by Diana Wynne Jones, it is set in Europe and features an 18-year-old girl, Sophie (Emily Mortimer), a shy young hat maker, who is transformed into a 90-year-old woman (Jean Simmons) by the jealous Wicked Witch of the Waste (Lauren Bacall), a sly name reflecting Miyazaki’s wonderful sense of humor. Looking in the mirror Sophie is shocked to see a stooped and gnarled old woman and it becomes her quest to somehow break the Witch’s spell. Unexpectedly she meets an attractive, inscrutable, shape-shifting Wizard, Howl (Christian Bale), who lives in a mobile, steampunkish, labyrinthine four-legged castle. This is a Miyazaki tale and Sophie’s adventure soon veers off in unexpected directions, involving a war, a fire demon (Billy Crystal), and even a silent, sentient scarecrow. As well, unlike many of Hollywood’s films aimed at a younger audience, Miyazaki does not draw deep lines between good and evil, often seeming more comfortable with the ambiguous. For example, the Wizard can seem both malicious and benign; Sophie comes to care for the Witch who cast the transformative spell. With regards to war, it’s never clear what side should prevail. The story also seems to ask the question whether war is not only futile but also an absurd human endeavor. All of the above is framed by understated humor and a sense of floating animé, which is vibrant, engaging, and filled with wonder. Note: Howl’s Moving Castle may be too intense for very young children, In addition, its plot is a bit convoluted, taking many different twists and turns. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004). Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. From Studio Ghibli and HBO Max. Animated, with the voices of Emily Mortimer, Billy Crystal, Jean Simmons, Lauren Bacall and Christian Bale. 2 hrs. Rated: PG.
articles.title: Howl’s Moving Castle another Miyazaki masterpiece

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Films such as The Karate Kid are, unabashedly, morality plays. The field of play is the context of choice given that sports are so ideally suited to this predictable yet compelling narrative. Adversity is confronted and overcome, the athlete prevails, then smash cut to cheers, raised arms. Get ready for a warm glow. The wildly popular 80s martial arts classic of the same name, starring Pat Morita and Ralph Macchio, was set in Los Angeles. The more recent incarnation takes place, interestingly enough, in Beijing and the sport is not karate but kung fu. Actually, it’s wushu, a more aggressive form of kung fu, involving punching and hard body contact. The template is familiar and the changes regarding geography and culture, when it comes to the core story, superficial. A young kid, Dre (Jaden Smith), from the streets of Detroit, arrives in China with his single mom, Sherry (Taraji P. Henson), who has a job with a car company. Dre is the new kid on the unfamiliar block and soon becomes the target of some local school bullies who are schooled by a cruel sensei in the art of kung fu. Dre’s life quickly becomes intolerable until he is rescued, literally, by the unassuming Mr. Han (Jackie Chan), the apartment building maintenance man, a man generally laconic yet deeply schooled in the martial arts, which he quickly makes obvious when Dre is attacked. Of course, there is a tween love interest, Mei Ying (Wen Wen Han), a gifted violinist, who befriends Dre. And so, Dre’s training begins, including the familiar wax on, wax off, only involving a jacket. Jacket on, hang up, jacket off. Rinse and repeat. Dre is undisciplined and angry; he wants to go home and feels like a stranger in a strange land. He is, nevertheless, quietly and firmly instructed in the lessons of Kung Fu and in the lessons of life, all leading to the familiar climactic match where he meets his nemesis, Cheng, on the mat. The ending is foregone, the building tide of good feelings and anticipation are finalized with Dre performing a slo-mo kicking somersault that is the money moment in the film. Take note: Jaden Smith is the son of actor Will Smith and his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith, who were the film’s producers. His debut acting role was with his father in The Pursuit of Happyness. It must be nice to have a mom and dad who can gift wrap a movie and let you carry it on your pre-teen shoulders. Of course, Jackie Chan’s crew helped with Jaden’s intense training and execution. Tweens will love the story, for them fresh and interesting as well as a nice introduction to China. To the filmmakers’ credit, the neighborhoods of Beijing are not scrubbed, but nicely frayed and crowded giving a solid sense of the bustling and crowded Beijing. It feels like the real deal. And so, once again, does the movie. The Karate Kid. A remake starring Jaden Smith, Jackie Chan, Taraji P. Henson, Wang Zhenwei and Wen wen Han. Directed by Harald Swart. 2 hrs., 20 min.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2020 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS Howl’s Moving Castle another Miyazaki masterpiece A scene from Howl’s Moving Castle. Review by Chris Honoré Howl’s Moving Castle represents another tour de force from the extraordinary imagination of writer-director Hayao Miyazaki and his world-renowned Studio Ghibli. Adapted from the novel by Diana Wynne Jones, it is set in Europe and features an 18-year-old girl, Sophie (Emily Mortimer), a shy young hat maker, who is transformed into a 90-year-old woman (Jean Simmons) by the jealous Wicked Witch of the Waste (Lauren Bacall), a sly name reflecting Miyazaki’s wonderful sense of humor. Looking in the mirror Sophie is shocked to see a stooped and gnarled old woman and it becomes her quest to somehow break the Witch’s spell. Unexpectedly she meets an attractive, inscrutable, shape-shifting Wizard, Howl (Christian Bale), who lives in a mobile, steampunkish, labyrinthine four-legged castle. This is a Miyazaki tale and Sophie’s adventure soon veers off in unexpected directions, involving a war, a fire demon (Billy Crystal), and even a silent, sentient scarecrow. As well, unlike many of Hollywood’s films aimed at a younger audience, Miyazaki does not draw deep lines between good and evil, often seeming more comfortable with the ambiguous. For example, the Wizard can seem both malicious and benign; Sophie comes to care for the Witch who cast the transformative spell. With regards to war, it’s never clear what side should prevail. The story also seems to ask the question whether war is not only futile but also an absurd human endeavor. All of the above is framed by understated humor and a sense of floating animé, which is vibrant, engaging, and filled with wonder. Note: Howl’s Moving Castle may be too intense for very young children, In addition, its plot is a bit convoluted, taking many different twists and turns. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004). Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. From Studio Ghibli and HBO Max. Animated, with the voices of Emily Mortimer, Billy Crystal, Jean Simmons, Lauren Bacall and Christian Bale. 2 hrs. Rated: PG. articles.text: The COVID-19 pandemic has unsettled the country’s employment picture for months and will likely continue to do so for a while. However, the nature and terminology of this disruption varies greatly among individuals – some have seen their jobs disappear, others have been “furloughed” and still others have been offered an early retirement. If you’re in this final group – those either offered, or feeling forced to accept, an early retirement, how should you respond? Try to look at your situation holistically, rather than strictly in a short-term manner. Consider these four areas: • RETIREMENT What does retirement really look like to you? Are you ready to fully retire or would you like to work part time? Are you confident that you can work somewhere else for a few years before retiring on your own terms? If you’re not certain you can work elsewhere, how can you adjust your desired retirement lifestyle – what you planned to do, where you hoped to live, etc. – to meet your new reality? • INCOME Just how financially affected you’ll be from an early retirement depends on several factors: how much you’ve already saved and invested, whether you’re married and have a working spouse, whether you’ve paid off your mortgage, and so on. In any case, though, you’ll need to answer several questions, including these: Do I need to start taking withdrawals from my IRA and 401(k)? If so, how much can I afford to take out each year without running the risk of outliving my resources? Should I adjust my current investment mix? If I haven’t yet started collecting Social Security, should I do so now, or can I afford to wait until my monthly payments will be bigger? Are there any other sources of income I can leverage? You may want to work with a financial professional to address these and other key income-related issues. • INSURANCE If you received health insurance through your employer, an early retirement could present you with a dilemma, especially if you’re not quite old enough for Medicare. You might be eligible for COBRA, which provides ex-employees and their dependents the option of continued health insurance for potentially up to 36 months, but this coverage can be expensive. As an alternative, you might be able to negotiate an extended severance package, which could provide you with health insurance for several months. Or, you might be able to get on the health insurance plan of your working spouse. • LEGACY Many people want to take care of their family while they’re alive – and leave something behind when they’re gone. If you take an early retirement, you might lose your employer’s group life insurance. Of course, if this plan was not sufficient, you may have already supplemented it with your own policy, but, if you haven’t, you may need to shop around for some coverage, particularly if you have children still at home. You also may want to take this opportunity to review your key financial accounts to make sure your beneficiary designations still accurately reflect your wishes. Going through an unplanned career transition is certainly challenging. But looking closely at the four areas describe above, and making the appropriate moves, may help you reduce some of the stress and can put you in a better position to start the next phase of your life. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Tj Stevko is a financial advisor with the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue. Tel. (510) 4589.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group took on one of its more challenging reads for its monthly discussion on Monday, August 3, when it tackled The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable, by author and former options trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb. Written in 2007 and updated in 2010, the book provides an understanding of rare and unpredictable events, their extreme impacts, and the tendency for people to find simplistic explanations for these events after they have happened. Taleb calls them “Black Swans”, using 9/11 is an example. The book was on the New York Times best-seller list for 36 weeks and was published in 32 languages. Taleb explains there are different types of events and probabilities associated with them. We cannot anticipate the black swans that dramatically affect us. Taleb does not suggest attempting to predict Black Swan events, but rather wants readers to develop the capacity to handle them and have the ability to take advantage of them when they unexpectedly occur. His central thesis is that we have a blindness with respect to randomness, particularly those with large deviations; and the consequences for us are profound. Taleb is a philosopher, mathematician, psychologist, social scientist, and financial trader, all wrapped up in one very intelligent man. He covers literary topics, psychology, science, business, and advises his readers on how to conduct themselves in the face of uncertainty. Following his thoughts requires focus and effort from the reader, but the group of thirteen readers was up to the challenge. Participating in the virtual meeting were Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Susan Ode, Jeri Lockhart, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Sally Arney, Margie Blodgett, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Most members of the group were happy to have read the book. They felt it will affect the way they will perceive and react to the uncertainties they experience. It was worth reading, but not the type of book that many of them usually read. Some readers felt that reading the book was like going back to school for better or worse. Others had issues with the book and the author’s style. Some found Taleb’s writing imperfect. There is humor, but sometimes Taleb takes what the readers felt were snarky shots at people with whom he disagrees. Taleb seems to have particular issues with the French, which might in part be explained by his Lebanese ancestry. Reading The Black Swan may be somewhat like going through boot camp – it is hard. Not all the experiences are enjoyable, but you are better off from doing it. Reading this book is another example of the benefits of a participating in the First Mondays Reading Group. It asks its members to read good books that they might not otherwise read. Ultimately, they enjoy and benefit from the mental stretching this requires. With their book discussion complete, the group discussed what to read next. They had previously made White Fragility by Robin DiAngelo and The Dutch House by Ann Patchett their SepFirst Monday Reading Group discusses Black Swan tember and October selections. However, during July some concerns with White Fragility had been expressed. With the recent death of Civil Rights leader, Congressman John Lewis, and our society’s current focus on racial justice, the group decided to replace White Fragility with Across That Bridge, a book by Rep. Lewis, for their September read. The group will read The Dutch House for an October discussion. Assuming social distancing is still in place, the readers will meet again in a September Zoom call. However, that discussion will not be on the first Monday of September, which is Labor Day, but rather the group will have its next discussion on Monday, September 14 at 1:30 p.m. New members are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Please contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department, jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov, for more information.

articles.text: All Oakland Public Libraries are closed, including the Piedmont Avenue branch library, but they continue to provide virtual services with online resources. Here is just a small sample. These and many more are available from this site: https://oaklandlibrary.org/online-resources/articles-and-databases. Click on whichever you want and enter your library card number to see the full resource. CreativeBug This is free with your library card. Librarian Mickey Vo of Teen Services says: “Creativebug offers a variety of arts & crafts video lessons, taught by expert designers and artists. Topics include art & design (like ceramics and painting), sewing, quilting, food & home, and much more! Classes welcome all skill levels and ages, and the tutorials are self-paced, making it easy to take your time in learning.” Tutor.com Free homework help is offered, including test preparation for students in all grades, kindergarten through 12th grade. It is also offered for adult learners. The site includes job search support, such as help writing a cover letter for a job, and resume writing. Live one-on-one assistance is available every day from 12 noon to midnight. Live Spanish-speaking support is also available for math, science, and social studies. Tumblebooks A site for kids, these are animated talking picture books that can be played on your computer. The Story Book collection includes a fun variety of stories for different age levels. The pace of the stories can be controlled by the reader. The Tumble Readables are large print “read on your own” children’s books. CustomGuide A variety of online training modules in computer basics and software, it includes Microsoft Excel, Word, and Outlook. Tutorials are self-paced and let you your own progress. You can also print out one-page resource sheets for most popular software applications. Clinton’s Auto Repair This includes thousands of combinations of year, make and model covering the most popular vehicles of the past 30 years. It also includes information on specialty models, and is designed so you can service or repair virtually any system on your vehicle. A total of 10 branch libraries now providing sidewalk service. Effective March 16, the Oakland Public Library closed all Library locations to help limit the spread of coronavirus (COVID-19). These closures will remain in effect until further notice. All programs, other than online, are canceled while our library is closed. The Friends of PAL will send out a notice when we know the date the library will reopen. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, August 26, 2020 FIRST MONDAY READING GROUP First Monday Reading Group discusses Black Swan The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group took on one of its more challenging reads for its monthly discussion on Monday, August 3, when it tackled The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable, by author and former options trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb. Written in 2007 and updated in 2010, the book provides an understanding of rare and unpredictable events, their extreme impacts, and the tendency for people to find simplistic explanations for these events after they have happened. Taleb calls them “Black Swans”, using 9/11 is an example. The book was on the New York Times best-seller list for 36 weeks and was published in 32 languages. Taleb explains there are different types of events and probabilities associated with them. We cannot anticipate the black swans that dramatically affect us. Taleb does not suggest attempting to predict Black Swan events, but rather wants readers to develop the capacity to handle them and have the ability to take advantage of them when they unexpectedly occur. His central thesis is that we have a blindness with respect to randomness, particularly those with large deviations; and the consequences for us are profound. Taleb is a philosopher, mathematician, psychologist, social scientist, and financial trader, all wrapped up in one very intelligent man. He covers literary topics, psychology, science, business, and advises his readers on how to conduct themselves in the face of uncertainty. Following his thoughts requires focus and effort from the reader, but the group of thirteen readers was up to the challenge. Participating in the virtual meeting were Sarah Johnson, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Susan Ode, Jeri Lockhart, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Albert Chen, Sally Arney, Margie Blodgett, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Most members of the group were happy to have read the book. They felt it will affect the way they will perceive and react to the uncertainties they experience. It was worth reading, but not the type of book that many of them usually read. Some readers felt that reading the book was like going back to school for better or worse. Others had issues with the book and the author’s style. Some found Taleb’s writing imperfect. There is humor, but sometimes Taleb takes what the readers felt were snarky shots at people with whom he disagrees. Taleb seems to have particular issues with the French, which might in part be explained by his Lebanese ancestry. Reading The Black Swan may be somewhat like going through boot camp – it is hard. Not all the experiences are enjoyable, but you are better off from doing it. Reading this book is another example of the benefits of a participating in the First Mondays Reading Group. It asks its members to read good books that they might not otherwise read. Ultimately, they enjoy and benefit from the mental stretching this requires. With their book discussion complete, the group discussed what to read next. They had previously made White Fragility by Robin DiAngelo and The Dutch House by Ann Patchett their SepFirst Monday Reading Group discusses Black Swan tember and October selections. However, during July some concerns with White Fragility had been expressed. With the recent death of Civil Rights leader, Congressman John Lewis, and our society’s current focus on racial justice, the group decided to replace White Fragility with Across That Bridge, a book by Rep. Lewis, for their September read. The group will read The Dutch House for an October discussion. Assuming social distancing is still in place, the readers will meet again in a September Zoom call. However, that discussion will not be on the first Monday of September, which is Labor Day, but rather the group will have its next discussion on Monday, September 14 at 1:30 p.m. New members are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Please contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department, jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov, for more information. articles.text: Observations of the built environment of a beautiful city The landscaping, the streets, the buildings and the resulting neighborhoods are in some cases nice, in many cases outstanding, and sometimes incredible! My focus is walking with the purpose of soaking in the design of the city and then reflecting on why it is the beautiful place it is—and what makes it this way? My daily excursions of the last months have led to a number of observations, thoughts, and a few conclusions on the built environment of Piedmont, which I would like to share with people. But first a word on walking itself. There is an old Steve Martin movie, LA Story, where, needing to visit his next door neighbor, he walks out the front of his house, gets in his car, and drives the 60 feet or so to his neighbor’s house. This scene is funny, but also of course a statement on our car-dependent culture, ramifications of which spread to all parts of the places in which we live. Simply walking mitigates this dependency and many of its related side effects. Not only does going on foot have obvious health benefits, but it adds zero traffic and pollution to our lives. Further, it facilitates meeting and talking to other people, to neighbors—it facilitates community. Although not always possible for some people because of physical limitations or geographical difficulties, going on foot is also, and perhaps most importantly, the best way to truly see, reflect on, and appreciate a neighborhood, a building or a place. The built-in slow pace of walking can’t be duplicated on a bicycle, and certainly not in a car. When I am walking and looking, the main questions I always have is: Is this nice? Is this beautiful? Or, is this lacking? Is this bad? And then, why? The answers are sometimes easy and obvious, but sometimes not. A viable evaluation depends on reflection and an understanding of the different components and design principles involved. And like a work of art, there are intangibles that are a result of, but transcend all the pieces. Because we are all so greatly affected by the built environment in which we live, I believe we all can benefit from this kind of discussion. In this column over the next number of weeks I will be focusing on various of my design observations from walking through Piedmont, including those related to the urban design, the landscaping architecture, and of course, the architecture. I encourage others to do the same, looking, evaluating and forming their own opinions as well. Next: Landscape Architecture in Piedmont: An Overview Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has been a resident of Piedmont for 30 years. articles.text: Dog Dear Abby: I’ve noticed a lot of dog poop bags left near the sidewalks around town. Why do people leave them by the sidewalks? Wouldn’t it be better to pop the bags in someone’s garbage can? Piedmont Poop Alert. Max the mix puppy and Amelia Dear Abby: It seems that many of the animal adoption centers do not have puppies. We need a smallish dog to bring us a smile while we work from home. It’s the perfect time for us to train a puppy, but we’re striking out. Any suggestions who might have a lucky puppy? Perplexed, Toni and Amy Dear Max and Amelia: Here are three possibilities. 1. Used poop bags are typically left by dog owners (near sidewalks) with the idea that they’ll pick them up on the way back home. Sometimes routes are changed and the bags are left and forgotten. 2. Some dog walkers drop the bags with the understanding that other dog walkers will pick them up and drop them in a public waste can. However, they might be picked up but they might not. 3. The idea of dropping a poop bag in someone’s garbage is complicated. Would I mind if you did that in our cans? Some non-dog owners say absolutely not. They don’t want the bags slipped into their garbage— the smell is not welcome. So it’s best to hang onto those bags and drop them in the public waste or when you return home. That’s the scoop on the poop, –Abby Dear Toni and Amy: There is a wonderful organization called Dog is My Co-Pilot that brings dogs and cats from Texas which seems to have a lot of adoptees to the western states, which are running out of dogs of all sizes to adopt. Dr. Peter Rork, a retired orthopedic surgeon, flies his own plane to Houston every two weeks and brings dogs of all ages to Merced, Portland, Salt Lake City, and other locations. Dr. Rork says he brings back mostly dogs on his trips, as many as 200, but also a few kittens too. In total, he thinks he’s helped place over 15,000 animals in adoption, one tail at a time. Look up Dog is My Co-Pilot; we hope you’ll get lucky. Wags to Dr. Rork! –Abby Send your dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at Melandogs@gmail.com.

articles.text: Map asserts southeastern part of Piedmont is part of zone, which may expand in the future The City will officially adopt a map as part of its City Code that asserts a portion of southeastern Piedmont is part of a Very High Fire Severity Zone on Wednesday, September 16. The map detailing the zone was set by CalFire several decades ago in the wake of the Oakland Hills Fire in 1991. State law gives local cities the option to work with CalFire authorities to adopt fire prevention ordinances revolving areas that are at a higher fire risk. These ordinances require properties in these high-risk zones to maintain fire defense improvements. In 2019, all cities were required to adopt CalFire’s Very High Fire Severity Zone map by ordinance. The map was last updated in 2008, and state authorities are pushing to update it but have been delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic. Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black said that when the map is updated, new methodologies will be used and it is likely that the Very High Fire Severity Zone in Piedmont will expand. Right now, the Very High Fire Severity Zone includes most of the area between La Salle Avenue to Park Boulevard, although a few neighborhoods are exempt. It also includes the area surrounding Tyson Lake. This amounts to roughly 20 percent of the City. The zone is part of wider designation that runs through the Oakland Hills. All of Piedmont is part of a state-designated Wildland Urban Interface Fire Area. “Piedmont’s unique topography and geography make the entire City particularly susceptible to fires,” the ordinance, which had a second reading unanimously approved by City Council on Monday, August 17, states. All of the City must follow state vegetation maintenance standards, with homeowners living the Very High Fire Severity Zone following stricter standards. These standards require residents to cut down and remove hazardous vegetation, like dead trees or brush, from the property. There must be a 30-foot perimeter around each structure that is a “defensible space,” meaning an area where wildfire prevention practices are in place. Roadways must be kept clear of vegetation. Additionally, roofs and gutters need to be regularly cleaned and maintained. The full standards can found in the City Code. Black told the Post that the Piedmont Fire Department has been applying California’s vegetation management standards in the Very High Fire Severity Zone and around the rest of the City for years, but now Piedmont has adopted the official state map. PFD has been conducting inspections of properties for fire risk since the 1990s. He noted that all Piedmont residents are required to maintain defensible space, officially defined as “the area adjacent to a structure or dwelling where wildfire prevention or protection practices are implemented to provide defense from an approaching wildfire or to minimize the spread of a structure fire to wildlands or surrounding areas,” regardless of if they live in the Very High Fire Severity Zone. “We are making our Code match our practices,” Black commented. articles.text: On Friday, August 21, the Alameda County Public Health Office issued a revised shelter-inplace order, effective this Friday, August 28. The revised order allows the reopening of pools, permission for outdoor personal care services, and permission for outdoor tasting at wineries. Pools may open but with a reduced number of swimmers, and will require appointments. Lane limitations will be utilized to allow for physical distancing. Aquatic fitness classes are allowed with these restrictions. Poolside and deck furniture is not permitted, and lounging by pool areas is still not permitted in the county. Sanitation practices must be observed. All indoor areas associated with the pool, including locker and shower areas, with the exception of restrooms, will remain closed, including common areas, snack bars, lounging and sunbathing areas. This is the first guidance issued by Alameda County for the reopening of pools. The City of Piedmont has said it will spend the next two weeks determining whether the conditions imposed by the order can be applied to reopen the Piedmont Community Pool. City staff developed reopening frameworks based upon guidance from other health jurisdictions in Northern California. “The city understands the importance of the pool to the community and will examine whether reopening under the requirements imposed by the order is practicable. It is likely a decision on whether to reopen the Piedmont Community Pool will be considered by the city council at its meeting of September 8,” wrote City Clerk John Tulloch. Personal Service Providers, a term used by the county and state that includes hair salons, barbershops, nail salons, skin care, waxing, and non-medical massage providers, may provide services outdoors starting August 28. These services are subject to applicable state and local guidance Wineries may now allow patrons to visit outdoor tasting facilities. Previously, wineries were only permitted to serve wine or allow for wine tasting with a meal or food order. The county confirmed that schools must continue distance learning, and not accept waivers for in-person learning at this time. In-person instruction is permitted for children in psychiatric health facilities, or crisis housing units. Extracurricular activities at schools are permitted on school campuses for groups up to 14.
articles.title: Pools, outdoor salons given go-ahead to reopen

pages.text: Wednesday, August 26, 2020 29 City to adopt Very High Fire Severity Zone map next month Map asserts southeastern part of Piedmont is part of zone, which may expand in the future By Barry Eitel The City will officially adopt a map as part of its City Code that asserts a portion of southeastern Piedmont is part of a Very High Fire Severity Zone on Wednesday, September 16. The map detailing the zone was set by CalFire several decades ago in the wake of the Oakland Hills Fire in 1991. State law gives local cities the option to work with CalFire authorities to adopt fire prevention ordinances revolving areas that are at a higher fire risk. These ordinances require properties in these high-risk zones to maintain fire defense improvements. In 2019, all cities were required to adopt CalFire’s Very High Fire Severity Zone map by ordinance. The map was last updated in 2008, and state authorities are pushing to update it but have been delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic. Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black said that when the map is updated, new methodologies will be used and it is likely that the Very High Fire Severity Zone in Piedmont will expand. Right now, the Very High Fire Severity Zone includes most of the area between La Salle Avenue to Park Boulevard, although a few neighborhoods are exempt. It also includes the area surrounding Tyson Lake. This amounts to roughly 20 percent of the City. The zone is part of wider designation that runs through the Oakland Hills. All of Piedmont is part of a state-designated Wildland Urban Interface Fire Area. “Piedmont’s unique topography and geography make the entire City particularly susceptible to fires,” the ordinance, which had a second reading unanimously approved by City Council on Monday, August 17, states. All of the City must follow state vegetation maintenance standards, with homeowners living the Very High Fire Severity Zone following stricter standards. These standards require residents to cut down and remove hazardous vegetation, like dead trees or brush, from the property. There must be a 30-foot perimeter around each structure that is a “defensible space,” meaning an area where wildfire prevention practices are in place. Roadways must be kept clear of vegetation. Additionally, roofs and gutters need to be regularly cleaned and maintained. The full standards can found in the City Code. Black told the Post that the Piedmont Fire Department has been applying California’s vegetation management standards in the Very High Fire Severity Zone and around the rest of the City for years, but now Piedmont has adopted the official state map. PFD has been conducting inspections of properties for fire risk since the 1990s. He noted that all Piedmont residents are required to maintain defensible space, officially defined as “the area adjacent to a structure or dwelling where wildfire prevention or protection practices are implemented to provide defense from an approaching wildfire or to minimize the spread of a structure fire to wildlands or surrounding areas,” regardless of if they live in the Very High Fire Severity Zone. “We are making our Code match our practices,” Black commented. articles.text: Alameda County remains on State watchlist Six cases of COVID-19 have been reported in Piedmont so far in August, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department as of yesterday, August 18. The new cases bring Piedmont’s total caseload to 29. Officials said that an electronic reporting problem in the county has been resolved this week. Some of the newly reported cases are due to delayed reports from earlier this year. It is not clear if the new Piedmont cases are all from August or were from prior months. In all of Alameda County, there have been 14,956 cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by coronavirus. Tragically, 224 people have died due to the disease in Alameda County since the pandemic began in March. Oakland, the most populous city in the county, now has 6,206 cases. Hayward counted 2,199 cases and Fremont has 1,013. The state still has Alameda County on a COVID-19 “watchlist” along with most other counties in California. Alameda County has been on the list since July 12, meaning many indoor businesses and activities are prohibited by state regulations. As of Monday, August 17, the state recorded 632,667 COVID-19. California is the only state in the nation with over 600,000 cases. There have been 11,342 deaths due to COVID-19 in California. In Piedmont, Linda Beach Playfield was closed on July 24 due to overcrowding and non-compliance concerns, and Witter Field was shuttered a week later due to continued non-compliance of county restrictions of social distancing. Witter Field had closed down during the initial weeks of the pandemic in March, and then reopened in June. Piedmont School District started classes this week, but all classes were remote due to the pandemic. The City of Piedmont keeps its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/covid-19
articles.title: Piedmont COVID-19 caseload jumps to 29

articles.text: A look at how faculty members prepared for the 2020 school year Amid coronavirus concerns, Piedmont School District made the ultimate decision last month for classes to remain fully remote. The community was made aware in an e-mail message sent on July 14 to parents of Piedmont students, in which Supt. Randy Booker announced that the academic year would begin with no in-person instruction. This left teachers and staff approximately 30 days to create lesson plans that would transition smoothly to digital instruction. Piedmont Middle School Principal Ryan Fletcher provided information on how his faculty prepared for the unusual academic year. As is customary before the start of any academic year, all district staff participated in professional development, and a one-day orientation was held for new teachers on August 6. Collectively, teachers and classified staff engaged in four days of professional learning, with collaboration and planning time held between August 10 and 13. “Piedmont Middle School teachers attended workshops covering topics on leveraging best practices for distance learning, discussions and reflections on equity and anti-racist curriculum as well as strengthening restorative justice practices,” Fletcher said. Educators will also receive two additional professional development days, one in October and one in January. Schools in California are required to have 180 days of instruction, which has not been waived during the COVID-19 crisis. Piedmont teachers are expected to provide 180 full days of instruction this academic year; albeit some days, or possibly all, will be done virtually. Students in 4th grade and

articles.text: City Council instructs staff to conduct more public hearings Piedmont’s City Council has deferred a second reading of ordinances implementing Reach Codes, originally scheduled for its August 17 meeting. Instead, council has instructed staff to conduct additional public outreach to better educate residents and to allow for more public input. The building code amendments, as proposed in the first reading held on July 6, were drafted following two public surveys and five public outreach forums – to an overall favorable view by residents. Survey results brought to council on July 6 showed that 66 percent of surveyed Piedmonters supported the proposed reach codes. Amendment ideas and language were first introduced to residents and contractors for feedback during five outreach events that were held in January and February of this year. articles.text: Editor: On July 29, you published an article about viciously bigoted anti-police graffiti here in Piedmont. The article didn’t run in the front page, and it offered no condemnation against those who defaced property with their hatred. Rather, the article ran on the back page, with a bland observation that the California penal code prohibited such actions. Don’t our police deserve more support than that? - Vernon M. Winters
articles.title: Police deserve more support

articles.text: First, let us be clear that the proposed Reach codes address only new constructions or large renovations. Once adopted they will set the direction for future expansions of their applicability and will be politically difficult to change direction. I show that the CO2 emission impact of installing electric heat pumps in place of natural gas heaters (whether for new structures or as replacement for existing natural gas installations) is positive. I am not addressing the capital costs and potential operational savings incurred by the homeowners. At the State of California level, the sources of electrical energy fluctuate during the day. [There is a] large drop in available renewable energy (wind and solar) at night, in the morning, and in the evening. articles.text: We are living through the worst pandemic of the past 100 years, with no end in sight. The United States GDP shrank at a record 32.9% in the second quarter of 2020, the sharpest economic contraction in history. Unemployment was over 10% in July, and Congress has failed to agree on an additional stimulus package. Piedmont revenues are being affected. In the first seven months of this years, the dollar volume of home sales in town (per MLS) dropped $33,494,500 from $187,956,500. This represents a reduction in revenue of over $435,000; annualized, the number would be almost $750,000. Piedmont will not see the usual increase in property taxes that have padded its coffers in years past. According to the city’s financial statement of June 30, 2019, almost 75% of the City’s revenue come from “Taxes and fees”. It is clear that this line item will take a hit. Given this scenario, is the first thing to come to mind, “Let’s borrow another $20 million dollars?” It probably didn’t come to your mind, but it did to the City Council, which has put it on the ballot for the November election in order “to fund new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas.” They approved it on August 4th, giving opponents only ten days to submit arguments against the proposition to the City Clerk.

articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter We installed solar panels in 2016 and reduced our electric bill from a really high number to an average of about $35 per month. In July 2018 we bought an electric vehicle (EV), and a few months later – when our charger was installed – we switched to PG&E’s EV1-A rate. It had low rates from 11 PM to 7AM plus weekends and holidays, but much higher rates the rest of the time. Because our panels generated excess electricity during daylight hours, we could charge our car at night and still keep our bill low. A year ago, PG&E stopped enrolling customers in our rate plan. I felt pretty lucky that we had gotten in – until we received a letter stating that we were being thrown off the plan because we had enrolled later than July 31, 2018. I thought I would choose my best rate plan. How bad could it be? The answer turned out to be VERY bad. Under our old plan, we paid about $550 per year. We had three alternative plans to choose from. They were estimated to cost us between $1,150 and $1,250 per year. So, by forcing me to switch to a new plan, they more than doubled my annual bill. How did they do this? In a nutshell, they dramatically increased the number of hours during the day when they charged low rates. Solar customers typically generate excess electricity from late morning to late afternoon. Under the old plan, this was sold back to PGE at higher prices, sometimes four times as much as the midnight to 7AM rate that was used to charge EVs. It was a classic example of “buy low, sell high”. Under any of the rate plans I was forced to use, PG&E slashed the price they paid me for excess electricity. My old bill in July was $10; the new bill was $70, a 600% increase. This makes good business sense to PG&E, at the expense of customers with an EV and solar. Solar customers without EVs have also been taking a hit. PG&E has slashed what it pays for excess power generated by all customers during the day. To beat PG&E at its own game, install a smart battery backup system. You can bank excess power during the day. There are two drawbacks. You lose about 10% of your excess power in the process of storing it and then passing it on, and it is quite expensive. The cost of a backup system can be as much as an entire solar system. Log on to your account at PG&E and use their rate tool. If you don’t use a lot of electricity, a tiered usage plan might be best. If you do, then a time of day plan may be best if you can minimize your usage during peak hours. If you have way too much disposable income, you can also install solar panels that generate more power than you use. Or you can simply move to another state. I guess we’ll have to change the old maxim to: “Nothing is sure but death, taxes…and big increases in PG&E bills.” Wiley Hoag, a Piedmont resident, is the Post’s Consumer Affairs Reporter. “The way I look at it, we have accidentally become a non-profit organization.”
articles.title: PG&E just (quietly) doubled

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters has embarked upon a fundraising and food collection drive this month in support of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. A recent LWV meeting led by Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the County Food Bank, spurred on the project. She spoke at a League event on August 4 that was live-streamed on the League’s YouTube channel. The fundraising drive runs until August 31. In her August 4 discussion Bateson described why the need for food during the COVID-19 pandemic has increased 1,000 percent. The Food Bank provides food for those in need, and includes fresh fruits and vegetables. To learn more and to donate, see https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=E7JelmIoZxc. The League has raised over $5000 to date. To view the August 4 discussion with Bateson, search “League of Women Voters Piedmont” on Youtube. For more information, visit www.lwvpiedmont.org.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified is in Distance Learning until further notice. Distance learning worsens educational inequalities. Students are estimated to lose months of learning which could harm an entire generation. What happens when Alameda County satisfies the Governor’s criteria and the school board regains autonomy? This question should be answered by all candidates for our school board. On June 24 Dr. George Rutherford attended our school board meeting as an epidemiologist familiar with Piedmont and our schools. I was thrilled because I knew he had the right expertise having published a scientific paper on reducing hospitalizations working closely with epidemiologists. Rutherford testified that with precautions, including masks and social distancing, it is next to impossible for a student to infect a teacher and that student infections rarely result in complications requiring hospitalization. The school district took Dr. Rutherford’s advice and crafted a hybrid option to allow parents to choose 50% classroom instruction or 100% distance learning. The hybrid option required daily clearances prior to student and staff participation, daily deep cleanings of classrooms, frequent air changes per hour within all classrooms, and many other precautions. The majority of parents were convinced of the safety of this modified classroom instruction. That majority persists in my recent survey as well as a Gallup survey of parents nationwide. An even larger percentage of parents were happy with having the choice of learning options. It was not a matter of either distance or hybrid learning but a choice based on risk assessments by individual households, as recommended by the Center for Disease Control. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Since my freshman year of high school, I have ended each summer with a backpacking trip with the High Adventure Crew, a coed teen Venturing Crew under the auspices of the Piedmont Scouts. Many of us had our summer plans canceled because of COVID-19, so we looked forward to the backpacking trip July 27-30 in Desolation Wilderness. It brought a larger group than past years. To prepare, we created a social bubble for two weeks prior to the trip, and wore masks whenever we encountered other people in the wilderness. Day 1 started with a celebration of crew advisor Ken Li’s 65th birthday. We met at the Glen Alpine trailhead at noon and began hiking after lunch. Birthday doughnuts were accompanied by singing Happy Birthday, and then an icebreaker discussion of what each of us hoped to gain from the trip. “I’m in my 14th year as Crew Advisor, and I’ve always loved the chance to share the joys of backpacking, camping, and hiking. Getting to know the members is a treat for me during these physically and mentally demanding trips,” said Li. With the sound of thunder in the distance, we were prepared for rain at our first destination, Gilmore Lake. Instead, it was warm and dry, just in time for a quick swim before dinner of Szechuan-inspired peanut noodles, one of Ken’s specialties. We began Day 2 with a morning climb of 1,400 feet to the summit of Mt. Tallac, which, at 7,671 feet elevation, overlooks all of the Tahoe basin. After returning to Gilmore for lunch, we made our way to Lake Aloha (3.2 miles), notable for its crystal-clear waters circled by mountains, endless rocks and trees. Surprisingly, there were no other campers in sight. Everyone decided to sleep under the stars without tents. articles.text: High school students discussing their personal stories as minorities in Piedmont in a video. Pictured are (top left to right): Harmonee Ross, August Thigpen, and Anthony Wong. Bottom left to right: Jenna Kim, Sage Mosley, and Anjuli Turner. With the school year starting, students in Piedmont will return to a classroom, albeit virtually, to study the usual subjects of English, math, and science. But some Havens students this fall will also get the opportunity to learn more about their own cultural backgrounds and explore their racial identities, all while guided by local high schoolers. Created through a partnership between the student-led Advocacy for Asian Americans (AAA) and Black Student Union (BSU) clubs at Piedmont High, and with two faculty advisors from Havens and the high school, the new mentorship program aims to provide support for students of color at Havens in their personal relationships with race. The program falls in line with the Board of Education resolution in July to create “meaningful” studies of race and an “inclusive environment” free of discrimination. “We each felt like this was something that was missing in our elementary school experience,” explained sophomore Sage Mosley, a BSU member in a video introducing the program. “Having another person that shares the same ethnic experience as you is valuable.” Jean Takazawa, an instructional aide at Havens and an advisor for the program, said she originally applied for a grant last year with the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC) to create a program where Asian students could have a place to acknowledge their cultural identities. In January she invited three Asian students from Piedmont High to speak about their cultural traditions at a Havens school assembly during Lunar New Year. After that, she started to involve high schoolers in the project. The partnership with BSU was created later. A newly released video presentation about the program, which was viewed by Havens staff members during last week’s professional development meetings, features six AAA and BSU leaders and members talking about their experiences as Asian and Black students in Piedmont schools, and served as their motivation for leading the program. Ina Bendich, a restorative justice consultant with Piedmont School District, said that watching the video is “an opportunity for the community to have some insight into what [students] experience,” which she said is key to creating a shift in the status quo. PHS senior Anthony Wong, co-president of AAA, said in the video that he wants to help kids “bridge the gap between their own families’ cultures at home and the culture at school” through mentoring. Wong was also one of the speakers at the Lunar New Year assembly. Meanwhile, PHS junior and BSU member August Thigpen said she wanted to make younger Black students feel empowered, creating a more “tight-knit” Black community in Piedmont. “The culture of predominantly white schools creates a space where Black students can feel unwelcome,” Thigpen said in the video. “Not having a group for us makes us feel more distanced from the community.” Mosley, along with senior Anjuli Turner, said they sometimes felt alone at school with no one to turn to on issues regarding race. Harmonee Ross, a Millennium HS senior and BSU leader, added that she wanted to provide safe places for kids of color to “feel comfortable and valued” in ways that current high schoolers of color did not feel. Bullying was also addressed in the video, with senior and AAA co-president Jenna Kim talking about her experiences dealing with hurtful comments about how Asian kids look. Bendich, who helped start BSU this year, said she felt high school students were “a natural place” to turn to for leadership. Piedmont School District does not have many teachers of color, and high school students understand the experiences of younger kids. Wong said that the new mentorship program aligns with AAA’s goals of outreach and advocacy, and that it could grow soon to include more schools. “The larger the program, the more support we can give to our communities,” Wong said. Takazawa and Bendich both said that they wanted to include more groups of students in the future. As Havens students approach the new school year – adjusting to being at home without their peers for distance learning – this new program may help them better connect in a time when it has become difficult to connect with others. To view the video, click on https://bit.ly/3hesqmx.
articles.title: High school students create restorative justice efforts at Havens

articles.text: As the strangest of summers ends, a bizarre school year begins. The first day of classes for all Piedmont grades began on Monday, August 17, but without students or teachers in classrooms. The worldwide coronavirus pandemic has changed everything. All instruction will be online as Piedmont parents and young scholars face a novel challenge: to learn exclusively through a computer screen. Columnist Mike Royko of the Chicago Daily News summed up the end of summer back in 1978. “When I was a kid, the worst of all days was the last day of summer vacation. We were in the schoolyard playing softball, and the sun was going down and it was getting dark. But I didn’t want it to get dark. I didn’t want the game to end. It was too good, too much fun. I wanted it to stay light forever...But the sun always went down. And now it’s almost dark again.” The summer of 2020 was stymied by COVID-19, but still, somehow, parents figured out how to get their kids ready for the school year. Alameda County remains on the state’s watchlist, meaning Piedmont will not be able to open school campuses until receiving clearance from the county. Some Piedmont parents have gotten creative this year, learning to instill a sense of normalcy and excitement for the first day and all the days that follow, In addition to being the mother of 5th, 9th and 10th graders, Christine Schooley began teaching in Oakland public schools last week. She employs unique strategies this fall, “My three are going to head out the door and walk or bike to school each morning so when they return to the house they are ready to sit down and start school. We also had a bunch of end-of-summer ‘lasts’: last ice cream for lunch, last backyard movie night, last marathon video game session.” Some parents like Jenna Caldwell are keeping with school traditions. “We went through all of our normal motions – annual back-toschool photo shoot in front of the house, back-to-school shopping for supplies, a few new clothes, and new tennis shoes. We have to look good for screen time! “The house was definitely buzzing with back-to-school energy!” she said. Other parents have held out on some of the traditions, but have focused on transforming their new work environment. “It seems like a good year to use up some of those partially used notebooks and still goodenough colored pencils,” commented mom Buffy Yeh. “ We Lily Caldwell, who enters her freshman year at Piedmont High School, in a traditional first dayof-school photo. did get a few things to make the living room into more of a school room, like office chairs and desk organizers. The most exciting thing will be breakfast before 8:00, made by mom,” she said, smiling. Students got a taste of online learning during the spring. With pass/no pass grading and without mandatory attendance or a set class schedule, many were left underwhelmed. Now there are set times for class, attendance is taken and new etiquette for video conferencing is in place. A few Piedmont students shared their first-day-of-school experience with the Post.
articles.title: Piedmont students return to school – virtually

articles.text: Welcome back to school. We are staying in distance learning for God knows how long. Although this is better than nothing, we all had hoped the school district would figure out a way for us to go back to school in person. Schedules were released last week for the online classes. So for most of the day everybody was frantically calling and texting friends to see if they had classes together. We told each other that it was going to be alright because it wasn’t as if we were going to be in a real building with live teaching. With no in-person learning, being trapped inside of a house with your family and glued to the screen on Zoom calls for six hours a day this school year, it is definitely going to be interesting. In other news the first of the high school buildings is almost done. I am actually really happy about that because it is such a beautiful building. But the big question many people are asking is what is going to happen with it? With new buildings that will be empty until students and teachers return to classrooms, I think that we should start a roller blade club. Bored kids can grab a pair of skates and just go crazy racing up and down in the empty hallways. Otherwise we are left with a $30 million classroom building empty and silent as a ghost. Some people think that construction should stop. I understand why people who live close to the school and can hear all the banging and clanging on a new building that’s not going to reopen for a year are complaining. Some now are asking why the bond money for construction should instead be spent for boosting our distance learning platform, or on safety measures that would allow us to attend school in person. I guess it is better to look at a new building and one just being built, than to look at a pile of rubble if construction were to stop. Now that we are back to virtual school, I wish the best to all the teachers for working through the hardships of COVID, and to the students who have figured out how to study remotely. This year is going to be a roller coaster, with ups and downs. For sure, it will be an adventure. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.
articles.title: Oh boy – it’s back to school

articles.text: By: Kaelin Campbell Piedmont for Oakland Public Schools (POPS) is a group of Piedmont High School students and alums working to bring the Piedmont community together to support Oakland-based organizations that fight for educational equity. The first POPS campaign raised over $62,000 for three organizations, State of Black Education Oakland, Planting Justice, and Black Organizing Project. With plans to continue the momentum, a second campaign has been launched to centralize donations to two organizations working to combat digital inequity in Oakland: The A to Z fund, and Oakland REACH. The systemic educational divides that POPS targeted in the first campaign will be exacerbated by the coronavirus pandemic as public schools are solely online this fall. In a survey conducted in 2019, 45% of Oakland students don’t have access to home internet. The lack of access will result in even higher teacher turnover rates, will detract from parents’ abilities to work outside the home, and create more socioemotional stress on everyone. Everyone is encouraged to attend the Zoom event this Friday, August 21, at 6 p.m. to hear from Oakland teachers and students, as well as representatives of our two organizations that your donations will be benefiting from. We hope the Piedmont community will continue to come together to show our Oakland neighbors the same care we show Piedmont. The webinar will also be recorded and posted on the POPS website: www.popsproject.org. Sign up for the webinar at: bit.ly/ Popthebubble2.
articles.title: Back2School: POPS event this Friday

articles.text: When I think about the next years of my life, senior spring, college applications and internships come to mind. The only housing I am worried about is whether it will be on or off campus in my freshman year in college. But for 1,700, kids ages 14-24, l who are homeless in Alameda County, their concerns are focused on finding housing, education, food, and safety. The Bay Area has the third highest homeless population in the United States, behind New York City and Los Angeles. But one group doing something about remedying this crisis is Youth Spirit Artworks. YSA has plans to make a Tiny House Village that will serve as transitional housing for two years for teens age 18-24. During these two years, residents will participate in job training, community upkeep, and cooking regularly. Last year, Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) funded and volunteered to make a Tiny house to contribute to the Village. Through this project, PCSC members learned how to build the framing for a house, install insulation, drywall, skylights, doors and windows. Participating in this project, in addition to helping combat the housing crisis, is helping the Piedmont volunteers appreciate all of the work that goes into building a house. Recently that house, currently in a residential driveway in town, was bestowed with a Claire Lichty (left), Shelby Cavanaugh and Elena Blanco near the end of a full day of finish work on Youth Spirit Artworks Tiny houses in July. They spent many days over the summer working on these houses and plan to use their experience when the Piedmont Community Service Crew builds a second Tiny house this fall. mural designed by crew member Quelam Tran Perez. Crew members plan to build a second Tiny house, but it needs funding from the community to reach a goal of $12,500 to cover the material costs. The deadline is August 31. Community Service Crew members will do all the planning and volunteer work, and they welcome community adults to help guide the youth members on the more technical aspects of construction. The Tiny House project changes the lives of everyone involved. To make a donation, contact PCSC Crew Advisor Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net. To become involved, high school students may sign up now to be part of PCSC, and middle school students may sign up for the Piedmont Service Club. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, August 19, 2020 Back2School: POPS event this Friday By: Kaelin Campbell Piedmont for Oakland Public Schools (POPS) is a group of Piedmont High School students and alums working to bring the Piedmont community together to support Oakland-based organizations that fight for educational equity. The first POPS campaign raised over $62,000 for three organizations, State of Black Education Oakland, Planting Justice, and Black Organizing Project. With plans to continue the momentum, a second campaign has been launched to centralize donations to two organizations working to combat digital inequity in Oakland: The A to Z fund, and Oakland REACH. The systemic educational divides that POPS targeted in the first campaign will be exacerbated by the coronavirus pandemic as public schools are solely online this fall. In a survey conducted in 2019, 45% of Oakland students don’t have access to home internet. The lack of access will result in even higher teacher turnover rates, will detract from parents’ abilities to work outside the home, and create more socioemotional stress on everyone. Everyone is encouraged to attend the Zoom event this Friday, August 21, at 6 p.m. to hear from Oakland teachers and students, as well as representatives of our two organizations that your donations will be benefiting from. We hope the Piedmont community will continue to come together to show our Oakland neighbors the same care we show Piedmont. The webinar will also be recorded and posted on the POPS website: www.popsproject.org. Sign up for the webinar at: bit.ly/ Popthebubble2. Piedmont Post For more information on placing an ad call... 626-2468 or email: nancy@cmc-ads.com By Crystal Vacker Welcome back to school. We are staying in distance learning for God knows how long. Although this is better than nothing, we all had hoped the school district would figure out a way for us to go back to school in person. Schedules were released last week for the online classes. So for most of the day everybody was frantically calling and texting friends to see if they had classes together. We told each other that it was going to be alright because it wasn’t as if we were going to be in a real building with live teaching. With no in-person learning, being trapped inside of a house with your family and glued to the screen on Zoom calls for six hours a day this school year, it is definitely going to be interesting. Oh boy – it’s back to school In other news the first of the high school buildings is almost done. I am actually really happy about that because it is such a beautiful building. But the big question many people are asking is what is going to happen with it? With new buildings that will be empty until students and teachers return to classrooms, I think that we should start a roller blade club. Bored kids can grab a pair of skates and just go crazy racing up and down in the empty hallways. Otherwise we are left with a $30 million classroom building empty and silent as a ghost. Some people think that construction should stop. I understand why people who live close to the school and can hear all the banging and clanging on a new building that’s not going to reopen for a year are complaining. Some now are asking why the bond money for construction should instead be spent for boosting our distance learning platform, or on safety measures that would allow us to attend school in person. I guess it is better to look at a new building and one just being built, than to look at a pile of rubble if construction were to stop. Now that we are back to virtual school, I wish the best to all the teachers for working through the hardships of COVID, and to the students who have figured out how to study remotely. This year is going to be a roller coaster, with ups and downs. For sure, it will be an adventure. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time. Community Service Crew to build 2nd Tiny house By Claire Lichty When I think about the next years of my life, senior spring, college applications and internships come to mind. The only housing I am worried about is whether it will be on or off campus in my freshman year in college. But for 1,700, kids ages 14-24, l who are homeless in Alameda County, their concerns are focused on finding housing, education, food, and safety. The Bay Area has the third highest homeless population in the United States, behind New York City and Los Angeles. But one group doing something about remedying this crisis is Youth Spirit Artworks. YSA has plans to make a Tiny House Village that will serve as transitional housing for two years for teens age 18-24. During these two years, residents will participate in job training, community upkeep, and cooking regularly. Last year, Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) funded and volunteered to make a Tiny house to contribute to the Village. Through this project, PCSC members learned how to build the framing for a house, install insulation, drywall, skylights, doors and windows. Participating in this project, in addition to helping combat the housing crisis, is helping the Piedmont volunteers appreciate all of the work that goes into building a house. Recently that house, currently in a residential driveway in town, was bestowed with a Claire Lichty (left), Shelby Cavanaugh and Elena Blanco near the end of a full day of finish work on Youth Spirit Artworks Tiny houses in July. They spent many days over the summer working on these houses and plan to use their experience when the Piedmont Community Service Crew builds a second Tiny house this fall. mural designed by crew member Quelam Tran Perez. Crew members plan to build a second Tiny house, but it needs funding from the community to reach a goal of $12,500 to cover the material costs. The deadline is August 31. Community Service Crew members will do all the planning and volunteer work, and they welcome community adults to help guide the youth members on the more technical aspects of construction. The Tiny House project changes the lives of everyone involved. To make a donation, contact PCSC Crew Advisor Ken Li at Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net.
