articles.text: Member I make it my mission to be a strong partner for schools. 2 - As a long-time volunteer and community leader, I have a passion for public service. As a City Council member for the last four years, my priority is to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. We are a small city with limited resources and staff, and it is essential that we budget conservatively and address past unfunded liabilities, including our streets and sidewalks, parks, and recreation facilities. Essential long-term investments will ensure a beautiful, sustainable city for our kids and grandkids. I also continue to emphasize more immediate priorities such as wildfire prevention, disaster preparedness, community health and public safety. As a Council member I have leveraged my deep community connections to engage and promote diverse perspectives, develop mutually beneficial solutions, and increase equity and inclusiveness. We have great work ahead of us and the right leadership in place to reach our goals. I look forward to continuing that work so that together we can pass on to our children and grandchildren a city as beautiful and safe as the one we live in today. CONNIE HERRICK 1 - Piedmont has been my home for 51 years. My early years were spent travelling and living in Japan and Thailand. When my dad retired from the Army, we moved to Oakland for a short time before settling in Piedmont in 1969. I attended Piedmont Middle School, graduated from Piedmont High in 1975 and still have close friendships from our high school class. My husband Mark and I purchased our Greenbank home in 1992 and are fortunate to have neighbors who we’ve known for over 25 years. Our son Matt attended Beach Elementary, Piedmont Middle School and graduated from Piedmont High in 2009. We are proud to have two PHS Highlanders in the family. 2 - Running for Council was a decision I made more with my heart than my head. Living in unprecedented times has not been easy for any of us. Every day we face challenges to our health, safety and financial stability. I felt that if there was ever a time to step up, contribute and affect positive change, it was now. I thought about the skills I’ve amassed over a 40-year career and realized that my financial expertise, operational experience and solution-based project management approach would well serve our City. As a longtime Piedmonter, I have an unwavering dedication to maximizing every dollar we pay in property taxes. Most of all, I have a strong desire to give back and a deep commitment to volunteerism and civic duty. That is the root of why I feel a strong pull to serve and run for office. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 - In 1989, my husband and I were expecting our first child and we wanted a home near our extended families. I grew up in San Francisco and Peter in Danville, so our primary focus was Piedmont. We bought our first home and soon discovered we had invested in much more than a convenient location. We were enchanted with Piedmont’s tree lined streets, detached homes, pristine parks and exceptional schools. And now, 30 years after this beautiful city and its residents welcomed us, I am running for City Council because I want to contribute to the decision-making that will keep Piedmont a special place to live. 2 - I was raised in a family passionate about service. My father spent 30 years in elected office in California. I have memories from about age 5, standing with my dad at local grocery stores, greeting people entering or exiting, trying to engage them in conversations about needed services in their neighborhoods. I learned that governing provides a unique opportunity to improve the lives of others. Throughout my years of volunteer leadership in Piedmont, I have been encouraged to run for City Council. Over the last three years, as enthusiasm for my candidacy increased, I consciously prepared for elected service by earning a position on the Recreation Commission and by leading the 2019 Civic Improvement Projects committee. I have the experience, the ability, and the passion to be an effective member of Piedmont City Council. NANCY BOSTROM No reply received

Like many Piedmonters, we were drawn to Piedmont for the quality public education and beautiful city. I grew up in the Midwest and didn’t have family nearby, so we were looking for a community with shared values in which we could put down roots and raise our family. I quickly became involved in our schools once my oldest started kindergarten. My three kids all attend(ed) Piedmont public schools and as a Council

I grew up in the Midwest and didn’t have family nearby, so we were looking for a community with shared values in which we could put down roots and raise our family. I quickly became involved in our schools once my oldest started kindergarten. My three kids all attend(ed) Piedmont public schools and as a Council Election Preview – City Council candidates Q&A Member I make it my mission to be a strong partner for schools. 2 - As a long-time volunteer and community leader, I have a passion for public service. As a City Council member for the last four years, my priority is to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. We are a small city with limited resources and staff, and it is essential that we budget conservatively and address past unfunded liabilities, including our streets and sidewalks, parks, and recreation facilities. Essential long-term investments will ensure a beautiful, sustainable city for our kids and grandkids. I also continue to emphasize more immediate priorities such as wildfire prevention, disaster preparedness, community health and public safety. As a Council member I have leveraged my deep community connections to engage and promote diverse perspectives, develop mutually beneficial solutions, and increase equity and inclusiveness. We have great work ahead of us and the right leadership in place to reach our goals. I look forward to continuing that work so that together we can pass on to our children and grandchildren a city as beautiful and safe as the one we live in today. CONNIE HERRICK 1 - Piedmont has been my home for 51 years. My early years were spent travelling and living in Japan and Thailand. When my dad retired from the Army, we moved to Oakland for a short time before settling in Piedmont in 1969. I attended Piedmont Middle School, graduated from Piedmont High in 1975 and still have close friendships from our high school class. My husband Mark and I purchased our Greenbank home in 1992 and are fortunate to have neighbors who we’ve known for over 25 years. Our son Matt attended Beach Elementary, Piedmont Middle School and graduated from Piedmont High in 2009. We are proud to have two PHS Highlanders in the family. 2 - Running for Council was a decision I made more with my heart than my head. Living in unprecedented times has not been easy for any of us. Every day we face challenges to our health, safety and financial stability. I felt that if there was ever a time to step up, contribute and affect positive change, it was now. As a longtime Piedmonter, I have an unwavering dedication to maximizing every dollar we pay in property taxes. Most of all, I have a strong desire to give back and a deep commitment to volunteerism and civic duty. That is the root of why I feel a strong pull to serve and run for office. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 - In 1989, my husband and I were expecting our first child and we wanted a home near our extended families. I grew up in San Francisco and Peter in Danville, so our primary focus was Piedmont. We bought our first home and soon discovered we had invested in much more than a convenient location. We were enchanted with Piedmont’s tree lined streets, detached homes, pristine parks and exceptional schools. And now, 30 years after this beautiful city and its residents welcomed us, I am running for City Council because I want to contribute to the decision-making that will keep Piedmont a special place to live. 2 - I was raised in a family passionate about service. My father spent 30 years in elected office in California. I have memories from about age 5, standing with my dad at local grocery stores, greeting people entering or exiting, trying to engage them in conversations about needed services in their neighborhoods. I learned that governing provides a unique opportunity to improve the lives of others. Throughout my years of volunteer leadership in Piedmont, I have been encouraged to run for City Council. I have the experience, the ability, and the passion to be an effective member of Piedmont City Council. articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved an agreement with Vintage Contractors for refurbishment of the Park Tennis Courts in the amount of $97,000. The unanimous approval was made at an August 17 meeting. The city’s four tennis court facilities are resurfaced, and repairs are completed on a rotation. The scheduled repair of courts began with Linda Beach, Hampton Park, Recreation Courts (now the Corey Reich Tennis Center), and now the courts in the Main Park. Repairs to the Linda Beach courts was completed in 2016. Hampton Park required more substantial repair and was completed in 2017 as part of the comprehensive Hampton Park Improvement Plan. The Rec Tennis Courts project was completed in 2019 with strong financial support from the community, led by the non-profit Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization. The Park Courts are the last to be refurbished. Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King said it is the right time to move forward in fixing the courts. “Hats off to Sara [Lillevand] for placing this item on the agenda. Everyone loves those courts and [the refurbishment] is the right thing to do with city resources,” King said. The scope of the project will include resurfacing two tennis courts with a slip sheet overlay system, similar to the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and installing new net posts and nets similar to the courts on Vista Avenue. All Piedmont tennis courts reopened on May 18 after a twomonth closure due to COVID-19 and shelter-in-place restrictions.
articles.title: Park Courts to be refurbished

articles.text: Photo by Jay Russell Piedmont Recreation Department is offering 3-week and 6-week programs for live, in-person classes. Registration is now open for Piedmont Recreation Department’s fall programs. Outdoor activities will be similar to this past summer and will adhere to current Alameda County Health Department safety guidelines for camps and extra-curricular activities. Programming has been expanded from the summer, based in part on knowledge gained in how to provide safe activities. The lineup for sports clinics has greatly increased, including, to include four levels of tennis camps, flag football, youth soccer and lacrosse, fencing, running. and basketball clinics though Triple Threat Academy. There are camps and classes for kids of all ages including Art and Action Camp where kids will work with clay and jewelry and also play games. Camp Games with Schoolmates favorite Michael Murphy helping during retirement, Hip-Hop dance, Move and Groove Yoga and Bike Fun will also keep kids active. Four levels of Debate Team are also offered to exercise the mind. Adults can have fun too this fall with an introduction to Quang Ping Yang-style Taijiquan and Morning Yoga with Nest owner Kim Lally. Some programs start the week of August 24 and others begin in September. View the full catalog with pricing, scheduling and details at: https://issuu. com/piedmontrecreation/docs/ piedmont_guide_fall_session_1 For more information, call the Rec. Dept. at (510) 420-3070.

articles.text: The City Council received a report on the 2023–2031 Housing Element and Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) plan at its August 17 meeting as the basis for a discussion on future housing. Since 1969, California law has required that all jurisdictions within the state create a plan to meet the housing needs of everyone in the community. Each local government must update its housing element and zoning, if needed, to show how it plans to accommodate its share of the regional need. The housing element is one of the mandatory elements of the Piedmont General Plan. Consultant Barry Miller, who works with the city to develop its detailed housing report, provided a presentation at Monday night’s meeting. He described RHNA as “a unique element, the only part of the general plan that has to updated on the cycle that is set by the state legislature.” The housing element must demonstrate Piedmont’s ability to accommodate its “fair share” of the region’s housing needs. The RHNA process is not new. In two years, Piedmont will enter its sixth cycle in the process. Some changes at the state level mean new requirements for this RHNA cycle. “There is a greater emphasis on social equity in the way housing allocation is made among jurisdictions,” Miller explained The total number of units for the Bay Area is substantially higher in this RHNA cycle than the last, Miller added. There is expanded California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) oversight on methodology and allocations. Miller pointed out that there are more factors to consider in allocations, such as: overpayment, overcrowding, greenhouse gas target, and jobs to housing fit, as well as new requirements for identifying housing sites or where housing can be built in Piedmont in the future. In the 2007 to 2014 RHNA cycle, Piedmont met its entire allocation for very-low income households, through the rent-restricted second unit program. Although the program proved The Fremont Bank Way.

articles.text: activity. With our team growing every year, and the swim team and girls’ team doing the same, the demand is here for a new pool. We have been told by the school that this year we need to come up with the funds for the pool rental. “Asking for $10,000 per year is a challenge; asking for $20,000 per year might be a death knell,” said Savage. Boys’ polo has become one of the most successful teams at the school despite its lack of pool space. If we’re going off building talent, it’s hard to determine a more deserving group. Since Savage returned to his hometown to teach at the high school and coach the water polo team, PHS has sent six athletes to nationally ranked collegiate water polo programs, including: Sarah Mooney (Class of 2015) to Bucknell; Kelsey Fennell (’16) to UC Santa Barbara; Adam Low (’17) and Annika Disney (‘18) to Santa Clara; Henry Saunders (‘19) to NCAA champion USC; and Patrick Conn (19) to the University of Toronto. Mooney came back to the school as head coach of the girls’ team for the last two seasons. Members of Piedmont’s Class of 2020 and onward certainly have the talent to continue water polo at the next level. Seniors Max Wagener and Spencer Stein form a formidable 1-2 punch with sophomore goalie Dariush Kashani already a first-team selection as a freshman. The girls have senior Ella Wright and sophomore Rosie Feldman leading the charge into 2021, both play club polo. The Piedmont City Council recently voted 5-0 in favor of putting a bond measure on the November 3 ballot. -PHS water polo coach John Savage The Piedmont Pool faces an imperative vote in November to pass a $19.5 million bond measure. With sports at Piedmont High already being sidestepped due to the effects of COVID-19, the water polo program was already facing its own pressing situation: the life of the Piedmont Pool. Requiring a 2/3 majority vote to pass a bond measure toward funding construction, the water polo program has only gained in size over the years while the water around them has shrunk – literally and figuratively. “The current pool has been on life support for some time. It is currently leaking about 1,000 gallons of water a day and is in need of repairs. These repairs would only be band-aids, as it has been noted, and the pool is quite old. The existing pool also does not meet the needs of the community,” said boys’ water polo coach John Savage. Both high school teams – boys and girls – have used the city’s community pool since the teams were created because Piedmont High School, unlike many schools throughout California, never built a pool for its swim teams in the spring and water polo teams in the fall. For now, they have been traveling to Laney College, while the swim team rents out space in Montclair and Emeryville; hardly a secure home for the future. “The swim team, the water polo teams, swim lessons, and community-use all require a larger facility than the one that exists,” explained Savage. Savage, who grew up in Piedmont and was on the swim and water polo teams, has seen water polo grow in popularity in his eight years coaching the high school boys’ team. With their requirement to practice at Laney or other pools, water polo is required to pay over $10,000 to operate, which would double in price should a new pool not get funded. Savage explains he’s been told it’s up to them to the team to find funding for 2021. “It would be very difficult and expensive for the water polo teams to continue to operate. It would add strain onto the athletes and families with the greater commute and time spent on the Photos by Nancy Brahm Boys’ water polo coach John Savage explains they are forced to pay $10,000 annually for operating costs. The girls’ team has sent numerous students to college, including head coach Sarah Mooney who played for Bucknell University.
articles.title: November ballot crucial for water polo program

articles.text: Staff photo Witter Field has been closed until further notice by Piedmont School District due to repeated reports of non-compliance of County Public Health orders by users of the field. Piedmont School District announced the closure of Witter Field as of Monday, August 3. The closure includes the main football-soccer-lacrosse field, the baseball and softball fields and their batting cages, and the field house. Though school began online classes this week on August 17, the field remains closed. The closure resulted from “persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County Public Health Department’s Shelter in Place orders” according to Supt. Randy Booker. Despite repeated warnings, field users have continued to play group sports in violation of COVID-19 health orders. Similar complaints led the City to close the Linda Beach Playfield last week. In a press release, Booker wrote, ”The District regrets having to take this action and the inconvenience this may cause the community. Continued lack of compliance of physical distancing and large groups gathering on both City and District fields poses a serious public health risk, necessitating these closures.” Many calls to the police were made recently and throughout the pandemic about safety violations at the field, particularly for soccer players using shared equipment in large groups and playing without masks. The school district said it will work with the City to determine when it is safe and appropriate to reopen Witter Field. For more information, contact Pete Palmer, Director of Facilities, at ppalmer@piedmont.k12.ca.us. S E N D T H E P E R F E C T G I F T W I T H F R E N C H S O A P D E P O T . pages.text: 12 Wednesday, August 19, 2020 Sports November ballot crucial for water polo program activity. With our team growing every year, and the swim team and girls’ team doing the same, the demand is here for a new pool. We have been told by the school that this year we need to come up with the funds for the pool rental. “Asking for $10,000 per year is a challenge; asking for $20,000 per year might be a death knell,” said Savage. Boys’ polo has become one of the most successful teams at the school despite its lack of pool space. If we’re going off building talent, it’s hard to determine a more deserving group. Since Savage returned to his hometown to teach at the high school and coach the water polo team, PHS has sent six athletes to nationally ranked collegiate water polo programs, including: Sarah Mooney (Class of 2015) to Bucknell; Kelsey Fennell (’16) to UC Santa Barbara; Adam Low (’17) and Annika Disney (‘18) to Santa Clara; Henry Saunders (‘19) to NCAA champion USC; and Patrick Conn (19) to the University of Toronto. Mooney came back to the school as head coach of the girls’ team for the last two seasons. Members of Piedmont’s Class of 2020 and onward certainly have the talent to continue water polo at the next level. Seniors Max Wagener and Spencer Stein form a formidable 1-2 punch with sophomore goalie Dariush Kashani already a first-team selection as a freshman. The girls have senior Ella Wright and sophomore Rosie Feldman leading the charge into 2021, both play club polo. The Piedmont City Council recently voted 5-0 in favor of putting a bond measure on the November 3 ballot. Witter Field remains closed “Asking for $10,000 per year is a challenge; asking for $20,000 per year might be a death knell.” -PHS water polo coach John Savage The Piedmont Pool faces an imperative vote in November to pass a $19.5 million bond measure. By Jonathan Comeaux With sports at Piedmont High already being sidestepped due to the effects of COVID-19, the water polo program was already facing its own pressing situation: the life of the Piedmont Pool. Requiring a 2/3 majority vote to pass a bond measure toward funding construction, the water polo program has only gained in size over the years while the water around them has shrunk – literally and figuratively. “The current pool has been on life support for some time. It is currently leaking about 1,000 gallons of water a day and is in need of repairs. These repairs would only be band-aids, as it has been noted, and the pool is quite old. The existing pool also does not meet the needs of the community,” said boys’ water polo coach John Savage. Both high school teams – boys and girls – have used the city’s community pool since the teams were created because Piedmont High School, unlike many schools throughout California, never built a pool for its swim teams in the spring and water polo teams in the fall. For now, they have been traveling to Laney College, while the swim team rents out space in Montclair and Emeryville; hardly a secure home for the future. “The swim team, the water polo teams, swim lessons, and community-use all require a larger facility than the one that exists,” explained Savage. Savage, who grew up in Piedmont and was on the swim and water polo teams, has seen water polo grow in popularity in his eight years coaching the high school boys’ team. With their requirement to practice at Laney or other pools, water polo is required to pay over $10,000 to operate, which would double in price should a new pool not get funded. Staff photo Savage explains he’s been told it’s up to them to the team to find funding for 2021. “It would be very difficult and expensive for the water polo teams to continue to operate. It would add strain onto the athletes and families with the greater commute and time spent on the Witter Field has been closed until further notice by Piedmont School District due to repeated reports of non-compliance of County Public Health orders by users of the field. Piedmont School District announced the closure of Witter Field as of Monday, August 3. The closure includes the main football-soccer-lacrosse field, the baseball and softball fields and their batting cages, and the field house. Though school began online classes this week on August 17, the field remains closed. The closure resulted from “persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County Public Health Department’s Shelter in Place orders” according to Supt. Randy Booker. Despite repeated warnings, field users have continued to play group sports in violation of COVID-19 health orders. Similar complaints led the City to close the Linda Beach Playfield last week. In a press release, Booker wrote, ”The District regrets having to take this action and the inconvenience this may cause the community. Continued lack of compliance of physical distancing and large groups gathering on both City and District fields poses a serious public health risk, necessitating these closures.” Many calls to the police were made recently and throughout the pandemic about safety violations at the field, particularly for soccer players using shared equipment in large groups and playing without masks. The school district said it will work with the City to determine when it is safe and appropriate to reopen Witter Field. articles.text: Witter Field has been closed once again. For many, this fall will be the first time without sports in town. COVID-19 continues to force communities all over the world to change how they think and alter many of their cherished traditions. In Piedmont, for the first time since world War II, there won’t be any sports this fall. No helmets cracking and pads smacking at Witter. No matchpoints at the tennis courts. No PRs being set by cross country runners. No goals being scored by Max Wagener or Ella Wright in the Piedmont Pool. No spirit week on campus. No student rooting section. No senior nights. No taco vendor. No food booths. Witter Field remains closed, meaning the school stays under county guidelines toward official activities. California is among 15 states committed to deferring all high school sports until 2021. “We still need some clarity ahead of December toward having access to kids and having a full offseason,” said football coach Jerome Johnson in anticipation of being able to start practices sometime that month. Witter shutting down has caused the budding stars of the Highlander soccer program to commute to new training locations. “We’re not practicing in Piedmont and have had to find other homes,” said Dan Chubbock, PHS women’s coach and Coaching Director of Piedmont Soccer Club. “That’s just how it is right now. We’ve had to move to Hayward and other locations.” At this time last year, the football program was beginning double days, the final preparation before its first scrimmage games that historically mark the beginning of the season. Piedmont has a five-year tradition of playing Justin Siena in the first week of the season. The Highlanders are still set to play the Braves for its opener, but not until January 2021. And question remains unanswered: will parents, students, or even journalists be allowed at games? A shining light around town is the Corey Reich Tennis Center at the corner of Vista and Bonita Avenue. The four-court complex remains open for residents and Jim Landes’ youth programs. But this fall what won’t be seen are the many players on the high school girls’ tennis team practicing and playing matches as they set their sights on another league championship. It is the first fall season without a girls’ team in action. Despite the headlines of other sports, Piedmont girls’ program’s 20-year unbeaten league championship remains among the top state records. For a girls’ team that saw that record come to an end last season, the team’s development of its younger players this year was critical. But coach Landes is skeptical about the possibility of even having a JV team because the season was both compressed and postponed to next spring. “I had over 15 incoming freshman girls reach out to me. We have a big turn out every year, and normally I’ll take 35-40 kids between JV and varsity. Now we’ll be lucky if we do half that,” said Landes. The big problem is that CIF has scheduled boys; and girls; tennis season to run concurrently, and in the spring. Piedmont has 8 courts available at three separate sites blocks from one another. If both programs run separate seasons, Landes and assistant Corey Reich would be pulling double-duty for some 70-plus kids. “We’ll have to be flexible with how we structure and run things. Running both teams is going to be difficult. If we keep teams around the same size, I would need all four courts for each practice. We’d have to do one practice followed by another, and you have to consider time availability of the tennis courts and school hours for kids,” Landes added. This isn’t the first time in recent memory the girls’ tennis team hit a roadblock. In 2018, the North Coast Section vacated its team tennis championship after the Butte County wildfire smoke and the following rain eliminated competition as schools transitioned from fall to winter semesters. This time, high school sports fans can only hope the teams reach the necessary phase to return. No tennis at the Corey Reich Tennis Center is a first for the girls’ tennis program.

articles.text: Disney also notched nine goals against American Canyon, eight at Berkeley, Dougherty Valley and Castro Valley, seven on St. Patrick, Berkeley, and Benicia, and six against San Leandro. Mooney returned last year a first-year head coach, hoping to regain its success under Aileen Finney, when it won WACC titles in 2012 and 2013 by going 21-2 and 17-5. Mooney was then in her sophomore and junior years. The team reached the second round of NCS both years. The next season, PHS went 16-6 but lost to Alameda in the finals and lost in the first round of the NCS playoffs. In her first year as head coach, Mooney’s team went 7-10 last season and narrowly missed NCS playoffs. She eyes this year’s team that returns a wealth of starters. with Ella Wright, Rosie Feldman, Alex and Bella Kjellen, Lindsey Wolin, Maya Galbreath, Annika Nillson, and Gwen Jones. Adam Low won the Posts’ 2017 Athlete of the Year award after scoring 103 goals, 25 assists and 76 steals in the 2016 season. He went on to play for Santa Clara University. With attention on a November ballot item that would raise money to build a new community pool in Piedmont, we take a look back at the recent success of the high school’s water polo program – the 2016 boys and 2017 girls. The 2016, the boys’ team under coach John Savage set the stage for four consecutive years of success and the growth of its popularity as a fall sport. In the prior years, the team went 11-11 in 2015, 8-6 in 2014, and won only two games in 2013, Savage’s first year as head coach. The 2016 team went 19-9 and reached the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seeded team. They lost to No. 1 Tamalpais, 17-9. The team featured the Post’s 2017 Athlete of the Year, Adam Low, who went on to play for Santa Clara University, a Div. 1 program. That season Low scored 103 goals, 25 assists, 76 steals to depart Piedmont as its all-time leading scorer – at the time. 2016 also had two future All-American players, sophomores Henry Saunders, and Patrick Conn, who eclipsed Low as the school’s all-time leading goal scorer the following two years. One thing that still has eluded Savage and Piedmont High is: a Western Alameda County Conference trophy, with Bishop O’Dowd as the perennial nemesis. Piedmont lost in the 2016 league finals to O’Dowd 16-11 then were upset by the Dragons the following year 8-4 in the opening round. In 2018, led by seniors Conn and Saunders, Piedmont had perhaps its strongest roster of all time with a 22-6 overall record and was undefeated in league prior to the playoffs. But in the 2018 finals, PHS relinquished a 15-10 lead going into the fourth quarter to O’Dowd and once again came up short, losing 17-16. Girls’ team The girls’ 2017 team was headlined by the school’s single season scoring record, Annika Disney, who scored 99 goals in 19 games that season after missing some time due to injury. Like Low, she now plays at Santa Clara. That year the team was 10-13 and missed out on NCS playoffs. Disney had some illustrious performances, including a single-game record of 12 goals against Pinole Valley, which snapped Sarah Mooney’s record of nine goals in 2013. Annika Disney set Piedmont High’s school record in a single season for goals with 99. She also plays for Santa Clara. articles.text: Photo courtesy of CalBears.edu An empty Memorial Stadium at UC Berkeley. The Pac-12 Conference recently postponed all fall sports until 2021. Much like the rest of the United States, no one in college football can seem to get on the same page in regards to the 2020… or 2021 season. It’s a mess. Conferences have changed and re-changed schedules, canceled postseasons or championship games, have had players threaten to boycott and players demand to play, while some schools have shut down sports altogether, such as Stanford. Of the power-five conferences, the Pac-12 and Big-10 are the only two leagues to officially postpone their season to January. Meanhwile, SEC, ACC, and Big- 12 are set to continue playing. Photo courtesy of SEC Among leagues still set to play, the SEC. Other leagues to opt-out of 2020 include the Mountain West Conference, which includes San Jose State, Fresno State, Nevada, and San Diego State. The Mid-American Conference also canceled its season. The Pac-12 and Big-10’s decision has ultimately been met with skepticism, given the NFL has continued its plans to start its 2020 season on-time in September and host its 2021 NFL Draft by the spring. This means that professional prospects risk missing out on the draft and NFL activities, therefor forcing many players to make a decision on whether to play. Several players from both conferences have already announced they will forego a prospective 2021 spring football season in favor of entering the draft. Of the Big-10 Conference, Ohio State quarterback Justin Fields posted a petition to “immediately reinstate the 2020 football season.” But a decision to continue playing, has come with obvious pushback from the West Coast. “We are in the middle of a pandemic, our country is one of the worst controlled on the planet,” said University of Washington head trainer Jon Drezner on CBS Sports. “We have more deaths than any country. We have cases surging all over the place. We haven’t done what we needed to do to play fall sports. And that is really sad.” CAA chief medical officer Dr. Brian Hainline said flatly that college football cannot continue until there are better protocols with nationwide testing. “We’re not in a place today where we could safely play sports,” said Hainline, per The Athletic. The advantage for the NFL, which they never correlated to college football programs throughout the country, is the isolated protocols professionals are privileged to have. The NFL and Players’ Association agreed to a Collective Bargaining Agreement last month that guaranteed some players a salary should they opt out. For college football and the NCAA, a wide-standing CBA has been delegated to each conference in a, “figure it out for yourselves,” manner. While the Pac-12 issued a 12-page statement covering their concerns about returning amidst the global pandemic, Big-12 commissioner Bob Bowlsby publicly said their decision to continue playing was to keep the status quo. “Ultimately, our student-athletes have indicated their desire to compete in sports. They love this season and it is up to all of us to deliver a safe, medically sound, and structured academic and athletic environment for accomplishing that outcome,” said Bowlsby. Photo courtesy of GoBlue.edu The Big House of the University of Michigan. The Big-10 Conference also postponed its season.
articles.title: Pac-12, Big-10 postpone until 2021; SEC, ACC, Big-12 still set to play

articles.text: Another week has passed for UEFA’s 2020 competitions, Champions and Europa league, the highest tiers of European club football. This year’s change for UCL and UEL due to COVID-19 has resulted in the leagues scrapping the usual two-round format on aggregate scores in favor of single game eliminations. As a reminder to American sports fans not in the know, last year’s finalists both had breathtaking comebacks in the semifinals. Liverpool overcame a 3-0 deficit to win 4-3 over top ranked Barcelona, while Tottenham, down 3-0, prevailed over Ajax thanks to Lucas Moura’s second-half hat trick. This year, the upsets have returned. And with just one game instead of the usual double-leg, players and clubs are forced to play as perfect as possible without the comfort of a second attempt. Here’s a rundown of the recent headlines in Europe. But the story of the weekend was the unprecedented dismantling of Barcelona by Bayern Munich, 8-2, leading to Barca firing its manager Quique Setien on Monday. It was just Setien’s first season as manager; unable to live up to expectations of accomplishing a three-peat as La Liga champs, relinquishing to Real Madrid, while getting utterly embarrassed by the German side. Although Bayern entered pre-game as the favorites, the hype couldn’t have been higher after Barca’s midfielder Arturo Vidal responded to trash talk on social media by saying, “We’re no Bundesliga team. We’re Barca, the best team in the world.” But for the Catalonians, their representation as La Liga’s stalwarts has its supporters out of sorts. Next year’s club president elections have been moved up from June 2021 to March, while players like Antoine Griezzman may get sent packing. The Guardian reports that Ronald Koeman is set to be hired as manager. He is a former Barca star from 1989-1995 and the current manager of the Netherlands’ national team. But when it comes to the Finals, PSG punched its ticket with a 3-0 win over Leipzig on Tuesday. Bayern and Lyon play today, August 19. If all goes as expected, 21-year old superstar Kylian Mbappe and Neymar face their toughest task yet against Bayern’s ultra-consistent (and expensive) ways behind Robert Lewandowski, Thomas Muller, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, & Co. Europa League The finals are now set, with Inter Milan of Italy’s Serie A vs. La Liga’s Sevilla on Friday, August 21. Everyone expected Manchester United to get the job done against Sevilla, and should have with 20 shot attempts. But for the small Spanish club, with an estimated worth of $316 million to United’s $1.65 billion, big money was needed to beat spotty defense. Champions League This year’s Cinderella has undoubtedly been Olympique Lyon of France’s Ligue 1. They reached the semifinals after beating Juventus in the Round of 16, then posted a major 3-1uspet of Premier League favorite Manchester City in the Quarterfinals on Saturday, August 15. For Man City, it means manger Pep Guardiola’s woes in UCL continue. There is no doubt that Guardiola will go down in history as one of the best coaches ever, but when it comes to Champions League, no one is a snake-bit as Pep. He has won the UCL since 2011, but never got past the semifinals at Bayern Munch (2013- 2016) and City. Lyon’s win becomes all the more illustrious when considering their net worth. By measure, the French club’s estimated total value is $394.63 million to City’s astronomical $1.41 billion and Juventus’ $1.51 billion. For Ligue 1 and Paris St. Germain also in the semis, it marks the first time two French teams have reached the latter stages. Another small team on the rise, RB Leipzig of Germany’s Budesliga, also pulled off a major upset of Atletico Madrid 2-1 on August 13. Not many people expected Atleti to fall after sending Liverpool home in the Round of 16. In fact, Los Rojiblancos were considered favorites to reach the finals. 2020-2021 seasons starting soon Players aren’t getting much rest when it comes to the start of next season. For English organizations, the first round of the Carabao Cup starts in two weeks on August 29. Ligue 1 kicks off August 21 in France; England’s Premier League and Spain’s La Liga starts on September 12; Bundesliga and Serie A begin September 19 in Germany and Italy. Photo courtesy of PSG.FR Paris St. Germain’s Neymar (left) and Kylian Mbappe punched their ticket to the Champions League finals on Tuesday. Photo courtesy of Telegraph.co.uk Bayern Munich absolutely embarrassed Lionel Messi and his Barcelona team with a 8-2 route in the Champions League quarterfinals. Their manager was fired this week.
articles.title: Man. City, Atletico Madrid, Man. United, Barcelona stunned

This year, the upsets have returned. And with just one game instead of the usual double-leg, players and clubs are forced to play as perfect as possible without the comfort of a second attempt. Here’s a rundown of the recent headlines in Europe. But the story of the weekend was the unprecedented dismantling of Barcelona by Bayern Munich, 8-2, leading to Barca firing its manager Quique Setien on Monday. It was just Setien’s first season as manager; unable to live up to expectations of accomplishing a three-peat as La Liga champs, relinquishing to Real Madrid, while getting utterly embarrassed by the German side. Although Bayern entered pre-game as the favorites, the hype couldn’t have been higher after Barca’s midfielder Arturo Vidal responded to trash talk on social media by saying, “We’re no Bundesliga team. We’re Barca, the best team in the world.” But for the Catalonians, their representation as La Liga’s stalwarts has its supporters out of sorts. Next year’s club president elections have been moved up from June 2021 to March, while players like Antoine Griezzman may get sent packing. The Guardian reports that Ronald Koeman is set to be hired as manager. He is a former Barca star from 1989-1995 and the current manager of the Netherlands’ national team. But when it comes to the Finals, PSG punched its ticket with a 3-0 win over Leipzig on Tuesday. Bayern and Lyon play today, August 19. If all goes as expected, 21-year old superstar Kylian Mbappe and Neymar face their toughest task yet against Bayern’s ultra-consistent (and expensive) ways behind Robert Lewandowski, Thomas Muller, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, & Co. Europa League The finals are now set, with Inter Milan of Italy’s Serie A vs. La Liga’s Sevilla on Friday, August 21. Everyone expected Manchester United to get the job done against Sevilla, and should have with 20 shot attempts. But for the small Spanish club, with an estimated worth of $316 million to United’s $1.65 billion, big money was needed to beat spotty defense. Champions League This year’s Cinderella has undoubtedly been Olympique Lyon of France’s Ligue 1. They reached the semifinals after beating Juventus in the Round of 16, then posted a major 3-1uspet of Premier League favorite Manchester City in the Quarterfinals on Saturday, August 15. For Man City, it means manger Pep Guardiola’s woes in UCL continue. There is no doubt that Guardiola will go down in history as one of the best coaches ever, but when it comes to Champions League, no one is a snake-bit as Pep. He has won the UCL since 2011, but never got past the semifinals at Bayern Munch (2013- 2016) and City. Lyon’s win becomes all the more illustrious when considering their net worth. By measure, the French club’s estimated total value is $394.63 million to City’s astronomical $1.41 billion and Juventus’ $1.51 billion. For Ligue 1 and Paris St. Germain also in the semis, it marks the first time two French teams have reached the latter stages. Another small team on the rise, RB Leipzig of Germany’s Budesliga, also pulled off a major upset of Atletico Madrid 2-1 on August 13. Not many people expected Atleti to fall after sending Liverpool home in the Round of 16. In fact, Los Rojiblancos were considered favorites to reach the finals. 2020-2021 seasons starting soon Players aren’t getting much rest when it comes to the start of next season. For English organizations, the first round of the Carabao Cup starts in two weeks on August 29. Ligue 1 kicks off August 21 in France; England’s Premier League and Spain’s La Liga starts on September 12; Bundesliga and Serie A begin September 19 in Germany and Italy. Photo courtesy of Telegraph.co.uk Bayern Munich absolutely embarrassed Lionel Messi and his Barcelona team with a 8-2 route in the Champions League quarterfinals. Their manager was fired this week.

articles.text: With the current heat wave, your options to escape this tropical warmth can be few and far between with digits reaching the high 90s in Piedmont and the surrounding Oakland Hills. Escaping toward the ocean could be a safe bet, but with COVID-19, sudden beach, parking lot, and trail closures could leave explorers in unfortunate situations far from home. Going early to trails was already important with COVID to escape the heavy crowds of people in popular areas throughout Joaquin Miller, Redwood Regional, Tilden, and other frequented parks. And now add heat to the equation. Trails are most heavily used around noontime, so consider starting your trail at 7 a.m. It is already 70 degrees, but it’s better than later in the morning. Here are a group of trails and parks for you to consider to keep you shaded and out of the sun: Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve This 2.4 mile-loop is dug out of a canyon along Skyline Boulevard. The trail is often less than a few feet wide, so it’s increasingly important to hit this park early to avoid contact with lots of people. Make sure you bring – and wear – your mask. The trail offers just under 450 feet of elevation gain and is easy to navigate, so you can continue on a second loop for an added workout without worry. If you want an increased lower body workout, multiple long stairwells are available to create your own circuit amidst the trees. The park is an oasis for wildflowers, ferns, trees, and information on them. Along the trail are panels identifying the vegetation with a year-round display of blossoming plants throughout the 241-acre preserve. You’ll find the glistening red bark of Pallid Manzanita, fragrant groves of California Bay Laurels, Brittleleaf Manzanita, Coast huckleberry, Douglas Iris, three different fern species (western bracken, coastal wood, and western sword), Pacific madrone, and the edible California Hazelnut. Leona Canyon/Leona Heights Leona Canyon and Leona Heights are two shady conjoining parks in the Oakland hills near Merritt College. Leona Canyon has trailheads on Campus Drive and the Merritt College parking lot, offering a quick 1.7 mile walk alongside Rifle Range Creek. Hikers and dog walkers often sit next to the creek, under the shade of Oak trees and beside groves of ferns. About midway into the park, an abandoned 1940s car sits in the creek. There’s also the foundation of an old logger’s home a few hundred yards down the trail. Leona Heights is a shorter 1.5 mile trail by Horseshoe Creek, which is much more active than the creek at Leona Canyon. The trail has a graffiti-covered foundation from an old factory building and a brief glimpse of the old Leona Heights Sulphur Mine, which was active from the 1890s until 1934. Although there are no recent reported sicknesses, it’s important to mention that a portion of the old sulfur mine has runoff leading into the creek. Parents and dog owners should be wary of the water after a rain. Dimond Canyon Dimond Canyon’s Bridgeview trail is just 1.5 miles from Montclair. It spans the Montclair Golf Course driving range (considered a hidden treasure to locals) beneath Redwood trees and the usual assortment of Oaks and Bays. The trail heads down into Dimond Park of Oakland and also travels next to Sausal Creek. It’s an ideal spot to escape the sun and isn’t a difficult hike with 400 feet in elevation gain, pending where you start. For an ascent, start at the El Centro Trailhead on El Centro Avenue. For a decline that starts closer to Montclair, begin on Monterey Boulevard. Leona Canyon in Oakland will keep you out of the sun and shaded by oaks, ferns in the midst of local history. Although Huckleberry Preserve only has a 2.4 mile loop, there are many sections of stairs for individual workouts. Dimond Canyon’s Bridgeview Trail is a short 1.5 mile walk between Montclair and Dimond Park. Dimond Canyon takes you along the Montclair Golf Course driving range. There should be enough distance to protect you from bad golfers.

articles.text: Here are 8 steps to succeed with distance learning responsible for ensuring their students keep up. Listed below are eight things you can do to help your students succeed: 1. Keep a schedule Shelter-in-place education is chaotic and discordant, which can make it even harder for students to focus. To help minimize these effects it is important to keep your students on a schedule. This can add consistency and normalcy to your children’s academic lives and help them keep focused on learning. Try to maintain consistent bed and wake times, study hours, free time, exercise routines, meals, and family hours. Many students will initially resist regular schedules, but if forced to stick to it, they will often become calmer and achieve more. but cutting is cutting, regardless of the vehicle. Once a student has “broken the seal” and skips a class, cutting can become normalized or even become a habit. Unfortunately, just getting them on the computer isn’t enough, because cutting can involve anything from not logging in at all, to logging in but leaving the room, to logging in but tuning out. Since most online classes meet less often than physical classes, attending every online class is essential. In addition, since meeting with teachers is more difficult, it can take twice as much effort to catch up once a student falls behind. 5. Get a Tutor: Tutors used to be available only to those with extensive disposable income. There are still many expensive tutors available, and they can be very helpful for those who can afford them, but distance learning has changed the tutoring landscape. You are no longer limited by geography, so expand your search to the entire nation, or even internationally. You never know, a British English tutor, Bolivian Spanish tutor or Armenian math tutor might be significantly less expensive. You may also be able to find a variety of free online tutoring resources. Find out what is available through your school district, library, government, Rotary Club or other local organization. 2. Make a Classroom It doesn’t matter if it’s the kitchen table, the living room or your kid’s bedroom, but a student needs a quiet, distraction-free place that they associate with learning. Figure out where your student’s “school room” is going to be ahead of time and start making arrangements now for their “classroom” space. 3. Don’t skip class Few parents accept cutting class in physical schools, so why do parents accept it in online education? It just doesn’t seem as serious to miss a Zoom meeting, 6. Stay Organized: Without the physical and structural supports of traditional school, more of the organization work will fall to students (or their parents or tutors). Remember that for teenagers, being organized is very difficult. They are not just being lazy. Their brains don’t have the organizational cognitive pathways hard wired yet. This doesn’t mean that you have to do all their organizing for them, but they will most likely need help figuring out how to set up an organizational system and sticking to it. If you know an organizational whiz, whether a friend, relative or paid professional, it’s time to bring them in to help your students set up a system that will work for them. 7. Understand strengths and weaknesses: Chances are, you’ve been aware of your children’s academic strengths and weaknesses for a while, and you have already made adjustments. But now it’s time to take an assessment of their life skills – how they do in a more isolated social environment; how they organize their lives; how they manage their priorities. You may 4. Go for the grade, not the pass: It was understandable for parents to lower their standards when distance learning was sprung upon them in the spring. Classes were truncated, no one knew what to expect, and we were all just focused on survival. Things are going to be different this year. Classes and grades will be similar to traditional schools. Even if schools switch to pass/ fail, teachers will know who is putting in the effort. This will reflect directly in letters of recommendation, which will play a larger role than ever before in college applications. In addition, distance learning isn’t going to last forever, and when students go back to school, their graded classes will build on the information taught online. If students don’t learn the online material, they will have a harder time succeeding when they return to school.

articles.text: Literally every parent I know is at their wit’s end about how to help their children weather the COVID storm. Just the other day I spoke with the mother of two boys who has been feeling the loss of normality acutely. She sees her sons spending too much time alone, too much time online, too much time sitting, sleeping, eating. It’s all too much of some things and not enough of some others, and she doesn’t know what to do. A few weeks ago, in her quest to bring her sons’ lives back into balance, she had a great idea. She would take the boys on a trip. They would leave the city and have some fun in the country. She was thrilled at her plan and excited about the possibilities, and she gave herself a hearty pat on the back for orchestrating what was sure to be a transformative experience. And it was transformative – but not for her sons. The trip unfolded as planned. The family went to the country, got plenty of fresh air, played and relaxed, and afterwards – the cherry on top – her sons thanked her for all of her efforts. And yet . . . they returned A hug and a juice box. home and instantly slipped back to their pre-trip routines. She was devastated. For many parents, the pandemic is the first time they haven’t been able to fix, or even make a dent in a child’s problem. Kids suffer all kinds of hardships growing up, but attuned and creative parents are quick to find remedies ranging from a hug and a juice box to tutors, therapists, and now, learning pods. But COVID is unlike any problem we’ve ever seen in our lifetimes, and there are no real solutions Pediatric Speech & Language Therapy Reading • Writing 3666 G r a n d A v e n u e • S u i t e A • ( 5 1 0 ) 8 3 5 - 2 7 5 7 until a vaccine is developed. It took a trip to the country for this mom to finally accept this fact. For months, she felt not only responsible for fixing an unfixable situation, but also felt like a failure as a parent. Even though she knew intellectually that the pandemic wasn’t her fault, she felt it was her job to right every single wrong COVID has visited upon her kids. But, of course she can’t. None of us can. What we can do is give ourselves credit for what’s going right, even if it’s just putting food on the table. And it wouldn’t hurt to have a good cry, give ourselves a hug and a juice box, and know that we’re not alone. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” An online broadcast is live every Friday at 4 p.m. on Aurora’s YouTube channel. In its first season of online productions the theater invited leading industry professionals to discuss Aurora’s upcoming shows and season, and hold interviews with question and answer segments and roundtable discussions. The company began its second season on August 14 featuring a discussion with Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Throughout Costello’s career, he has worked to make theater more accessible for more people, sharing a passion for the visceral experience of live theater with new audiences and underserved communities. He was the founding Artistic Director of Impact Theatre, which focused on audiences in their teens and twenties. articles.text: Music Director Michael Morgan introduces Florence Price’s Symphony No. 2 Oakland Symphony is offering a weekly, archival concert series featuring past performances, with performances every Friday at 6 p.m. The current concert, Florence Price’s Symphony No. 3 in C minor, was originally premiered by the symphony on January 25, 2019 at the Paramount Theatre. Price was an African-American composer who lived from 1887 to 1953. Her First Symphony was the first work by an African-American woman to be played by a major American orchestra, the Chicago Symphony, in 1933. “She is now seeing a great rediscovery, and for me her Third Symphony is her masterpiece,” said Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan. “It is in four movements – classical in form, but American in outlook – with the melodiousness of American folk music, and the extended harmonies we have come to associate with jazz.” You can watch this performance and others in the rePAST series at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/repast/. Florence Price, an early 20th century American composer.

articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players has ennouncd plans for two new series of virtual concerts: Bach Shorts and Main Stage Concerts. The first series, Bach Shorts, consists of three one-hour, livestreamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of Bach’s Cello Suites . Three leading Bay Area cellists partner with professors, composers, and musicians from around the globe for uniquely personal performances and collaborations. The series begins on Sunday, September 13 at 4 p.m. with cellist Christopher Costanza, from the St. Lawrence String Quartet. He will perform Bach’s Second and Sixth Cello Suites and will partner with Stanford Professor Jonathan Berger, who will discuss the effect music has on the brain, hence the concert title, Bach and the Dancing Brain . On October 11, GCCP presents Bach Inspired, a cncert featuring Jennifer Kloetzel, former cellist with the Cypress Quartet. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler . Elena will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. The Bach Shorts series concludes on Sunday, November 8 with Bach Connections, with cellist Robert Howard from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra. He will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. More Music Next Year After the New Year, we plan to offer four live-streamed Main Stage performances with a feeling similar to what Gold Coast audiences have come to enjoy. Tickets for the Main Stage concert series will go on sale later this year. Bach Shorts tickets are $20 per concert, or $50 for all three performances in the series. Concerts are live-streamed via YouTube LIVE. Purchase online at Christopher Costanza, cello www.GCCPmusic.com or by calling (925) 283-3728. See the website, gccpmusic.com, for regular updates about concert offerings, to purchase tickets and to make donations. articles.text: Did you know that Franklin Delano Roosevelt wanted to be a concert pianist? He went to the Metropolitan Opera House with his mother on November 29, 1887 to hear the young prodigy, pianist Josef Hofmann. After the concert little Franklin asked his mother: “do you think I can be a great pianist, also?” As you know, FDR did not become a great pianist. But he did rather well in another endeavor. We now will play the game of “what if”. The only difference is that everything here is the absolute truth. All the names will be familiar, but the stories behind them are not. Famed comedian Jack Benny took his music seriously. He wanted to be a great violinist more than anything else in the world. He said, somewhat ruefully, that he would gladly trade his success as a comedian if he could be a great violinist. While he rubbed shoulders with many of the greatest violinists, he never got any better; despite his disciplined practice regimen. In an effort to sound better, he purchased an outstanding Stradivarius violin and two very expensive bows. Professor Albert Einstein, on the other hand, never had any delusions about his musical ability. He loved the violin but played only for his own relaxation. Some have taken the route of glamour. The glitziest of entertainers was certainly Liberace. He realized early on that he could never compete with great concert pianists of his time, so he developed a flamboyant style and rode it to incredible success. Don’t for a minute let Liberace‘s showbiz persona fool you. He really was a fine pianist. Another person who went down the Glamour Trail was the noted cellist-composer Nina Kotova. Her reasons were completely different from Liberace‘s. Nina always wanted to be a serious concert artist, and she became an important fashion model for the sole reason of financing her concert career. The last czar of Russia, the ill-fated Nicholas II, was another violin-playing enthusiast. As was fitting a Czar, Nicolas noodled on a Stradivarius. Perhaps he should have continued down that path and avoided any military delusions. The Czar’s Stradivarius was sold by the subsequent communist government in an effort to raise money. Famed radio violinist and personality Dave Rubinoff bought the violin and used it as a successful publicity ploy. Rubinoff was another one whose musical ability far exceeded his pop musician notoriety. Such was his fame that he was the most known violinist in America. A young Jascha Heifetz wanted to go in the front door of Carnegie Hall. The doorman told him to use the musician’s entrance. Heifetz said to the doorman: “I am Jascha Heifetz”. The doorman said: “I don’t care if you’re Rubinoff. Use the musician’s entrance.” Just to be clear, Heifetz and Rubinoff were very good friends. Charlie Chaplin was not only a famous Hollywood actor, he was a composer of note and wrote some of the memorable musical themes in his movies. He, too, was an enthusiastic violinist… And a left-handed one at that. Operatic tenor Enrico Caruso was told continuously that he had no future as a singer. Somehow he managed not to be discouraged. Many of us regard Caruso as the greatest singer of all time. If he hadn’t achieved fame on the operatic stage, he would most assuredly have become a successful commercial artist. He was a featured caricaturist in newspapers and even considered syndication. And now we return to the pianist who dashed the musical career of Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Josef Hofmann is considered one of the greatest, if not THE greatest pianist of all time. He could easily have given up his musical career for that of an inventor. He had at least 70 patents to his name. He invented an improved action for the Steinway piano. Another success was his pneumatic shock absorber which was used on Pullman train cars and also for airplanes. One of his strange inventions was a house with a movable foundation so that every room of your house would always be in the sun. As a pianist, Hofmann made lots of money. But he made more money from just one of his inventions than he ever made as a famous pianist. So… as you see… the path to fame and success is often delusionary and circuitous. Pianist Joseph Hoffman made more money as an inventor than a concert pianist.
articles.title: Finding another line of work – stories behind the fame

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet recently premiered a new film by Benjamin Millepied, titled Dance of Dreams. The film features SF Ballet dancers performing choreography by Justin Peck, Dwight Rhoden, Janie Taylor, and Christopher Wheeldon, all of whom donated their time to the project. It premiered on August 13 at 12 p.m., and is now available to the public on the ballet company’s live-stream “SF Ballet @ Home,” YouTube, Facebook, and IGTV. Commissioned by Helgi Tomasson and filmed in iconic San Francisco locations including the Palace of Fine Arts and the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, the six-minute film is set to “Scène d’Amour” by Bernard Hermann from the Alfred Hitchcock film Vertigo. SF Ballet Orchestra Music Director Martin West mixed and mastered the recording, which incorporates more than 150 tracks recorded remotely by more than 60 musicians in the Orchestra. Social distancing rules were observed during the filming process. The pas de deux are danced by dancers who have been sheltered in place together. You can watch the movie, and learn more about its production at https://www.sfballet.org/ sf-ballet-home/.
articles.title: SF Ballet premieres film Dance of Dreams

He went to the Metropolitan Opera House with his mother on November 29, 1887 to hear the young prodigy, pianist Josef Hofmann. After the concert little Franklin asked his mother: “do you think I can be a great pianist, also?” As you know, FDR did not become a great pianist. But he did rather well in another endeavor. We now will play the game of “what if”. The only difference is that everything here is the absolute truth. All the names will be familiar, but the stories behind them are not. Famed comedian Jack Benny took his music seriously. He wanted to be a great violinist more than anything else in the world. He said, somewhat ruefully, that he would gladly trade his success as a comedian if he could be a great violinist. While he rubbed shoulders with many of the greatest violinists, he never got any better; despite his disciplined practice regimen. In an effort to sound better, he purchased an outstanding Stradivarius violin and two very expensive bows. Professor Albert Einstein, on the other hand, never had any delusions about his musical ability. He loved the violin but played only for his own relaxation. Some have taken the route of glamour. The glitziest of entertainers was certainly Liberace. He realized early on that he could never compete with great concert pianists of his time, so he developed a flamboyant style and rode it to incredible success. Don’t for a minute let Liberace‘s showbiz persona fool you. He really was a fine pianist. Another person who went down the Glamour Trail was the noted cellist-composer Nina Kotova. Her reasons were completely different from Liberace‘s. Nina always wanted to be a serious concert artist, and she became an important fashion model for the sole reason of financing her concert career. The last czar of Russia, the ill-fated Nicholas II, was another violin-playing enthusiast. As was fitting a Czar, Nicolas noodled on a Stradivarius. Perhaps he should have continued down that path and avoided any military delusions. The Czar’s Stradivarius was sold by the subsequent communist government in an effort to raise money. Famed radio violinist and personality Dave Rubinoff bought the violin and used it as a successful publicity ploy. Rubinoff was another one whose musical ability far exceeded his pop musician notoriety. Such was his fame that he was the most known violinist in America. A young Jascha Heifetz wanted to go in the front door of Carnegie Hall. The doorman told him to use the musician’s entrance. Heifetz said to the doorman: “I am Jascha Heifetz”. The doorman said: “I don’t care if you’re Rubinoff. Use the musician’s entrance.” Just to be clear, Heifetz and Rubinoff were very good friends. Charlie Chaplin was not only a famous Hollywood actor, he was a composer of note and wrote some of the memorable musical themes in his movies. He, too, was an enthusiastic violinist… And a left-handed one at that. Operatic tenor Enrico Caruso was told continuously that he had no future as a singer. Somehow he managed not to be discouraged. Many of us regard Caruso as the greatest singer of all time. If he hadn’t achieved fame on the operatic stage, he would most assuredly have become a successful commercial artist. He was a featured caricaturist in newspapers and even considered syndication. And now we return to the pianist who dashed the musical career of Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Josef Hofmann is considered one of the greatest, if not THE greatest pianist of all time. He could easily have given up his musical career for that of an inventor. He had at least 70 patents to his name. He invented an improved action for the Steinway piano. Another success was his pneumatic shock absorber which was used on Pullman train cars and also for airplanes. One of his strange inventions was a house with a movable foundation so that every room of your house would always be in the sun. As a pianist, Hofmann made lots of money. But he made more money from just one of his inventions than he ever made as a famous pianist. So… as you see… the path to fame and success is often delusionary and circuitous. Madison Keesler and Benjamin Freemantle make use of the Palace of Fine Arts for their “Dance of Dreams” segment with the San Francisco Ballet. SF Ballet premieres film Dance of Dreams By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet recently premiered a new film by Benjamin Millepied, titled Dance of Dreams. The film features SF Ballet dancers performing choreography by Justin Peck, Dwight Rhoden, Janie Taylor, and Christopher Wheeldon, all of whom donated their time to the project. It premiered on August 13 at 12 p.m., and is now available to the public on the ballet company’s live-stream “SF Ballet @ Home,” YouTube, Facebook, and IGTV. Commissioned by Helgi Tomasson and filmed in iconic San Francisco locations including the Palace of Fine Arts and the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, the six-minute film is set to “Scène d’Amour” by Bernard Hermann from the Alfred Hitchcock film Vertigo. SF Ballet Orchestra Music Director Martin West mixed and mastered the recording, which incorporates more than 150 tracks recorded remotely by more than 60 musicians in the Orchestra. Social distancing rules were observed during the filming process. The pas de deux are danced by dancers who have been sheltered in place together. You can watch the movie, and learn more about its production at https://www.sfballet.org/ sf-ballet-home/. articles.text: Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill in a scene from Moneyball. Review by Jonathan B. Moy Our beloved, local, perennial hard-luck Oakland A’s and General Manager Billy Beane are the focus of Director Bennett Miller’s new film Moneyball, which had its world premiere on Monday night at the Paramount Theatre in downtown Oakland. It was the first major Hollywood release premiered in Oakland in 20 years. At the end of an incredible yet disappointing 2001 season in which the A’s are eliminated from post-season playoffs by the New York Yankees, Beane (with much hoopla, played by Brad Pitt) is faced with the problem of losing three key players to bigger teams with bigger money: outfielder Johnny Damon, first baseman Jason Giambi and pitcher Jason Isringhausen. Ownership will not give him the funds to replace them, so he is faced with the challenge of building a winning team with one of the smallest payrolls in Major League baseball. but it does include an improbable 20-game winning streak, the likes of which had never been seen in professional sports. The story of Moneyball is the emergence of a revolutionary, sabermetric style of baseball player evaluation, originated by statistician Bill James, and made known throughout the world from its use by Beane and Assistant GM Paul DePodesta during the early 2000’s. Flying in the face of traditional scouting methods, “moneyball” was a way to see value in traditionally undervalued players, and hence build a successful and competitive team with very limited funds. The model Beane and DePodesta created in 2002 is now utilized in some way by nearly all other major league teams, including the 2004 World Champion Boston Red Sox. Author Michael Lewis’ Moneyball must’ve been a difficult adaptation for screenwriters Steven Zaillian (a San Francisco State film school graduate who has Schindler’s List and Searching for Bobby Fischer to his credit), and Aaron Sorkin (A Few Good Men, The Social Network, “The West Wing”). Essentially it is a book about evaluating baseball players with a laptop as opposed to a scouting manual. Thankfully they were able to evoke a humanity and a meshed narrative involving the life of Beane himself. An extremely promising outfielder drafted out of high school, Beane could not rediscover his talent in the big leagues. Zaillian and Sorkin relate his lifelong frustration to the theory of “moneyball.” which values the talents of those who have been wrongly prejudged by traditional evaluation. Moneyball is actually an attempt at inclusion in a culture where exclusion is the norm. Key to the film’s success is the relationship between Beane and Brand, and the onscreen chemEnter Peter Brand (acted by Jonah Hill), youthful advisor to the Cleveland Indians, who has a new way of evaluating players that traditional scouts balk at. Facing tremendous opposition and criticism from the baseball world, including A’s manager Art Howe (played by Philip Seymour Hoffman), Beane and Brand stick to their plan of hiring those who have been written off by other teams, but who have the right numbers, including a high on-base percentage. The 2002 season does not bring a World Series Championship to Oakland,

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The films of Hayao Miyazaki, master storyteller and animator and often referred to as the Walt Disney of Japan, have been difficult to find in America. Through a collaboration between Studio Ghibli and HBO Max, an impressive list of Miyazaki films are now available. This week’s recommendation is Kiki’s Delivery Service, made in 1989. The film was adapted from a popular Japanese novel written by Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s anime and storytelling talents, incorporating fantasy and benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young god-hearted witch on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home. She takes her cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom-flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service for his freshly baked products. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on coming-of-age issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, Kiki’s Delivery Service is also a wonderful adventure. Equally important, it is also a personal crossroads for Kiki, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. It is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service (1989). Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the Englishdubbed voices of Kirsten Dunst, Debbie Reynolds and Matthew Lawrence. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated G. Scene from Kiki’s Delivery Service.
articles.title: Kiki’s Delivery Service a masterpiece by Miyazaki

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Who are these pulp fiction superheroes and why do they resonate with our children? Whatever the answer, Hollywood is in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel. This summer’s big tent blockbusters are once again defined by the superhero: Thor; X-Men: First Class; Green Lantern. And not to forget Transformers. Plus Harry Potter, a superhero to be sure. Just ask Voldermort. Now comes Marvel’s Captain America: The First Avenger. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), is desperate to join the army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), But he can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. What 90-pound kid wouldn’t love to suddenly have the washboard abs of Captain America, an all-American hero who goes off Chris Evans stars as Captain America. to fight not just the Nazis, but a cranked up version of evil doers, an outfit called Hydra, led by Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), who also possess some serious weaponry. The first Captain America is an original film (beginning in 1942), and act one is devoted to how Rogers morphs into his present incarnation. It’s all nicely done, albeit with holes in the logic, requiring serious suspension of disbelief as well as a huge assist by CGI. But then, that’s what defines these wonderfully imagined movies. “No way” some literalists might say. Response: a chorus of kids saying, “Yes, way!” Captain America fights for truth, justice, and VE-day, which means serious combat with the Hydra. Captain America. Directed by Joe Johnston. Starring Chris Evans, Haley Atwell, Tommy Lee Jones, Hugo Weaving and Stanley Tucci. Rated PG-13. Originally printed in the Post on July 27, 2011.
articles.title: It’s summer – time for Captain America

articles.text: Rosemary Orozco (left) in a dress from her Fall collection, and designer Azadeh Riaz. The two have created a new women’s clothing line that will be available online. Piedmont resident and KTVU TV meteorologist Rosemary Orozco is teaming up with Couture Fashion expert Azadeh Riaz to create a classic, chic, fun collection described as suitable for all women. Orozco and Riaz met more than two decades ago at a time when Orozco was a model before becoming a TV journalist and meteorologist. Azadeh in the meantime built her fashion line into a multi-million-dollar company. Azadeh’s extensive experience in the design and manufacturing of couture garments and her dedication to the fit and technique of constructing each piece of a garment has earned her a respected reputation in the high fashion industry. While the idea of designing dresses brought these two together, COVID-19 has caused a slowdown in the industry. As a result, the two women have created a plan to focus on the challenges that women face today. “We’re focusing on professional, comfortable designs that women can wear during on-line work meetings and still pretty enough to leave for after-hour social distancing gatherings and entertainment allowed by law,” explained Orozco. When the two aren’t talking fashion, they’re often chatting about the uncertainty and pain felt by so many people right now. They have decided that part of their effort will be to give back to the community and will be able to serve women in need. “We want to help build confidence among these women, whether it’s a nice outfit for work or for someone seeking a fresh start,” Orozco said. The new company will be donating to charity and those hit hard by COVID-19. Understanding the fashion world and the toll it takes on the environment, Azadeh said they plan to use eco-friendly packaging for shipping and that the manufacturing will be in the U.S. The Rosemary Orozco By Azadeh collection will be sold online with the goal of offering clothing and accessories at a handful of Bay Area stores once customers are allowed to return to indoor shopping. For more information, see: https://www. atelierazadeh.com/collection/ wearable-fashion/.
