articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

The timeline for a cure or even a treatment for ALS may be very long, and we may not be around long enough to see it, but the goal is worthy of our effort and hopefully your dollars. Any contribution, no matter how small (or large!) will be appreciated and will help fund research into the causes and cures of ALS. Your tax-deductible gift will make a difference in the lives of many! It is faster and easier than ever to support this great cause. You can make your donation online by simply clicking on the link at the bottom of this message. If you would prefer, you Once again, the bicycle team Linda and Marvin will be riding in memory of Linda Lettieri and Marvin Stern, both of whom passed away from ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, better known as Lou Gehrig¹s Disease). July 9 marked the 13th anniversary of Linda¹s passing and the 15th year our bicycle team, Team Linda and Marvin, will be participating in the Ride to Defeat ALS. This is truly a science fiction-like disease in its progressive reduction of your ability to move, speak and eventually, breathe. Since ALS is currently not well understood, has no cure or effective treatment path, we are working hard to fund-raise to find a cure through the ALS Association, Golden West Chapter. Finally, there are some glimmers of hope that some of the genetics of ALS are being discovered, although we are a long way from effective treatments and the eventual cure. The ALS Association is the only non-profit organization fighting Lou Gehrig’s Disease on every front. It is the first public open space to be closed due to non-compliance of County Health guidelines during the coronavirus pandemic. The Piedmont Police Department has received a slew of complaints from residents in the last two weeks regarding people using the field. The most frequent and ongoing complaint is of young adults playing organized, pick-up sports – primarily soccer – on the field without masks on, and without social-distancing. Despite repeated warnings from city staff and park ambassadors, users of the facility have continued to play group sports in violation of public health orders from Alameda County and the city. articles.text: Part 1 in a series providing a detailed history of the Community Pool located next to the Piedmont Recreation Department. The future of the Piedmont Community Pool will be up to the voters this fall in the form of a bond measure that would redesign the facility. On November 3, Piedmonters will vote to either support or reject a bond issue initially pegged at $19 million. Numerous City Council and Recreation Commission meetings have alerted the public of ongoing, long-term issues with the aquatic facility, including an outer-shell leak causing a loss of 1,000 gallons of water a day. At each digital meeting, calls poured in from concerned residents over the future of the city’s only public pool (the school district has none). The majority of callers supported the decision to place a bond on this year’s ballot, and showed interest in a redesign of the facility. This is not the first time that a redesign has been offered for the 56-year-old pool. It originally opened in 1964 and has had no major renovations. In May 2002, a proposed swim center project was brought to City Council and community members to consider. At the time, the proposition received both proponents and opponents, but was ultimately tabled at future council meetings. The plan, designed by Piedmont resident and nationally-acclaimed aquatics architect Clarence Mamuyac, envisioned a 30-meter competition pool, a recRendering of pool design from 2002 when the city was being lobbied to renovate the already inadequate-sized Piedmont Pool.

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council on July 24. Editor: I want to compliment you on the great jobs you are doing for our city under very trying circumstances. I imagine you never ever thought that your jobs would involve working during a Pandemic. Please accept my sincere thanks. I do have some very serious concerns about REACH rules and regulations proposed to be instituted within our city building code. Of course, I am speaking about my own situation, but I would guess that there are many others in the same boat. My husband and I are in our twilight years (81 and 78) and living on a fixed income. We also live in a home that is about to be 100 years old. We have lived in it for 48 years. Our home has a tile roof as well as a boiler/circulating hot water system that is powered by natural gas. Should I be required to change out that heating system, it would be a tremendous financial burden and may not even be possible without remodeling every room in the house and cost many thousands of dollars. Likewise, if I wanted to do a roof repair and was told that I had to add solar, it would be extremely complicated and costly. I might choose to take all the tile off and put on a composition roof that would make for a change that would ruin the character of the house. I can see this happening to a lot of homeowners who have been in Piedmont in older homes for many years. At this point in our lives, we want to stay in Piedmont and do the best we can with repairs and not be forced to leave because of REACH. I would like to suggest that for these older homes and older people, REACH would only be triggered by the sale of the house. This would allow the seller and buyer to negotiate upon whom the financial burden would fall. I would hate these REACH rules to be the factor that forced people to leave our beautiful city. In my case, that would mean leaving a city that has been my home for 78 years. I believe that there are many similarly situated homeowners who are not aware of what you are proposing, and if they knew, they would be outraged. Please consider the above as you make your decisions about REACH. Thank you, –Fran Wolfe
articles.title: REACH codes have big impact on older homes

I would like to suggest that for these older homes and older people, REACH would only be triggered by the sale of the house. This would allow the seller and buyer to negotiate upon whom the financial burden would fall. I would hate these REACH rules to be the factor that forced people to leave our beautiful city. articles.text: Piedmont’s brand-new fire engine was assigned to the Gold Fire in Modoc County last week. Its 4-man crew is expected to be there for at least a week. Piedmont Fire Engine 2841 was assigned to the Gold Fire in Modoc County and departed to the far northeastern corner of the state on the morning of July 22. The fire started near the town of Adin, 29 miles southwest of AltuPiedmont’s 4-member crew, led by Lt. Zach Heliker, was assigned to a helicopter base for the Gold Fire. It is expected that Piedmont will rotate in a new 4-man crew later this week. “Tanker 944, the largest firefighting tanker in the world, is working the Gold Fire,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. “It holds about 20,000 gallons and is operating out of McClellan Air Force Base in Sacramento. The tanker is active all year long, relocating where needed in both hemispheres.” Upon arrival, PFD firefighters were stationed at a location for 13 helicopters assigned to the fire. “They became familiar with various safety systems on all the aircraft, including emergency shutdown procedures,” Black said. The Gold Fire started on July 20 and the cause is still under investigation. Cal Fire released the following update on July 27: “Today, a brief break in weather is expected and firefighters will take advantage of the opportunity to aggressively improve fire lines and extinguish burning material within the fire perimeter. Gusty afternoon winds and dry conditions are still a possibility in the afternoon hours, building through the week. The incident continues to burn in areas that include private residences as well as ranch and commercial operations. Several cultural and sensitive resources remain threatened,” the report stated. As of press time 13 structures have been destroyed, five structures damaged, and three people have been injured. The fire, which has burned 21,870 acres, was 65 percent contained as of yesterday afternoon.

articles.text: Over the past seven days, three additional new cases of COVID-19 were counted in Piedmont according to the Alameda County Department of Public Health. The county’s caseload is now over 10,000. Its Public Health Department announced there had been 10,633 cases as of yesterday, Tuesday, July 28. Officials said that 181 people have died in Alameda County since the coronavirus pandemic was declared in March, an increase of 14 people in the past seven days. Week over week, COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the coronavirus, cases have increased by roughly 8 percent countywide. While Piedmont’s caseload of 23 shows that July has been the City’s worst month since the first weeks of the pandemic. Heading into July, Piedmont had only 10 reported cases. No cases were reported in June, and three were reported in May. In Oakland, the most populous city in the county, officials recorded 4,218 cases. Hayward now has a total of 1,537. Fremont has reported 584 cases, San Leandro has reported 551 cases and Berkeley has reported 374 cases. Alameda County is the hardest hit in the San Francisco Bay Area and is the only county with over 10,000 cases in the region. On July 12, Alameda County was placed on a statewide COVID-19 “watchlist” and currently remains on this list. Currently all counties in the Bay Area except San Mateo are on the watchlist. As per California regulations, counties on the watchlist cannot allow for indoor activities like dining and museums, however those indoor activities were already prohibited by Alameda County orders. Indoor malls have been closed and indoor religious services are currently prohibited. Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials at the end of June. July has been a disheartening month for all of California as a continued surge of COVID- 19 cases followed weeks of the state’s efforts to control the spread of the virus. With a caseload of 466,550 as of yesterday, California now has more cases than any other state, including New York. Last Friday In Piedmont the City closed Linda Beach Playfield due to repeated incidents of non-compliance with city and county restrictions. Field users had been issued warnings about the requirement to wear masks and observe social distancing. “Despite repeated warnings from city staff, users of this facility have continued to play group sports in violation of COVID-19 health orders,” the City said in a release last week. “We regret having to take this action, but the actions of field users have necessitated it.” The City of Piedmont keeps its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ covid-19 “Since becoming president you made but one mistake...unfortunately it was a lulu.”

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont will host a discussion on food insecurity in the East Bay, led by Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. The event will be livestreamed on the League’s YouTube channel (https://www. youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg) from 4:00-5:00 p.m. on Tuesday, August 4, 2020. Viewers will learn about Alameda County’s significant food problems which have been exacerbated by COVID-19. Bateson will describe how every citizen can help create a hunger-free community. Bateson, the Food Bank’s Executive Director since 2001, will describe their programs, including fresh food distribution to the community and efforts to eliminate the causes of hunger in the East Bay. During her tenure, the Food Bank has tripled its annual food distribution. In 2016 it won Feeding America’s National Food Bank of the Year Award. The Food bank has also ended the distribution of carbonated beverages and increased its farm-fresh produce from 1 million to 20 million Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank, will be the guest speaker at an event hosted by the Piedmont League of Women Voters on August 4. pounds annually. Bateson was inducted into the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame in 2017 and currently is Chair of Feeding America’s Western Region. Viewers may participate on August 4 by submitting questions to the YouTube livestream comment section, or by e-mail to LWVpiedmont@gmail.org. For more information, visit www. lwvpiedmont.org. articles.text: 2 seats open on council, 3 on school board The nomination period for the two vacancies on Piedmont City Council and three vacancies on the School Board opened on July 13. Elections for both bodies will occur in the General Election on November 3. The deadline for filing papers for candidacy is Friday, August 7 at 5 p.m. Thus far four residents have obtained papers to run for seats on the city council, and six have obtained papers to run for school board. Council incumbent Jennifer Cavenaugh is filing for a second 4-year term. Other candidates to pick of papers include Connie Herrick, Conna McCarthy and Nancy Bostrom. As of press time, McCarthy is the only candidate who has qualified for the ballot. Mayor Bob McBain will term out after serving on the city council for more than eight years. Hari Titan, who has twice been a candidate, has picked up papers for filing. Also intending to file as candidates are Hilary Cooper, Veronica Anderson, James Crawford-Jakubiak, Jason Kelley, and Bostrom, who has signed up for both elective bodies. Cory Smegal, nearing the completion of her first four-year term, is eligible to run for a second four-year term. School board members Sarah Pearson and Andrea Swenson will term out, leaving two definitive vacancies. The city publishes a guide to nomination and candidacy, which provides details about the nomination and candidacy process which prospective candidates might find useful. That information is available on piedmont. ca.gov/government. California Elections Code requires that nomination papers be issued in person to the prospective candidates, who are required to take out nomination papers in person at the City Clerk’s office. Residents with questions about the process and those who wish to make an appointment may call the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040, or email: cityclerk@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: City, school election on November 3

articles.text: The U.S. Census Bureau will be hiring more than 300 people to conduct door-todoor canvassing in the coming weeks. Census takers (enumerators) interview the residents of households that have not responded to previous invitations to complete the census survey online, by phone, or by mail. Applicants must be at least 18-years-old, have a driver’s license, an email address, and be able to pass a background check. The job is temporary, has flexible hours, and pays $30/hour. Census takers serve as the last line of defense for getting an accurate count, which is critical for federal funding and fair political representation. You can help your community and yourself by applying now at 2020census.gov/jobs or calling 1-855-562-2020.

articles.text: Piedmont Grocery employee Brian Hanley frequently sanitizes handled surfaces in the store. Piedmont Grocery, in business for 118 years, has remained open during the entirety of the COVID-19 pandemic and has implemented some of the most rigorous and comprehensive safety adjustments to fight the viral spread. On April 8 they were dealing with an influx of people hoarding and engaging in panic buying of so-called essentials, primarily paper products. As the challenges have changed, owner Dave Larson and his grocery staff have kept vigilant and adapted to the health standards required by Alameda County. In March and April, the store shortened its hours, created a senior hour each morning, and closed Thursday for restocking. In time they were able to return to a seven-day schedule, and now are back to regular hours of 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. every day, and 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Sundays. Senior hour from 9:00-10:00 a.m. has proven to be efficient and popular, eliminating lines of customers that sometime occur during the day. At Piedmont Grocery the carts and baskets are diligently separated into clean and carts just returned by customers but not yet cleansed with wipes. Some grocery stores have resorted to leaving out a sanitizing bottle and paper towels for self-cleaning, but Piedmont Grocery, takes the responsibility to clean everything properly. The store is small, so while the aisles may be tighter, there is not a huge crowd inside, and shoppers don’t have to linger inside. The store hired six additional

articles.text: Staff photo After making an appointment, Piedmont resident Lee Alering (left) was able to drive to the Carriage House and leave donations with Dress Best for Less with DBFL employee Sharon Sanford. Dress Best for Less, the community’s thrift shop, is now accepting donations at the Carriage House at 799 Magnolia Avenue, but by appointment only. Its retail shop next to Piedmont Grocery at 4020 Piedmont Avenue has been open since June 17, but it does bit have adequate storage space for accepting donations. The Carriage House, which houses a sorting and marking room for the store, recently received clearance to accept donations by appointment. Appointments to donate must be made at www.dressbestforless.org. DBFL can no longer sell directly out of the Carriage House. It will be used for drive-up donations and sorting only. Sales will occur at its store on Piedmont Avenue, but only higher end goods can be accepted. Recommended items for donation include nearly new: women’s summer tops, handbags, purses, jewelry, men’s tops, home decor, kid’s clothes, toys & puzzles, books, designer items, and even ski and snowboard apparel. Many people have backlogs of “pandemic spring cleaning” donations in wait, but patience will be required. “If we opened up to regular donations in our bin out front, we would get dumped on again,” said DBFL chair Linda Smith Munyan, noting the double function of donations by appointment only. “It gives the store a chance to re-educate our donors. People have been used to giving us everything. It’s more effective to explain this in a conversation vs. signs on the building,” she said. Dress Best for Less has experienced slow sales since its reopening, around 50 percent of normal. Much of their proceeds benefit Piedmont schools. On Thursday July 30, appointments are available from 9-12. Future schedules will be be Tuesdays and Wednesdays from 9-12 and Saturdays from 10-1. Everyone must wear a mask and adhere to social distancing.
articles.title: Dress Best for Less accepting donations – by appointment

By Jay Russell Dress Best for Less, the community’s thrift shop, is now accepting donations at the Carriage House at 799 Magnolia Avenue, but by appointment only. Its retail shop next to Piedmont Grocery at 4020 Piedmont Avenue has been open since June 17, but it does bit have adequate storage space for accepting donations. The Carriage House, which houses a sorting and marking room for the store, recently received clearance to accept donations by appointment. Appointments to donate must be made at www.dressbestforless.org. DBFL can no longer sell directly out of the Carriage House. It will be used for drive-up donations and sorting only. Sales will occur at its store on Piedmont Avenue, but only higher end goods can be accepted. Recommended items for donation include nearly new: women’s summer tops, handbags, purses, jewelry, men’s tops, home decor, kid’s clothes, toys & puzzles, books, designer items, and even ski and snowboard apparel. Many people have backlogs of “pandemic spring cleaning” donations in wait, but patience will be required. “If we opened up to regular donations in our bin out front, we would get dumped on again,” said DBFL chair Linda Smith Munyan, noting the double function of donations by appointment only. “It gives the store a chance to re-educate our donors. People have been used to giving us everything. It’s more effective to explain this in a conversation vs. signs on the building,” she said. Dress Best for Less has experienced slow sales since its reopening, around 50 percent of normal. Much of their proceeds benefit Piedmont schools. On Thursday July 30, appointments are available from 9-12. Future schedules will be be Tuesdays and Wednesdays from 9-12 and Saturdays from 10-1. Everyone must wear a mask and adhere to social distancing. Piedmont Grocery employee Brian Hanley frequently sanitizes handled surfaces in the store. By Jay Russell Piedmont Grocery, in business for 118 years, has remained open during the entirety of the COVID-19 pandemic and has implemented some of the most rigorous and comprehensive safety adjustments to fight the viral spread. On April 8 they were dealing with an influx of people hoarding and engaging in panic buying of so-called essentials, primarily paper products. As the challenges have changed, owner Dave Larson and his grocery staff have kept vigilant and adapted to the health standards required by Alameda County. In March and April, the store shortened its hours, created a senior hour each morning, and closed Thursday for restocking. In time they were able to return to a seven-day schedule, and now are back to regular hours of 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. every day, and 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Sundays. Senior hour from 9:00-10:00 a.m. has proven to be efficient and popular, eliminating lines of customers that sometime occur during the day. At Piedmont Grocery the carts and baskets are diligently separated into clean and carts just returned by customers but not yet cleansed with wipes. Some grocery stores have resorted to leaving out a sanitizing bottle and paper towels for self-cleaning, but Piedmont Grocery, takes the responsibility to clean everything properly. The store is small, so while the aisles may be tighter, there is not a huge crowd inside, and shoppers don’t have to linger inside. articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation recently announced that Colleen Allan, Amelie Kappes, and Teebie Saunders will be co-chairs of this year’s Giving Campaign for Piedmont schools. They will lead the community-wide effort to raise $3 million to keep Piedmont schools strong. “Every school year it costs the Piedmont Unified School District roughly $18,000 to educate each student in Piedmont. Federal, state, and local funding pays for all but $1,700-2,000 per child of that amount,” said Kappes. “As a community, we are responsible for closing this gap, and each year Piedmont has stepped up and shown we are committed to doing this.” The three chairs have been working throughout the summer to prepare for a campaign kickoff on September 1. An extensive committee of parents representing Piedmont’s six schools is also on board to amplify the outreach of the campaign. For more information on the Piedmont Education Foundation and its annual Giving Campaign, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org. The Fremont Bank Way.
articles.title: Ed. Foundation names Giving Campaign co-chairs

Meg Adler, illustrator of Outside the Lines: A Coloring Book for Rebels. Meg Adler, a Piedmont High School alum, recently published a coloring book with a Bay Area collaborative focus. Adler was born and raised in Piedmont, and her parents, Wayne and Melissa Batavia, still live in the same house in which she grew up. She is a proud alum of Wildwood elementary, Piedmont Middle School, and Piedmont High School. Her interest in art started when she was a young girl, but other than taking a semester of art in high school, she is primarily selftaught. She drew inspiration from her grandmother’s calligraphy. Adler said that her real interest in art as a career came through art therapy, when she was 12 years old. own marks. There’s little prompts throughout,” Adler said. A big aspect of the book, she said, is that it challenges the artist to think outside the norm. “A big part of my art is to think creatively, and to try and represent that,” Adler said. Adler owns a small illustration business called Letters, Aligned. She started the business in 2014. She describes the mission of her business as inspiring awe and imagination, embracing imperfection, and connecting people through collaborative art supporting local businesses. “[The company] started as simple designs for friends, and “It was really formative for me, to think of art not just in a classroom setting, but by creating things,” she said. She said that she hasn’t stopped making art, in some form or fashion, since then. “All kids start drawing. At some point, some of us stop and some of us keep going. And it has generally tied to whether or not we’ve been deemed ‘good at it or not,’ or whether or not we’re good at representational, realistic art, as opposed to whether or not we have an interesting idea, or use materials in an interesting way,” Adler said. Adler’s art is always free hand. She uses simple materials like pen, pencil and paper. Her art, she added, is meant to celebrate the “wiggles and wonders of daily life.” Her debut coloring book, Outside the Lines: A Coloring Book for Rebels, was inspired by her commute from Alameda to San Francisco. The pictures detail her bike from her apartment in Alameda to the ferry, then on the ferry to the Embarcadero in San Francisco, and then the two-block walk to her office. “Some things I would see throughout the city and just think, ‘oh, I want to draw that.’ Now that I’m not commuting, it’s almost like an homage to my commute,” she laughed. From the flower kiosk in at the Ferry Building to the bridge she traveled under every day, each detail that stood out to Adler is chronicled in Outside the Lines. The coloring book is designed for all ages, she said. “It kind of functions as an adult coloring book. You can just color it in if you want, and that’s for any age. You can also add to the drawing, using your San Francisco Ferry Building, illustrated by Meg Adler.

articles.text: If you could design your own rover, where would you want it to go? What would it look like? Complete the challenge below to sketch, label, then design your own rover. Materials: • Pencil or Pen • Scissors • Tape or Glue • Markers or Crayons (to decorate) • Reusable Materials: • Cardboard • Construction Paper • Paper cups • Toothpicks • Foil • Straws • Pipe Cleaners • Popsicle Sticks • Egg Cartons • Toilet Paper or Paper Towel Procedure: 1. Build the body of your rover. You can use a variety of materials for the body, but it should be something sturdy that you can attach other materials to. 2. Decorate the base. You can paint, color, or wrap your body however you’d like. 3. Build the wheels and legs of your rover. For help making a rover that rolls, follow steps (4-9) below. Materials that are round and can roll make great wheels. Straws are a helpful material if you’d like to build a rover that rolls. 4. Tape a straw, or cylinder of paper horizontally across the bottom of your rover. 5. Repeat with one, two, or three more straws/paper cylinders. Try to make them equally spaced out on your rover. 6. Identify the materials you will be using as wheels, and as axles. The axel will hold your two wheels together. You will need the same number of axles as paper cylinders or straws, and twice the number of wheels. 7. Thread your axle material through the straws or paper cylinders underneath your rover. 8. Use tape or glue to attach the center of your wheel to one end of an axle. Make sure the axel is still threaded through the straws on your rover! 9. Repeat so that each axle has two wheels attached to it and is suspending on the bottom of your rover. 10. Add the arms, neck, and head to your rover. Use glue, tape, or poke them through the body of your rover to hold them in place. Strong, skinny materials that can stand up make good arms or necks. Get creative and add different tools to the ends of your rover arms, too. 11. Add a brain, and an energy source to your rover. You can make them out of paper, cardboard, or whatever material you think works best. 12. Add logos, a flag, even passengers to your rover. 13. Encourage others to build their own rover, too. They can even use different materials than you to build their rover. Find more activities and at-home experiments on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Be sure to share your rovers with us on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter @chabotspace. Ellie Morris is a Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland.
articles.title: Want to explore Mars? Design your own rover

articles.text: Julia Banuelos This year the Piedmont Community Service Crew was faced with the cancelation of the annual Pancake Breakfast on the 4th of July, a fundraiser run by the crew for the past three years. After a lot of brainstorming, we came up with the Barbecue Basket idea, which started simply and then evolved into a carefully planned project. Through some hard work, lots of advertising, and direct emails to everyone we knew, we were able to successfully replace Piedmont’s traditional Pancake Breakfast fundraiser and turn it into a fun at-home holiday. Thanks to the generosity of Dave Larson at Piedmont Grocery. Keith Trimble at Village Market, and Lee Chin of Oakland Flower Mart, the teen coed crew was , and Oakland Flower Market, we were able to raise over $2,500. Not only was it a financial success, crew members received lots of positive feedback from their customers. All the proceeds will go toward supporting the crew’s philanthropic efforts, including some of our larger projects, such as working with Rebuilding Together Oakland and a project to build a second Tiny House for homeless teens. We were new PCSC members at the start of our freshman year and worked our way up to our current roles as VPs of fundraising. In May, we began talking about the big responsibility of creating fundraisers that would fit under the restrictions and limitations of COVID-19. Because of the pandemic, a lot of the physical work for the barbecue baskets had to be done by two people to minimize spread of the virus. In addition, publicizing the event and finding people who were interested in purchasing a basket was difficult as well. To solve this problem, we had to make many calls, write emails, post on different social media platforms and publish a lot in local newspapers. The plan did get messy, but even through spontaneous refrigerator malfunctions and unexpected summer plans, this fundraiser became a success. Ken Li, the crew’s advisor was very supportive and told us that our idea was “a perfect example of what [he] dreamed would happen more often–brand new crew members discovering the potential of PCSC and all it has to offer”. Keiko Hayashi, a crew parent, sent a message immediately after receiving her personally delivered barbecue basket. “Wow! We love our 4th of July Basket! You’ve done a tremendous job organizing and pulling these beautiful baskets together! We are so impressed with all of your careful labeling and instructions too.” Sofia Prieto Black holds a newly created Fourth of July Barbecue Basket, a fundraiser by the Piedmont Community Service Crew.
articles.title: July 4th Barbecue Baskets a successful fundraiser

articles.text: Oakland Zoo Outdoor Zoo – Now Open The zoo reopens to the general public on July 29. Mandatory reservations and safety precautions are new at the zoo. The zoo has been closed since March and is the last to reopen in the state. If you haven’t visited in a while, check out the California Trail which was added in 2018. The trail doubled the zoo’s space and provides a habitat for seven species including American buffalos, jaguars and bald eagles. The San Francisco Zoo Outdoor Zoo – Now Open The San Francisco Zoo reopened on July 15th. Reservations must be made at least a day in advance online for specific times to enter. Take the kids to see the 2,000 exotic, endangered and rescued animals at the beautiful zoo right by the ocean. Travel times to San Francisco may never be shorter. The SF Zoo opened in 1889 with a lone grizzly bear, Monarch, believed to be the last in California; he was later sketched on the California flag. Take part in the zoo’s history with a trip the kids will love. Watch videos about chin-strap penguins, how high animals can jump and the world record set for hiccups. The site also has kid-friendly articles and information about various animals. Kids will enjoy the educational computer games available too, try the “Dung Beetle Derby” or “On the Trail of Captain John Smith.” PBS Kids Online Games and TV Shows Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) has provided content that kids and families love for over 50 years. Check out their website, which has tons of fun computer games for kids to play like Cookie Monster’s Food Truck, Dinosaur Train’s Dino Flight, and Clifford the Big Red Dog’s adventure stories. Choose from hundreds of science, reading, Spanish and music games. The site also has kids’ TV shows, including Sesame Street, Curious George and The Cat in the Hat. articles.text: City alleges new FCC rules would further limit local control of cell towers T h e P i e d m o n t Pl a n - ning Department released an announcement on Tuesday, July 21 outlining its opposition to new guidelines recently passed by the Federal Communications Commission that limit how local governments can regulate cell towers. “We believe there are ways for wireless communication devices to be deployed in an aesthetically appropriate manner,” Kevin Jackson, the Director of Planning and Building, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, the FCC seems intent on making that much more difficult, if not impossible.” The announcement came one day after Piedmont City Council voted to join a coalition of cities opposing the rules. On June 9, the FCC adopted a new ruling that altered how municipalities handle permits for wireless facilities. Specifically, the FCC modified Section 6409(a) of the Spectrum Act of 2012. The section requires cities like Piedmont to approve requests from wireless infrastructure companies to modify existing wireless towers and base stations if the physical dimensions do not undergo a “substantially change.” The new decision alters the meaning of “substantial change.” As long as a wireless infrastructure company follows FCC rules, cities cannot deny height or size increases of existing cell antennae even if the modifications would violate aesthetic conditions, such as vegetation screening or fencing requirements, that were initially imposed when the antennae were first approved. The FCC now allows antenna to be up to 20 feet tall and there is no height maximum for new antennae built outside the public right-of-way. Furthermore, the FCC allows that wireless infrastructure companies can install more equipment cabinets per request to make modifications to existing structures. The FCC also changed the definition of “concealment” in regard to wireless facility building requests so that concealment only means “stealth” design, meaning a cell tower that is meant to look like something else, like a tree. Under the order, cities requesting concealment of cell towers could not require screening by a rooftop or tree line. Additionally, timing requirements were altered by the FCC as part of the rule change. Cities must make decisions on wireless facility application within a standardized 60-day “shot clock” period. The new rules mean that the “shot clock” period starts earlier in the application process, when the applicants start the first procedural steps of submitting a proposal. This tightened timeline gives cities less opportunity to publicize and have public discussions about the applications. In response, Piedmont joined a coalition of cities, organized by law firm Best Best & Krieger (BBK), in opposition to the new FCC rules. Comments against the rule change must be filed by August 10. “Unless there is a court-ordered injunction, the new FCC rules will further reduce Piedmont’s ability to control the installation of wireless communication facilities,” Jackson continued. The action is the latest volley between Piedmont and the FCC over cell tower regulations, especially since Ajit Pai was appointed Chairman of the commission by President Trump in 2017. Publicly, the cell tower issue has been a major point of controversy in Piedmont for more than three years. In late 2016, wireless infrastructure builder Crown Castle submitted plans to build several small cell antennas around the City. After years of protest and legal battles, Council approved several of plans from the company last year as part of a settlement with Crown Castle. While the City has had wireless communication facility regulations on the books for decades, a recent push to expand next generation 5G wireless coverage nationwide has brought cell tower builders, cities and the federal government into conflict. In 2018 and 2019, the Council agreed to join organized coalitions in opposed to new FCC rules that make it harder for cities to regulate cell towers. Some of these FCC decisions are now awaiting decision from federal courts. The 2012 Spectrum Act was modified before in 2014 and the changes in June were passed 3-2 by the FCC. “The pandemic has highlighted the need for all Americans to have broadband connectivity as soon as possible,” Pai said after
articles.title: Piedmont announces opposition to new FCC wireless facility rules

articles.text: Grace Foster, a 2017 graduate of Piedmont High School, was named to the 2020 Dean’s List at Lawrence University. The Dean’s List is an annual honor roll of students demonstrating exemplary academic performance. The Dean’s List is compiled at the end of the academic year once all grades have been recorded. To qualify for the Dean’s List a student must earn a minimum of a 3.5 GPA. About Lawrence University Founded in Appleton, Wisconsin in 1847, Lawrence University uniquely integrates a college of liberal arts and sciences with a nationally recognized conservatory of music, both devoted exclusively to undergraduate education. Lawrence draws its 1,500 students from nearly every state and more than 50 countries.
articles.title: Foster named to Dean’s List at Lawrence University

ADVERTISE IN THE POST July 4th Barbecue Baskets a successful fundraiser By Sofia Prieto Black and Julia Banuelos This year the Piedmont Community Service Crew was faced with the cancelation of the annual Pancake Breakfast on the 4th of July, a fundraiser run by the crew for the past three years. After a lot of brainstorming, we came up with the Barbecue Basket idea, which started simply and then evolved into a carefully planned project. Through some hard work, lots of advertising, and direct emails to everyone we knew, we were able to successfully replace Piedmont’s traditional Pancake Breakfast fundraiser and turn it into a fun at-home holiday. Thanks to the generosity of Dave Larson at Piedmont Grocery. Keith Trimble at Village Market, and Lee Chin of Oakland Flower Mart, the teen coed crew was , and Oakland Flower Market, we were able to raise over $2,500. Not only was it a financial success, crew members received lots of positive feedback from their customers. All the proceeds will go toward supporting the crew’s philanthropic efforts, including some of our larger projects, such as working with Rebuilding Together Oakland and a project to build a second Tiny House for homeless teens. We were new PCSC members at the start of our freshman year and worked our way up to our current roles as VPs of fundraising. In May, we began talking about the big responsibility of creating fundraisers that would fit under the restrictions and limitations of COVID-19. Because of the pandemic, a lot of the physical work for the barbecue baskets had to be done by two people to minimize spread of the virus. In addition, publicizing the event and finding people who were interested in purchasing a basket was difficult as well. To solve this problem, we had to make many calls, write emails, post on different social media platforms and publish a lot in local newspapers. The plan did get messy, but even through spontaneous refrigerator malfunctions and unexpected summer plans, this fundraiser became a success. Ken Li, the crew’s advisor was very supportive and told us that our idea was “a perfect example of what [he] dreamed would happen more often–brand new crew members discovering the potential of PCSC and all it has to offer”. Keiko Hayashi, a crew parent, sent a message immediately after receiving her personally delivered barbecue basket. “Wow! We love our 4th of July Basket! You’ve done a tremendous job organizing and pulling these beautiful baskets together! We are so impressed with all of your careful labeling and instructions too.” Sofia Prieto Black holds a newly created Fourth of July Barbecue Basket, a fundraiser by the Piedmont Community Service Crew. Piedmont announces opposition to new FCC wireless facility rules City alleges new FCC rules would further limit local control of cell towers By Barry Eitel T h e P i e d m o n t Pl a n - ning Department released an announcement on Tuesday, July 21 outlining its opposition to new guidelines recently passed by the Federal Communications Commission that limit how local governments can regulate cell towers. “We believe there are ways for wireless communication devices to be deployed in an aesthetically appropriate manner,” Kevin Jackson, the Director of Planning and Building, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, the FCC seems intent on making that much more difficult, if not impossible.” The announcement came one day after Piedmont City Council voted to join a coalition of cities opposing the rules. On June 9, the FCC adopted a new ruling that altered how municipalities handle permits for wireless facilities. Specifically, the FCC modified Section 6409(a) of the Spectrum Act of 2012. The section requires cities like Piedmont to approve requests from wireless infrastructure companies to modify existing wireless towers and base stations if the physical dimensions do not undergo a “substantially change.” The new decision alters the meaning of “substantial change.” As long as a wireless infrastructure company follows FCC rules, cities cannot deny height or size increases of existing cell antennae even if the modifications would violate aesthetic conditions, such as vegetation screening or fencing requirements, that were initially imposed when the antennae were first approved. The FCC now allows antenna to be up to 20 feet tall and there is no height maximum for new antennae built outside the public right-of-way. Furthermore, the FCC allows that wireless infrastructure companies can install more equipment cabinets per request to make modifications to existing structures. The FCC also changed the definition of “concealment” in regard to wireless facility building requests so that concealment only means “stealth” design, meaning a cell tower that is meant to look like something else, like a tree. Under the order, cities requesting concealment of cell towers could not require screening by a rooftop or tree line. Additionally, timing requirements were altered by the FCC as part of the rule change. Cities must make decisions on wireless facility application within a standardized 60-day “shot clock” period. The new rules mean that the “shot clock” period starts earlier in the application process, when the applicants start the first procedural steps of submitting a proposal. This tightened timeline gives cities less opportunity to publicize and have public discussions about the applications. In response, Piedmont joined a coalition of cities, organized by law firm Best Best & Krieger (BBK), in opposition to the new FCC rules. Comments against the rule change must be filed by August 10. “Unless there is a court-ordered injunction, the new FCC rules will further reduce Piedmont’s ability to control the installation of wireless communication facilities,” Jackson continued. The action is the latest volley between Piedmont and the FCC over cell tower regulations, especially since Ajit Pai was appointed Chairman of the commission by President Trump in 2017. Publicly, the cell tower issue has been a major point of controversy in Piedmont for more than three years. In late 2016, wireless infrastructure builder Crown Castle submitted plans to build several small cell antennas around the City. After years of protest and legal battles, Council approved several of plans from the company last year as part of a settlement with Crown Castle. While the City has had wireless communication facility regulations on the books for decades, a recent push to expand next generation 5G wireless coverage nationwide has brought cell tower builders, cities and the federal government into conflict. In 2018 and 2019, the Council agreed to join organized coalitions in opposed to new FCC rules that make it harder for cities to regulate cell towers. Some of these FCC decisions are now awaiting decision from federal courts. The 2012 Spectrum Act was modified before in 2014 and the changes in June were passed 3-2 by the FCC. “The pandemic has highlighted the need for all Americans to have broadband connectivity as soon as possible,” Pai said after See FCC Rules on page 30

articles.text: In collaboration with the Oakland League of Women Voters (LWVP), the Piedmont League of Women Voters presented Part 2 of “New Models for Social Justice – Police Reform” on Monday, July 20 with guest speaker Anne Janks, Organizer at the Coalition for Police Accountability. Janks, a resident of Oakland for 25 years, has worked as a union organizer under varied labor laws. She has spent time with workers’ rights education, legislative campaigns, fundraising, website development, and social media advocacy. She began volunteering with the Coalition for Police Accountability in 2016 during the campaign for a ballot measure to create an independent community body to oversee the Oakland Police Department. The resulting Oakland Police Commission is the strongest independent oversight body in the country, with authority to write policy, independently investigate and discipline officers, and fire the police chief. Janks was introduced by LWVP member Lois Corrin. Janks described her involvement with the independent oversight body. In the midst of their campaign in 2016, the Oakland Police Department made national headlines, chronicling some Oakland officers’ involvements in trafficking an underage female. “It had the collateral effect of ensuring that we ended up with the strongest oversight body of a police agency anywhere in the country,” Janks said. One of the largest capabilities of the citizen-led commission is the ability to hire and fire officers and the police chief, which was demonstrated earlier this year. Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf fired former Oakland Police Chief Anne Kirkpatrick, acting on the recommendation of the Oakland Police Commission. “The only challenge about having the commission is that there is an ongoing struggle for resources and independence. There are certainly [citizens] within the city who want to undermine [the commission’s] ability to function independently,” Janks said. Janks then described anecdotes that she said proved a need for police reform and accountability. “There was an instance [in 2018] where our police officers had been called to a scene where a man was sleeping in between two houses, and there was a gun nearby. Over about 40 minutes, they couldn’t come up with a plan with what to do,” Janks said. The result in that encounter, Janks said, was that officers tried to wake up the man who became agitated, and then was shot to death by an officer. “Ad vo c a t e s f r o m t h e un-housed community who had known [the man] came to say they didn’t understand why this would happen,” she said. The result was an organized hearing on policing in the homeless community. It became overwhelming clear, Janks said, that most interactions between homeless community members and Oakland police officers were negative. MACRO, or mobile assistance community responders of Oakland, is a pilot program formed to combat social issues that may be better handled by community members than police officers. The pilot program is heralded by the Coalition for Police Accountability, which began pushing for the city to adopt a MACRO-like program since early 2019. Although nationwide calls for defunding the police have now become commonplace, the pilot program is really the product of years of grassroots research and advocacy, Janks said. “The structure of the pilot is that we will use people from the community as much as possible. Counselors will have some combination of doing similar outreach work, and provided training,” Janks said. After her presentation, Janks answered questions from viewers. You can watch the presentation on Yout ube at ht t p s://w w w.yout u b e.c om / watch?v=9oFnOxpP5zU. This was the second part of a two-part series on police reform hosted by the LWVP. Part one featured Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Deputy Attorney General Nancy Beninati.

articles.text: July is one of the best times to shop in Paris. SOLDES (Sales) literally merchandise promotion, and the sign streaks across every store’s front picture windows in town. Sunday especially brings out the shoppers, and the streets are full of people enjoying sunny weather and floating in and out of the shops with a collection of name-brand bags swinging from their arms. July is a busy month. It’s when world class brands – Karl Lagerfeld, Gucci, Prada, Bulgari, Calvin Klein, Hermès, Chanel, Lanvin – discount their creations. So do many other medium and modest class purveyors of goods all over Paris. The luxury stores are lovely, and an eye-opening to browse, but no one is shocked that even hefty discounts equate to affordability. In July, everyone in Paris is shopping. July Sales July and January are the legally ordained time of year for promotional discounts in France. The precise calendar dates are announced one year in advance. Couture and fashion-forward stores alike use the promotional sale (unsurprisingly) to push last season’s inventory out the door to make space for new arrivals. Discounts are printed on large signs splashing across the windows starting at 30-40% reductions. In a few weeks, new window signs will boast the second markdown (2 ème démarque jusqu’à -50%). A week later, the sales and discounts go deeper to 70-75% to sell off whatever is left. French clothing is expensive compared to clothes-shopping in the U.S. Most point out the VAT Soldes at Maje, where at least twenty of their stores pepper Paris neighborhoods, now advertising July’s second markdowns. On the right, a synthetic-knit from SCOTCH & SODA at €89 with 50% off to €44.50. Both are past-season garments, as I plan ahead for cooler weather in the fall.

Another factor appears to be the difference in volume of manufactured clothing; in the U.S., clothing manufacturing runs are enormous relative to France. I’ve also read that design work in France is a much more intense, lengthy process than what American designers churn out. French clothes are expensive, and the French buy fewer pieces, it appears. Confession: the July sale season has caught my fancy. For months of lockdown I’ve been lamenting my boredom with the same clothes. During the winter, I lacked a truly warm coat, one where I felt content enjoying a stroll across the ponts over the Seine. Instead of gazing at the moon, I was breaking into a trot to escape the chill. I simply refused to buy another coat. It’s not so odd really for someone having left the San Francisco Bay Area last September to arrive in Paris without a wool garment of any sort except for a cozy scarf. I had packed two large suitcases filled to the gills with clothes to cover four seasons: warm, cold, rainy, and dressy. Two holiday evenings qualified as dressy, and we haven’t yet had an actual formal affair. What else doesn’t rise to the occasion is a bit of a jumble. Sweatpants are bulky to store and seldom worn. My over-the-knee black leather boots Continued on next page The EU’s 20% VAT is circled on Galeries Lafayette store receipts. A traveler is eligible for tax rebate with minimum €175 purchase; but not for us: as Parisians, we are in the local economy.

Wednesday, July 29, 2020 11 In barely more than an hour of shirt shopping at Galleries Lafayette L’Homme on Boulevard Haussmann, Michael carries away the goods in an array of brands’ shopping bags. Clothes are expensive in Paris: a man’s cotton short-sleeved shirt priced at €145, now 70% off, but the last one and only in size Small. now feel clunky. The one blazer I packed is somehow wrong. Four pairs of one-inch heeled shoes get chewed to scrap-leather on the cobblestones as well as poke through the thin leather soles, so I stopped that nonsense. Shoes that do well under any conditions on Paris streets are flat rubber soles. These are not chic, and I bought two pairs of necessity. I did indeed pack well in the category of accessories, however: scarves, belts, and earrings to mix and match with any clothes. Scarves are a bright spot and magical for versatility, and so light to pack. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Scott Hill A team photo of the 1976 Piedmont football team, the only football team to win a NCS title. Last week, we published an article regarding Piedmont’s only football team to win the North Coast Section championship. With apologies, it contained a number of factual errors. The year was 1976, and legendary coach Bob Muenter had retired after 25 years as head coach to become the school’s Athletic Director, a position he held until 1983. Kevin McNair was named head coach of the powerhouse football program, and with Clark Ransom as his Defensive Coordinator, they became the best football team in the area, bar none. McNair’s team was undefeated and won the league title. It went on to win the North Coast Section championship in a two-game format, a 20-8 win over Salesian in the finals after defeating Sunset high of Hayward 14-7 in the semi-finals. Sunset closed its doors as a school in 1990. Piedmont’s Mike Humphries, for whom the current baseball field is named, was a scout coach for the football team in 1976. He recently described McNair as one of the most fiery coaches he has known. “He was so intense it was unbelievable,” said Humphries. “He had this red face that would just get redder; he looked like he was going to blow up. There’d be moments where Clark would have to call some offensive plays because Kevin had gotten so emotional,” he added. McNair, who also coached track & field at Piedmont, went on to coach Occidental College’s track and field program, and Ransom turned his focus on a career in real estate. Jeff Dreher, the namesake of the football teams perpetual Offensive Lineman award, was part of the team, as was Sports Hall of Fame fullback and linebacker Jeff Haile, then the league’s Player of the Year. Haile was also an All-League track and field athlete in shotput and to this day holds the school’s record in the event. He went on to play football and rugby for Stanford and was elected to the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2014. With video footage discovered on YouTube, you can witness Haile barreling through the line in games against Encinal, San Leandro, Miramonte, and Albany, as the Highlanders beat Sunset at Pacific Field in San Leandro, now Burrell Field. Humphries said the 20-8 championship win over Salesian came on a blustery night late that fall. “It was a stormy night with big winds,” he recalled. “In the fourth quarter, Salesian had the wind at their face, and we knew then we would win. I’ll never forget coming back to Piedmont on the bus and the lights were out in Oakland and tree limbs were down everywhere. It was a wild and crazy night.” Those Piedmont years were characterized by its stout defense and aggressive linemen, featuring Seth Bobbitt, Ken Chan, Scott Guel, and Kent Jordan, who briefly signed with the Raiders. Peter Craig was a running back, pairing in the backfield with Haile. Bob Brueckner was quarterback, and David Loomis the receiver. Watching the film of that team you can witness some Piedmont supporters in the small visiting stands with signs reading “Upset Sunset,” and classic cars along the fence line. After Piedmont’s only NCS championship, it took five years before they got to the semifinals, losing to 28-14 to San Lorenzo. Piedmont didn’t reach the NCS semifinals again until Scott Coats coached the 2014 program to a school-record 12-1 season and a WACC league title. Seeded No. 2, Piedmont was upset by No. 3 Justin-Siena 14-3 in the semi-finals. The 2016 team under James Holan also advanced to the NCS semi-finals, but lost to No. 1 Cardinal Newman.

articles.text: Photo by Robert Davis Nikolai Littleton set Piedmont High’s single season scoring record with 49 goals back in 2010. With the Premier League now over and Champions and Europa League on the docket, we take a look back to one of the Piedmont High boys’ all-time bests performances, the senior years of soccer player Nikolai Littleton, who set a school record with 49 goals. It was 10 years ago, and Piedmont High was coming off hallmark Bay Shore Athletic League championship seasons in 2007 and 2008 under coach Peter Hayton during Littleton’s freshman and sophomore years – both undefeated seasons. In 2009, Marques Dillard was hired to lead the team and coached them to another Bay Shore championship and Division 2 North Coast Section semifinals berth. At that time, NCS had only two soccer brackets. It’s now up to four with PHS in the smallschool Div. 4 bracket. Littleton and the team lit up scoreboards that season with a bundle of impressive shutouts and one-sided victories, including: 4-0 and 5-1 wins on St. Patrick, 9-0 and 10-2 against St. Joseph, 7-0 vs. Swett, and 4-0 against both Salesian and Encinal. Litttleton set a school record with the number of games in which he scored three goals. He closed his career at Witter Field with two goals against El Cerrito in the opening round of the NCS playoffs. The team was 12-3-1 in league and 16-5-3 overall. Littleton received a first-team All-League selection and briefly went on to play overseas in the U.K. before returning home. He’s now a wingback on the Oakland Roots pro soccer club and earned starting minutes before the season was shut down due to the coronavirus. “Littleton’s 49 goals led the East Bay. Albany’s Gabriel Borges was a distant second with 26 goals,” wrote the Post’s James Bucci in 2010. Also, on that team was Christian Smit, who received a firstteam all-league selection as a junior, and defender Ralston Louie with second-team honors. It seems that in 2010 with Littleton’s scoring record and departure from the school, the stature of the Piedmont boys’ program went with him. In the years to follow, there have been a number of coaches, including Rory O’Connor from 2012 until Todd Sullivan’s hire in 2016. Sullivan wound up hiring Littleton as his assistant coach at PHS, a decision that led to huge dividends. Coming full circle, Sullivan, Littleton, and the 2019 team won the school’s first league title since 2009 after going 9-0-1 in the Shoreline Division of the WACC. Photo by Robert Davis Christian Smit was a part of that team, a first-team All-League recipient. articles.text: Bay Area finalizes Levi Stadium bid for World Cup 2026 Photo courtesy of OaklandAs.com Baseball is back with cardboard cutouts of fans at the Oakland Coliseum. (At least they don’t leave peanut shells behind.) Since the start of the global pandemic, the fraternity of sport has seemingly gotten closer. The European soccer tables are finalized and, here in the states, baseball, basketball, and soccer are back. Here’s a rundown of the professional sports going on this summer. Major League Baseball Baseball, also known as The Great American Pastime, is back with a greatly reduced schedule of 60 games. For the Oakland A’s, there’s some optimism for a playoff berth as a Wildcard, with a solid lineup and a 3-1 start. However, for the Giants, even-year magic doesn’t look like it’ll be coming around in 2020 with AllStar Buster Posey opting out of the season. Some rule changes include a National League teams adopting the designated hitter role, teams will be given a runner on second to start extra innings in an attempt to shorten games, and no restrictions on position players pitching. National Basketball Association The NBA is back underway tomorrow, Thursday, July 30, picking up its season with an eight-regular season game model for 22 teams, excluding the last-place Golden State Warriors. Games are expected to run through August. All games are being played in Orlando, Florida. Major League Soccer Major League Soccer got back into action on July 8 and has concluded their Group Stage and Round of 16 matches. The San Jose Earthquakes have moved on to the quarterfinals. The Quakes will play Minnesota on August 1 at 8:00 p.m. All of the MLS’ games are also being played in Orlando, Florida at ESPN’s Wide World of Sports complex. Tennis For the tennis world, the ATP Tour is set to return on August 22-28 with the Western & Southern Open. But the big news is the first Grand Slam tournament since the Australian Open in January will be the U.S. Open in New York Starting August 31. It could mean the return of Mackenzie McDonald, former Piedmont tennis star. He made his return from hamstring surgery at the Australian Open, where he lost to Daniel Evans in five sets. McDonald last appeared in the Indian Wells tournament in March, where he won 6-0, 6-4 win over Blake Mott, but lost 7-5, 7-6 (6) to Japan’s Taro Daniel. Bay Area to bid for 2026 FIFA World Cup The Bay Area made its official pitch to finalize itself as one of the 10 hosting communities in the United States for the 2026 FIFA World Cup from North America. The co-hosts would be the U.S., Canada and Mexico. The Bay Area’s games would be held at the 49ers’ Levi’s Stadium, while the San Jose Earthquakes would provide grounds for a training facility at Avaya Stadium. “Levi’s Stadium was built to host the world’s biggest sports and entertainment events and there simply is no event larger than the FIFA World Cup,” said 49ers President Al Guido in a statement. “The San Francisco Bay Area is globally recognized as one of the world’s most popular destinations with a successful history of hosting epic events including the first FIFA World Cup in this country, the 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup, and two Super Bowls. This, along with being a global tech and innovation epicenter, makes us as qualified as any city to host this storied event.” For many soccer fans, they’ll be saying: “It’s about time” after the 2022 World Cup was unexpectedly awarded to Qatar. The 2022 World Cup in the Middle East will be the first time the events are played in winter months, given Qatar’s heat can swelter well over 100 degrees in the summer months.

articles.text: The 38th and final Premier League game was played on Championship Sunday, July 26, finalizing qualification for Champions League and Europa League by way of the table. But Monday, July 13’s ruling of Manchester City winning their appeal against UEFA’s two year ban from UEFA games (Champions and Europa) was perhaps the biggest news. It also reduces their $32.5 million fine to $11 million and notes no wrongdoing of Financial Fair Play rules, which are cost controls to mitigate the gap between bigger and smaller clubs. Back in February, UEFA ruled that City committed multiple violations related to club licensing by overstating its sponsorship revenue and break-even information from 2012-2016, while the organization failed to cooperate in the investigation. City’s ownership, the City Football Group, and the Court of Arbitrations cited that UEFA’s own rules prevent them from handing an immediate ban against their organization due to a five-year time limit for breach of Financial Fair Play rules, effectively barring an official investigation. It’s a massive win for City on a technicality. Some around the league, like Tottenham manager Jose Mourinho, had harsh words about the ruling: “If they are guilty, they should be banned. In any case, the decision is a disaster. If you are not guilty, you should not pay [an $11 million fine]. I am not saying Man. City is not guilty. I know money for them is easy, but it’s a principle. Even a pound. Why are you paying eight, nine million? It is a disgrace,” said Mourinho in his naturally brash style. Photo courtesy of Manchestercity.com Manchester City and manager Pep Guardiola have won their appeal against UEFA’s two-year ban from Champions League and Europa League. Final Table The Manchester City ruling means that the usual top-four in the Premier League table qualified for Champions League: Liverpool (99 points), City (81 points), Manchester United (66 points) and Chelsea (66 points). The Red Devils, as expected, catapulted above Leicester City (62 points) for a Champions League spot by defeating them 2-0 on Sunday, sending the Foxes down to a fifth place Europa League qualification spot. The difference between Champions League and Europa, you ask? Around €60 million from prize money alone; a max earning from UCL scored 2019 champions Liverpool €82.45 million. From UEL, Chelsea earned €21.34 million. With TV deals, advertising revenue, and ticket sales for Champions League added in there, the difference between the two is closer to €100 million. But for 2019 UCL runner up Tottenham (59 points), pushing into Europa with the sixth spot on the table should be taken as a huge win. They overtook the Wolves of Wolverhampton, who also finished with 59 points but had a worse goal differential with a 2-0 loss to Chelsea on Sunday. Their 1-1 draw with Crystal Palace was enough to get the job done for the Hotspur and new manager Mourinho, who took over the job in November from former manager Mauricio Pochettino with Tottenham near bottom of the table in 14th. Hotspur’s North London counterpart Arsenal did itself no favors on Tuesday, July 21 with a 1-0 loss to Aston Villa. The Gunners finished 8th, out of a Europa qualification spot and lowest it’s finished on the table in 25 years. But their hopes are not all forgotten. Arsenal and Chelsea square off in a London Derby for the FA Cup Trophy, which would automatically qualify the Gunners for Europa. As for Chelsea, they got bigger fish to fry. Champions and Europa League Finales With the Premier League gone, we’re onto the European tour of Champions and Europa League—where the top teams from England, Italy, Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, and even Greece, Turkey, Croatia, and Russia compete. Both leagues finished on the second leg’s games in the Round of 16. UCL returns Friday, August 7 with Cristiano Ronaldo, Paulo Dybala, and Juventus fighting from a 1-0 deficit against Lyon of France. Manchester City currently holds a 2-1 aggregate advantage over Real Madrid, where superstar Sergio Ramos will be unavailable due to a Red Card received on February 26’s first leg. Chelsea also plays German giant, Bayern Munich. Leo Messi and Barcelona are drawn 1-1 with Italy’s Napoli. UEL is back sooner on August 5, Manchester United are the hands-down favorites, up 5-0 over LASK of Austria from the first leg. Inter Milan of Serie A’s Italian league and the Wolves are two more teams to keep an eye on. The winner of Europa gets automatic qualification to next year’s Champions League. Photo courtesy of ManUnited.com Manchester United solidified a Champions League qualification spot by finishing 3rd. They have more matches to play in the Europa League Round of 16 starting August 5. Photo courtesy of tottenhamhotspur.com Tottenham manager Jose Mourinho and his coaching staff are all smiles after bringing the Hotspur from 14th to 6th after he was hired during the season in November.

14 Wednesday, July 29, 2020 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 13th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. WALTER TEITELBAUM Cross Country & Track Eduardo Calvo-Salinas, PHS Class of 2017, transferred from the University of Portland to Seattle Pacific University and is their starting midfielder. EDUARDO CALVO-SALINAS Soccer Piedmont High Class of 2017 Seattle Pacific University Class of 2021 Eduardo Calvo-Salinas joined the University of Portland’s Div. 1 soccer program coming out of Piedmont High in 2017 but transferred to Seattle Pacific University in 2019 as a sophomore and quickly entered the starting lineup as a midfielder. In 2019, Calvo-Salinas appeared in 16 games and started 12, scoring one goal and two assists while logging 1,170 minutes on the pitch. During his senior year at PHS, he earned first-team All-League honors for the 2016-2017 season under then first-year head coach Todd Sullivan and was the team’s leading scorer as a midfielder. What is your workout program this summer? I’ve made sure to stay fit by doing different types of workouts every day. My workouts include: - 5-8 mile runs to keep my cardio and fitness levels up. - Lifting weights for upper and lower body strength and other core, full body routines. - Doing technical drills to make sure my touch stays sharp. - Using the stationary bike at home, or going on rides with the mountain bike. I’ve also been playing pickup soccer at Stanford with some talented college players from around the area; even a couple of professional players joined us as well. What are your fitness goals for the summer? To stay as fit and sharp as possible while staying healthy to prevent any sort of injury. Lastly, I have been paying close attention to my nutrition and have been eating very healthy since the start of the pandemic. Nutrition is very important and can definitely help avoid injuries and boost performance. How are you measuring your development? By timing all of my runs and workouts. I am also gradually increasing the amount of weight I lift, the amount of distance I run, and the amount of time that my workouts last. I’ve also been tracking my sleep patterns and how that relates to my performance. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? On my own and with other college soccer players from around the area. However, I normally train with Nikolai Littleton, who I believe is the best certified trainer in the Bay Area and a talented wingback on the Oakland Roots pro team. He has helped my development tremendously ever since I got to Piedmont in 2014. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Being able to maintain consistent workouts every day since late-March. I’ve managed to stay fit and sharp throughout this whole process as a result of completing these daily routines while also being able to take care of my online summer courses, schoolwork, and work. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Never stop working on your crafts, to not make any excuses, to work extremely hard, be disciplined, fight for their dreams and goals, and always stay true to themselves. Hard work pays off. In these difficult times, it is important to stay positive and always believe in yourself. Walter Teitelbaum, PHS Class of 2018, is entering his junior year on the UC Santa Cruz cross country and track programs. He hopes to help the Banana Slugs reach the NCAA Div.3 National Championships for a secondconsecutive season. Piedmont High Class of 2018 UC Santa Cruz Class of 2022 Walter Teitelbaum graduated from Piedmont High in 2018 and is currently running for the UC Santa Cruz cross country and track programs, embarking on his junior campaign this fall. Teitelbaum was among his team’s top finishers in the 2019 Division III NCAA West Region Cross Country Championship, helping his school finished 3rd. He also competed with the Banana Slugs in the Division III NCAA Cross County Championships. He graduated from Piedmont High in 2018. He earned a firstteam All-League selection in 2017 after helping lead the PHS cross-country team to a berth in the State Championship. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I moved to Boulder, Colorado with my friend so I could train at altitude to improve my overall fitness while taking summer classes online because of the virus. My summer training has mostly been the following: Monday: Rest day or an easier 30-50 min run. Tuesday: 10min warmup jog; drills and speed development; 40-65 min training run Wednesday: Pre-Meet (20min jog, drills, strides); Aerobic Tempo (4-8 miles depending on assigned pace; Cooldown, 15-30min shakeout later in the day. Thursday: Mid-Week Long Run (60-80min). Friday: Pre-Meet (20min jog, drills, strides); 10-30 min Cooldown Saturday: Either Progression, 50-60 min cutting down every mile to about 5:30, or just a 50-75 min training run. Sunday: Long run day, 80-100 min. What are your fitness goals for this summer? This summer training plan has allowed me to do the work that I feel like my body can handle without feeling too tired in order to avoid the long term effects of burning out from overtraining. This summer I am gradually working up to about 70 miles per week, last summer I was at about 60, and the summer before that, 50. I am very proud of the success I have had by doing consistent summer running and I feel like it has made the biggest impact on my running ability as well as injury prevention. How are you measuring your development? By timing my results and measuring my weekly progress and energy output. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out on my own with athletic instruction and workouts from my coaches, David Klech and Shawn Gallup. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I was able to help score for my team all season and qualify us for the West Regional XC Championship, where I placed top 35 and earned all-region awards. We also reached the National XC Championship, where our men’s program placed 22nd overall. This last track season, as short as it was, I was able to run 15:30 in the 5k, 8:30 in the 3k, and 4:04 in the 1500m, way better than I ever would’ve imagined when in high school. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? My advice for anyone who is interested in getting into running would be to set goals for yourself and make it a habit to go out and run in the morning, despite how hard it is. Running is an accumulation of experience as well as fitness, and although it can take months or even years to see improvement, it becomes worth it when you realize the organization that it can bring to your life and the friends you will make along the way. For a high schooler who might be interested in running competitively in college, I couldn’t recommend choosing a Division III school more. Running at a D3 level has allowed me to continue to focus on my school and learning as my first priority without any compromise to my running. My teammates and coaches are my favorite humans on the planet and they help in all aspects of college life, whether it’s doing schoolwork, getting good sleep, eating right, or making the right decisions (things that are very difficult to do in college these days). BEN LEVINSON Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Ben Levinson is set to enter his senior year and has the potential to be among the baseball team’s strongest arms on the mound and a strong hitter. The Highlanders were 3-2 prior to the stoppage of play this spring Levinson was 1-1 with a team-leading nine strikeouts as a starting pitcher. As a batter, he carried a .400 average with six hits, four RBIs, and three runs scored. Levinson was named an Honorable Mention player of the year by the Post in his sophomore year in 2019 after he went 6-1 with 36 strikeouts in 49 innings of work and opened the season with a no-hitter against Head-Royce. What is your workout program this summer? I’ve been given workout plans from my brothers [Owen and Nate Levinson], who both play college baseball, and also getting instruction from coaches. For pitching, it’s really important to have strong legs so I’ve been focusing on strengthening my lower body. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goal is just to get stronger. Throwing harder will help pitching at the next level. How are you measuring your development? I’ve been throwing a lot of bullpens recently and tracking my velocity. I’ve been able to steadily increase my velocity, which is a good sign. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’ve mostly been working on my own but also work with pitching coach Steve Thobe, who has also helped me to get stronger and develop more as a pitcher. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Recently, I recorded my highest pitching velocity. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Find time whenever you can to put in work, whether that’s lifting weights, or skill-work for a specific sport. As you reach higher levels, the competition only gets harder. If you don’t work hard and aren’t motivated to get better in any way that you can, you might not get as far and be able to play as much as you would want to. Ben Levinson is entering his senior year at Piedmont High. After his junior year was canceled due to the coronavirus, Levinson has his eyes set on a big senior campaign.

Guidelines for hiking amidst the coronavirus include: • Start with research parking or trail restrictions. Plan your route. • Be mindful. Always bring a face cover of some sort. • The earlier the better. Trails are most trafficked past noon. • No large groups. The bike and pedestrian path opened in November of 2019 and to my surprise isn’t as popular as one would imagine. On a Friday at noon, I saw just seven bikers throughout the day, meaning I would go miles without passing another person. There were no groups, and just one man with his daughter and a few fishermen hanging around Point San Quentin. The path on the Richmond Bridge is 10-feet wide, giving ample space for hikers and bikers. The trail is not as developed as the similar Bay Bridge Trail, which has a guard rail and fair amount of space separating you from traffic. On the Richmond Bridge it’s just you, concrete barriers, and cars zooming by on I-80.
