articles.text: Maestro Michael Morgan with Oakland Symphony musicians at the November 2015 performance of the Third Symphony of Victor Bendix. Oakland Symphony is offering weekly, archival concerts featuring past performances, to be available online every Friday at 6 p.m. This week’s concert is Victor Bendix’s Symphony No. 3 in A Minor, Op. 25, originally premiered by the Symphony on November 13, 2015 at the Paramount Theatre. The selected music is from 1895. Bendix, who lived from 1851 to 1926, was the first composer played in the symphony’s “Lost Romantics” series. “Pieces from the romantic era have fallen out of the repertory for reasons that I couldn’t explain. Bendix was a Danish-Jewish composer, which could somewhat account for his music getting lost during the World War II period,” explained Maestro Michael Morgan. “This symphony is in three movements, full of melodic and harmonic inventiveness. I particularly call to your attention the second subject of the first movement about four minutes in. At that point, any doubts are cast aside and you are all in,” Morgan said. You can listen to this week’s archival concert at: https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/repast/.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony rePAST: Victor Bendix’s, Symphony No. 3

articles.text: Each week, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English invites playwrights to join him for a half-hour conversation about playwriting, inspiration, and the future of theatre. Playwright Luis Alfaro will join English for a discussion tomorrow, evening, Thursday, July 30, at 7 p.m. C u r r e n t l y t h e p l a y - wright-in-residence at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival in Ashland, he is an associate professor in the School of Dramatic Arts at the University of Southern California. He is the recipient of numerous awards, including the MacArthur Foundation Fellowship, and the 1998 National Hispanic Playwriting Competition Prize. In 2013, he began a three-year residency program with OSF in Ashland, Oregon through the National Playwright Residency Program. It is funded by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation. Playwright Luis Alfaro Alfaro’s plays and fiction are set in Los Angeles’ Chicano barrios, including the Pico Union district, and often feature LGBTQ+ and working-class themes. His most noted plays include “Bitter Homes and Gardens,” “Pico Union,” “No Holds Barrios,” and “Black Butterfly.” Many of his plays have also been published as stories or poetry. You can watch the fireside chat live at 7 p.m. on Youtube. Visit https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=eux5IToFDaI&feature=youtu.be.

articles.text: Kip Cranna, Dramaturg Emeritus of San Francisco Opera. San Francisco Opera is offering “Opera Aficionado”, an educational, interactive lecture series that gives opera-goers around the world front-row seats to scholarly discussions. The theme on Sunday, August 2, at 1 p.m. is “Social Themes in Opera: Past and Present,” and the first lecture series of the month will focus on operas about liberation. The guest speaker is Dramaturg Emeritus of San Francisco Opera, Dr. Clifford “Kip” Cranna. Cranna has served on the staff for 40 years and was Director of Music Administration for over 30 years. In 2008, he was awarded the San Francisco Opera Medal, the company’s highest honor, and in 2012 he received the Bernard Osher Cultural Award. The lecture will focus on ideas about liberty and freedom from oppression that have inspired opera composers through the centuries. Cranna will take viewers on a video journey, exploring the many varied ways that operas have expressed in drama and song the basic human aspiration of freedom. To register, visit https://sfopera.com/discover-opera/education/community-programs/ aficionado/. GET UP TO

articles.text: Pianist Eric Zivian The Valley of the Moon Music Festival, which this year is online, will conclude its series of concerts this Sunday, August 2. You can tune in at 4 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday, through August 2 for a total of six concerts. Patrons can livechat on YouTube with musicians and lecturers during the concert, and join afterwards for a Zoom reception. If you miss the 4 p.m. livestream, you can still watch videos of the virtual festival, made available on valleyofthemoonmusicfestival.org. Saturday, August 1 will feature Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 24 in F-sharp major, Op. 78 (a Therese), and Cello Sonata No.2 in G minor, Op. 5, No. 2. Musicians featured on Saturday include festival founders Tanya Tomkins (cello) and Eric Zivian (piano), and guest artist, pianist Audrey Vardanega, founder of Musaics By the Bay in San Francisco. The closing concert, on Sunday, will feature Beethoven’s Violin Sonata No. 4 in A minor, Op. 23, and Piano Trio in E-flat major, Op.70, No.2. Sunday’s featured musicians include Francisco Fullana (violin), Tomkins, Zivian and Vardanega. Cellist Tanya Tomkins Bob Taylor, of Sonoma TV, filmed the July 19 and 25 concerts in the restored ruins of Issac DeTurk’s 1863 winery at Yulupa Ranch in Bennett Valley. Sonoma TV will also be re-broadcasting the Valley of the Moon Music Festival, with a schedule to be announced soon. Festival musicians and scholars in the festival’s Blattner Lecture Series will introduce each concert and provide commentary. Speakers include Nicholas Mathew, author of Political Beethoven and associate professor in the Department of Music at UC Berkeley, Nicholas McGegan, former Artistic Director at Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra, and Kate van Orden, Harvard University’s Dwight P. Robinson, Jr. Professor of Music. “Conversations with Kate” will be repeated at 3 p.m. on August 2, in which van Orden leads a fascinating conversation with musicologists and cellist Elaine Fitz Gibbon, about Mauricio Kagel’s film Ludwig van: A Report. All musicians originally contracted for the 2020 festival have received 50 percent of their fee. You can view the full program at htt ps://valleyofth e m o o n m u sicfe s t iv a l .o r g / beethoven-festival-2020/. articles.text: Oakland Symphony musicians and directors have released their own personal Pandora playlists during the months of shelter-in-place. The most recent director to release a playlist is Chorus Director Dr. Lynne Morrow. Morrow became Director of the Oakland Symphony Chorus in 2005. During her tenure the scope of the Chorus has expanded to include contemporary, international, and neglected works, along with traditional choral repertoire. She conducts the Chorus’ workshop performances of major works; hosts summer choral outreach “Sing-ins;” and prepares the Chorus for work with Oakland Symphony. “I have sung or conducted all of this music. The process for choosing the list was to think back to music that gave me chills or great joy when I remembered performing them. The music is often heartbreaking or soulful. The characters are always searching, deeply within, or out into the universe. The text is always clearly sung and intentional,” Morrow said. articles.text: Melanie Laurent and Ewan McGregor star in Beginners. Movie review by Chris Honoré There is a line in Beginners, spoken by Oliver (Ewan McGregor), thirty-something, reflecting on the recent death of his father, Hal (Christopher Plummer): “My personality was created by someone else and all I got was this stupid T-shirt.” And therein is the essence of this wonderfully insightful, poignant and uplifting film. Any attempt to sort out our personalities, such as they are, and the connection to our families of our values and quirks and subtle dysfunctions, is likely a lifelong endeavor. In a sense we all get a T-shirt, at some point, worn with joy and resentment and surrendering delight. Everything about families is like a Chinese puzzle, that tube into which you stick your forefingers, one at each end, and when you begin to pull them out, the tube tightens, failing to release. To be free, if freedom is the goal, then you must do what is contraindicated. Oliver has recently lost his mother, Georgia (Mary Page Keller), to cancer. Months after her death, Hal decides, with flair and abandon, to declare that he is gay and always has been, a fact that catches Oliver completely by surprise. He had always assumed his parents loved each other but just weren’t in love. Hal’s new life inspires him, and he embraces fully his honesty and his new friends, to include a younger lover, Andy (Goren Visnjic). Hal says to Oliver, with kindness and conviction, when questioned about his coming out, “I don’t want to be theoretically gay.” From a distance, Oliver watches in wonder and amazement, leavened with love. But then, this is a film about love, about elusive, contradictory, ever-present affection, about old baggage that is packed and unpacked through a series of insightful flashbacks, beginning when Oliver’s parents marry in the 1950s. The backstory is conveyed seamlessly using old photographs and small vignettes that are filled with humor both winsome and mysterious. But then Beginners is replete with riptides of emotions, never framed by resentment or anger, but by a will to understand and accept – and always touched by regret. But then regret is an emotion that can stalk us like a dim shadow, a reminder of what could have been. Oliver’s understanding of love, as wondrous and harrowing as it can be, is challenged when, at a costume party, he meets Anna (Melanie Laurent), a lovely, enigmatic young French actress. Not only is this a love story about father and son, but about two newly met people, in their own way a bit damaged, both moving inextricably toward one another. Beginners is astonishingly well cast and acted. Christopher Plummer, as Hal, is a treasure. And Ewan McGregor, who carries the film’s point of view, is perfect. As is Melanie Laurent. All deliver understated but emotive performances that take the film to its poignant and hopeful conclusion. As an aside, Hal’s Jack Russell terrier, Arthur, who is telepathic (don’t ask, but know that it works, with subtitles, and is delightful), chews up every scene that he’s in. Beginners. Starring Ewan McGregor, Christopher Plummer, Melanie Laurent, Goren Visnjic and Mary Page Keller. Written and directed by Mike Mills. Rated R. Originally printed in the Post on July 13, 2011. Christopher Plummer and Ewan McGregor in a scene from Beginners.
articles.title: Beginners a lovely film about love

articles.text: Spielberg directs, Coen brothers write a winning film Movie review by Chris Honoré In retrospect, the Soviet Union and the United States managed to navigate almost 50 years of adversarial encounters without a confrontation that would have taken us past the brink of the deterrence known as mutual assured destruction (aka MAD). Part of the kabuki dance that the two superpowers engaged in, however, was elaborate and sustained spying. Steven Spielberg’s Bridge of Spies, is a taut, well-made film based on a true story. It begins in 1957 with the arrest by the FBI of a Soviet spy, Rudolf Abel (Mark Ryance). The government, certain it has overwhelming evidence of his clandestine activity, decides to put him on trial. James Donovan (Tom Hanks), an insurance attorney, is selected to defend Abel who has stoically resisted all attempts by the CIA to extract information from him. What the government does not anticipate is that Donovan decides to mount a rigorous defense on Abel’s behalf, followed by an appeal of his conviction. Donovan is denigrated for carrying out what he felt was his constitutional obligation. He also suggests to the trial judge that Abel not be given the death penalty, arguing that should one of our spies be captured, we just might need Abel should there be a proffered swap. And that’s the protracted set streets are awash in institutional blues and grays. Donovan, suffering from a tenacious cold, walks ever closer to a precipice, lost in a world of duplicity and obscure signals. He never knows if he is in discussion with the decisionmakers or straw men. All that has occurred, from 1957 to 1962, leads to that intersection on a bridge which divides East from West. The outcome is always in doubt, the distrust between the players palpable. Tom Hanks gives a nuanced and spot-on performance, his portrayal likely to earn him a nomination when the awards season takes hold. Ditto the movie. And do not forget Mark Ryance, an accomplished stage actor, as Abel. His character is laconic in the extreme while laced with a humor so dry that it crackles. He is superb in scene stealing. As is this very entertaining film. Bridge of Spies. Starring Tom Hanks, Mark Ryance and Amy Ryan. Directed by Steven Spielberg. 2 hrs., 15 min. Rated PG-13. Originally printed in the Post on October 21, 2015. up. But Bridge of Spies, written by the Coen brothers, Joel and Ethan, is a remarkable two-act story. Act one is the Abel capture and trial. Act two involves Donovan’s prescient statement about a possible trade at some point in the future: our guy for your guy. Our guy, as it turns out, is Francis Gary Powers, the U2 spy plane pilot, shot down in 1960 by the Russians. What could go wrong does go wrong and he’s captured and put on trial. The Soviets now have their spy. This is wonderful, spare, retro moviemaking, delivered as only Spielberg can. Act two is launched. Donovan is selected to negotiate the exchange and arrives in East Germany just after the Berlin wall has been built (1961). He has been given the task of talking to the Soviets and the East Germans about how to achieve a grudgingly agreed upon trade. It’s winter, the skies are leaden, East German buildings and Tom Hanks in a scene from the new Spielberg film Bridge of Spies.
articles.title: Bridge of Spies displays fine craft of filmmaking

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré If there are tweens or early teens somewhere in the house, don’t hesitate to make the case that Dolphin Tale is a family movie way worth seeing. The youngsters will relish every minute. It is sweet, moving, with just enough high-risk high-gain drama to keep the young audience on the edge of their seats. The film is based on the true story of Winter, a young dolphin that became entangled in a crab fisherman’s lines and was washed up on the Gulf Coast, near Clearwater, Florida. Seriously injured, she is nursed back to health by the staff at the Clearwater Marine Aquarium. And so the story begins. Sawyer Nelson (Nathan Gamble), abandoned by his father some years before, resisting spending his summer enrolled in summer school, discovers the bleeding dolphin on the beach and cuts her loose from the entangling ropes. And in that moment he and Winter bond, changing his life forever. Drawn to the aquarium, he soon discovers a world where people are dedicated to rescuing and caring for marine mammals so they can eventually be released back into the environment. And it is at the Clearwater Aquarium that he meets young Hazel Haskett (Cozi Zuehlsdorff); her father, the lead marine biologist, Dr. Clay Haskett (Harry Connick); and Reed Haskett (Kris Kirstofferson), Clay’s father. But most importantly, he finds Winter, struggling to survive. With regret, Dr. Haskett makes the decision to surgically remove Winter’s tail in order to save her life. How Winter’s life is changed parallels the changes brought about in the life of Sawyer, his family, and everyone at the Aquarium. All are transformed and in some way rescued in a wonderful, uplifting way. The movie’s embedded message: “Family is forever.” Nice. Dophin Tale is a family movie not to be missed. Dolphin Tale. Starring Nathan Gamble, Harry Connick, Ashley Judd, Cozi Zuehlsdorff, Kris Kristofferson and Morgan Freeman. Directed by Charles Martin Smith. Rated PG. Originally printed in the Post on September 28, 2011. Nathan Gamble with a dolphin in a scene from Dolphin Tale.
articles.title: Dolphin Tale – families are forever

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré A Monster Calls is extraordinary and a heartfelt surprise. But take seriously its rating of PG-¡3. While the trailer seems to promise a child’s tale, involving an enormous monster in the humanoid shape of a gnarly yew tree, this British film is so much more. There is not a hint of Disney to be found, and the narrative goes far beyond the familiar palliative, “happily ever after.” At the film’s center is 12-yearold Conor (Lewis MacDougall) who is in a place in his young life that is almost more than he can bear. He is relentlessly bullied at school, haunted by a traumatic nightmare that causes him to wake in the deep of night, and coping with the life-threatening cancer that is consuming his mother (Felicity Jones). He is also unable to turn to his rigid and distant grandmother (Sigourney Weaver). His father (Toby Kebbell) has been, for most of his life, absent, living in America and though he arrives briefly due to his ex-wife’s illness, he offers little comfort to Conor. And then one night, as he sits in his room sketching in his notebook, strange things begin to happen, a pencil rolls across his desk, onto the floor. Things begin to move. And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him. He tells the boy that he will return and tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to believe yet boldly resistant to what cannot be. And so, just after midnight, the monster appears to share with Conor a fable that is gorgeously animated in watercolors (which are thematic throughout the film). The stories are puzzling, seemingly unrelated, and at first beyond Conor’s comprehension. And, as the monster points out, each is contradictory; they are not what they seem. Meanwhile, Conor goes to school and deals with the bullies and attempts to cope with the reality that his mother is slipping away from him and there is nothing he can do. Together the two of them cling to hope: his, that she will live and that each new treatment will be a cure; hers, that she can prepare her son for his life without her. Deeply conflicted, he rages against the punishment inflicted by his mother’s cancer, his anger uncontrollable, his helplessness ever with him. A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative, and it never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. While it could have dropped into a well of melodrama, instead it grasps life and looks at both the darkness and light and searches for a truth that is often absent from such stories. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book of the same title written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. Starring Lewis MacDougall, Felicity Jones and the voice of Liam Neeson. Directed by J.A. Bayona. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Originally printed in the Post on January 11, 2017.
articles.title: A Monster Calls – a beautiful children’s allegory from England

articles.text: Ghibili Studios, the much-revered Japanese producer of anime classics, has long depended on home video sales and avoided digital platforms, insisting they A scene from Studio Ghibil’s Spirited Away were anathema to its philosophy of care and mindfulness. But now tucked into HBO Max’s platform of some 10,000 hours of programing is a gem of a film list from Ghibili Studio, which has garnered accolades and critical praise in its 35-year history. Founded in 1985 by filmmakers Hayao Miyazaki, Isao Takahata, and Toshio Suzuki, the studio has made 21 animated feature films, earned five Oscar nominations and one statuette for Miyazaki’s Spirited Away, reported to be Japan’s highest-grossing film. The studio has long been the recipient of almost cult-like adoration. For decades collectors have been in the hunt for DVD releases. Known worldwide, Ghibili Studios,has been a tourist attraction in Mitaka, Japan, since opening in 2001, similar to PIXAR in the U.S. Now their elusive titles can be found in one place, HBO Max, a mass-market mainstream where 21 of the Studio’s classics and lesser-known anime favorites can be found. It comprises an extraordinary catalog of complex, beautifully written and illustrated stories. For access, simply Google HBO Max and you will be guided through multiple options, depending on personal preferences. Since the list can seem overwhelming, The Post will run recommendations weekly, beginning with the classics, each with brief annotations. dio Ghibil’s imaginative redefiSpirited Away — one of Studio Ghibil’s animated film nition of animation, we suggest starting with Spirited Away – considered essential viewing. It’s about a young girl, Chihiro, who stumbles into a dark spirit world and searches for a way out. Filled with fantastical creatures, strange demons, and a powerful sorceress who looms over them all, it is considered one of Miyazaki’s most thrilling and immersive films.
articles.title: Welcome to the animated world of Studio Ghibil

A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative, and it never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. While it could have dropped into a well of melodrama, instead it grasps life and looks at both the darkness and light and searches for a truth that is often absent from such stories. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book of the same title written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. By Chris Honoré Ghibili Studios, the much-revered Japanese producer of anime classics, has long depended on home video sales and avoided digital platforms, insisting they A scene from Studio Ghibil’s Spirited Away Welcome to the animated world of Studio Ghibil were anathema to its philosophy of care and mindfulness. But now tucked into HBO Max’s platform of some 10,000 hours of programing is a gem of a film list from Ghibili Studio, which has garnered accolades and critical praise in its 35-year history. Founded in 1985 by filmmakers Hayao Miyazaki, Isao Takahata, and Toshio Suzuki, the studio has made 21 animated feature films, earned five Oscar nominations and one statuette for Miyazaki’s Spirited Away, reported to be Japan’s highest-grossing film. The studio has long been the recipient of almost cult-like adoration. For decades collectors have been in the hunt for DVD releases. Known worldwide, Ghibili Studios,has been a tourist attraction in Mitaka, Japan, since opening in 2001, similar to PIXAR in the U.S. Now their elusive titles can be found in one place, HBO Max, a mass-market mainstream where 21 of the Studio’s classics and lesser-known anime favorites can be found. It comprises an extraordinary catalog of complex, beautifully written and illustrated stories. For access, simply Google HBO Max and you will be guided through multiple options, depending on personal preferences. Since the list can seem overwhelming, The Post will run recommendations weekly, beginning with the classics, each with brief annotations. It’s about a young girl, Chihiro, who stumbles into a dark spirit world and searches for a way out. Filled with fantastical creatures, strange demons, and a powerful sorceress who looms over them all, it is considered one of Miyazaki’s most thrilling and immersive films.

articles.text: French-Romany guitarist Django Reinhardt who overcame an injury to his hand early in life to create what is now known as gypsy jazz. The news media is full of stories of “Bad Guys”. With the exception of the Piedmont Post, they all tell us “that’s what sells the news”. These days, we need as much inspiration as we can get. The annals of history are loaded with the names of “Tough Guys”. Let’s forget those who push women around and pick on puny guys. Let’s take a look at those who turn adversity into victory. Our first example is violin virtuoso Maud Powell (1867- 1920). Why? First, she was a woman. Sure, history acclaims the cigar-chomping, pants-wearing George Sand; she who flung society’s norms in their faces. But Maude Powell came from a very cultured American family. The most damning thing about her was that she was American, something that was a huge impediment. at the time. The bias against American musicians was what we used to refer to as “an international conspiracy”. But she became America’s first great violinist and popular with the masses, I might add. At the opposite side of the spectrum was Ray Charles. Blindness was only one of his obstacles. And what a success he was. Crossing racial, societal and musical barriers, he earnied entry into the musical pantheon. Next, we need to mention three one-armed pianists. Count Geza Zichy (1849-1924) is the first on record. He was a Hungarian nobleman who lost his right hand in a hunting accident. Undaunted, he established himself as one of the most important pianists of the 19th century. He inspired composers to write lefthand pieces for him. So did another nobleman, Paul von Wittgenstein (1887- 1961). He was already an established concert pianist when drafted into the Austrian army in WWI. His right arm was shot off and he was imprisoned in Siberia. Also undeterred, he re-established his career and commissionied a whole library of left-hand compositions. Ravel’s piano concerto for the left hand is a famous example. These days, we are thankful for the one-handed pianist Nicholas McCarthy. Unlike those other pianists, McCarthy was born without a right hand, but chose to pursue a career as a pianist. Look him up. He is an inspiration. Michael Tilson Thomas is also noteworthy for his toughness. I was with him backstage before a concert. He fell down and broke his right wrist. I pushed him onto the stage where he played a brilliant concert at the piano. That’s toughness. Jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt also overcame a disfiguring injury. The son of a gypsy family in Romany, he suffered severe burns in a fire at the gypsy camp and lost the use of two fingers. Again, undeterred, he firecely pursued his love of playing the guitar and became world famous for his “three-fingered-lightning” and his merging of Slavic and jazz harmonics. Austrian violinist Rudolf Kolisch (1896-1978) overcame a childhood injury to his left hand, and learned to play the violin as a lefty. And now we have the international catastrophe of the coronavirus. Many segments of society are coming unglued. At the same time, many people have found ways to make considerable advancement. Viennese violinist Thomas Christian was in the hospital undergoing foot surgery. While hospitalized he still managed to practice his violin 6 to 7 hours every day. Somehow he also found time to compose cadenzas for the Beethoven violin concerto. And Hungarian violinist Antal Zalai continues to put up more videos than any violinist I can think of. So, as you can see, we have choices. We can find every excuse under the sun or use the time to our best advantage. The decision is ours.
articles.title: Overcoming adversity: Where do we go from here?

articles.text: Bonita Avenue School was Piedmont’s first public school, built in 1909 and designed by Albert Farr. uary 30, 1907. The first order of business was to build a city hall and a school. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had 8 classrooms for 8 teachers who taught 8 grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The fires and smoke were visible for days from the Piedmont hills as over 15,000 lost their homes in the fire. As Oakland looked to the hills to annex more land for this influx of earthquake survivors, a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents did not want Piedmont to become part of Oakland. Hugh Craig and James Ballentine immediately began an effort to incorporate Piedmont as a city. They quickly drew up a map of Piedmont’s borders using an existing Piedmont Sanitary District map and filed the map in Sacramento. On January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate. The vote passed, and Piedmont officially became a municipality four days later, JanA photo from 1926 shows Ellen Driscoll, then the principal of Havens School, with her students. Bonita Avenue School was Piedmont’s first public school, built in 1909 and designed by Albert Farr. uary 30, 1907. The first order of business was to build a city hall and a school. While the Board of Trustees debated the location of City Hall (some wanted it on Highland Avenue), plans progressed for Piedmont’s first public school. The Bonita Avenue School was built in 1909. It had 8 classrooms for 8 teachers who taught 8 grades and 318 students. The Lake School (now the Egbert W. Beach School) on Lake Avenue) was built three years later to provide more classrooms for students. The first school was built on the east side of Bonita Avenue between Oakland and Vista Avenues, hence the name, Bonita Avenue School. When Frank C. Havens died in 1918, the school was renamed in his memory. Albert Farr designed the school in the Spanish Colonial or Spanish Mission design that he would use the following year for Piedmont’s City Hall and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. The school had two large, square Spanish towers with shallow balconies and ornate cupolas on each side of the main building. Classroom wings on each side extended to the front and rear, making the building an H-shape with the school’s entry set between the two wings. Large arched windows flanked the arched entry, and Mission tile covered the roofs and capped the walls to the courtyard entry. Clara Crumpton was the first principal of the Bonita Avenue School and taught first grade. On the occasion of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco in 1915, Miss Crumpton had her students recreate the “Tower of Jewels” in front of the school. In 1910 Ellen Driscoll began teaching at the school, and became principal of Havens School from 1920 to 1940. She was a popular teacher and was known for her keen memory as a principal. She knew the names of each of her 300 students. The 1947 photo shows the school with its courtyard and classroom wings. The long, rectangular building at the rear is a 5-classroom addition completed in 1937 by the Federal government as a Work Projects Administration project. In 1940 the Board of Education contracted again with the WPA to build auditoriums for what by then were three elementary schools. The auditorium at Havens was dedicated as the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. Hand-painted panels in the ceiling of all three school auditoriums were executed by 5th and 6th grade students in a paintby-number fashion. At the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, they depict California history. In 1953, the Piedmont Board of Education considered the 1909 Havens School to be inadequate to meet the school enrollment at the time. The number of students had grown to the point where some classrooms were in temporary buildings. A bond issue was passed, and the new Frank C. Havens School, designed by nationally recognized architects Miller-Warnecke, was completed in 1955 with 12 classrooms, a library, an administration office and cafeteria. By 2010 the sleek modern design of 1955 was considered an earthquake hazard and was replaced by the current Frank C. Havens School, designed by Mark Becker. articles.text: About six years ago I was on a wine trip to the Rhone River region of France. My friend Terry Hershey and I had several appointments each day at wineries to taste the wines and write up notes for the article I would be completing back home. The wine tasting experience in France is very different than what has developed here in California. You need to have an appointment, they never charge money, they will pour every wine they make and talk endlessly about them and show you every tank and barrel. We planned on (and needed) a couple of hours per winery. They treated us as honored guests. (This is true even if you are not a wine writer. It is the appointment that does the trick.) Except on Sunday. Disregard everything I wrote above if it is a Sunday. On Sunday you are supposed to be having a 4-hour lunch with your family and drinking wine. If you own a business and it is open, there is something wrong with you. (Except the boulangeries, which are open till noon.) So, on a Sunday afternoon in January, Terry and I were driving the small scenic roads between Chateauneuf du Pape and Gigondas, admiring the nearby jagged toothlike mountains called the Dentelles du Montmirail. We come across a sign for a winery called Notre Dame des Pallieres to which was attached a small sign saying “Ouvert” (open). What? You’re kidding! We headed down the dirt driveway and discovered a charming, small winery that was indeed… open. The owner, Claude Roux, greeted us and began a generous tasting of all 12 or so of his wines. Then came some earlier vintages for comparison and to see how they age. I asked if the wines were available in the U.S. “Yes,” he said. “We have an importer based in a town in California called Richmond.” “Wow, that’s next door to the town I live in,” I told him. And thus began my introduction to wine importer Grape Expectations in Richmond. When I got home I got acquainted with Grape Expectations founder Mike Apple and started exploring their portfolio. They import wines from almost everywhere – South America, Australia and New Zealand, Spain and Italy – but it was their French portfolio that intrigued me. They have hand-selected small, high quality growers in Languedoc, Provence, Rhone Valley, Loire Valley, Burgundy, Bordeaux and Alsace – previously overlooked, and have brought them to the U.S. market.
articles.title: Grape Expectations – a hidden gem in Richmond

articles.text: Photos by Deborah Quok There is no shortage of good ideas and good recipes in cookbooks, both old and new. So here we are in the midst of a health crisis – the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020. Everyone has been told to shelter-in-place, meaning stay at home. But what do we suddenly do to occupy ourselves 24/7? Spend more time cooking – baking in particular. Cooking and baking were destined to be a part of my DNA. I was raised in a food-centric family, growing up next door to our family’s neighborhood grocery, with our restaurant just a few miles away. I began cooking at a young age. Before I was a teenager, I was reading cookbooks and experimenting – mostly with baking projects as everyone in my family has a Huge. Sweet. Tooth. Even then I recognized that baking was a precise undertaking to achieve desired results. My early interest in cooking and cookbooks has become my fiercest hobby. My bookshelves and tabletops are stacked high. I read them for many reasons and sometimes I even cook or bake from them! There is considerable baking happening these days as we’re sheltering-in-place with time to prepare homemade treats. If you’ve not previously been much of a baker, now is as good a time as any to get into the kitchen and start practicing. Baking from scratch need not be intimidating. There are a few principles to follow that help towards a successful finish. 1. Read through the recipe – in its entirety. Several times if needed. You must understand the list and amounts of ingredients as well as understand the directions. Some recipes are very clear and step-by-step. Others are not as clear, for example combining total amounts of an ingredient in the list, only to later describe how they should have been divided for adding at different times in the process. (This after you’ve used the full amount in Step 1, which may or may not be a recoverable error.) 2. Set out all the ingredients and measure them in advance to ensure you don’t overlook any ingredients and have accurate amounts. The French call this mis en place or “putting in place”. This practice is commonly seen on many cooking shows, so has become very mainstream. 3. Follow the directions! Especially if you’re new to baking, take the time to understand and follow the directions closely. Even slight adjustments to ratios of flour or sugar to fat, or dry to

Even then I recognized that baking was a precise undertaking to achieve desired results. My early interest in cooking and cookbooks has become my fiercest hobby. My bookshelves and tabletops are stacked high. I read them for many reasons and sometimes I even cook or bake from them! There is considerable baking happening these days as we’re sheltering-in-place with time to prepare homemade treats. If you’ve not previously been much of a baker, now is as good a time as any to get into the kitchen and start practicing. Baking from scratch need not be intimidating. There are a few principles to follow that help towards a successful finish. 1. Read through the recipe – in its entirety. Several times if needed. You must understand the list and amounts of ingredients as well as understand the directions. Some recipes are very clear and step-by-step. Others are not as clear, for example combining total amounts of an ingredient in the list, only to later describe how they should have been divided for adding at different times in the process. (This after you’ve used the full amount in Step 1, which may or may not be a recoverable error.) 2. Set out all the ingredients and measure them in advance to ensure you don’t overlook any ingredients and have accurate amounts. The French call this mis en place or “putting in place”. This practice is commonly seen on many cooking shows, so has become very mainstream. 3. Follow the directions! Especially if you’re new to baking, take the time to understand and follow the directions closely. articles.text: • The American Red Cross strongly urges healthy, eligible individuals who are feeling well to give blood or platelets to help maintain a sufficient blood supply and prevent shortages as concerns about the outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019, or COVID-19, rise in the U.S. Cold and f lu season has already impacted the nation’s ability to maintain its blood supply. As the number of coronavirus cases grows in the U.S., the number of people eligible to give blood for patients in need could decrease further. “We’re asking people to help keep the blood supply stable during this challenging time. As communities across the country prepare for this public health emergency, it’s critical that plans include a readily available blood supply for hospital patients,” said Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Blood Services. “As fears of coronavirus rise, low donor participation could harm blood availability at hospitals, and the last thing a patient should worry about is whether lifesaving blood will be on the shelf when they need it most.” Make an appointment to donate blood now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or calling the Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 510-658-6456. Donating blood is a safe process and people should not hesitate to give or receive blood. There are no data or evidence that this coronavirus can be transmissible by blood transfusion, and there have been no reported cases worldwide of transmissions for any respiratory virus, including this coronavirus, from a transfusion. The Red Cross only collects blood from individuals who are healthy and feeling well at the time of donation – and who meet other eligibility requirements, available at RedCrossBlood.org. At each blood drive and donation center, Red Cross employees follow thorough safety protocols including wearing gloves, routinely wiping down donortouched areas, using sterile collection sets for every donation, and preparing the arm for donation with an aseptic scrub. These mitigation measures will help ensure blood recipient safety, as well as staff and donor safety in reducing contact with those who may potentially have this respiratory infection. The Red Cross has implemented new blood donation deferrals out of an abundance of caution. Individuals are asked to postpone their donation for 28 days following: • Travel to China and its special administrative regions, Hong Kong and Macau, as well as Iran, Italy and South Korea; Diagnosis of COVID-19, contact with a person who has or is suspected to have the virus. As the situation evolves, the Red Cross will continue to evaluate all emerging risks in collaboration with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and industry partners to determine if additional intervention strategies are needed. Together, we stand ready to keep the American public informed and prepared. Blood donation process A blood donation takes about an hour from start to finish, but the actual donation itself only takes about 8-10 minutes. Donors can also save up to 15 minutes at the blood drive by completing a RapidPass®. With RapidPass®, donors complete the pre-donation reading and health history questionnaire online, on the day of donation, from a mobile device or computer. To complete a RapidPass®, follow the instructions at RedCrossBlood.org/RapidPass or use the Red Cross Blood Donor App. To donate blood, individuals need to bring a blood donor card or driver’s license or two other forms of identification that are required at check-in. Individuals who are 17 years of age in most states (16 with parental consent where allowed by state law), weigh at least 110 pounds and are in generally good health may be eligible to donate blood. High school students and other donors 18 years of age and younger also must meet certain height and weight requirements. Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue. Call 510-547-6456 for hours.

articles.text: Terry Smith is a gardener with a mission. “Mine is a habitat garden. Nearly everything that grows here has a purpose to feed, nurture or shelter creatures, human or otherwise,” says Smith, a former Havens Elementary School science teacher, co-founder of Piedmont Connect (www.piedmontconnect.org) and cofounder of the Pollinator Posse (www.pollinatorposse.org). Since Smith and her husband bought home at Jerome and Oakland Avenue 38 years ago, they have transformed both front and back yards from lawn and eucalyptus trees to native and/or drought-tolerant plants, pollinator habitat and edibles. Their front garden is now an orchard underplanted with pollinator-friendly plants and designated an official Monarch Butterfly Waystation. The backyard features raised vegetable beds surrounded by fruit trees, a water feature, seating areas and more host plants. Many of the 27 fruit trees are multi-grafted to produce different varieties from the same trees. “By planting year-round and preserving the bounty, I can eat something from the garden every day of the year,” Smith says. “I freeze, can, dehydrate and share any extra. We’re so lucky with our climate here that the garden is often more productive in the winter months than a typical summer harvest.” Smith’s gardening strategies Water conservation: “Water is efficiently applied only as needed. I recently learned that homegrown vegetables and fruit use 1/30th the water of those raised commercially. Our water use is far less than when the garden was lawn, but the land is far Photo by Rob Smith Terry Smith’s Pollinator Posse creation of super-sized, silk Monarch Butterflies and caterpillars won the “Most Artistic” award in Piedmont’s 2020 Fourth of July “Celebrate in Place” competition. She created the giant butterflies originally for the 2019 Autumn Festival of Lights at Lake Merritt. more productive.” Toxin free: “No pesticides or herbicides ever, and plants are purchased from carefully vetted nurseries, or grown from seed to avoid those treated with neonicotinoids. Neonics are systemic poisons that render a plant toxic throughout its life cycle. Most wholesale growers apply these to plants and often don’t inform the nurseries that buy them. Even more disturbing is the use of these systemic, addictive and toxic chemicals on many food crops. Diverse habitat to nurture pollinators: “I choose many plants for their affiliation with wildlife, especially pollinators. The incredible decline in recent years of insect populations — the base of our food chain — is primarily the result of pesticides and climate change.” “The benefit of providing habitat and sustenance for these creatures includes a high yield of fruits and vegetables – nothing goes unpollinated – and their pleasant company. Since butterflies in particular need specific plants to complete their life cycles – caterpillars are the original picky eaters – I make sure I have as many of those plants as possible.” Climate Corner is a collaboration between the city of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect, a local environmental nonprofit, to raise awareness about climate actions in the community. One of those villages is Cairanne – a charming medieval looking hill town. This wine is an improvement from your average Cote du Rhone. It has good cherry fruit with a touch of earth and spice. It is lush and full in the mouth and has a long, lingering, easygoing, supple finish. • 2017 Crous St. Martin Gigondas “Les Espaliers”, $25 Gigondas is often called the “poor man’s Chateauneuf du Pape”. I have been at many tastings where the Gigondas is greatly preferred to the Chateauneuf. This wine is dense ruby/purple with notes of blackberry intermixed with smoke, earth and flowers. articles.text: J. Harper Gaston M.D. died on July 12, 2020 in Atlanta, Georgia due to complications of dementia. He was 88. Dr. Gaston was a most caring father and grandfather, a loving husband of sixty-seven years, and an honorable, dedicated, and talented physician, who was beloved by his many patients, family, and friends. He worked for the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group of Northern California for over 20 years, and later founded and served as the first Medical Director and Physician-in-Chief of the Kaiser Permanente Southeastern Medical Group in Atlanta, Georgia. Born J. Harper Gaston IV on November 2, 1931 in New York City, he was the son of Joseph H. Gaston III M.D and Louese Hays Gaston. Raised in Columbus, Georgia, where his father practiced orthopedic medicine, Harper Gaston attended city schools in Columbus and graduated from the Darlington School in Rome, Georgia. After his father’s death, Dr. Gaston worked as a grocery clerk to help support his mother and to earn his tuition money. At age 16, he entered Emory University, where he received both his Bachelor (1952) and Medical Degree (1955). While attending Emory Medical School, he met and married the love of his life, his medical school classmate, Dr. Anne Elizabeth Hendrick. Both doctors completed their internships and residencies at Grady Memorial Hospital. He was named the first fellow in Cardiology under the direction of world-renown cardiologist, Dr. J. Willis Hurst. Upon completion of his residency program, Dr. Gaston enlisted in the U.S. Air Force and was stationed at Kessler Air Force Base in Biloxi, Mississippi. With the rank of Capt., he served as a general internist and (oddly) Chair of the Dermatology department while his wife, Dr. Anne Gaston worked as a civilian pediatrician in the Kessler Air Force Base General Hospital. In 1961 he and his wife moved first to Oakland, and then to Piedmont, where they joined the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group in the KPMG’s first medical office in San Leandro. Their decision of the home games in the World Series from 1972-1974. In Atlanta, Dr. Gaston continued his community service, by serving the Emory University Medical School in many capacities for over 50 years, including as an adviser to the Emory University System of Healthcare Board of Directors, as a member of the Emory Board of Visitors, and as Co-Chair with his wife of the National Council of Medicine. The Drs. Gaston also established the Gaston Service Scholarships for Emory University Medical School students who exemplified community volunteerism and service. “Service in and of itself is the greatest reward that our profession can offer us. It is the heart of medicine,” he said. He was awarded the Emory Medal in 1997, Emory’s Highest Honor, for his service to Emory and the community. Dr. Gaston remained an avid sports fan of the Oakland A’s, the Oakland Raiders, the Atlanta Braves, and the Georgia “Dawgs” for all of his life. He loved to travel and traveled with one of the first groups of physicians to visit the USSR in the late 1960s. He also loved horse racing and was a co-owner of Dogwood Stables in Aiken, South Carolina. His one disappointment in life was when Dogwood’s horse, Summer Squall, won the 1990 Preakness, but despite being the favorite to win, came in second in the 1990 Kentucky Derby. His greatest achievement was his generosity of spirit and his tremendous love for his wife and family. Dr. J. Harper Gaston is survived by his wife, Dr. Anne Elizabeth Hendrick Gaston, his only child, Lisa Anne Gaston, his sonin-law Michael Gerard Reff, and his two granddaughters and their spouses, Allison Elizabeth Stalla (Timothy Zeid Stalla) and Hayley Harper Swarbrick (Andrew John Swarbrick). A private service will be held at Greenville Presbyterian Church Cemetery, where Dr. Harper Gaston will be laid to rest. A public memorial service will be planned and announced at a later date. Condolences may be expressed online at www.mckoon.com. Dr. Harper Gaston, a Board-Certified Internist and Cardiologist with Kaiser Permanente in Northern California for over 20 year, died on July 12, 2020 in Atlanta, Georgia. was based primarily upon the fact that the KPMG was one of the only medical groups in the country which would allow a husband and wife to both practice medicine for equal pay. Dr. Harper Gaston was appointed the Assistant-Chief of Medicine at the new Kaiser Permanente Hospital in Hayward in 1966. He became Chief of Medicine in 1971, Assistant Physician-in-Chief in 1976, and was elected Physician-in-Chief from 1977 to 1984. That year he was chosen to return to his home state of Georgia to establish the Kaiser Permanente Southeastern Medical Group, where he served as its founding Medical Director. In addition to his work with the Permanente Medical Group, Dr. Gaston also served as an Assistant Clinical Professor in Internal Medicine at Stanford University. Dr. Gaston was also active in the State of California Heart Association, where he served on the Board of Directors, and served as President of the Alameda County Heart Association. His many years of work with the California Heart Association was responsible for securing and installing a cardiac defibrillator station at the Oakland Coliseum. It was the first staffed cardiac defibrillator station in a sports venue on the West Coast. This activism led to one of his fondest memories where he acted as personal game-day cardiologist, sitting next to Charlie O. Finley, owner of the Oakland A’s, for all

articles.text: Richard “Dick” Brooks passed away peacefully at age 92 on July 18, 2020 at the Terraces in Boise, Idaho. He was a 22-year resident of Piedmont through 1987, and long-time resident of Ketchum, Idaho. Born in 1928 in Akron, Ohio, Dick marked his life in Milwaukee, Yale University, Dallas, and San Francisco, then Piedmont before retiring to Ketchum. Linguistically precise and athletically adept, Dick spent his career in finance and was the architect of one of the first interest-rate currency swaps, recognized in 1983 as “the most noteworthy financial swap” by Institutional Investor magazine. Outside of work, he had a penchant for the precise: the structure of a sonnet, the turn of a phrase, the fine cut of woodworking. Known to many family members as “Squeak”, he was a loving dad and grandfather who taught his family what it was to be respected and respectful. He loved song and was an orator of notable skill. His voice will live on in our hearts as we focus on being aware of life’s moments, often with ice cream and/or Scotch. During his time in Piedmont, he was a member of the executive council of the Boy Scout Council in the 1970s, and helped to maintain the independence of the Piedmont Council, which continues to this day. Dick is survived by his wife Sidney, and his children Dave (wife Ann, daughter Jennings), Scott (wife Emily, sons Alexander, Zachary, and Mitchell), and Susie (husband Patrick, daughters Katie and Sammie). A memorial service will be held on August 7 at St. Thomas Episcopal Church in Sun Valley, Idaho, where he will be laid to rest in the columbarium. Dick Brooks, who lived in Piedmont from 1965 through 1987, passed away on July 18, 2020 in Boise Idaho. Je was 92.
articles.title: Dick Brooks, former Piedmont resident, dies at 92

articles.text: Two residents of The Lake Merritt enjoy a stroll at the lake. There aren’t many major cities where you can drive from the grocery store to the middle of a redwood forest in five or 10 minutes/ A little secret is that you can in Oakland. Residents of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living have been exploring our wonderful local parks in a safe and distanced way. The City of Oakland boasts nearly 6,000 acres of parks and trails, many of which connect to larger park networks. The East Bay Regional Parks features nearly 125,000 acres and has a very good website that is continuously updated with COVID-related closures and other information. We also use alltrails.com to search for easy hikes, and read user reviews about trail width and busyness. Locally, you can walk for days without retracing your steps. Recently, our residents enjoyed a great presentation by Stan Dodson, the founder of Oakland Trails (oaklandtrails.org), as part of our weekly public speaker series, “Topics of Merritt.” This and our other Zoom programs are free and available to the public, so call us or register online. Dodson is a person who knows his local trails. He is a recipient of the Parkland Steward Award from Oakland Public Works Department, and the Anne Woodell Community Award, Oakland’s highest honor for community service in parks. Dodson recommends visiting Oakland’s gorgeous parks in the afternoon on weekdays to avoid crowds. He also recommended to our audience some easy and accessible trails within the Oakland City Parks system. On the Eastern side of Joaquin Miller Park there is a nearly flat maintenance road that can be accessed from a parking pullout on Skyline Boulevard near the Big Trees Trailhead. This road takes you through the redwood forest toward the Sequoia Horse Arena in Roberts Park. This trail is wheelchair accessible and peaceful. Within the nearby Sausal Creek watershed, Dodson recommends entering the Dimond Canyon Trail at El Centro Avenue in the Glenview District. There you will find a flat, wide trail that attracts families and is suitable for nearly all abilities. In addition to these spots, The Lake Merritt residents have several favorites to share. One resident particularly likes the Montclair Railroad Trail, the steepest part of which is a gentle ramp to get onto the trail (behind the Montclair Parking Garage). He says, “the trail is not too crowded. It’s very wide and paved and it’s flat. I could do one of those walks every day.” Another series of trails we’ve visited more than once are in Redwood Regional Park. This gorgeous woodland features wide, paved trails, as well as an impressive network of dirt paths. We usually enter through Redwood Gate and explore the Stream Trail. Another of residents said, “There are times when I come back from our nature walks feeling almost ecstatic.” If you’d like to do even more research on area walks and trails, you can view Dodson’s two short films through Oakland Trails. This all-volunteer organization is dedicated to promoting, maintaining and enhancing the City of Oakland’s wildland parks and trails. Trailhead is Dodson’s first film. It provides an overview of Oakland’s largest wildland trail system that connects neighborhoods to redwood forests. Old Survivor, Dodson’s second film, highlights the only remaining old-growth redwood tree in the East Bay hills and tells the story of Oakland’s resilient, ecologically amazing and now-protected redwood forest. Both documentaries can be viewed for free and are found at oaklandtrails.org. It is possible for older adults and families to enjoy easy and immersive nature walks in Oakland. They are food for the soul. Get out and enjoy the rest of the summer. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living located at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland, call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: We often talk of “meaningful” engagement or activity as if there is just one type of meaning. The truth is that what is meaningful to one person may not be so to another, especially when that person needs assistance with activities of daily living. When something is meaningless, it lacks purpose, value or significance. Certainly no one is striving to spend their time in a meaningless way, and yet maintaining boring routines can feel futile to people. There can be a lack of joy or inspiration when people are stuck in a rut of meaningless activity. Here are some examples of meaningless activities: • Checking email just because • Scrolling through social media feeds • Viewing TV alone or watching the same programs repeatedly Conversely, when something is meaningful it is “full of significance” and has purpose. When caring for someone who might need elder care due to age or chronic conditions that have altered their physical abilities, it is important to find ways to spend time together that is worthwhile to them. Here are some examples of meaningful activities: • Gardening can be meaningful if it brings someone the joy of growing their own food or waiting for the flowers to bloom. This also can engage all of one’s senses, which tends to increase the meaning of an activity. • Making a photo album for sharing memories with someone in your life. It can be to give as a gift or have as a keepsake. • Listening to music which can evoke memories to be shared or be part of creating new ones. In order to find out what is meaningful to another person who needs your help, you might ask what they love to do or what they are good at. Even if they physically cannot do it alone, maybe you can assist so they still have the feeling of engaging in this activity. Remember that one person may find coloring in pictures to be relaxing and rewarding while someone else might think it is mind-numbing and pointless. Creating a shared activity in which people need to talk or rely on one another to complete a larger task can be meaningful, so it is not just about one or two people. Think of a letter-writing campaign or making a meal together for group activities. For more ideas on how to create meaningful activities visit the Changing Aging blog at changingaging.org. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. watch?v=67keaaWOKzE Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a MacBook Pro, and since I am not going into work, I have time to learn how to use it. I am coming from the PC world, so everything is different. Where do I start? -Leslie G., Oakland Dear Leslie: Congrats on your new purchase, and luckily, there are many good sources that provide information on becoming comfortable on the Mac platform. You can find help with books, online print sources, and videos. Here are some of my favorite sources. Books: I am still a page turning learner, and if I am learning something new, I like to sit with a highlighter and a book, and study like the old days! There are some excellent books on switching to Mac, whether you are a tech savvy user, or more of a beginner. The “For Dummies” series is excellent, and there is a “Switching to a Mac for Dummies”. Anything by David Pogue is great, although a bit more technical. One that I would strongly recommend is “macOS Catalina for Dummies” by Bob LeVitus. Also, the “for seniors” volumes are usually well written, specifically Mac OS Catalina for Seniors” by Scott La Counte. Be aware, that if these volumes are not current (2019 or later), the info might be outdated. Websites: Apple itself has a web page devoted to folks who switched to Mac from PCs: https://support. apple.com/en-us/HT204216 You can find lots of good info here. I also really like the “How to Geek”: https://www.howtogeek. com/437168/how-to-switch-froma-windows-pc-to-a-mac/. Another good source is wired. com. If you do a Google search “switching from PC to Mac” there are countless links from established sites. Videos (YouTube): This is most likely your best bet. Anson Alexander has really good video series and his Mac tutorial for beginners is excellent: https://www.youtube.com/ Another good video is by macmost.com, including a video on “Questions New Mac Owners Have When Switching from Windows”: https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=vau_4NpkEB8. Of course, there are plenty of videos by helpful pros, and if you just got a new mac, you can always call AppleCare with any questions: 1-800-275-2273. I think you will find that there are many similarities, and the differences are mostly for power users. Of course, the file structure is different, and the user experience is also a bit different. If you are a photographer, artist or musician, you will appreciate the amount of software for you. And these days, the current version of Microsoft Office apps like Word and Excel are almost exactly the same on the Mac as PC. I would say, that within a month or so, you will feel like a pro. If you need more guidance, contact me, I am doing all of my support appointments remotely these days. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 3820 Broadway, Oakland

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

Piedmont Grocery employee James Obendorf, a Piedmont resident, took the time to share with the Post his experience as an essential worker. “It’s a family owned business, and for the most part everyone gets along, which makes the work environment great. Customers feel safe. A few customers have been rude by ignoring the mask requirement, so the manager will ask them to leave. We also watch for people not putting the mask over their nose and tell them they have to.” Larson commented on the average mindset of his customers. “There still is concern, but they aren’t as panicky as they were initially. We have got it pretty much organized and under control. They don’t mind waiting to go in, keeping their distance and the seniors haven’t make a fuss.” The grocery store has run into a few problems of not being able to stock all of its usual products. “We were operating really well for a while, and now suddenly we are starting to miss a few things. It’s nothing quite as serious as before, but we still Piedmont Grocery set up tents outside to shade customers from the direct sun while waiting to get into the store. Taking a few simple steps now can make a big difference in reducing the risk of wildfire and increasing the safety for you and your family. Piedmont Firefighters have already begun preparing for the upcoming fire season, and we are asking Piedmont residents to do the same. A great place to start is online at: • Identify vegetation hazards and make a plan to deal with them • Make a simple plan in case of evacuation. • Pay attention to information and instructions in the event of an emergency. Look for additional information and tips that will make the community as safe as it can be this upcoming summer. If you have any questions or need assistance, feel free to contact the Piedmont Fire Department at 510-420-3030.

Piedmont Grocery employee James Obendorf, a Piedmont resident, took the time to share with the Post his experience as an essential worker. “It’s a family owned business, and for the most part everyone gets along, which makes the work environment great. Customers feel safe. A few customers have been rude by ignoring the mask requirement, so the manager will ask them to leave. We also watch for people not putting the mask over their nose and tell them they have to.” Larson commented on the average mindset of his customers. “There still is concern, but they aren’t as panicky as they were initially. We have got it pretty much organized and under control. They don’t mind waiting to go in, keeping their distance and the seniors haven’t make a fuss.” The grocery store has run into a few problems of not being able to stock all of its usual products. “We were operating really well for a while, and now suddenly we are starting to miss a few things. It’s nothing quite as serious as before, but we still Piedmont Grocery set up tents outside to shade customers from the direct sun while waiting to get into the store. can’t get any flour,” he explained. But again, his staff has adapted by being creative. “We buy flour in bulk from restaurant supply [people] and then repack it into smaller containers.” Larson explained the brief nationwide spike in meat prices wasn’t too unusual, noting that meat prices normally increase a bit in the summer, and that now they are back to normal. Their extensive hot lunch bar has been closed, but they do offer pre-packaged hot lunches now, with daily changing items, like whole chickens, salmon, and mac and cheese. Orders may be placed by phone at 658-8181. Since 1902, Piedmont Grocery has been a part of the community of Piedmont. Through good times and lean times, the Larson family has made a point of contributing back to the community. Long a part of the 4th of July festivities in town, when the announcement came that the parade had been canceled, Piedmont Grocery offered to provide meat and buns to the coed teen Piedmont Community Service Crew for their Fourth of July BBQ basket fundraiser. Located at 4038 Piedmont Avenue, Piedmont Grocery has been a cornerstone in the local community for 118 years. Visit their website at https://piedmontgrocery.com/ for staff picks and vendors of the week or call 658-8181. articles.text: Barbara Addleman and sons Blaise and Kleed Cumming were awarded the Highland Saucer this week for the “Most Patriotic” entry in the Piedmont Fourth of July Front Yard Decorating Contest. In the absence of a parade this year – the first in the parade’s 55-year history – the Fourth of July Committee invited the community to compete in a “celebrating in place” contest. The Addleman-Cumming family transformed their yard into a history of civil protests in the U.S., replete with 23 cardboard protest signs, and 40 additional signs in a bay window. On the front of the house was a large “Power to the People” banner. Their entry, called “This is What Democracy Looks Like,” was sparked by the Black Lives Matter demonstrations and the family’s keen awareness of social issues. “We have always been active politically and socially by joining demonstrations for the women’s march or against Monsanto and climate change,” Addleman said. Signs at their house included a range of statements, including “Google Fred Hampton,” “Who Watches the Watchers,” “Water is Life,” ”Medicare for All,” and “Freedom of the Press.” Kleed Cummings explained Barbara Addleman’s front yard filled with signs representing an entry in the 4th of July Yard Decorating contest titled, “This is What Democracy Looks Like.” Carla Betts, Chair of the July Fourth Parade committee, presents the Highland Saucer to Kleed Cumming (left)and brother Blaise, and their mother Barbara Addleman for the “Most Patriotic” entry into Piedmont’s first ever Fourth of July “Front Yard and Car Decorating Contest.” the importance of their project, “Piedmont is definitely an affluent town that is pretty privileged and might not necessarily be acknowledging these social movements going on right now. We just thought it would be good to highlight them for everyone.” “Demonstrating is ingrained in being patriotic and being American,” his mother added. “It goes back to the Boston Tea Party. People going out, demonstrating, and participating in democracy is part of why we have all the things that we do have.” The three started planning out their July 4 entry a week ahead of time and spent three long, but fun, afternoons in the yard making the signs from recycled material. Their hard work paid off, Addleman admitted. “I was totally surprised when I got the call from Carla Betts. We sort of said, ‘oh well, we haven’t heard from them, but it was fun to do.’ But then we got the call and we said, “Oh my god, they actually called!” Piedmonters can still check out their award-winning front yard on Carmel Avenue. When thinking of taking their installment down recently, the Cumming-Addleman family decided to leave something out there. “If nothing else, just to continue it will support the people in Portland,” she said.
articles.title: Cumming-Addleman family wins Highland Saucer

articles.text: Over the weekend of July 18, graffiti with anti-police messages popped up at two locations in Piedmont. With graffiti a hot topic nationwide, especially in Portland and Oakland, Piedmont has discovered it is not immune. At the Hall Fenway, which connects Wildwood and Crocker Avenue, a bench, street sign and the sidewalk were tagged. The messages included “ACAB,” anti-police sentiment and a message about “one percent.” On Guilford and Highland similar messages, with the same color spray paint, targeted the sidewalk and a street sign. According to California penal code 594, “If the amount of defacement, damage, or destruction is four hundred dollars ($400) or more, vandalism is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by a fine of not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000).” Under $400 in damage can be punished with up to one year in county jail and up to a $1,000 fine. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers weighed in on the delicacy of the situation. “I understand the raw emotional state which comes from a number of factors, but vandalizing property isn’t going to move the needle. Constructive, purposeful engagement will,” he said. Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan has not seen much graffiti of any kind in his three years in the City, so this represented something of a first. “We had a little bit of anti-police graffiti right after George Floyd. It was nothing dramatic like in the big cities,” he explained. “There was a little chalk graffiti around the civic center. Beyond that, we have had very, very little – and hopefully will not have any.”
articles.title: Graffiti in Piedmont – a follow-up

articles.text: The summer of 2006 brought a life-changing journey for the Ensemble group of the Piedmont Choirs. A two-week tour of performances I the Far East gave the young vocalists an opportunity to compete in Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore. In addition to a rigorous competition schedule, the group got to see the sights and taste the flavors of the Far East while meeting other youth singers from international choral groups.

articles.text: Piedmont joined a coalition of cities on Monday, July 20 to oppose new rules from the Federal Communications Commission that the City contends make it harder for local governments to regulate cell towers. On June 9, the FCC adopted a new ruling that altered how municipalities handle permits for wireless facilities. Specifically, the FCC modified Section 6409(a) of the Spectrum Act in 2012. “We believe the City should continue to push to restore local control over wireless infrastructure: current rules greatly reduce our ability to decide what and where these facilities can be installed,” Mayor Bob McBain told the Post. In a report about the coalition, Planning Director Kevin Jackson highlighted several issues with the ruling. For example, cities must make decisions on wireless facility application within a standardized 60-day “shot clock” period. The new rules start the “shot clock” period earlier in the application process. The ruling also outlines how cities cannot require cell towers to look concealed within their environment. Additionally, the ruling gives more leeway to wireless infrastructure companies in adjusting and updating facilities in certain regards. In response, City Council unanimously agreed to join a coalition of cities, organized by law firm Best Best & Krieger (BBK), in opposition to the new FCC rules. Comments against the rule change must be filed by August 10. The action is the latest volley between Piedmont and the FCC over cell tower regulations, especially since Ajit Pai was appointed Chairman of the commission by President Donald Trump in 2017. Publicly, the cell tower issue became a nexus of controversy in Piedmont since 2016 when wireless infrastructure builder Crown Castle submitted plans to build several small cell antenna
articles.title: Council supports joining coalition opposing new FCC cell tower rules

articles.text: Last zoo in state to reopen welcomes visitors starting July 29 Oakland Zoo, the last zoo in California to be given authorization to reopen during the coronavirus pandemic, will be opening to the public starting next Wednesday, July 29. The news came on Wednesday, July 15, after a push for it to be reclassified as an outdoor museum. The zoo had to wait for an approval for an application sent by the county’s Board of Supervisors for state variance. The variance gave the zoo permission from state health officials to re-open. “This is a great day for us,” Dr. Joel Parrott, the zoo’s president and CEO said about the approval. “This gives us a chance to survive.” during its four-month closure, but Parrott made it clear that re-opening was key to keeping the zoo operative. Now that the zoo is able to re-open, zoo officials have instituted an extensive range of new protocols that comply with county and state health authorities. Oakland Zoo will resume operations in phases, starting with limiting the number of guests at any given time through a new online reservation-based ticketing system. There will be limited dining and shopping experiences, frequent cleaning and sanitization of high-touch areas, with sanitizing stations available throughout the zoo. Face coverings for guests age 3 and older will be required, Photo courtesy of Oakland Zoo Dr. Joel Parrott, president and CEO of Oakland Zoo. The zoo closed on March 17 due to COVID-19 and was at risk of permanent closure due to re-opening restrictions. Community support and philanthropic efforts helped keep the zoo afloat
articles.title: Oakland Zoo finally given green light to reopen

articles.text: A proposed distance-learning model for the coming school year was discussed at length at a special Piedmont School Board meeting on Thursday July 16. In an e-mail message sent on July 14 to parents of Piedmont students, Superintendent Randy Booker announced that the academic year will begin with no in-class instruction, and 100 percent remote learning. With five weeks left before the first day of school, Booker acknowledged that families and faculty need time to prepare for the proposed distance-learning model. This factored into the decision to begin with 100 percent remote learning, he said. “We’re starting with a distance-learning environment, because that is what the conditions are indicating at this point. I would rather start this way, than start in-person and face such a dramatic shift to distance learning,” Booker said. In-person classes would have to be shifted in the event that a student or faculty member were to test positive for COVID-19. Booker acknowledged that the upcoming school year will be “very tumultuous” but held firm that the uptick in coronavirus cases across the state prompted the decision. He also addressed the model that was conducted in the spring and called it “crisis learning” rather than distance-learning. “At first we thought it would be for two weeks, so teachers were organizing lessons, thinking it would be a short period of time. Then [health officers] extended it another month,” Booker said. “That was a lot of crisis planning, learning, training and testing.” A set, consistent bell schedule, where students will have to report to teachers in real-time before class begins, is likely.
