articles.text: California Interscholastic Federation, the governing body for high school sports in the state, announced on Monday, July 20 an historic change to schedules for all high school sports. There will be no fall sports throughout California, and both fall and winter sports will begin their schedules in January 2021 in response to the global COVID-19 pandemic. Instead of its usual three sports seasons – Fall, Winter and Spring – the CIF has compressed schedules into just two seasons, Winter and Spring. Football, water polo, cross country, and volleyball will have their first day of practice on December 14, with their seasons ending by mid-March. Football Staff Photo Will there be sports at Witter Field? CIF announced its plan for the 2020-2021 sports calendar. playoffs will stretch until April 10. In the spring, Piedmont High will have 10 sports with a total of 17 teams. Girls and boys soccer teams will begin on February 22 – historically the week of the NCS championships, and girls and boys basketball won’t begin until March 15. Girls’ tennis, a fall sport, will be played concurrently with boys’ tennis as a spring sport alongside the boys’ program. This means coaches like Jim Landes and assistant Corey Reich will be pulling double duty. The question of finding extra court and field space remains unanswered, as does the logistical question of providing officials for all sports in the compressed time period. The availability of Witter Field becomes an intriguing question with prospective varsity and JV teams requiring field space. In spring, teams vying for space at Witter will include football, boys’ and girls’ soccer, boys’ and girls’ lacrosse, and track and field.
articles.title: Radical changes in sports schedules announced by State

articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved the first reading of a proposal to implement Reach Codes at a July 20 virtual meeting, with direction for amendments to be explored by staff before a second reading. A package of proposed local amendments to the California Electrical Code, Residential Code, and Building Energy Efficiency Code were considered. The amendments, referred to as “reach codes,” would alter the requirements for home construction and renovation in Piedmont to facilitate building insulation, electrification, and solar panel installation. Staff proposals would set new standards in both new and already existing buildings to reduce gas use and help meet Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan’s goals. “Piedmont adopted a Climate Action Plan first in 2010, and again in 2018 to address this crisis. Actions in the plan include measures to reduce natural gas use, and to increase the use of solar energy systems. The proposed amendments do just that,” said City Planning Director Kevin Jackson. Reach codes, he added, would improve air quality and be cost-effective. Survey results brought to council on July 6 showed that 66 percent of surveyed Piedmonters supported the proposed codes. City staff also held five outreach events in January and February, where amendment ideas were first introduced to residents and contractors for feedback. CivicSpark Fellow Justin Szasz, who will be completing his 11-month fellowship with the city of Piedmont this month, provided detailed information in a presentation to city council members. The proposal, as presented, would require that newly constructed low-rise residential building must use all electric building appliances, and would be prohibited from being connected to natural gas service. This would also apply to new, detached accessory dwelling units. When an existing, low-rise residential building gets a new upper level, or increases its roof area by 30 percent or more, the installation of solar panels is required. Renovations of lowrise residential buildings with a construction value of $25,000 or more must include at least one item from a list of energy efficient insulation or electrification measures. Renovations of $100,000 or more in value must include two of the items. While other jurisdictions have been vocal about wanting to address natural gas use in existing buildings, few have done so. “Piedmont’s proposed amendments will provide leadership to other jurisdictions on this crucial issue,” Szasz said. Results from previous surveys, and information provided by a public engagement program, offered revisions to the proposed amendments that were discussed on July 20. City councilmembers dissected some of the costs associated with the proposal that residents may encounter when renovating. Councilmember Betsy Andersen pointed out that solar panel installation is still a large up-front cost, despite the return in investment after approximately 30 years. She also asked if there would be temporary exemptions for residents who have already been proactive in their sustainable efforts in home improvement. “There are so many folks who keep adopting the incremental changes that they can afford. There are tipping points here where some stuff may become unaffordable with a lot of Piedmonters,” said Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King. Szasz responded by stating that staff believes the proposal to be beneficial to residents, because it meets the climate action plan demands with consideration of upfront costs. “We tried to always make the additional upfront costs proportional to the triggers for the requirements. Because [staff] understands that there is a significant upfront cost for solar panel installation, we weren’t looking at requiring it on every single new roof. We really wanted to hone in on projects that are significantly costly, so it would only be a small increase in the upfront cost,” said Szasz. The goal, he added, is to help residents make these changes without putting any undue cost burden on them. On a 3-2 vote, the council approved a first reading of the proposal, with modifications. Councilmember Anderson and Mayor Bob McBain dissented. The council may hold a second reading on the subject as early as soon as August 3. City staff would then file all amendments to the California Electrical Code and California Energy Code.
articles.title: Council approves first reading of proposed “Reach Codes”

articles.text: FCC further reduces decision-making power of local governments At its meeting on July 20, 2020, the Piedmont City Council joined a coalition to oppose new Federal Communications Commission rules regarding wireless communications facilities. The new rule, approved by the FCC on June 9, 2020, significantly reduces the already limited decision-making power held by local governments to minimize the impact of wireless communication facilities on their community. “We believe there are ways for wireless communication devices to be deployed in an aesthetically appropriate manner. Unfortunately, the FCC seems intent on making that much more difficult, if not impossible,” said Kevin Jackson, Piedmont Planning Director “Unless there is a court-ordered injunction, the new FCC rules will further reduce Piedmont’s ability to control the installation of wireless communication facilities.” Section 6409 of the Spectrum Act requires a city like Piedmont to approve an “eligible facilities request” for a modification of an existing wireless tower or base station that does not “substantially change” the physical dimensions of such tower or base station. The FCC has changed the definition of “substantial change,” as well as other important changes. Changes in the new Eligible Facilities order include, but are not limited to: • The 60-day “shot clock” is now triggered when the applicant takes the first procedural steps, giving the city less time to review for the compliance with the City’s codes. • The definition of concealment has been narrowed so that concealment is only “stealth” design, e.g. look like something other than a wireless tower or base station. Now under the new FCC order, concealment of a facility at a specific location would not include screening by a rooftop or placement behind a tree line or fence. • In addition, the FCC order specif ies that aesthetic requirements or iginally imposed as conditions of approval, such as vegetation cover, fencing, screening, and similar requirements will not be grounds to deny an expressly allowed height or size increase. The order allows the installation of additional antenna up to 20 feet, plus there is no cap to the height of new antenna, for towers outside the public right-of-way. On an existing structure such as a utility pole, the FCC made modifications to the number of equipment cabinets that can be installed per an eligible facilities request. For more information, contact Piedmont Director of Planning and Building Kevin Jackson at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. “Someday, son, this vast chain will all belong to you, your mother, your sisters, Uncle Harry or Aunt Lilly Belle.”
articles.title: Piedmont joins coalition of cities opposing FCC rules on wireless communications

Warnings are currently being given out to ease car owners back into the obeying the parking limitations The reduced demand for parking in the civic center area during the pandemic has led to a relaxing of enforcement on the parking spots on Bonita and Vista Avenue. City employees have noted the inability to have access to their parking spots which are reserved from 8 a.m.-5 p.m. Some of the spaces are being used by construction workers at the high school. “We have been receiving some complaints from City staff about vehicles without city employee parking permits parking in city employee parking spots,” said Staff photo Warning Only parking violations are now being issued by the city. articles.text: An issue with paperwork and variance approvals caused Alameda County to shut down outdoor dining for the second time, only to allow restaurants to reopen again last weekend. After months of being limited to providing takeout and delivery only, the county re-opened for sitdown dining on June 19. But on Friday, July 13, new guidance from the state made clear that the county did not file all necessary paperwork required to reopen. On Saturday in the middle of the day, restaurant owners were blindsided by an abrupt order to close. “I saw it on the 11 o’clock news [on Friday],” said Alan Carlson, owner of Italian Colors, a popular restaurant in Montclair Village. “We didn’t get a robocall [from the county], no email, nothing,” he said. Like other restaurant owners, Carlson brought employees out of furlough to work, adding to the confusion. With outdoor dining eliminated, he was worried he would have to furlough those same employees again. “It breaks your heart to have to do that. They’ve been off for three, almost four months,” Carlson said. Luckily, the county rushed Alan Carlson, owner of Italian Colors, prepares dinners for guests pre-COVID-19. to complete paperwork that would allow for outdoor dining. Restaurant owners in Alameda County were in limbo for about five days. On Wednesday afternoon, July 15, public health officials announced that outdoor dining once again could resume in the county after the state approved a variance to proceed. All restaurants in the county that can adequately provide socially-distant outdoor dining areas now may do so. Restaurants are still allowed to conduct takeout and delivery operations.

articles.text: Fenton’s Creamery on Piedmont Avenue, Piedmont’s s iconic ice cream parlor since 1894, has endured wars, depressions, and earthquakes without once having to shut down their ice cream plant. Only a fire closed them temporarily for rebuilding. And then came COVID-19. Scott Whidden and his family have owned Fenton’s since 1987, when they bought the business from a national dairy corporation to bring it back to local ownership. Fenton’s has a large following and is beloved by many for providing a perfect atmosphere for celebrations, nostalgia and indulgence. When COVID-19’s shelter-inplace went into effect and Fenton’s was given permission to serve only takeout, they were in a spot of trouble. Takeout normally accounts for 20 percent of their business, and parties bring in half of the total revenue. They had to furlough 40 of their 65 workers and encouraged them to file for unemployment. In April when it became clear the pandemic was not going away, the furloughs turned into layoffs. Whidden said, “It is ghastly. These are people that have worked at Fenton’s for 10-15 years. We don’t want to fire anyone. They are a part of the Fenton’s family.” Fenton’s does have some advantages, however. It has two sets of double doors at the entry, making for an easy flow in and out now. And they have 24 seats outdoors with benches and tables in the parking lot. They can accommodate a lot After shutting down ice cream production for the first time since a fire many years ago, Fenton’s Creamery is back serving ice cream and food for takeout. It is offering delivery and outdoor dining on an expanded patio on the parking lot. of people and maintain the county’s required six-foot distancing. They have expanded their delivery service, mostly through Doordash, and their website allows for easy ordering and payment for pickup. With these revenues they have been able to return to roughly half of their normal production. “At 50 percent, we are at a self-sustaining level,” said Whidden. “But in terms of economics, we are losing week over week, just because of the size of the building and its overhead. We will have to tread water probably until Spring Break 2021, hopefully not beyond that.” “If this is a ‘new normal’, we have to ask the question, ‘Does Fenton’s even need a party room or dining room?’ To cue up just for takeout, that would be tragic,” he said. “Our essential workers are basically putting their lives at risk to serve a scoop of ice cream. It’s mind-boggling to get your arms around that. But that is the reality of it.” Fenton’s may be in the food industry, but they are also in the entertainment business. Going to Fenton’s has always been an event – a celebration. “Ice cream is like a sweet, reminisce treat for people. Sitting there and being a part of that carnival of activities is a big part of it. People come to celebrate what is going on with them or just park themselves to indulge a little bit,” said Whidden.

articles.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom At a press briefing on Friday, July 17, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued strict guidelines for reopening schools across the state. School can only open for in-person classes if their county has been off the state’s watch list for two weeks. Schools that don’t meet those criteria must begin with classes this fall with distance learning. Alameda County leads the Bay Area in total COVID-19 cases and is on the state’s watch list, delaying some anticipated re-openings. On Friday morning, San Francisco County was also added to the state’s coronavirus watch list. San Francisco, Oakland, and Sacramento school districts all have announced plans to begin school in August with remote learning. If school districts in the state want to reopen, their county health officials must prove two weeks of declining coronavirus cases. Districts that may reopen would require all school staff and students in 3rd grade and above to wear masks and with desks six feet apart. Staff members are also expected to keep a six-foot distance from students. Piedmont School District made the decision to begin the academic year virtually and proposed a distance-learning model at a July 16 school board meeting. “Since we’ve issued our guidance, conditions have changed dramatically,” State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond said during a media briefing last Wednesday, July 15, adding that he expects more districts will decide to begin the term virtually. “In any place where there is uncertainty, we should proceed with caution. In many cases, that’s going to [mean] distance learning.” Thurmond initially left the decision to reopen schools up to individual school districts throughout the state. If Alameda County experiences a decline in coronavirus cases, it may reopen under restrictions. S E N D T H E P E R F E C T G I F T W I T H F R E N C H S O A P D E P O T . articles.text: Jenessa Joffe, a 1994 Piedmont High graduate, recently directed and co-produced a second season of the award-winning digital series “Radical Cram School.” The short Youtube videos address social activism with kids by way of host Kristina Wong, a San Francisco comedian and performance artist. Radical Cram School is a kid-centric, entertaining and informative series that empowers Asian girls and kids of all ethnicities color to embrace their identities, fight for social justice, and be the revolution. For Joffe, this project feels just right. “I’m a storyteller and I love comedy. To be able mix those with social activism feels like the truest expression of who I am and who I want to be in the world,” Joffe said. The episodes involve kids enrolled as Young Rebels in “Radical Cram School” which engages in difficult topics like undocumented migration, the Black Lives Matter protest and gender identity. Some of the episodes have a format in which kids provide the dialogue for Wong, who lip-synchs a costumed reenactment on fun sets utilizing puppets. Joffe sees a current demand for comedic activism. “I think there is a call now for content that is giving a way for kids to talk about some of these issues they have been wondering about. Kids are going to protests and they are seeing things on TV and they are wondering, ‘Why are they wearing masks?’” “You can’t hide things from kids,” Joffe added. The show got its start last year with crowdfunding as financial support. It now has a fan club, so it raised even more money for its second season. Joffe is pitching the series as a TV show through “Yes. And Laughter Lab,” which allows the show to be viewed by film and entertainment professionals like Comedy Central as well as social justice organizations. Joffe has seen a shift in the nonprofit entertainment world. “More and more social justice organizations and nonprofits are wanting to hire comedy people to make content because they Director and Producer Jenessa Joffe (right) with Creator and Host Kristina Wong and Producers Anna Michelle Wang and Teddy Chao at the Season 2 premiere party for “Radical Cram School.” realize that people will pay more attention when it is entertainment. Maybe Jon Stewart was the first big one to do it,” Joffe said. “Comedy has the power to open people’s hearts and allow us to make a change internally that is non-violent and uplifting. That’s why I’m attracted to it, it’s pretty powerful actually,” she added. This current project aims to create space for voices often underrepresented in public conversations. The series can be used as a fun resource to spark conversation with kids about identity, civil rights, and progressive values. Radical Cram School zooms in on social changes through the lens of Asian-American identity and female empowerment but explores many hot topics. Joffe admitted that with this project, she feels good about her career as a director and producer. Her advice to young people interested in a career in film? “Start making films and never stop; that’s really all there is,” she stated. “You will find likeminded people by making films with others, and that’s how you build a community.” Joffe’s collection of videos can be viewed at www.jenessajoffe.com and Radical Cram School via Youtube, and on www.jenessajoffe.com/projects/ radical-cram-school.

Until rapid daily testing or vaccines are available, the upcoming school year is going to be an almost unrecognizable experience for students, parents, and teachers alike. Here are some tips to help parents come to terms with the above realities: Practice radical acceptance. The school experience as we knew it is over. Sounds harsh, I know, but it’s true. The sooner parents can accept this, the better. An attitude of acceptance will make it easier for parents to partner with teachers, administrators, and school districts that are doing their best to navigate a canoe through a typhoon. Live in the present moment. Literally no school on the planet can predict what the school year is going to look like, so it’s best to take things one day at a time. Don’t trip about the future because, well, there’s nothing we can do about it. Practice gratitude. When we can muster a sense of gratitude for what’s going well in our lives-- and there’s always something--it helps ease the frustration about what’s going not so well. Help your children do all of the above. We are all in this together, and when children see their parents practice acceptance, remain present, and give thanks, they will be reassured that things will be okay in the long run. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@ orindaacademy.org. • Now is the time for parents to accept the reality of what school is going to be like next year and to prepare themselves for it. Here are two important things for parents to understand: • School is going to feel completely different than it did before the pandemic. While kids may be back at school with their friends and classmates some of the time, their behavior will be regimented in a way that will feel unnatural. No doubt students have harbored fantasies about returning to school and having fun with their friends and engaging in their favorite activities; the reality will be much different than imagined, especially for older students. School is going to be radically altered, and this may be surprising, upsetting, and frustrating for many kids. The school year will be marked by uncertainty. • • • School will look different this year.

articles.text: Bruno Banuelos As middle schoolers with a lot of time on our hands, we want to make sure we are spending some of it helping others. We are lucky enough to have a program in our community that gives us the ability to give back to people who are less fortunate. The Piedmont Service Club (PSC), affiliated with Piedmont Community Service Crew (for high schoolers), connects middle schoolers to service opportunities in nearby neighborhoods. Under normal circumstances we participate in events that range from tutoring refugee kids to volunteering at local plant nurseries, among other activities. Since it is not currently safe to meet in person, the club has found new ways to serve the community. We decided to take advantage of an event that took place on June 6 which had crew members collectively cook a meal for 75 needy people, but cook from our own homes. Through a carefully planned sign-up, we chose which meal components we wanted to prepare. Then we packed up our food and drove it to the College Avenue Presbyterian Church in Oakland where it was packaged into individual dinner boxes so the recipients could take it with them. As we carried the food to the serving tables on the side of the church, we saw the homeless people sitting on the steps waiting to be served and felt sympathy for them. We all felt grateful for the opportunity to help them. Despite it being hard work, we felt a sense of reward knowing that we were helping provide meals to people who needed them. COVID-19 makes it difficult to find ways to volunteer right now, but this is one way to make a big impact on many people’s lives. It is more important now than ever that we come together as a community and support each other. Meet PSC – a service organization for middle schoolers By Klara Zietlow and Bruno Banuelos As middle schoolers with a lot of time on our hands, we want to make sure we are spending some of it helping others. We are lucky enough to have a program in our community that gives us the ability to give back to people who are less fortunate. The Piedmont Service Club (PSC), affiliated with Piedmont Community Service Crew (for high schoolers), connects middle schoolers to service opportunities in nearby neighborhoods. Under normal circumstances we participate in events that range from tutoring refugee kids to volunteering at local plant nurseries, among other activities. Since it is not currently safe to meet in person, the club has found new ways to serve the community. We decided to take advantage of an event that took place on June 6 which had crew members collectively cook a meal for 75 needy people, but cook from our own homes. Through a carefully planned sign-up, we chose which meal components we wanted to prepare. Then we packed up our food and drove it to the College Avenue Presbyterian Church in Oakland where it was packaged into individual dinner boxes so the recipients could take it with them. As we carried the food to the serving tables on the side of the church, we saw the homeless people sitting on the steps waiting to be served and felt sympathy for them. We all felt grateful for the opportunity to help them. Despite it being hard work, we felt a sense of reward knowing that we were helping provide meals to people who needed them. COVID-19 makes it difficult to find ways to volunteer right now, but this is one way to make a big impact on many people’s lives. It is more important now than ever that we come together as a community and support each other. If you find you want to use your time to help others, join the Piedmont Service Club, an organization for 6th, 7th and 8th graders, or if you are in high school, join the Piedmont Community Service Crew. Take the kids to see the 2,000 exotic, endangered and rescued animals at the beautiful zoo right by the ocean. Travel times to San Francisco may never be shorter. articles.text: Part 3 in a series High in the Piedmont hills, a sunny canyon is surrounded by eucalyptus trees and protected from the Bay breezes. It’s filled with houses now, but 130 years ago the United States Experimental Silk Culture Station was raising silkworms and promoting silkworm culture there. In the 1880s, there were only three types of cloth – cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government came to believe that silk could be produced in America as well and as cheaply as in China and began a program of funding and providing incentives to encourage the production of silk and the establishment of experimental silk producing stations. The Ladies’ Silk Culture Society of California believed the raising of silkworms and processing silk was an excellent way to provide hundreds of jobs for women, eliminate unemployment and add to the family income. Women could raise silkworms as a home industry or work at a silk culture station. The Society purchased 15 acres at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue (today’s Dudley and Littlewood). The silk promoters planted over three acres of mulberry trees and built a two-story, eight-room building to serve as a cocoonery. Piedmont residents called it the “Silk Farm.” was thriving and the property was expanded to seven acres. With $5,000 in federal aid from Congress in 1887 and in 1888, the Society soon employed 100 women at Piedmont’s silk farm. The Silk Culture Society also demonstrated the raising of silkworms and distributed silkworms and mulberry trees to those who wanted to raise them at home. Raising silkworms was labor intensive, however. Hundreds, if not thousands, of silkworms lived on trays filled with mulberry leaves at the Silk Farm. Silkworms ate their own weight 50 times over during their fast growing life. Women harvested the leaves, chopped them up and fed the voracious worms four times a day. In 35 days, the silkworms reached maturity and climbed onto wood racks to spin their cocoons. In just three or four days, the cocoons were ready to harvest. They were fumigated with sulphur to kill the silkworm pupa before it ate through the cocoon, cutting the silk thread. Fumigated cocoons could be stored for unreeling at a later time, providing year-round employment at the silk farm. To unreel the silk, the women softened the cocoons in hot water to separate the silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 2000-3000 feet long, and several filaments were later spun together to form one silk thread. The silk culture did not prosper in Piedmont. The canyon was not quite warm enough for the worms. Also, in the 1880s and 1890s silk workers in the U.S. would not work for less than one dollar per day. In contrast, workers in China were paid six cents per day. mulberry leaves before they are fed to the silkworms. The sign reads “U.S. Experimental Silk Culture Station, Oakland Cal.”

Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop named their popular store “Mulberry’s Market” in recognition of this little-known piece of Piedmont history. Their logo is a leaf with silkworm bites. Mulberry trees were also planted at the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Field in memory of the role they played in Piedmont’s early history. articles.text: Part 2 in a 3-part series. Previously published in the Post on March 28, 2018 Out of Portugal’s Bairrada region come two local gastronomic points of pride. One is the grape varietal baga, which requires a stubborn devotion on the part of wine producers and something of an open mind from the wine drinker. The other is leitão, an ovenroasted suckling pig. On our first day, a tasting with winemaker Mario Sergio, carrying on the third generation at Quinta das Bágeiras, turned into an invitation for lunch. At Mugasa, the hot spot to eat and pass an afternoon in the one-rotary town of Fogueira, we had the opportunity to sample Bairrada’s delicacies as they were meant to be – enjoyed together. Our caravan to Mugasa included Mario, his assistant Ana and his wife, their five friends visiting from Luxembourg and Basel, and 10 open bottles from that morning’s tasting. Our little international coalition, along with our oversized ice bucket that included a 1991 bottle of espumante (sparkling wine) took over a corner table of the top floor. Espumante finds a nice home in Bairrada, with its cool climate, clay soils and the acidic baga. The dishes came out family style, with the leitão as the centerpiece. It was a type of Thanksgiving, with the leitão taking the place of the turkey. All differences in nationality or language were set aside to come together in the commonality of sharing good food and wine. The next day was spent with Luís Pato, known as Bairrada’s “rebel” and something of a living legend for infusing traditional baga with enough modernity to bring this beloved, if somewhat difficult, grape to the world’s attention. Highly tannic, baga can be harsh when young and traditionally requires many years in the bottle to mellow and reveal its other notes of dark fruits. Most markets do not have such patience to allow baga its proper aging. The trick to softening a grape like baga is to add oak, always a controversial subject as it unleashes a long list of choices on the part of winemakers. appellation. Luís, a chemical engineer by training, took the lead in 1980 and began tinkering with modern techniques and outside methods. Wine is the ongoing pursuit of balance and Luís discovered how to polish baga’s edges so that In regions such as Bairrada, where oak is not part of the winemaking past, it is held in even greater skepticism, even suspicion or cynicism, as something that obscures the natural characteristics of the varietal. Luís managed to find the sweet spot. His father, João, became the first in the region, in 1970, to bottle under his own name after Bairrada was made a distinct everyone could see – and taste – the diamond in the rough. Kate Fratar is Court of Master Sommeliers certified sommelier and a former Post writer currently on special assignment in Portugal. Known as the “rebel” for having revolutionized Portugal’s Bairrada region, winemaker Luís Pato strikes his famous label pose joined by a rebel U.S. reporter from California. Espumante (sparkling wine) made in the traditional method finds a natural home in Bairrada, with its cool climate and clay soils. The cellars for Caves São João stretch far underground. articles.text: No fall sports; Football starts in Jan.; basketball, soccer now spring sports; boys’ & girls’ tennis to resume in spring Staff Photos Sports at Witter Field is officially set to return in January 2021, starting with football. On Monday, July 20, the California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) and North Coast Section (NCS) announced their sports calendar for the 2020-2021 school year. In an historic decision, the CIF ruled there will be no fall high school sports in California. Traditional fall sports, such as football, cross-country, water polo and volleyball, will begin in January 2021 The customary three sport seasons – fall, winter and spring – will be condensed into two seasons, late winter and spring. “In examining the most effective way to deliver Fall, Winter and Spring sports for the 2020- 2021 school year, the decision was made to condense three seasons of sport into two seasons, primarily to help with the spacing between particular sports and the overlap of certain sports between seasons,” wrote NCS commissioner Pat Cruikshank in a July 20 press release. Cruikshank noted that NCS is aiming at completing a full season for each sport, which, given its history of playoff scheduling blunders was refreshing to hear. This means sports like football will have 10 weeks to play 10 games. “It is important to point out that no reduction in the number of contests has taken place, meaning that a sport that generally allows 24 contests and 2 scrimmages during a normal season is still allowed the same number of contests. We hope that this allows all schools the opportunity to attempt to play a full schedule, albeit in some cases during a smaller window,” he continued. Fall sports that would typically begin action next month will have their official first date of practice set for Monday, DecemBaseball at Humphries Diamond will return in April for its start of play. ber 14. Each season is anticipated to stretch until late-March, including football, cross country, volleyball, and water polo. Although this will be the latest North Coast Section football playoffs in history, it is not uncharted waters for the Southern Section, which held its football championship in March 1919 due to the Spanish Flu. Spring sports’ start of practice is scheduled to for the last week of February and early March. Here’s a further look at the effects of the new CIF sports calendar: Get Ready for Spring: 10 sports, 17 varsity teams New spring sports: both soccer teams, girls’ tennis, and both basketball programs have their official start of practice set to February 22, March 8, and March 15 respectively. Other active sports at Piedmont from February 22 to lateJune will include: badminton, both swim teams, boys’ tennis, baseball, both golf teams, both lacrosse, softball, and track and field. Aside from the expected date change, the largest change will be girls’ tennis getting moved from fall to spring and being assigned to play a single season concurrently with boys’ tennis. Many questions arise, starting with the number of courts available, their locations, and how veteran coach Jim Landes and assistant coach Corey Reich will be able to coach two teams concurrently. He’s still waiting for the NCS plans on the variables for schools like Piedmont with limited court space. “They haven’t told me any details as to how the seasons are going to work in February,” said Landes. “It just says boys’ and girls’ seasons start then. They haven’t said whether it will be a co-ed team or somehow run them simultaneously. I don’t know,” said Landes. Should both boys’ and girls’ programs run at the same time in separate seasons, Landes points out an obvious factor that each coach at the school is worried about, field-space. “Running both teams is going to be difficult with only four courts. If we keep teams around the same size, I would need all four courts for each practice. We’d have to do one practice followed by another, and you have to consider time availability of the tennis courts and school hours for kids. I’ll just have to be flexible,” he said. Landes could see this resulting in the JV programs dissolving given the lack of space at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Landes is expecting 15 incoming freshmen to play when the season starts. “With this many kids, we may not be able to have a JV team. I’m worried about kids who may miss out on playing. We have a big turnout every year, normally I take 35-40 kids between JV and varsity for each team (girls and Lacrosse coach Carlton Chan discusses some of the inherent changes and problems with the State’s altered sports seasons. boys), “Now we’ll be lucky if we do half that,” he added. Field sports For field sports, it poses an interesting question. Who gets to use Witter Field in the spring – football, boys’ and girls’ soccer teams, boys’ and girls’ lacrosse teams, or track and field? PHS Coaches Meeting A meeting for all Piedmont High School coaches has been scheduled for this Friday, July 24, though no detailed notice has been received as of press time, including the time and format of the meeting, which will be virtual. “It’s interesting how the CIF is compressing the schedule in the spring. I’m not sure how they’re going to do it, basically sticking all the field-sports together around the same time,” commented girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan. required. crossroad.

Chubbock said he is unaware of why the CIF pushed for a full season in a shorter amount of time. “The statement said teams can still play the same number of games, which I thought was a little bit strange. I’m surprised they didn’t reduce the number of games, especially for sports like soccer where we don’t need 24 games and generally only play 18. You have football, then soccer right after it, then lacrosse soon after,” said Chubbock. Chubbock expects most of the games will be against local teams in the Western Alameda County Conference, which consists of 12 teams all with boys’ and girls’ soccer programs. Lacrosse – how will this work? For lacrosse, it’s a different story. It’s not as easy for Piedmont’s defending 2019 NCS championship boys’ and girls’ teams. The League (WACC) has just five boys’ teams and six girls’ teams, meaning some of the newer teams, such as Oakland Tech, Newark Memorial, and Washington could go without lacrosse. “There’s no way we’d only play amongst our conference,” said girls lacrosse coach Carlton Chan. “I could see playing within our local [area], like the Diablo Valley League with Miramonte, Acalanes, and Campolindo. There are certainly a lot of options, but they will require traveling,” Overlapping schedules All sports moving to 2021 also brings the issue of overlapping schedules amidst the most popular sports at the school. With Piedmont’s small enrollment size. Multi-sport athletes are the basis for the success of many of the school’s sports programs. For football, the NCS schedule will get underway on March 26-27 and run through April 10. But many members of the football team also play soccer, lacrosse, and baseball, raising the question of who will get left on the sidelines? Boys’ soccer’s first day of practice is February 22 and play set for April 4, meaning those transferring from the gridiron to the pitch will have only a few days to prepare. Lacrosse starts practice March 15 and plays games starting April 21. Those players will miss the first month of training after finishing their football season, another physical sport. Baseball, meanwhile, starts practice March 15, with games starting on April 25. “Having ample time to train and prepare for a season is a safety issue,” explained football coach Jerome Johnson. “Those are things that are up in the air right now until we know what practices are possible,” For girls’ sports, the notable overlapping of soccer, tennis, softball, and lacrosse will put many in a Catch 22. Each sport is set to be active from March through June, playing simultaneously. It means that some girls, who are key players on multiple teams may have to decide on a single sport during the season. “Some of these kids never would’ve thought they’d have to make this decision. People even play club sports, and there’s only so many hours in a day. Families will have to make some tough decisions, and we’ll be behind whatever they choose,” said Chubbock. Chubbock, who has had countless prominent student-athletes pursue college ambitions away from sports, noted the importance of allowing teenagers to have time to discover their passions. “No coaches at the school will put pressure on their students. It’s like three busses arriving at the same time, ‘Which one do I choose?’ We have to support their long-term plans. Are they learning a musical instrument, seeing a tutor twice a week, are they part of A Capella or the school play? As educational-athletic coaches, we need to really focus on the kids now more than ever,” he said. “I know it sounds cliché, but they are all obviously going through the toughest time,” Chubbock stated. “In the past, players like Ashley Nelson would have had a very tough time,” added Chan of the former PHS athlete who starred in both lacrosse and soccer. “It would be unfortunate if kids wanted to play more than one sport and weren’t allowed to. “You hope it doesn’t add stress,” he stated. Tennis at the Corey Reich Tennis Center will be packed this spring, as both boys’ and girls’ teams are scheduled to play simultaneous seasons. Continue working hard and surround yourself with people who make a positive impact on your life. Piedmont High Class of 2021 Aya Troyer is an incoming senior at Piedmont High with three years as a varsity runner on both the cross-country and track teams. She was 12th out of 60 runners at the WACC Cross-Country Championships with a time of 19:15.7 and placed 25th of 130 at the NCS Championship in 20:14.10; She’ll be among the captains of the Purple Train this year alongside Ellie Black, Adri McAullife, and Valerie Xiong. What is your workout program this summer? This summer, I have been primarily social-distance running with a couple of other teammates. We run between 3 to 9 miles about five times a week at Witter Field, Lake Merritt, Berkeley, and other places. I have been running between 15 and 30 miles per week for the last few months of quarantine. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals have been to maintain a solid mileage every week and avoid injury. Running during quarantine also gives me a safe way to leave the house and stay active. How are you measuring your development? I use the app “Strava” as well as “Xcstats” to record my times and distances of every run. It allows me to keep track of my workouts and also see the workouts my teammates have been doing. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am mostly running on my own or with one or two other teammates. However, I do receive workout ideas and plans from my coach. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Although I haven’t been able to run any races recently, I am glad that I have been able to continue running throughout the summer. Most years, I struggle to keep up my running during this time and that leads to injuries in the fall, so I am happy that I have been able to maintain my mileage. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Joining the cross country and track Everyone is friends with everyone on the team, so not being able to interact as much with these people during quarantine has been hard. I recommend that younger athletes try out for the team! U.C Berkeley Class of 1978 U.C Irvine Class of 1981 Peter Harvey began competing in triathlons at age 53 and fell in love with the sport after qualifying for the U.S.A National Team. He is a two-time U.S. National Champion and All-American in the Aquathlon. This is his 11th consecutive year on Team U.S.A, and has competed in the Aquathlon (bike and run) and Long Course Triathlons in seven different counties. He was training to compete in the 2020 Long course Championships in the Netherlands next month, but they were recently canceled due to the global pandemic. What is your workout program this summer? My training was just beginning in March with goals of competing in the Long Course Triathlon World Championships in Holland in September. The race was a 3 km swim, 160 km cycle and 30 km run and my goal was to get on the podium. Training was going well, but by mid-March, my gym closed due to COVID-19, so I had to rethink where to train. Instead of a pool, I used Monterey Bay and saw many dolphins, seals, and even whales. For those interested, the best place to swim is Lovers Point Park. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goals were to continue my fitness in preparation for our competition. How are you measuring your development? For long triathlons, one builds up endurance in all three categories by going longer by about 10 percent per week, and every fourth week taking it back down a bit in order to rest. As the training Christian Turner, PHS Class of 2017, is set to attend Bemidji State in Minnesota on a full baseball scholarship. CHRISTIAN TURNER Baseball Piedmont High Class of 2017 Bemidji State Class of 2023 Christian Turner, PHS Class of 2017, was recently recruited to join the Bemidji State baseball team after competing for Sierra College and Los Medanos College in California the last two years, He will be eligible for three years of baseball due to the shortened 2020 season. Turner graduated from Piedmont High as a four-year starting pitcher and amassed 146 strikeouts over his high school career. As the team’s Ace pitcher, Turner helped lead the Highlanders to the quarterfinals of the North Coast Section playoffs and nearly upset No. 1 ranked St. Mary’s. What is your workout program this summer? My new coaches at Bemidji State are requesting me to throw and stay consistent toward keeping my arm healthy for next season. I have been throwing long toss with my brother Julian, and doing bullpens with Piedmont coach Steve Thobe, while working out with my old pitching coach out in Pittsburg. I have also been lifting weights and have begun throwing live sessions against other ballplayers. What are your fitness goals for this summer? My goal is to work with different grips and arm angles to improve my slider, changeup, and fastball to be more consistent in the strike zone. How are you measuring your development? Staying in the strike zone with improved command and if I’m lifting heavier weights, I’m getting stronger. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working with some former coaches while I’m in the Bay Area. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I transferred from Sierra College last year to Los Medanos College in Pittsburg. In my limited innings pitched, I maintained a 0.0 ERA. Also, our Los Medanos team made it to the NorCal JUCO Championships and were among the final eight teams in the state. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Aya Troyer embarks on her senior season as a distance runner at Piedmont High. articles.text: For many in the football world, these fall months will be the first without the sport for the first time since their childhood. The California Interscholastic Federation announced on Monday that due to COVID-19, Fall sports will not begin until next January. So this week, with football at Witter Field arriving the latest in school history, we’re going back – way back. In 1976, coach Bob Muenter’s Highlanders were a powerhouse in the East Bay and winners of the school’s only football North Coast Section championship. It was Muenter’s final year as coach before becoming the school’s athletic director until 1983. Muenter, the namesake of the PHS Football’s Perpetual Spirit Award, led the football program from 1950-1976, building championship teams in 1959, 1960, 1965, and 1972. The team known as Muenter’s Boys went undefeated in 1976 in winning the Alameda County Athletic League title, then went on to win the North Coast Section 2A championship with a 14-7 win over the Sunset High of Hayward, a school that closed in 1990. Jeff Dreher was a part of the program, the honorary namesake of PHS’ Most Valuable Offensive Lineman award. Another Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer Jeff Haile was a member of the 1976 team. For this week’s look back in Piedmont sports history, we examine the NCS champion 1976 football team and its legendary coach, Bob Muenter member of the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame, running back and linebacker Jeff Haile, was the league’s Player of the Year in ‘76. Haile was also an All-League track and field athlete in shotput and is the school’s record holder in the event. He went on to play football and rugby for Stanford and was elected to the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2014. Thanks to footage on YouTube we can witness Haile barreling through the line in games against Encinal, San Leandro, Miramonte, and Albany on the way to the NCS Championship at Pacific Field in San Leandro, now Burrell Field. While Haile made headlines as Piedmont’s premier running back, Muenter’s defense was the hallmark with a rough, efficient style that is reminiscent of Jack Tatum’s and George Atkinson’s Oakland Raiders of the 1970s. Using a 4-3 defense that is still used by pro-teams, the Highlanders were seemingly in the backfield on every play, tackling quarterbacks and running backs with frequent blitzes. The school reached the NCS semifinals in 1981 in a 28-14 loss to San Lorenzo, and 2014 under coach Scott Coats after posting the school’s best record in football, 12-1 and a league championship (WACC Shoreline). Entered as the No. 2 seed, they were upset by No. 3 Justin-Siena 14-3. Two years later, 2016, the team also advanced to the NCS semifinals.
articles.title: A look back: the 1976 NCS Champion football team

articles.text: It’s been an offseason unlike any other for football teams throughout the country. So far this summer, NFL, college, and prep-teams have all been in the same boat: processing information and learning, but none of it on a football field due to the continuing coronavirus pandemic. “We’re doing as much Zoom as possible given it’s a non-contact situation. We’re doing a lot of teaching online; that’s how we’ve been doing our summer prepping,” explained PHS head coach Jerome Johnson “It’s really educational football; it’s all about teaching, all about the fundamentals and principals of offense and defense,” said Johnson, who is set to embark on his second season at the helm. The name constantly heard with sports’ programs this summer: Zoom, the virtual meeting app designed for camera-based chat rooms. Basically, every football team – big to small, professional to amateur – have been utilizing Zoom for their sessions. “We can really go step-bystep. As weird as it may seem, it’s almost better, because we have a captive audience. Kids are engaged, ask a lot of questions and we can go over so many nuances of teaching the game of football,” described Johnson. While at this time last year, helmets and pads would be cracking at Witter Field with annual scrimmages at Laney College and Miramonte. Now, without Xs and Os being taught on the sidelines or on a chalkboard, student-athletes are putting their brains to work instead of legs. “Now the teachable moments are unique. Usually during the summer, kids have a lot of open space and are more engaged with each other instead of paying attention within a classroom setting,” said Johnson. “The advantage of what we’re doing is putting players in certain situations and have them draw up the offensive or defensive scheme based on what we’re asking them. When you put them in scenarios mentally, we hope it will translate when we hit the field,” he added. At this time last year, Piedmont would be participating in summer scrimmages. Pictured here is senior wide receiver Alex Hilton working against an Oakland High defensive back in a scrimmage last year. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! We need to have time to teach our kids how to form-tackle and angle-tackle properly because these are things that are a safety issue. We need that,” he emphasized Football will embark on its first official day of practice on December 14 with January 6 as the date of the first game. Due to the physical nature of football, Johnson was clear that necessary preparation for a season has the utmost importance to avoid injuries. “We need that time to teach; that’s something we’re concerned about. The NFL has a heads-up program and I’ve been a part of that for years. I believe “Eyes to the Skies” is very important to get kids in position to tackle properly. It’s a safety issue; you can’t put a kid right onto the practice field and think he’s ready to play in a game. That’s not how football works,” reiterated Johnson. “What we’re instructing kids to do is sending out as many highlights and clips as they can. We’ve talked to numerous coaches and many of them are concerned about their careers and students may go into a dead-period where they don’t hear from them,” explained Johnson. “The things we are getting our kids to do is to promote themselves. There’s only so much time in the day for recruiters to do things now,” he added. NCS football playoffs will overlap with the start of play for soccer on April 4. Lacrosse, baseball, and tennis start practices in mid-March. This means teams could be at risk of losing athletes coming in without time to train. “I understand if a student’s spirit is on another sport, we’re here to support all of what our kids want to do. Kids want to play multiple sports, and it certainly could be difficult on some families. Hopefully it can lead to more conversations between students, parents, and other coaches. It’s an unprecedented time; we’re a small school, but we’ll work it out,” said Johnson.
articles.title: Piedmont football underway with virtual sessions

articles.text: Each week, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English invites playwrights to join him for a half-hour conversation about playwriting, inspiration, and the future of theatre. Playwright Aaron Posner will join English for a discussion tomorrow, Thursday, at 7 p.m. Posner is an American playwright and theater director and is co-founder of the Arden Theatre Company in Philadelphia. He has directed over 250 productions at major regional theater companies across the country. He has won many awards, including five Helen Hayes Awards, two Barrymore Awards, the Outer Critics Circle Award, the John Gassner Prize, and the Eliot Norton Award. Posner has adapted novels as plays, and later created new variations of classic plays, including some by Shakespeare and Chekhov. Among Posner’s most wellknown adaptions are The Chosen, Playwright Aaron Posner based on Chaim Potok’s 1967 novel of the same name, and My Name is Asher Lev, also based on Potok’s 1972 novel. Posner is also an adjunct professor of acting and directing at American University in Washington, D.C. To view tomorrow’s livestream, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/fireside-chats/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse fireside chat with Aaron Posner on July 23

articles.text: The Oregon Shakespeare Festival, having cancelled its 2020 season due to Covid-19, is offering on-demand streaming service with full-length plays from its 2020 season. The performances will be accessible on laptops, tablets and mobile phones. This season’s offerings began with The Copper Children by Karen Zacharias, and continues with the Shakespearian comedy, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, which ends today, July 22. The Festival has emphasized that its productions are not readings or previews; rather, they are shown in their entirety with a full cast of OSF actors and were filmed on stages during their short runs earlier this year. The intent is to give patrons a live theater experience with the cameras having been placed directly in front of the stage so the show is experienced as if you are sitting in a front row seat. This is a pilot program, with plans are underway for additional offerings in the months ahead. The productions are handled by Uscreen, a provider of video-on-demand services. Subscribers will be able to access the play at a cost of $15 per show by setting up an account on the hosting site. Information can be found online by searching Oregon Shakespeare Festival or email OSF directly at streaming@osfashland.org, an email established for the purpose of assisting subscribers with access to content. A list of FAQs can be found online at Oregon Shakespeare Festival on their website. Photo by Jenny Graham, Oregon Shakespeare Festival. A Midsummer Night’s Dream (2020): Daniel T. Parker (Nick Bottom), Michele Mais (Tom Snout), Cristofer Jean (Francis Flute). L M B I N T E R I O R S .C O M | 51 0 . 5 3 1 .8 4 3 8

articles.text: Michael Stehr Art lecture on Sunday, July 26 Mike & patron Join art historian Michael Stehr for a Zoom adventure to Paris and a visit to the Louvre. The illustrated lecture will be a detailed walk through one of the world’s greatest museums. The art lecture will take place this Sunday, July 26 at 5 p.m. on Zoom. Download the Zoom app to join the lecture: https://zoom. us/ To join the Zoom event, click on: https://us02web.zoom. us/j/84959657863?pwd=UGx- 1RDdzYUhBR2ZKeDBOOGRramxZdz09. Meeting ID: 849 5965 7863. Password: 569213. A visit to the Louvre is a highlight of any visit to Paris, and certainly a high point in the life of any traveler. When one stands before I.M. Pei’s Glass Pyramid, what awaits are encounters with some of the greatest achievements yielded by some of the most talented craftsman ever to walk the face of the Earth. Michelangelo, Leonardo, David, and Corot. The Slaves, The Mona Lisa, The Oath of the Horatii, and the View of the Roman Forum. It’s an impressive guest list, to be sure. A visit to a museum of this scale can be daunting. Join Michael Stehr for a 50-minute tour of the Louvre. Stehr will celebrate this incredible location by highlighting his favorite works, spanning all three wings of the museum. For more information click on: piedmontcenterforthearts.org.
articles.title: A Day at the Louvre

articles.text: Ragazzi Boys Chorus As a farewell performance from the graduating senior class of the Ragazzi Boys Chorus Young Men’s Ensemble, the chorus chose Shenandoah by James Erb for their final virtual performance. The song was first sung as an ensemble when they were freshman four years ago. In March, rehearsals for the Ragazzi Boys Chorus Ensemble, located in Redwood City, were abruptly halted due to the coronavirus pandemic. Like many other ensembles, the group continued to rehearse virtually. Singers range in age from 5 to 18. The Grammy-Award winning chorus has been training singers in both treble and changed-voice repertoire since 1987. View their final performance on YouTube at https://www. youtube.com/watch?time_continue=6&v=OZ3tD1RQv8g&feature=emb_title.
articles.title: Ragazzi Boys Chorus presents Shenandoah

articles.text: Photo by Cory Weaver German soprano Nadja Michael sings the lead in Janacek’s The Makropulos Case. Each week, the San Francisco Opera streams an archived opera as part of its “Opera is On” virtual streaming series. This Saturday, July 25, Leos Janacek’s The Makropulos Case will be streaming for 24 hours. More than 300 years ago an alchemist named Makropulos was employed by the Hapsburg Emperor Rudolf II to create an elixir to give the Emperor eternal life. Not trusting Makropulos’s finished potion, the Emperor forced him to administer it to his own daughter, Elina. When she became seriously ill Makropulos was put in prison, but Elina eventually recovered and escaped. What was not apparent at the time was that the elixir actually worked, granting Elina some 300 additional years of life. During the time that she has lived, Elina has had many identities, many names (always with the initials E.M.), and many affairs. One of her more passionate affairs was with Baron Josef Ferdinand Prus, by whom she had a son. While Prus left his estate in writing to this illegitimate son, the will has long gone missing and there has ensued a century-long dispute between two branches of the family, Gregor and Prus, over rights to the estate. The opera, originally premiered during the 2016–17 season, is sung in Czech with English supertitles. To view this weekend’s upcoming opera, visit https://sfopera. com/opera-is-on/?gclid=Cj0KCQjw9b_4BRCMARIsADMUIyrjmT3GiYT7kJ28ktDf5CQl23ZdBV36DGcghIUs_PUUv53FsP- 3m864aAoTTEALw_wcB. Donors and subscribers can still stream past productions of Mephistopheles, The Capulets and the Montagues, Moby-Dick, and Lucrezia Borgia by logging on to their account on SFopera.com.
articles.title: SF Opera streaming The Makropulos Case on July 25

articles.text: Photo by Barbara Mallon Erin Sanzero (;eft) as Lucia and Christopher Bengochea as Edgardo in Livermore Valley Opera’s production of Lucia di Lammermoor. Livermore Valley Opera is streaming archival premieres for patrons while its doors remain closed due to COVID-19. You can view their 2015 season finale, a rendition of Donizetti’s Lucia di Lammermoor, free on Livermore Valley Opera’s YouTube channel. The opera, noted for its complex plot and exceptionally lyrical score in the bel canto tradition, was performed in Livermore’s Bankhead Theatre. Conductor Alexander Katsman led the opera with a small orchestra and a capacity crowd of 500. The opera was directed by Candace Evans. By Allyson Aleksey Each week, the San Francisco Opera streams an archived opera as part of its “Opera is On” virtual streaming series. This Saturday, July 25, Leos Janacek’s The Makropulos Case will be streaming for 24 hours. More than 300 years ago an alchemist named Makropulos was employed by the Hapsburg Emperor Rudolf II to create an elixir to give the Emperor eternal life. Not trusting Makropulos’s finished potion, the Emperor forced him to administer it to his own daughter, Elina. When she became seriously ill Makropulos was put in prison, but Elina eventually recovered and escaped. What was not apparent at the time was that the elixir actually worked, granting Elina some 300 additional years of life. During the time that she has lived, Elina has had many identities, many names (always with the initials E.M.), and many affairs. One of her more passionate affairs was with Baron Josef Ferdinand Prus, by whom she had a son. While Prus left his estate in writing to this illegitimate son, the will has long gone missing and there has ensued a century-long dispute between two branches of the family, Gregor and Prus, over rights to the estate. The opera, originally premiered during the 2016–17 season, is sung in Czech with English supertitles. articles.text: Liam Neeson and Julianne Moore in a scene from Chloe. Movie review by Chris Honoré To suggest that Chloe is simply an erotic thriller is to diminish what is an intriguing film – a character study and examination of a woman’s attempt to bridge what seems an insurmountable distance between herself and her husband. At its center, the story is not about seduction but about abiding loneliness, perhaps best captured by those stark scenes where Catherine (Julianne Moore), a successful gynecologist in Toronto, stands looking out the window at the street below, gazing at her husband as he sits in his den working on his computer, and as she observes her patients in the waiting room. She is suffused with a feeling of disconnection, as if all she has known is now inaccessible, emotionally elusive. She has grown older. She feels less desirable. Her viewpoint has grown clinical. Because she and her husband, David (Liam Neeson), a professor of music, married some 20 years, have lost contact, and she observes him being flirtatious with his students and with other women, she suspects he is having an affair. What she does at this moment, at this intersection in her life, is profoundly human and understandable, but immensely destructive. She hires a young prostitute, Chloe (Amanda Seyfried), to test her husband’s fidelity and sets in motion a series of events filled with unintended consequences. She she insists that Chloe report back to her the details of her time with David. Unexpectedly, Catherine finds herself in the position of a voyeur, more comfortable with hearing about and imagining the intimacy shared by Chloe and David than searching for a path toward intimacy herself. But then isn’t her voyeurism the handmaiden to pornography? Ultimately she finds nothing satisfying about hearing about David and Chole, and yet she cannot stop herself. She might have hired a private detective, of course, but then perhaps she was looking for something else, something she divines from the outset. There are no substitutes, no amount of triangulation will ever point the way back, though Catherine tries – at great risk and potentially great harm, to herself and her family. Chloe has its moments as a studied thriller, and it spirals nicely toward a taught conclusion. Some might find the premise far-fetched, balking at the idea that any professional, highly educated woman would make such an extreme choice. But an aspect of truth is seen in Moore’s portrayal of Catherine that sustains the film, a portrayal supported by the fine performances of Liam Neeson and Amanda Seyfried, who is perfectly cast in the role of the young seductress Chloe. Chloe. Starring Julianne Moore, Amanda Seyfried, Liam Neeson and Max Thierot. Directed by Atom Egoyan. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on March 31, 2010. Amanda Seyfried and Julianne Moore in Chloe.

articles.text: Jennifer Lawrence in a scene from Winter’s Bone. Mobie review by Chris Honoré The first stark images of Winter’s Bone are of two children playing in a yard, surrounded by trees winter bare, the sunlight diffuse, without warmth. The house is more a shack than not, wood frame and hard used. Dead cars and appliances sit deep in weeds. The setting is a hamlet in the southern Missouri Ozarks, a place apart, where people – hard scrabble, insular – live on the frayed edges of society. Many are off the grid, suspicious, even paranoid, their source of income the cooking and sale of methamphetamine. The children in the yard, a brother and sister, are the siblings of Ree Dooly, 17 (played by Jennifer Lawrence), who carries the full weight of her family. Her mother is paralyzed by a deep depression and her father, Jessup, recently arrested for cooking meth, has just made bond and been released from jail. What Ree soon learns from the local sheriff is that in order to post bond, Jessup has put up the house and the surrounding acreage, some of it rich with timber, as collateral. If he fails to make his court date all will be forfeited. She and her family will be homeless. Ree sets out to find her father, a journey that takes her to the center of the Dolly clan where she discovers that family ties will only protect her to a certain point and no further. She’s told to leave it alone by men and women who look at her with cold eyes and grimly set mouths, their secrets impenetrable. For Ree, the stakes are high, finding her father crucial, and she’s prepared to risk all. Winter’s Bone is a remarkable film, one of the best thus far in a paper thin, spring-summer season. The performance by Lawrence is astonishing as she captures with a steely grittiness the intractable place in which Ree finds herself. As a character, Ree is the anchor of her family, a person who faces a reality she barely understands. Lawrence demonstrates an uncanny subtlety and power in her portrayal, considering that the dialogue is laconic, stripped of all excess language. So authentic is this film that it borders on cinema-verite’. As the story unfolds, it’s easy to forget the actors are not locals but are delivering exceptional performances. At its core, Winter’s Bone is a woman’s film. For all of their truculence and need to control, leavened with a subtext of violence, the men are almost peripheral. It’s the women, and, of course, Ree, who are central to the events as they slowly, ominously develop. It’s the women who place Ree in harm’s way. This fact gives the story an interesting and compelling dimension. If you love movies that illuminate, films that are an unsettling and penetrating window into the human condition, Winter’s Bone is not to be missed. Winter’s Bone. Starring Jennifer Lawrence, John Hawkes, Dale Dickey and Garret Dillahunt. Directed by Debra Granik. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on July 28, 2010. Jennifer Lawrence in a scene from Winter’s Bone.

articles.text: An image from the film How to Train Your Dagon: The Hidden World. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World is the last installment of what has been a very successful franchise, first released in 2010. This final wrap may lack the punchy and fresh stories of the first two, but it is beautifully animated with glorious scenes of dragons in flight, all circling the island refuge of Berk. This medieval village is home to a cohort of Vikings, now led by the aspirational chief, Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), and supported by his girlfriend, Astrid (America Ferrera). It is filled with characters both young and old and is wonderful. Hiccup’s best friend, Toothless, who is a special breed of alpha dragon, is alive and well and the two still ride the skies as one. The computer graphics are breathtaking. This is distinctly not your grandfather’s painstaking, Disneyesque animation. Naturally there is a villain, a malevolent dragon hunter called Grimmel (F. Murray Abraham) who speaks with a strange accent. His mission is to kill Toothless and take control of the dragons living peacefully in Berk. Luckily, he’s a bit of a klutz – good at planning, not so much at execution. Unexpectedly, two budding love stories surface. One is telegraphed in the previous films, a romance between Hiccup and Astrid (they’re now talking marriage). The other is between Toothless and a kindred young female dragon, who, unlike the obsidian Toothless, is white as the driven snow. I wondered how these two story lines would work since the audience is decidedly young, not even teenagers. I did find the dialogue charming, nicely contemporized, though I don’t think Hiccup ever says or even whispers the word “Dude!” The final act, which takes Hiccup and Astrid to the Hidden World, is remarkable – a veritable feast of color. Having found this place at the edge of the world, Hiccup realizes that there is a safe place for Toothless and his love interest. Separation is now inevitable – or maybe not. There’s enough in this film for the youngsters to have the chance to fully say goodbye to a nifty crew of dragon riders and their dragons. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World. Animated with the voices of Jay Baruchel, America Ferrera, and F. Murray Abraham. Directed by Dean DuBlois. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG. Originally published in the Post on March 6, 2019.
articles.title: How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The template for Brave is decidedly familiar, which is surprising for Pixar, a studio that has pioneered computer-generated animation with original and compelling stories (Wall-E, Ratatouille, The Incredibles). Brave is, nevertheless, a beautifully rendered work, an example of detailed and sumptuous animation that creates breathtaking scenes as its heroine, Princess Merida (Kelly Macdonald), rides her Clydesdale Angus through the emerald green countryside of 10th century Scotland. What makes Brave familiar is the tension between the headstrong teenager, Merida – wildly spirited, with tangled persimmon-colored hair, a deadeye archer, possessing an unyielding wish to fashion her own destiny – and her mother, Queen Elinor (Emma Thompson), who wishes only that her rebellious daughter behave as a demure, corseted, wimple-covered princess should. And, of course, marry one of the doofus sons from a neighboring clan. Merida, ever willful, forgetting that she should always be careful what she wishes for, changes her mother’s life, literally, with horrifying and unintended consequences with the help of a witch she encounters deep in the woods. It’s at this point that the narrative veers off in an entirely new direction that proves to be less satisfying than anticipated. Meanwhile, the clans, always at odds, are a bit too slapstick. Merida’s father, King Fergus (Billy Connolly), is preposterously large and thick-headed. It all becomes a bit silly at times. On the plus side, Merida is the first female lead for Pixar, and she is both marvelous and maddening. But not to forget that the audience is young, embracing, and ready for an adventure. And make no mistake: Brave is an adventure. Brave. Animation. Starring the voices of Kelly Macdonald, Billy Connelly, Emma Thompson and Julie Walters. Directed by Brenda Chapman and Mark Andrews. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Originally published in the Post on June 26, 2012. A still shot from the Pixar movie Brave. articles.text: Let me pose a question to you. Is classical music relevant in today’s world? The devotees are diminishing and with it, the market. Those are the facts. So, what is so popular in pop music? Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc, ad infinitum. And don’t forget one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. And, as for lyrics, a steady stream of profanity - all spoken in monotone. Not sung. Monotone speech. Wow! The knock against classical music is that it is boring. Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. I ask you, which is boring? A friend observed that pop music always accents the second beat. How boring is that? one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. Compare the utter predictability (i.e. boring) rhythm of pop music with multi- hued classical music. Take, for example, a 3-beat rhythm. The nobility of the Polonaise, the whirling lightness of the quick Viennese waltz, the elegant regularity of the Minuet, the second beat emphasis of the slow Sarabande, or the third-beat emphasis of the Mazurka… and that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Versus... Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. Psychiatrists and psychologists have studied the effects of classical music on the general public. The “Mozart effect” is not a psychological fantasy. Listening to classical music actually makes us smarter. It does. Playing it is even better. While pop music (whether rock, heavymetal, hip-hop, or rap) beats us into intellectual Dementia Pugilistica, classical music, by its very nature, encourages thought and imagination. For those of you who think classical music is boring, I will leave you to your Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc ad infinitum. As for me, give me Bach and Mozart and Beethoven. NEXT WEEK: Where do we go from here? The nuances of nature. Are they needed in music? Just listen to Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6, the “Pastorale.”
articles.title: An open letter to pop music fans

articles.text: Annual soirée, concet & auction goes online this year The Community Women’s Orchestra annual Soirée, titled Grand Pause this year, will be held Sunday, August 9, at 3 p.m. It will be streamed live on YouTube and Facebook. The Community Women’s Orchestra ( CWO) has been a part of the East Bay’s cultural life for over 35 years. It was founded as a community orchestra in 1985 and has grown to include over 60 musicians. It is the only allwoman orchestra in California. CWO, a non-profit, is passionately committed to engage, inspire, and celebrate women in classical music. Our efforts would not be successful without the help of our donors. CWO’s fundraising efforts provide critical operating support to present our season of concerts and education and community engagement activities. Without support from individuals, foundations, companies, and government, our season would not be possible. For more information, see the CWO website at: https://www. communitywomensorchestra. org/.
articles.title: Community Women’s Orchestra benefit Concert on Aug. 9

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley has launched a series of weekly live broadcasts, “Aurora Connects”, online. A broadcast will go live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. An upcoming episode featuring Maggie Whitaker and Cliff Carruthers will premiere this Friday, July 24. Whitaker is a costume designer with numerous Broadway, film, television, and international credits. Carruthers is a sound designer with a particular talent for working on plays and creating complex sound worlds for complicated texts. He is currently a lecturer at San Francisco State University, and previously lectured at Stanford University. Each episode is hosted by Aurora’s Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Costello was appointed artistic director in 2019 following a national search. At Aurora, he has directed, among others, Exit Strategy, The Importance of Being Earnest, Detroit, and the award-winning world premiere of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day. Williams has been Aurora’s Associate Artistic Director since August 2019. An Oakland-native, she was Artistic Associate and a resident artist at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival for six seasons. To view the upcoming episode via YouTube, visit https://www. auroratheatre.org/auroraconnects. You can listen to Aurora Connects on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Google Podcasts by visiting http://auroraconnects.buzzsprout. com/.
articles.title: Maggie Whitaker and Cliff Carruthers featured this Friday

articles.text: Jazz vocalist Stella Heath, Reich & Fabricante this Sunday Piedmont Piano has launched a series of concerts being streamed live, titled “The Showroom Sessions.” Headlining an online concert this Sunday, July 26, at 5 p.m. are jazz vocalist Stella Heath, with pianist & accordionist Rob Reich and bass player Daniel Fabricant. Heath will take the listener on a transatlantic journey of song. From the Great American Songbook to French Chanson, the group will cover music from the 1920’s through 1960’s, including works by Gershwin, Berlin, Rodgers and Hart, Edith Piaf and Serge Gainsbourg. Singing since the age of eight, Heath has been strongly influenced by the music of Billie Holiday. She grew up in the North Bay and before creating a career as a jazz vocalist, studied acting at Interlochen Arts Academy and Syracuse University, where she Jazz vocalist Stella Heath will hep inaugurate Piedmont Piano’s series of virtual concerts. received a degree in classical acting and cultural geography. The live sessions, produced by Jordan Perlman, are streaming every week from Piedmont Piano on San Pablo Avenue. For more information, visit https://www.piedmontpiano. com/calendar/2020/7/26/stella-heath-rob-reich-daniel-fabricant.
