pages.text: 20 Wednesday, July 22, 2020 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet An open letter to pop music fans By Joseph Gold Let me pose a question to you. Is classical music relevant in today’s world? The devotees are diminishing and with it, the market. Those are the facts. So, what is so popular in pop music? Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc, ad infinitum. And don’t forget one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. And, as for lyrics, a steady stream of profanity - all spoken in monotone. Not sung. Monotone speech. Wow! The knock against classical music is that it is boring. Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. I ask you, which is boring? A friend observed that pop music always accents the second beat. How boring is that? one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. Compare the utter predictability (i.e. boring) rhythm of pop music with multi- hued classical music. Take, for example, a 3-beat rhythm. The nobility of the Polonaise, the whirling lightness of the quick Viennese waltz, the elegant regularity of the Minuet, the second beat emphasis of the slow Sarabande, or the third-beat emphasis of the Mazurka… and that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Versus... Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. Psychiatrists and psychologists have studied the effects of classical music on the general public. The “Mozart effect” is not a psychological fantasy. Listening to classical music actually makes us smarter. It does. Playing it is even better. While pop music (whether rock, heavymetal, hip-hop, or rap) beats us into intellectual Dementia Pugilistica, classical music, by its very nature, encourages thought and imagination. For those of you who think classical music is boring, I will leave you to your Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc ad infinitum. As for me, give me Bach and Mozart and Beethoven. NEXT WEEK: Where do we go from here? The Community Women’s Orchestra now has more than 60 musicians. articles.text: Maestro Michael Morgan in rehearsals with Oakland Symphony musicians for Louise Farrenc’s Symphony No. 3. Oakland Symphony is offering a weekly, archival concert series featuring past performances, to debut every Friday at 6 p.m. This week’s episode is Louise Farrenc’s Symphony No.3 in G minor, Op. 36, originally premiered on March 22, 2019 at the Paramount Theatre. The selected music is from the Romantic Period – in the case of Farrenc, the early Romantic Period. “Over the years, we’ve played a series of pieces we’ve called lost romantics,” explained the symphony’s artistic director Michael Morgan. “I’ve heard Louise Farrenc described as ‘criminally underplayed’ and I agree. A revered teacher and performer at the Paris Conservatory, it is said that on the success of this symphony, she demanded and finally got pay that was equal to her male colleagues.” The symphony was originally written by Farrenc in 1847. You can listen to this week’s archival concert at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/repast/.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony opens archives with “rePAST” concert series

articles.text: Opera San Jose is presenting Schumann’s Dichterliebe with baritone Eugene Brancoveanu Opera San Jose is currently presenting a recital of Robert Schumann’s Dichterliebe (“A Poet’s Love”) for virtual streaming through August 15. The opera will feature resident artist, baritone Eugene Brancoveanu, and resident conductor Christopher James Ray. “The timeless beauty of the music speaks for itself,” Brancoveanu said. “It is at one turn minimalist before raging into a full orchestral sounding polyphony of boisterous emotions and eruptions.” Tickets are “pay what you choose,” with a recommended $15 - $50 per household. Viewing instructions will be accessible after an order confirmation. The run time is approximately 30 minutes, followed by a 15-minute interview with the artists. Opera San Jose is utilizing its Fred Heiman Digital Media Studio, which can serve as both a rehearsal and chamber performance space and be streamed to remote audiences. Dichterliebe is the first concert to be streamed in this way. “With this new space we will be able to safely perform smaller scale operas with theatrical lighting, sets, and appropriate musical accompaniment, utilizing stateof-the-art cameras and audio equipment to create works that can be enjoyed by at-home audiences. This thrilling new venture will enable us to continue our work as an incubator for emerging artists and producer of accessible, world-class operatic performances, while maintaining mitigation efforts to avoid the spread of COVID-19,” said General Director Khori Dastoor. To view the opera, visit https:// www.operasj.org/dichterliebe/.
articles.title: Opera San Jose streams Schumann’s Dichterliebe

articles.text: Brock the parrot sings the blues with San Francisco-based trio Dirty Cello. The Oakland Zoo, after an unprecedented 121-day closure, will reopen to the general public on July 29. Receiving a variance from Alameda County and the State of California to classify the zoo as an outdoor museum was the biggest hurdle to re-opening the zoo, confirmed Neeta Balram, Public Information Manager with the Alameda County Public Health Department. “The Healthcare Services Agency [in Alameda], on the direction of County Board of Supervisors, submitted a letter to the state to consider the zoo an outdoor museum rather than a zoo,” she said. At the time, the Oakland Zoo was the only zoo in the state that could not re-open. The county needed approval from the state after it appeared on the state’s COVID-19 monitoring list, signifying a spike in cases. When East Bay residents learned of this hurdle, they jumped at the chance to support the zoo’s reclassification as an outdoor museum. Caephren McKenna, a firstgrade teacher at Frank Otis Elementary School in Alameda, created a petition on change.org urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to allow Oakland Zoo to reopen as an outdoor museum. The petition quickly collected 2,480 signatures. “Our entire class, 100 students, goes to the zoo every year. It’s definitely a highlight for the kids. It’s a great resource and educational place for the public,” McKenna said. She also confirmed that saving the zoo was near to her heart because of her personal interest in the zoo’s sanctuary efforts. “The Oakland Zoo is home to many animals that have been rescued from being euthanized or orphaned, including mountain lions, grizzly bears, and black bears. It also houses a pair of gray wolves that had pups in May 2019,” she said. Managed by the Conservation Society of California, the nonprofit Oakland Zoo has invested over $1 million in contributions supporting its 25 partnering conservation organizations in saving animal species worldwide. As an accredited member of the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA), the Zoo is part of the largest conservation organization in the nation. 230 AZA-accredited zoo and aquarium institutions contribute over $160 million every year to wildlife conservation. articles.text: Back Yard Miracle – the ups and downs of hillside retaining walls When building outdoor landscaping projects in hillside settings, there are a number of challenges – along with amazing possibilities – that one should consider. This detailed example of a recent extensive retaining wall and patio project should show how these issues came to light and how they were dealt with over the course of a yearlong project. The initial scope of work was to replace a 9-foot tall block retaining wall and patio that was beginning to fail. This impressive home in the Oakland hills was rebuilt after the fire, but as is typical, things like drainage work and retaining walls in the yard were a lower priority compared to the main house. Poor detailing and inexpensive construction were not holding up to the test of time. Without any reinforcement or real footings, this large block wall was starting to shift downhill and the patio had sunk, exaggerated by a lack of appropriate drainage. During the design phase the owner decided to create a lower patio as well. This required another 9-foot wall, but the planning and zoning department would only allow a 6-foot height for any new walls. The plan was to build a set of new reinforced curved concrete walls and stairs that were faced with stone. This required a fair amount of engineering to start. pages.text: Wednesday, July 22, 2020 23 Can You Dig It? Back Yard Miracle – the ups and downs of hillside retaining walls By Jim Gardner When building outdoor landscaping projects in hillside settings, there are a number of challenges – along with amazing possibilities – that one should consider. This detailed example of a recent extensive retaining wall and patio project should show how these issues came to light and how they were dealt with over the course of a yearlong project. The initial scope of work was to replace a 9-foot tall block retaining wall and patio that was beginning to fail. This impressive home in the Oakland hills was rebuilt after the fire, but as is typical, things like drainage work and retaining walls in the yard were a lower priority compared to the main house. Poor detailing and inexpensive construction were not holding up to the test of time. Without any reinforcement or real footings, this large block wall was starting to shift downhill and the patio had sunk, exaggerated by a lack of appropriate drainage. During the design phase the owner decided to create a lower patio as well. This required another 9-foot wall, but the planning and zoning department would only allow a 6-foot height for any new walls. We decided to create a shorter 3-foot wall at the front for a planting area, with a 6-foot wall at the bottom of the lower patio. The plan was to build a set of new reinforced curved concrete walls and stairs that were faced with stone. This required a fair amount of engineering to start. The new walls required reinStonework was installed. Photos by Jim Gardner Construction The plan was to build new reinforced concrete walls and stairs that were faced with stone. Installation of a membrane, piping and gravel for drainage. READ IT IN THE POST Custom railings were added. forced concrete piers averaging a depth of 13 feet. Unfortunately, the drilling was time consuming, ironically because the soil was good and hard, with the drilling slowing substantially below the 9’ mark. Since drillers are paid by the hour, this added to the cost as the last 4-feet or so and took about twice as long to drill as the first 9 feet. Because of the steep rear yard and limited access via stairs from the front, the holes had to be drilled with a portable rig, which was slow and time consuming to move around. The drilling alone took around 2 months to complete. Once the piers were reinforced and concrete was poured, we began the process of installing the rebar and forms for the footings to the concrete walls connecting between the piers. As you can in the photos, the amount of steel was extensive. All of the materials had to be brought to the site down a long stairway on one side of the house. To facilitate that process, we installed a series of large plastic tubes to bring material down to the job (primarily gravel) and larger 24” diameter tubes at the bottom of the site to carry dirt down to the street below and into a large dump trailer. At the bottom of the site the yard dropped off at an extreme slope. After excavating for the lower 6-foot wall we realized that we were too close to the edge of the drop-off on one side, so we had to add a fourth wall, 6-feet tall on one end, that was tied into our original lower wall to help stabilize it. By the end of the job, we ended up drilling over 50 piers in total. Once the new walls were poured, we installed a membrane, piping and gravel for drainage. Conduits were installed for lighting and irrigation. The spaces behind the walls were backfilled, and reinforced concrete was poured for the patio and stairs. Stonework was installed to face the upper 2 walls, along with slate for the patio. Stone caps were fabricated on-site for the walls. Custom railings were fabricated and installed for the taller walls and stairs. Landscaping, lighting and irrigation were put in as the final touches. Thoughts upon completion There are several takeaways from this work that are important to consider for hillside structural and landscaping projects. The requirements to design and create a properly engineered job that will stand the test of time can be significant. Pier drilling may be slow, especially with portable equipment. Excavation can affect the area adjacent to the site if the space is limited and the grade is steep (it required us to build an additional wall). Access to the site can be a major factor in how long the project lasts. Carting tons of materials back and forth via a long set of stairs added substantial time to the job. Custom curved walls, footings and railings are slow and expensive to produce in comparison to rectangular structures. The bottom line is that you have to consider the site conditions carefully when planning a large project such as this. Given the serious slopes and tall walls, this approach was necessary here. For projects with less severe conditions and options for doing shorter (non-structural) tiered walls, there may be block or rock wall options. For non-engineered walls (typically shorter than 4 feet), that would dramatically simplify the job, particularly when the walls are not close to the house and are more landscaping in nature. This article was written by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. Jim is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair in your neighborhood since 1983. To schedule an estimate or for more information please go to our website at jimgardnerconstruction.com.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: City Council unanimously approved a list of streets to be repaved next year in a project that will cost an estimated $1.35 million at a meeting on Monday, The 2021 paving project would include asphalt overlays on portions of Grand Avenue, Hampton Road, Hill Lane, Wildwood Avenue and Requa Road. The list did not include the city’s main thoroughfare, Oakland Avenue, a bus route with noticeable and ongoing The council approved a list of streets for the paving project this month in order to secure paving funding from the state, though work won’t begin until July next “Piedmonters take pride in the condition of their streets,” Director of Public Works Chester Nakahara told Council at the virtual meeting. “It’s something we continue to work on even though funding is a challenge.” In November 2019, the City conducted a study of its 39 miles of streets and found that their condition has improved in recent years. According to the Department of Public Works’ system, the average Piedmont street had a Pavement Condition Index score of 67, which is a “good” rating, as of last November. A PCI score above 70 is considered “very good to excellent” according to the system. The score was an improvement from 2017, when the average score was 64. City Engineer John Wanger said this improvement was “pretty significant.” Wanger noted that the improvement was due to Council putting a significant amount of money toward repaving in recent years as well as an aggressive approach to ensuring utility companies repair roadways as they do maintenance. The roadway portions highlighted for repaving next year were selected for several reasons, including PCI scores, budget constraints, ongoing sewer replacement projects, utility company projects and the streets’ proximity to each other. The total 2021 repaving project will likely cost about $1.35 million, although the funding will span two fiscal years because the project will take place next summer. If the plans are approved, the state is expected to provide about $200,000 this fiscal year through Senate Bill 1 funds, while the City would pay an anticipated $258,000. The remainder would be paid from the following fiscal year. Council did not approve costs at the meeting last week. The selection of the streets was required to qualify for SB-1 funds from the state. This decision has been met with disdain from some community members. A petition initiated by parents, entitled “Piedmont Partners for PUSD Reopening,” asked the district to present a five-day instructional calendar before any formal action is taken by the board. “What worries me a lot, especially as a physician myself, is what will happen [because] parents are now scrambling. We have to swallow the unintended consequence that will happen with us moving to distance learning, and what will result with [families] figuring it out on their own,” resident Lauren Hartman said during public comment at the July 16 meeting. “As a parent, I felt the communication was not where it needed to be,” resident Jennifer Rego said. “We thought tonight [July 16] would be a presentation of what a distance-learning plan would look like, but we’re not hearing a lot of specifics of how that works,” resident Rob Philips said, echoing concerns over effective communication between parents and the district. Board member Megan Pillsbury, a former educator, acknowledged some teachers’ fears if in-person instruction were to be implemented. “My daughter in an educator in New York, where 50 teachers have died. Another educator, who is now a parent [in Piedmont] had two colleagues who have passed away,” she said. Pillsbury then listed a myriad of questions that she has considered in the event of a re-opening. “Where would [we] have lunch? How will we manage the hallways? These are things, as an educator, I [wonder] how [they] would all be manageable,” she said. Booker addressed a long list of questions beyond the learning model that have risen throughout the decision-making process. Questions he addressed were focused on state funding, federal funding, attendance, and communication throughout the district, among others. As of press time, there is no definitive date of when in-person classes may begin in the district. One day following the school board meeting in Piedmont, Gov. Newsom barred school districts from reopening in the state if their county is on the State’s coronavirus Watch List. Board members uniformly urged community members to continue to practice social distancing and CDC-guidelines, which they assert would be necessary for in-person instruction. “I think we can get to this place of safety and [in-class instruction] if our community is following rules by limiting social contact,” Swenson said. Virtual classes will begin on Monday, August 17. SUDOKU SOLUTION CROSSWORD SOLUTION Oakland Zoo Continued from page 1 along with social distancing practices. Guests are asked to arrive at the zoo with only individuals from their household. Patrons are asked not to visit the zoo if individuals within their group are feeling unwell, or have an above normal temperature. Some areas will remain closed. For guest and staff safety, all indoor exhibits are closed, including the Bug House, Reptile and Amphibian Discovery Room, California Conservation Habitarium, and all rides at Adventure Landing. Additionally, the playground and picnic areas are closed for the time being. Since the closure of the zoo on March 17, some new “residents” have joined the zoo, including Kijiji the giraffe, Aluna, a newborn Hamadryas baboon, and seven newborn American Buffalo calves. With admissions now limited to one-third of normal capacity, revenue is expected to fall short of meeting the zoo’s normal operating costs of $1.3 million monthly. articles.text: Over the weekend two separate sites in Piedmont were vandalized with anti-police graffiti. The spray-painted messages appeared on a sidewalk near Guilford and Highland Avenue, and at the Hall Fenway pathway near Wildwood and Crocker Avenue. On Highland and Guilford, “ACAB” and another anti-police slogan were sprayed in large lettering in black and red. The vandalism likely occurred Saturday night. A resident with experience in removing graffiti took the initiative of removing it after taking photos as evidence. The other location tagged was the Hall Fenway, a quarter-acre landscaped parklet connecting upper Wildwood Avenue with Crocker Park. That graffiti appeared on Saturday night or Sunday morning on a bench, the pavement, a stop sign, and a city traffic barricade. They have all been removed. A message about ”one percent” was scrawled in spray paint. The traffic barricade was painted to say Pigsville instead of Piedmont and the same anti-police messages from Guliford were painted on the pathway. A stop sign was also altered. The Hall Fenway graffiti was also in black and red, and the handwriting looked similar to the location on Guilford. These were quickly painted messages. The city estimated the damage as costing $550 to repair. Anyone with information on the identity of the suspects is asked to contact the Piedmont Police Department at 420-3000.
articles.title: Graffiti with anti-police messages surface in Piedmont

articles.text: Armed purse snatcher on Arbor On Friday, July 10, a man armed with a firearm wearing a gray hoodie and a dark colored Covid- 19 mask robbed a woman of her purse in front of her home on Arbor Drive at 7:07 p.m. Items stolen included a credit card, driver’s license, and two iPhone 8s, with a total value of approximately $900. The suspect was seen running down Arbor Drive, jumping in the passenger side of a white vehicle, and escaping. The suspect’s license number was captured on the City’s plate reading cameras and a follow-up by detectives is in progress. Man caught with 2 stolen cars Shortly after 12 noon on Saturday, July 11 the license plate reader at Grand Ave. was triggered by a stolen 1994 Acura Integra. Officers found the car on Cambridge Way with a man standing next to it. Parked behind the vehicle was a Honda Prelude with a female in it. Both vehicles were confirmed as having been stolen. The man and the woman were identified and cited for two counts auto theft, possession of burglary tools, mail theft, possession of stolen property and misappropriation of property. Mail addressed to another person was found in the car. Sergio Flores, 33, of Hayward, was cited and released due to COVID-19 jail capacity concerns. The woman was also cited and released. Thief caught with stolen car, catalytic converters On Monday morning July 13, at 6:53 a.m., a 2004 Chevy Monte Carlo set off the automatic license plate reader eastbound on Wildwood. The car was listed as stolen, and an officer conducted a high-risk traffic stop. Officers detained and handcuffed the female in the passenger seat, but the driver ran away. Five minutes later the suspect was found hiding in a resident’s vehicle. A search of the stolen Monte Carlo revealed a portable Milwaukee Sawzall and four catalytic converters. William Casados, 36, from Hayward, admitted to driving the car and claimed he stole the converters from a junkyard in Hayward. Casados was arrested for possession of a stolen vehicle and stolen property and was sent to Santa Rita jail. The female passenger was released. Police interrupt burglary in progress On Friday morning, July 17 at 10 a.m. police were alerted to a burglary in progress at a home on Arroyo Ave. Tamara Rucker, 29, of Emeryville, was found sitting in a vehicle with the engine idling near the crime scene. She was arrested for burglary and conspiracy, sent to Santa Rita jail. The victim suffered a loss of $220 in jewelry lost and $800 in damages to a sliding glass door.

articles.text: California now poised to have more cases than any other state as COVID-19 continues its spread Three more cases of COVID- 19 were added to the count amongst Piedmont residents within the past week, raising the total for Piedmont to 20 as of July 21. This is in addition to four cases reported earlier in July. Three were reported in May and 10 were reported prior to April 13, when the county began delineating cases by cities. The caseload for Alameda County is now 9,383, the highest in the greater Bay Area. More than 1,000 new cases have been added in one week, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. A total of 167 people have died in the county due to COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, this year in the county. Oakland now has 3,687 cases, Hayward has 1,379. Fremont has reported 483 cases, San Leandro has reported 474 cases and Berkeley, which has its own Health Department, has a total of 332 cases. Alameda County, the hardest hit in the Bay Area, was placed on the State’s COVID-19 “watchlist” on Sunday, July 12. Counties on the watchlist cannot allow indoor activities like dining and museums. Alameda County had abruptly shut down outdoor dining on Saturday, July 11, but issued a notice on Wednesday, July 15, that allowed outdoor restaurant dining to resume. Of particular note, County officials notified Oakland Zoo on July 15 that it had been approved as an outdoor museum and that it could reopen for outdoor activities. Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials at the end of June. California has seen a surge of cases in recent weeks and on Monday, July 13, the state ordered the closure of many indoor businesses, from restaurants to movie theaters. After California appeared to slow down the rate of COVID-19 spreading for weeks, cases surged upward in June and July. Now the state is poised to soon have more cases than any other state in the U.S., including New York, the leader for several months. As of yesterday, there have been at least 401,000 cases in California according to a New York Times database, and 7,776 people have died. On Thursday, July 16, the Piedmont Board of Education announced the upcoming school year would have 100 percent remote learning. A day later, Gov. Gavin Newsom ordered that all public and private schools on the state watchlist must continue remote learning until their respective county has been off the watchlist for 14 days. This guidance was echoed by Alameda County officials. The City of Piedmont keeps all of its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/covid-19.
articles.title: Piedmont COVID-19 cases jump to 20

The spray-painted messages appeared on a sidewalk near Guilford and Highland Avenue, and at the Hall Fenway pathway near Wildwood and Crocker Avenue. On Highland and Guilford, “ACAB” and another anti-police slogan were sprayed in large lettering in black and red. The vandalism likely occurred Saturday night. articles.text: The nomination period for the two vacancies on Piedmont City Council and three vacancies on the School Board opened this week on Monday, July 13. articles.text: Local restaurants limited again to serving takeout only On Saturday late afternoon, July 11, restaurant owners throughout Alameda County were suddenly notified to stop serving meals at their outdoor locations. The decision came less than two hours before dinner time on Saturday night, typically the busiest night of the week. The decision came when the California Office of Public Health added Alameda County to the state’s “monitoring list” because of a rise in COVID-19 cases. New restrictions include the rollback of restricted outdoor dining; restaurants may now serve only takeout and delivery. Though Alameda County’s Health Officer Order had allowed outdoor dining, under this stricter state guidance, all restaurants, wineries and bars throughout the county may only be open for drive-through or pick up and delivery options. “We are moving toward obtaining a variance from the state, and a letter of support for a variance is on the agenda for Tuesday [July 14] Board of Supervisors’ meeting,” said Neetu Blaram, Public Information Manager for the county’s Public Health Department. Alameda County hit pause on reopening on June 29 due to rising case rates and hospitalizations, but subsequently delayed plans to apply for a variance. Alameda County has the highest number of cases in the seven-county Bay Area. In recent days, seven states, including California, set new records for daily COVID-19 related deaths. This news comes nearly a month after outdoor dining launched in the region. As of press time, Alameda County remains one of only two counties in the state that has not yet applied for a variance. Imperial County, at the southern border of the state, is the other holdout. “It’s difficult to put a timeline [on this], because the first step in obtaining a variance would be the Board of Supervisors approving a letter of support, then the assumption would be that if they voted to approve the letter, then we can take the steps that are required to become a variance county,” Blaram told the Post. According to the Alameda County roadmap for reopening, outdoor dining was permitted on June 19, with restrictions. Each new development in reopening the county is contingent upon local COVID-19 indicators, at intervals of two and four weeks. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a press conference Monday afternoon, July 13, said, “We’re continuing to see hospitalizations rise and we continue to see an increase in the rate of positivity in the state. As a result, we are moving back into a ‘modification mode’ of our original stay-athome order, effective today.” Alameda County and 29 other counties fall under these stricter modifications. Gov. Newsom did not provide a guideline for when restaurants would be given authorization to reopen.
articles.title: State orders Alameda County to abruptly end outdoor dining

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the Piedmont School Board on June 25. Thank you for the discussion last evening and your work. I think that my comments and the comments of many others were misinterpreted yesterday, and I would like to clarify. Distancing learning must exactly duplicate 5 day per week in-person classes. This can easily be done by live-streaming the classes (just video on teacher, which would not be hard, as teachers will not be mobile to achieve distancing anyway) and sharing any in class materials (worksheets and handouts) via schoology. If this is not done, it would require much extra work for teachers to create separate content and the distancing students will get a lower quality of instruction, given the experience during this past spring. Piedmont does in class teaching well, so that should be the basis for distance learning. Having distance learning separate from a duplicate of in-class learning in the spring did not work. I have yet to find a single parent saying that distance learning in the spring was as good as in-class learning. Piedmont does in-class learning well, we just need to duplicate it for the distancing learning students. Having even one day per week that does not have in-class learning will result in that day of school being of lower quality. If distance learning in the spring that was different than in-class learning was woefully inadequate, and months of time was available to develop it, how would it be any different starting in just 1 and 1/2 months? As mentioned by school board members last night. Half of the kids could go in the morning, with the other half in the afternoon (or some other split by days over a two-week period of 10 days). This split would not be even for every class but should allow a reduction from a class size of 22 to 15 in all classes. Cohorts are not possible in high school. Exceptions would be with a change to a few tracks with the same classes. Cohorts with individualized schedules will not work in high school with very individualized class selection. It could work with several different choices (maybe 2 or 3) with all kids within those choices having the same classes. With this 2- or 3-track method, splitting the kids into two groups for AM or PM attendance would result in each class having 1/2 have kids in each. Numbers in each in class at less than 15, if the average class size were 22 (and still 15 with class sizes of 30). Need to establish full mask compliance. This can be done by suspending students for several days if they violate even once (they can distance learn for that suspension period). Further, as I outlined in a separate email to you within the last 12 hours, we need to establish full mask compliance by adults and children while outside this summer via more signs and police enforcement. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 922-8711 email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Barry Eitel Allyson Aleksey Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Piedmont resident Peter Sherris received a rare honor on June 25, 2020., when Oakland Mayor Libby Schaff declared it Peter Sherris Day. It marked the end of his term as President the Rotary Club of Oakland, the third oldest in the U.S. Sherris’ resume of public service covers all spheres, from local to international. He has long been a Scoutmaster associated with Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop One, and has helped lead many backpacking trips in the high regions of the Sierra Nevada. Council Commissioner Rich Harms recalled Sherris’ impact on the Boy Scouts. “He was a good leader: he led by example with his formidable outdoor skills,” Harms said. “He took his troop of Piedmont Scouts on trips that they will remember for the rest of their lives. He led the troop on snow camping trips every winter and we were the only troop doing that at the time. We would build snow huts and sleep in those.” When not leading the Scouts in the Sierra or in the Yukon, Sherris worked his day job as a cardiologist and internist for 34 years with Kaiser Permanente. Through the Rotary Club he twice volunteered in the fight to eradicate malaria in Kenya. He returned to school to earn a Masters of Public Health at UC Berkeley. With Sherris at the helm of the Rotary Club this past year, Rotarians were prepared to undertake community service projects when COVID-19 hit. “Before 2020 started, Peter made sure we had consistent live streams of our meetings for members that couldn’t make it. articles.text: Justin Szasz, Piedmont’s CivicSpark Fellow and leader of the city’s Climate Plan for the past year, will be completing his 11-month program with the city at the end of July. His next stop will be a PhD in Sociology from the University of Oregon. A native of Santa Cruz, he obtained a Bachelor’s Degree in Social Studies from Harvard University in 2018, and for the past year has displayed considerable leadership with Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, notably with the creation of a Climate Challenge. “I started [gaining interest] in climate change partway through college, I was primarily a Middle East studies major. By the time I was a junior, I was interested in what was then a very popular academic theory, that a drought connected to climate change played a role in sparking the Syrian civil war,” he explained. After some lengthy research, Szasz came to the conclusion that drought did play a role in the growth of existing problems. “An exacerbation of existing problems is in itself a real issue. So I became interested in the human impacts of climate change first, before I became interested in the determinants of climate change,” he said. From the fall 2018 to the next summer Szasz worked as a Research Assistant at the Harvard University Center for the Environment, studying the intersection of political economy and climate change. His studies followed how economic policies affect carbon emissions trajectories and how weather events connected to climate change interact with economic policies to affect populations. During that time, he applied for a CivicSpark Fellowship as Justin Szasz is leaving the Piedmont Planning Department to pursue a doctorate at the University of Oregon. a chance to learn how emissions reduction plans are created and implemented on a local level. He also took the opportunity as a chance to get involved in reducing California’s carbon emissions. CivicSpark is an AmeriCorps program in which fellows are matched with project partners throughout California, including the Central Coast, San Joaquin Valley, Los Angeles, San Diego, Sacramento, Sierra Nevada, and the San Francisco Bay Area. Fellows are matched with project partners to serve on at least one project, benefiting at least one local public agency. Szasz said that the Piedmont community was at the top of his list when considering where to work. After an interview with Planning Director Kevin Jackson, he was hired. “When I started this position a year ago, the first thing I did was read our climate action plan, which gives a lot of specific information on what goals city council has set out for us in terms of emission reduction, and where all the current emissions categories are,” Szasz said. Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 (its second comprehensive plan) calls for a reduction of emissions by 40 percent below 2005 emissions levels by 2030, and by 80 below 2005 emissions levels by 2050. What became apparent, he added, was that emissions should be reduced in two major categories to achieve the goal Piedmont has set: car transportation, and natural gas use in appliances and buildings. “Just looking at the numbers, to accomplish these goals, we’d have to significantly reduce natural gas use in buildings and vehicle use. The question for me became what programs can I work on that will best help Piedmont transition off of gas use in buildings and gas for transportation?” he explained. articles.text: In collaboration with the Oakland League of Women Voters, the Piedmont League of Women Voters will present Part 2 of “New Models for Social Justice – Police Reform” on Monday, July 20 at 4 p.m. with guest speaker Anne Janks, Organizer at the Coalition for Police Accountability. The Community Conversation is free and open to the public and will livestream on YouTube and not on Zoom. Janks will describe a proposed Oakland pilot program to respond to some 911 calls with a counselor and EMT rather than with armed police. This program does not propose abolishing the police department but emphasizes public safety. Janks will speak for the first half of the program, to be followed by a Question & Answer session moderated by Piedmont LWV President Lorrel Plimier. Participants may submit questions through YouTube livestream comments, or email them in advance to: lwvpiedmont@gmail.org. For more information, visit www.lwvpiedmont.org.”

articles.text: The U.S. Census Bureau will be hiring more than 300 people to conduct door-to-door canvassing in the coming weeks. Census takers (enumerators) interview the residents of households that have not responded to previous invitations to complete the census survey online, by phone, or by mail. Applicants must be at least 18-years-old, have a driver’s license, an email address, and be able to pass a background check. The job is temporary, has flexible hours, and pays $30/hour. Census takers serve as the last line of defense for getting an accurate count, which is critical for federal funding and fair political representation. You can help your community and yourself by applying now at 2020census.gov/jobs or calling 1-855-562-2020.

articles.text: With caseload of more than 8,000, Alameda County added to State’s watchlist Three new cases of COVID- 19 were confirmed in Piedmont during the past seven days as cases in Alameda County soared above 8,000 as of Tuesday, July 14. It brings Piedmont’s total to 17 cases. One Piedmont case was reported last Wednesday, July 8, another was reported on Thursday, July 9, and a third was reported this week on Monday, July 13. Before the new cases in the past seven days, a new case was reported on July 3. Three cases were reported in May and 10 reported before April 13. Countywide, the caseload is now 8,321, an 11.6 percent increase from one week ago, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department. In total, 152 people in the county have died due to COVID- 19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, this year in the county. Alameda County is the hardest hit county in the San Francisco Bay Area. Santa Clara County now counts 6,542 cases and 167 total deaths. In Contra Costa County, the caseload is 5,023 and there have been 92 deaths. In San Francisco, the caseload is 4,640 and there have been 50 deaths. A total of 3,172 cases have been reported in Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County. Hayward now has a total of 1,277. Fremont has reported 425 cases, San Leandro has reported 419 cases and Berkeley has reported 278 cases. Due to its increasing numbers, Alameda County was placed on a statewide COVID-19 watchlist on Sunday, July 12. Counties on the watchlist cannot allow indoor activities like dining and museums. Those indoor activities were already prohibited by county orders. Outdoor restaurant dining was suddenly shut down by the County late Saturday afternoon, July 11. “Alameda County is experiencing a continued increase in reported COVID-19 cases in recent weeks, indicating elevated disease transmission,” the county said in a statement. “The magnitude of the change is above what would be expected as a result of the County‘s substantial expansion of testing.” Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials at the end of June. In the announcement this week, county officials noted that although Alameda County had the most cases in the region, other counties in the area and statewide had higher case rates. California has seen a surge of cases in recent weeks and on Monday, July 13, the state ordered the closure of many indoor businesses, from restaurants to movie theaters. As of yesterday, there have been 336,508 total cases in California and 7,087 deaths. Piedmont’s annual Fourth of July Parade was canceled, although a socially distant, front yard decoration celebration took place. At a City Council meeting on Monday, July 6, City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted that the pandemic numbers were “not trending favorably” and predicted at that time that that Alameda County likely would be placed on the state’s watchlist. The City of Piedmont keeps all of its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/covid-19.

articles.text: Triple Threat Basketball Camp, operating camps for Piedmont’s Recreation Department for the 13th year, has moved its summer program outside to Hampton Park, rather than in the school gyms. The camps last three weeks and consist of pods of 12 players ages 6-12 playing three hours a day. The founder of the program, Tony Ferraro, wasn’t sure if any camps would be open this summer. “We had no intention of doing anything in Piedmont, but then got a call four weeks ago saying we can now do it outside,” he said. Camp registration filled up quickly like all the other in-person summer camps. Triple Threat had been operating at other locations since June 1. “We already had the protocols and the guide to reopen. The biggest difference with the Piedmont camp is that kids can actually play against each other and interact. Camps at our other locations have zero contact.” Players are screened for their temperature every day, and hands are frequently sanitized. Many kids show up with masks on, and some play with masks on. “I think they are trying to feel it out. Since we started there has not been one instance of someone withdrawing from the camp,” said Ferraro. Signs are posted at the camp outlining the limitations and A Piedmont basketball player got on a roll, making the other players wait for his hot streak to end. A race for a loose ball at the Hampton Courts. Players are divided into smaller groups and more instructors are added to prevent mixing. Shooting and rebounding in the summer sun never felt so nice. restrictions during the coronavirus. According to Ferraro, the response from parents has been encouraging. “There are a lot of kids signed again up for the next session. The parents are probably happier than the kids for a little free time,” he said. This is the first time the basketball camp has been held outside, and the weather could not be better. A tent nearby offers players shade if needed. Normally the camps are one week and may focus on a particular skill, like defense or offense. With the county restrictions, camps have to stay together for the three weeks, so the programs are more all-encompassing. The program consists of about 70 percent skill development, and 30 percent scrimmaging. Ferraro played basketball in Australia and has worked at basketball camps his entire life. He began Triple Threat Academy when he returned to the U.S. “It took a little while, but once it got going, we have been really fortunate to have lots of families trust us to do the camps and the classes. We even have teams now and have blossomed into quite a program,” he confirmed. Kids are happy to see their friends, to move around and catch some sun, and Ferraro is happy to provide this outlet for participation and socializing. “The silver lining is you are seeing that people still want to do it. articles.text: Science Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center This is a hands-on experiment our young scientists won’t soon forget. We all know the importance of thoroughly washing our hands, but how clean are our hands? How clean are these household and classroom items we touch multiple times a day? MATERIALS: • Enough slices of fresh, white bread for each item you’d like to test • 1 plastic sealable sandwich bag for each slice of bread that you’ll test • A control slice of bread that has not been touched (use gloves or clean tongs) • Whatever items are frequently touched in your home or classroom: • Clean hands: warm water and soap for 20 seconds • Clean hands: hand sanitizer • Dirty hands • Your face • Anything with a touch screen • Keyboard • TV remote or gaming controller • Door handle • Light switch • Your pillow PROCEDURE: 1. Using new gloves or clean tongs, remove 1 slice of fresh white bread and seal it into a plastic sandwich bag. Number and label the bag as Control (bag #1) 2. Wipe dry, clean hands that have been washed thoroughly for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm water on the next slice of bread. Number and label the bag as Clean hands- Soap and Warm Water (bag #2) 3. Continue to repeat this process for each surface you’d like to test. Make sure to correctly label and number each bag. 4. Leave the sealed bags with their labels on a table or counter for up to one month. 5. Make predictions about which slices of bread will grow the most mold. Which slices will get moldy the fastest? Why? Find more activities and at-home experiments on Chabot’s Learning Launchpad at chabotspace.org. Be sure to share your observations with us on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter @chabotspace. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, July 15, 2020 SchOOLs Taking it outside: basketball camp goes to Hampton SUMMER THOUGHTS By Jay Russell Triple Threat Basketball Camp, operating camps for Piedmont’s Recreation Department for the 13th year, has moved its summer program outside to Hampton Park, rather than in the school gyms. The camps last three weeks and consist of pods of 12 players ages 6-12 playing three hours a day. The founder of the program, Tony Ferraro, wasn’t sure if any camps would be open this summer. “We had no intention of doing anything in Piedmont, but then got a call four weeks ago saying we can now do it outside,” he said. Camp registration filled up quickly like all the other in-person summer camps. Triple Threat had been operating at other locations since June 1. “We already had the protocols and the guide to reopen. The biggest difference with the Piedmont camp is that kids can actually play against each other and interact. Camps at our other locations have zero contact.” Players are screened for their temperature every day, and hands are frequently sanitized. Many kids show up with masks on, and some play with masks on. “I think they are trying to feel it out. Since we started there has not been one instance of someone withdrawing from the camp,” said Ferraro. articles.text: –John Savage Piedmont High Science Teacher Parents and families involved with Piedmont Makers have led a fundraising campaign to finish the designated engineering lab in the new 3-story STEAM classroom building on the site of the former high school theater. The STEAM building, set for completion in four weeks, will house science, technology, art, engineering and mathematics classes. The capstone of the $30 million building is expected to be an engineering lab, long touted as the school’s future. But the project has come up short. The cost to outfit the engineering lab was estimated at $420,000. That work appears not to have been included in the overall cost of the building. The Piedmont Makers organization leaped to the rescue, launching a campaign to raise $420,000. As of a week ago, $320,000 had been raised, but the outfitting of the lab is not expected to be completed until late January 2021 at the start of the second semester. At a presentation at the July 7 school board meeting, PHS Principal Adam Littlefield said, “We’re still creating the vision for the use of the engineering lab, but at this point it includes project-based learning integrated into curriculum, and really a space to build things.” There will be a focus on engineering and technology-based activities, Littlefield continued, with a goal to allow students to design and manufacture using state-of-the art equipment. A “library-like” resource center, with software driven tools and traditional manual tools, is included in the vision. Littlefield added that he would like to see the lab available for community members beyond students and district staff, clearing the way for the space to be utilized by members of the Piedmont Makers. “The STEAM building, including the engineering lab, would be open to community groups, as would the facilities within PUSD,” said Littlefield. Piedmont Makers, a nonprofit founded in 2014, helped convert the Piedmont Middle School woodshop to a robotics and maker space. It sponsors more than 30 teams in the Youth Robotics League. In the first quarter of this year, Piedmont Makers worked with Supt. Randy Booker and Littlefield to discuss outfitting the engineering lab, and then worked with Facilities Director Pete Palmer to develop a layout and an equipment list. Highlander Robotics worked with several non-profits to obtain plastic, and then cut and designed into personal protective equipment (PPE) for nurses, back in March when there was a significant shortage. “PPE is a simple project and could be translated to a project that the class or community could work on. It’s a great way to connect the community to the STEAM lab,” said Charlie Lambert. Sally Aldridge is leading the fundraising campaign to outfit the lab. “We started this effort quite a while ago, before COVID, and were fortunate enough to get some large anchor donors on board early,” she said. Maker Space created a detailed three-year operating budget of $420,000, including district-certified lab staff. “This budget is over and above the H1 plans, so there’s no need to dip into any existing funds,” Aldridge said. “We think of this plan much like the Wellness Center at the high school, which started with outside donations.” A future goal is to raise $50,000 from the community and $50,000 to be matched by an anonymous donor. To recognize these donors, a Donor Wall will be placed in the hallway outside the lab. “The school budget is so tight, and I appreciate the thoughtfulness put [into this budget], and thinking through relieving pressure from the district budget,” school board member Cory Smegal said. Outfitting the lab did not specifically fall under the Bond Project List of the measure H1 bond to fund the STEAM building, which passed in 2016. The project list includes: “construction of a new Piedmont High School STEAM building, renovation, refurbishment or replacement of existing Piedmont High School, middle school, and Millennium High School buildings, addition of classrooms to elementary schools sufficient to meet higher educational standards for kindergarten, energy efficiency measure and addition of security measures, and the furnishing of new, renovated, and existing buildings, including modern technology.” Some of the school’s most respected educators expressed concern at the lack of faculty input on the project. “We have a variety of teachers who want input on this. It’s important to have teacher input for [this],” said PHS science teacher Marna Chamberlain. “I’d like to see an engineering lab that would promote robotics, guitar [manufacturing] and more. I would like to see it being classdriven rather than just a club after school, and to be utilized as much as possible,” she said. John Lambert, Vice President of Fundraising for Piedmont Makers, offered a rendering concept of the new engineering lab, which would include 3D printers, laser cutters, and computer numerical control (CNC) routers. PHS junior Charlie Lambert, a member of Highlander Robotics, explained some of the projects the group has worked on in the “mini-lab” thus far, and what the group plans on continuing in the proposed engineering lab. With Extended hours to Fit Your Busy Schedule Dr. Gutlaizer and Sandy with Sasha and Morgan.
articles.title: Parents to the rescue on completion of PHS engineering lab

articles.text: Right now, you probably are sobbing in your room because you missed out on your Paris trip, or how you couldn’t go to Greece. It’s okay. I was supposed to go to Hawaii with my family, but since COVID hit and Hawaii closed its doors for tourists, we weren’t able to go. To my surprise, we quickly found a solution. We booked a hotel in Pismo Beach and in Yosemite - a whole week of vacation! I was so excited to finally get out of my house for longer than an hour. In less than a week we were packed and ready to go to Pismo Beach, near San Luis Obispo. At first, I was a bit shocked because nobody was wearing a mask. There were so many people it looked like summer in Disney World, not DisneyLand, folks, But don’t get me wrong, I loved Pismo Beach, although it has a few faults. For those of you who haven’t gone on vacation during the quarantine, not much has changed, except that you have to wear a mask and observe social distancing. Hotel restaurants are mostly takeout. My sister and I went down to the beach and as soon we arrived. It was like Hawaii. The sand at Pismo is so white and soft. The water was still cold but, not as cold as in Northern California, especially Point Reyes. Walking down the beach was a workout because walking on sand is not easy when you’re walking on a shifting surface and it’s hot. I didn’t last 20 minutes. Some people at our hotel were quite self-absorbed. There was a family that took up three outdoor fireplaces and just left their stuff on the chairs and left. That made it kind of touch for other people who were freezing from sitting by the comfort of a warm fire (my family included). Quite rude, but then nobody asked me. After spending three days in Pismo Beach we drove to Yosemite, a four-hour trip. In that time, it was amazing to see the coastal terrain turn into mountains with lush forests. Initially we stayed at the Pines Resort at Bass Lake, which was like one small town. There were restaurants, convenience stores, even a post office. The housing units were called chalets, each with an individual name. Ours was the “Sunrise Chalet”, with a view of the hills and the lake. One of the perks at this resort was that we could rent boats – plus the fact that we were only 13 miles from Yosemite. After settling in, we went outside to explore the resort. We were alerted by an employee in a golf cart that there was a bear running loose through the area. When I asked her whether this happened often, she said, “You’re in the mountains, sweetheart,” I almost died from laughter. Kind of like “You’re not in Kansas, Anymore.” The next day we drove to the park. On our way we made jokes about how when you get to Yosemite it’s supposed to be a spiritual awakening. But when we came out of the tunnel we were stunned. Mountains jutting out from the side. Bridalveil Falls in the distance. The Merced River winding through the trees. It was spectacular. After taking many pictures, we drove into the Valley, and at some point we realized that we had lost the permit that let us in the park, So we put a note that said “lost” (it, not us), and hoped for the best. Walking under the towering redwoods and oaks was an amazing experience. Unlike in Pismo, many people were wearing masks, which was comforting. We wanted to go up to MIrror Lake but didn’t find the trail entrance. Instead we took the Mist Trail to Vernal Falls. When I tell you it was hard, you do not understand unless you yourself have attempted this hike. I’m not kidding, it just went up and up, and it was hot. But we kept our masks on the whole time. But in the end, the torturous hike was well worth it. The thundering falls blocked out sound and all you could see was the beauty of this massive waterfall. What utterly confused me was seeing people in their 60s and 70s and children walking on the steep trail on the way back down like it was flat. Maybe there is something wrong with us. Who knows? After a long day at Yosemite we went to Glacier Point, watched the gorgeous sunset and drove back to Bass Lake. The next day we could barely move, but nonetheless got up because we had reserved a boat for a couple of hours. There is something you need to know: At Bass Lake there are different cliques of teenagers. My sister and I went down to the beach and as soon we arrived. It was like Hawaii. The sand at Pismo is so white and soft. The water was still cold but, not as cold as in Northern California, especially Point Reyes. Walking down the beach was a workout because walking on sand is not easy when you’re walking on a shifting surface and it’s hot. I didn’t last 20 minutes. Some people at our hotel were quite self-absorbed. There was a family that took up three outdoor fireplaces and just left their stuff on the chairs and left. That made it kind of touch for other people who were freezing from sitting by the comfort of a warm fire (my family included). Quite rude, but then nobody asked me. After spending three days in Pismo Beach we drove to Yosemite, a four-hour trip. In that time, it was amazing to see the coastal terrain turn into mountains with lush forests. Initially we stayed at the Pines Resort at Bass Lake, which was like one small town. There were restaurants, convenience stores, even a post office. The housing units were called chalets, each with an individual name. Ours was the “Sunrise Chalet”, with a view of the hills and the lake. One of the perks at this resort was that we could rent boats – plus the fact that we were only 13 miles from Yosemite. After settling in, we went outside to explore the resort. We were alerted by an employee in a golf cart that there was a bear running loose through the area. When I asked her whether this happened often, she said, “You’re in the mountains, sweetheart,” I almost died from laughter. Kind of like “You’re not in Kansas, Anymore.” The next day we drove to the park. On our way we made jokes about how when you get to Yosemite it’s supposed to be a spiritual awakening. But when we came out of the tunnel we were stunned. Mountains jutting out from the side. Bridalveil Falls in the distance. The Merced River winding through the trees. It was spectacular. After taking many pictures, we drove into the Valley, and at some point we realized that we had lost the permit that let us in the park, So we put a note that said “lost” (it, not us), and hoped for the best. Walking under the towering redwoods and oaks was an amazing experience. Unlike in Pismo, many people were wearing masks, which was comforting. We wanted to go up to MIrror Lake but didn’t find the trail entrance. Instead we took the Mist Trail to Vernal Falls. When I tell you it was hard, you do not understand unless you yourself have attempted this hike. I’m not kidding, it just went up and up, and it was hot. But we kept our masks on the whole time. But in the end, the torturous hike was well worth it. The thundering falls blocked out sound and all you could see was the beauty of this massive waterfall. What utterly confused me was seeing people in their 60s and 70s and children walking on the steep trail on the way back down like it was flat. Maybe there is something wrong with us. Who knows? After a long day at Yosemite we went to Glacier Point, watched the gorgeous sunset and drove back to Bass Lake. The next day we could barely move, but nonetheless got up because we had reserved a boat for a couple of hours. There is something you need to know: At Bass Lake there are different cliques of teenagers. But this year the event is constrained by the Covid-19 virus. Attendance by dense crowds is incompatible with social distancing. French deaths from the virus now exceed 30,000; and there are 171,000 confirmed cases. In comparison, the United States, with nearly five times France’s population, has 137,000 deaths and 3,300,000 confirmed cases. articles.text: Makenna Thiel has committed to the University of California wehre she will pursue her tennis career. Makenna Thiel, an incoming Piedmont High senior and the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2018, has officially committed to the University of California tennis program in Berkeley. “I grew up going to every Cal men’s basketball game with my family. When I started looking into each school, I found that Cal was perfect in every way for me. It has a great balance between athletics and academics. “I am grateful for this opportunity,” said Thiel. Thiel said her decision came down to Cal and USC, but her familiarity with Berkeley and the Golden Bears ultimately won her over. “It was always a dream of mine to stay in the Pac 12. I feel like a part of the team already. I’ve hit with some of them in the past and met a few at tournaments, so I feel already close with some of the girls already. “That was a huge draw; it’s great to know people where I’m going,” she added. Thiel will be playing under head coach Amanda Augustus and assistant Zach Warren, who helped lead the school to the second round of the 2019 NCAA Championships. “Both Amanda and Zach are great coaches. I’ve played on the Cal courts a few times and I’d see them at tournaments. I noticed that I played better when they watched me; I realized that I was already comfortable in their presence despite not knowing them on a personal level yet,” said Thiel. Thiel is a four-star recruit and has continuously been ranked among the top prospects in the state. She’s competed in top-level regional tournaments since her pre-teen years and remains a premier competitor. She helps solidify the Cal tennis program’s best recruiting class of all time, giving Augustus and Warren possibly their best shot at topping archrival and back-to-back NCAA champs, Stanford. Alongside Thiel as freshmen will be five-star recruit Cami Brown of Irvine, Canadian champion Jada Bui, and Hannah Viller Moller of Denmark. “We worked very hard to bring in a group we feel includes outstanding young women who are great fits at Cal athletically and academically. I believe this is the highest rated recruiting class in program history,” said Augustus. “In combination with the class we brought in this past year and with our veteran players, we’re really excited about the upcoming 2020- 21 season,” he added. Thiel’s time on Piedmont High’s tennis team was only two years, but she made it count. She won all but one match in over 20 appearances and was named the Western Alameda County Conference’s MVP for the fall of 2017 and 2018. She won the Div. 1 NCS doubles’ championship with Lauren Young. Thiel was part of Piedmont’s run of five consecutive Division 2 North Coast Section Team Championships, which started with her older sister, Kaelli Thiel, in 2013. “I remember Makenna at 11-years old saying she wants to play professional tennis, which was rare for someone at that age,” recalled former PHS tennis coach and Hall of Fame inductee. “She always had that John McEnroe attitude and is a fierce player.” “Even as a fifth grader Makenna would always came to our matches. We’d bring her into our circle when we did announcements. She was always a part of the team.” Piedmont’s 2018 team was among the school’s most talented team of all time. That year Makenna. as a sophomore, played with Angela Huang, who now plays for Washington University in St. Louis. As for Thiel’s possible major, she said, “I’m not 100 percent sure, but I think business. Haas is a great business school.” Makenna Thiel was named Athlete of the Year by the Piedmont Post in 2019, and Freshman of the Year in 2018.

articles.text: With the summer months rolling along, athletes at Piedmont High face an unconventional offseason ahead of the fall. You may see some members of the girls’ cross-country team working on their mileage on runs around town. The entire team is taking part in the Athletes as Leaders’ program with coach Jeanine Holmlund. The program provides a weekly topic and a video to watch, discuss and reflect on in terms of values. “Within our group we give each student a platform to discover and articulate her thoughts. At the very least, we are sharing our feelings and becoming a tighter group through this experience,” said Holmlund. The program enables student-athletes to deal with issues like social awareness, civil rights, mental health and understanding societal stereotypes. It also aids teenagers toward processing personal matters like self-image positivity and developing healthy relationships. “I want the girls to recognize they are more than athletes and students. I want them to believe in themselves and have confidence in their ideas as they move forward and out of high school. Our running programs offer coping skills and life skills, a place to reflect and to grow as individuals,” explained Holmlund. Aya Troyer embarks on her senior campaign with some familiar faces around her, including Adri McAullife, Mara Lovric, Molly McWeeny, Valerie Xiong, Katie Korn, and the Posts’ Sophomore of the Year, Ellie Black. Troyer will eb a four-year varsity runner. “Aya Troyer, Katie Korn and Valerie Xiong have joined. They are running over 35 miles a week and are a really committed group,” added Holmlund. It will be the first time in four years that the team has not had Sofia Zalewski as a team leader. A record-setting runner, she finished her high school career as Valedictorian and will be attending Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburg. Holmlund is hopeful that the Athletes as Leaders program facilitates a leader-mentality going into the fall. “We have a committed girls’ team. We have a core group of upperclassmen, lowerclassmen, and incoming Freshmen participating weekly on our online Zoom sessions,” added Holmlund. When looking ahead to the fall, the NFHS classified cross country as a “low risk” sport if athletes are given staggered starts—meaning racers would start individually instead of the traditional herd of runners at the starting line. Homlund said she hasn’t heard anything from section officials, but expects many plans to be announced in the coming days. “There have been many ideas put forward on how to run races within CDC guidelines. NCS and our league will have their plans announced soon,” said. Let’s hope. The state’s decision on fall sports is scheduled to be made public on July 20, less than a week away.

She won the Div. 1 NCS doubles’ championship with Lauren Young. Thiel was part of Piedmont’s run of five consecutive Division 2 North Coast Section Team Championships, which started with her older sister, Kaelli Thiel, in 2013. “I remember Makenna at 11-years old saying she wants to play professional tennis, which was rare for someone at that age,” recalled former PHS tennis coach and Hall of Fame inductee. “She always had that John McEnroe attitude and is a fierce player.” “Even as a fifth grader Makenna would always came to our matches. We’d bring her into our circle when we did announcements. She was always a part of the team.” Piedmont’s 2018 team was among the school’s most talented team of all time. That year Makenna. as a sophomore, played with Angela Huang, who now plays for Washington University in St. Louis. As for Thiel’s possible major, she said, “I’m not 100 percent sure, but I think business. Haas is a great business school.” Makenna Thiel was named Athlete of the Year by the Piedmont Post in 2019, and Freshman of the Year in 2018.

articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Will there be sports at Witter Field this fall? The CIF’s decision on sports comes on July 20. Student-athletes, coaches, parents, and high school sports supporters are all intently waiting for Monday, July 20, when the California Interscholastic Federation – the governing body for high school sports in the stet – has said it will announce plans for fall sports – if, when and how they will take place. On June 10, the CIF announced its two phases toward safely re-opening with some training guidelines and a July 20 deadline for the specifics. In May, the National Federation of State High School Associations and Sports Medicine Advisory Committee released its classifications for sports deemed “High Risk” to “Low Risk”. • High Risk: Wrestling, football, boys’ lacrosse, competitive cheer, and dance. • Moderate Risk: Basketball, volleyball, baseball, softball, soccer, water polo, gymnastics, ice hockey, field hockey, tennis, swimming relays, pole vault, high jump, long jump, girls lacrosse, crew with two or more rowers, 7 on 7 football. • Low Risk: Individual running events, throwing events (javelin, shot put, discus), individual swimming, golf, weightlifting, alpine skiing, sideline cheer, single sculling, and cross country running with staggered starts. The NFSH marked several “Moderate Risk” sports could be considered “Low Risk” with appropriate cleaning of equipment and athletes using masks, including volleyball, baseball, softball, gymnastics, tennis, pole vault, high jump, and long jump. Coaches at Piedmont High have confirmed that as of now, everything is up in the air. Cross country coach Jeanine Holmlund said, “I don’t expect to know anything sooner. NCS, WACC and Piedmont will be making decisions within the CIF’s framework.” Water polo coach John Savage said, “I haven’t heard anything else.” “The CIF has been very quiet about their decision,” commented football coach Jerome Johnson. Many coaches at Piedmont have indicated that they’d be “surprised” by a fall season, giving a dark cloud over the July 20 announcement date. For fall contact sports like football and water polo, the risk classifications could bring serious alterations to the schedule. “You always hear rumors, but we’re taking clues from the NFL and NCAA. If colleges are beginning to shut down or push back, we know we’re next. We do have a feeling that we could start sometime in the winter months,” explained Johnson. Sports like tennis, golf, and cross-country are deemed “low risk”, so the possibility of a season might exist. A push back for fall sports will, without a doubt, affect the schedule of winter sports like basketball and soccer. The CIF said last month that is “prepared to offer alternative calendars” for sports by July 20. For heavy contact sports like football, Johnson is well aware that player-safety comes with requisite time and preparation. “Yes, we need a full offseason program because we can talk to them and prepare them for a season. These are things that we need for our kids; learning how for form-tackle and angle-tackle properly. That is a safety issue. We need that time to teach,” added Johnson. In the meantime. Stay tuned for a July 20 announcement.

articles.text: With our 2019 Athlete of the Year Makenna Thiel having committed to UC Berkeley after she graduates from Piedmont in May 2021, we look back to 2013 at the start of five consecutive Division 2 North Coast Section tennis team championships stretching until 2017, Thiel’s freshman year. In 2013, Makenna’s older sister, Kaelli Thiel, led the charge for Piedmont as a sophomore after the Highlanders lost to Branson 6-1 in the 2012 NCS Finals. The five-year run of dominance starting the 2013 has helped solidify Piedmont as a “tennis school.” In 2014, they beat Branson 4-3 as the No. 2 seeded school, and then beat the Bulls 5-2, once again as the No. 2 team in 2015. Former coach Neil Rothenberg joked that he considered retiring after the 2014 championship win, but Thiel convinced him to stay until she graduated. He said, “OK, but only if you play Division 1singes as a senior.” She did. She won, and the rest is history. “That run was pretty amazing when we started with Kaelli. I’ve always been proud of all the teams, but that whole run was really special,” said Rothenberg. Kaelli Thiel graduated in 2015 as one of the most decorated PHS tennis player of all time. She finished with a four-year overall record of 94-10 and won both the Div. 1 and Div. 2 North Coast Section singles championships. This week, we look back to the start of the girls’ tennis program’s fiveyear Division 2 NCS Championship run. Pictured here is former coach Neil Rothenberg getting the honorary Gatorade bath. “We seemed to always peak at the end of the season, which is sometimes really difficult to do when coaching,” said Rothenberg. “That was the start of some amazing camaraderie between the players.” Kaelli departed from the school in 2015 among the most accomplished in the program’s history. She compiled a record of 94-10 over her four years at the school, won a Division 2 singles title as a junior, and came back to win the Division 1 title as a senior and finished 23-0. “Kaelli is the most decorated high school player that Piedmont’s ever produced on the women’s side, there’s no doubt about it. She was very tenacious; she would’ve played more matches if I let her. She easily could have won 120 matches if I played her against the weaker schools,” added Rothenberg. The start of the run in 2013 was Piedmont’s first section title in 15 years span. It was the third time in a row that PHS had faced Branson dating back to 2011. The Bulls and Highlanders famously continued to square off for the section title annually until the 2018 cancelation by the NCS. It was one of the more famous rivalries in Bay Area tennis. “In case you weren’t counting. For the Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team, the third time’s a charm… It was only the second time Piedmont team has won the NCS title, and its first since 1998,” wrote the Post back in 2013. Following Rothenberg’s retirement in 2015, Jim Landes took over the program. In 2016 and gained two more NCS championship wins over Branson prior to the 2018 vacated year due to the Butte County fire pollution. The 2016 team featured Angela Huang as a sophomore winning the Division 2 NCS singles title and completed its 18th consecutive undefeated league championship season. In 2017, Makenna Thiel made her first appearance at the school and wound up winning the league’s MVP award and Post’s Freshman of the Year honors. With a 5-2 win over Branson, it marked their fifth and final championship year. Thiel was undefeated at 10-0, and only lost one set. The elder Kaelli Thiel played on Harvard’s tennis team for one year, then switched sports to polo, though she was not an equestrian. She has graduated and intends on attending medical school. Piedmont’s 2017 tennis team was the last of five straight NCS Championships. Staff Photo
