14 Wednesday, July 15, 2020 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 13th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. JUKKA VALKONEN Triathlon Piedmont High Class of 1985 Cal State East Bay Class of 1991 Piedmont’s Jukka Valkonen is a member of the US National Team as a triathlete. He currently is training for the USAT Off-road Triathlon National Championships in September. A professional trainer and physical health expert, Valkonen is working as the Chief Health Officer for the largest AI tech-enabled medical practice that is aiding with the global impact of COVID-19. He shares an important message regarding athletes, teams, and being safe during the global pandemic. What is your workout program this summer? With COVID19, the focus has been keeping the mind, body and spirit healthy. Early in the year and pandemic, I reminded my fellow athletes we are going to be in a storm and as humans we are designed to get out of the rain and hunker down. That meant keep the body healthy but not stressed. Training for competition puts one right on the thin line of illness and race readiness. My program has been focused on a balance of endurance, power and technique work all while having fun and not stressing. I’m not training any less, but I’m also not stressing over a regimen and weight. What are your fitness goals for the summer? The focus is being resilient. Right now, my National Championships in September hasn’t been cancelled, so that’s the focus without stressing the body. How are you measuring your development? I have many years of benchmark data and also know what I need to accomplish in order to achieve my competition goals. For fun, I unofficially came close to matching the world record in the Murph, an exercise test common in CrossFit and many sports. I’m currently focused on the Abbate, which at the competition level weight is still a little out of my reach. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I work on my own and with a couple of racing buddies. I’ve been a pro sports trainer so I know what I need to do. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Unofficially close to matching the world record in the Murph, and am at an elite level with the Abbate. I also did possibly the first ever Swim/Run from Emeryville to Richmond. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? As a rugby coach, I always say to the athletes and parents: the main two objectives are safety and fun. COVID has, for now, tremendously changed sports. Super pros, Olympians, college and HS athletes are testing positive. All it takes is one teammate to be irresponsible. I see way too many kids (and adults) not heeding public health requirements, especially with masks. While the team that gets infected may not have very sick athletes, not only do they put others at risk, but they put their opportunity to play their sport at risk. We aren’t in the same boat, but we are in the same storm. Sasha Liu, PHS Class of 2019, recently finished her freshman year at Brown University as a member of the swim team. SASHA LIU Swimming ress with my times in practice. I have noticed my repeats improve in the last month, which is very motivating. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? In the time pools were closed, Elie Cole [former All-American lacrosse athlete] and I would go on long walks and we were able to get up to 15 miles walking from Lafayette to Walnut Creek. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Completing my freshman year at Brown. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Try to find the positives in what you’re doing. The break I had from swimming gave me perspective on things I had taken for granted. I used to feel really unmotivated after really hard sets, but after not being in the pool for so long; I realized how much I missed the sport and have a newfound motivation to get back! Jukka Valkonen is a triathlete and rugby coach who competes in offroad and ITU world championship races. Piedmont High Class of 2019 Brown University Class of 2024 Sasha Liu just finished her freshman year at Brown University. She made a big impact on the swim team in just seven meets prior to the COVID-19 shutdown. She won one events as a newcomer, defeating Yale in a dual meet in the 200 individual medley while also placing third in the 100 breaststroke. She also placed fourth in the 500 freestyle against Cornell, second against UConn in the 100 breast, and second and third respectively in the 200 IM and 100 breast in a meet with Penn. During her high school career in Piedmont, Liu was an NCS qualifier as a freshman, sophomore, and junior before missing her senior season after undergoing surgery. Her list of accomplishments at Piedmont includes: • Led PHS relay team to NCS Finals as a sophomore. • Placed 2nd in the 200 IM at NCS her sophomore and junior years. • CIF state qualifier as sophomore and junior. • USA Swimming Junior National qualifier • Qualified for USA Swimming Scholastic All American as sophomore and junior. • Set WACC record for 100 Breast and 500 Freestyle. What is your workout program this summer? I am training with my club team in Concord. Before pools opened up, I would do online workouts with my team and go on runs a couple times a week. What are your fitness goals for this summer? Just to get back into swimming shape. With pools being closed for around three months, I had to take the longest break from swimming that I ever have taken in practically my entire swimming career. While I could run and do other strength training, nothing is quite the same as swimming. How are you measuring your development? I’ve been measuring my progWIDDY TEVIS Lacrosse Piedmont High Class of 2020 Trinity College Class of 2024 Widdy Tevis graduated from Piedmont and will be playing lacrosse at Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut. Her senior campaign at PHS was cut short due to COVID-19. Tevis entered the spring as the leading scorer on the 2019 NCS Championship team. It is the women’s lacrosse program’s only NCS banner. She finished last season with 56 goals and 16 assists and was named a first-team All-League selection. As a sophomore, she burst onto the scene to lead the team in goals with 60. As a junior, Tevis scored at least three goals in 10 games including two fivegoal performances, in addition to four games with four goals. In 2020, she scored 11 goals and five assists in four games before the season was canceled. What is your workout program this summer? This summer, my lacrosse coaches sent us a strength (both with weights and with bodyweight, depending on access to gyms) packet, an agility packet, and stickwork drills in order to improve this summer. I am also taking advantage of the outdoors this summer. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals are to keep a fast mile – typically 6:30 or under for midfielders – as well as quick sprints on the field and track. I have the goal to perfect our wallball test which our coaches sent us. I’d like to get 100 quick sticks in one minute. How are you measuring your development? I use timing to measure my development, it’s very reliable. I know I’m improving when my times are faster. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I have been working out on my own and occasionally with girls on my club lacrosse team. We can easily stay distanced while having fun working together and pushing each other. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Graduating from high school. Even though my season was cut short, I was able to focus on school, my craft, and spending time with family. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Set achievable goals that can be accomplished to build up confidence and consistency. Also, have fun! Get a partner to do it with you -- a brother, sister, teammate, parent, neighbor, etc. At the end of the day, just remember to enjoy the process and communicate how you’re feeling. Widdy Tevis is a recent PHS graduate who will be playing lacrosse at Trinity College in Connecticut.

articles.text: Visitors to Mt. Tamalpais’ East Peak are afforded a million-dollar view of San Francisco, the Marin Headlands, Sausalito, and the North Bay.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON

articles.text: For this week’s hike, we return to Marin County and its landmark, Mt. Tamalpais, to seek out some views and a steady incline for an adequate lower-body workout. After many trails were closed in March at the start of the pandemic, county officials declared Mt. Tam re-opened for the public last month for hikers. For this trip, we start at Mt. Tam’s Quarry Parking Lot heading 1.5 miles down the Rock Spring Trail until intersecting with the historic West Point Inn. Our ascent starts from there, trekking two miles up to the East Peak, 2.4 miles to the opposite West Peak, and 1.2 miles back to the car. Once again, the spread of COVID-19 is still a concern for everyone. If you go out, do it responsibly. Here are our guidelines for hiking amidst the virus: • Research parking or trail restrictions for whatever park you choose. • Be mindful. Always bring a face cover of some sort. • The earlier the better. Trails are most trafficked past noon. • Find lesser used trailheads. Hiking on weekdays provides less traffic. • Go solo or plus-one. No large groups. To my surprise, there were just two other cars at the Mt. Tamalpais Quarry Lot upon my arrival after driving past many other lots filled to capacity. It’s been some time since our last trip to Mt. Tam when we visited Cataract Creek, an often-visited site. The 1.5 miles trip on the Rock Spring Trail was mostly level and downhill toward the West Point Inn with continuously improving views of San Francisco, the Marin Headlands, Sausalito, and the Pacific Ocean below. On your way to the West Point Inn, you’ll go through groves of California Bay Laurel trees and a stretch of a serpentine rock formation with a striking green hue. The West Point Inn, although closed due to COVID-19, has accommodated visitors since 1904 when it was a stopping point on the Mill Valley and Mt. Tamalpais Scenic Railway. From there, you’ll travel along the backside of the Inn on the Old Railroad Grade to East Ridgecrest Boulevard toward the East Peak’s parking lot. Gaining some 750 feet in elevation, you’ll reach the Gardner Fire Lookout for another sweeping view of the North Bay. It’s worth mentioning that the East Peak is among the most popular destinations of Mt. Tam, meaning you’ll be passing by lots of people just there for a quick view. I observed 17 people in the 3.5 miles toward the East Peak. On the walk up to Gardner Lookout, however, there were more than 30 people from the parking lot. Leaving the crowd, we traveled 2.4 miles down East Ridgecrest toward the West Peak – a much less visited and less developed area. I saw no other hikers on my walk down the boulevard. The walk toward the peak continued, with stellar views of San Francisco and the Marin Headlands, while gaining another 450 feet of elevation. West Peak is being restored and is fenced off. A large radio toward sits on the hill, but aside of a glimpse of the A view of the empty parking lot at the Quarry Lot, a. great starting point to avoid crowds. The Gardner Lookout point was created in 1937 and remains a popular destination.

articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will host a virtual concert, titled The Earthly and the Ethereal, with newly recorded music of Ludwig van Beethoven, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, Chevalier de Saint-Georges, and a world premiere by CMSSF co-founder Jory Fankuchen. The Chamber Society’s virtual events are structured to resemble its live concerts, but all pieces will be pre-recorded. The music will be introduced live, giving context and anecdotes about each piece, and will feature a live conversation with the musicians. The Chamber Music Society of SF quartet includes violinists and co-founder Fankuchen and Natasha Makhijani, violist Clio Tilton, and cellist Samsun van Loon. The virtual concert will be available for viewing and listening on Friday, July 24 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, July 26 at 6 p.m. Tickets are $25 and are available on Eventbrite at: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/ virtual-quartet-concert-the-earthl y - a n d - t h e - e t h e r e a l - t i c kets-110238688886. The concert will be a Zoom stream, and information to log into it will come with the purchase of a ticket. The quartet of the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco: Natasha Makhijiani (left), Jory Fankuchen, Clio Tilton, and Samsun van Loon.

articles.text: The world famous Alexander String Quartet, with violinists Zakarias Grafilo and Frederick Lifsitz, violist Paul Yarbrough, and cellist Sandy Wilson, announced their retirement last year. The Alexander String Quartet – violinists Frederick Lifsitz and Zakarias Grafilo, violist Paul Yarbrough, and cellist Sandy Wilson – kicked off San Francisco Performances ‘Sanctuary’ Series of concerts with a live-stream performance from St. Stephen’s Church in Belvedere on June 12, 2020. The all-Brahms performance included Brahms’ Opus 51, No. 1 in C minor, and No. 2 in A minor; also the Intermezzo from Opus 118, No. 2. In introducing the pieces, Violinist Frederick Lifsitz said, “These quartets by Brahms are interesting because Brahms started with the string quartet form very early on, thinking it would be something he could surmount relatively easily, compared to the symphonies. But he kept on feeling the ‘tramp of giants’ as he said, behind him. Beethoven in particular looking over his shoulder in Vienna. It took 18 quartets that he wrote and destroyed before he finally had two that he would share publicly.” You can watch the performance on Youtube at https:// www.youtube.com/watch?time_ continue=278&v=CYdZ76AwuXw&feature=emb_title.
articles.title: ASQ kicks off SF Performances ‘Sanctuary’ series

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will host a virtual event showcasing the work of Giancomo Puccini, considered the greatest composer of Italian opera after Verdi. One of Puccini’s most revered operas, La Boheme, will be discussed at the event. The composer is often disdained within intellectual circles, but adored by the public, a contradiction that will be explored. The discussion will be led by Robert Hartwell. Hartwell is a professor of music history and Department Chair at Foothill College, where he teaches classes in music history, music of multicultural America, and contemporary American culture. The discussion is part of a weekly series offered by San Francisco Opera in lieu of in-person events due to COVID-19. Entitled “Opera Aficionado,” the program includes interactive lectures, scholarly talks, and open dialogue between experts and patrons. Each Robert Hartwell, Music Department Chair at Foothill College. month will be focused on a concept or theme; this month’s theme is “emotions in opera.” The event will take place virtually on Sunday, July 19, at 1 p.m. Each interactive lecture costs $20, and subscription pricing will be available soon. For more information, visit https:// sfopera.com/discover-opera/education/community-programs/ aficionado/.
articles.title: Passion, Paris and Puccini: SF Opera virtual event on Sat.

articles.text: Cellist Gabriel Martins Musaics of the Bay is offering another presentation from its “Stay-at-home Symposium” series. The fourth in the series, released last week, is a solo cello piece by composer Milad Yousufi and performed by Gabriel Martins. The work, titled “Mystery,” is a work inspired by a photograph by Dale Carter called “Ridges in Sand 1.” The photograph was, in turn, inspired by the paintings of Mark Rothko. “There is a gentle sense of serenity and contemplation in [Rothko’s] paintings that I attempted to capture in this series,” Carter told Musaics of the Bay founder Audrey Vardanega. “Like Rothko, I took a meditative approach to this piece, with the soft color scheme. My main focus, though, was on capturing those fleeting, beautiful moments in nature when it reveals itself.” The Stay-at-home Symposium is a community collaboration and series of broadcasts featuring music premieres based on the creativity of community members – composers, performers, and artists of all types. “We believe in the power of classical music to enrich and heal us, especially in these uncertain times,” Vardanega said. You can watch the fourth installment of the series on Youtube by visiting https://www. youtube.com/watch?time_continue=276&v=fQM-wogxCRs&- feature=emb_title.
articles.title: Musaics of the Bay continue stay-at-home symposiums

articles.text: As the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra ensemble shelters in place, Music Director Ben Simon has put his time in quarantine to good use by launching the “Simon Says Show.” In the first episode, Simon shares two examples of famous composers stealing from “our planet’s greatest musicians: the birds.” He explores how birdsongs made their way into classical works by Vivaldi and Beethoven. Simon provides some historical background to these two works, and explains how the music was influenced by birdsong, quoting Vivaldi’s own words. Simon breaks up the short explanation with some musical humor, for which he is well known (and well loved): “What does a lawsuit and a viola have in common? Everyone is relieved when the case is closed.” Watch Ben Simon’s first episode of the Simon Says Show on YouTube by visiting https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=8Z_lT7cdwF8&feature=emb_title. articles.text: A scene from Capernaum Movie review by Chris Honoré The title Capernaum comes from French literature and means chaos. And indeed, chaos is the essence of this film, permeating the narrative with a bleakness that is unrelenting. The story, however, is wondrous, and is testimony to the resilience of the human spirit. If there is beauty and hope in Capernaum it is revealed through a 12-year-old boy, Zain (Zain Al Refeea). It’s from Zain’s point of view that we are introduced to the squalid, desperately mean streets of Beirut. Everywhere and everything conveys this. The flatroofed, square, crumbling houses and shops, stacked one on top of the other are barely habitable. Everyone has a hustle, and if Zain is to survive, he must make his way, using all the street smarts he can muster. He endures the snarls and slaps and abuse from his mother and father (Kawthar Al Haddad and Fadi Kamel Youseef), both grifters and drug dealers, resisting and ignoring their threats, all the while working the streets and watching other kids going to and from school. There is only one person he cares about, truly loves, and that is his sister, Sahar (Cedra Izam), one year younger. He is fearful, even desperate, that his parents do not discover that she is on the cusp of her menarche, lest she be sold to their landlord’s son as part of a forced marriage bargain. When he learns that that is what they have done, in a rage, he runs away. And so begins act two in which he is befriended by a young Ethiopian woman, Rahil (Yordanos Shiferaw), who has a small child. She is an undocumented refugee. Zain becomes the babysitter while Rahil goes to work. It is a responsibility he takes most seriously, his courage and empathy evident, his concern for the small boy constant. But then events change everything. Capernaum has been nominated for Best Foreign Film, and has a documentary feel about it. It is a searing close up, a brutal window through which we see a brittle humanity in granular detail. Chaos defines everything, until it doesn’t. The last image on the screen is of a smiling Zain. Capernaum. Directed by Nadine Labaki. In Arabic with English subtitles. Starring Zain Al Rafeea, Yordanos Shiferaw and Cedra Izzam. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R. Zain Al Rafeea in a scene from Capernaum.
articles.title: Capernaum – nominated for Best Foreign Film of 2018

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honore’ Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood is not surprisingly an off-center homage to, well, Hollywood. The year is 1969. The film glows with SoCal sunshine, blue skies, prologue traffic with airplane-size cars, and is more introspective than director Quentin Tarantino’s previous oeuvre. I’ve always been ambivalent about his movies (Pulp Fiction was made 25 years ago), yet interested, maybe even captivated, by their quirky plots and strong characters. Still, I’ve bridled at what has always seemed to me to be gratuitous, over-the-top violence and sideways action. The Hateful Eight is a good example. I knew nothing about the movie upon entering, and had not seen the trailer if there was one. I only knew that Brad Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprio starred in what, at first glance, seemed a buddy movie. For much of act one I worked at giving the movie a chance as it moseyed from one digression to the next as the Pitt and DiCaprio characters, Cliff Booth and Rick Dalton, were introduced. Rick is a fading TV star who appeared just long enough in a western series titled Bounty Law to give him name recognition and offers of Movie of the Week guest gigs as villainous characters. Cliff was Rick’s stunt double in the TV series and has remained his friend and salaried assistant/ go-fer who only works when Rick does. The narrative focuses on these two men, both aging-out of mainstream Hollywood and both reacting in decidedly different ways. Rick is a bundle of insecurity in the grip of a tormenting angst, which he buffers with alcohol. In one scene, on a movie set and in his trailer, he berates himself for missing his lines, looking in a mirror threatening to take a gun to his head if he doesn’t pull it together. Cliff, in contrast, takes life as it comes, is studiously content to support Rick, keeping him and his fragile self-confidence barely moving forward and running errands as needed. Gradually, the film engages, cutting back and forth from Rick’s latest villain gig to Cliff hanging out, or at home in his trailer with his dog. While both now work at the edges of the industry, there’s still work to be had. The story’s through line is the headline-grabbing murder that occurred in August of 1969. A sometimes actress Sharon Tate and others are killed by the Manson Family, a group of psychotic followers of Charles Manson, perpetrators of what later became known as the Tate-LaBianca murders. But consider the title of the movie: Once Upon a Time…. This is a Tarantino fantasy, viewed through the prism of pop culture and Hollywood road signs, framing how tragic events might’ve been, could’ve been, if only. In Act II, Tarantino seems to find a nice rhythm, crafting some excellent, very watchable scenes. One captures Tate (Margot Robbie), a second tier movie star married to director Roman Polanski (Rosemary’s Baby), out running errands. She goes into a movie theater to watch herself in a film. The camera holds on her face, a smile touching her eyes as the audience reacts to her scenes. It’s a tender moment, though a bit ominous given what has been so indirectly foreshadowed. There is also a vignette that is both wonderful and foreboding when Cliff picks up a young hippy girl hitchhiking (Margaret Qualley). She tells him she lives with her friends at the Spahn Ranch and begins to give him directions. He, however, knows the way since it’s been a familiar location for westerns. It’ is now where a cohort of hippies is living/squatting. When Cliff and the girl arrive, he is not greeted with flower power, or a groovy vibe. Standing on the front porches are feral young women – ranch denizens, suspicious and unwelcoming. Cliff knows that the ranch is owned by a cantankerous, partially blind geezer, George Spahn (Bruce Dern). He insists on saying hello to him, just to see that all is well. There is is a long, harrowing scene as Cliff tries to judge George’s well-being. Though not quite satisfied, he leaves, taking a slow walk back to his car, past the hostile gathering of hippie women. What shouldn’t surprise, given Tarantino’s predilection for reactionary violence, is that he turns the Hollywood hippies into foils. In one scene, Rick, who is drunk, hearing a car entering his private cul-de-sac walks out to the street while holding a blender of margaritas and in a scatological rant tells the hippie driver and his passengers to back up and get out. Tarantino skips all the counterculture good feeling gestalt of the 60s, choosing instead to portray them as deranged cultists. Which, hewing to a semblance of history, the Manson clan was, though not representative. This scene leads to the harrowing climax of the film, one that is breathtakingly outrageous, pure Tarantino, yet fits into the farrago of myth and fact that has always permeated Hollywood. Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. Directed by Quentin Tarantino. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Brad Pitt and Margot Robbie. 2 hrs., 39 min. Rated R. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on August 7, 2019
articles.title: Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood – Tarantino’s latest offering

What shouldn’t surprise, given Tarantino’s predilection for reactionary violence, is that he turns the Hollywood hippies into foils. In one scene, Rick, who is drunk, hearing a car entering his private cul-de-sac walks out to the street while holding a blender of margaritas and in a scatological rant tells the hippie driver and his passengers to back up and get out. Tarantino skips all the counterculture good feeling gestalt of the 60s, choosing instead to portray them as deranged cultists. Which, hewing to a semblance of history, the Manson clan was, though not representative. This scene leads to the harrowing climax of the film, one that is breathtakingly outrageous, pure Tarantino, yet fits into the farrago of myth and fact that has always permeated Hollywood. Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. Directed by Quentin Tarantino. Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Brad Pitt and Margot Robbie. 2 hrs., 39 min. Rated R. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on August 7, 2019

articles.text: A scene from Spielberg’s movie, The BFG. Movie review by Chris Honoré The BFG (Big Friendly Giant), based on Roald Dahl’s children’s book, proves to be a soft, beautifully imagined film that captures the power of enchantment that only film can fully create, especially when crafted by a director with the skill of Steven Spielberg. Visually, it is wondrous to behold. With the aid of computer graphics, Mark Ryance (from Bridge of Spies) is transformed into an enormous giant whose face is deeply creased by smiles, possesses enormous ears, and eyes that capture the sparkle and joy of his job. He’s Merlin, an alchemist, a gentle soul who lives in an out-ofplumb house. He visits, beneath a canopy of stars, the dream tree where he captures small whizzing stars and dreams (not unlike Tinkerbell) and bottles them for later. It is a stunning scene, breathtaking in all aspects. And what does he do with those glowing, luminous stars? At night, when all are sleeping, BFG goes forth from giant land, stealthily visiting the city, and with his trumpet-like, spiraling horn that has attached a bottle of captured dreams, he blows them, one at a time, into the mouths of kids and adults. It’s on one such outing that he is spotted by 10-year-old Sophie (Ruby Barnhill), a plucky, precocious orphan who climbs out of bed and stands on a narrow balcony staring at this enormous creature in complete disbelief. Afraid that she will reveal his presence, he kidnaps her and takes her back to his digs in Giant Land. His home is a marvelous place filled with inventions and bottled dreams, each container glowing and carefully labeled. Sophie is mere inches tall by comparison and suddenly finds herself in a world of huge items, to include the strange talking conjurer of dreams, the BFG. If there is a dark side to The BFG, it’s the nine stupendously massive dunderhead giants who live near BFG. They also happen to be carnivores of “human beans” (or just “beans”). Apparently they’ve been taking small children and consuming them and would love to find Sophie for the same reason. Hence their visit to BFG’s cavern-like home. BFG, of course, is desperate to keep her hidden among the jars and bowls set on the shelves and the tables, lest her fate follow that of the other children. However, these really big giants (far taller than BFG, called “Runt” by the crew) never seem to present a serious threat to Sophie. Spielberg, and his screenwriter, the late Melissa Mathison (famous for E.T.) are content to keep Sophie out of any real jeopardy, meaning the sense of excitement never rises to any real breathtaking level. And so there’s a sense of brief longueur in act two. Things don’t really gain any real momentum until act three when Sophie goes to the Queen of England (Penelope Wilton) and most humbly asks for her help with the nine giants. After introducing her to BFG, of course. For kids watching this film, the question of whether there is enough story in The BFG to stand alone, absent the many joyous and visually captivating scene is not relevant. The answer, aimed at the adults who will be sprinkled throughout the audience is, well, sort of. But it’s not a story in which the stakes seem precariously high. In essence, the nine giants are cannibals who relish feasting on “beans.” Shudder. But in some strange way they seem rather harmless. Instead, The BFG is testimony to Spielberg’s love of the magic that film can create on a grand scale. Today, given the astonishing technology available to filmmakers, there is nothing imagined that cannot be created, meaning a story can transcend all limitations that were once thought of as constraints. From an adult point of view, I’m not sure that Dahl’s 1982 book was ever well suited to be made into a movie; however, what is clear is that in The BFG, Spielberg has made a wondrous attempt. Kids will love it. When it concluded, they clapped. Tangentially, I’ve always believed that one of his best children’s movies – well, quasi-children’s movies – is The Empire of the Sun, in which the stakes are enormous for a young boy struggling to survive at a POW camp during World War II. The BFG. Starring Mark Ryance, Ruby Barnhill and Penelope Wilton. Directed by Steven Spielberg. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on July 6, 2016.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS The BFG a wondrous story, wondrous film

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The character “Astro Boy” was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books) and anime (movie and television animation), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries. Now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. They will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment (others will likely follow) explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy superhuman. He can fly, has x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. At first unaware he’s a robot, Astro sets out to find his place in the world, meaning Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City and all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. The kids long for Astro’s powers and he longs for their humanity. He also grieves for the loss of his father. There’s an evil Mayor of Metro City (Donald Sutherland) who covets Astro’s “blue power,” and a duplicitous hustler named Hamegg (Nathan Lane) who wants only to use Astro. It’s a long journey back to the arms of his father. While the story brings to mind Transformers and even Pinocchio, kids will find Astro appealing and will look forward to The Return of Astro Boy. Astro Boy. Animated. With the voices of Nicolas Cage, Freddie Highmore, Nathan Lane, Kristen Bell and Bill Nighy. Directed by David Bowers. Rated PG. Reprinted from Piedmont Post on October 28, 2009.
articles.title: Astro Boy – a charming story from Japanese animator Tezuka

articles.text: If you have kids pacing back and forth with that “there’s nothing to do” look in their eyes, I would suggest that you convince them to do a deep dive into the world of animation. Think of it as a tutorial, beginning with the proliferation of the animated films of Hayao Miyazaki. A world-renowned Japanese animator, filmmaker, screenwriter, author, and manga artist (Japanese comic books), he strongly influenced Pixar and Disney in the U.S. in their storytelling and art of animation. Miyazaki began what has been an extraordinary career in 1963, immersing himself in the world of manga and film animation (anime), with hand drawn and later computer-generated animation originating in Japan. He co-founded Studio Ghibli in 1985 where he and fellow animators found critical and commercial success throughout the world with the films Castle in the Sky, My Neighbor Totoro and the hugely successful Princess Mononoke (released in 1997). He went on to win an Oscar at the Academy Awards in 2001 for the animated feature, Spirited Away. Hayao Miyazaki, Japan’s world-famous animator and founder of Studio Ghibli, who strongly influenced both Pixar and Disney in the U.S. Using colorful graphics, vibrant characters, and fantastical themes, which thread through films such as Kiki’a Delivery Service, The Wind Rises, Spirited Away, Nausica of the Valley, Ponyo and From Up on Poppy Hill, Miyazaki has explored humanity’s relationship with nature and technology as well as capturing the perpetual sense of wonder inherent in young people. In his work he has also examined the obstacles encountered as one tries to maintain a pacifist ethic in a violent world, while also examining themes that touch on love, family and feminism. Many of his protagonists are young women, never objectified, who struggle with the complexities inherent to their gender. In 2012, Miyazaki was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his cultural contributions, and, in 2014, he received the Academy’s honorary award for his impact on animation and cinema worldwide. Note: Netflix has a large trove of anime and is a remarkable resource for animated films. Cover art: My Neighbor Totoro Cover art: Spirited Away
articles.title: Hayao Miyazaki – the world’s iconic animator

articles.text: Arturo Toscanini was the greatest orchestra conductor of his time. He achieved the highest quality performances from his orchestras with an uncontrolled temper that rivaled the explosion of Krakatoa. Many of his rehearsals were recorded. These document the eruptions which seem to be over absolutely insignificant things. Yelling and screaming and insults were his modus operandi. He was unbelievably severe with his musicians. He could also be brutal with his own mistakes. In order to placate him and put him in a good mood, his musicians presented him with a very expensive gold-encased pocket watch. It lasted less than one rehearsal. His temper flared and he took out that very expensive watch, flinging it to the ground and breaking it to smithereens. His musicians learned their lesson. They gave him another watch. This time it was a cheap one… which he smashed during the very next rehearsal. One time, Toscanini yelled at a musician telling him to play mezzo forte. They played the passage again, but the musician played exactly the same way the second time. Toscanini yelled even louder. “I told you to play mezzo forte!” The musician looked blandly at the maestro and calmly said, “Maestro, do you want me to play louder or softer?” It was the perfect thing to say and it was said with great cleverness and A caricature of Arturo Toscanini by Enrico Caruso – all angles and oblique lines. diplomacy. Toscanini’s temper tantrums were famous throughout the world. The curious thing is that the musicians in his orchestras did not seem to take offense. They usually responded to these eruptions with calmness and understanding. But that made no difference to Toscanini. A raging temper, fortified with insults was his way of life. But there is a curious twist to this story. Toscanini was a raging, temperamental maestro, but only when at the podium. Off the podium he was the epitome of a calm gentleman. While conducting he demanded absolute perfection in music. But off the podium he became a shy, self-effacing mouse. If he went to a restaurant and the waiter brought him the wrong thing…he said...absolutely nothing! Buon appetito. Showing the mild side of Arturo Toscanini, in a telegram he thanks an RCA executive for some cheese and wine.

articles.text: Copper Children, Midsummer Night’s Dream currently being shown The Oregon Shakespeare Festival, having cancelled its 2020 season due to Covid-19, is offering on-demand streaming service beginning with full-length plays from its 2020 season. The performances are accessible on laptops, tablets and mobile phones. This season’s offering has begun with The Copper Children by Karen Zacharias and is streaming from July 2-15. Zacharias previously wrote Destiny of Desire that won the Edgerton Foundation new play award and was featured as part of the 2018 season in Ashland. Copper Children is set in Arizona at the turn of the 20th century and is based on the true history of what was known as the orphan trains, a welfare program that sent predominantly Irish orphaned and homeless children from Eastern U.S. cities across the country to foster homes in the Midwest. Oregon Shakespeare Festival is also featuring the Shakespearian comedy, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, with music. It is streaming July 9-22. The productions are complete shows with a full cast of actors filmed on stage during their short runs earlier this year. The intent is to give patrons a live theater experience with the cameras having been placed directly in front of the stage, so the show is experienced as if you are sitting in a front row seat. The productions are handled by Uscreen, a provider of video-on-demand services. Subscribers will be able to access the play at a cost of $15 per show by setting up an account on the hosting site. Information can be found online by searching Oregon Shakespeare Festival or by e-mailing: streaming@osfashland.org Photo by Jenny Graham, Oregon Shakespeare Festival. The Copper Children (2020): Carla Pantoja (Sister Anna), Armando Durán (George Swayne), Sarita Ocón (Sister Francis). The Copper Children (2020): Ensemble. Photo by Jenny Graham, Oregon Shakespeare Festival. Photo by Jenny Graham, Oregon Shakespeare Festival. A Midsummer Night’s Dream (2020): Lauren Modica (Titania), Al Espinosa (Oberon). articles.text: Reprinted from May 6, 2015. This cake will be the highlight of your summer brunch or tea time. It pulls together easily enough for kids and dads alike to prepare, yet has a simple elegance that fits this special occasion. I’ve added a hint of orange to the cake for that je ne sais quoi complement to the strawberries. Select perfectly ripe fruit to maximize the berries’ flavor. Medium-sized fruit is best for distribution on the cake and ease when it comes time to slice and serve. Helpful tip: Set a timer to track the initial 10 minutes of baking so you will know when to reduce the oven temperature. Reset the timer for 45 minutes to begin checking the cake to see if it done. Fresh Strawberry Cake Adapted from Martha Stewart INGREDIENTS • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus additional for the pan • 1-1/ 2 cup all-purpose flour • 1-1/ 2 teaspoon baking powder • 1/ 2 teaspoon salt • 3/4 cup granulated sugar, preferably super-fine; plus an additional 2 tablespoons for topping • 1 large egg, room temperature • 1/4 cup whole milk, approx. • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1 medium orange • 1 pint fresh strawberries, approximately 16 berries; hulled and halved lengthwise INSTRUCTIONS Adjust oven rack to the lower 1/ 3 position in the oven and preheat to 350°F. Butter a 9-inch pie pan. Whisk together the flour, baking powder and salt in a small bowl. Set aside. Remove the zest of the orange using a microplane or very fine grater, avoiding the white pith. This yields about 1 teaspoon of zest. Set aside. Cut the orange in half and extract the juice into a measuring cup. This yields about 1/ 4 cup of juice. Add enough whole milk to bring the combined liquids to measure 1/ 2 cup total. Set aside. Put 6 tablespoons of butter and 3/ 4 cup of sugar into a large mixing bowl. Beat on medium-high speed until they become pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Reduce the mixer speed to medium low and add the egg, orange zest, vanilla and juice-milk mixture. It will look curdled. This is OK. Reduce mixer speed to low and gradually add the flour mixture. Mix until just incorporated, do not overmix. You can use a silicone spatula to combine the last bits of flour clinging to the bowl. Transfer the batter into the buttered pie pan, smoothing to level it with a spatula. Place the strawberries on top of the batter, cut sides down and close to each other but not overlapping. Sprinkle the remaining 2 tablespoons of sugar evenly over the berries. Bake the cake for 10 minutes, then reduce the oven temperature to 325° F. Bake until cake is golden and a toothpick inserted into the center of it comes out with only a few crumbs clinging to it, about 45-50 additional minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool on a wire rack. Cake may be served warm or at room temperature with a bit of whipped cream and sliced berries. For more information or to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok at PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: Celebrating summer with Strawberry Cake

articles.text: Whether you’re planning a refresh or a complete kitchen remodel, the first step is to examine your space. Take a moment to think about how you use and move throughout your kitchen. Kitchens are no longer just for cooking. Integrating dining and additional workspaces into your new kitchen can make it a multi-functional room. Including a workstation to make the kitchen the home’s command center will allow the family to work at home. Consider incorporating a casual space for dining via a counter or breakfast nook. Kitchen Remodel Taking Shape The next step is to determine the most functional use of space. Think about how the space works and any pain points you’d like to solve. There are three common kitchen layouts: U-shaped, I-shaped, and L-shaped kitchens. U-Shaped Kitchen This common kitchen layout is versatile, functional, and great for busy cooks. The workspace surrounds the cook for maximum efficiency and keeps everything within easy reach. This layout is also great for entertaining. I-Shaped Kitchen In this layout, the appliances are concentrated along a single wall. This simple kitchen design is great for small spaces and the biggest benefit is its cost effectiveness. However, the limited workspace of this kitchen layout can make it challenging for multiple cooks to operate at the same time. L-Shaped Kitchen This layout works best within a large kitchen footprint. It is the most ergonomically correct kitchen design and is perfect for a family with multiple chefs in the kitchen at the same time. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, July 15, 2020 Features HOME REMODELING TIPS Celebrating summer with Strawberry Cake By Deborah Quok Reprinted from May 6, 2015. This cake will be the highlight of your summer brunch or tea time. It pulls together easily enough for kids and dads alike to prepare, yet has a simple elegance that fits this special occasion. I’ve added a hint of orange to the cake for that je ne sais quoi complement to the strawberries. Select perfectly ripe fruit to maximize the berries’ flavor. Medium-sized fruit is best for distribution on the cake and ease when it comes time to slice and serve. Helpful tip: Set a timer to track the initial 10 minutes of baking so you will know when to reduce the oven temperature. Reset the timer for 45 minutes to begin checking the cake to see if it done. Fresh Strawberry Cake Adapted from Martha Stewart INGREDIENTS • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus additional for the pan • 1-1/ 2 cup all-purpose flour • 1-1/ 2 teaspoon baking powder • 1/ 2 teaspoon salt • 3/4 cup granulated sugar, preferably super-fine; plus an additional 2 tablespoons for topping • 1 large egg, room temperature • 1/4 cup whole milk, approx. • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1 medium orange • 1 pint fresh strawberries, approximately 16 berries; hulled and halved lengthwise INSTRUCTIONS Adjust oven rack to the lower 1/ 3 position in the oven and preheat to 350°F. Butter a 9-inch pie pan. Whisk together the flour, baking powder and salt in a small bowl. Set aside. Remove the zest of the orange using a microplane or very fine grater, avoiding the white pith. This yields about 1 teaspoon of zest. Set aside. Cut the orange in half and extract the juice into a measuring cup. This yields about 1/ 4 cup of juice. Add enough whole milk to bring the combined liquids to measure 1/ 2 cup total. Set aside. Put 6 tablespoons of butter and 3/ 4 cup of sugar into a large mixing bowl. Beat on medium-high speed until they become pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Reduce the mixer speed to medium low and add the egg, orange zest, vanilla and juice-milk mixture. It will look curdled. This is OK. Reduce mixer speed to low and gradually add the flour mixture. Mix until just incorporated, do not overmix. You can use a silicone spatula to combine the last bits of flour clinging to the bowl. Transfer the batter into the buttered pie pan, smoothing to level it with a spatula. Place the strawberries on top of the batter, cut sides down and close to each other but not overlapping. Sprinkle the remaining 2 tablespoons of sugar evenly over the berries. Bake the cake for 10 minutes, then reduce the oven temperature to 325° F. Bake until cake is golden and a toothpick inserted into the center of it comes out with only a few crumbs clinging to it, about 45-50 additional minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool on a wire rack. Cake may be served warm or at room temperature with a bit of whipped cream and sliced berries. articles.text: Staying at home seems to be making greater readers of everyone. The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Monday Reading Group opened July with a large turnout of 19 people on Monday, July 6. The group continues to meet virtually through Zoom technology. The July book selection, The Library Book by Susan Orlean, is a non-fiction account of the unsolved mystery of the most catastrophic library fire in American history. On the morning of April 29, 1986, a fire in the Los Angeles Main Public Library raged through its stacks. It reached 2000 degrees, burned for over seven hours, destroyed 400,000 books and damaged 700,000 more. The library was closed for seven years. An investigation into the cause of the fire led to the arrest of Harry Peak, a struggling actor who constantly changed his story about his activities during the day of the fire. His role in the fire remains a mystery, and its cause has never been conclusively determined. Peak was charged, but the evidence was not definitive and the charges were eventually dropped, after he countersued. Peak’s guilt or innocence was a question for the readers to discuss, and there was no consensus. While the fire and the story of Harry Peak provide the thread that weaves through the book, it is more than a fire mystery who-done-it. With a life-long love of books, Orlean fondly recalls the happy trips to her library that she had with her mother. Orlean expands the fire story and her personal experiences into a history of the Los Angeles Library, libraries more broadly, the city of Los Angeles, library staff, along with those who run and use libraries. The author shows us the larger role that libraries now play in our society, how they are more than just books. Many in the reading group loved the book. They appreciated how Orlean provided so much information about libraries, their history and the people associated with them. The author was also able to make an emotional connection with readers. Some could relate to Orlean’s library experiences and the library time she spent with her now declining mother. Some readers had similar library experiences when they were young. An interesting reader dynamic was the split between the women and men about the book. There were 16 women and three men in the group. All three men liked the book, though they did not have the level of passion for it that the women did. It was suggested that possibly young girls have more positive, emotional experiences with books and libraries than boys do. Participating in the discussion were: Rumi Ueno, Margie Blodgett, Jeri Lockhart, Sarah Johnson, Sally Arney, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Heidi Shale, Laura Goldman, Albert Chen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Bella Almanzan, Pat McSwain, Adriene Hamlin, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Carol Long and Priscilla Wanerus. Next came a discussion to select the next book to read. They had previously made The Black Swan by Nassim Nicholas Taleb and The Dutch House by Ann Patchett their August and September selections. However, with society’s current focus on racial justice, the group decided to read White Fragility by Robin DiAngelo for September. Assuming social distancing is still in place, the readers will meet again for a Zoom discussion on Monday, August 3 at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration with the Recreation Department is required. For more information, contact John Wilk at Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov). articles.text: Book review by Ann P. McCauley The Perfume Collector by Kathleen Tessaro is a novel about the sensual awakening of two young women. It is set in glamorous Parisian apartments, stylish New York hotels, English country gardens in the spring, and warm, midnight beaches near Monte Carlo. Readers revel in descriptions of these lovely places before learning of an evil character who ends up on a dairy farm in Minnesota. One young woman is born to poverty but has extraordinary gifts that allow her to create a world of style and excitement that beguiles those around her. She flits around glamorous casinos in a shimmering dress and silver sandals, pausing in the doorway to catch the light. The other woman is an English debutante who complains that food with onions and garlic has too much flavor and who considers luxurious clothing garish. A French hairdresser turns her into a beauty, and a shop saleswoman puts her into a flattering Balenciaga “architecturally cut” dress. A charming, sensitive French man introduces her to…well…onions, garlic and other pleasures. Central to the novel is the appreciation, description, and enjoyment of the sense of smell. Fragrance, a character notes, is an aspiration. Perfume transports us from life as it is into a lovely place filled with our most sensually delicious moments, and so each person needs a perfume that reminds them of things they love – clean rain, jasmine in a flower garden, newly mown grass. It is a pleasure to spend time in the world of this novel. The Perfume Collector, Discovering Life Through the Senses, not the Mind, by Kathleen Tessaro. Ann McCauley studied Anthropology at Cal and works in international health. She loves stories with sympathetic, wise characters who engage in humorous conversations and travel to exotic places. articles.text: Neil Guiney, a resident of Piedmont for 24 years, passed away peacefully at home in Oakland on May 7, 2020 after a brief struggle with cancer. Born Neil Terrence Guiney on February 14, 1945 in San Francisco, he was the son of Katherine Sullivan Guiney and Neil Joseph Guiney and a lifelong Bay Area resident. He was a member of the first graduating class of St. Francis High School in Mountain View. After graduating from St. Mary’s College in Moraga, he earned a Master’s Degree in English with an emphasis on Irish Theater from San Francisco State University in 1969. Upon completing his education in the arts, he became a carpenter, obtaining his General Contractors License in 1976. He married Julie Ann Fielder in 1973, and in 1979 they moved from San Francisco to Piedmont where they raised their two children. In 2003, they moved to Oakland, where they ultimately retired. As a builder he created beautiful homes, remodeling each of his houses to his exacting taste and specifications, just as he did for scores of clients over the years. His workshop in the garage was his favorite place to be, where he crafted furniture and worked on myriad projects. Neil was a Renaissance man at heart. He enjoyed playing many instruments throughout his life, from the piano to the fiddle. He loved literature, his vegetable garden, handwoven textiles and a wide variety of music and art. He spent many happy hours in museums throughout the world. In 2018, after a painstaking search of family records, Neil was very proud to obtain the necessary documentation that allowed him a dual citizenship in Ireland and the U.S. Though an avid 49ers and Warriors fan, his true love was the San Francisco Giants, a love he shared with his father. In 1958 Neil Guiney, a resident of Piedmont for 24 years, passed away on May 7. He was 75. Neil’s father watched the parade welcoming the Giants to San Francisco in front of his financial district office. Fifty-two years later, in 2010, when the SF Giants finally won a World Series title, Neil stood proudly in front of that same building with his own son, watching the parade go by and knowing his father was with them in spirit. Above all he loved his family and demonstrated that in gestures both grand and small. The family is devastated by his loss. Neil is predeceased by his parents, and is survived by his wife Julie, daughter Ann, son Dennis (wife Micaela Garcia), granddaughter Teresa, his brother Stephen (wife Brooke), brother and sister-in-law (John and Susan Fielder) and loving nieces and nephews Sean, Katherine and Connor Guiney, Jane Fielder and Robyn Fielder Pichel. He was a man who lived by the Henry Kaiser maxim: “When your work speaks for itself, don’t interrupt.” A celebration of Neil’s life has been indefinitely postponed due to current public health concerns. The family suggests that memorial donations in the name of Neil Guiney may be made to the St. Anthony Foundation or to an arts organization of your preference. about you, it’s possible that you’ll care about others. You are special, and so is your neighbor – that part is essential: that you’re not the only special person in the world. The person you happen to be with at the moment is loved, too.” We don’t have saints in the Protestant church. But, if we did, I’d nominate Mister Rogers. Saint Fred – the patron saint of neighborliness. Rev. Dr. William McNabb is Senior Minister of Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont. articles.text: Julia Burke’s wildflower sidewalk strip in front of her house. As ongoing shelter-in-place takes its toll on daily life, many Piedmonters have found new and continued pleasure in their backyards. Just ask Eric Dam, manager of ACE Garden Center. “Everyone is gardening” Dam said. “They’re creating Victory Gardens. In the spring, we ran out of vegetable seeds. Now there’s a shortage of bark and soil, and our native plant supply clears out every week.” Julia Burke, a member of the Piedmont Garden Club and an avid native-plant gardener and beekeeper, is delighted to see more gardens springing up in town, especially with drought-tolerant and native species. She is hoping to see more city properties and sidewalk strips planted with wildflowers. “People need to know that native gardens can make a difference for wildlife and for drought,” she says. “These plants have evolved over thousands of years to withstand six months of drought. Non-natives don’t attract the insects that birds need to survive and feed their young. They need diversity. ‘The whole food web depends on natives, and it’s just as easy to grow them as non-natives,” she said. As the city’s Climate Challenge notes, replacing 1,000 sq. ft. of lawn with drought-tolerant plants can save up to 20,000 gallons of water a year. (See www. piedmontclimatechallenge.org/ action/replace-lawn.) Burke replaced the lawn in front of her house on LaSalle five years ago. Since then she has transformed the area into a hillside of colorful wildflowers including California poppies that reseed every year. Her fenced backyard is devoted to more wildflowers, vegetables, and beekeeping. She lets her lettuce, chard, and broccoli flower go to seed for the bees. This year, Burke planted all of her vegetables from seed and gave away six-packs of seedlings to friends. “Sunflowers are also a wonderful addition to attract birds and bees,” she said. “My yard is not landscaped, and I would never have anyone blowing it to disturb the leaves or the soil.” Burke’s interest in beekeeping began when she learned about it from Piedmonters Carter and Patty Dunlap (whose beekeeping and fruit tree garden will be featured in a future Climate Corner). “I thought I was allergic to bees,” Burke said, “but after getting stung a few times, I found I wasn’t allergic. It’s Zen-like to watch the bees coming and going.” Plus, they give her 30 pounds of honey a year – a pretty sweet deal. You are special, and so is your neighbor – that part is essential: that you’re not the only special person in the world. The person you happen to be with at the moment is loved, too.” We don’t have saints in the Protestant church. But, if we did, I’d nominate Mister Rogers. Saint Fred – the patron saint of neighborliness. Rev. Dr. William McNabb is Senior Minister of Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont. articles.text: The American Red Cross strongly urges healthy, eligible individuals who are feeling well to give blood or platelets to help maintain a sufficient blood supply and prevent shortages as concerns about the outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019, or COVID-19, rise in the U.S. Cold and f lu season has already impacted the nation’s ability to maintain its blood supply. As the number of coronavirus cases grows in the U.S., the number of people eligible to give blood for patients in need could decrease further. “We’re asking people to help keep the blood supply stable during this challenging time. As communities across the country prepare for this public health emergency, it’s critical that plans include a readily available blood supply for hospital patients,” said Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Blood Services. “As fears of coronavirus rise, low donor participation could harm blood availability at hospitals, and the last thing a patient should worry about is whether lifesaving blood will be on the shelf when they need it most.” Make an appointment to donate blood now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or calling the Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 510-658-6456. Donating blood is a safe process and people should not hesitate to give or receive blood. There are no data or evidence that this coronavirus can be transmissible by blood transfusion, and there have been no reported cases worldwide of transmissions for any respiratory virus, including this coronavirus, from a transfusion. The Red Cross only collects blood from individuals who are healthy and feeling well at the time of donation – and who meet other eligibility requirements, available at RedCrossBlood.org. At each blood drive and donation center, Red Cross employees follow thorough safety protocols including wearing gloves, routinely wiping down donortouched areas, using sterile collection sets for every donation, and preparing the arm for donation with an aseptic scrub. These mitigation measures will help ensure blood recipient safety, as well as staff and donor safety in reducing contact with those who may potentially have this respiratory infection. The Red Cross has implemented new blood donation deferrals out of an abundance of caution. Individuals are asked to postpone their donation for 28 days following: • Travel to China and its special administrative regions, Hong Kong and Macau, as well as Iran, Italy and South Korea; • Diagnosis of COVID-19, contact with a person who has or is suspected to have the virus. As the situation evolves, the Red Cross will continue to evaluate all emerging risks in collaboration with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and industry partners to determine if additional intervention strategies are needed. Together, we stand ready to keep the American public informed and prepared. Blood donation process A blood donation takes about an hour from start to finish, but the actual donation itself only takes about 8-10 minutes. Donors can also save up to 15 minutes at the blood drive by completing a RapidPass®. With RapidPass®, donors complete the pre-donation reading and health history questionnaire online, on the day of donation, from a mobile device or computer. As the number of coronavirus cases grows in the U.S., the number of people eligible to give blood for patients in need could decrease further. “We’re asking people to help keep the blood supply stable during this challenging time. As communities across the country prepare for this public health emergency, it’s critical that plans include a readily available blood supply for hospital patients,” said Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Blood Services. “As fears of coronavirus rise, low donor participation could harm blood availability at hospitals, and the last thing a patient should worry about is whether lifesaving blood will be on the shelf when they need it most.” Make an appointment to donate blood now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or calling the Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 510-658-6456. Donating blood is a safe process and people should not hesitate to give or receive blood. There are no data or evidence that this coronavirus can be transmissible by blood transfusion, and there have been no reported cases worldwide of transmissions for any respiratory virus, including this coronavirus, from a transfusion. The Red Cross only collects blood from individuals who are healthy and feeling well at the time of donation – and who meet other eligibility requirements, available at RedCrossBlood.org. At each blood drive and donation center, Red Cross employees follow thorough safety protocols including wearing gloves, routinely wiping down donortouched areas, using sterile collection sets for every donation, and preparing the arm for donation with an aseptic scrub. These mitigation measures will help ensure blood recipient safety, as well as staff and donor safety in reducing contact with those who may potentially have this respiratory infection. The Red Cross has implemented new blood donation deferrals out of an abundance of caution. Individuals are asked to postpone their donation for 28 days following: • Travel to China and its special administrative regions, Hong Kong and Macau, as well as Iran, Italy and South Korea; • Diagnosis of COVID-19, contact with a person who has or is suspected to have the virus. As the situation evolves, the Red Cross will continue to evaluate all emerging risks in collaboration with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and industry partners to determine if additional intervention strategies are needed. articles.text: The Gray family’s front yard decorations won the Highland Cup as best entry in 2020. It featured a “Smash the Virus” piñata, and a sign that read “Don’t Forget True Beauty.” Piedmont’s Fourth of July Front Yard and Car Decorating Contest ultimately had 21 entries, up from seven one week earlier. On the evening of Friday, July 3, members of the 4th of July Parade Committee toured all locations and settled on the top entries as winners of the city’s perpetual trophies and awards. Due to the coronavirus and health restrictions, Piedmont’s annual parade was canceled and replace with a house and car decorating contest titled “Celebrating in Place.” The big winner for best entry and recipient of the coveted Highland Cup was the Gray family at 23 Piedmont Court. All decorations were created by the Grays’ creative sons, s Austin, 1st grade, and Mason, 4th grade. Their entry “Bloom Where You are Planted,” refers to their dad, Mike, being a second generation Piedmonter, now living with wife Kim and two sons in the house in which he grew up. The home, front yard, and driveway were elaborately decorated with red, white, and blue and included a piñata with a sign reading “Smash the Virus.” The Grays described their entry as such, “We have been trying to thrive and bloom during these uncertain times. Nearly all of our decorations are items we have gathered or created from around our house including the piñata.” The parade committee caravan wove through town, in a lengthy event that spanned over two hours. There were so many good entries that two additional prizes, Most Artistic and Best Spirit, normally awarded only to parade floats, were given out. The Best Spirit Award went to “Do the Right Thing,” by Sydney Proctor and Team Proctor at 385 Moraga Ave. Their decorations extended into blocked off parking spots and had a collection of signs promoting racial justice and focusing on Black Lives Matter. The Most Artistic Award went to “Pollinator Posse” by science teacher Terry Smith, at 121 Fairview Avenue. Her front yard was filled with five-foot wide butterfly and bee models and facts on pollinators. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer enjoyed her first Fourth of July event in Piedmont. “I loved that neighbors and families collaborated on their decorations from traditional patriotic to butterflies-such a great way to celebrate in place this 4th of July,” she said. articles.text: Bond for new pool to be on ballot Nov. 3 Piedmont Community Pool After a lengthy discussion at a July 6 meeting, the Piedmont City Council directed the city staff to prepare documents to place a general obligation bond on the ballot on November 3, 2020 that would create a new Piedmont Community Pool. The decision follows a series of discussions in the past four years and was a more detailed discussion of the pool’s fate at a June 29 meeting. At that meeting, more than 100 community members participated in a virtual meeting on Zoom, and at least 30 residents voiced their opinion. A majority of those residents were in favor of having a community pool, either by restoring the current facility or creating a new one. The council will move forward with a possible bond to appear on the November 2020 ballot. The estimated bond amount is currently $15 million, but staff is waiting on updated cost estimates for the conceptual master plan adopted in November 2016. A conceptual master plan went through a rigorous community process four years ago, and an operational analysis proved that it was favorable. “[When] taking inf lation into account, the city is engaging a consultant to evaluate on a number that feels realistic. There is always some risk for the unknowns, but a solid number will be given before a first reading on this item,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. Details on cost estimates will be presented to council on July 20. Residents poured in during public comment on Monday to show support of a new pool facility, and a subsequent bond to fund it in November. Steve Collins, President of Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO), said that the organization would support enhancing the city’s aquatic facilities.
articles.title: Council makes history –

articles.text: Oakland Zoo is at risk of permanent closure in July due to the loss of income due to the zoo’s closure to the public and may be forced to close this month. The zoo has been closed since March 16 due to the current health crisis, but employees and directors are fighting to reopen as an “outdoor museum.” Outdoor museums in Alameda County were allowed to reopen with certain health and safety restrictions on June 19. –Nik Dehejia, Executive VP, Oakland Zoo “The governor issued regulations [in June] that put us in the category of indoor museums. The county of Alameda needs to apply for a variance from the The iconic sign over the entrance to Oakland Zoo. state. Every county in California has applied for a variance, and Alameda County is the last and has yet to apply,” explained Nik Dehejia, Executive Vice President of the zoo. The variance would allow the county to have local control in the decision of reopening the zoo. Every zoo in California is now open or has the ability to reopen, except for Oakland Zoo and San Francisco Zoo. A proposal made to the Alameda County Board of Supervisors on behalf of the zoo would allow admission by reservation, and masks and social distancing would be required. Indoor exhibits, concession stands and restaurants, and amusement rides would remain closed. The number of daily visitors would not exceed 2,500. Summer months are critical to sustaining the zoo’s yearly operating costs. During the pandemic, the zoo initiated “Behind the Scenes,” a daily interactive livestream program that virtually connects guests with animals
articles.title: Zoo needs County approval to be classified as outdoor museum

articles.text: Editor: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on June 30. Thank you for your tireless dedication to the city. We have been fortunate that 56 years ago, a group of visionary citizens saw fit to raise funding to enable this city to have a public pool. After having heard the eloquent pleas from the city’s young people, I hope that one of the take-aways you gleaned is that the pool has a broad base of support across ages because it is an affordable public asset that reflects Piedmont’s inclusive civic values. As last night’s speakers pointed out, the pool supports physical and mental health & well-being for young and old, including learn-to-swim for the very young, aquatic sports & exercise for students, special education, and adults. As a number of the young people pointed out, not everyone in Piedmont can afford to join a private club with a pool. The pool’s broad public benefit justifies an ongoing subsidy. As Jon Sakol pointed out, the outside consultant hired by the city had expressed that the level of subsidy the city has had to incur to date is, on average, within the range, if not slightly lower, compared to other city pools. Consequently, as you consider whether or not to re-open the pool in the near term and the longer term ballot measure for a bond to finance a new pool, I urge you to adopt a frame of mind along the lines of “how best to maintain a pool in Piedmont” versus one of “whether to have a pool in Piedmont”. To that end, in the interests of preserving this important inclusive cultural legacy, I urge you to propose a ballot measure that combines the pool with other infrastructure projects so that voters can choose to invest in preserving our infrastructure that benefits a broad cross section of our community as a package. -Jackie Khor Liu For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: And so the MAGA magical thinking tour continues, driven by the engine of denial and delusion, the rhetorical umbrella remains that Covid-19 will “go away without a vaccine.” No matter that as of this writing, 2.5 million people in the U.S. have been infected, 126,494 people have died, and 29 states are today reporting new highs in reported cases. The reality is haunting, deadly and ignored. Our shambolic pandemic policy continues to be shaped by a needy, ego-driven president who refuses to wear the totemic mask, now appearing to be a surreal symbol of conservative defiance and a statement of personal freedom. And there are, of course, the virus denying, maskless MAGA rallies, such as those recently held in Tulsa and Phoenix, where, from the podium, Trump voiced his rejection of testing (fewer tests, fewer cases to, “slow the testing down”), committing once again political malfeasance on an extraordinary level, and his rejection of science simply breathtaking. Meanwhile the culture wars continue, and the defense of Confederate statuary leads while hospitalizations rise and the ICUs once again begin to fill and the white noise of ventilators surrounds gown shrouded family members, standing in stark hospital rooms, pleading to say goodbye. But as we move into the heart of summer, I find that I also worry that the tone of desperation and incoherence revealed by Trump in the Tulsa and Phoenix speeches were but precursors to what awaits us in the months ahead as the campaign heats up.
articles.title: The man behind the resolute desk

If Trump concludes he is losing, our democracy will enter what I believe will be the most fraught and dangerous period of his presidency. Recall that the one chip he was expecting to play was a red-hot economy, made manifest by a robust stock market (the go-to barometer of his success). And so, Trump is left with sowing the seeds of chaos, already calling into question the legitimacy of the 2020 election, allegations steeped in conspiracy, buttressed by foreign intervention. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will hold its General Municipal Election on November 3, 2020. The nomination period for two vacancies on the Piedmont City Council and three vacancies on the Board of Education opens on Monday, July 13. The deadline for submitting completed paperwork is Friday, August 7 at 5:00 p.m. There is no cost to file for election. The City Council and Board of Education are Piedmont’s two elected bodies and guide the operation of City government and the Piedmont Unified School District respectively. Members of these bodies may serve a maximum of two consecutive four-year terms. The City publishes the Guide to Nomination and Candidacy, which provides details about the nomination and candidacy process which prospective candidates should find useful. This election will take place in the context of the COVID- 19 pandemic. While there have been some changes to election procedures on a statewide scale to provide for social distancing, many of the steps in getting a candidate’s name on the ballot involve person to person contact. Among other requirements, candidates must turn in at least twenty, but no more than thirty valid signatures to have their name placed on the ballot. The Alameda County Health Officer’s Shelter in Place Order specifically defines signature gathering as an essential government function, which is allowed under the order. The California Elections Code requires that nomination papers be issued in person to the prospective candidate at City Hall. Because many city staff are working at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic, prospective candidates are required to schedule an appointment to take out nomination papers with the City Clerk’s office. An appointment will also be required to submit the nomination papers once the candidate has completed their work. These appointments generally last between 30 minutes and one hour. Residents with questions about the process or wishing to make an appointment can call the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040 or send an email to cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Nomination period begins July 13 for Nov. election

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will present Part 2 of “New Models for Social Justice – Police Reform” on Monday, July 20, with Anne Janks, Organizer at the Coalition for Police Accountability, as guest speaker. The Community Conversation is free and open to the public and will livestream on YouTube from 4-5 p.m. and not on Zoom. Janks will describe a proposed Oakland pilot program to respond to some 911 calls with a counselor and EMT rather than with armed police. This program does not propose abolishing the police department but emphasizes public safety. Janks will speak for the first half of the program, to be followed by a Question & Answer session moderated by Piedmont LWV President Lorrel Plimier. Participants may submit questions through YouTube livestream comments, or email them in advance to: lwvpiedmont@ gmail.org. For more information, visit www.lwvpiedmont.org. About Anne Janks Anne Janks, a resident of Oakland for 25 years, has worked as a union organizer under varied labor laws. She has spent time with workers’ rights education, legislative campaigns, fundraising, website development, and social media advocacy. She began volunteering with the Coalition for Police AccountAnne Janks, an organizer with the Coalition for Police Accountability, will be the guest speaker at a July discussion sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. ability in 2016 during the campaign for a ballot measure to create an independent community body to oversee the Oakland Police Department. The resulting Oakland Police Commission is the strongest independent oversight body in the country, with authority to write policy, independently investigate and discipline officers, and fire the police chief. Despite ongoing disputes over their mandated independence and resources, the commission has drafted new policy protecting residents from disparate stops and limited OPD access to military equipment, fired officers who killed a sleeping homeless man, and fired the police chief.
