articles.text: Photo of an electric vehicle charging station in Los Angeles. Piedmont’s Park Commission was asked to consider a recommendation to City Council to install electric vehicle charging stations in the city. Commission members unanimously approved the recommendation, and the proposal will be considered at a City Council meeting in the near future. Due to costs and other criteria, the city has been ineligible for grants from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District for the installation of public electric vehicle chargers. The new proposal would provide five chargers with a total of nine charging ports, at no cost to the city. The charging stations would be owned, operated and maintained by East Bay Community Energy, which services electricity to Piedmont. Piedmont Climate Action Fellow Justin Szasz introduced the proposal to the commissioners at a July 1 meeting, held via Zoom. The proposal would place electric vehicle chargers on streetlights in Piedmont. These would be “Level 2” chargers, which would charge vehicles for 10 to 20 miles of range an hour. A second proposal would include “DC fast kiosk chargers,” which can charge an electric vehicle for 360 miles of range in an hour. That proposal includes the Community Hall and Ace Hardware locations. Suggested locations for chargers are near Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue, in the parking lot at the Community Center, and on Highland and Craig Avenue next to Havens School. But the city’s failure to provide advance notice of the project drew criticism from some. “I am writing to urge the Park Commission not to approve the EV Charging Station Proposal at its meeting later today. The total lack of time for public input on this proposal is egregious. The notice is dated June 26, just last Friday. I have seen no news of this proposal, either in the Post or the Exedra. That is not surprising since there has not been time for either news source to publish news of its existence,” resident Cameron Wolfe said. Each charging port would be next to a parking space, which would be reserved specifically for electric vehicles. The price would be competitive with other electric chargers and would be less expensive than gas for non-electric cars. “It is staff’s belief that this program may help to meet the general plan and climate action plan goals in emission reduction,” Szasz said.
articles.title: Park Commission approves Electric Vehicle charging station plan

Although operating a kitchen allowed Cato’s to stay open during the current shelterin-place restrictions, their business is fighting for its life. Operating now as only a restaurant, with wine and beers to go, Cato’s business has dropped and they are in danger of closing permanently. Engineering lab not ready till Jan. The district plans to outfit the Engineering Lab this fall, with plans to open the lab in January 2021. Piedmont Makers has already secured a CNC router with donated funds to create precision machined objects and it is ready to be installed as soon as construction of the lab is finished. Other equipment will include a laser cutter, 3D printers, drill presses, compressed air cooling systems, sawdust collection systems, and bandsaws. Funds raised will also provide for a staff member to supervise the lab as well as implement safety certifications for all students. Piedmont Makers continues to drive the growth of robotics in Piedmont. From a single team a decade ago, there will be 35 robotics teams this fall and well over 200 students participating from grades K through 12. Although robotics will look different in Piedmont this fall as everyone adjusts to COVID, leaders of the Makers movement see a strong, growing cohort of students at the high school and at the lower grades. A 3D rendering of the proposed Engineering Lab by Piedmont architect Jane Lin and UC-Berkeley architecture student Amy Chen As excitement builds around the new STEAM classroom building on the high school campus, scheduled to open in mid-August, Piedmont School District still needs to raise $100,000 to outfit the new building with equipment necessary to meet its 21st century curriculum needs. articles.text: Piedmont High School head tennis coach Jim Landis made the start of summer official. He began operating tennis clinics last week, and suddenly the courts at the Corey Reich Tennis Center came to life. To abide by the Alameda County’s restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic, all participants were wearing masks, and the groups, now called pods, were limited to 12 kids at a time and instructors stayed with their pod for three weeks. During each hour and half session, campers have several water breaks during which everyone is required to use hand sanitizer. Landis confirmed that quite a few parents stayed to watch on Monday, the first day, to see how the camp would operate during the coronavirus. He received few concerns from parents. The tennis clinic, running from Monday to Friday each week has three sessions each day based upon age. Campers from age 8-12 are in the first group, players 13-18 are in the second group, and advanced players comprise the final group. In total, there are 60 players throughout the day, similar to prior years. The difference in 2020 is that there are more instructors, creating a four to one player to instructor ratio. Current restrictions in Alameda County require that instructors not be in more than one pod of campers.

articles.text: Quarantine is boring, no doubt about that, but if you’re bored you can always try work. Last week, I remodeled my room because I needed to do something with my hands and give myself a change of scenery. The project took me about a week and gave me something to do and something to look forward to. I started by going to Ace Hardware to get painting supplies (you’ll need brushes, trays, drop clothes, tarp to cover your furniture and spackle to cover up holes in your walls.) And as soon as I walked in, I was out of my element and walked around completely lost. The store was packed, which made my navigation even harder. Eventually I got to the paint section and asked a very kind worker to point me in the right direction for all my supplies. There I chose the three colors that I wanted – blue, yellow and grey. I got samples and took them home, put them on my wall and looked at them until I knew which one I liked the best. ( I chose blue.) The following day I went back to Ace to get the remaining supplies and the buckets of paint. The next few days were chaotic. We had to move all of my furniture out of my room and that took a long time. My dad had to step off some of his calls and help me put primer on my walls (that’s basically like white paint to block out the old color – purple in my case). That took four hours and it smelled horrible, and when I say horrible, I mean worse than locker room horrible. After the primer dried overnight, I got my sister and my dad to help me paint. Then we let the walls dry and moved the furniture back in, but not all of it. It seemed like a good time to unclutter the room. Not everyone was happy; my mom had to find a place for the stuff I didn’t want back. The whole project took about a week, but it was well worth it because now my room finally looks aesthetically pleasing. The hardest thing about room remodeling is not figuring out what color you want; it’s securing your family’s support. Some members might not be that excited about adding remodel to the quarantine. My dad was supportive, and my sister was a mix of seven different emotions. Personally, I was very confident with the decision to re-paint my room, even when my mother said that the blue color I’d chosen looked like a hospital room color, the yellow too much like the kitchen, and the grey was depressing. But in the end, everybody, even Mom, was happy. As a first-time painter I learned that there are a lot of do’s and don’ts.
articles.title: Saga of a quarantine room remodel

articles.text: • Do put a drop cloth on the floor unless you want an angry mom yelling at you about the paint ruining the hardwood. • Do wear a mask because the fumes will get to you. • Do open a window to lessen the amount of fumes. • Don’t put a lot of paint on your roller, or brush because the paint will splatter everywhere. • Don’t paint straight out of the bucket. • Don’t put your curtain rods in the middle of the dining room if you don’t want your mom to impale herself. So, if you are looking for something to do during quarantine, I would suggest remodeling your room. If you aren’t ready to repaint your walls, just rearrange everything. You can always put it back the way it was if you don’t like it. (Not so much with the walls.) Although remodeling a room is one of the many ways to spend quarantine, it is certainly one of the more hands-on activities. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time. In addition to the live webcams, the site has a large collection of “Kid’s Corner” episodes produced by the zoo, which kids are sure to enjoy. Videos on wizardingworld.com combine both of these as actors from the Harry Potter films and celebrities read the Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone chapter by chapter. Hear from Daniel Radcliff, Whoopi Goldberg, David Beckham, Dakota Fanning and more. Register for free on the wizardingworld.com website or find the readings on Spotify. California Academy of Sciences Online Resources The Academy of Sciences in Golden Gate Park has a robust selection of online resources for kids (and adults). Meet marine biologists, astronomers and naturalists to inspire a healthy interest in science. Take virtual dives in the kelp forest, learn how to identify birds in the wild and discover how to create your own compost bin. Cal Academy of Sciences has tons of videos and instructions for activities and projects. He’ll read kids’ books on Mondays at 9 a.m., Young Adult books on Wednesdays at 3 p.m., and advanced-level books on Fridays at 6 p.m. Take a look, it’s in a book. It’s LeVar Burton Reads. articles.text: Residents with Oakland Library cards may now pick up holds reserved online for books, DVDs, and CDs. You can also reserve a WiFi hotspot at the library doors. Indoor areas remain closed to the public. It’s easy! Here’s how it works: Search for Books, DVDs, and CDs at oaklandlibrary.org. Use the “request it” button to place items on hold. You’ll need your library card number and PIN. Select the branch library most convenient for you. If you already have items on hold, log in to your account and select an open location to send your hold. Branch Pickup When you are notified that your items are ready, come to the selected branch between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. You will receive an email, text, or phone notification when your hold is available for pickup. Please note: Wait times for holds may be longer than usual. If you have multiple items on hold, you will get a separate notification for each one. You have 14 days after you get the notification to pick up your item. You’ll need to have your library card number with you. Be mindful of the ongoing health crisis. Wear a face covering and observe social distancing. Keep 6 feet apart from other patrons in line. Sidewalk Pickup Star ting now, sidewalk pickup of books will be available locally at the Main Library and Rockridge Branch Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Summer Reading Programs to begin Readers of all ages can now register to participate in our annual Summer Reading program. You’ll be able to qualify to win prizes at the end of the program by completing your reading log, participating in the online programs, and getting involved in your community. Register for Summer Reading by visiting www.oaklandlibrary.org/ summer. Complete information is at https://oaklandlibrary.org/. For questions, please call 510-238- 3134 or email eanswers@oaklandlibrary.org.

articles.text: County reopening plans put on pause A new case of COVID-19 was confirmed in Piedmont on Friday, July 3. As the global pandemic continues into July, Piedmont’s surrounding area has been much harder hit by COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus. Cases across Alameda County increased to 6,887 by Monday, July 6, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Tragically, another five people have died of the disease since June 23, increasing the number of total fatalities in Alameda County to 140. Alameda County continues to be the hardest hit county in the San Francisco Bay Area. Santa Clara County, the initial epicenter in the region, now counts 5,478 cases and 165 total deaths. In San Francisco, the caseload is 4,020 and there have been 50 deaths. In total, there have been 14 cases reported in Piedmont. 10 were reported before April 13 and three during May. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, 2,712 cases were reported. Hayward now has a total of 1,116. Fremont has reported 362 cases and San Leandro has also reported 345. Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials on Monday, June 29 as concerns mount about COVID-19 hospitalizations. The new order does not reverse previous reopening orders, but the county is now postponing its plan to phase in the next stage of reopening, which would allow for indoor dining, salons, barbershops, pools and professional sports, although without the presence of fans. An order that went into place on June 19 allowed for outdoor museums, outdoor restaurant dining, some religious services, indoor retail, mall shopping and outdoor fitness classes. On Thursday, July 2, county officials urged residents to stay home during the Independence Day holiday. “We can all help protect our families, friends and neighbors by celebrating the Fourth of July at home this year,” wrote Dr. Nicholas Moss, who is taking over for Dr. Erica Pan as the Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Cases and hospitalizations are rising across the region and COVID-19 spreads most easily when people who don’t live together gather in groups.” In Piedmont, the City’s annual Fourth of July Parade was canceled, although a socially distant, front yard decoration celebration took place. While the county had been opening up new sectors of the economy about every two weeks through June, that process has been paused for the time being. The department said that last week and this week will be critical for assessing how to reopen more activities. Statewide, 271,684 COVID-19 cases were reported as of Sunday, July 5, an increase of over 55,000 in a week. In California, 6,337 people have died since the outbreak began. Last week, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that 19 counties were on a “watchlist” and must close down many indoor businesses and restaurants. He added four counties to the list on Monday, July 6, including Marin County. Contra Costa and Solano Counties were also on the watchlist. Alameda County is not on this watchlist, but at a City Council meeting this week, Piedmont officials said it was likely that the county will be added to the list in the future. In a notice from June, Piedmont noted that Alameda County’s face covering requirements are still in effect – face coverings must be work at all times in public, even if a person is exercising. Face coverings can only be removed if a person will not be within 30 feet of another person from outside the household. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, July 8, 2020 HIKING WITH JON Mt. Diablo State Park: Burma Road Trail to Moses Rock Ridge Six miles with 2,000+ feet in elevation gain By Jonathan Comeaux COVID-19 remains a concern despite National, State, and We’re back for another edition of our outdoors series. Back in December, the Chronicle’s Tom Steinstra called Mt. Diablo State Park’s Burma Road Trail the “most challenging” trail in the Bay Area, so I had to see it for myself. Let me tell you – he wasn’t lying. You’re going to need proper hydration, correct footwear for steep descents, and hiking sticks to help you along the way. Before we start, spread of Regional parks officially becoming open for summer festivities. Here are our guidelines for responsible hiking: • Research parking or trail restrictions for whatever park you choose. • Be mindful. Always bring a face cover of some sort. • The earlier the better. Trails are most trafficked past noon. • Hike during the week instead of Sat. or Sun, if possible. • Go solo or plus-one. No groups. This sign marks the start of your trail off of North Gate Road. The first half mile of Burma Road includes two steep hills where you gain 530 feet in elevation. After a mile, keep left to stay on Burma Road. Mothers Trail provides a 1,000-foot climb in one-mile to Moses Rock Ridge. Staff Photos Last week we headed to Mt. Diablo’s Burma Road: a climb of 2,000 feet to Moses Rock Ridge. Burma Road to the Moses Rock Ridge is an out-and-back 3.1 miles hike. Your trail starts on North Gate Road, which is already an epic understatement itself. Be prepared to climb at a rate of 1,000 feet per mile. There were times I was walking purely on my toes given the steep grade of Burma Road. The hike starts with a bang, requiring you to ascend 530 feet in just a half mile, followed by an easier 230 feet climb in 0.4 of a mile to your first junction. But any ease will quickly be forgotten after turning left onto Mothers Trail. A tenth of amile in you’ll turn right and into your final ascent to the top, gaining some 550 feet in elevation within the next half mile to the next junction. Prior to turning right to continue on Burma Road, you’ll pass a man-made watering hole, presumably left for cattle that used to graze the fields. Etched into the round concrete walls of the miniature pond is “Burma Springs, 1968. A school of koi fish swam undisturbed in the remote hillside location. After the junction, you’ll climb another 500 feet in one mile to the Moses Rock Ridge and Deer Flat Road junction. Continuing down Deer Flat Road for another half mile will add 400 more feet of elevation and close out the 3.1 mile trek to the Diablo Valley Overlook, which provides a sweeping view of Contra Costa County, Diablo Valley, and all the way to Suisun Bay. Throughout your trail, your view gets more magnificent by the step. With each rest after ascents, the view of the rolling foothills of Mt. Diablo were enough to revitalize for, albeit, A unique sight along Burma Road: a pond of koi fish with an inscription “Burma Springs, 1968.” The view of Mt. Diablo from the Moses Rock Ridge trail. short moments. With just a few groves of treecover along the hike, bring sunblock and other sun-protective gear. The inland Contra Costa heat may take a toll, especially on the steep trails, so be sure to arrive early. Despite Mt. Diablo’s popularity, there were no other hikers on my entire trek. Given Mt. Diablo has a population of mountain lions and rattlesnakes, bringing a friend may be wise. Keep in mind that rattlers enjoy resting on trails during the summer months. Being wary of your surroundings is imperative on lesser-known back country hikes like this. Enter “Burma Road Trail” into your GPS device to locate the trailhead about one-mile past the State Park kiosk. Entrance fee to the park is $10. The Diablo Valley Overlook is the final destination on this 3-mile climb.

articles.text: Alex Weekes, PHS Class of 2020, is working out at Team Prep USA’s summer running camp in Colorado. A senior leader from the upcoming Piedmont High class of 2021, Alex Weekes, is eying a big campaign for the end of his high school career. Currently in Colorado at the Team Prep USA camp, he is using the altitude to his advantage. “We were in Boulder one week, which is around 5,000 feet in elevation. Now, I’m in Gunnison around 7,700 feet, so it feels a lot different. We’re doing a lot of runs up to 9,000-10,000 feet. I’ve been here for a while, but I’m still getting used to this elevation,” explained Weekes. It marks his second summer program at Team Prep USA. The camp has hosted former Olympic champions like 3000-meter steeplechase winner Emma Coburn. Former Piedmont Post 2018 Athlete of the Year Reece Proctor is also a former attendee. “I came to the camp last year and really enjoyed my experience, so I wanted to return this summer,” said Weekes. “We’re focusing on two longer runs throughout the four-week course, and we’re doing a lot of base training. Every run is on a dirt road or on trail-type courses, but the elevation really makes a difference,” he added. “It’s among the only overnight summer camps that is happening this year. We have to follow a lot of protocols, like wearing masks when not running or eating and social-distance from people not within your pod of 10 runners,” he said. Last year Weekes emerged as a team leader and was named to the second-team All-League after finishing 10th of 74 at the WACC Championship meet in 16:31. “By the end of last season, we saw we had a chance to qualify for State but didn’t make it. It seemed to light a fire under everybody,” said Weekes, noting that Piedmont finished 5th of 22 team at the North Coast Section championship and failed by two places to advance to the State meet. Weekes will be joining a group of upperclassmen, including firstteam recipient and classmate Collin Mortimer, who finished fifth at the league finals. Rowen Connelly is another senior, and according to PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund is running 30 miles weekly. He clocked a 16:48.9 at the league championship, finishing 18th. Juniors Seamus Chamberlain Carr and Cooper Downing are were two more runners to frequently finish as the boys’ topfive group. “We really started to believe as the year went on. We have a strong five already right there. If we have a season, we have the potential to do very well. We have the mindset going in this time,” said Weekes. With the close of the spring track season and powering through an offseason program unlike any other, Weeks says he’s just looking forward to seeing some familiar faces again. “With losing the spring track season, it was a strange way to walk away. I’m definitely excited to get back, talk to friends, and see how they’re doing,” added Weekes. As for the standing of fall sports, the CIF is expected to make an announcement on July 20. The NFHS has regarded running sports as a “low risk” transmission, so there is some optimism toward a cross country schedule.
articles.title: X-C runner Alex Weekes trains at camp in Colorado

articles.text: The 2003 girls’ team won the school’s only North Coast Section championship in soccer. With the Premier League and European soccer as the marquee sport during the worldwide pandemic, we take a look back at Piedmont High’s only North Coast Section soccer championship – the girls’ team in 2003. In 2003 Giants’ legend Barry Bonds won the third of four consecutive Most Valuable Player awards. Cristiano Ronaldo made his Manchester United debut at age 18. In Piedmont, it was year of history. Twins Courtney and Ashley Paris led the basketball team to the school’s first state championship in any sport, then repeated it in 2004. With a group of friends who had played and competed together for seven years, the girls’ soccer team won the NCS championship ­ also a first in school history. They remain the only Piedmont High soccer team – boys or girls – to win a section title. Their team finished with a school-record 24-1-1 overall record and a Bay Shore Athletic League championship, securing the top-seed in the 2A playoffs. But they never had it easy in the playoffs, defeating No. 8 El Cerrito 4-1 but requiring a win by penalty kicks against No. 5 Las Lomas in the semifinals. In the championship game, Piedmont faced crosstown rivals Bishop O’Dowd, then the lead team in the Hayward Area Athletic League. After regulation, the game was still scoreless at 0-0. In penalty kicks, Catherine Betts scored the game-winner in sudden death overtime. That year’s team featured two athletes signing with Division 1 programs: Whitney Temple to Loyola Marymount and Catherine Betts to Oregon State. Temple was a four-year starter at Piedmont and led them in scoring during that time. She was a three-year starter at LMU and team captain. “As a freshman, Temple became an equal scoring threat on Piedmont’s team with Liz Dosa [who went on to play at Michigan]. In four years, Temple helped lead the Highlanders to four league championships and two appearances in the semifinals of the North Coast Section championships,” wrote Post editor Gray Cathrall in 2003. Betts played for Oregon State and eventually transferred to the University of the Pacific. At the time she told the Post that she wanted to pursue a career in sports therapy and seemingly has pursued that dream. Betts, who briefly returned to Piedmont as an assistant coach for the girls’ team in 2009-2010, became health and performance coach and launched Betts Fit LLC, which patented an innovative sports bra design. Whitney Temple, Class of 2003, was a four-year starter at Piedmont and played college soccer at Loyola Marymount. Catherine Betts, Class of 2003, went on to play for Oregon State and UOP before starting a career in sports sciences.
articles.title: A look back: the 2003 NCS Champion girls’ soccer team

With the close of the spring track season and powering through an offseason program unlike any other, Weeks says he’s just looking forward to seeing some familiar faces again. “With losing the spring track season, it was a strange way to walk away. I’m definitely excited to get back, talk to friends, and see how they’re doing,” added Weekes. As for the standing of fall sports, the CIF is expected to make an announcement on July 20. The NFHS has regarded running sports as a “low risk” transmission, so there is some optimism toward a cross country schedule. The 2003 girls’ team won the school’s only North Coast Section championship in soccer. By Jonathan Comeaux With the Premier League and European soccer as the marquee sport during the worldwide pandemic, we take a look back at Piedmont High’s only North Coast Section soccer championship – the girls’ team in 2003. In 2003 Giants’ legend Barry Bonds won the third of four consecutive Most Valuable Player awards. Cristiano Ronaldo made his Manchester United debut at age 18. In Piedmont, it was year of history. Twins Courtney and Ashley Paris led the basketball team to the school’s first state championship in any sport, then repeated it in 2004. With a group of friends who had played and competed together for seven years, the girls’ soccer team won the NCS championship ­ also a first in school history. They remain the only Piedmont High soccer team – boys or girls – to win a section title. Their team finished with a school-record 24-1-1 overall record and a Bay Shore Athletic League championship, securing the top-seed in the 2A playoffs. But they never had it easy in the playoffs, defeating No. 8 El Cerrito 4-1 but requiring a win by penalty kicks against No. 5 Las Lomas in the semifinals. In the championship game, Piedmont faced crosstown rivals Bishop O’Dowd, then the lead team in the Hayward Area Athletic League. After regulation, the game was still scoreless at 0-0. In penalty kicks, Catherine Betts scored the game-winner in sudden death overtime. That year’s team featured two athletes signing with Division 1 programs: Whitney Temple to Loyola Marymount and Catherine Betts to Oregon State. Temple was a four-year starter at Piedmont and led them in scoring during that time. She was a three-year starter at LMU and team captain. “As a freshman, Temple became an equal scoring threat on Piedmont’s team with Liz Dosa [who went on to play at Michigan]. In four years, Temple helped lead the Highlanders to four league championships and two appearances in the semifinals of the North Coast Section championships,” wrote Post editor Gray Cathrall in 2003. Betts played for Oregon State and eventually transferred to the University of the Pacific. At the time she told the Post that she wanted to pursue a career in sports therapy and seemingly has pursued that dream. Betts, who briefly returned to Piedmont as an assistant coach for the girls’ team in 2009-2010, became health and performance coach and launched Betts Fit LLC, which patented an innovative sports bra design. Whitney Temple, Class of 2003, was a four-year starter at Piedmont and played college soccer at Loyola Marymount. Catherine Betts, Class of 2003, went on to play for Oregon State and UOP before starting a career in sports sciences.

High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. JORDAN MARCUS Triathlon Lily Keville, PHS Class of 2019, just finished her freshman year as a member of the Pomona-Pitzer lacrosse program. LILY KEVILLE Lacrosse Piedmont High Class of 2019 Pomona-Pitzer College Class of 2023 Lily Keville just completed her freshman year at Pomona-Pitzer College after graduating from Piedmont High in 2019 and being a part of the school’s NCS Championship team. As a member of Pitzer’s attack, Keville made six appearances before the season was cut short this pasts spring. In her brief time, she scored three goals and had an assist, along with three ground ball recoveries and four forced turnovers. One year ago, she helped PHS finish with the school’s most wins of all time at 20-2 overall and its longest winning streak ever at 16 games. In high school she was a threeyear starter and part of two league championship teams, in 2018 and 2019. She scored 47 goals, had 16 assists, and 45 ground balls and 11 takeaways as a senior. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program currently consists of daily runs to help increase my endurance and bodyweight exercises at home to improve my strength. What are your fitness goals for this summer? My goals are to lower my mile-run time and gain more muscle. How are you measuring your development? My endurance development is being tracked on the Nike Run Club phone app, while our strength-training numbers are tracked on TeamBuildr. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Last summer, he returned to the Bay Area for numerous events like the Oakland Triathlon and Ironman in Santa Rosa. He is training for more competitions in California this summer. As a senior at PHS in 2017, Marcus finished in 16:32 at the NCS Cross Country Championship meet. He also competed on the track team, running the 800, 1600, 3200, and in relays. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program is a bit jumbled this summer without access to a pool, but I am still able to get the same number of hours in biking and running. I was initially training for the SF Marathon, but once that got postponed has made it a little more difficult to train without a specific race on the calendar. What are your fitness goals for the summer? To feel satisfied with where I am in my training; to feel fit enough to complete more rigorous workouts and longer distances. My goal is to be content with the results of my baseline workouts. How are you measuring your development? I recently started using heart rate to track my development. Seeing as my weekly schedule consists of many of the same workouts, which leads to hitting many of the same paces, I can track my progress with the average heart rate of each workout. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am mainly working on my own this summer. I was initially using a training book, “Daniels’ Running Formula,” to help prepare for the marathon. Savage helped Jordan Marcus start the Piedmont Triathlon Club in 2015, helping spark Marcus’ interest in triathlon as a sport. What is your workout program this summer? Without a pool, my focus has switched to riding and running. I’m doing structured indoor rides three days a week, with a longer ride on the weekend and a track workout once a week. I’m doing a little more than 200 miles of riding and about 40 miles of running a week. I also do core work once or twice a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Without any races, my goals have been to be consistent, build strength on the bike, and speed on the run. This involves doing shorter intervals on the bike at a higher intensity, and running “fast” on the track. How are you measuring your development? Some of my friends have organized some socially distanced races where we pick an event, and then go do it by ourselves. We’ve John Savage, PHS chemistry teacher and boys’ water polo coach, is also a triathlete and annually competes.

articles.text: A map of the 2020 Tour de France, which starts on August 29. The 107th edition of the Tour de France is set to begin after being rescheduled from August 29 in Nice to September 20 in Paris after COVID-19 forced the tour to reschedule from June 27. The Tour anticipates a course that starts with the 2020 Grand Départ from Nice; a 170 km ride into France’s Var Valley to Sisteron. Stage 2 climbs 187 km to the Nice Haut Pays with nearly 4,000 meters of ascent. Another critical point will be the back-to-back mountain courses of Stage 8 and 9, which are respective 140 km and 154 km courses. Like the first mountain stage, Stage 8 will include three cols (mountain passes) and require more than 4,000 meters of elevation gain for cyclists. Stage 9 has one steep ascent up Cole de la Hourcere at 1,440 meters. From there, Stages 16, 17, and 18 are three consecutive mountain stages and could certainly form the eventual Yellow Jersey winner. Stage 16 goes 164 km from La Tour de Pin to Villard de Lans; Stage 17 travels 168 km from Grenoble to Col de la Loze; and 18 goes another 168 km from Méribel to La Roche-sur-Foro. But before the official Grand Boucle, the tour is hosting online virtual unofficial session using Zwift until July 19—a homebased interactive video game where contestants use their bike on a stand. The big trio from Team INEOS in competing in the virtual event, including 2019 Tour winner Egan Bernal, 2018 winner Geraint Thomas, and 2017 Chris Froome, who won in 2013, 2015, and 2016 as well. Other elite men’s riders include Julian Alaphilippe, Greg Van Avermaet, Mathieu van der Poel, Nairo Quintana, Mads Pedersen, and Romain Bardet. The tour’s women’s ladder also has many prominent pros, including time trial world champion Chloe Dygert alongside others like Marianne Vos, Coryn Rivera, Marta Bastianelli, Lisa Brennauer, Kirsten Wild, Tiffany Cromwell, and Lizzie Deignan. The Tour de France is hosting a virtual race via Zwift. Several of the world’s top riders are competing.
articles.title: Tour de France returns on August 29

articles.text: Playwright Geetha Reddy joins SF Playhouse Artistic Director in a “fireside chat” on Thursday, July 9. Each week, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English invites playwrights to join him for a half-hour conversation about playwriting, inspiration, and the future of theatre. Playwright Geetha Reddy will join English tomorrow, July 9, at 7 p.m. for a fireside discussion. Reddy’s work has been produced by the Playwrights’ Foundation, San Francisco Playhouse, Central Works and Crowded Fire’s Matchbox Series. She has written a short film, “Obit,” which appeared at LA Shorts and the New York Indie Fest. Her most recent play, Far, Far Better Things, premiered at the Live Oak Theatre in Berkeley in a co-production by TheatreFirst and Shotgun Players. The play is loosely inspired by A Tale of Two Cities and juxtaposes the lives of a South Asian doctor and her Latina nanny and housekeeper. The live stream of the discussion will be available tomorrow at 7 p.m. You can watch the live stream at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=-KzqBuwxl88&- feature=youtu.be. Throughout the current health crisis, all fireside chats will be streamed online for listeners. Past chats can are available at https:// w w w.sf playhouse.org /sf ph / fireside-chats/. articles.text: Shotgun Players’ Kill the Debbie Downers is an adaptation of Chekhov’s 1901 play, Three Sisters. Shotgun Players is offering past performances on its website throughout the current health crisis. This week, patrons can view Kill the Debbie Downers, Kill Them, Kill Them, Kill Them Off, a theater piece inspired by Anton Chekhov’s Three Sisters. Checkhov wrote Three Sisters in 1901, four years before an attempted revolution in Russia. “One can already feel that revolution on the horizon in Three Sisters, its rumble of change exciting and unnerving the characters. And yet as in a Beckett play ‘they do not move.’ What revolutions are rumbling on our horizon?” read the program notes. The cast includes Nathaniel Andalis, Gabby Battista, Amanda Farbstein, Sam Jackson, Erin Mei-Ling Stuart, and Billy Raphael. The cast of six switches roles throughout the production. The play is directed by Mark Jackson and Beth Wilmurt, and was originally performed in March and April last year. The video has been made available through the Shotgun Players’ website for patrons to enjoy during shelter-in-place regulations. You can watch the full play on Youtube at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=-nUmgLJXSGU&- feature=youtu.be. The play is approximately 120 minutes. Erin Mei-Ling Stuart plays Masha.
articles.title: Shotgun Players presenting 2019 performance of Debbie Downers on Youtube

articles.text: The Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra took to Zoom to release the capstone of their 2019–2020 season. The young musicians performed Dvorak’s Symphony No. 9 (New World Symphony). Each musician recorded their segment at home due to current shelter-inplace restrictions. Full rehearsals and the final concert were cancelled due to COVID-19. Nevertheless, students continued to rehearse along with Oakland Symphony coaches. In a moving display of hope and determination, the entire youth orchestra came together virtually to perform this season’s capstone. The video was edited by their conductor, Omid Zoufonoun. You can view the performance at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/virtual-performances/ dvoraks-symphony-no-9/. articles.text: on the cusp of old age. Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field, a consummate actress, creates a person who, while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues), is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood living in a van; she is also in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. To add to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of unread magazines decades old). Her packrat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology; rather, like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train long ago has left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it and now, suddenly, has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Starring Sally Field, Max Greenfield and Tyne Daly. Directed by Michael Showalter. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on April 27, 2016. Sally Field stars in a scene from Hello, My Name is Doris. Movie review by Chris Honoré I try to imagine what Sally Field thought when she first read the screenplay for Hello, My Name is Doris. I assume she was both moved and excited. She recognized in the role of Doris Miller a character that, while eccentric, was also deeply human. This was a substantive part. And she must have immediately understood that while the story had its comedic moments, there was also a sad, lonely quality to Doris that transcended all of her peculiar idiosyncrasies. This is a film about isolation and regret and a life not fully lived. The movie opens with a funeral. Only a few friends and family members are in attendance. Doris sits alone, grieving; the deceased is her mother, whose profile is barely visible in the coffin. Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with bric-a-brac. Now in her 60s, Doris works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry. Despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves – she remains, to most of her young co-workers, essentially invisible. Seen but not seen. That is until a new co-worker, John Fremont (Max Greenfield), thirty-something, arrives and for a few moments on a crowded elevator sees Doris… really sees her. articles.text: He runs up and down the vacant aisles, calling out for Guddu… for anyone. The train does not stop until it reaches a station in Kolkata (formerly Calcutta), and massive numbers of people, waiting on the platform, begin to board. Saroo pushes his way off the train, looking around for anything familiar. What he is unaware of is that he is 1,000 miles away from home and at a complete loss as how to get back. And he doesn’t know where back is. He is suddenly alone. Lost. Endless crowds of people move around him, ignoring him, like a small rock in a rushing stream. This long first act is gripping, breathtaking, filled with heartfelt tension. How will small Saroo ever survive on the urban mean streets where predatory adults victimize abandoned children. And so begins a brief act two, which leads into act three and we meet a grown Saroo (Dev Patel) whose life has been completely changed forever. But this older Saroo who once was lost now must be found. Be prepared to be caught up in this wonderful film. It will touch you as you absorb not only little Saroo’s circumstances, but as you later engage with him as a young man. Not incidentally, Both Dev Patel and Nicole Kidman were nominated for Golden Globes for their very fine performances. Lion. Starring Dev Patel, Sunny Pawar, Rooney Mara and Nicole Kidman. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, July 8, 2020 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Bravura performance by Sally Field in Hello, My Name is Doris on the cusp of old age. Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field, a consummate actress, creates a person who, while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues), is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood living in a van; she is also in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. To add to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of unread magazines decades old). Her packrat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology; rather, like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train long ago has left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it and now, suddenly, has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Starring Sally Field, Max Greenfield and Tyne Daly. Directed by Michael Showalter. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated R. Movie review by Chris Honoré I try to imagine what Sally Field thought when she first read the screenplay for Hello, My Name is Doris. I assume she was both moved and excited. She recognized in the role of Doris Miller a character that, while eccentric, was also deeply human. This was a substantive part. And she must have immediately understood that while the story had its comedic moments, there was also a sad, lonely quality to Doris that transcended all of her peculiar idiosyncrasies. This is a film about isolation and regret and a life not fully lived. The movie opens with a funeral. Only a few friends and family members are in attendance. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré For all of its CGI-animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creator of the Toy Story franchise, has never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple yet inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Saoirse Ronan and Eliza Scanlen in a scene from Little Women. Movie review by Chris Honoré All fiction, however thin the thread, inevitably is autobiographical. The writer’s persona, in some way, reveals itself. And so it is with Louisa May Alcott’s iconic 19th century novel, Little Women, in which the central character, Jo March (Saoirse Ronan), is unabashedly Alcott. It should not be a surprise that writer/director Greta Gerwig would place Jo’s writing, first her short pieces and plays, and then the creation of her book, at the center of what proves to be a remarkable adaptation of this resilient and timeless story. Of course, the contrasts between the 1860s and today are stark; yet, there is a prescient, rebellious modernity to Little Women that is inescapable. The world of women then was defined by norms that, in the main, rendered them powerless. There was an absence of civil rights, including, and they were bound and diminished by an insidious inequality. The way forward for most women, especially those of little means, was a path of narrow options, most often limited to marriage and motherhood. And yet, in this milieu of such cultural expectations, Gerwig focuses on Jo, one of four sisters – Meg (Emma Watson), Amy (Florence Pugh), Beth (Eliza Scanlen), and their mother, Marmee (Lora Dern). It is Jo who is headstrong, intent on becoming a writer, her dresser drawer filled with plays and stories, a young woman fiercely independent, often finding herself at odds with the reactions by others to her abrasive, outspoken points of view. It is Jo’s intention to be a person apart. She declares emphatically that she will never marry and will make her way financially with her pen. Above all, as she insists defiantly, she will row her own canoe. And yet – and this is a tender, complex and powerful contradiction with which Jo struggles – she realizes that she thrives in the loving embrace of her family. Jo wants above all for the March family – this warm, eruptive, loving group of women – to remain as it is, as it has always been, and wills it never to change. In one scene, on the eve of Meg’s wedding, she pleads with her sister not to marry, arguing that in two years she will have grown tired of all of it. Better to remain at home, no matter that she, Jo, will make her own journey to New York to work as a tutor while submitting her stories to a local publisher. As writer and director Gerwig takes risks, not only in her creative interpretation of the novel, but in constructing a narrative that bifurcates the film, moving from the early years of the March sisters to that period when they are adults. Into that mix she adds dream-like scenes that focus on alternative outcomes that are unrealized, implying that in Jo, when reacting to the realities of life, we do not always have a reliable narrator. It’s an aspect of the film that enhances and never detracts, for it reveals the tension between what is and what should be, if only life were fair. Little Women is also nimbly and wonderfully filled with moments that resonate because of their humanity and their inherent decency. Jo looks out a window, and watches her sister Meg and her husband, John (James Norton), touchingly embrace. Jo and Beth rest side by side on a windswept beach, lost in conversation (a foreshadowing of what lies ahead for Beth). And there are the steely, sororal bonds made manifest, their history inextricably binding them together, this band of young sisters. G e r w ig, u nexp e ct e d ly, includes a scene when Jo looks into the camera and speaks to an empty room while not breaking the fourth wall (a film, like a play, has, typically, only three dimensions); rather she lets her thoughts become concrete sounds, words to be weighed and considered, ripe for reflection. It’s audacious but effective. Little Women is a beautifully made film, superbly acted. It is Gerwig’s best work to date. As well, perhaps it’s an antidote to our driven, cynical times; or a universal reminder that the best of who we are can emerge and define us when encouraged and nurtured by family. And yet Gerwig’s adaptation makes clear that while the bars of sunlight beam throughout the March house with raw energy and unabashed happiness, the world still intrudes. Life happens. Events must be sorted out. The March women anxiously await the safe return of the father, gone to fight in the Civil War. Their gentle and raucous chatter, the sheer vitality of these little women, represents a hybrid of modern consciousness as well as an acceptance of the decorum and social constraints of their time, made especially concrete by Meg and Amy. Don’t miss this film. It’s worth seeing on the big screen. In so many ways, it is larger than life. Little Women. Written and directed by Greta Gerwig. Starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Eliza Scanlen, Laura Dern and Timothée Chalamet. 2 hrs., 14 min. Rated PG. Originally published in the Post on January 8, 2020. A scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 3.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Little Women a faithful adaption of the Alcott classic

articles.text: Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a day care center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat-of-your-pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a coming of age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes and Toy Story 3 may turn out to be the sweetest and best-told story of the summer. Toy Story 3 (Animation). Starring the voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack and Don Rickles. Directed by Lee Unkrich. Rated PG.

articles.text: A town hall style meeting was convened on June 29 via Zoom by Berkeley Symphony in collaboration with the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco. Ref lections Town Hall, a panel discussion on social justice co-presented by The Commonwealth Club of California and Berkeley Symphony, took place through Zoom technology on Monday, June 29. The town hall-type gathering convened a panel of thought leaders to examine the role of arts organizations in addressing racial injustice. The discussion included Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young, Dr. Deborah L. Gould, Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan, educator Charles McNeal, Cal Performances Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen, and Jeff Benson, Executive Director of SWAG Foundation. The discussion was organized by Berkeley Symphony Board President Shariq Yosufzai, with Joseph Young serving as moderator. “I’m always reminded to remember that the fight for social justice is no sprint. The work that institutions must do to demolish centuries of systemic racism will still take years, and even decades of individual reflection and action,” Young said, before introducing the panel of thought leaders. The panel convened a few weeks after the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis, and subsequent protests nationwide and worldwide. Young began the discussion with a question to the panelists: “Why do you think there is such a big reaction now from whites, blacks, and even arts organizations about police brutality?” Morgan opened by pointing to the current health crisis and shelter-in-place regulations. “The single upside of the COVID crisis, is that everyone is home and is able to focus on what’s going on in the world. None of this is new; we’ve always been so busy where we can sort of look away and keep going on with our lives,” Morgan said. Morgan observed that the young protestors are “the real heroes right now, taking up the torch.” “I feel like this modern movement was really sparked by Trayvon Martin, because that was where the catalyst began, where we began to see a crystal-clear element of racial divide and racism,” noted Charles McNeal, San Francisco Opera’s Director of Diversity. “We have environmental distress, political distress, we have an education system in shreds. The wound has been opened.” McNeal agreed that COVID- 19, and regulations related to it, helped fuel the nationwide discussion surrounding racial equity. “We’ve all been devastated by [COVID-19], and that was an awakening of the integral nature of things, we’re all connected. Your freedom is my freedom, and your pain is my pain,” he said. Young asked the panel for suggestions on how organizations can be held accountable for their social impact. McNeal said that organizations should be “engaged learning organizations,” implementing ongoing, sustainable plan in approaching this complex issue. “If you do not change, you become extinct,” Dr. Gould added, referencing Spencer Johnson’s Who Moved My Cheese? “Listening with humility, and working to transform requires trust and a culture where everyone feels valued,” she said. The town hall concluded with a song from the Oakland Interfaith Community Choir. “As a message of standing together, and of Black Lives Matter, the choir published a video titled ‘Hear my Prayer.’ As we all reflect, even as we can’t come together as artists, we still sing,” Young said. You can view the panel discussion on Youtube at https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=0IMN_ XFT1WE&feature=youtu.be. The panel discussion concluded with a song from Oakland Interfaith Community Choir in support of Black Lives Matter. reported, 4,750, was the total number of entries for all categories.

articles.text: There are many social issues hitting us in the face these days. Whether it’s pretense or poverty, we find ourselves on the ropes. Music can do more than soothe the savage beast… much more. Throughout history, those who aspired to upward mobility utilized a number of stratagems. Sports comes to mind first. Just think of the many sports heroes who rose to fame and inspired all of us. The Irish can claim John L Sullivan; and many others of ALL ethnicities followed him in the boxing ring. Joe Louis was honored by President Franklin Roosevelt as an honor to the human race. What an inspiration he was! Likewise, the Latin-Americans and the Asians. Jews also fought their way out of the ghetto via the boxing ring. But they also did it in the concert halls. The instrument of choice most often was the violin. As a people, they were kept in poverty. Pianos were expensive but violins were cheap. Pianos were also big and heavy. So, if you got expelled from your town or from your country you couldn’t move easily with the monster piano. But you could with a small violin. The violin was also an expression of an entire peoples‘ emotional outcry. Do these things sound familiar? Do these issues really change? Music was also a financial passport out of misery. But other factors played a big part. Music, you see, has many contradictions. In the first place it teaches literacy. Education is the first step forward. But at the same time the language of music is both specific and merely suggestive. In other words, you must follow directions and at the same time you must think for yourself. A musician must practice alone in order to be expressive and emotional in public. How about that for a contradiction! Music teaches us to be, at the very same time, a team player and a self-centered star. Music does not know the prejudice of age nor the prejudice of religion nor the prejudice of ethnicity or the prejudice of sexual orientation. Oh sure, there have been a few bad apples. But their numbers are so small when compared to those who can see beyond the horizon. A perfect example of this is the generous former conductor of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, Edgar Braun. He was made administrator of a government- sponsored orchestra back in the 1970s. The government bureaucrat who was in charge wanted to establish quotas for the players. Edgar told me that he hired one black player. The government administrator said: “the quota of black players has now been set at one.“ Not long after this, Edgar hired another black player. The government administrator phoned Edgar saying: “You are in violation of your quota. Your quota is one black player and you now have two.“ Edgar, thinking very fast replied: “I don’t know how to tell you this, Sir, but my ears are colorblind.” There was silence at the other end of the phone. The bureaucrat did not know what to say. After a little while he said: “OK.” That was the end of it. I wonder if the bureaucrat learned anything. The great Greek philosopher Aristotle had a lot to say on the importance of music. In fact, the ancient Greeks advocated that music was the equal to mathematics/science and sports. Those were the three most important subjects during the golden age of Greece. Where will we find another Aristotle to enlighten those who need enlightenment? I am sure that Aristotle could say it simple enough even for those folks to understand. “Music has proven its worth in society. What we need is more music… especially in our schools.” NEXT WEEK: Famous temper tantrums in the world of music.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, July 8, 2020 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Reflections Town Hall examines the role of arts in addressing social justice The Musical Gourmet Edgar Braun, former conductor of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra. Contradictions of music Exactly why everyone should learn music By Joseph Gold There are many social issues hitting us in the face these days. Whether it’s pretense or poverty, we find ourselves on the ropes. Music can do more than soothe the savage beast… much more. Throughout history, those who aspired to upward mobility utilized a number of stratagems. Sports comes to mind first. Just think of the many sports heroes who rose to fame and inspired all of us. The Irish can claim John L Sullivan; and many others of ALL ethnicities followed him in the boxing ring. Joe Louis was honored by President Franklin Roosevelt as an honor to the human race. What an inspiration he was! Likewise, the Latin-Americans and the Asians. Jews also fought their way out of the ghetto via the boxing ring. But they also did it in the concert halls. The instrument of choice most often was the violin. As a people, they were kept in poverty. Pianos were expensive but violins were cheap. Pianos were also big and heavy. So, if you got expelled from your town or from your country you couldn’t move easily with the monster piano. But you could with a small violin. The violin was also an expression of an entire peoples‘ emotional outcry. Do these things sound familiar? Do these issues really change? Music was also a financial passport out of misery. But other factors played a big part. Music, you see, has many contradictions. In the first place it teaches literacy. Education is the first step forward. But at the same time the language of music is both specific and merely suggestive. In other words, you must follow directions and at the same time you must think for yourself. A musician must practice alone in order to be expressive and emotional in public. How about that for a contradiction! Music teaches us to be, at the very same time, a team player and a self-centered star. Music does not know the prejudice of age nor the prejudice of religion nor the prejudice of ethnicity or the prejudice of sexual orientation. Oh sure, there have been a few bad apples. But their numbers are so small when compared to those who can see beyond the horizon. A perfect example of this is the generous former conductor of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, Edgar Braun. He was made administrator of a government- sponsored orchestra back in the 1970s. The government bureaucrat who was in charge wanted to establish quotas for the players. Edgar told me that he hired one black player. The government administrator said: “the quota of black players has now been set at one.“ Not long after this, Edgar hired another black player. The government administrator phoned Edgar saying: “You are in violation of your quota. Your quota is one black player and you now have two.“ Edgar, thinking very fast replied: “I don’t know how to tell you this, Sir, but my ears are colorblind.” There was silence at the other end of the phone. The bureaucrat did not know what to say. After a little while he said: “OK.” That was the end of it. I wonder if the bureaucrat learned anything. The great Greek philosopher Aristotle had a lot to say on the importance of music. In fact, the ancient Greeks advocated that music was the equal to mathematics/science and sports. Those were the three most important subjects during the golden age of Greece. Where will we find another Aristotle to enlighten those who need enlightenment? I am sure that Aristotle could say it simple enough even for those folks to understand. “Music has proven its worth in society. What we need is more music… especially in our schools.” NEXT WEEK: Famous temper tantrums in the world of music. A town hall style meeting was convened on June 29 via Zoom by Berkeley Symphony in collaboration with the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco. By Allyson Aleksey Ref lections Town Hall, a panel discussion on social justice co-presented by The Commonwealth Club of California and Berkeley Symphony, took place through Zoom technology on Monday, June 29. The town hall-type gathering convened a panel of thought leaders to examine the role of arts organizations in addressing racial injustice. The discussion included Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young, Dr. Deborah L. Gould, Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan, educator Charles McNeal, Cal Performances Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen, and Jeff Benson, Executive Director of SWAG Foundation. The discussion was organized by Berkeley Symphony Board President Shariq Yosufzai, with Joseph Young serving as moderator. “I’m always reminded to remember that the fight for social justice is no sprint. The work that institutions must do to demolish centuries of systemic racism will still take years, and even decades of individual reflection and action,” Young said, before introducing the panel of thought leaders. The panel convened a few weeks after the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis, and subsequent protests nationwide and worldwide. Young began the discussion with a question to the panelists: “Why do you think there is such a big reaction now from whites, blacks, and even arts organizations about police brutality?” Morgan opened by pointing to the current health crisis and shelter-in-place regulations. “The single upside of the COVID crisis, is that everyone is home and is able to focus on what’s going on in the world. None of this is new; we’ve always been so busy where we can sort of look away and keep going on with our lives,” Morgan said. Morgan observed that the young protestors are “the real heroes right now, taking up the torch.” “I feel like this modern movement was really sparked by Trayvon Martin, because that was where the catalyst began, where we began to see a crystal-clear element of racial divide and racism,” noted Charles McNeal, San Francisco Opera’s Director of Diversity. “We have environmental distress, political distress, we have an education system in shreds. The wound has been opened.” McNeal agreed that COVID- 19, and regulations related to it, helped fuel the nationwide discussion surrounding racial equity. “We’ve all been devastated by [COVID-19], and that was an awakening of the integral nature of things, we’re all connected. Your freedom is my freedom, and your pain is my pain,” he said. Young asked the panel for suggestions on how organizations can be held accountable for their social impact. McNeal said that organizations should be “engaged learning organizations,” implementing ongoing, sustainable plan in approaching this complex issue. “If you do not change, you become extinct,” Dr. Gould added, referencing Spencer Johnson’s Who Moved My Cheese? “Listening with humility, and working to transform requires trust and a culture where everyone feels valued,” she said. The town hall concluded with a song from the Oakland Interfaith Community Choir. “As a message of standing together, and of Black Lives Matter, the choir published a video titled ‘Hear my Prayer.’ As we all reflect, even as we can’t come together as artists, we still sing,” Young said. You can view the panel discussion on Youtube at https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=0IMN_ XFT1WE&feature=youtu.be. The panel discussion concluded with a song from Oakland Interfaith Community Choir in support of Black Lives Matter. Many of these visitors enjoyed the mild weather and views of San Francisco Bay and decided to build their homes here. Raised on a dairy farm in Vermont with 11 siblings., Walter was born In 1851. He and his brother William sailed around Cape Horn to get to San Francisco. Within months, they rowed across the Bay and discovered the fertile lands in the Piedmont hills. In 1852, Walter purchased 600 acres from the U.S. government at $1.25 per acre of what is now central Piedmont, with property that extended from Scenic Avenue west to Grand Avenue. The brothers selected a level site just south of Moraga Avenue near a freshwater spring and built a modest one-room cabin. They named the pathway from Moraga to their home “Vernal” for the abundant ferns and shrubs that grew around that nearby spring. Vernal Avenue was renamed Highland Avenue in 1911. The Blair brothers planted wheat and barley on their land, purchased cattle from the neighboring ranches and established a dairy near what is today Dracena Park. The dairy quickly became known for its high quality milk, cream and butter, and soon the Blairs were delivering their milk and butter to residents in Oakland and even across the Bay to a few wealthy San Francisco customers. It was difficult for the horses hauling those wagons filled with ten-gallon milk cans. The roads were filled with muddy ruts in the winter and covered in thick dust in the summer. Blair realized that a hard surface was needed for these roads. Always the entrepreneur, Blair hired Chinese laborers to quarry rock from a basalt outcropping near his dairy and sold crushed rock to lay over the muddy/dusty streets in Oakland. The walls of the quarry are still visible in lower Dracena Park. Walter Blair went on to develop the first horsecar line to Piedmont and Blair’s Park. (More on that in a later column.) William Blair established a nursery near Mountain View Cemetery and sold eucalyptus seedlings. Lombardi Introduction The City of Piedmont is now celebrating its 111th anniversary, In cooperation with the Piedmont Historical Society, the Piedmont Post is pleased to announce the beginning of a biweekly series of snapshots of moments in time, from the city’s founding in 1907,its growth resulting in part to the earthquake and fire in San Francisco in 1906, and the city’s earliest settlers. He built the first house in the Piedmont hills (see photo) and established a dairy and rock quarry. In the 1860s, long before bridges spanned the Bay, he developed the first horse car line bringing visitors and picnickers into the Piedmont hills. articles.text: Photo by Jennifer Graham Laura Bovard meditates in her living room envisioning what she wants more of in her life. Now more than ever, we need our homes to really support us in our journey. I believe that when we feel filled up and our hearts are open and we have an environment that supports us in feeling that way, then we can actually go out into the world and give our gifts to humanity. We all need to be filled up and fully-resourced in order to really, truly go out and give of ourselves, supporting our families, our employees, coworkers, clients, and communities, and the causes we believe in, the change we want to see in the world. These days, we are sitting around our houses a lot. And many of us may be thinking about what we might like to have different, maybe even popping onto the internet for some inspiration, starting a Pinterest board, flipping through a catalog that came in the mail. In this column, I am offering you a tool for envisioning the most soulful, connected, personal, restorative space you can create. This is actually the same tool I use in my life whenever there is tension between me and another person. When there is upset, the thing I know to be true is, we cannot create from the energy that made this mess. I imagine you know this, too. Especially if you are a couple and have kids. Taking a time-out to calm down usually yields better solutions and a fresher perspective than continuing to argue. A calming corner in the master bedroom is designed for inspiration and repose. TJ Stevko, CFP® Financial Advisor 370 Highland Avenue Suite 201 Piedmont, CA 94611 510-547-4589

It’s so appealing that my friend, watercolor artist Gary Bukovnik, painted this pie for a show several years ago. Quick and cold are best for success. 2. Select freestone peaches. The flesh of the peach will come away easily from the pit. If you use cling peaches, you must cut the fruit from the pit, detracting from the pie’s appearance (but not its taste). 3. Cool the pie sufficiently for the juices to thicken slightly before slicing. articles.text: Jon Sigurdson, a resident of Piedmont since 1970, passed away at home with his family on June 16, 2020. He was 86. Born Jon Frederick Page Sigurdson in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada on July 2, 1933, he was the third child of Larus Arthur and Helen Page Sigurdson. After completing his Bachelor of Arts at the University of Manitoba, Jon followed in his father’s footsteps by studying medicine. In 1959 he received his Doctor of Medicine from the University of Manitoba with an emphasis in Anatomy and Physiology. While in medical school, Jon met the love of his life, Margaret Jean Watson. They were married on July 19, 1958. After completing his internship at Winnipeg General Hospital, Jon and Margaret moved to Philadelphia in 1960 for his orthopedic residency at the University of Pennsylvania. While in Philadelphia, their only child, Helen Margaret Jean, was born. In 1964, the family moved to Oakland, CA where Jon joined the Kaiser Permanente Medical Group. In 1970, Jon went into solo private practice in Oakland with Margaret as his office manager. Jon was very active in the orthopedic community and served on the Board of Councilors of the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons from 1983 to 1989. He enjoyed a successful orthopedic practice and retired in 2011. Jon was a passionate student of the arts. He received a Music degree as a Piano Solo Performer from the Royal Conservatory of Music of Toronto in 1956. His love of music led Jon and Margaret to be long time patrons of the San Francisco Symphony and the San Francisco Opera. His memberships in the Canadian and the British Orthopedic communities led them to medical meetings and an opportunity to meet new friends all over the world. Jon enjoyed studying art, history and geography. Together, he and Margaret took classes at the De Young Museum and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. As voracious readers, they were long-time members of two book clubs. Jon and Margaret were also avid hikers. They hiked the West Highland Way in Scotland, the full length of the Thames, and the Milford Track in Australia. He delighted in taking his family to historical sites throughout the U.S., Canada and Europe. Jon was a devoted, husband, father and grandfather. He passed his love of arts and outdoors to his daughter and granddaughters. Jon was an active member of the First Presbyterian Church of Oakland for over 50 years and was instrumental in the installation of the church organ. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, July 8, 2020 By T.J. Stevko When facing illness, take control of finances In light of the coronavirus pandemic, virtually all of us have considered health-related issues. But for people facing a serious, chronic illness, such as Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, diabetes or cancer, health concerns are an everyday matter. If you’re fortunate, you may never be afflicted with such maladies, but the future is unpredictable. Of course, going through these health challenges bring physical and emotional concerns – but also financial ones. How can you prepare for them? Essentially, you’ll need to consider four key areas: investments, insurance, legal arrangements and taxes. Let’s take a quick look at each of them: • Investments You’ll likely need to draw on your investments for at least some of the expenses associated with your illness. So, within your portfolio, you may want to establish a special fund devoted entirely to these costs, whether they be health care, modifications to your home, transportation and so on. A financial professional can help you choose investments for this fund, as well as make recommendations for your overall investment strategy, including techniques for boosting your income, such as adding investments that can provide an income stream that kicks in when you think your costs will rise. • Insurance Depending on your health status, you may be able to collect Medicare earlier than the traditional starting point at age 65. Even so, you’ll likely need to supplement it with additional coverage. But you may also want to look beyond health insurance. For example, you might be able to purchase a “chronic illness rider” that allows you to tap into life insurance benefits while you’re still alive. Or you might consider adding a “long-term care rider” to a life insurance policy; this rider offers financial benefits if you ever require daily care that you can’t provide for yourself. And some foundations, states and drug companies offer programs that can help pay for some costs that your insurance won’t cover. • Legal arrangements If you haven’t already done so, you may want to establish the legal documents most appropriate for your situation, such as a durable power of attorney for finances, which gives someone the authority to manage your financial affairs if you become temporarily incapacitated, possibly due to flare-ups of your chronic disease. Once you’ve recovered, you regain control of your financial decisions. You might also want to consider a health care proxy, which appoints an individual to make medical decisions for you if you can’t. In creating or revising these documents, you’ll need to consult with your legal professional. • Taxes You might qualify for Social Security disability payments, which, like other Social Security benefits, are taxable, so you’ll need to be aware of what you might owe. But you might also be eligible for some tax breaks related to your condition. If you still itemize tax deductions, you may be able to deduct some medical expenses, as well as certain home improvements, such as wheelchair ramps, bathtub grab bars, motorized stairlifts and so on. Your tax advisor may have suggestions appropriate for your situation. Dealing with a chronic illness is never easy. But by considering how your illness will affect all aspects of your life, getting the help you need, and taking the right steps, you may be able to reduce the financial stress on you and your loved ones. Jon enjoyed studying art, history and geography. Together, he and Margaret took classes at the De Young Museum and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco.
