articles.text: Piedmont needs to decrease emissions another 13.5% by 2030 to meet CAP goals Greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont have decreased in recent years, according to a report presented by Justin Szasz, Climate Fellow, to City Council on Monday, July 6. The report was an inventory of greenhouse gases emitted in 2018 and found that total emissions were down over 26 percent compared to 2005. In 2018, the City estimates there were 34,340 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, compared to 48,818 metric tons in 2005 and 38,101 metric tons in 2017. The report noted 934 metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2018 were attributed to activities done by the City government. In the past 15 years, greenhouse gas emissions have dropped mostly due to a reduction in appliance use. “The reductions since 2005 are largely due to decreases in emissions from building appliances,” the report explained. Piedmonters appear to be using less natural gas appliances at home. The report notes the increased use of electric utility systems appears to have contributed to the decrease. However, much of the decreased use of appliances can be ascribed to the fact that winters have been warmer in recent years, a trend that scientists blame on global warming. Although reported emissions decreased almost 10 percent from 2017 to 2018, the City attributed this decline to changes in methodology. In fact, the City believes did not change significantly in this time period. “Reductions between 2017 and 2018, by contrast, are largely attributable to changes in in the protocols for estimating emissions, not to emission reductions happening in Piedmont,” the report said. The inventory suggests that the report for 2019 emissions will show a notable decrease, though, because the City has enrolled in an electricity plan that powers Piedmont with 100 percent renewable energy. This action was part of the Climate Action Plan (CAP) adopted by the City in 2018. While the amount of emissions from appliances decreased, emissions from vehicles have held steady from 2015 to 2018. The CAP goals adopted in 2018 push Piedmont to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 40 percent below 2005 levels by 2030. By 2050, the CAP sets forth the goal of reducing emissions to 80 percent below 2005. The inventory released this week shows that Piedmont still has some work to do in order to reach its goals in 10 years. “The inventories completed thus far reveal that, for the most part, the changes from year to year are caused by external forces, and that the City still has a long way to go to make substantive changes to the building energy sector and the transportation sector so that it can meet the City’s 2030 and 2050 goals,” the report said. The City must reduce 2018 emission levels another 13.5 percent in order to reach the CAP goals by 2030.
articles.title: Piedmont greenhouse gas emissions 26% lower than 2005

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: The American Red Cross strongly urges healthy, eligible individuals who are feeling well to give blood or platelets to help maintain a sufficient blood supply and prevent shortages as concerns about the outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019, or COVID-19, rise in the U.S. Cold and f lu season has already impacted the nation’s ability to maintain its blood supply. As the number of coronavirus cases grows in the U.S., the number of people eligible to give blood for patients in need could decrease further. “We’re asking people to help keep the blood supply stable during this challenging time. As communities across the country prepare for this public health emergency, it’s critical that plans include a readily available blood supply for hospital patients,” said Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Blood Services. “As fears of coronavirus rise, low donor participation could harm blood availability at hospitals, and the last thing a patient should worry about is whether lifesaving blood will be on the shelf when they need it most.” Make an appointment to donate blood now by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or calling the Oakland Blood Donation Center, 6230 Claremont Avenue, at 510-658-6456. time of donation – and who meet other eligibility requirements, available at RedCrossBlood.org. At each blood drive and donation center, Red Cross employees follow thorough safety protocols including wearing gloves, routinely wiping down donortouched areas, using sterile collection sets for every donation, and preparing the arm for donation with an aseptic scrub. These mitigation measures will help ensure blood recipient safety, as well as staff and donor safety in reducing contact with those who may potentially have this respiratory infection. The Red Cross has implemented new blood donation deferrals out of an abundance of caution. Individuals are asked to postpone their donation for 28 days following: • Travel to China and its special administrative regions, Hong Kong and Macau, as well as Iran, Italy and South Korea; • Diagnosis of COVID-19, contact with a person who has or is suspected to have the virus. Donating blood is a safe process and people should not hesitate to give or receive blood. There are no data or evidence that this coronavirus can be transmissible by blood transfusion, and there have been no reported cases worldwide of transmissions for any respiratory virus, including this coronavirus, from a transfusion. See it filled with your own objects and art. Visualize that the space is clean and clutter-free. Next, ask yourself, what do I want for this room? And notice what arises. Do you imagine rearranging it? Are you willing to let go of certain pieces? Are there items in that room that you’ve been telling yourself a story about, justifying why you should hang onto it? Have them envision the same space, or their own spaces. See what everyone comes up with. Thought becomes form. If we can dream it, we can create it. But without a clear sense of our own vision, we might find ourselves just grabbing whatever looks good at the retail furniture outlet or being swayed by the marketing story on page 34 of a print catalog. Maybe you don’t want to sit and do vision work. If that is the case, try this: Simply notice the energy that you’re in when you are thinking about making a change to your home. Is it the energy of, “I want my home to look good because I care what other people think,” or is it, “I want it to feel good so that I will be able to be more connected to myself”? Which of these thoughts is more inspiring for you? Adjust your inner monologue as needed. Another way that we can create a more connected environment is to be visioning when we are in an energy-rich state. So, be very mindful about how you are feeling when you are looking for things for your home. Try this: Meditate (if that is your jam) or go for a walk in nature before going online to shop for furnishings. Notice if you suddenly find things more easily, or make decisions more effortlessly, when you are resourced by stillness. If you fill your home with pieces that you collect when you are really connected to yourself, then your environment will be far more soulful, and far more welcoming, and far more you. An interior designer can help you get you clear on your vision; and with that vision, create a thoughtfully designed home environment that invites you to tap into your higher self. This is why I am so inspired by what I do. I get to help people create home environments that support them in the most magnificent way possible, so that they may share their gifts with the world. Expected users of public electric vehicle chargers include renters, employees of the school district and city government, and visitors to local residences or commerce, in other words, owners of electric vehicles who do not have their own chargers at home. “Some residents of Piedmont have [an electric vehicle], but currently no appropriate plug for a charger in their garage,” Szasz explained. “There are similar projects in London and Los Angeles, but this [proposal] would be the leading example in Alameda County”, said Zac Thompson, East Bay Community Energy program associate. Transportation is one of the leading causes of greenhouse gas emissions, Thompson explained. Many residents in Piedmont have already converted to electric vehicles, as evidenced in the Piedmont Climate Challenge that was held earlier this year. Both Thompson and Szasz asserted that a greater transition to electric vehicles will ultimately reduce Piedmont’s carbon footprint, while also improving air quality. The Piedmont Planning Department conducted a five-day sample survey of Piedmont residents from June 17 to 22 to gauge what residents think of various potential programs. City Planning Director Kevin Jackson presented the findings of that survey to commissioners. “About 85 percent [of that sample group] believe that climate change is caused mostly by human activities, and three-quarters believe that they will see a difference in their own lives as a result of climate change,” Jackson said. One-quarter of respondents own an electric vehicle, and four in five support the project. Renters were found to be especially supportive of increasing electric vehicle charging stations in Piedmont. “Approximately half of non-electric vehicle drivers say they would be more likely to acquire one if chargers were more widely available,” Jackson explained. Commissioners weighed the pros and cons of installing charging stations throughout the city. Commissioner Amber Brumfiel pointed out the loss of parking space if the proposal were to advance. “Because residents can charge at home, the tradeoff of loss of parking doesn’t seem worth it,” Brumfiel said. “I’m wondering if this greatly impacts Piedmont’s carbon footprint.” Resident Cameron Wolfe, Jr. echoed Brumfiel’s concerns. “Further reductions in available general parking in the Community Center lot is a bad idea. articles.text: In time-honored tradition, the Piedmont 4th of July Parade Committee toured the city the nigh before the parade to observe locations of all parade entries. With the cancellation of the parade due to concerns of COVID-19, there were no floats this year. Instead, with a theme of Celebrating in Place, residents submitted entry forms describing the decorations on their homes and cars. After viewing the 20 entries, the committee is presenting the following awards: Highland Cup Best Entry: Mason & Austin Gray, 23 Piedmont Court, “Bloom Where You Are Planted” (2nd generation owners) All decorations were created by sons Mason & Austin, including a large sign on the garage reading ”Don’t forget true beauty.” Highland Saucer Most Patriotic: Barbara Addelman, 225 Carmel Ave., “This is What Democracy Looks Like” Large collection of handmade signs from historic civic protests in the U.S, going back to the rallies by Native Americans at Standing Rock, North Dakota. Highland Spoons Best Quaranteam: Buffy Yeh & Neighbors, 223 Park View Ave, “Celebrating with Patriotism and Protests” Mayor’s Award “E Pluribus Unum – Out of Many, One”, Julia Elitzer, 128 Greenbank Ave. Handmade flags of every state in the U.S., and a dozen countries outside the U.S. Best Car in Place Rod Boothby, 1132 Oakland Ave. Most Artistic Award “Pollinator Posse,” Terry Smith, 121 Fairview As a science teacher, the display calls attention to importance of creating pollinator-friendly gardens. Best Spirit Award “Do the Right Thing”, Sydney Proctor and Team Proctor, 385 Moraga Ave. A collection of signs promoting racial justice, include Black Lives Matter.

articles.text: At 8:12 a.m. on Thursday morning, July 2, the Piedmont Police received a call about an attempted robbery, attempted stolen vehicle and death threat by a person with a knife and in possession of burglary tools. A contractor hired to paint the inside of a Piedmont home went outside to his vehicle and saw a man inside his vehicle. The contractor chased the suspect down Highland Ave. The suspect then turned around and brandished an 8-10” black knife toward the contractor, who immediately ran back away from the suspect. The suspect then chased the contractor. When the contractor fell to the ground, the suspect demanded the contractor’s wallet. The contractor refused and the suspect was unable to take any property from him or his vehicle. The suspect then fled in a grey Toyota Camry southbound on Highland Ave. The suspect’s vehicle had been stolen from Fairfield. Police issued a BOLO (Be on the lookout for) alert notice to other jurisdictions.
articles.title: Attempted robbery, car theft by suspect with knife

One of the best entries was saved for last. Barbara Addelman and family on Carmel Avenue set up a yard filled with handmade signs based upon the theme, “This is What Democracy Looks Like”. The impressive assemblage of included historic civic protests in the U.S, going back to the rallies by Native Americans at Standing Rock in North Dakota. Signs for social causes filled up dozens of small windows out front and cutout protesters held up pickets. Signs read “Black Lives Matter,” “Water is Life,” “Google: Fred Hampton,” “We Stand with Hong Hong,” and dozens more. This installation and fan favorite won the Highland Saucer for Most Patriotic entry. articles.text: The future of the Piedmont community pool was discussed extensively at a special city council meeting held via Zoom on Monday evening, June 29. More than 100 people tuned and over 30 residents spoke during the public comment portion of the meeting. According to City Administrator Sara Lillevand the city currently does not have the capital to revive the pool to optimum standards. A minimal upgrade on the pool would cost at least $1.5 million, in addition to a lengthy closure. “We need to focus our attention on a new aquatic facility. Using more and more duct tape to keep this current one alive doesn’t make sense from a fiscal perspective,” Lillevand said. Lillevand added that it would cost approximately “$15 million to build a facility that would serve the community well.” A bond measure, which could appear as early as this November, would be required to make this happen. The council noted that the Piedmont Community Pool adjacent to the Recreation Center on Hillside Avenue.

articles.text: The city commissioned a herd of 500 goats through Ecosystem Concepts in Dixon, a company that pioneered the use of goats to take out undergrowth that fuels the flames of wildfires. The company emerged after the 1991 wildfire in Oakland in order to “provide a sustainable solution.” The goats came to Piedmont on June 20 and will return to a quieter area away from the sound of fireworks tomorrow, July 2. The herd will be moved before Independence Day weekend because the sound of fireworks can make the goats anxious, Fire Chief Bret Black explained. Goatherd Martin Matarrese answered questions from residents on Tuesday afternoon at a public event created by Chief Black. The herd can clear unwanted, dry brush in areas and steep hills where machinery or chemicals cannot. Each goat will eat approximately 10 pounds of brush or grass a day, Matarrese said. The goats cleared approximately 50 percent of the undergrowth in Blair Park in two days. The goats stay in one place until they collectively eat about four to six inches of vegetation and grass. Staff Photos A group of 500 goats were brought to Piedmont for the past week to help clear brush and weeds on the hillside above Coaches Field and in Blair Park. The herd of 500 that arrived in Piedmont is young, with an average age of one year, Matarrese said. “The sites [in Piedmont] are mostly steep, and the soil is soft. These are lighter-weight goats, as opposed to the up to six-yearold goats in some of our bigger herds,” he said. Their life expectancy is about seven to eight years. At that age, the goat’s teeth begin to soften, and they can no longer graze. Two dogs stayed on-site with the herd to protect them from natural predators, such as mountain lions or coyotes. Matarrese said that coyote sightings have recently become more prevalent in the Bay Area, so the dogs stay with the goats throughout the night to ensure their safety. Border Collies are used as “sheep herders,” and assist the goatherd in transporting the goats from one location to the next. Ecosystem Concepts has a total of about 5000 goats, and has contracts with a number of cities, including Oakland, Roseville, and Menlo Park. They are also used by homeowners associations across northern California.
articles.title: Goats come calling in Piedmont

articles.text: Oakland firefighters blamed fireworks for an early morning brushfire in the Oakland hills on Sunday, June 28, days after the Piedmont Fire Department warned that the use of any fireworks, including sparklers, can cause wildfires. Reported in the middle of the night, at 3:09 a.m. on Sunday, the three-alarm fire burned about 2.5 acres near the intersection of Crest Avenue and Fontaine Street by Interstate 580. No structures were threatened by the fire and no one was injured, but Oakland Fire Department confirmed that it took 56 firefighters several hours to extinguish the intense fire. Oakland firefighters said that the cause was the use of illegal fireworks. On Thursday, June 25, Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black released a warning about the danger of fireworks ahead of the Fourth of July. “As the 4th of July approaches, Piedmont Fire and Police Departments want to remind the community that all forms of fireworks are prohibited in Piedmont, even ‘sparklers,’” Black proclaimed. Even though it may be tempting to shoot off fireworks to interrupt the boredom of Alameda County’s shelter-at-home orders See Fireworks on page 30 The Goats, Redux ................1 Banks remain closed . ............3 Question Man......................4 Businesses reopen. ...............5 School reopening.................6 Nick Millosovich. ..................8 PPD Blue. ...........................9 Americans in Paris . ............ 10 Sports............................. 12 Goats – photo page............. 15 Museum tours. ................... 16 Music.............................. 17 Kid Movies. ....................... 19 Musical Gourmet................ 20 Travels with Kate. ............... 21 Bookmark deliveries. ........... 22 Humor by Phil Witte............ 24 Crime Report. .................... 32 Goats come calling in Piedmont By Allyson Aleksey The city commissioned a herd of 500 goats through Ecosystem Concepts in Dixon, a company that pioneered the use of goats to take out undergrowth that fuels the flames of wildfires. The company emerged after the 1991 wildfire in Oakland in order to “provide a sustainable solution.” The goats came to Piedmont on June 20 and will return to a quieter area away from the sound of fireworks tomorrow, July 2. The herd will be moved before Independence Day weekend because the sound of fireworks can make the goats anxious, Fire Chief Bret Black explained. Goatherd Martin Matarrese answered questions from residents on Tuesday afternoon at a public event created by Chief Black. The herd can clear unwanted, dry brush in areas and steep hills where machinery or chemicals cannot. Each goat will eat approximately 10 pounds of brush or grass a day, Matarrese said. The goats cleared approximately 50 percent of the undergrowth in Blair Park in two days. The goats stay in one place until they collectively eat about four to six inches of vegetation and grass. Staff Photos A group of 500 goats were brought to Piedmont for the past week to help clear brush and weeds on the hillside above Coaches Field and in Blair Park. The herd of 500 that arrived in Piedmont is young, with an average age of one year, Matarrese said. “The sites [in Piedmont] are mostly steep, and the soil is soft. These are lighter-weight goats, as opposed to the up to six-yearold goats in some of our bigger herds,” he said. Their life expectancy is about seven to eight years. At that age, the goat’s teeth begin to soften, and they can no longer graze. Two dogs stayed on-site with the herd to protect them from natural predators, such as mountain lions or coyotes. Matarrese said that coyote sightings have recently become more prevalent in the Bay Area, so the dogs stay with the goats throughout the night to ensure their safety. Border Collies are used as “sheep herders,” and assist the goatherd in transporting the goats from one location to the next. Ecosystem Concepts has a total of about 5000 goats, and has contracts with a number of cities, including Oakland, Roseville, and Menlo Park. They are also used by homeowners associations across northern California. See more photos on page 15.

articles.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a budget emergency in order to release funds to help pay for resources needed to combat the COVID-19 pandemic. Citing a $54.3 billion state budget deficit, Newsom declared the emergency on Thursday morning, June 25. The proclamation states that the ongoing pandemic “requires future expenditures of state funds for personal protective equipment (PPE), medical equipment and other expenditures as necessary to support a potential hospital surge, to provide necessary services to vulnerable populations, and other expenditures necessary to respond to the threat and spread of COVID-19.” The proclamation specifies that the state must use a portion of the reserves in the Budget Stabilization Account in the 2020-21 fiscal year to fund expenditures related to COVID-19 and provide other needed services. California has experienced a sharp increase in hospitalizations for more than a week and last week set daily records for new cases since the mandate to lockdown in March. The state broke a record on Tuesday, June 23 with an increase of more than 7000 cases in 24 hours. Newsom suggested that the rise in cases is due to Californians’ cavalier attitude toward the virus. “Many of us understandably developed a little cabin fever. Some of us, I would argue, developed a little amnesia. Others have frankly taken down their guard,” the governor said during a June 24 press briefing. “People are mixing and that is increasing the spread of the virus,” he added.
articles.title: Gov. Newsom declares budget emergency to fund COVID-19 response

articles.text: All three banks in Piedmont – Wells Fargo, Citi Bank, and Bank of America – have remained closed to customers throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. The three banks officially closed on March 16, without warning to customers. Banks and related financial institutions, including money lender and check cashing services, are considered essential businesses and are permitted to remain open throughout the health crisis. However, the decision to remain open is ultimately up to each bank and its district manager. Some brick-and-mortar banks closed their doors to customers in anticipation of lower foot traffic. Wells Fargo District Manager Munir Ahmad said that the decision to close the location at 344 Highland Avenue was due to a shortage of employees. “We closed about 35 percent of our branches, including Piedmont, Rockridge and Claremont. Most of our team members [at the Piedmont location] chose to self-quarantine due to high risk of exposure,” Ahmad said. When asked why customers were not notified of the closure, Ahmad said that developments related to countywide restrictions were happening very quickly, making it difficult to alert customers in a timely manner. In the event of a second closure, customers will be notified by mail, according to Ahmad. Wells Fargo has said that its Piedmont branch would reopen on Monday, June 29, but the doors remained locked throughout the day. Markers have been placed outside the entrance to designate social distances of six feet, but with the bank closed, there is no evidence of customers waiting to get inside. The banks two ATM machines are the only source for banking, although two employees have been in the bank throughout shelter-in-place to assist with safety deposit box appointments. Bank of America a no show Bank of America, located at 346 Highland Avenue, closed on March 16. Numerous signs on the front door direct customers to a location at 6201 College Avenue and provide a phone number customers may call if they have Citi Bank at 333 Highland Avenue. Bank of America at 345 Highland Avenue. Staff photos Markers have been placed around the Wells Fargo location at sixfoot distances. questions. The phone number provided, 415-985-3137, is a dead line. A sign taped on the front door states that employees have been directed to do their jobs from home, if possible, and not to come to the branch bank if sick. It is unclear when or if the bank will reopen. The bank has offered no statement thus far. No plans to reopen by Citibank Citibank, located at 333 Highland Avenue, has remained closed throughout the pandemic. Customers are directed to Citi Bank at 4101 Piedmont Avenue by a sign posted on the front door. The ATMs at each branch are still operable, but safe deposit box access must be scheduled in advance during business operating hours. Maggie Monaghan, a Citibank Public Affairs employee in New York, said that there is no set date on when Citibank will reopen its Piedmont location. “We are closely monitoring the data on COVID-19 cases to ensure that we are providing a safe environment for clients and employees as we reopen branches that were temporarily closed. We encourage customers to use Citibank.com or the Citi Mobile App for everyday banking needs and to check on the status and hours of our branches. Additionally, there is a nearby Citibank branch that is open only a mile or so away at 4101 Piedmont Ave in Oakland, California,” Monaghan said. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Editor: Farewell Piedmont. We came as a young couple, not for the schools, but to shorten Michael’s commute. We fell in love with your charming streets, beautiful homes and lovely parks. We became a family here. Soon after moving in, our first child arrived. Holding her in our arms, the doorbell rang. “Trick or Treat”, said the neighborhood kids. “Cute baby”, they chimed in. We knew we would like life in Piedmont. Neighbors and Newcomers club, playground conversations, tearful goodbyes on the first day of Kindergarten; all the fond memories of this gracious little city. Bird Calling and Beach Review, Pancakes on the Playground and Dad’s Softball games, A Cappella concerts and football at Witter Field, the Fourth of July Parade and concert in the park; we will cherish them all. Most of all, we cherish the friends we made, our neighbors now and those long gone. We wish to thank the teachers, administrators and staff of PUSD, our city leaders and staff, for their dedication to our little city. It is the people who make Piedmont the special place that it is. We leave having raised two great kids with loads of memories. The next chapter begins. While our life is taking us to new places and on new adventures, we will always call Piedmont our hometown. With love and fondness, -Michael Coen and Deidre Brodeur-Coen
articles.title: A love letter to our hometown of 24 years

articles.text: Editor: Last night, (Monday, June 29) the Piedmont City Council held a special online meeting on the short and long term prospects for the Piedmont Community Pool, given the age of the pool, maintenance issues resulting from the age, and the current COVID crisis. The meeting was well attended (virtually) and Piedmonters of all ages spoke overwhelmingly in favor of keeping the pool open, and working toward the replacement facility envisioned in the Aquatics Master Plan in 2016. I encourage the City Council to continue the strategy developed in 2016-17 to seek a bond measure to support city facilities as a bundled package, with the pool as one of the projects in the package. I believe that the strategy discussed last night to seek a bond for the pool by itself, competing with other bond measures on the ballot, would likely not be successful and would result in the permanent loss of a pool for Piedmont. This would be a sad loss for the many Piedmonters who enjoy the pool, and use it for recreation, exercise, and for all of the multitude of programs for young people that it has always supported. I urge the Council to stick with the prior strategy of bundling improvements in one measure. -Duncan Watry
articles.title: Council urged to create bond for new city pool

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council will consider the first reading of an ordinance implementing Reach Codes, or amendments to the state’s Building Energy Efficiency Standards and state Electrical Code, which are designed to promote efficient building methods in homes in Piedmont. The first reading will be conducted during a regular city council meeting on July 6 at 7:30 p.m. The council will also consider an ordinance requiring home energy audits under certain circumstances. These measures are being proposed because Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 calls for the community to reduce its annual greenhouse gas emissions from the building, transportation, waste, and wastewater sectors. The goal is to reduce emissions from about 38,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions in 2017, to just 9,800 metric tons in 2050. Currently, a large percentage of the city’s emissions come from natural gas appliances in buildings, especially gas furnaces and water heaters. To meet CAP goals, the community must decrease natural gas use in buildings by improving insulation, and by switching out natural gas appliances for electric appliances powered by renewable energy. The proposed requirements are as follows: newly constructed low-rise residential buildings, including new detached accessory dwelling units (ADUs), must use all electric building appliances. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, July 1, 2020 Local Items A love letter to our hometown of 24 years Editor: Farewell Piedmont. We came as a young couple, not for the schools, but to shorten Michael’s commute. We fell in love with your charming streets, beautiful homes and lovely parks. We became a family here. Soon after moving in, our first child arrived. Holding her in our arms, the doorbell rang. “Trick or Treat”, said the neighborhood kids. “Cute baby”, they chimed in. We knew we would like life in Piedmont. Neighbors and Newcomers club, playground conversations, tearful goodbyes on the first day of Kindergarten; all the fond memories of this gracious little city. Bird Calling and Beach Review, Pancakes on the Playground and Dad’s Softball games, A Cappella concerts and football at Witter Field, the Fourth of July Parade and concert in the park; we will cherish them all. Most of all, we cherish the friends we made, our neighbors now and those long gone. We wish to thank the teachers, administrators and staff of PUSD, our city leaders and staff, for their dedication to our little city. It is the people who make Piedmont the special place that it is. We leave having raised two great kids with loads of memories. The next chapter begins. While our life is taking us to new places and on new adventures, we will always call Piedmont our hometown. With love and fondness, -Michael Coen and Deidre Brodeur-Coen July 1 - 5 Wednesday, July 1 6 a.m. June 30 Special School Board meeting 11 a.m. June 29 Special City Council meeting 5:30 p.m. Park Commission mtg. - Live By Jay Russell QUESTION: What are your plans for the Fourth of July? Council urged to create bond for new city pool Editor: Last night, (Monday, June 29) the Piedmont City Council held a special online meeting on the short and long term prospects for the Piedmont Community Pool, given the age of the pool, maintenance issues resulting from the age, and the current COVID crisis. The meeting was well attended (virtually) and Piedmonters of all ages spoke overwhelmingly in favor of keeping the pool open, and working toward the replacement facility envisioned in the Aquatics Master Plan in 2016. I encourage the City Council to continue the strategy developed in 2016-17 to seek a bond measure to support city facilities as a bundled package, with the pool as one of the projects in the package. I believe that the strategy discussed last night to seek a bond for the pool by itself, competing with other bond measures on the ballot, would likely not be successful and would result in the permanent loss of a pool for Piedmont. This would be a sad loss for the many Piedmonters who enjoy the pool, and use it for recreation, exercise, and for all of the multitude of programs for young people that it has always supported. I urge the Council to stick with the prior strategy of bundling improvements in one measure. -Duncan Watry 6 a.m. June 30 Special School Board meeting 11 a.m., 5 p.m. Celebrate in Place – Piedmont’s 4th of July Celebration 12 p.m. Past July 4th Parades 3 p.m. July 1 Park Commission mtg. 6 p.m. June 29 Special City Council meeting Due to the COVID 19 emergency, live meetings are being held virtually and NOT at City Hall. Council to consider Reach Codes at July 6 meeting By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont City Council will consider the first reading of an ordinance implementing Reach Codes, or amendments to the state’s Building Energy Efficiency Standards and state Electrical Code, which are designed to promote efficient building methods in homes in Piedmont. The first reading will be conducted during a regular city council meeting on July 6 at 7:30 p.m. The council will also consider an ordinance requiring home energy audits under certain circumstances. These measures are being proposed because Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 calls for the community to reduce its annual greenhouse gas emissions from the building, transportation, waste, and wastewater sectors. The goal is to reduce emissions from about 38,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions in 2017, to just 9,800 metric tons in 2050. Currently, a large percentage of the city’s emissions come from natural gas appliances in buildings, especially gas furnaces and water heaters. To meet CAP goals, the community must decrease natural gas use in buildings by improving insulation, and by switching out natural gas appliances for electric appliances powered by renewable energy. The proposed requirements are as follows: newly constructed low-rise residential buildings, including new detached accessory dwelling units (ADUs), must use all electric building appliances. Projects proposing an entire new upper level on a low-rise residential building, or that increase a low-rise residential building’s total roof area by 30 percent or more, are required to install solar panels on their roof. Additionally, a housing renovation on a low-rise residential building, that costs $25,000 or more, will require the applicant to include one item from a list of energy efficient insulation or electrification fixes. The council will also consider other amendments to the building code and policy changes that will help reduce natural gas use. Residents are encouraged to participate by submitting comments and by attending the council meeting, which will be held virtually through Zoom technology. Comments regarding the proposed code amendments may be sent to the council via email at citycouncil@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Dress Best for Less opened its new storefront location at 4020 Piedmont Ave on March 7, only to have their red carpet rolled right back up seven days later due to COVID-19. Located next to Piedmont Grocery it reopened Friday, June 17 after an uneasy three months in which they employed new business strategies. Dress Best for Less (DBFL) is a non-profit thrift store stocked with donations from Piedmont’s carriage house donation center across the street from the high school. In addition to providing some funding for Piedmont schools, it contributes to charitable organizations. About one month into the county’s required shutdown due to the coronavirus, members of the DBFL board realized the restrictions were not ending anytime soon, so they created a website. Thrift stores rely on in-person browsing, so sales were low through the site. Board member Melanie Marcus saw a silver lining. “We kept our name out there and kept active. We showcased the nice labels and brands and the quality of the merchandise,” she said. The store also beefed up its presence on social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook while reaching out to customers new and old with the Manager Julia Kirillova keeps the new location for Dress Best for Less on Piedmont Avenue clean, organized and sanitary. constant contact email service. The store’s non-profit status did not exempt them from the concerns all businesses have faced. The DBFL president Linda Smith Munyan said, “We moved quickly and were able to get some funding through the CARES act to help us pay our rent.” “We were also able to keep paying our salaried manager and our two other part-time employees throughout the closure. It was important to keep paying our employees and the CARES act helped us with that. It wasn’t a big amount, but our bookkeeper jumped right on it,” said Munyan. Dress Best for Less did well on their first day of reopening, with business primarily from new customers. Kirillova outlined their new stringent sanitary precautions, “We have hand sanitizer everywhere and spare new masks for guests who forget theirs. The clothes that people try on will be steamed before they go back out. Every 45 minutes all the surfaces get cleansed.” Donations cannot be accepted at this time according to Alameda County health restrictions. Many households have items waiting to be donated, so when they receive a green light from the County, DBFL will be able to receive donated items and essentially restock the store. Current hours are 11:00 a.m.- 5:30 p.m. Tuesday - Saturday. The store at 4020 Piedmont Avenue is next to Piedmont Grocery. View their new website at dressbestforless.org, or call 510-658-8525.

This includes ensuring that students have computer and internet access, documenting daily student participation in a weekly log and creating a system to track non-participating students, setting procedures for reengaging students who are absent for more than 60 percent of instruction per week, and communicating with parents about learning processes. The bill also sets requirements for districts to ensure that teachers interact with students daily to instruct, monitor progress, and maintain parent-student relationships. AB 77 section 43503 states that distance learning may be offered under either circumstance: as a result of an order or guidance from a state public health official, or for pupils who are medically fragile or would be put at risk by in-person instruction. “What this means to us, is that the idea of [full] distance learning is essentially pulled off the table for board consideration,” Booker said. That’s very importThe Piedmont School Board has provided an opportunity for the public to comment and provide suggestions for board policies on equity and racial justice. Cheryl Wozniak, Director of Curriculum, presented the renewed board policy at a June 24 meeting, which was up for review as a first reading. “For many years, members of our community and PUSD staff have really had a strong interest and goal of bringing diversity work to Piedmont,” Wozniak said. A Diversity Task Force was formed in 2011, comprised of district staff and community members to create a mission and vision development. The task force formed a partnership with Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC), a community-based committee with a mission to promote and practice inclusiveness in Piedmont and surrounding communities. In 2011, the task force came before the school board to present their development mission statement, which was later incorporated into the District’s mission and goals. Wozniak said that this was a starting point for the district’s commitment to fostering inclusion and beginning to recognize structures that raise barriers, preventing all from feeling welcome and receiving an equal education experience. In 2017, the board adopted a three-year Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP). This was comprised of two goals: to ensure that all students feel physically safe, emotionally cared for, and academically as well as socially included in their school environment. The second goal was to commit to equity, diversity, and social justice partnerships and community engagement. “We can make wise decisions about what text we put in front of our students, so that they see themselves in the curriculum and have windows to the experiences of others who have different backgrounds,” Wozniak said, adding that the district has been adopting curriculum over the past few years that celebrates diversity through a social justice lens. In the past year, students have written and shared their own stories through a series entitled “I Am Here: Conservations About Identity.” Mentorship programs for Asian-American students, where high school students have partnered with elementary students, is continuing to progress. The proposal presented by Wozniak stated, “The district shall commit to anti-racist work in order to proactively identify class and cultural biases as well as practices, policies, and institutional barrier that negatively influence student learning and impede equal access to opportunities for all students.” The draft calls on the board and superintendent to develop and implement policies and strategies that promote equity by recognizing the existence of institutional racism and working to dismantle systems of oppression within district programs and activities. This includes educating staff about key elements of antiracist education, including: identifying and counteracting bias and stereotyping in learning material, dealing with racial tensions and conflicts, examining historical roots and contemporary manifestations of racial prejudice, and more. “We will continue to meet with Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee and the city of Piedmont leaders in recognizing that this has to be a city wide effort, with all of us coming together. We all acknowledge we have a lot to learn,” Wozniak said. The district is seeking input on Board Policy 0415: Equity and Racial Justice. Please read the Board Background on BP 0415 at https://docs.google.com/ document/d /18nJeaEhR KUuNdpMOUdO3RpekxwBkbNQxQeZfW_8MlQs/edit, and the Draft Board Policy at https://docs. google.com/document/d/1keNQA7g rq0j1T bLD2r tN7 VSxP G k p5G jW b - p q wX UQPl4 / edit. To provide feedback or input for changes, email Cheryl Wozniak at cwozniak@piedmont. k12.ca.us by this Friday, July 3.

articles.text: Residents with Oakland Library cards may now pick up holds reserved online for books, DVDs, and CDs. You can also reserve a WiFi hotspot at the library doors. Indoor areas remain closed to the public. It’s easy! Here’s how it works: Search for Books, DVDs, and CDs at oaklandlibrary.org. Use the “request it” button to place items on hold. You’ll need your library card number and PIN. Select the branch library most convenient for you. If you already have items on hold, log in to your account and select an open location to send your hold. Branch Pickup When you are notified that your items are ready, come to the selected branch between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. You will receive an email, text, or phone notification when your hold is available for pickup. Please note: Wait times for holds may be longer than usual. If you have multiple items on hold, you will get a separate notification for each one. You have 14 days after you get the notification to pick up your item. You’ll need to have your library card number with you. Be mindful of the ongoing health crisis. Wear a face covering and observe social distancing. Keep 6 feet apart from other patrons in line. Sidewalk Pickup Star ting now, sidewalk pickup of books will be available locally at the Main Library and Rockridge Branch Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Summer Reading Programs to begin Readers of all ages can now register to participate in our annual Summer Reading program. You’ll be able to qualify to win prizes at the end of the program by completing your reading log, participating in the online programs, and getting involved in your community. Register for Summer Reading by visiting www.oaklandlibrary.org/ summer. Complete information is at https://oaklandlibrary.org/. For questions, please call 510-238- 3134 or email eanswers@oaklandlibrary.org.

It will be immediately next to the 3-story classroom building and create a formidable entry to the high school campus. The building housing the new Alan Harvey Theater is scheduled for completion in August 2021. Over the next month, Overaa will work on more prep work. “Grading and other preparations for building the foundation of the [theater] are now underway,” Palmer continued. The one-story Alan Harvey Theater with distinctive architecture matching the rest of the campus was demolished in April of 2019 and now a nearly finished massive three-story classroom building stands in its place. Scaffolding on the classroom building will be removed in the coming weeks as Overaa finishes working on the stucco exterior. “The [new] building will include a new Alan Harvey Theater, a green room and dressing rooms, space for a classroom and small [black box] theater, and a conference room,” Palmer continued. articles.text: Our library, like all other offices and stores, is closed as a precaution to help limit the spread of coronavirus (COVID-19). During this period all due dates are extended and you do not need to return materials until Oakland Public Library is back in full operation. The library is closed, but there are lots of continuing library services. If you have internet you can access electronic books, audio books, periodicals, music and movies from home. It’s easy! Need a library card? You can complete an online application to set up your account at: https://www.oaklandlibrary.org/ using-library/library-cards. To see everything that is available, go to https://www.oaklandlibrary.org/online-resources/e-books-and-digital-content. Follow the instructions to download Google Play or the App Store and sign in with your library card number and pin. You can watch movies and TV online with Kanopy, more movies and audio books with Hoopla, even learn a new language with Pronnunciator. Screen-free activities for family fun Sheltering in place while working from home with kids out of school can lead to a lot of screen time. When you’re ready to cut down on the screens for a bit, visit this site for recommended activities: https://oaklandlibrary.org/blogs/childrens-services/ screen-free-activities-family-fun Tutor.com – Live homework help The library can provide one-on-one homework help for students – and parents. Oakland Public Library is happy to provide access to Tutor. com, a trusted resource for students and adult learners that offers live and FREE one-on-one tutoring, homework help and test preparation for students in Kindergarten through 12th grade in a variety of subjects. Live Spanish-speaking support is also available for math, science, and social studies subjects. Live one-on-one assistance is available every day from 12 noon to midnight: https://oaklandlibrary.org/blogs/childrens-services/tutorcom Effective March 16, the Oakland Public Library closed all Library locations to help limit the spread of coronavirus (COVID-19). These closures will remain in effect until further notice. All programs are canceled while our library is closed.

articles.text: Kimberly Bonacum, an Occupational Therapist, has worked in Piedmont schools for 16 years. In that time, she has worked with a wide range of students, including a number of them who fidget due to being hyperactive. To help them, she has designed and is now producing a wearable “fidget” spinner wristband that is mindful of the learning environment. It helps keep their attention during school. The product was released in March. Her company, called Mindful Fidget, has created an adaptation of the popular fidget spinner but is smaller, quieter and less likely to be misplaced because it’s attached to the wrist. “It’s great for overall calmThe Mindful Fidget has tactile bumps on its edges and a quick release to easily swap out wristbands. ing of anxiety and for overall self-regulation. It helps to get students in just the right state to learn,” explained Bonacum. She works as an OT with Piedmont students at all grade levels. OTs are sometimes asked to assist in curriculum development for handwriting and social skills, or recommend modifications to classroom environments or assignments that help all students participate. Former Havens 4th grade teacher Catherine Knowland, a Piedmont resident, sees a need for products to improve the focus of students. “The ability of students to focus has gotten worse over time. When I first started teaching in the 80s, there might have been six students in a class that needed some sort of distraction or fidget. Into the 90s with the invention of the computer and video games their attention spans got worse. Nearly all of them needed to be entertained with a hands-on item to manipulate.” The large, and loud handheld fidget spinner had an explosion of popularity in 2017. Students began to use them as toys and had competitions with each other. This became a distraction in class and eventually most schools had to ban them. Bonacum’s design is focused on being school friendly. She picked a bearing that is quiet and does not spin for too long, requiring active participation. Bonacum sees applications for patterns. adults as well. out.”
articles.title: Piedmont resident designs watch spinner for fidgeters

Oakland Public Library announces 5 branches for sidewalk pickup Residents with Oakland Library cards may now pick up holds reserved online for books, DVDs, and CDs. You can also reserve a WiFi hotspot at the library doors. Indoor areas remain closed to the public. It’s easy! Here’s how it works: Search for Books, DVDs, and CDs at oaklandlibrary.org. Use the “request it” button to place items on hold. You’ll need your library card number and PIN. Select the branch library most convenient for you. If you already have items on hold, log in to your account and select an open location to send your hold. Branch Pickup When you are notified that your items are ready, come to the selected branch between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. You will receive an email, text, or phone notification when your hold is available for pickup. Please note: Wait times for holds may be longer than usual. If you have multiple items on hold, you will get a separate notification for each one. You have 14 days after you get the notification to pick up your item. You’ll need to have your library card number with you. Be mindful of the ongoing health crisis. Wear a face covering and observe social distancing. Keep 6 feet apart from other patrons in line. Sidewalk Pickup Star ting now, sidewalk pickup of books will be available locally at the Main Library and Rockridge Branch Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Summer Reading Programs to begin Readers of all ages can now register to participate in our annual Summer Reading program. You’ll be able to qualify to win prizes at the end of the program by completing your reading log, participating in the online programs, and getting involved in your community. Register for Summer Reading by visiting www.oaklandlibrary.org/ summer. Complete information is at https://oaklandlibrary.org/. For questions, please call 510-238- 3134 or email eanswers@oaklandlibrary.org. articles.text: Nick Millosovich stepped in as Piedmont’s Public Works Department Supervisor of Maintenance on April 1, six months after former Supervisor Dave Frankel retired after a 30-year career. Millosovich held the role of interim supervisor for a sixmonth period before his contract with the city was formally approved. He has worked with the city for 13 years, since 2007, the year of the city’s Centennial. Millosovich will work under the direction of Chester Nakahara, Director of the Public Works Department. “Public Works is very pleased with the appointment of Nick as our Public Works Supervisor. In his 13 years with the city, he has proven to be a caring leader with a high level of technical skills, and is a great ambassador for the department and the City of Piedmont. Going forward, I think the city is in good hands with Nick,” Nakahara said. Prior to taking on the role of Public Work Supervisor, Millosovich worked with Diamond Tree Service for approximately 16 years. Diamond Tree Service offers brush chipping, land clearing, stump removal, insect management, and cabling and bracing. Millosovich is a certified arborist with experience working in the professional tree care industry. He began working with Diamond Tree Service after the 1991 firestorm in the Oakland hills. The blaze, which raged for three days, destroyed more than 3,000 homes and burned 1,520 acres. “On my first day, I walked in wearing nice blue jeans. They told me to take this cable, wrap it around this log that was burned. When I got up, I was pitch black, covered in soot,” he said. The work that summer was taxing, but Millosovich said that he “had the best office in the world” looking over the hills. His work with Diamond Tree Service served as a catalyst for his decade-long tenure with the city, with whom Diamond Tree owner Kent Donaghy has done contract work for decades. The transition to working with the city’s Public Works Department was seamless. Piedmont’s public works department is responsible for oversight of all functions relating to infrastructure systems; this include sanitary and storm sewers, coordination of utility company systems, street maintenance and improvement, sidewalks, street lighting, parks maintenance, street trees, and more. Millosovich explained the priorities within the department had been handed down to him from Dave Frankel, who retired on October 1 last year after more than 30 years on the job. “Nick has worked with the city for 13 years, so he really knows his stuff,” said Frankel. “Nick has the best demeanor; he never gets rattled. It’s important [in that position] because there are a lot of demands. He knows what’s important and how to deal with the emergencies we have.” “Our guys have an incredible Former Piedmont City Administrator Paul Benoit, who had worked with Millosovich closely before Benoit retired one year ago, praised him for his knowledge of the city’s infrastructure. “Nick is a long-time Public Works employee,” said Benoit. “What always impressed me about Nick was his quiet and steady manner, as well as his confidence and competence. To do that job well you have to have a deep understanding of Piedmont’s assets and infrastructure and you need to have a strong commitment to public service. Nick has those qualities.” “The irrepressible Dave Frankel is hard to replace, but Nick is fully up to the task,” Benoit said. When Millosovich formally took over the position, the city had just declared a state of emergency and implemented shelterin-place regulations due to the coronavirus. . “With our veteran crew, it’s been pretty simple, because they know exactly what needs to be done,” said Millosovich, adding that three members of his street department have each worked for the city for 30 years or longer. Marilyn Weber, Chair of the Piedmont Turkey Trot, the city’s second largest event after the 4th of July Parade, worked alongside Millosovich before he took on the title of supervisor. “Nick is such a kind, thoughtful and generous person,” she said. “I have had the pleasure of working with him as both a community member and as a volunteer on several community events and every interaction with Nick exceeds all expectations. He is a consummate professional and is very adept at dealing with many different circumstances. “The City of Piedmont is fortunate to have Nick leading the team,” Weber stated. Staff photo Nick Millosovich, Piedmont’s new Public Works Superintendent. capacity to do a lot of things. It’s a great team,” Frankel added with a strong sense of pride. One of the primary responsibilities as Supervisor will be to check sewer lines regularly through the year using a closed circuit television (CCTV) van. Millosovich and his crewmembers check for broken pipes, conduct spot repairs, and check storm drain lines. As testament to the work they do, Piedmont is the only city in a group of eight Bay Area cities that was not fined by the EPA for sewage leaking into the San Francisco Bay. But there is still work to be done. Once finished, about 85 percent of the city’s pipe system will be brand new. The public works department has still identified “problematic spots” throughout the city. “The bad pipes we have are still bad pipes, and we have a list of problematic spots throughout the city. We visit them at least once a year, and the ones along our creek lines are checked at least twice a year,” said Millosovich. articles.text: Chabot Space and Science Center Online Talks and Sky Viewings Fri, July 3 8-9 p.m. - Moon Mash-Up Sat, July 4 9:45-11:00 p.m.- Telescope Viewing Be a part of Chabot Space and Science Center’s exciting online lineup. Friday, join astronomers as they talk about the moon, show off moon rocks and take peaks at our closest neighbor in the sky with Chabot’s telescopes. Saturday, cap off your Fourth of July with a look into the sky and the expanses of the universe. Witness the splendor of the cosmos through Chabot’s most powerful telescope, Nellie. The videos stream on their facebook page. Piedmont’s July 4 Decorating Contest. Celebrating in Place – House & Car Decorating Contest This Fourth of July there won’t be a parade on Highland, but you can make your own showcase at home as many other residents are. Get the kids involved with decorations, chalk drawings, and fun pageantry. Kids should jump at the opportunity to decorate their homes with patriotic items or as a replica of a favorite vacation spot. To be in the running to win one of the five awards presented by the fourth of July Committee, see the entry form in today’s Post. McLaughlin Shoreline State Park State Park With the opening of state parks, you can now take the kids to the East Bay shoreline of McLaughlin Eastshore State Park. The park spans 8.5 miles along the East Bay shoreline from the Bay Bridge to Richmond. The 1,833 acres of beach and tidelands offer unique views of the bay from walking and bike trails. It starts at 40th Street in Oakland and continues past Golden Gate Fields all the way to Point Isabelle and the Richmond Marina. California Academy of Sciences Online Resources The California Academy of Sciences in Golden Gate Park has a robust selection of online resources for kids (and adults). Meet marine biologists, astronomers and naturalists to inspire a healthy interest in science. Take virtual dives in the kelp forest, learn how to identify birds in the wild and see how to create your own compost bin. Cal Academy of Sciences has tons of videos and instructions for activities and projects. More Info: Chabot Space and Science Center, Oakland www.facebook.com/ChabotSpace Piedmont’s July 4 Home and Car Decorating contest Email carlabetts@hotmail.com for competition consideration McLaughlin Eastshore State Park www.ebparks.org/parks/eastshore California Academy of Science Golden Gate Park, San Francisco https://www.calacademy.org/blogs/landing/educator-news

Report of a smashed dashboard on a BMW. 2:08 p.m. El Cerrito Ave. Report of 3 kids jumping fence with “Do Not Climb” sign onto Witter Field. Officer escorts them out. 4:20 p.m. Alta Ave. Auto Burglary. Report of theft of car registration. Owner has video of suspect in White Dodge Charger. 10:31 p.m. Magnolia Ave. Report that tree limb is blocking Magnolia. Officer moves it off roadway. Public Works notified. Saturday, June 20 8:22 a.m. Grand Ave. Residential Theft. Report of a man entering through garage door, stealing items and driving off. Extent of loss unknown. 9:26 a.m. Dracena Ave. White road bike found near second set of stairs in Dracena Park. 12:24 p.m. Grand Ave. Report of a man aggressively panhandling & jumping in front of cars. Pictured is Tottenham Hotspurs’ Dele Alli with his first raised. The catalyst clearly is midfielder Paul Pogba. The World Cup champion from France has only made 10 appearances this season due to injury but has already made a dynamic pair with The Red Devils’ recent addition, fellow midfielder Bruno Fernandes. The two created a goal in Tuesday’s 3-0 win over Brighton after Pogba dished a quick ball to Fernandes, while adding the attacking combination of strikers Anthony Martial and Marcus Rashford may create the most dynamic offense in the league. Another team to keep an eye on is the Wolverhampton Wanderes in 6th place with 52 points. Also a club considered over-performing, they have big matches with Arsenal and Chelsea to close the year. Chelsea, in 4th with 54 points, could already be the most improved team after agreeing to transfers with Bundesliga star Timo Werner and Netherland’s Ajax midfielder Hakim Ziyech. Additionally, the Blues have American superstar Christian Pulisic, who scored the game winner in their 2-1 win on Man City. Champions League This year’s UEFA Champions League will continue on August 7 with the second leg of the round of 16. Last year’s champ, Liverpool, was already bounced out by Atletic Madrid by 4-2 on aggregate. La Liga The Spanish league’s table, predictably, is coming down to Real Madrid in first with 71 points and Barcelona in second with 70. In third is Atelico Madrid with 59 points and six match days remaining. Should all go as expected, both Real Madrid and Barca will win out their remaining matches, giving Real this year’s table. Serie A Italy’s Serie A is a bit more intriguing. Nine match days remain. with Cristiano Ronaldo and Paulo Dybala’s Juventus club holding first with 72 points, ahead of Lazio’s 68 and Inter Milan’s 61. At this rate, it would be a shock if anyone but Juve’s star-studded cast wins the league championship. Juventus’ and Lazio’s match on July 20 will should ultimately determine the final order. articles.text: Golfer Henry Lambert (right), PHS Class of 2021, is charging through an aggressive schedule on the Nor-Cal junior tournament circuit this summer. Henry Lambert never got a chance to show what he can do. A junior and the leader of the Piedmont High School golf team this spring, his season was cut short due to the coronavirus. He was able to complete only one round of golf But deprived of interscholastic sports, Lambert isn’t taking any days off. He is competing in two different golf competitions this summer – the Junior Tour of Northern California and the Junior Golf Association of Northern California He is currently competing in the Johnny Miller Junior Championship at Napa’s Silverado Resort and is set to compete again on July 6 at the GANC/NCGA NorCal Players Championship at the legendary Pebble Beach. “I am competing in a bunch of tournaments this summer. I’m currently in Napa at the same place the PGA hosts the Safeway Open,” confirmed Lambert. “I’m just staying sharp; working on my short-game and hitting the ball straighter and controlling the curve of my shots,” he added. Before the COVID shutdown, Lambert shot one-under in their tri-match with San Leandro, Alameda, and Bishop O’Dowd. It was Piedmont High’s only match last spring. He has appeared in four tourneys this month, including two rounds of 75 at PGA course Cherry Island on June 23-24, then turned around to play in the June 25-26 Mountain View Jr. Championship at the Shoreline Golf Links, with rounds of 74 and 75. “I feel like I’ve been playing some of my best golf within the last couple of weeks. I think my best rounds are ahead of me,” added Lambert. Lambert, a team captain as a junior, earned an All-League selection as a sophomore. Entering his senior year, Lambert feels he has more control of his swing. “When I was younger, my swing at times would come from behind my body, which would force my ball to sway from the right to a hard left. Over the years, I’ve worked at coming at the ball straighter; it’s creating a straighter shot, “said Lambert. Soon to be a senior, Lambert will head to each of the courses around the Bay Area with added knowledge after playing most of them several times. “With how I’m playing lately, it feels that my experience on each course will help a lot.” Lambert heads into his senior year alongside classmate Nate Wilson, another four-year starter on the golf team. Players are back on the pitch in Europe with the winding down of the Premier League, Bundesliga, La Liga, and Serie A seasons. All are back in action after each soccer league was halted due to COVID-19’s global impact. The German Bundesliga was the first of the EU super leagues to return, starting action on May 17. Bayern Munich won its eighth consecutive league title. But when it comes to European soccer, perhaps no other league has more attention from Americans than England’s Premier League. As an American football writer, watching how the Premier League handles civil rights situations compared to the NFL is eye-opening. In stark contrast to American politics and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell’s stance on Colin Kaepernick prior to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Movement, the Premier League in unison has all players, coaches, and officials kneel in solidarity. Premier League also inscribed all players jersey’s with “Black Lives Matter” instead of player names through the first week of play, as did the women’s professional soccer league in the U.S. Since the start of Kaepernick’s civil rights campaign in 2016, the NFL and its fans were at odds on how to handle players kneeling during the National Anthem. Now, with the strength and broad support of Back Lives Matter, Goodell admitted his failure on handling player protests. Back to the UK. Liverpool officially won its first title since 1990 with some help from Chelsea beating Manchester City 2-1 on June 25. The Reds accomplished the quickest Premier League championship in history. But when it comes to Champions League qualification, the pack remains crowded, especially considering the possible two-year ban of Man City after allegedly mismanaging player funds. If City’s ban is upheld, it will enable the fifth-ranked team in the Premier League table to qualify for Champions League and the sixthranked team to Europa League instead of the usual top-four to UCL and fifth to UEL. Just seven match days remain for the Premier League to determine the final standings with 12 points separating Leicester City in 3rd and Arsenal in 10th. When predicting the final outcome, Leicester is a team that could certainly move down. Already considered a team over performing, the Foxes have tough games with teams well above their payroll like Arsenal on July 7, Tottenham on July 18, and close the season on July 26 against Manchester United – arguably the best team in the league right now. United hasn’t lost a match in 16 appearances dating back to January 19 with a 2-0 loss to Liverpool. Since the return, they drew 1-1 with Tottenham, manhandled Sheffield United 3-0, Norwich 2-1, and Brighton 3-0 on Tuesday, June 30.

Bayern Munich won its eighth consecutive league title. But when it comes to European soccer, perhaps no other league has more attention from Americans than England’s Premier League. As an American football writer, watching how the Premier League handles civil rights situations compared to the NFL is eye-opening. In stark contrast to American politics and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell’s stance on Colin Kaepernick prior to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Movement, the Premier League in unison has all players, coaches, and officials kneel in solidarity. Premier League also inscribed all players jersey’s with “Black Lives Matter” instead of player names through the first week of play, as did the women’s professional soccer league in the U.S. Since the start of Kaepernick’s civil rights campaign in 2016, the NFL and its fans were at odds on how to handle players kneeling during the National Anthem. Now, with the strength and broad support of Back Lives Matter, Goodell admitted his failure on handling player protests. Back to the UK. Liverpool officially won its first title since 1990 with some help from Chelsea beating Manchester City 2-1 on June 25. The Reds accomplished the quickest Premier League championship in history. But when it comes to Champions League qualification, the pack remains crowded, especially considering the possible two-year ban of Man City after allegedly mismanaging player funds. If City’s ban is upheld, it will enable the fifth-ranked team in the Premier League table to qualify for Champions League and the sixthranked team to Europa League instead of the usual top-four to UCL and fifth to UEL. Just seven match days remain for the Premier League to determine the final standings with 12 points separating Leicester City in 3rd and Arsenal in 10th. When predicting the final outcome, Leicester is a team that could certainly move down. Already considered a team over performing, the Foxes have tough games with teams well above their payroll like Arsenal on July 7, Tottenham on July 18, and close the season on July 26 against Manchester United – arguably the best team in the league right now. United hasn’t lost a match in 16 appearances dating back to January 19 with a 2-0 loss to Liverpool. Since the return, they drew 1-1 with Tottenham, manhandled Sheffield United 3-0, Norwich 2-1, and Brighton 3-0 on Tuesday, June 30. European soccer is back with Premier League on the forefront Photos courtesy of TottenhamHotspur.com The Premier League has had all players, coaches, and officials kneel in solidarity with the Black Lives Matter Movement. Pictured is Tottenham Hotspurs’ Dele Alli with his first raised. The catalyst clearly is midfielder Paul Pogba. The World Cup champion from France has only made 10 appearances this season due to injury but has already made a dynamic pair with The Red Devils’ recent addition, fellow midfielder Bruno Fernandes. The two created a goal in Tuesday’s 3-0 win over Brighton after Pogba dished a quick ball to Fernandes, while adding the attacking combination of strikers Anthony Martial and Marcus Rashford may create the most dynamic offense in the league. Another team to keep an eye on is the Wolverhampton Wanderes in 6th place with 52 points. Also a club considered over-performing, they have big matches with Arsenal and Chelsea to close the year. Chelsea, in 4th with 54 points, could already be the most improved team after agreeing to transfers with Bundesliga star Timo Werner and Netherland’s Ajax midfielder Hakim Ziyech. Additionally, the Blues have American superstar Christian Pulisic, who scored the game winner in their 2-1 win on Man City. Champions League This year’s UEFA Champions League will continue on August 7 with the second leg of the round of 16. Last year’s champ, Liverpool, was already bounced out by Atletic Madrid by 4-2 on aggregate. La Liga The Spanish league’s table, predictably, is coming down to Real Madrid in first with 71 points and Barcelona in second with 70. In third is Atelico Madrid with 59 points and six match days remaining. Should all go as expected, both Real Madrid and Barca will win out their remaining matches, giving Real this year’s table. Serie A Italy’s Serie A is a bit more intriguing. Nine match days remain. with Cristiano Ronaldo and Paulo Dybala’s Juventus club holding first with 72 points, ahead of Lazio’s 68 and Inter Milan’s 61. At this rate, it would be a shock if anyone but Juve’s star-studded cast wins the league championship. Juventus’ and Lazio’s match on July 20 will should ultimately determine the final order. Photo courtesy of Liverpoolfc.com Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp and The Reds captured the quickest Premier League title in history. Photo courtesy of ManUtd.com Paul Pogba (right) and Anthony Martial (left) have provided Manchester United with a dynamic attack since the return of play.

articles.text: Bryce Chu was named the North Coast Section’s Most Valuable Player after posting an 0.93 ERA and 18 strikeouts in the postseason. Pitcher Jordan Remer set a Piedmont High single-season record for strikeouts in 2008 with 102. This week, we look back at the Piedmont’s only North Coast Section champion baseball team back in 2008. It was the spring of 2008 the Boston Celtics beat the Los Angeles Lakers in six games, and Barack Obama was gearing up for his presidential run in the Democratic Primaries. But it was the Piedmont baseball that came out of nowhere to win the school’s only North Coast Section championship – then and now. The team didn’t win the league championship and was seeded No. 7 in the NCS post-season playoffs. They pulled off upset victories one after the other, eventually beating No. 1 Northgate in a game played at the Oakland Coliseum. “The Highlanders dogpiled in the infield. They pointed to the fans and family in the stands. Jordan Remer sat down on the grass with his head in his hands, overwhelmed by what the Highlanders just accomplished,” wrote the Post sportswriter Benjamin Bombard after the game. . To win the game, Piedmont tallied on two runs in each of the fourth, fifth, and sixth innings. Northgate piled on five runs in the fifth to take a 5-4 advantage, but Jeremy George, the underweight football quarterback that led the football and soccer teams to successful seasons, smacked a clutch two-run double over the head of the center fielder to take the lead in the sixth inning and win the game. George, PHS Class of 2009, was a three-sport star in high school, and opted to not play sports at UC San Diego. He was elected to the PHS Sports’ Hall of Fame in February 2020. Under first-year manager John Nelson, the Highlanders went 20-7-1 and finished second to St. Mary’s in the Bay Shore AthPhoto by Ken deCrosta letic League. Given a #7 seed, they began a series of dramatic post-season upsets, first defeating No. 2 St. Mary’s in the quarterfinals, then completely dominating No. 3 Campolindo in the semis, 13-7. Nelson was the school’s first coach after Mike Humphries retired after coaching baseball for roughly 30 years. Nelson left PHS following the 2009 season and became St. Mary’s head coach from 2011 to 2013. He closed his career there with a 7-6 win over Eric Olson’s Highlanders, which marked Olson’s first year at the school. Between Nelson’s departure and Olson’s arrival, PHS went 10-14 and 6-16 under Josh Muldau, then went 18-10 under Brent Weisbrod until losing to Nelson’s Panthers in the NCS quarterfinals. Olson has been at the helm for Piedmont ever since, making two NCS Finals appearances – his second was a 5-4 loss to Redwood Christian in 2018. Pied mont’s 2008 team received five All-League selections in the BSAL, including pitcher Bryce Chu receiving firstteam honors and NCS Most Valuable Player honors. Chu posted a 0.93 ERA throughout the NCS playoffs and struck out 18 batters. He was the closing pitcher in PHS’ 6-5 win over Northgate. Chu smacked a home run to centerfield in the NCS Semis and went 6-3 as a starting pitcher with 65 strikeouts. Remer was another firstteam selection and still holds the school’s single-season strikeout record with 102. Alexander Menke was another first-team selection with a 3.49 average, 22 hits, 26 runs, and two home runs. Piedmont first-year baseball John Nelson took the Highlanders to the school’s only NCS Title in 2008. He coached only two years in Piedmont. Ryan Patte and Kyle Bonacum were honorable mentions. Patte, the first baseman played the season without any errors, and Bonacum. the right fielder, finished with 16 hits.
articles.title: 2008: PHS baseball team’s only NCS Championship
