14 Wednesday, July 1, 2020 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 13th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. Tennis player Angela Huang, PHS Class of 2019, completed her abbreviated freshman season at Washington University in St. Louis. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out alone. In the past I would work out with my trainer in Berkeley. Our athletic trainer from school helps us from afar. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Something I am proud of is that I was able to play in the lineup in college as a freshman for both singles and doubles. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Balancing sports in college is definitely not an easy thing to do, but it provides you with a unique experience many others don’t get to have. ANGELA HUANG Tennis CAMILLE CREIGHTON Softball What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main fitness goal for this summer is to maintain the strength and endurance that I had in my freshman season. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development through the tracking of weights, sets, and endurance for cardio exercises. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am working out on my own, but our trainer has developed the workouts for us from home. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone has been my ability to replicate squat and bench press weights with household objects, i.e. backpacks filled with textbooks. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? My advice: Don’t let COVID- 19 discourage you from staying active! Workouts come in many shapes and forms, and in these difficult times, it’s important to remember that hiking our local trails is just as beneficial as lifting in a gym. Piedmont High Class of 2019 Washington U. of St. Louis Class of 2023 Angela Huang had her freshman year at Washington University in St. Louis cut short after appearing in seven matches, after competing at No. 2 and 3 singles, while also playing No. 1 doubles alongside captain Ally Persky. Huang graduated from Piedmont High in 2019 after finishing her career as only the school’s second player to win back to back North Coast Section championships. She won the singles title in both Div. 1 and Div. 2, duplicating the feat of Kaelli Thiel in 2014-2015. She helped PHS complete its 20th consecutive undefeated League Championship, it was the final year of the school’s state record winning streak. In the Division 1 individual tournament, Huang won all four of her matches in straight sets after entering the brackets as an unseeded entrant. She made quick work of Camilla TarpeySchwed of Tamalpais in the finals, 6-1, 6-2. What is your workout program this summer? Our athletic trainer has given us weekly workouts to complete at home. They are of similar structure to the ones we do at school, but we are allowed to update it to adjust from working out at home. These workouts include body weight exercises and also weight-training routines. What are your fitness goals for this summer? To just stay in my best shape so that I’m ready to compete again in the fall, hopefully. Between stay-at-home orders, internships, and classes, it’s become even more important to keep tennis a top priority. How are you measuring your development? Each week we meet with our trainer online and discuss our workouts. A lot of our workouts include increasing intensity and weight, so that is how we can measure our progress. Piedmont High Class of 2019 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2023 Camille Creighton finished her freshman softball season at Pomona-Pitzer after appearing in two of the 11 games before the COVID shutdown. She graduated from Piedmont High in 2019 after starting on varsity all four years and took over at shortstop as a senior. Creighton was a three-time firstteam All-League selection and also received a second-team selection as a senior. Creighton helped win back-toback undefeated league championships in 2017 and 2018, which got the program promoted to the WACC’s upper Foothill Division in 2019. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program this summer is run through the app Teambuildr. Our workouts rotate between body weight circuits and cardio exercises. CAL BARNA Baseball & Football Cal Barna prepares for his senior campaign at Piedmont High as a twosport athlete in baseball and football. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goals include gaining 10-15 pounds to increase my strength tremendously, and being able to settle myself and truly focus when pitching. How are you measuring your development? I have metrics in certain lifts or workouts. Progress from the start to the end of the summer is based on how these numbers improve. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? With friends for lifting, a coach for pitching, and teammates for football. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Pitching 91 mph consistently, benching 230 pounds for film purposes, and throwing a baseball 365 feet. Prior to the COVID shutdown I could complete 12 pull ups; now, I am currently at 40. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Work harder than what you initially think is necessary. Don’t worry about your peers or feel pressure from what they are doing. Instead, truly examine what you want to accomplish, how badly you want it, then sacrifice everything to stay on your path. Camille Creighton, PHS Class of 2019, recently finished her freshman season on Pitzer’s softball program. Piedmont High Class of 2021 Cal Barna is the starting quarterback for the football team and also plays catcher, pitcher, and utility fielder for the baseball team. On the gridiron, Barna is known for his ability to air out deep passes with good velocity. One of his most productive games was a 235-yard performance on 11 completions against San Leandro. In baseball, Barna earned a key role as a sophomore as a catcher and pitcher. He racked up nine hits with five RBIs as a sophomore, to go along with one save and five strikeouts as a relief pitcher. Prior to his junior season being cut off, Barna was off to a hot start with .357 average with five hits and three RBIs, including a double and triple. On the mound, Barna had two strikeouts in one inning of work. Barna describes that he’s been in contact with baseball recruiters from Hawaii, Northwestern, and Duke. He’s hopeful to gain consideration from the Alabama Crimson Tide, his dream school. What is your workout program this summer? I am lifting with friends and teammates six-times per week starting at 8 a.m. Five nights a week, I complete a home workouts on my own. With limited weights and time, it’s easier to incorporate both. Baseball occurs five times a week. Football practices still happen without coach involvement.

Goatherd Martin Matarrese and Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black provided a “goat talk” for kids and interested residents on June 30. Residents gather to view the goats as they remove brush and weeds in Blair Park. The goats are most active in the early morning. You can visit all of them virtually as we continue to shelter in place. also spurred a debate amongst the art world: many scholars called for museums throughout Europe to return thousands of artifacts looted from Africa during the colonial period. You can learn more about the museum’s history by watching CGTN Africa’s introductory video at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=Eri0OMwG-es Museum of Black Civilizations, Dakar, Senegal The Museum of Black Civilizations, inaugurated in 2018, acts as a creative hub for Senegal as well as the entire African continent. The museum both celebrates African cultures while detailing the struggle their people have faced throughout history. The museum was the vision of Senegal’s first president, Leopold Sedar Senghor, who vowed to build an institution honoring African art and identity. The Museum of Black Civilizations now holds one of the largest collections of artifacts on the continent. While Senghor passed before the museum’s opening, his legacy lives on in the curated art selections and striking displays that fill its galleries. The opening of the museum Museum of the Royal Tombs of Sipan, Chiclayo, Peru The Museum of the Royal Tombs of Sipan was built to honor and display what has been considered one of the most important archaeological discoveries in South America. Guests can view lavish jewels, regal vessels, and other stunning artifacts of Peru’s ancient community. The museum, which was officially inaugurated in 2002, contains most of the important artifacts found at Huaca Rajada by archeologist Walter Alva in 1987, including relics of Lord of Sipan and his entourage. The architecture of the museum was designed to resemble the ancient Moche tombs. Museum of the Royal Tombs of Sipan in Chiclayo, Peru. GET UP TO

articles.text: The total number of Botanical Gardens in the United States is more than 1,000 – ranging from small botanic spaces to large arboretums. There are approximately 40,000 different species of flower and fauna in these gardens. Here’s a look at some lesser known, but incredibly unique, botanical gardens throughout the country that are well worth a visit. Cheyenne Botanical Gardens, Cheyenne, Wyoming The Cheyenne Botanical Gardens are located in Lions Park in Cheyenne, with an associated High Plains Arboretum five miles from town. The gardens began as a vision in 1977 to build a nonprofit, solar heated greenhouse. Today, the 6,800 square foot conservatory consists of three greenhouses. The first is filled with tropical plants, herb and cacti gardens and a waterfall pond filled with Koi fish. The second is primarily used for growing vegetables, and the third is focused on propagation of bedding plants and flowers for the botanic garden grounds and all flowers for the Cheyenne park system. Outside are many gardens featuring flowers and cacti. Visit https://www.botanic.org/ for more information. Crapo Park and Gardens, Burlington, Iowa The 85-acre Crapo Park in Iowa contains an arboretum and botanical garden next to the Mississippi River. The park’s arboretum contains more than 200 varieties of trees and shrubs, as well as botanical gardens of annuals and perennials. As of 2003, the following trees were on Iowa’s statewide “Big Tree” list: Arizona Cypress, Black Hickory, Pawpaw, and Black Walnut. The park and its gardens were added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976. Crapo Park is also reputed to be the site where the American flag was first raised on Iowa’s soil, by Zebulon Pike in 1805. For more information on the park and its gardens, visit https:// www.burlingtoniowa.org/2328/ Crapo-Park. Sayen Park Botanical Garden, Hamilton Township, New Jersey Sayen Park Botanical Garden is a 30-acre municipal park that is open year-round from dawn to dusk without charge. Park activity is at its peak in the spring. The park was opened to the public in 1991, and was expanded in 2003. It is home to more than 1,000 azaleas, 500 rhododendrons, and more than 250,000 flowering bulbs for spring display. There are also ponds, bridges, gazebos, and walking trails. You can learn more about Sayen Park and its gardens at http://www.hamiltonnj.com/ SAYENGARDENS. Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens, Boothbay, Maine The Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay opened in 2007 and invites visitors of all ages to create and explore meaningful connections to plants and nature at their own pace. The gardens have been named one of Maine’s top attractions. Its gardens and landscape include nearly a mile of tidewater shoreline, which provides unique soil and climate for a wide range of plants native to the New England coast. It is the largest botanical garden in New England, comprising 295 acres, 17 of which are gardens featuring native plants of Maine. Yearly, the gardens are visited by an average of 200,000 guests. Alaska Botanical Garden, Anchorage, Alaska The Alaska Botanical Garden, the largest in the state, is an independent non-profit organization which opened in 1993. Its mission is to enhance the beauty and value of plant material through education, preservation, recreation and research. The garden’s land consists mainly of spruce and birch forest. It features eight developed demonstration gardens and a special location for junior master gardeners. The gardens include over 1,100 species of perennials, more than 150 that are native to Alaska. It also includes an herb garden, a rock garden, and a wildflower walk. To learn more about the garden, visit http://www.alaskabg.org/. Tulips at the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens .

articles.text: The Guardians is John Grisham’s 40th novel. In most, he focuses on some aspect of legal practice and he always educates the reader about both the necessary legal procedures and the many ways that practitioners elude or obscure the intent of the law. Here Grisham writes about a lawyer who seeks release for prisoners who have been wrongly convicted. The subject is close to Grisham’s heart because he has served on the Board of the Innocence Project, which seeks to reverse the convictions of innocent inmates. In the novel, the characters speculate that this happens in about 10% of cases, which means that there may be thousands of innocent people in prison today. Grisham is a master of characterization, plot, narrative and dialogue. Here he introduces Cullen Post, a sweet and caring man who is both a lawyer and, after a nervous breakdown, an Episcopal priest. Post is building a legal case to introduce new evidence that will lead to the release of a Black man named Quincy Miller who was framed for the murder of a Florida lawyer. The story wanders through a collection of interesting individuals – Southern lawyers who drink too much, weak prison guards who have been corrupted by dangerous criminals, forthright women in power, and angry officials who don’t want to admit they are wrong. All are well described but none are so overwhelmingly evil that they are unbelievable. This novel does not have the astonishing turns of plot found in Grisham’s early novels such as The Firm, but it is a well-constructed, engaging narrative with characters that one might like to know. It is also a painless and detailed way to learn about the way the legal system malfunctions for many people. Ann McCauley studied Anthropology at Cal and works in international health. She loves stories with sympathetic, wise characters who engage in humorous conversations and travel to exotic places.
articles.title: What if the courts convict an innocent person?

articles.text: The Gold Cost Chamber Players practicing at Reve Bistro in Lafayette for their concert on June 28. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, and shelter-in-place guidelines that have come with it, the Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players is offering “Immersive Experience” packages that allow patrons to enjoy concerts at home with some extra perks. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Life is fragile, tenuous, each day a gamble. Until it isn’t. The idea that bad things happen to good people is an abstraction. Suddenly what we take for granted – another dawn, and all that follows – can no longer hold our weight, like fragile ice on a winter’s pond. Still Alice is about such a life; it may be more truth than some viewers care to confront in a film. The movie is a tour de force by Julianne Moore. She portrays Dr. Alice Howland, a professor of linguistics at Colombia University, married to John (Alec Baldwin), a research scientist. She is the mother of three lovely children (Kristen Stewart, Kate Bosworth and Hunter Parrish). Accomplished, cherished by her family and colleagues, just 50, she relishes in every way this moment in her life. But ever so gradually she begins to notice small moments when her memory hits a speed bump. What was automatic – a word during a lecture, the destination of a morning run – eludes her. And so begins a cruel and insidious journey, one in which all that she is, all that she has become, begins to abandon her. With John, she visits a neurologist who confirms that she has familial early onset Alzheimer’s disease. It’s a betrayal of her mind that is unexpected and will be, with unyielding certainty, catastrophic. Like a flower in full bloom, every pedal vibrant with life, she begins to close ever so slowly. What is so tragic is that Alice – bright, scholarly, educated, loving – is told in detail what awaits her. The path that stretches before her is detailed, like a photograph of familiar colors and images left out in the sunshine that slowly begins to fade. The irony of the film is its title: Still Alice. From the moment of her diagnosis, when she is told that the disease she has is very rare and also genetic (it’s possible that the gene she inherited came from her father, an alcoholic, and she may have passed it on to her children), Alice is no longer still Alice. She is now that person who struggles to find the courage and grace to face each day, to suffer each moment of forgetfulness, clinging to any remnant of who she was and wishes she still could be. Though this subject matter is not unique (recall The Notebook), what gives Still Alice its deeply human essence is the performance by Moore. She has been nominated for an Oscar as Best Actress. She is remarkable and restrained and finally a broken mirror. The camera lingers on her in tight, intimate shots, her every feature conveying the hope and sheer terror and brief moments of panic and lucidity that are now her life’s experiences. Moore is astonishing. She is just so good. As is the film, which is never gratuitous or purposively maudlin or sentimentalized. Do the filmmakers flinch? Of course. It’s just too hard. Yet when we leave the theater and look around and remember to breathe we know that we have been given one more day. A gift. As well as a thoughtful and moving story to ponder. Still Alice. Starring Julianne Moore, Alec Baldwin and Kristen Stewart. Directed by Richard Glatzer and Wash Westmoreland. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG-13. Originally published by the Post on February 18, 2015. Julianne Moore portrays Dr. Alice Howland who is battling early onset Alzheimer’s disease in Still Alice.

Movie review by Chris Honoré The just released film, Motherless Brooklyn, loosely adapted from the award-winning 1999 novel by Jonathan Lethem, is a wonderfully pulpy noir-mystery gumshoe classic, set in the 1950s, offering a plethora of fine actors and stylishly period atmospherics. This movie is also a passion project by actor-filmmaker-writer Edward Norton who moved what was originally a contemporary story back to the mid-20th century, bringing to mind not only the noir movies of that period, such as Double Indemnity, but also of those later films, such as the iconic Chinatown as well as L.A. Confidential. But Motherless Brooklyn is, at its center, a compelling character study of one Lionel Essrog (Edward Norton) who works for a detective agency owned by Frank Minna (Bruce Willis), a boss and father figure to not only Lionel, but a crew of men who long before were rescued from a Catholic orphanage (Bobby Cannavale, Dallas Roberts, Ethan Suplee). But it’s Lionel who is the most reliable factotum to Frank, though plagued by an unnamed affliction (Tourette’s syndrome comes to mind) that erupts at inappropriate times. His words are a loud sing-song mnemonic stream, accompanied by obsessive-compulsive tics (touching someone three times, ditto with doors). In one scene he describes his mannerisms akin to having an anarchist inhabiting part of his brain, completely detached from his will. However, Lionel is also gifted with near perfect memory, unyielding empathy, and razorsharp intelligence all masked by his twitchy outbursts. The film opens with Lionel and one of his P.I. cohorts offering backup for Frank, who is taking a clandestine meeting with some sketchy types in bulky overcoats and wide-brimmed fedoras. Presuming likely Oscar marPonyo will be available on Anime fans on an international Then again, Totoro never won Ponyo is based loosely on the It is five-year-old Sousuke, ments and gentle terrors that come with childhood. The DVD release is the latest product of the Disney/Ghibli distribution deal. The film has some more-than-proven talent; the enjoyable Tina Fey, Matt Damon, Liam Neeson, Cate Blanchett, Betty White, Lily Tomlin and Cloris Leachman all lent their vocal talents. Although Ponyo has won numerous international accolades, there are some who are quick to emphasize the film’s “lack of social importance” compared to Miyazaki’s other more broadly ecological films. Ponyo resembles Miyazaki’s masterpiece, Totoro, in that the plot is completely secondary to its characters and their experiences. The spectacle of Ponyo, as a little girl, running atop a tsunami wave, or chasing after a speeding car is less important emotionally to the same little girl seeing a plug-in lantern for the first time, basking in its glow and gazing in wonderment. Is Ponyo a masterpiece akin to Totoro? Only time will tell, but it certainly feels similar. It is another slow-moving epic teeming with imagination and innocence. Ponyo is the fourth of Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli features to be released in American theaters in the last 12 years, and his 10th overall. It is refreshing that Miyazaki and company continue to hand-draw their animation cels one at a time in a relatively unrushed pace, thereby not churning their films out like factory products. The fact that Miyazaki still directs, writes, storyboards and key animates his own stuff, and the perpetual rumor of his retirement at the completion of every film makes every film that we get to see a very special experience. Ponyo (also known as Ponyo on the Cliff By the Sea) (2008). Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Featuring the voices of Cate Blanchett, Noah Lindsey Cyrus, Matt Damon, Tina Fey, Frankie Jonas, Cloris Leachman, Liam Neeson, Lily Tomlin and Betty White. Presented by Studio Ghibli & Disney DVD. Originally published in the Post on February 24, 2010. romance begins. When she is rescued by her father, Fujimoto, she rebels against him to be with Sousuke and magically wills herself to become human. When she goes back to Sousuke in now human form, the imbalance in nature causes a tremendous tsunami, flooding the island town. Ponyo’s mother, the sea goddess Granmamare decides to test Sousuke and see if he can truly love her with all of his heart. If he can, Ponyo will become human and nature will return to normal, and if not, she will turn to sea foam. First and foremost Ponyo is a fantasy film. Like many of Miyazaki’s works, it looks as if it takes place in our own reality, but there are utterly fantastic elements at work as well and both combine in a very organic and non-chalant kind of way. In My Neighbor Totoro, there are anxieties, there are boxes to unpack, there are vegetables, but then again there are also forest spirits and magical feline vehicles. In Ponyo, we have an isolated island town with inhabitants who have jobs, have to pick up and drop off their kids, and have to make dinner, but there are also goldfish-children, ocean goddesses and prehistoric fish returning from extinction. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E – Up will delight and entertain audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail breathtaking, and the story a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, square-faced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed. Years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. All that is absent from this touching retrospective is that one, magnificent adventure. Sadly, having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties some 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning he floats away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well-equipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of lift-off. And so the journey begins with the unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. You can’t make this stuff up. Well, actually, in the case of Pixar, you can, and that is exactly what these filmmakers do with unbridled imaginations and an inexhaustible well of stories that captivate and entertain. In Up they even manage to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell. Carl uses a poignant aphorism about how life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). Up. Animated, with voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Written and Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Petersen. Pixar Studios, 2009. Rated PG. Originally published in the Post on June 3, 2009. Pixar’s Up is a movie for all ages.
articles.title: Up an all-time winner from Pixar

Moy Presuming likely Oscar marketing buzz for director Hayao Miyazaki’s and Studio Ghibli’s Ponyo, Disney decided an early March (2008) street date would be the best time for a DVD release. Ponyo will be available on March 2nd, a full five days before the Academy Awards ceremony. Miyazaki and company received an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature in 2004, yet for some misalignment of the universe, Ponyo is not included among the list of nominees for Academy Awards this year. Anime fans on an international scale must be aghast, especially because in many ways Ponyo is Miyazaki’s most subtle film since his seminal My Neighbor Totoro, one of the most revered children’s films in history. Then again, Totoro never won an Oscar either. Ponyo is based loosely on the Hans Christian Andersen tale The Little Mermaid, but within a much more childlike vein. Brunhilda is an adventurous goldfish princess who runs away from her undersea sorceror father one day and is trapped in a bottle. It is five-year-old Sousuke, who lives in a house on the cliff above, who rescues her and names her Ponyo. He pledges to always care for her and a young Ponyo a stunning film by the legendary Miyazaki ments and gentle terrors that come with childhood. The DVD release is the latest product of the Disney/Ghibli distribution deal. The film has some more-than-proven talent; the enjoyable Tina Fey, Matt Damon, Liam Neeson, Cate Blanchett, Betty White, Lily Tomlin and Cloris Leachman all lent their vocal talents. Although Ponyo has won numerous international accolades, there are some who are quick to emphasize the film’s “lack of social importance” compared to Miyazaki’s other more broadly ecological films. Ponyo resembles Miyazaki’s masterpiece, Totoro, in that the plot is completely secondary to its characters and their experiences. The spectacle of Ponyo, as a little girl, running atop a tsunami wave, or chasing after a speeding car is less important emotionally to the same little girl seeing a plug-in lantern for the first time, basking in its glow and gazing in wonderment. Is Ponyo a masterpiece akin to Totoro? Only time will tell, but it certainly feels similar. It is another slow-moving epic teeming with imagination and innocence. Ponyo is the fourth of Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli features to be released in American theaters in the last 12 years, and his 10th overall. It is refreshing that Miyazaki and company continue to hand-draw their animation cels one at a time in a relatively unrushed pace, thereby not churning their films out like factory products. The fact that Miyazaki still directs, writes, storyboards and key animates his own stuff, and the perpetual rumor of his retirement at the completion of every film makes every film that we get to see a very special experience. Ponyo (also known as Ponyo on the Cliff By the Sea) (2008). Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Featuring the voices of Cate Blanchett, Noah Lindsey Cyrus, Matt Damon, Tina Fey, Frankie Jonas, Cloris Leachman, Liam Neeson, Lily Tomlin and Betty White. Presented by Studio Ghibli & Disney DVD. Originally published in the Post on February 24, 2010. romance begins. When she is rescued by her father, Fujimoto, she rebels against him to be with Sousuke and magically wills herself to become human. When she goes back to Sousuke in now human form, the imbalance in nature causes a tremendous tsunami, flooding the island town. Ponyo’s mother, the sea goddess Granmamare decides to test Sousuke and see if he can truly love her with all of his heart. If he can, Ponyo will become human and nature will return to normal, and if not, she will turn to sea foam. First and foremost Ponyo is a fantasy film. Like many of Miyazaki’s works, it looks as if it takes place in our own reality, but there are utterly fantastic elements at work as well and both combine in a very organic and non-chalant kind of way. In My Neighbor Totoro, there are anxieties, there are boxes to unpack, there are vegetables, but then again there are also forest spirits and magical feline vehicles. In Ponyo, we have an isolated island town with inhabitants who have jobs, have to pick up and drop off their kids, and have to make dinner, but there are also goldfish-children, ocean goddesses and prehistoric fish returning from extinction. Ponyo, like all of Miyazaki’s works, resembles a child’s dream. It is filled with all the associated wonderA scene from Pixar’s Up, directed by Piedmont’s own Pete Docter. Up an all-time winner from Pixar Movie review by Chris Honoré Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E – Up will delight and entertain audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail breathtaking, and the story a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, square-faced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed. Years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. All that is absent from this touching retrospective is that one, magnificent adventure. Sadly, having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties some 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning he floats away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well-equipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of lift-off. And so the journey begins with the unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. You can’t make this stuff up. Well, actually, in the case of Pixar, you can, and that is exactly what these filmmakers do with unbridled imaginations and an inexhaustible well of stories that captivate and entertain. In Up they even manage to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell. Carl uses a poignant aphorism about how life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). Up. Animated, with voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Written and Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Petersen. Pixar Studios, 2009. Rated PG. articles.text: Musicians have always led the best of lives. We have friends everywhere. We get to travel and eat good food. After all, as Shakespeare once said: “ If music be the food of love, play on.” In times like these, some inspiration is needed. Let’s sample the good life as exemplified by some famous musicians. Rossini must be mentioned first, because he was the most famous gourmet of all - and a notable gourmand as well. But first we need some music to whet our appetites. The German composer Handel was a noted gourmand. He wrote music for virtually every festive occasion – sailing, fireworks, eating and more. It didn’t matter what the occasion was, Handel wrote for it. On the other hand, history does not include Telemann as a gourmand, but he was more specific when it came to the music. After all, Telemann’s most famous composition is Tafel Musik (music for the banquet). Beginning with breakfast, we would expect some good espresso. Johann Sebastian Bach wrote a miniature opera which is known to us as the “Coffee Cantata”. This is a tongue-in-cheek satire in praise of coffee and the addiction thereof. So, get the espresso ready. Don’t let anyone tell you that Bach was devoid of humor. The hero of this satirical opera is a character named Stick In The Mud. To accompany this good espresso, may I suggest Melba toast. Opera singers have been the inspiration for many famous dishes, and Melba toast was named for the Australian opera singer Nellie Melba. She was always watching her weight, so the noted chef Escoffier invented a twicebaked toast especially for Melba. Strangely, the other dish named for Melba is the extremely rich Peach Melba. Escoffier’s original version is a large portion of vanilla ice cream topped with a lightly poached peach and that topped with sweetened raspberry sauce. Let me offer a less caloric version of Peach Melba. Mix equal amounts of ricotta cheese and cream cheese. Add sugar to taste. Put a half peach on top of your cheese mixture and top it off with some raspberry jam. This is the easy version of Peach Melba, and it is just about as good as the original version. Returning to the great Rossini as gourmet-gourmand, we must select tornadoes of beef a la Rossini. The recipe appeared in one of my previous columns, but it is easy to find on the Internet. When you prepare these tornadoes, be sure to use the very finest fillet of beef available. The original recipe calls for fois gras, but you could substitute pate fois gras if you like. Now, for the main course. Two more opera stars figure in our Gourmet Hall of Fame. Soprano Luisa Tetrazzini takes credit for the dish named for her, Chicken Tetrazzini. Her friend, the immortal Neapolitan tenor A gala dinner in the Parisian home of virtuoso violinist Pablo de Sarasate on Sept. 29, 1907. Sarasate’s house was designed by the artist Janes McNeil Whistler. The guests included the famed female violinist Teresina Tua and composer Enrique Fernandez-Arbos. Enrico Caruso, offers a contribution with Spaghetti a la Caruso. For this one all you need is spaghetti with marinara sauce. Mix in some lightly sautéed chicken livers and you have Chicken a la Caruso. If you don’t like chicken livers, leave them out and enjoy spaghetti marinara. Caruso loved his hometown of Naples, but he refused to sing there. At his operatic debut, the Neapolitans gave him a very cool reception. He said he would go to Naples only to eat spaghetti, but he would never sing for them. Two of the most successful virtuosos were the Spanish violinist Pablo de Sarasate and the Polish pianist Ignatz Jan Paderewski. Both were so successful that they traveled in their own private railroad cars. Paderewski’s was plushly appointed and included a drawing room to play cards and a fully stocked kitchen. Needless to say, butlers were engaged on every trip. A menu from one of Sarasate’s banquets accompanies this article. And now for dessert One of Sarasate’s Spanish dances is a song in praise of chocolate. The Spanish version is hot drinking chocolate thickened with cornstarch. If you wanted, you could encore peach melba or take inspiration from the French pianist-composer Saint-Saens. One of his most brilliant compositions is another satire in music. You can just about taste the whipped cream in this effervescent trifle. It is called “Wedding Cake,” a strange combination for a man who had no interest in women. So…Whether you are a gourmet or a gourmand or just a “grazer”, I leave you with the absolute final thought on the subject of food. The English would call something like this a savory. Noted social critic Weird Al Yankovic said it all in his seminal opus “Eat it” – just eat it. Enjoy. Next week: The contradictions of music and why you should play a musical instrument.
articles.title: Living the good life – musicians and food

articles.text: The view from Alves de Sousa overlooks neighboring vineyards in the Douro valley that use patamares, the new terracing system. in kind, increasing the duty on French wines and later forbidding their import entirely. The short version of the story from here is that British merchants looked south to Portugal to fill the wine gap. It was the red varietals of the Douro, which had the additional benefit of river transport over mountainous land passage, that came to be preferred. For the wine to survive the sea voyage, however, it needed to be fortified – spiked with a brandy that increased the alcohol content and served as a preservative. What started as necessity was cultivated into style. Brandy came to be added earlier, in effect stopping the fermentation process so that more residual sugar remained and the end result is a wine at once sweet and high octane. There are many variations of port and tasting the range of styles is one of the treats of the Douro. Smaller producers such as Alves de Sousa, once a supplier of grapes to larger houses and now an independent estate, continue the port tradition with a strong sense of family heritage. The 20-year-old tawny port from Alves de Sousa is the handiwork of three generations of winemakers. For another taste of Portugal, I recommend the pastries. There is the pastéis de nata, a bite-sized wonder of layers of flaky crust with egg custard filling and the lightest of toasted, caramelized topping. Legend has it that they started at Mosterio dos Jerónimos in Lisbon and that the recipe was sold by a monk to a bakery in the city’s Belém district. Pastéis de nata are found across the country, alongside highly localized delights. Near Lisbon there are Sintra’s travesseiros, translated roughly as “pillows.” Dusted in a light sprinkling of sugar and cinnamon these almond cream fillings are couched in layers of dough. In Amarante, the crossing point between the Douro and Minho wine regions, confeitarias line the cobblestone streets of 31 de Janeiro like Starbucks in New York. It is impossible to leave one without walking into another. The train-station city of Pinhão remains at the center of Portugal’s Douro, and port, region. With layers of flakey crust and an egg custard filling, pastéis de nata (center) are Portugal’s flag-bearing pastry in a country filled with regional delights.

pages.text: Wednesday, July 1, 2020 21 TRAVELS WITH KATE Pastries and Port in Portugal The view from Alves de Sousa overlooks neighboring vineyards in the Douro valley that use patamares, the new terracing system. By Kate Fratar In the world market, the most easily recognizable Portuguese product may be port. The sweet, fortified wine comes from the Douro valley, traditionally traveling by rabelo, a long cargo boat, to Vila Nova de Gaia for storage before being shipped from Porto. The hitch in claiming port as thoroughly Portuguese is that the history of the wine is at least half British. Trade between the two nations goes back centuries, with the 1386 Treaty of Windsor as a cornerstone. Geopolitical motivations aside, the treaty also buttressed a growing commercial relationship by granting each country the right to trade on the same terms as subjects of that country and encouraging settlement with the right for subjects of either country to dwell in the domain in the other. By 1654, a new commercial treaty gave a further boost to English and Scottish merchants living in Portugal with preferential custom duties. The stage was well set, then, when Colbert, acting as the first minister of Louis XIV of France, sparked something of a trade war, enacting a series of measures in 1667 to limit the import of British goods to France. Charles II of England reacted in kind, increasing the duty on French wines and later forbidding their import entirely. The short version of the story from here is that British merchants looked south to Portugal to fill the wine gap. It was the red varietals of the Douro, which had the additional benefit of river transport over mountainous land passage, that came to be preferred. For the wine to survive the sea voyage, however, it needed to be fortified – spiked with a brandy that increased the alcohol content and served as a preservative. What started as necessity was cultivated into style. Brandy came to be added earlier, in effect stopping the fermentation process so that more residual sugar remained and the end result is a wine at once sweet and high octane. There are many variations of port and tasting the range of styles is one of the treats of the Douro. Smaller producers such as Alves de Sousa, once a supplier of grapes to larger houses and now an independent estate, continue the port tradition with a strong sense of family heritage. The 20-year-old tawny port from Alves de Sousa is the handiwork of three generations of winemakers. For another taste of Portugal, I recommend the pastries. There is the pastéis de nata, a bite-sized wonder of layers of flaky crust with egg custard filling and the lightest of toasted, caramelized topping. Legend has it that they started at Mosterio dos Jerónimos in Lisbon and that the recipe was sold by a monk to a bakery in the city’s Belém district. Pastéis de nata are found across the country, alongside highly localized delights. Near Lisbon there are Sintra’s travesseiros, translated roughly as “pillows.” Dusted in a light sprinkling of sugar and cinnamon these almond cream fillings are couched in layers of dough. In Amarante, the crossing point between the Douro and Minho wine regions, confeitarias line the cobblestone streets of 31 de Janeiro like Starbucks in New York. It is impossible to leave one without walking into another. There, one of the concoctions to come out of mixing sugar and egg yolks is a cookie named ponte after the Roman bridge. For the best news of all, yes, many of these delicacies would go well with port. Kate Fratar is Court of Master Sommeliers certified sommelier and a former Post writer currently on special assignment in Portugal. articles.text: Dear Abby: Recently I’ve seen a lot of poop bags on our sidewalks, and even on the street. Why do people leave their poop bags on the sidewalk? Why can’t they just take the bag with them and throw it away in a garbage can? In this day of not wanting to pick up strange germs, I think it’s best if people pick up their dog’s poop and dispose of it themselves. That’s our task as dutiful dog lovers. A puzzled and perturbed pet lover, -Pat and Bingo the Mutt Dear Pat and Bingo: I agree. For some reason, a few years ago dog walkers started leaving used poop bags by the side of the sidewalk or trails when they were on a walk with multiple dogs. They just didn’t want to carry the poop with them. The thought was that they would pick it up on the return or someone else would pick it up for them. (Eventually they would even pick up somebody else’s left behind bag and return the favor.) But it doesn’t make sense in these days of Covid-19 – particularly in Piedmont where garbage cans are never too far away. Dog walkers of all shapes and sizes should pick up after their beloved friends and toss the waste into garbage cans. We don’t want our doggies digging into those bags, nor do we want it laying by our homes where our children ride their bikes or walk. We all need to pitch in and keep our city safe and clean. And please, if you have a dog walker, mention our concerns. I’ve seen them drop the bags recently. No poop left behind. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Mexican rice from Diana Kennedy’s cookbook, My Mexican Kitchen. Diana Kennedy is one of my culinary heroes. There’s a recently released documentary film Diana Kennedy: Nothing Fancy that’s available to stream from home. The film is an insightful telling of the feisty Kennedy’s life and travels throughout Mexico. Kennedy, now 97 is British, but has spent most of her adult life living in Mexico; and is widely recognized as the world’s leading authority on Mexican cuisine. Her most approachable recipes are from My Mexican Kitchen, Techniques and Ingredients. It is from this book that I prepare her Arroz a la Mexicana; the familiar rice served at your favorite Mexican restaurant, and easy to prepare to enjoy at home. Whilst Diana will surely chide one for using canned, crushed tomatoes in place of fresh, I say go with what is most flavorful and available. Vine-ripened tomatoes that taste truly tomato-y are available in our summer months, but many are still cooking out of the “pandemic pantry”. I’ve halved the ingredients from the cookbook’s recipe as I most frequently cook for two these days. Just double the ingredients if you need to scale it up for a larger quantity. Arroz a la Mexicana Makes 3 cups Adapted from Diana Kennedy’s My Mexican Kitchen INGREDIENTS • 3/4 cup long-grain white rice • 2 tablespoons vegetable oil • 3/4 cup ripe tomatoes, coarsely chopped • 1 tablespoon white onion, coarsely chopped • 1 clove fresh garlic, coarsely chopped • 1-1/2 cup chicken broth • 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1 tablespoon peas (optional) • 1 serrano chile (optional) INSTRUCTIONS 1. Pour hot water to cover the rice and let soak for about 5 minutes. Strain, rinse in cold water and strain again, shaking the strainer to remove any excess water. Do this when ready to cook the rice, not ahead of time, to minimize the rice absorbing too much water. 2. Place the tomatoes, onion, and garlic in a blender jar and blend until smooth. Set aside. 3. Heat the oil in a heavy 2-quart saucepan over medium heat. The one I use is about 3-inches deep and 8-1/2 inches in diameter. Stir in the rice – it should sizzle as it hits the oil.
articles.title: It’s July – time for Diana Kennedy’s Mexican Rice

articles.text: Winifred Walters, a longtime Bookmark volunteer (and Piedmont Post subscriber) stands on her porch while a young volunteer with Friends of Oakland Public Library delivers books to the house. Starting on June 19, The Bookmark non-profit bookstore in Old Twon Oakland, began selling books and magazine from the store through its Virtual Bookstore. One of its principal features is the offer of delivery of books to residents’ homes, or curbside pickup. Customers can browse and purchase select books and media from the current store inventory. How it Works • Shop for books from the online photo galleries in the Virtual Bookstore (click on fopl.org). • When you see a title you want, click on the “Go to link” at the bottom of the photo page and e-mail it to The Bookmark at: bookmark@fopl.org. • In your email, let us know which book(s) and/or media • • you’re interested in We will respond with item availability, pricing, and payment instructions We prefer PayPal in advance, but you may also pay at pickup with a gift card, debit, or credit card Pickup & Delivery options • Curbside pickup will be available for all purchases each week on Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday from 11am-2pm. Note: masks will be mandatory for pickup. • Purchases over $25 will be eligible for free delivery (via car or bike) in Oakland and Piedmont. That’s our new motto. -Abby Dear Abby: I’m troubled by the masks that seem to be falling off everyone’s faces and littering the streets. Everyone is walking and biking more, trying to get exercise, and masks are now part of our daily routine. Sometimes they do fall and my Gio loves to devour them. He seriously loves to sniff them and when he’s licking my hands later, I can’t help but wonder what bacteria I’m getting. I always wash afterwards but still... Please ask everyone to pick up their masks and save our sniffers. -Eddie & Gio the Italian German Shepherd Dear Eddie and Gio: All dogs live to sniff those dropped masks and discarded tissues. Our puppy tries to eat them. Not sure why! And yes, it does make one wonder if we can be infected with something after they’ve examined it, licked it, chewed it. Please if you drop a mask, drop down and pick it up. Our habits can save lives. As Smokey the Bear said, “Only You Can Prevent...” We can prevent. Go dog lovers, go! -Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston and Ellen Stem at MSJ312@aol.com or fifiafoot@yahoo,com. Photo by Deborah Quok Mexican rice from Diana Kennedy’s cookbook, My Mexican Kitchen. By Deborah Quok Diana Kennedy is one of my culinary heroes. There’s a recently released documentary film Diana Kennedy: Nothing Fancy that’s available to stream from home. The film is an insightful telling of the feisty Kennedy’s life and travels throughout Mexico. Kennedy, now 97 is British, but has spent most of her adult life living in Mexico; and is widely recognized as the world’s leading authority on Mexican cuisine. Her most approachable recipes are from My Mexican Kitchen, Techniques and Ingredients. It is from this book that I prepare her Arroz a la Mexicana; the familiar rice served at your favorite Mexican restaurant, and easy to prepare to enjoy at home. Whilst Diana will surely chide one for using canned, crushed tomatoes in place of fresh, I say go with what is most flavorful and available. Vine-ripened tomatoes that taste truly tomato-y are available in our summer months, but many are still cooking out of the “pandemic pantry”. I’ve halved the ingredients from the cookbook’s recipe as I most frequently cook for two these days. Just double the ingredients if you need to scale it up for a larger quantity. Arroz a la Mexicana Makes 3 cups Adapted from Diana Kennedy’s My Mexican Kitchen INGREDIENTS • 3/4 cup long-grain white rice • 2 tablespoons vegetable oil • 3/4 cup ripe tomatoes, coarsely chopped • 1 tablespoon white onion, coarsely chopped • 1 clove fresh garlic, coarsely chopped • 1-1/2 cup chicken broth • 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1 tablespoon peas (optional) • 1 serrano chile (optional) INSTRUCTIONS 1. Pour hot water to cover the rice and let soak for about 5 minutes. Strain, rinse in cold water and strain again, shaking the strainer to remove any excess water. Do this when ready to cook the rice, not ahead of time, to minimize the rice absorbing too much water. 2. Place the tomatoes, onion, and garlic in a blender jar and blend until smooth. Set aside. 3. Heat the oil in a heavy 2-quart saucepan over medium heat. The one I use is about 3-inches deep and 8-1/2 inches in diameter. Stir in the rice – it should sizzle as it hits the oil. While it would make One of San Francisco’s best a great partner to a grilled steak, tastings of the year occurs in to me it is delicious just by itself. April when the Rhone Rangers roll into town. This year the tasting was located at a beautiful new venue in Richmond with breathtaking views overlooking the Bay. This trade group of wineries and growers was formed over 20 years ago to promote the classic Rhone varietals in California. For a refresher course, the main ones for red wines are Syrah, Grenache, Mourvedre and Petite Sirah and, for white wines, Viognier, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne and Marsanne. Amazing progress has been made in the past 20 years, and the vast majority of these wines are now much better than they were years ago. It took a while to find the right growing areas and to develop the right vineyard management techniques, but many of these wines rival their French cousins. This year, the top wines from the tasting list include a couple of perennial favorites plus some really interesting newcomers. Ridge and Tablas Creek, two of the best Rhone producers, were omitted from this article as I have recently published articles reviewing all their wines. • 2010 Qupe Syrah Sawyer Lindquist Vineyard “Sonnies”, $55 Every Rhone Ranger owes a huge debt to Qupe’s Bob Lindquist, one of the first people in the country to specialize in Rhone grapes. This bottling celebrates their 30th anniversary. Its explosive aromatic profile offers up scents of cassis, raspberries and jasmine. Deep and plump with good acid and abundant tannin, this serious Syrah will be even better in a few years and will last a decade. L’Aventure is an outstanding producer from Paso Robles. • 2011 L’Aventure Côte à Côte, $85 Stephan Asseo was a successful French winemaker in Bordeaux when he up and left that region to start a winery in Paso Robles. It was all about freedom, he said. Well, the results are in the bottle. He is crafting what are perhaps the best wines in the Paso Robles region. This combination of Syrah, Grenache and Mouvedre is opulent yet elegant. It has beautiful berry fruit with hints of smoke and earth. It is big • 2010 Pull “CdR”, $18 (BEST VALUE) This is the second label of the Broken Earth Winery in Paso Robles. The name refers to Côtes du Rhône, the everyday drinking wine of most of France, and it reminds me of a good juicy Côtes du Rhône from the likes of Guigal. The wine has a deep ruby/ purple color as well as sweet aromas of berry fruit, cassis and earth. It is medium bodied with good intensity, plentiful fruit and sweet tannins. This easygoing wine would make a great “house wine” for everyday drinking. • 2010 LeCuvier Viognier – $46 This was the best white wine I tasted at the Rhone Rangers event. It has an enchanting nose of honeysuckle and jasmine followed by a huge volume of peach and apricot fruit. It is one of the biggest bodied white wines I have ever tasted and reminds me of the great Condrieus of France. Well done. • 2011 Alta Colina Mourvedre Mourvedre is the bad boy of the Rhone varietals. Not only is it difficult to grow, you never quite know what it is going to do. There are wide variations in the flavor profiles based on terroir and handling. This one reminds me of a really nice Châteauneuf-du-Pape from Beaucastel. It has a beautiful nose of jammy fruit, anise, spice and vanilla. It has intense berry fruit and a viscous texture yet is light on its feet. Very impressive effort. • 2011 Austin Hope Grenache, $42 This is a perennial member of my top Rhones list. It is one of the finest Grenaches in America. Light ruby in color it has a sumptuous bouquet of kirsch liqueur, spice box and licorice. Full-bodied and fleshy with low acidity, it is a sweet, seductive offering with no hard edges and a rich mouth-feel. This is a wine to drink now as it is not built for long-term aging. • 2009 Peterson Syrah Bradford Mountain Vineyard Gravity Flow Block, $48 This big blockbuster Syrah has 7 percent of the white grape

This is a wine to drink now as it is not built for long-term aging. • 2009 Peterson Syrah Bradford Mountain Vineyard Gravity Flow Block, $48 This big blockbuster Syrah has 7 percent of the white grape Viognier included in the final blend. This technique, which is common in Cote Rotie and Hermitage, works here to give the wine a nice flowery perfumed nose. It is followed by blockbuster fruit in the mouth with flavors of blackberries, plums overlapped with a nice layer of minerality. This firmly structured wine will last for two decades. • 2012 Wrath Muscat Blanc “Ex Anima” I fell in love with this wine the minute I tasted it and was saddened to hear that this is the last vintage of the wine as the vines are being budded over to something else. This is Alsatian-style Muscat, which means a vibrantly floral nose with gardenia and honeysuckle so you think it’s going to be a sweet wine, but in the mouth it turns out to be bone dry. Utterly enchanting. I was assured they still have some of the wine for sale direct from the winery but better move fast. • 2009 Pipestone Mourvedre, $38 This interesting bottling combines the earthy, gamey, herbal flavors of a French Mourvedre like Bandol with the sunny, bright fruit that Paso Robles supplies so plentifully. It is medium-bodied with a smooth tannin-free finish. A perfect guest at your next BBQ. • 2007 Edenvale Grenache, $18 (GREAT VALUE) Hailing from Oregon’s Rogue Valley, this light-bodied, ethereal wine reminds me of Pinot Noir but with the distinctive floral Grenache nose. It is well balanced and has adequate acid and structure. It shows round berry fruit in the mouth and has a clean finish. Perfect picnic wine. • 2011 Chacewater Petite Sirah, $20 Of all the Rhone varietals Petite Sirah is the only one that is not widely planted in France. There it is called Durif and is a minor player. But pioneering wineries like Ridge and Stag’s Leap, have shown what amazing wines can be made from this grape. Robert Parker called it “America’s Overlooked Great Wine.” This bottle from Lake County shows the full-bodied power and huge mouth-feel of the grape along with the abundant tannins. This wine should be cellared for a few years and then will last for a couple of decades. • 2012 Folin Cellars Petite Sirah Blanc This wine from Oregon’s Rogue Valley stopped me in my tracks. I have never seen anyone even try to make a white wine from Petite Sirah – the darkest of red grapes. I have no idea how they prevented the red skins from turning the wine pink, but they did. This has an understated nose of flowers and citrus with big full-bodied, mouth-filling flavors of melons and peaches. It is a dead ringer for a white Hermitage. Amazing. • 2011 Ranchero Cellars Revolver, $40 This Paso Robles winery was new to me. The Carignane grape, which is increasing but still somewhat rare in California, is married to 50 percent Syrah, resulting in an interesting blend. It shows the light-hearted fruit and elegance of Carignane and the sturdy brawn of Syrah. It has blackberry and plum fruit with highlights of tobacco and spice. Delicious now it should last for seven or eight years. • 2012 Skinner Mourvedre, $24 El Dorado is an up-and-coming wine region, and this bottle shows how well the area is suited to Rhone varietals. This Mourvedre, which is called Monastrell in Spain and Mataro in Australia, is a medium-bodied wine with brambly fruit mixed with earthy, gamey flavors that give it a nice complexity. It is ready to drink now and should last for five or six years. • 2009 Cypher “The Peasant”, $40 This quirky winery – they have the absolute best labels – from Paso Robles produces really interesting, characterful wines, like this blend of Mourvedre, Grenache and Syrah. This wine shows an extraordinary perfume of blackberry liqueur with anise and pepper. The explosive aromatics are followed by equally bold massive flavor concentration on the palate with a long, smooth finish. • 2009 Still Waters Syrah, $32 This was my first encounter with Still Waters, a small family-owned winery in Paso Robles. The Syrah shows a sweet perfume of blackberry fruit intermixed with earth and subtle wood. It is a chewy, dense, pure, succulent effort to enjoy over the next six to seven years. • 2011 Villa Vallecito Grenache, $34 This is very fresh, light-bodied wine from the Sierra foothills with aromas of cherries and spice. It is soft and round in the mouth and shows no tannins on the finish. Eminently quaffable, this charmer is ready to drink now and should last for four or five years. • 2011 Page Mill Winery “GPS”, $28 The often overlooked Livermore AVA is a perfect location for big Rhone-style wines. This wine is named for the blend of Grenache, Petite Sirah and Syrah. The wine starts with aromas of roasted meats, blueberries, tar and smoke. It’s a huge generous wine with a big, round mouthfeel. Dark and intense, it has the stuffing to last for over a decade. • 2011 Onx “Mad Crush”, $45 Rather than having the traditional Grenache, Syrah, Mouvedre blend, this wine swaps out the Syrah for Tempranillo, Spain’s greatest grape. The wine exhibits aromas of flowers, blueberries and cherries. It is layered, full-bodied, beautifully crafted and unctuously textured with gorgeously ripe flavors and a superb finish. • 2011 Caliza “Azimuth” Crafted from a blend of Grenache, Syrah, Mourvedre, Petite Sirah and Tempranillo this wine has a nice nose of cherries, violets and earth. It is medium to full bodied with layers of dark berry fruit and a good amount of tannin. This well structured wine will gain complexity with a few years of aging. Reprinted from May 7, 2014. articles.text: Spike in reported COVID cases; total in county nears 6,000 Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials on Monday, June 29, as concerns mount about COVID-19 hospitalizations. The new order does not reverse previous reopening orders, but the county is now postponing its plan to phase in the next stage of reopening. The number of COVID-19 cases in Alameda County was 5,964 as of yesterday, Tuesday, June 30, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. There have been 824 new cases since last week, a 16 percent increase. Another 15 people have died of the disease since last Tuesday, June 23, increasing the number of total fatalities to 135. Alameda County continues to be hardest hit county in the San Francisco Bay Area. Santa Clara County, the initial epicenter in the region, now counts 4,370 cases and 156 total deaths. In San Francisco, the caseload is 3,603 and there have been 50 deaths. No new cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, were reported in Piedmont in June. In total, there have been 13 cases reported in Piedmont. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, 2,352 cases were reported. Hayward now has a total of 987. Fremont has reported 290 cases and San Leandro has also reported 290. In its announcement about pausing the county’s reopening schedule this week, the Alameda County Public Health Department noted that the case rate per 100,000 people had increased from 63.2 to 71.1. Daily hospitalizations had been decreasing through Monday, June 22, but have been increasing daily since then. “We recognize the multifaceted challenges presented by a slow reopening and are grateful for the sustained effort and sacrifices made by our residents and businesses,” the department said in a statement. “As the pandemic evolves, we will need to remain flexible and nimble in our response.” While the county had been opening up new sectors of the economy about every two weeks, that plan has been put on hold for the time being. The department said that this week and next week will be critical for assessing how and when to reopen more activities. An order that went into place on June 19 allowed for outdoor museums, outdoor restaurant dining, some religious services, indoor retail, mall shopping and outdoor fitness classes. The timetable for reopening activities such as indoor dining, barber shops, pools and gyms is now delayed until further notice. The surge of COVID-19 cases across the state over the past few weeks has caused officials on all levels in California to act to reduce the spread of the disease, a shift from earlier hopes that the pandemic was trending toward its endpoint. “Until recently, our state managed to do so well that our experience has been dubbed ‘The California Miracle,’” tweeted University of California, San Francisco Department of Medicine Chair Bob Wachter on Monday, June 29. “But let’s say it clearly: The Miracle is over. The sooner we acknowledge that, the better off we’ll be.” While Wachter said state officials and residents mostly acted responsibly, relaxing restrictions starting in mid-May appears to have led to increases in cases. Statewide, 216,550 COVID-19 cases were reported as of Sunday, June 28, an increase of over 33,000 in a week. In California, 5,936 people have died since the outbreak began. The City of Piedmont has been following Alameda County’s guidance. The City announced in May that the annual Fourth of July Parade is cancelled this year due to the pandemic. In a notice earlier this month, the City of Piedmont reminded residents that Alameda County’s face covering requirements are still in effect. The State recently ordered that face coverings must be work at all times in public, even if a person is exercising. Face coverings can only be removed if a person will not be within 30 feet of another person from outside the household. The City of Piedmont keeps all of its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/covid-19
articles.title: Alameda County pauses reopening of economy

articles.text: Satire by Phil Witte Schedule of Classes At Overdone Fitness, we offer the widest and most idiosyncratic range of classes of any chain fitness center with 10 or fewer employees. Our converted basketball half-court serves as ground zero for an explosion of fun-filled exercises endorsed by the private armies of some of the world’s most exclusive dictatorships. Here’s a rundown of our classes ranked in terms of fewest injuries: 12:00 AM — Midnight Madness Liftathon This drop-in “class” begins at the stroke of midnight and ends when we officially open five and a half hours later. It’s perfect for stragglers in an impaired state of sobriety, swing shift workers, and people walking on dark streets who feel they’re being followed. We offer absolutely no supervision to inhibit your individualized sense of what’s proper and safe technique. Weights will be scattered throughout the facility for you to lift, sketch, or ignore. Turn off the lights when you’re done, or else stick around for— 5:30 AM — Wake-up and Smell the Sweat Our trainers promise to arrive for this predawn boot camp class, but if they’re late, an enormous urn of coffee will be wheeled in for maximum consumption. A great class for new moms who have been awake all night and just need a reason to leave the house so as not to do something regrettable. 7:00 AM — Yoga Beyond Limits If your idea of yoga is a discipline unifying mind, body, and spirit through a series of prescribed positions, you haven’t tried our modern “twist” (get it?) on yogic fun. Led by Grihamani “Gumby” Chakrabarti, you’ll experience the full range of pain and delight by launching into such updated positions as Jammed Telephone Booth, Clown Car, and Kiss One’s Own Ass. All levels are welcome, although participants are grouped by body mass index, so that impossibly fit and flexible people don’t have to look at chubbies. 10:00 AM — Aqua Aerobics with Bernice Our own beloved Bernice will lead the class in the swimming pool’s shallow end in resistance training exercises, such as leg lifts and flutter kicks. You won’t be doing any of that. Instead, you’ll stand behind a one-way mirror laughing at people who think that this is a form of exercise. Fact: a half-hour of hearty laughter burns more calories than one hour of aqua aerobics. 12:00 PM — TRXYY This TRX class is designed especially for men with an extra Y chromosome. In addition to the usual equipment, the club provides speed bags, heavy bags, and an attack dog trainer in a bite suit. 2:00 PM — Hauling Furniture At our only off-premises class, you’ll get a full afternoon of exercise moving sofas up flights of stairs and carrying armoires through narrow hallways. Your instructor, Vinnie, will hand you a slip of paper with the address before going on his coffee break. We provide the truck and driver. You provide the muscle. Remember to smile because a tip could be in your future. Note: all gratuities must be shared equally with Overdone Fitness. 4:00 PM — Nothin’ But Burpees The title says it all: dozens of variations on the basic burpee until you’re ready to puke. A typical sequence may include burpees while someone is clinging to your back, burpees using only one arm and one leg, and burpees plus a slap in the face. 5:00 PM — #MeToo Kickboxing What makes this class special is the motivational video playing in a continuous loop featuring accused sexual harassers, including Harvey Weinstein, Charlie Rose, Matt Lauer, Les Moonves, R. Kelly, Roy Moore, Bill Clinton, Donald Trump, and we could go on and on. 6:00 PM — Shame-Shame Motivational Class For a different type of motivational class, try one using an old technique that has enjoyed a recent revival based on a scene from Game of Thrones. If you fail to meet the goals set randomly by our personal trainers, you’ll be marched naked (except for mud splashed on you) through a crowd of angry strangers in our Workout Enthusiasm Readjustment Room. During these sessions, our no-video rule is sometimes strictly enforced. 7:00 PM — Silent Exercise Perhaps the only class in any fitness studio anywhere without a soundtrack blasting beatheavy music. The instruction is purely via pantomime. The only sound you’ll hear is collective grunting and the voice in your head asking why you’re still a gym member. 8:00 PM — Roomba Zumba Has Zumba become routine for you? Then try this class. The gimmick here is that you’ll attach a Roomba vacuum cleaner to each foot and go wherever they go, as you slide to Latin tunes. It’s a complete cardio workout and a great way of giving back to Overdone Fitness by cleaning the club for other members. 9:00 PM — Hot Lava Yoga End your workout day with a soothing yoga session at our hot lava studio. A fire-resistant net is the only thing between you and a river of white-hot lava, while you perform a series of one-leg poses designed to improve your balance and connectedness to Mother Earth. Until management fixes the door lock, please wedge something like a gym shoe in the door to avoid locking yourself in the soundproof lava room.
articles.title: Overdone Fitness, where opportunities are endless

articles.text: Stir until the grains are evenly coated and continue frying over medium heat until they just take on a golden hue, about 7 - 8 minutes. 4. Stir the puree into the rice and continue frying over medium high heat, scraping the bottom of the pan to avoid sticking, until the rice has absorbed most of the liquid, about 4 – 5 minutes. 5. Add the broth and the optional ingredients; stir the rice well, add salt and cover the pan leaving the lid slightly ajar to allow steam to escape. Continue cooking over medium heat until most of the broth is absorbed and small holes appear on top. Reduce the heat to the lowest setting, place the lid on tightly, and cook another 4 – 5 minutes until no liquid is visible. Turn off the heat and let the rice continue steaming for about 10 minutes. 6. When serving, gently stir the rice from the bottom with a fork to ensure all the flavorings that may have settled get reincorporated into the rice. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

In a notice earlier this month, the City of Piedmont reminded residents that Alameda County’s face covering requirements are still in effect. The State recently ordered that face coverings must be work at all times in public, even if a person is exercising. Face coverings can only be removed if a person will not be within 30 feet of another person from outside the household. Overdone Fitness, where opportunities are endless Satire by Phil Witte Schedule of Classes At Overdone Fitness, we offer the widest and most idiosyncratic range of classes of any chain fitness center with 10 or fewer employees. Our converted basketball half-court serves as ground zero for an explosion of fun-filled exercises endorsed by the private armies of some of the world’s most exclusive dictatorships. Here’s a rundown of our classes ranked in terms of fewest injuries: 12:00 AM — Midnight Madness Liftathon This drop-in “class” begins at the stroke of midnight and ends when we officially open five and a half hours later. It’s perfect for stragglers in an impaired state of sobriety, swing shift workers, and people walking on dark streets who feel they’re being followed. We offer absolutely no supervision to inhibit your individualized sense of what’s proper and safe technique. Weights will be scattered throughout the facility for you to lift, sketch, or ignore. Turn off the lights when you’re done, or else stick around for— 5:30 AM — Wake-up and Smell the Sweat Our trainers promise to arrive for this predawn boot camp class, but if they’re late, an enormous urn of coffee will be wheeled in for maximum consumption. A great class for new moms who have been awake all night and just need a reason to leave the house so as not to do something regrettable. 7:00 AM — Yoga Beyond Limits If your idea of yoga is a discipline unifying mind, body, and spirit through a series of prescribed positions, you haven’t tried our modern “twist” (get it?) on yogic fun. Led by Grihamani “Gumby” Chakrabarti, you’ll experience the full range of pain and delight by launching into such updated positions as Jammed Telephone Booth, Clown Car, and Kiss One’s Own Ass. All levels are welcome, although participants are grouped by body mass index, so that impossibly fit and flexible people don’t have to look at chubbies. 10:00 AM — Aqua Aerobics with Bernice Our own beloved Bernice will lead the class in the swimming pool’s shallow end in resistance training exercises, such as leg lifts and flutter kicks. You won’t be doing any of that. Instead, you’ll stand behind a one-way mirror laughing at people who think that this is a form of exercise. Fact: a half-hour of hearty laughter burns more calories than one hour of aqua aerobics. 12:00 PM — TRXYY This TRX class is designed especially for men with an extra Y chromosome. In addition to the usual equipment, the club provides speed bags, heavy bags, and an attack dog trainer in a bite suit. 2:00 PM — Hauling Furniture At our only off-premises class, you’ll get a full afternoon of exercise moving sofas up flights of stairs and carrying armoires through narrow hallways. Your instructor, Vinnie, will hand you a slip of paper with the address before going on his coffee break. We provide the truck and driver. You provide the muscle. Remember to smile because a tip could be in your future. Note: all gratuities must be shared equally with Overdone Fitness. 4:00 PM — Nothin’ But Burpees The title says it all: dozens of variations on the basic burpee until you’re ready to puke. A typical sequence may include burpees while someone is clinging to your back, burpees using only one arm and one leg, and burpees plus a slap in the face. 5:00 PM — #MeToo Kickboxing What makes this class special is the motivational video playing in a continuous loop featuring accused sexual harassers, including Harvey Weinstein, Charlie Rose, Matt Lauer, Les Moonves, R. Kelly, Roy Moore, Bill Clinton, Donald Trump, and we could go on and on. 6:00 PM — Shame-Shame Motivational Class For a different type of motivational class, try one using an old technique that has enjoyed a recent revival based on a scene from Game of Thrones. If you fail to meet the goals set randomly by our personal trainers, you’ll be marched naked (except for mud splashed on you) through a crowd of angry strangers in our Workout Enthusiasm Readjustment Room. During these sessions, our no-video rule is sometimes strictly enforced. 7:00 PM — Silent Exercise Perhaps the only class in any fitness studio anywhere without a soundtrack blasting beatheavy music. The instruction is purely via pantomime. The only sound you’ll hear is collective grunting and the voice in your head asking why you’re still a gym member. 8:00 PM — Roomba Zumba Has Zumba become routine for you? Then try this class. The gimmick here is that you’ll attach a Roomba vacuum cleaner to each foot and go wherever they go, as you slide to Latin tunes. It’s a complete cardio workout and a great way of giving back to Overdone Fitness by cleaning the club for other members. 9:00 PM — Hot Lava Yoga End your workout day with a soothing yoga session at our hot lava studio. A fire-resistant net is the only thing between you and a river of white-hot lava, while you perform a series of one-leg poses designed to improve your balance and connectedness to Mother Earth. Until management fixes the door lock, please wedge something like a gym shoe in the door to avoid locking yourself in the soundproof lava room. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation.
